66186276B48953429733047.name: Idaho
66186276B48953429733047.summary: House Bill 752, signed by Governor Brad Little and effective 1 July 2026, makes it a crime for a transgender person to use a restroom or changing room that does not match the sex assigned at birth. It reaches government buildings and public-facing private businesses, including gas stations, restaurants, entertainment venues and hospitals. A first offence is a misdemeanour carrying up to one year in jail. The ACLU of Idaho filed suit on 30 April 2026 on due-process, equal-protection and privacy grounds, arguing the law targets no criminal conduct; six transgender Idahoans are plaintiffs in the challenge, brought before the effect date. According to the ACLU, Idaho's is the only state law extending bathroom criminalisation to private businesses, and it carries steeper penalties than other states' bans.

The suit argues House Bill 752 is unconstitutional.

sources.title: LGBTQ rights in Idaho (Wikipedia)
sources.summary: Idaho bans any change of sex on birth certificates under a 2018 implementation law allowed into legal effect in January 2026, permitting only biological male or female sex at birth, after a prior period from April 6, 2018 when transgender people could change birth certificates to reflect gender identity following a 2017 lawsuit, which Governor Brad Little sought to reverse with HB 509 signed March 30, 2020 that took preliminary effect July 1, 2020 but was ruled moot and unenforceable on August 7, 2020 by District Judge David C. Nye, with $321,000 in attorneys' fees awarded to Lambda Legal and approved in August 2022. Since March 2019 Idaho allows an "X" third-gender option on driver's licenses and state IDs, but under the August 7, 2020 ruling applicants changing gender markers must submit a physician letter certifying sex reassignment surgery, and in November 2019 the Board of Health and Welfare removed doctor-approval for gender change for transgender minors while retaining parental permission, emancipation, or court order. Gender-affirming medical care for minors is criminalized as a felony for doctors under HB 71 signed April 4, 2023 banning puberty blockers, hormones and surgeries, a ban upheld by the U.S. Supreme Court in April 2024, after an earlier HB 675 passed the House in March 2022 proposing felony liability and life imprisonment for parents taking children out-of-state but blocked by the Senate, while HB 668 effective July 1, 2024 further restricts care for minors and adults when provided by state/local/county professionals, through Idaho Medicaid, or on state property including hospitals, public colleges and prisons, excluding counseling/mental health but limiting HRT and gender-affirming surgery and barring tax deductibility. Transgender prisoners were permitted hormone therapy under a September 2024 federal judge ruling nullifying a 1997 law banning it, and in August 2024 the Governor signed an executive order barring application of any federal laws, regulations and guidelines regarding gender identity/ideology within Idaho. Schools and teachers are restricted by an April 2024 law banning use of pronouns not based on birth certificates for students/pupils by teachers and education agencies, while a February 2024 House-passed bill pending in the Senate would exclusively recognize male and female throughout Idaho Code. Transgender athletes are barred from public school and university sports teams matching gender identity under legislation signed March 30, 2020. Under a March 2026 law schools, childcare providers and medical professionals must out transgender minors to parents within three days of learning trans status, and a March 2026 bathroom law passed by House and Senate makes it a felony for a trans person to use a bathroom, changing room or other gender-segregated facility not matching assigned sex in any publicly owned building or private business, narrowed June 16 by U.S. District Judge Amanda Brailsford two weeks before effect to bar enforcement against single-stall use or multi-user use when no unoccupied single-user restroom is on same floor. No Idaho state law explicitly addresses discrimination based on gender identity, but Bostock v. Clayton County on June 15, 2020 provides federal Title VII workplace protection, about 40% of population is covered by county/city ordinances in Ada County, Bellevue, Boise, Coeur d'Alene, Driggs, Hailey, Idaho Falls, Ketchum, Lewiston, Meridian, Moscow, Pocatello, Sandpoint, Victor plus Latah County employee protection, while Idaho hate-crime law excludes gender identity but federal Matthew Shepard and James Byrd, Jr. Act of October 2009 allows federal prosecution for gender-identity-motivated crimes. Consensual same-sex sexual activity became unenforceable as crime under Lawrence v. Texas in 2003, remaining formally in Idaho Code until the Legislature passed repeal in March 2022 signed by the Governor effective July 1, 2022, after history including an 1864 sodomy statute punishing anal intercourse with five years to life, 1916 extension to fellatio in State v. Altwatter, 1971 repeal effective January 1, 1972 reversed April 1, 1972 after Catholic/Mormon opposition, and retention for married heterosexual couples until State v. Holden in 1995. Same-sex marriage has been legal since October 2014 after Latta v. Otter found 1990s statutes and the November 2006 constitutional amendment limiting marriage to man-woman unconstitutional on May 13, 2014, upheld by the Ninth Circuit October 7, 2014 without U.S. Supreme Court stay, with Governor Butch Otter ceasing defense and approximately 100 couples licensed in Ada County October 15, 2014. No Idaho state law explicitly addresses discrimination based on sexual orientation, with voters rejecting Initiative 1 on November 8, 1994 by 50.38% to 49.62% that would have barred minority status based on homosexual behavior, Senate State Affairs rejecting protections 7-2 February 10, 2012, House State Affairs rejecting 13-4 January 29, 2015 after Ways and Means 6-1 vote for hearing January 15, 2015 following Add the Words protests in April 2014, and a renewed bill in January 2021. Federal Title VII under Bostock v. Clayton County June 15, 2020 protects LGB employees from workplace discrimination based on sexual orientation, supplementing local ordinances covering sexual orientation in Ada County, Bellevue, Boise, Coeur d'Alene, Driggs, Hailey, Idaho Falls, Ketchum, Lewiston, Meridian, Moscow, Pocatello, Sandpoint, Victor representing about 40% of population plus Twin Falls city-employment and Latah County employee coverage, with Pocatello voters retaining its ordinance May 20, 2014 by 50.41% to 49.59% against Proposition 1 repeal. Idaho hate-crime law does not cover sexual orientation, but the federal Matthew Shepard and James Byrd, Jr. Hate Crimes Prevention Act signed October 2009 allows federal prosecution for crimes motivated by actual or perceived sexual orientation. Enforcement history includes 1956 State v. Moore and State v. Wilson imprisonments for consensual same-sex activity, a September 2020 suit by a man forced to register as sex offender for consensual oral sex with his wife 20 years prior in another state, and an April 2021 appeal by a Montana man required to register after a 1993 crimes-against-nature conviction at age 18 for consensual sex with two 16-year-old males at Pratt ranch in Gem County after serving a 7-year prison term, where heterosexual 16-18 sex is otherwise legal.

66186276B41335105066757.name: Louisiana
66186276B41335105066757.summary:
In August 2026 a mob beat a transgender couple, Aurora Rush and Shae Sanders, over restroom use at Cypress Black Bayou Park in Benton. Sanders, who has a pre-existing spinal injury, and Rush, who suffered a concussion and blood pooling, were both charged with disturbing the peace; the sheriff's office recorded no arrest of any attacker that day, and a plea deal had not been signed. Rush was denied hospital care and taken to a men's jail.

Rush was held in a men's facility and searched by a male guard even though her driver's licence carries a female marker. The marker on her licence did not determine her housing or her search procedure in custody.

In the same period the municipality of Benton voted one of the country's most severe anti-trans restroom ordinances.

Gender-marker changes on Louisiana documents require surgical proof. A driver's licence marker change requires a physician-signed statement confirming successful sex reassignment surgery; a new birth certificate requires a certified court order confirming surgical gender change, with proof of a diagnosis recorded as "transsexual or pseudo-hermaphrodite" and of anatomical change.

Louisiana's 1997 hate-crime statute provides penalty enhancements for offences motivated by sexual orientation or perceived sexual orientation but does not cover gender identity, so gender-identity bias crimes fall to federal prosecution under the Matthew Shepard and James Byrd Jr. Hate Crimes Prevention Act of October 2009.

Gender-affirming care for minors is banned: the Legislature overrode the governor's June 2023 veto in July 2023, and the ban on puberty blockers, hormones and surgery took effect on 1 January 2024.

Marriage is recognised in Louisiana after the 2015 invalidation of the state's 2004 constitutional ban on marriage and civil unions and its 1988 and 1999 Civil Code provisions; married couples hold full joint adoption and parental rights, following the 2014 Costanza v. Caldwell ruling that granted the state's first adoption by a same-sex couple.

The state's unenforceable sodomy statute remains on the books, carrying up to five years' imprisonment, a $2,000 fine and sex-offender registration; a repeal bill failed 66-27 in April 2014.

Louisiana has no state law prohibiting gender-identity discrimination in employment, housing or public accommodations. The Movement Advancement Project scores its gender-identity policy at -8.75 out of 25 and its overall policy at -8.75 out of 47 as of 12 October 2026, leaving federal employment-discrimination processes as the main recourse. New Orleans and Shreveport prohibit gender-identity discrimination in employment, housing and public accommodations; Alexandria, Baton Rouge, Lafayette, Lake Charles and Jefferson Parish extend protection only to public employees.

sources.summary: Metro Weekly (Aug 2026): a mob beat trans couple Aurora Rush and Shae Sanders over restroom use at Cypress Black Bayou Park, Benton; Sanders (pre-existing spinal injury) and Rush (concussion, blood pooling) were both charged with disturbing the peace while no attacker was arrested; Rush was jailed in a men's facility and searched by a male guard despite a 'female' marker on her driver's licence.

Erin in the Morning (5 Aug 2026): the same Benton mob attack — victims charged rather than their attackers, plea deal not signed; reports the municipality simultaneously voted one of the country's most severe anti-trans restroom ordinances; Rush was denied hospital care and taken to a men's jail, and no one else was arrested that day per the Sheriff's Office.

HRC memorial (11 June 2024): Yella (Robert) Clark Jr., a 45-year-old Black trans woman serving a life sentence at Angola prison, was killed in a fight with several inmates on 2 April 2024 — at least the 16th trans or gender-expansive person HRC had learned of killed in 2024 and the fifth in April alone, with such deaths systematically under- or mis-reported.

sources.title: LGBTQ rights in Louisiana (Wikipedia)
sources.summary: Transgender people may change the gender marker on a driver's license upon submitting a physician-signed statement confirming successful sex reassignment surgery, and may obtain a new birth certificate upon presenting a certified court order confirming surgical gender change with proof of diagnosis as transsexual or pseudo-hermaphrodite and anatomical change. In July 2023 the Legislature overrode the Governor's June 2023 veto to enact a ban on puberty blockers, hormones, and surgeries for minors, formally effective January 1, 2024, while two other related bills remained awaiting legislative action. Surgery, puberty blockers, hormone replacement therapy and other transition-related healthcare are excluded from health insurance and state Medicaid coverage. In June 2022 Louisiana banned transgender girls from sports in public schools with more than two-thirds support in both chambers, after a similar 2021 bill (House 77-17, Senate 29-6) was vetoed and the override failed by 2 votes. Employment discrimination based on gender identity is prohibited under the June 15, 2020 U.S. Supreme Court ruling in Bostock v. Clayton County applying Title VII, but state law provides no prohibition in housing, health care, education, credit or public accommodations. Only New Orleans and Shreveport prohibit gender-identity discrimination in employment, housing and public accommodations, while Alexandria, Baton Rouge, Lafayette, Lake Charles and Jefferson Parish limit protection to public employees. The 1997 state hate-crime law providing penalty enhancements covers sexual orientation or perceived sexual orientation but does not include gender identity, leaving gender-identity-based hate crimes to federal prosecution under the Matthew Shepard and James Byrd Jr. Hate Crimes Prevention Act of October 2009. Consensual same-sex sexual activity was decriminalized by the 2003 U.S. Supreme Court decision in Lawrence v. Texas and the 2005 Fifth Circuit ruling striking adult consensual anal and oral sex provisions, though the unenforceable sodomy law with up to five years imprisonment, $2,000 fine and sex-offender registration remains on the books after repeal failed 66-27 in April 2014. Same-sex marriage has been recognized since the June 26, 2015 Obergefell v. Hodges ruling invalidating 1988 and 1999 Civil Code bans and the 2004 constitutional bans on marriage and civil unions, with compliance confirmed two days later. Married same-sex couples are entitled to full joint adoption and parental rights, following the September 22, 2014 Costanza v. Caldwell ruling granting the first same-sex adoption, while single persons may adopt without explicit denial to same-sex couples. Employment discrimination based on sexual orientation is prohibited under Bostock, but state law provides no protection in housing, health care, education, credit or public accommodations, and executive orders barring sexual-orientation discrimination in state employment (1992, 2004, 2016) all lapsed, expired or were struck down and upheld on appeal in March 2018. The 1997 hate-crime statute, the first in the Deep South after five years lobbying, provides penalty enhancements for crimes motivated by sexual orientation or perceived sexual orientation. The June 2017 domestic-violence amendment removing opposite-sex language, passed 54-42 in the House and 25-13 in the Senate and effective August 1, 2017, ensures identical treatment irrespective of sexual orientation where same-sex offenders previously received lesser sentences. Louisiana maintains a no promo homo law prohibiting sex education classes from discussing male or female homosexual activity.

66186276B29106115751815.name: Texas
66186276B29106115751815.summary:
Texas restricts trans people's use of sex-separated facilities under the Women's Privacy Act, signed by Governor Greg Abbott on 22 September 2025 and effective 4 December 2025. The law requires restrooms to match the sex recorded on a person's birth certificate and applies to public schools, universities, prisons and Texas government buildings. Facilities face a $25,000 fine for a first violation and $125,000 for subsequent violations. The gender-placements statute reaches prisons only as to restroom use; it does not govern cell assignment or the housing placement of trans prisoners.

Enforcement began immediately. On 6 December 2025 Department of Public Safety troopers checked identification at women's restrooms outside the Capitol; trans women holding female identity markers were admitted. The Austin City Council moved to circumvent the law's intent, and opponents warned that unclear guidelines produce uneven and invasive enforcement. Protests followed at the Capitol.

In April 2026 Attorney General Ken Paxton's second complaint escalated the state's probe of the Austin Independent School District over its bathroom policy, with a renewed records demand after a tip-line complaint. It is the first state bathroom-law enforcement inquiry directed at a school district.

An independent legal-risk assessment places Texas in its top "Do Not Travel" tier for adult trans travellers, one of four states so graded alongside Florida, Idaho and Kansas, scored law-by-law across care bans, bathroom bans and enforcement posture.

House Bill 229, the Women's Bill of Rights, passed in May 2025, was signed in June 2025 and took effect in September 2025. It defines female as a person who can biologically produce ova and male as one who can biologically fertilise ova, requires people with disorders of sex development to select one binary gender with no third-gender recognition, applies across all state statutes, regulations and laws using gendered terms, and bans any change of sex on Texas driver's licences and birth certificates. Before that change, altering a birth certificate's gender indicator required a court order, with judicial discretion often referencing WPATH Standards of Care, a narrative statement from a doctor or therapist that care was appropriate and the change in the person's best interest, and no specific treatment requirement including surgery. On 30 January 2025 Governor Abbott separately directed state agencies to recognise only two genders.

Texas's hate-crime statute enhances penalties for crimes motivated by sexual orientation but does not cover gender identity, and it is rarely prosecuted. No state law bars employment, housing, public-accommodations or insurance discrimination based on gender identity. Texas courts recognised federal employment protections under Bostock v. Clayton County in March 2021. Austin, Dallas, Fort Worth, Plano and San Antonio prohibit gender-identity discrimination in private and public employment, housing and public accommodations; Denton, El Paso, Arlington, Brownsville, Corpus Christi, Houston, Irving, Lubbock, Mesquite and Waco have narrower city-employment or public-accommodation protections.

Same-sex sexual activity was decriminalised by Lawrence v. 66186276B52324970173776.name: Tennessee
66186276B52324970173776.summary:
Tennessee law regulates gender presentation in public. The Adult Entertainment Act of 2023 (SB 3/HB 9) defines "adult cabaret entertainment" to include male or female impersonators and makes it a criminal offence on public property or anywhere a child could see it. A first offence is a Class A misdemeanour carrying up to 11 months 29 days and a $2,500 fine; a second violation is a Class E felony with one to six years and fines to $3,000. A federal judge declared the statute vague and overbroad and unconstitutional in June 2023, but it was reinstated on procedural grounds after appeal, and in 2026 the U.S. Supreme Court refused to hear challenges to it, leaving the appeals-court ruling upholding the law in force. A separate suit remains ongoing.

Facilities access is restricted by birth sex. The "Riley Gaines Women's Safety and Protection Act," passed in April 2026, requires transgender people to use only facilities matching sex assigned at birth, bars trans women from women's shelters, and mandates that transgender inmates be housed by sex assigned at birth. Earlier provisions remain part of the statutory background: legislation of 2 May 2019 defines a transgender person using a bathroom corresponding with gender identity as committing indecent exposure, and May 2021 laws banned transgender students from public-school bathrooms matching their identity and required small businesses permitting transgender use of multi-person bathrooms to post warning signs under penalty of up to six months' jail. The business-sign requirement took effect 1 July 2021, was enjoined on 9 July 2021 and struck down entirely in May 2022 as a First Amendment violation; the school bathroom law drew further lawsuits from August 2021.

Gender-affirming medical care for minors is prohibited. Senate Bill 1, signed 1 March 2023, makes it illegal to provide such care to any person under 18 in Tennessee or through out-of-state telehealth. New care was barred after 1 July 2023 and existing care had to be withdrawn by 31 March 2024. The statute authorises regret-based lawsuits by parents, guardians and physicians, and $25,000 suits by the Attorney General against providers. The U.S. Department of Justice challenged the law with the ACLU and Lambda Legal on 26 April 2023; a partial injunction of 28 June 2023 was stayed on 8 July 2023, and the U.S. Supreme Court upheld the statute 6-3 in United States v. Skrmetti on 18 June 2025, holding it did not violate equal protection. A May 2024 law adds civil penalties for adults who help minors obtain such care elsewhere, and April 2024 legislation bans the care for inmates.

Custody is a site of specific harm. In April 2024 the Tennessee State Legislature passed a bill banning gender-affirming care for people held in state prisons, and under the 2026 Act transgender inmates are to be placed in prisons according to sex assigned at birth.

Identity documents are governed by a fixed statutory definition of sex. Tennessee has prohibited change of sex on an original birth certificate under Tenn. Code Ann. § 68-3-203(d) since 1977, and a 2023 law signed by Governor Lee defines "sex" as determined by anatomy and genetics existing at the time of birth. The Department of Safety denied a legally transitioned transgender woman a driver's licence gender change, prompting an ACLU suit filed 23 April 2024 in Davidson County.

Transgender students are excluded from school sport. Legislation of 26 March 2021 banning transgender youth athletes passed the Senate 27-6 and the House 71-16 with 5 abstentions; Public Chapter 1005 of 22 April 2022 requires proof of gender assigned at birth under threat of funding loss. Litigation over a Farragut student barred from boys' golf produced partial summary judgment on 29 March 2024. Public Chapter 448 of May 2023 shields teachers from suit and discipline for using birth-certificate pronouns, and a May 2024 mandatory-outing law took effect immediately requiring teachers to report to administrators, and administrators to parents, whenever a child requests a different name or pronoun.

Protection machinery is thin and partly federal. Tennessee's hate-crime statute has punished bias based on sexual orientation since 2001 without explicitly listing gender identity; a February 2019 Attorney General opinion holds that selecting a victim because she is transgender qualifies for enhancement under § 40-35-114(17) as an offence committed because of gender, and federal law covers gender-identity bias. Employment discrimination on the basis of gender identity is prohibited through Title VII as applied in R.G. & G.R. Harris Funeral Homes v. EEOC (Sixth Circuit, 7 March 2018) and Bostock v. Clayton County (14 June 2020), but state law provides no statutory ban on sexual orientation or gender identity discrimination, and local public-employment ordinances in Knoxville, Memphis, Franklin, Chattanooga and Nashville/Davidson County do not reach private employers and are blocked by the Equal Access to Intrastate Commerce Act.

Violence risk carries a documented mitigation in law. The gay and trans panic defence remains available to lower or eliminate punishment for fatal attacks, and reporting describes police and legal officials sympathetic to aggressors who turn a blind eye, calling same-sex attraction a sin. The Tennessee Bureau of Investigation recorded 0 anti-transgender incidents in 2019, 1 in 2020 and 2 in 2021; these are raw counts with no population denominator and no evidence of continued reporting after 2021. In April 2021 Tennessee was described as experiencing economic and social impacts similar to the 2016 North Carolina bathroom-law backlash, and in 2024 the Human Rights Campaign classified Tennessee among the lowest-ranking states for LGBTQ rights.

Marriage and shelter access carry direct exclusions. Marriage licences have been issued to same-sex couples since Obergefell v. Hodges on 26 June 2015, but HB 878, signed 21 February 2024, allows government employees to refuse to solemnize a marriage against their personal beliefs. Trans women are barred from women's shelters under the 2026 Act.

66186276B64014601259366.name: Kansas
66186276B64014601259366.summary:
Kansas Senate Bill 244 was enacted on 26 February 2026 when the Legislature overrode Governor Laura Kelly's veto, and it took effect immediately. The law confines transgender people to sex-segregated facilities matching sex assigned at birth in publicly owned buildings, a category the Human Rights Campaign records as covering schools, universities, airports and government offices. It creates civil and criminal penalties of up to $1,000 for using a non-matching facility and authorises bounty-style lawsuits of at least $1,000 by any private person who claims to have shared a bathroom with a transgender person.

The same law bars the updating of driver's licences and state identification cards and invalidates existing licences whose gender marker is inconsistent with sex assigned at birth. The Kansas Department of Revenue has been mailing written notice, and many holders have already been told their licence is now invalid. Reissue is at the holder's expense with no grace period, and surrender letters warn of additional penalties for driving without a valid credential.

Two transgender men filed Doe v. State of Kansas in Douglas County District Court within days of enactment, represented by the ACLU and Ballard Spahr, citing fear of violence under the facility-restriction and identification-invalidation provisions.

The identification rules rest on an earlier statute. Senate Bill 180 was enacted in April 2023 by veto override, defined biological sex in state law and barred agencies from recognising genders beyond sex assigned at birth. The attorney general then directed that new or updated driver's licences and birth certificates reflect only original sex at birth. A temporary restraining order barred gender-marker changes; the Kansas Court of Appeals reversed unanimously on 13 June 2025 for lack of evidence of irreparable harm to law-enforcement identification; and in October 2025 the Kansas Supreme Court rejected an appeal, allowing the Department of Revenue to continue the changes.

Kansas law has prohibited discrimination on the basis of gender identity in employment, housing and public accommodations since 2020, following Bostock v. Clayton County and Kansas Human Rights Commission action in August 2020 covering businesses with four or more employees. The state hate-crime law provides penalty enhancements for crimes motivated by sexual orientation but does not cover gender identity; federal law has covered both since October 2009.

Marriage for same-sex couples became available after U.S. District Judge Daniel D. Crabtree ruled the state ban unconstitutional on 4 November 2014, effective 12 November 2014, and became fully legal under Obergefell v. Hodges on 26 June 2015, with all judicial districts issuing licences by the end of that month. Consensual same-sex sexual activity is legal under Lawrence v. Texas (2003), which rendered Kansas's sodomy law unenforceable, though the Legislature has not repealed its same-sex-only sodomy provisions carrying historic penalties of six months in jail and/or $1,000.

The reclassification follows the new bathroom-bounty law, which lets private individuals sue trans people encountered in wrong-sex facilities. The assessment addresses interstate-travel exposure.

sources.summary: State law has prohibited discrimination on the basis of gender identity in employment, housing and public accommodations since 2020 following Bostock v. Clayton County on June 15, 2020 and Kansas Human Rights Commission action in August 2020 covering businesses with four or more employees, while the state hate-crime law provides penalty enhancements for sexual orientation but does not cover gender identity, though federal law has covered both since October 2009. In April 2023 the Legislature overrode Governor Laura Kelly's veto to enact SB 180 defining biological sex in state law and barring agencies from recognizing genders beyond sex assigned at birth, leading to Attorney General direction that new or updated driver's licenses and birth certificates reflect only original sex at birth, a temporary restraining order barring gender-marker changes, a June 13, 2025 unanimous Court of Appeals reversal for lack of evidence of irreparable harm to law-enforcement identification, and an October 2025 Supreme Court rejection of appeal allowing the Department of Revenue to continue changes. In February 2026 SB 244 was enacted via veto override effective immediately on February 26, 2026 to legally require state IDs including driver's licenses to reflect sex assigned at birth and to invalidate and reissue non-compliant documents at the holder's expense with no grace period, with holders receiving surrender letters warning of additional penalties for driving without a valid credential, prompting an ACLU of Kansas lawsuit. A legislative ban on transgender athletes in female sports teams passed in April 2021 and April 2022 and was vetoed twice, then passed again and after a March 2023 veto was overridden to take effect July 1, while the Kansas State High School Activities Association as of February 2023 left decisions case-by-case to schools. On health care, Governor Kelly vetoed SB 233 on April 12, 2024 to ban gender-affirming care for minors under 18 and the override failed by two votes, vetoed similar SB 63 in February 2025 which was overridden February 18, 2025, and in May 2026 State District Judge Carl Folsom III granted a temporary injunction blocking enforcement in an ACLU-backed parental lawsuit. SB 180 prohibited entering sex-segregated bathrooms, crisis shelters, prisons and other biology/safety/privacy accommodations not matching sex assigned at birth without enforcement mechanisms, while SB 244 added financial and criminal penalties up to $1,000 for using a non-matching gender-segregated facility in a publicly-owned building plus a bounty provision allowing private citizens to sue for up to $1,000, described as a February 2026 $1,000 bounty on transgender bathroom use. Roeland Park in June 2020, Lawrence in April 2021 and Prairie Village in October 2021 banned conversion therapy on minors, and in 2022 a Geary County middle-school teacher obtained a partial federal preliminary injunction allowing her to use students' non-preferred names and to out students to parents despite a school preferred-name requirement. Consensual same-sex sexual activity is legal under Lawrence v. Texas (2003) which rendered unenforceable Kansas's sodomy law, though the legislature has not repealed its same-sex-only sodomy provisions carrying historic penalties of six months in jail and/or $1,000 after the 1969 reform that legalized heterosexual sodomy, and State v. Limon invalidated harsher Romeo-and-Juliet statutory-rape sentences for same-sex parties. Same-sex marriage became available after U.S. District Judge Daniel D. Crabtree ruled the state ban unconstitutional November 4, 2014 effective November 12, 2014 after stays were denied, and became fully legal under Obergefell v. Hodges June 26, 2015 with 25 of 32 judicial districts issuing by June 29 and all issuing or intending to by June 30, replacing prior statutory and constitutional bans on same-sex marriage and all other same-sex unions. Married same-sex couples may adopt, lesbian couples may access in vitro fertilization with the non-genetic, non-gestational mother recognized only if married, and the state permits gestational and traditional surrogacy on equal terms for same-sex and different-sex couples, but adoption agencies may refuse placements violating religious or moral convictions and under In the Matter of Adoption of I.M. (Nov. 2012) and Frazier v. Goudschaal (Feb. 22, 2013) unmarried non-biological partners obtain rights only in limited best-interest circumstances. State law has prohibited sexual-orientation discrimination in employment, housing and public accommodations since 2020 under Bostock and Kansas Human Rights Commission enforcement, supplemented by city ordinances and prior executive orders from 2007, rescinded 2015 and reissued 2019, while voters in Salina and Hutchinson repealed local ordinances November 6, 2012. The state hate-crime law provides penalty enhancements for crimes motivated by sexual orientation, and in March 2024 the Legislature passed a law defining content containing "acts of homosexuality" as harmful to minors alongside pornography and requiring government ID-based age verification to access such material.

66186276B64014601259366.localsOnly:
Kansas banned transgender athletes from female school sports teams through a veto override in March 2023, effective 1 July 2023, after earlier bans passed in April 2021 and April 2022 were vetoed twice. The Kansas State High School Activities Association as of February 2023 left decisions case-by-case to schools.

Gender-affirming care for minors under 18 is banned. Governor Kelly vetoed Senate Bill 233 on 12 April 2024 and the override failed by two votes; she vetoed similar Senate Bill 63 in February 2025 and that override succeeded on 18 February 2025. In May 2026 State District Judge Carl Folsom III granted a temporary injunction blocking enforcement in an ACLU-backed parental lawsuit.

Three municipalities banned conversion therapy on minors: Roeland Park in June 2020, Lawrence in April 2021 and Prairie Village in October 2021. In 2022 a Geary County middle-school teacher obtained a partial federal preliminary injunction allowing her to use students' non-preferred names and to disclose students' gender identity to parents despite a school preferred-name requirement.

Married same-sex couples may adopt. Lesbian couples may access in vitro fertilisation, with the non-genetic, non-gestational mother recognised only if married. The state permits gestational and traditional surrogacy on equal terms for same-sex and different-sex couples, but adoption agencies may refuse placements that violate their religious or moral convictions, and under In the Matter of Adoption of I.M. (November 2012) and Frazier v. Goudschaal (22 February 2013) unmarried non-biological partners obtain rights only in limited best-interest circumstances.

Sexual-orientation discrimination in employment, housing and public accommodations has been prohibited since 2020 under Bostock and Kansas Human Rights Commission enforcement, supplemented by city ordinances and executive orders issued in 2007, rescinded in 2015 and reissued in 2019. Voters in Salina and Hutchinson repealed local ordinances on 6 November 2012. In March 2024 the Legislature passed a law defining content containing "acts of homosexuality" as harmful to minors alongside pornography and requiring government ID-based age verification to access such material.

66186276B69138566591314.name: Mississippi
66186276B69138566591314.summary:
Mississippi's own statutes, not the national framework, set the terms a trans visitor meets inside the state. The Movement Advancement Project's equality map records that Mississippi enacted bans on transgender people using public bathrooms and facilities according to their gender identity in 2024 and 2025, and that state statute defines sex by birth. The Anti-Trans National Legal Risk Assessment Map's July 2026 update places Mississippi in its "Worst Laws Passed" category, among states the assessment describes as having legislatively erased transgender people; the grading derives from a five-year legislation-tracking methodology with a scoring rubric.

Facilities rules bite first in schools. A law signed 13 May 2024 and effective immediately requires individuals in public schools to use bathrooms consistent with sex "determined solely by birth." In 2024 a Harrison County dress code requiring clothing to match sex assigned at birth led to a transgender girl being threatened with in-school suspension for wearing a dress to a regional band event. Two earlier bills, the SAFER Act restricting transgender people's use of public bathrooms, locker rooms and public university dormitories, and the Women's Bill of Rights codifying a binary definition of sex at birth, died on 29 April 2024 when House and Senate negotiators failed to agree on compromise versions; the 2024 and 2025 enactments followed that failure.

Identity documents are closed at state level. The Vital Records office issues an amended birth certificate with a new name and gender marker on a certified court order, a medical statement attesting to gender reassignment, and a fee, but the amended certificate lists both the updated and the original information. From 1 November 2021 to March 2026 a Gender Designation Form signed by a physician or psychotherapist allowed a driver's licence marker change; a March 2026 law prohibited markers not reflecting sex assigned at birth.

The state's highest court has ruled against recognition. On 17 April 2025 the Mississippi Supreme Court held 8-1 that a transgender teenager undergoing gender transition could not change his name, denying a petition filed nearly two years earlier by a then-16-year-old whose parents both consented. The majority opinion, written by Justice James D. Maxwell II, referred to the boy as a "minor female" and cited the 2023 REAP Act as Mississippi's express public policy against children receiving life-altering gender-transition assistance; a chancellor may grant a minor's name change only where it is clearly in the child's best interest. Minors may otherwise change names with parental consent.

Care access is restricted. The Regulate Experimental Adolescent Procedures (REAP) Act, signed 28 February 2023, bans gender-affirming care for people under 18. The University of Mississippi Medical Center's TEAM Clinic closed on 30 June 2023, leaving Spectrum: The Other Clinic in Hattiesburg, operating virtually, as the only LGBTQ+-specialising clinic in the state.

School sports participation is conditioned on proof of anatomy. SB 2536, signed 11 March 2021 and effective 1 July 2021, bars transgender students from school sports consistent with their gender identity and requires any athlete whose sex is disputed to provide a physician's statement verifying genitalia, DNA and hormone levels.

Anti-discrimination protection is absent at state level. Mississippi law provides no protection based on gender identity in employment, housing or public accommodations, and the 1994 state hate-crime statute does not include gender identity.

The Religious Liberty Accommodations Act (HB 1523) protects individuals, religious organisations and some businesses that refuse services on the belief that gender is determined at birth by anatomy and genetics.

Violence against transgender people in Mississippi has drawn federal prosecution. The U.S. Attorney's Office for the Southern District of Mississippi reported that Joshua Brandon Vallum was sentenced to 49 years in federal prison for the bias-motivated murder of a transgender woman in Lucedale, committed after he learned his former girlfriend was transgender.

Marriage is recognised. Same-sex marriage has been recognised in Mississippi since the Supreme Court's ruling in Obergefell v. Hodges on 26 June 2015, which overrode a 1996 executive order, a 1997 statutory ban and 2004 constitutional Amendment 1, approved by 86.01% of voters. Those bans remain unrepealed. A trans visitor in a relationship read as same-sex under birth-sex status can marry, and the then Attorney General Jim Hood directed clerks to comply or face lawsuits on 29 June 2015 after initial resistance.

sources.title: LGBTQ rights in Mississippi (Wikipedia)
sources.summary: Mississippi bans gender-affirming care for individuals under age 18 under the Regulate Experimental Adolescent Procedures (REAP) Act signed February 28, 2023, after which the University of Mississippi Medical Center's TEAM Clinic closed June 30, 2023, leaving Spectrum: The Other Clinic in Hattiesburg operating virtually as the only LGBTQ+-specializing clinic. State law bars transgender students from school sports consistent with gender identity under SB 2536 signed March 11, 2021 and effective July 1, 2021, requiring any athlete whose sex is disputed to provide a physician's statement verifying genitalia, DNA, and hormone levels. A law signed May 13, 2024 and effective immediately requires individuals in public schools to use bathrooms consistent with sex "determined solely by birth," and a 2024 Harrison County dress code requiring clothing to match sex assigned at birth led to a transgender girl being threatened with in-school suspension for wearing a dress to a regional band event. For identity documents, the Vital Records office issues an amended birth certificate with new name and gender marker upon certified court order, medical statement attesting to gender reassignment and fee but lists both updated and original information, while from November 1, 2021 to March 2026 a Gender Designation Form signed by a physician or psychotherapist allowed driver's license marker changes until a March 2026 law prohibited markers not reflecting sex assigned at birth. In April 2025 the Mississippi Supreme Court ruled a transgender teenager with parental support could not legally change his name until age 21 for "lack of maturity" while misgendering him, although minors may otherwise change names with parental consent, and a separate enacted measure prohibits inmate name changes after The Real You Act of 2022 died in committee. State non-discrimination law provides no protection based on gender identity in employment, housing or public accommodations, though federal Title VII per Bostock v. Clayton County on June 15, 2020 prohibits employment discrimination based on gender identity, and Jackson, Clarksdale, Holly Springs and Magnolia ban gender-identity discrimination in employment, housing and public accommodations while Hattiesburg, Oxford and Starkville protect city employees only. The 1994 state hate-crime statute does not include gender identity, but federal prosecution remains available under the 2009 Matthew Shepard and James Byrd Jr. Act, under which Joshua Vallum was sentenced in 2017 to 49 years in federal prison for murdering his former girlfriend after learning she was transgender, and the Religious Liberty Accommodations Act (HB 1523) protects refusal of services based on belief that gender is determined at birth by anatomy and genetics. Same-sex sexual activity has been legal since 2003 under Lawrence v. Texas, but Mississippi's sodomy statute originating in 1839 with up to ten years' imprisonment remains on the books unenforceable, and persons convicted before 2003 are still required to register as sex offenders under the 1995 registration law, prompting a 2016 federal lawsuit by five residents and $400,000 in taxpayer legal fees reported in 2023. Same-sex marriage has been recognized since June 26, 2015 under Obergefell v. Hodges overriding the 1996 executive order, 1997 statutory ban and 2004 constitutional Amendment 1 approved by 86.01% of voters, though those bans remain unrepealed and Attorney General Jim Hood on June 29, 2015 directed clerks to comply or face lawsuits after initial resistance. Mississippi banned adoption and fostering by same-sex couples in 2000 and was the only state still enforcing such a ban by 2015, until U.S. District Judge Daniel Porter Jordan III struck it down March 31, 2016 with final effect May 2, 2016 after no appeal, making it the last state to allow same-sex couple adoption. State law does not prohibit discrimination based on sexual orientation in employment, housing or public accommodations, though federal Title VII per Bostock in 2020 prohibits employment discrimination based on sexual orientation and Jackson, Clarksdale, Holly Springs and Magnolia have local ordinances banning sexual-orientation discrimination while Hattiesburg, Oxford and Starkville cover municipal employees. The Religious Liberty Accommodations Act (HB 1523), effective after the Fifth Circuit lifted an injunction June 23, 2017, protects individuals, religious organizations and some businesses acting on beliefs that marriage is between one man and one woman and sexual relations be confined to such marriage. The 1994 state hate-crime law does not cover sexual orientation, though federal coverage exists under the 2009 Matthew Shepard and James Byrd Jr. Act, and Mississippi maintains HIV criminalization making failure to disclose HIV-positive status to a sexual partner a felony even without transmission, with at least 43 arrests for HIV-related offenses between 2004 and 2021 per a 2024 Williams Institute report. A 2019 PRRI poll found that "68% of Mississippians favored laws that would protect gay, lesbian, bisexual, and transgender people from discrimination in jobs, housing, and public accommodations, with 23% opposed." By 2024, PRRI reported support for such a statewide anti-discrimination law covering sexual orientation and gender identity reached 67%. The article states that "Compared to national averages, Mississippi tends to show lower support for same-sex marriage and transgender rights, but opinion gaps have narrowed over time." It notes generational differences are pronounced, with younger Mississippians showing significantly higher support for LGBTQ rights than older residents. For visible local climate relevant to transgender visitors as part of the LGBTQ community, Starkville hosted its first pride parade March 24, 2018 after initial permit denial, drawing approximately 3,000 participants and becoming the largest parade in the city's history.

66186276B83300161667341.name: Oklahoma
66186276B83300161667341.summary:
Oklahoma is a state within the United States, so a visitor stands under the national framework recorded in the parent country's dossier. Within that framework, Oklahoma's own statutes and executive acts restrict a transgender visitor's use of facilities, documents, care and sport more narrowly than the national baseline.

The Movement Advancement Project's national tracker, current to 25 March 2026, lists Oklahoma among states banning transgender people from bathrooms and facilities matching their gender identity in K-12 schools, with enactments in 2022 and again in 2025. Senate Bill 615, signed in May 2022, requires transgender students and staff to use school bathrooms, changing rooms and similar facilities according to sex assigned at birth as stated on an original birth certificate rather than gender identity. That statute is associated with the 2024 death of 16-year-old non-binary student Nex Benedict, who was beaten in a school bathroom shortly before dying.

Facility and role definitions at state level were widened by an executive order Governor Kevin Stitt signed on 1 August 2023, requiring state agencies to define female, woman, girl and mother as a person whose biological reproductive system is designed to produce ova and male, man, boy and father as a person whose system is designed to fertilise ova, based on sex assigned at birth. The order applies to state and legal purposes including bathrooms and changing rooms in state-owned facilities, sports, domestic violence shelters, rape crisis centres, incarceration and statistics collection, which restricts legal recognition of transgender people for state agency purposes.

Birth certificates are the sharpest document exposure. Oklahoma recognised a non-binary birth-certificate option from October 2021 under Kit Vivien Loreleid v. Oklahoma State Department of Health, but in November 2021 Governor Stitt ordered the health department to block any gender-marker changes, and in April 2022 Senate Bill 1100 limited birth certificates to male or female only, banning other markers with immediate effect. House Bill 1225, which requires a male or female designation on Oklahoma birth certificates and prohibits changes with very little exception, passed its most recent vote 70-17 and on 6 May 2026 was headed to Governor Stitt's desk, still pending his signature. Its authors said it is designed to strengthen the existing law being challenged in federal court by transgender plaintiffs including a Tulsa resident, Rowan Fowler; the state Attorney General's office confirmed the bill clarifies that Oklahoma never permitted gender-marker changes, while critics called it further discrimination. In October 2026 the Oklahoma Supreme Court ruled retroactively that changing a birth-certificate gender marker was never legal, even to correct an error made for a cisgender person.

Transgender Oklahomans could previously change driver's licences on a notarised physician statement of permanent and irreversible transition; the source does not describe the operative licensing practice after the 2021 and 2022 birth-certificate restrictions, and equality-map research shows conditions for changing a gender marker on a licence or birth certificate differ state by state.

Sport is closed to transgender girls and women in public education. In March 2022 Governor Stitt signed a law barring transgender women and girls from women's and girls' athletic teams at public schools and universities, and in 2022 he signed S.B. 2 prohibiting transgender students from playing school sports consistent with their gender identity and excluding all transgender girls from school athletics.

Gender-affirming care is restricted on several fronts. An October 2022 law bars government funding to Oklahoma hospitals providing any gender transition services to minors. An April 2023 law, signed in May 2023, explicitly bans any gender-affirming healthcare practice on minors, making Oklahoma the 16th state with such a restriction, and a judge declined to block it in October 2023. Senate Bill 904, passed at the end of the 2026 session (77-14 in the House, 39-8 in the Senate) and signed on 14 May 2026 with immediate effect, bars use of public funds, Oklahoma Medicaid (SoonerCare) coverage or reimbursement, and state-owned properties and healthcare facilities for gender-affirming surgeries, puberty blockers, cross-sex hormones and other medications that delay puberty or develop secondary sex characteristics where they affirm a gender identity different from sex assigned at birth, for minors and adults alike. Intentional violations by state employees are a criminal misdemeanour; patients face no penalties. The ban exempts mental health counselling, anxiety and depression medication, precocious puberty treatment, intersex care, treatment of complications from prior gender-affirming care, and emergency treatment to prevent death or major impairment, leaving gender-affirming medical care available only at privately owned facilities paid by private insurance or out of pocket, without Medicaid. A February 2023 House-passed bill to bar publicly funded entities from providing or permitting gender-affirming care to transgender people of any age and to ban insurance coverage did not pass the Senate and did not become law.

State statutes provide no discrimination protection on the basis of gender identity. Norman prohibits discrimination in employment, housing and public accommodations on gender identity and sexual orientation, while Edmond, Oklahoma City and Tulsa prohibit it only for public city employment. Oklahoma is an at-will employment state, permitting dismissal without a stated reason.

State hate-crime law does not cover gender identity, so a bias-motivated assault against a transgender person is prosecuted without the state enhancement. Violence directed at trans and gender-nonconforming minors is documented: in 2018 a school in Achille closed for days after a 12-year-old transgender student received death threats, including threats of mutilation, whipping and castration, from classmates' parents.

An advocacy legal-risk assessment, the Anti-Trans National Legal Risk Assessment Map published in July 2026, assigns Oklahoma a per-state traveller risk grade alongside the other states; that edition added a fourth 'Do Not Travel' state and tracked changes to its 'Worst Laws Passed' tier, but the source does not state Oklahoma's specific grade.

Relationship recognition is settled in the opposite direction. Same-sex marriage and adoption by same-sex couples have been permitted in Oklahoma since October 2014, after voters approved Question 711 on 2 November 2004 banning same-sex marriage and its legal incidents, Judge Terence C. Kern declared it unconstitutional on 14 January 2014 in Bishop v. United States, the Tenth Circuit upheld that ruling on 18 July 2014, and the U.S. Supreme Court denied appeal on 6 October 2014. Oklahoma permits adoption by a couple or unmarried adult without regard to sexual orientation, and in August 2007 the Tenth Circuit in Finstuen v. Crutcher ordered the state to recognise a same-sex couple's adoption and issue a revised birth certificate. State law nevertheless allows agencies to refuse placements that violate their written religious or moral convictions. Lesbian couples can access fertility treatment and IVF, with state law recognising a married non-genetic, non-gestational mother as a legal parent, although a 2023 district judge stripped such a wife's rights in favour of a sperm donor where she was absent from the donor contract and had not adopted.

sources.title: Oklahoma Senate Bill 904 (2026) - Restriction on state resources for gender-affirming care

66186276B98021244841737.name: Alabama
66186276B98021244841737.summary:
Alabama is a state of the United States and stands under the national framework. Federal passport and visa rules, entry screening, federal custody and detention policy, and federal healthcare and funding measures apply in Alabama as they do elsewhere in the country.

Facility rules are the first thing a trans visitor encounters. The Movement Advancement Project's equality map tabulates state bans on transgender people using public bathrooms and facilities according to their gender identity, and records Alabama as enacting such bans in 2022 and 2024. The 2022 statute, House Bill 322, signed on 8 April 2022 as Act No. 2022-290, requires public school students to use bathrooms consistent with the gender recorded on their birth certificate, and the state Board of Education codified that rule in September 2022. A March 2024 measure extends the restriction to university facilities. Senate Bill 79, signed in February 2025, declares gender an immutable male-female binary determined by biological sex assigned at birth and authorises separate single-sex spaces where biology, privacy, safety or fairness are implicated.

The July 2026 Anti-Trans National Legal Risk Assessment Map places Alabama in its worst-law grouping of legislatively-erasing jurisdictions, citing a bathroom ban carried by the state's 'Don't Say Gay' legislation that reaches college campuses.

Gender-affirming care for minors is a felony in Alabama. The Vulnerable Child Compassion and Protection Act, Senate Bill 184, signed on 8 April 2022 and effective from 8 May 2022, makes it a Class C felony punishable by up to 10 years in prison for a medical provider to supply gender-affirming care, including puberty blockers, hormones or surgery, to anyone under 19. The Eleventh Circuit allowed enforcement on 21 August 2023, and the ban remains in force after the plaintiffs withdrew their challenge on 1 May 2025. A trans visitor accompanying a minor, or seeking care for one, is exposed to that prohibition.

Identity documents are closed to most trans people. Alabama permits amendment of birth certificates and driver's licences to a person's current sex only with documentation of sex "changed by surgical procedure" together with a name change. A January 2021 federal ruling in Corbitt v. Taylor invalidated the surgery requirement, but the Eleventh Circuit reversed it and the requirement stands. On 20 September 2024 the same court ruled that refusal to issue accurate licences did not violate the federal constitution; rehearing was denied on 13 November 2024 and judgment entered on 10 December 2024. Most transgender people cannot obtain an accurate licence and must carry daily identification showing the wrong gender, which the ACLU describes as exposing them to a high risk of harassment and violence during ID checks.

No statewide law prohibits discrimination based on gender identity in employment, housing, public accommodations, or student harassment and bullying. Alabama also has no ban on insurance exclusions for transgender healthcare and no transgender-inclusive health benefits for state employees. A trans visitor has no statewide public-accommodations recourse.

Alabama's hate-crime statute, in force since 1994, covers offences motivated by race, colour, religion, national origin, ethnicity, or physical or mental disability. Gender identity is not covered. Attempts to add sexual orientation failed: House Bill 533 passed the House 46 to 41 in April 2009 but received no Senate vote before adjournment on 15 May 2009, and House Bills 413 in 2016 and 8 in 2017 also failed.

Partner recognition is settled statewide. Eight counties were still refusing all marriage licences in 2017, but the Legislature required recording of marriage certificates in May 2019 and every county began recording for all couples, including couples read as same-sex under birth-sex status, on 29 August 2019. The 1996 Executive Order Number 24, the 1998 statute at Alabama Code § 30-1-19 and the June 2006 constitutional Amendment 774 remain unenforceable.

Violence data for Alabama is incomplete. A July 2026 national analysis drawing on TGEU and Williams Institute data records a killing rate of trans women in Alabama of 3.8 per 100,000 per year, a figure the source itself describes as an undercount floor, calculated on a 428-victim base covering 2008 to 2025. Alabama's general homicide rate does not appear in the source material, so the comparison that would show whether this exceeds background violence cannot be made, and the figure should not be read as a measure of severity on its own.

66186276B82803899326534.summary:
Indiana is a state of the United States, and a trans visitor here stands under the national framework on passports, visas, entry screening and federal custody, which the country record carries. What follows is the state layer.

Indiana's Bureau of Motor Vehicles ban on gender-marker changes to driver's licences and state identification cards took effect on 1 February 2026. It ended the route residents had used to obtain such a change, which ran through a court-ordered gender change or a physician's statement. The ban completed an administrative rule change the bureau initiated; LGBTQ advocates who testified against it said it would forcibly out transgender and nonbinary residents whose documents no longer match how they present. The ACLU has challenged the policy in court.

Governor Mike Braun's March 2025 executive order defining sex solely as assigned sex at birth directed the Indiana Department of Health to stop updating gender markers, and the bureau's 2026 rule extended that prohibition to licences and identification cards. Birth-certificate changes had been available by court order from 2014 until 2025. In May 2023 the Indiana Supreme Court declined in split votes to hear two cases brought by transgender girls seeking amended birth certificates, which left appellate rulings standing that trial courts have no authority to grant a change unless the General Assembly codifies it. One of those cases involved a nine-year-old transgender girl whose birth certificate's male designation her school used to restrict her bathroom access.

Indiana issued an X marker between March 2019 and January 2020, on presentation of an amended birth certificate or a physician's statement confirming permanent gender change. The bureau withdrew it after a public hearing, and a March 2020 opinion from the attorney general held that only the General Assembly could authorise nonbinary designations.

As of April 2026, Indiana law places no restriction on transgender people using restrooms that match their gender identity, and Indianapolis and Bloomington ordinances expressly protect that use. Proposals to criminalise it have died in committee since 2021, and in August 2023 a Seventh Circuit decision upheld a preliminary injunction barring schools from limiting a transgender student's bathroom use while litigation continued.

Senate Bill 182 passed the Indiana Senate 37-8 on 27 January 2026 on a party-line vote and went to the House. It would define sex and gender by reproductive biology at birth, permanently bar amendments to birth certificates, require public K-12 schools and state universities to designate multi-person restrooms, locker rooms and changing areas for use only by males or females as assigned at birth, and confine prison housing to a placement matching birth sex. Its author, Senator Liz Brown of Fort Wayne, said the proposal protects women's private spaces; opponents including GenderNexus warned that a provision allowing anyone directly or indirectly injured to sue a school would encourage harassment-style enforcement. The bill received no House hearing and is not law.

Gender-affirming care for minors is barred. Senate Bill 480, passed and signed in 2023 under an emergency clause, prohibits physicians from providing gender-transition procedures to anyone under 18 or from aiding such care, with a phase-out for existing patients. It was enjoined on 16 June 2023, took effect on 27 February 2024 after a stay, and was upheld in November 2024. The ban covers surgery, puberty blockers and hormone therapy. A trans visitor under 18 cannot obtain that care in Indiana.

Indiana's hate-crimes law, enacted in April 2019, allows harsher sentences where an offence was motivated by a victim's perceived or actual characteristics, gender identity among them. It creates an aggravating circumstance rather than a standalone offence; the state had tracked bias crimes without any sentencing enhancement from 2003 until then.

66186276B31593004124297.name: Utah
66186276B31593004124297.summary:
Utah restricts restroom and locker-room use by sex assigned at birth in public schools and government-owned buildings. HB 257, titled Sex-based Designations for Privacy, Anti-bullying, and Women's Opportunities, was introduced on 11 January 2024 and signed by Governor Spencer Cox on 30 January 2024. The statute does not reach private businesses, so hotels, gyms and commercial venues fall outside it. New government buildings must include single-occupant facilities. A person facing a complaint may answer it with documentation: a birth certificate and, where the marker on that certificate has been changed, proof of gender-affirming surgery. The defence rests on records a visitor will generally not carry, and the law provides no alternative route for someone whose documents were issued outside the state.

Enforcement runs through complaints rather than police action. A reporting form allows residents to report transgender people in privacy spaces such as changing rooms and restrooms, and complainants may choose whether their own names are included while the state investigates each reported violation. A procedure adopted in May 2024 allows officials and individuals to file formal complaints about suspected incorrect bathroom use in schools and government buildings. The ACLU of Utah opposed HB 257 on the ground that it invites discriminatory enforcement.

In March 2025 Utah enacted a ban on LGBTQ pride flags in public schools and government buildings. A May 2025 account places the signing on 7 May and describes Utah as the first state to prohibit such flags explicitly, with fines of $500 a day. Salt Lake City adopted the Sego Visibility Flag, modelled on the transgender pride flag, as an official city flag in May 2025. Utah Pride's executive director said the state leads the nation in anti-LGBTQ legislation.

Gender-affirming care for minors is banned. The ban passed the House on 26 January 2023 and the Senate 20-8 the following day, and was signed on 28 January 2023 with immediate effect; treatment already under way in January 2023 could continue. Clinicians may provide care to patients under 25, but those patients hold a retroactive right to disaffirm consent and sue. A legislative legal review found the ban potentially unconstitutional for targeting transgender people. A two-year systematic review commissioned under the ban and released in May 2025 concluded that the treatments are effective for mental health and psychosocial outcomes and for body changes consistent with an affirmed gender, and safe with respect to bone density, cardiovascular risk, metabolic change and cancer; the legislature dismissed the findings and kept the ban in force.

State-issued identity documents remain amendable. A transgender person may change the gender marker on a Utah birth certificate on submission of a certified court order changing name and gender; surgery is not required, and an X descriptor is available subject to judicial approval. In May 2021 the Utah Supreme Court held 4-1 that judges must grant sex and name changes when the clinical requirements are met.

Nondiscrimination protection is partial. SB 296, passed in 2015, bans discrimination based on gender identity in employment and housing but not in public accommodations, and exempts religious organisations and their affiliates, including schools and hospitals. The hate-crime statute amended in 2019 covers gender identity, carries enhanced penalties and requires the collection and publication of hate-crime statistics; those amendments passed the Senate 18-11 and the House 64-9, with Senate concurrence 22-3, and were signed on 2 April 2019.

Sports participation has been contested for several years. House Bill 11, barring transgender athletes from sports, athletics and the Olympics, passed in March 2022, was vetoed by Governor Cox on 22 March 2022, and was enacted over the veto to take effect on 1 July; on 19 August a judge partly reversed it and allowed transgender girls to be considered case by case for girls' sports in 2022-2023. On 3 October 2024 Southern Utah University and Utah State University forfeited matches against San Jose State University during litigation over a transgender player's eligibility. In 2024 the state also barred transgender students from university dormitories matching their gender identity, after a transgender woman was assigned to a women's dormitory at Utah State University.

Marriage equality reached Utah on 6 October 2014, after the Tenth Circuit affirmed a district ruling of 20 December 2013 striking the state's ban; the ruling displaced the 1995 non-recognition statute H.B. 366 and the 2004 constitutional amendment defining marriage as the union of a man and a woman, which voters approved 65.8 per cent to 33.2 per cent. Adoption follows from the recognition of the marriage. Foster care and adoption are otherwise limited to married or single persons, with cohabiting unmarried couples barred and priority given to married couples under 1998 H.B. 103. For couples using in vitro fertilisation, parental recognition of the non-genetic, non-gestational parent follows only from marriage. In August 2019 the Utah Supreme Court held the bar on same-sex surrogacy agreements unconstitutional.

Private consensual sexual conduct is not criminalised. The state's sodomy statute was invalidated by Lawrence v. Texas in 2003 and repealed by the legislature in 2019, following House approval 74-0 with one abstention on 29 January, Senate approval 25-2 with two abstentions on 22 February, and signature by Governor Gary Herbert on 25 March 2019. Earlier changes had reduced the offence from a felony to a misdemeanour in 1969 and created an exemption for married couples in 1973.

66186276B22881275445497.name: North Dakota
66186276B22881275445497.summary:
North Dakota stands under the United States national framework for passports, entry and screening; the findings below are those specific to the state.

North Dakota is listed among the worst states for legislation targeting transgender adults in a July 2026 legal-risk assessment published by Erin In The Morning, and among the states that prohibit any change to birth certificates, which forces transgender people to disclose their status when presenting documents.

Birth certificate markers are closed. A 2023 North Dakota law bans all gender-marker changes on birth certificates with a narrow exception for applicants who have had genital surgery. The Movement Advancement Project's identity-document policy tracker describes the surgical requirement as stricter and more explicit than in many other states and classifies North Dakota as a negative-law state. The regulations accompanying the 2023 law were rejected, leaving in place a 2008 regulation that restricts changes to applicants who have undergone a sex conversion operation.

Driver licence and state identification markers are handled separately. The state Department of Transportation updates the gender marker on a driver licence or state identification card on receipt of a letter from a physician or therapist stating that the applicant has completed a permanent gender role transition.

No North Dakota statute explicitly prohibits discrimination on the basis of gender identity, and the state hate-crime law does not cover gender identity.

An April 2023 law signed by the governor and effective 1 July explicitly allows transgender people's use of public bathrooms to be restricted in many state-run facilities.

A law signed in May 2023 and effective 1 July bars schools and government entities from requiring or prohibiting the use of preferred pronouns but requires that transgender students in state-run schools be disclosed to their parents. The 2023 legislative record for HB 1522, an act creating new sections of the North Dakota Century Code relating to preferred pronouns and providing accommodations to a transgender student, records a penalty provision and an emergency clause, with the governor's signature and the last official action filed with the Secretary of State on 9 May 2023. An earlier March 2023 bill requiring parental and administrative approval for preferred pronoun use in state-run schools and classrooms was vetoed. An April 2021 law allows student groups at colleges, universities and high schools to discriminate against LGBT students.

A 2021 bill to bar transgender girls from girls' school sports teams passed the House 69 to 25 and the Senate 27 to 20 and was vetoed by Governor Doug Burgum on 21 April 2021. Two bills signed in April 2023 ban individuals assigned male at birth from female sports and athletics in schools and in higher education respectively.

Providing gender-affirming care to minors is illegal under a bill passed by a veto-proof majority on 5 April 2023.

A June 2021 committee regulation bans conversion therapy by social workers, psychologists and counselors.

North Dakota is listed among 'the worst states' for legislation targeting transgender adults, and among the states that prohibit any changes to birth certificates, forcing trans people to out themselves when showing documents. Also documents that federal policies keep creating legal difficulties for transgender people nationwide.

66186276B38006515706420.name: South Dakota
66186276B38006515706420.summary:
South Dakota restricts transgender people from using bathrooms, locker rooms and changing areas matching their gender identity in public schools and state-owned buildings under House Bill 1259, signed by Governor Larry Rhoden on 20 March 2025 and announced the following day. The law took effect on 1 July 2025 and passed the state House 49-21. Its scope covers state-run facilities, primarily K-12 schools and state colleges, including off-campus activities. It is the first facilities restriction of its kind to be enacted in the state, after comparable bills failed in 2016, 2017, twice in 2018 and in 2022.

The law's "reasonable accommodation" clause and the floor debate around it raised the prospect that incarcerated transgender people would be placed in solitary confinement in order to comply.

No South Dakota statute explicitly prohibits discrimination on the basis of gender identity in employment, housing or public accommodations, and the state hate-crime law does not cover gender identity. Federal law supplies the only backstop: Title VII employment protection as construed in Bostock v. Clayton County (2020) and federal hate-crime prosecution under the 2009 Matthew Shepard and James Byrd Jr. Act.

Identity documents are closed to gender-marker change. On 5 March 2026 the South Dakota Supreme Court ruled that a transgender person cannot amend the sex designation on a South Dakota birth certificate to reflect gender identity, affirming the denial of Sigrid Nielsen's September 2024 petition to change the marker from male to female and holding that a change is permitted only to correct an error made at birth. A legal gender change on a driver's licence or state ID remains available by court order or a physician affidavit confirming sex reassignment surgery, and on a birth certificate by court order, photo ID, application and fee.

Gender-affirming care for people under 18 is banned under House Bill 1080, passed in February 2023 and signed on 13 February 2023. The law required prior puberty-blocker or hormone treatment to be systematically reduced, ending no later than 31 December 2023, and authorises affected people to sue until age 25 or within three years of discovering an injury.

An advocacy legal-risk assessment published in July 2026 lists South Dakota among the worst states for legislation targeting transgender adults, drawing on five years of daily legislative tracking and a rubric for the most severe bills.

State institutions have also acted against transgender health provision directly. On 16 December 2022 South Dakota terminated The Transformation Project's $136,000 federally funded Community Health Worker contract for LGBTQ+ and transgender community health in Sioux Falls. To settle the organisation's discrimination lawsuit, Health Secretary Melissa Magstadt issued an apology letter on 17 January 2024 acknowledging the termination and differential treatment compared with other Community Health Worker contractors, affirming equal treatment under law regardless of race, colour, national origin, religion, disability, age or sex; the state paid $300,000 covering attorney fees, committed not to discriminate against the Project in violation of state or federal law in any services, programmes or activities, and allowed the retention of community health worker Jack Fonder.

A March 2021 law signed by Governor Kristi Noem allows businesses to deny goods or services to LGBTQ people based on owners' purported religious beliefs, and in 2024 the Transformation Project won a discrimination lawsuit against the state. South Dakota hate-crime law does not cover gender identity, but federal prosecution has been available since the 2009 Matthew Shepard and James Byrd Jr. Act, and in September 2019 the Oglala Sioux Tribal Council passed hate-crime legislation protecting LGBT and two-spirit individuals by 14-2-1. Whitmarsh to include fellatio, with current age of consent at fifteen after initial thirteen. Same-sex marriage has been recognized since June 26, 2015 under Obergefell v. Hodges, superseding a November 2006 constitutional amendment and statutes defining marriage as man-woman and barring other recognition, following Rosenbrahn v. Daugaard filed May 22, 2014 where Judge Karen Schreier ruled for plaintiffs January 12, 2015 but stayed pending appeal. 66186276B10933057601622.name: Wyoming
66186276B10933057601622.summary:
Wyoming's facilities law is the most immediate exposure for a trans visitor. House Bill 72, the "Protecting privacy in public spaces act," was signed by Governor Mark Gordon on 3 March 2025 after passing the House 52-8 on 7 February 2025 and the Senate 25-6, and took effect 1 July 2025. It defines male and female by biological sex and requires public facilities to reserve multi-occupancy restrooms, changing areas and sleeping quarters exclusively for males or exclusively for females, prohibiting entry into a facility that does not match biological sex. Accommodations are permitted only where they do not include access to opposite-sex multi-occupancy facilities. The law creates a cause of action against a facility that permitted, or failed to prohibit, an opposite-sex person in a sex-designated restroom or changing area, and a separate cause of action for a person required by a correctional or educational facility to share sleeping quarters with the opposite sex.

A companion measure, Senate File 62, "Sex-designated facilities and public schools," requires public school students from pre-kindergarten upward, including charter school students, to use restrooms aligned with sex assigned at birth, and requires districts to provide a "reasonable accommodation" to any student who does not wish to use a multiple-occupancy restroom or locker room matching the gender at that student's birth. The Movement Advancement Project's equality map records the Wyoming facility bans as signed in March 2025.

Wyoming has no state law prohibiting discrimination on the basis of gender identity in employment, housing, public accommodations or credit and lending. As of 12 October 2026 the Movement Advancement Project rates the state's gender-identity policy score at -9 out of 25 and its overall score at -6.5 out of 47, a Negative rating. The only recourse for gender-identity employment discrimination is federal. Jackson, Casper and Laramie have ordinances prohibiting discrimination covering gender identity in employment, housing and public accommodations; Cheyenne and Gillette prohibit city employment discrimination on sexual orientation only.

Wyoming has no state hate-crime statute. Debate after the 1998 murder of Matthew Shepard near Laramie did not produce one.

Gender-affirming care for minors is banned under a measure passed by both houses in March 2024 and signed by the governor, effective 1 July 2024, barring sexual reassignment surgery and gender-affirming care for children.
