sources.title: LGBTQ rights in Wyoming (Wikipedia)
sources.summary: Wyoming state statutes do not address discrimination based on gender identity, but the United States Supreme Court ruling in Bostock v Clayton County protects LGBT employees from workplace discrimination under federal law, and the cities of Jackson, Casper and Laramie have ordinances prohibiting discrimination covering gender identity in employment, housing and public accommodations. Wyoming has no state hate crime law, but the federal Matthew Shepard and James Byrd Jr Hate Crimes Prevention Act of 2009 expanded the federal definition to include gender identity. Changing the gender marker on a Wyoming birth certificate requires undergoing sex reassignment surgery and obtaining a court order stating sex has been changed, with submission to Vital Statistics Services of a letter requesting the change, a photocopy of current ID, a certified copy of the court order, and a doctor letter confirming surgery was performed. Correction of the gender marker on a driver's license or state ID requires a completed Gender Designation Change Request Form signed by the applicant and a physician, therapist or counselor, psychiatric social worker or other medical or social service provider confirming gender identity. A bill passed in March 2023 explicitly bans transgender athletes from playing on any female sports and athletics teams, which became law without the governor's signature or veto and took effect July 1, 2023. A bill passed by both houses in March 2024 explicitly bans sexual reassignment surgery and gender-affirming care on children, which the governor signed to take effect July 1. House Bill 72 signed in April 2025 requires all public restrooms in the state to be segregated by biological sex and takes effect July 1, 2025. Consensual same-sex sexual activity has been legal since Wyoming decriminalized consensual sodomy in February 1977, with common-law liability for anal intercourse abrogated in 1982, and the age of consent for all consensual sexual activity is 17. Same-sex marriage has been recognized since October 21, 2014 after state officials declined to appeal the October 17 federal decision in Guzzo v Mead finding the ban unconstitutional, replacing a statutory ban in place since 1977 and made more explicit in 2003, under which legal relationships of same-sex couples had been recognized only for divorce. A 2013 domestic partnership bill to provide immediate-family rights was approved 7-2 in House committee on January 28 but rejected 24-35 by the full House on January 30. Married same-sex couples are permitted to adopt and lesbian couples can access in vitro fertilization, with state law recognizing the non-genetic, non-gestational mother as legal parent after donor insemination irrespective of marital status. State law does not authorize or prohibit gestational surrogacy contracts leaving review case-by-case, and an August 2021 law explicitly legalizing surrogacy contracts uses the terms mother and father instead of parent or parents to exclude single people and same-sex couples. State statutes do not address discrimination based on sexual orientation, with prohibitory bills rejected by the House on January 31, 2011 and by the Senate 15-13 on January 31, 2013, and bill SF 115 approved 24-6 by the Senate and 6-2 in House committee in February 2015 but rejected 26-33 by the House on February 24, 2015. Jackson, Casper and Laramie have ordinances prohibiting discrimination covering sexual orientation in employment, housing and public accommodations, while Cheyenne and Gillette prohibit city employment discrimination on sexual orientation only, and federal Bostock protections apply to sexual orientation in the workplace. Wyoming has no state hate crime law following hot debate after the 1998 murder of Matthew Shepard near Laramie, but the federal 2009 Act covers sexual orientation, and a state obscenity-material law affecting certain LGBT books was enforced in October 2021 when a Gillette librarian was charged by the district attorney and sheriff office.

66186276B64762166704956.summary:
West Virginia's controlling statute on sex and facilities is Senate Bill 456, the Riley Gaines Act, signed by Governor Patrick Morrisey on 12 March 2025 after passing the state Senate on 3 March and the House of Delegates on 6 March. It defines "woman" as an adult human of the female sex and "man" as an adult human of the male sex, and the law recognises no category beyond male and female; language requiring genital examination was struck before signing. At the ceremony the Governor said bathrooms, locker rooms, domestic violence shelters and rape crisis centres "should be kept private for women only."

The statute's stated reach covers locker rooms, bathrooms, rape crisis centres, dormitories and prisons, so exposure runs from a rest stop restroom to any shelter or correctional setting a visitor might enter. West Virginia's facility restrictions are catalogued in the Movement Advancement Project's equality map of state bans on transgender people's use of public bathrooms and facilities according to their gender identity.

An independent anti-trans legal risk assessment published 27 August 2026 places West Virginia in its "Worst States" group, one tier below the four states it rates "Do Not Travel," within a national frame it describes as "Worst Policies In Effect."

State identity documents remain changeable but the route is narrow. A gender marker on a West Virginia birth certificate requires a Birth Certificate Request Form with a court order for gender change and fees paid to Vital Registration; a driver's licence or state ID requires a Gender Designation Form signed by a licensed physician, with no surgery or sterilisation required. In July 2020 the West Virginia Supreme Court upheld a circuit court's refusal to allow a marker change even after reassignment surgery, so a court order does not guarantee approval.

House Bill 3293, passed in March 2021 and effective 1 July 2021, restricts transgender athletes from teams aligned with their gender identity by defining male and female solely on reproductive biology and genetics at birth. The Fourth Circuit held the ban unconstitutional in West Virginia v. B.P.J. in April 2024, and in July 2025 the Supreme Court agreed to hear the case, leaving the operative position unsettled.

Gender-affirming care for minors is restricted by a March 2023 law effective 1 January 2024 banning puberty blockers, hormone therapy and surgery except for severe dysphoria diagnosed by at least two physicians. For adults, a 1997 Medicaid ban on sexual reassignment surgery was ruled unconstitutional in August 2022 and coverage was required, but the Fourth Circuit overturned that ruling in 2026, holding that refusing funding is not irrational; Anderson v. Crouch, challenging the adult Medicaid exclusion, was argued on 9 December 2025 and remains unresolved.

An April 2025 bill passed both houses and awaited gubernatorial action that would require teachers and principals to immediately out transgender, non-binary and intersex students to parents and guardians.

West Virginia statutes provide no discrimination protection on gender identity, and the only statewide employment protection comes from Bostock v. Clayton County under federal Title VII. Fifteen cities bar gender-identity discrimination in employment, housing and public accommodations, with further protections for county and city employees in Kanawha County, Buckhannon and Elkins. House Bill 3042, passed 27 and 28 February 2023, is a Religious Freedom Restoration Act letting a person or corporation claim that a state or local law or government policy burdens religious belief and claim exemption from compliance, which permits denial of business service, housing and government service on grounds of gender identity, and it carries qualified immunity. On 26 March 2025 the state Senate approved by 25 to 8 a bill to nullify all city and county LGBTQ anti-discrimination ordinances, which awaited a House vote.

Marriage for couples the state would class as same-sex has been recognised since 9 October 2014, when Attorney General Patrick Morrisey ceased defending the ban and Governor Earl Ray Tomblin directed agencies to comply with federal rulings, despite a statute defining marriage as between a man and a woman that was never repealed.

66186276B86295910312663.summary:
Arkansas stands under the United States national framework on travel documents, and adds its own state-level restrictions. A bathroom bill became law on 11 April 2023 as Act 619, making Arkansas the fourth state to restrict transgender students' use of school bathrooms matching their gender identity; the law was amended and extended in 2025, and the Movement Advancement Project's equality-map citations record HB 1156 as a 2023 K-12 facility ban extended in 2025. Act 619 of 11 April 2023 separately creates a misdemeanour for transgender use of public bathrooms, locker rooms or changing facilities where a minor is present, dependent on intent of arousing or gratifying sexual desire.

Erin In The Morning's Anti-Trans National Legal Risk Assessment Map of July 2026 places Arkansas in 'The Worst States' group, one tier below the 'Do Not Travel' designation given to Florida, Idaho, Kansas and Texas. The grading reflects the state's own body of anti-trans law rather than any federal measure.

Arkansas was the first state, in 2021, to ban gender-affirming healthcare for trans minors, after the legislature overrode the governor's veto. HB 1570, banning puberty blockers, hormone therapy and surgery for under-18s, was vetoed on 5 April 2021 as overbroad and extreme but overridden on 6 April 2021; it was blocked and then struck down on 20 June 2023 by Judge James M. Moody Jr. for discrimination and constitutional violations, before the Eighth Circuit overturned that ruling on 12 August 2025 and allowed enforcement, citing United States v. Skrmetti. Litigation over the 2021 care ban continues, and a federal judge enjoined it for 'irreparable harm' to minors while litigation was ongoing.

Identity documents at state level have narrowed. Arkansas has permitted transgender people to amend birth certificates since 1981, when Senate Bill 256, the Arkansas Vital Statistics Act, passed 34-0 in the Senate and 92-0 in the House on 19 February 1981, codifying a surgery-based pathway requiring court order verifying sex reassignment surgery and a name change. Identity documents with an X sex descriptor were available from December 2010, but in March 2024 the Department of Finance and Administration rescinded X descriptors for driver's licences.

Arkansas law does not address discrimination based on gender identity, leaving protection only through the 2020 Bostock v. Clayton County nationwide ban. Little Rock, Conway, Hot Springs, North Little Rock and Pulaski County bar gender-identity discrimination in public employment, while the comprehensive ordinances in Eureka Springs and Fayetteville are unenforced under the Intrastate Commerce Improvement Act; the Arkansas Supreme Court struck down Fayetteville's ordinance in February 2017.

Arkansas has no hate-crime penalty-enhancement statute, and its civil remedy for intimidation, harassment, violence or property damage covers only racial, religious or ethnic animosity, not gender identity. The April 2021 state hate-crimes law, signed effective immediately, excludes sexual orientation or gender identity explicitly or implicitly. Federal law has covered gender identity since October 2009 under the Matthew Shepard and James Byrd, Jr. Act.

SB 289, signed 26 March by Governor Asa Hutchinson and effective immediately, allows medical practitioners to cite religious beliefs to deny healthcare to LGBT patients. In March 2021 the Legislature passed a ban on transgender athletes in sports, signed 25 March and effective immediately; ESPN records it as enacted 25 March 2021, prohibiting transgender women and girls from competing on school sports teams consistent with their gender identity across K-12 and collegiate sports, and allowing a student or school claiming harm to sue a school for violation.

In March 2023 the Legislature passed a gender-affirming litigation bill, signed 13 March 2023 by Governor Sarah Huckabee Sanders, allowing those who received such care as minors to sue providers 15 years after turning 18, versus two years for other care. On 21 March 2023 a law prohibiting trans people from using public school bathrooms matching gender was signed, making Arkansas the fourth such state.

66186276B76680759932915.name: Ohio
66186276B76680759932915.summary:
Ohio is a state within the United States; federal law and the federal document regime apply here and are carried at national level. What follows covers Ohio's own statutes, courts and agencies.

Erin In The Morning's Anti-Trans National Legal Risk Assessment Map of July 2026 places Ohio in "The Worst States," a group of sixteen states forming the second-highest tier beneath the four states graded "Do Not Travel," under the map's national frame of "Worst Policies In Effect."

Ohio's facility law, Senate Bill 104, the "Protect All Students Act," was signed by Governor Mike DeWine on 27 November 2024 and took effect 25 February 2025. It requires every K-12 school and every college and university, public and private, to designate bathrooms, locker rooms, changing and shower rooms and overnight accommodations for the exclusive use of males or females on the basis of sex assigned at or near birth, and requires students to use the facilities matching their birth certificate. Single-occupancy restrooms with controlled use are exempt. The bill was signed out of public view over the objections of Democrats, teachers' unions and civil rights groups; its sponsor was Republican state Senator Jerry Cirino. The statute contains no enforcement mechanism.

State identity documents are being narrowed. Amendment of the gender marker on an Ohio birth certificate was barred under the 1987 precedent In re Ladrach, challenged by four transgender Ohioans in March 2018 and invalidated as unconstitutional by federal Judge Michael H. Watson in Ray v. McCloud in December 2020; corrections have been officially permitted since 1 June 2021, although some counties continue to refuse them. Transgender people can change name and gender on Ohio driver's licences by court order together with a Declaration of Gender Change signed by a physician, nurse practitioner, social worker, therapist or psychologist, and an X marker has been available since April 2022. In August 2026 the Bureau of Motor Vehicles announced rules allowing only male or female markers and requiring an exact-matching birth certificate or passport.

Care and sport are governed by HB68, the Saving Adolescents from Experimentation Act, which bans puberty blockers, hormones and surgery for under-18s and bars transgender girls and women from women's high-school and college sports. It passed on 13 December 2023, was vetoed by Governor DeWine on 29 December 2023, and was enacted by House override on 10 January 2024 and Senate override on 24 January 2024. A court blocked it in April 2024, allowed it to take effect in August 2024 after finding the regulation of transgender individuals a legitimate state interest, and the Ohio 10th District Court of Appeals re-enjoined it on 18 March 2025, with Attorney General Dave Yost vowing to appeal. The operative position on any given provision should be checked before relying on it.

Protection is patchy. Ohio statutes do not address discrimination on account of gender identity, but gender-identity discrimination in state employment has been barred by executive order since 19 December 2018, and the Sixth Circuit held on 7 March 2018 that discrimination on the basis of transgender status is sex discrimination under Title VII. Thirty-three Ohio cities and counties have ordinances barring gender-identity discrimination in employment, housing and public accommodations.

sources.title: LGBTQ rights in Iowa (Wikipedia)
sources.summary: Since 2007 Iowa prohibited discrimination based on gender identity in employment, housing and public accommodations, but in February 2025 the Legislature passed a veto-proof bill removing gender identity from anti-discrimination laws, signed by Governor Kim Reynolds and effective July 1, making Iowa the first state to remove anti-discrimination protections for any class and the first to take a protected group away from civil rights protections. In 2025 Iowa stripped nondiscrimination protections from trans people and in 2026 passed a bill banning localities from maintaining civil rights protections stronger or broader than the state government, after several cities passed their own protections. As of July 1, 2025 under Senate File 418 transgender people may not alter legal gender on government IDs or documents or be legally recognized differently from assigned sex, stripping 2007 gender-transition language and imposing an unchangeable binary legal definition of sex determined at birth based on gametes expected to be produced later in life. Iowa hate-crime law provides penalty enhancements for crimes based on sexual orientation but not gender identity; a March 8, 2016 Senate bill to add gender identity passed 27-21 but died in the Republican-controlled House, though federal law has covered gender identity since October 2009. In March 2019 the Iowa Supreme Court required Medicaid coverage of sex reassignment surgery, but the General Assembly passed and Reynolds signed a ban on state funding a month later, a Polk County District Court ruled that ban unconstitutional in November 2021, and in June 2025 Reynolds signed another law banning Medicaid coverage for transgender surgeries and hormone treatments effective July 1, 2025. In March 2022 Iowa limited women's sports to cisgender females based on sex at birth, effectively barring transgender girls and women at all accredited public or private educational institutions including colleges and universities effective July 1, 2022, with civil lawsuit cause for any direct or indirect harm from violation. In March 2023 Senate File 538 banned provision of any gender-affirming healthcare to transgender minors effective immediately with 180-day wind-down for existing patients, and a separate March 2023 bill required written parental permission for students to use a single-person restroom at school. In May 2023 Iowa banned sexual orientation and gender identity lessons in Kindergarten through grade 6 classrooms, and only Davenport has banned conversion therapy on minors by 8-2 council vote April 22, 2020 after statewide Senate and medical and psychology board efforts failed. Iowa Territory adopted Wisconsin anti-sodomy law in 1838 punishable by up to three years, omitted sodomy in its 1843 code making it legal as noted in 1860 Estes v. Carter, re-criminalized sodomy in 1892 with one to ten years for heterosexual or homosexual consensual activity with first conviction in 1900 State v. Todd and fellatio criminalized in 1902, limited prosecution of heterosexual sodomy in a divided 5-4 1976 Supreme Court ruling requiring compelling state interest for private consensual adult opposite-sex conduct, and repealed same-sex criminalization in a 1978 comprehensive code with no mention of sodomy and age of consent 16 regardless of gender and sexual orientation. Iowa provided benefits to same-sex partners of state employees since 2003, recognized same-sex marriages since April 3, 2009 after unanimous Iowa Supreme Court affirmance in Varnum v. Brien, issued licenses from April 27, 2009 as fourth U.S. state to legalize same-sex marriage, defeated constitutional amendment and convention attempts to ban it, and removed three participating justices in November 2010 retention elections while retaining a fourth in November 2012. Joint adoption by married same-sex couples has been legal since a 2008 Supreme Court ruling with individuals and married couples allowed to adopt regardless of sexual orientation, state courts ordered listing of married lesbian non-birthing mothers on death certificates in December 12, 2012 Buntemeyer v. Iowa DPH and on birth certificates in Gartner v. Newton unanimously affirmed May 3, 2013 to ensure support and fundamental legal rights at birth, lesbian couples have IVF access with non-genetic, non-gestational mother recognized if married, and courts are generally favorable to gestational or traditional surrogacy despite no defined surrogacy laws. Since 2007 Iowa has outlawed discrimination based on sexual orientation in employment, housing and public accommodations with Des Moines protected since 1991, and hate-crime law provides penalty enhancements for crimes based on sexual orientation. On March 17, 2015 the Senate voted 26-24 to ban sexual orientation change efforts on LGBT minors but the bill died in the Republican-controlled House, the Board of Medicine and Board of Psychology declined in 2016 to ban conversion therapy by rule, and Davenport became the first city to ban conversion therapy on minors by 8-2 vote April 22, 2020. In March 2020 the House unanimously passed 95-0 a bill to abolish the gay panic defence twice, but the Republican-controlled Senate twice refused to take it up.

sources.title: Iowa Supreme Court March 2019 Medicaid ruling and legislative reversal
sources.summary: In March 2019 the Iowa Supreme Court ruled Iowa Medicaid cannot deny coverage for medically necessary gender confirmation surgery for transgender recipients under the Iowa Civil Rights Act and in late April 2019 the Iowa House and Senate passed a health and human services appropriations bill containing the Costello amendment allowing state and local government units to refuse taxpayer and Medicaid funds for sex reassignment surgery and any other cosmetic reconstructive or plastic surgery procedure related to transsexualism, hermaphroditism, gender identity disorder, or body dysmorphic disorder to overturn that ruling with the bill sent to Governor Kim Reynolds to sign or line-item veto.

sources.title: Iowa hate crime law and March 8, 2016 Senate bill
sources.summary: On March 8, 2016 the Iowa Senate voted 27-21 to pass a bill adding gender identity and gender expression to Iowa's hate crimes law to provide legal protection from hate crimes for transgender people, advancing the bill to the Iowa House of Representatives.

sources.title: LGBTQ rights in South Carolina (Wikipedia)
sources.summary: Changing legal gender on the birth certificate does not require sex reassignment surgery. State anti-discrimination law contains no explicit prohibition of discrimination on the basis of gender identity, but 2020 federal workplace protections against LGBT discrimination apply in South Carolina, with additional local employment protections for gender identity in Mount Pleasant, Myrtle Beach and Richland County and for city employees only in Columbia, Charleston and Latta. South Carolina has no state hate crime law, while hate crimes motivated by gender identity are prohibited federally under the Matthew Shepard and James Byrd Jr. Hate Crimes Prevention Act. In April 2016 Governor Nikki Haley said she opposed a transgender bathroom-restriction bill introduced in the Legislature and viewed it as "unnecessary". On May 17, 2022 the governor signed a transgender sports ban. In May 2024 legislation signed into law and effective immediately banned gender-affirming healthcare for individuals under 18 and banned federal funding going directly or indirectly toward gender-affirming care for adults, after which providers including the Medical University of South Carolina stopped providing such care regardless of age. The 2024-25 and 2025-26 budget appropriations bills require students to use bathrooms based on sex "at the time of birth", though on September 10, 2025 the U.S. Supreme Court allowed trans student plaintiff John Doe to continue using the boys' bathroom while his challenge proceeds, with all other trans students required to follow state law. Same-sex sexual activity is legal under the 2003 U.S. Supreme Court decision in Lawrence v. Texas, which invalidated South Carolina's sodomy law making "buggery" a felony punishable by five years in prison or a $500 fine, though the legislature has not repealed it. Voters adopted a November 2006 constitutional amendment defining marriage as the union of a man and a woman, which was overturned in Condon v. Haley on November 12, 2014, with stay denials by the Fourth Circuit on November 18 and by the U.S. Supreme Court on November 20, the first same-sex marriage on November 19, 2014 and general recognition and performance from the next day. South Carolina permits adoption by individuals with no explicit prohibition on adoption by same-sex couples or on stepchild adoptions, and since a February 15, 2017 federal order the state must list both same-sex parents on children's birth certificates without the adoption or Family Court order previously required only of same-sex couples. No state anti-discrimination provision explicitly covers sexual orientation, though 2020 federal workplace protections apply, supplemented by local employment protections in Mount Pleasant, Myrtle Beach and Richland County and for city employees in Columbia, Charleston and Latta. South Carolina is the only state not to include same-sex couples in domestic violence statutes, which explicitly cover only opposite-sex couples, and it has no state hate crime law, though crimes motivated by sexual orientation are covered federally under the Matthew Shepard and James Byrd Jr. Hate Crimes Prevention Act. In March 2020 a federal judge declared unconstitutional the 1988 law "banning homosexual or gay topics within school classrooms".

66186276B65591139260314.summary:
Florida stands under the United States national framework and adds a state layer that a trans visitor meets directly on the ground, most sharply in public facilities. Under the Facility Requirements Based on Sex Act (Fla. Stat. 553.865), in force since 1 July 2023, a trans person may not use a restroom or changing facility consistent with their gender identity in buildings owned or leased by state or local government: state offices, courthouses, legislative offices, prisons and jails, local immigration detention facilities, state parks, toll-road plazas, state schools and state universities. Refusing to leave when an authority figure orders departure can be charged as criminal trespass. The statute purports to cover all schools, public and private.

Private businesses fall outside the law's scope, so exposure concentrates in government and education settings rather than in shops, hotels and restaurants. ACLU Florida advises that each situation requires fact-specific judgement and legal counsel, reflecting that the statute has never been substantively tested.

Arrest risk is documented rather than theoretical. On 19 March 2025 Marcy Rheintgen, a 20-year-old trans college student, was arrested at the Florida State Capitol after police, alerted in advance, detained her washing her hands in a women's restroom; she had declared an intention to break the law. She was charged with misdemeanour trespass carrying up to 60 days in jail, in what was believed to be the first arrest under Florida's transgender bathroom restrictions. On 20 June 2025 Leon County Judge Lashawn Riggans threw the case out, holding that as a defendant charged under the act she had no standing to argue the law itself was illegitimate.

Enforcement machinery inside the education system is already built. On 23 August 2023 the State Board of Education approved firing employees of 28 public community and state colleges who enter a prohibited restroom, and on 18 October 2023 it voted to apply a comparable restriction to private college and university buildings including student housing, with compliance proof required by 1 April 2024.

Identity documents are closed at state level. Since January 2024 the Department of Highway Safety and Motor Vehicles has refused to issue any driver's licence bearing a gender marker different from sex assigned at birth, and treats holders, users or applicants as criminally guilty of fraud, with suspension and revocation of the licence. Since July 2024 transgender people born in Florida have been unable to update or change sex on birth certificates despite explicit legislation permitting it. Before that closure, an amended birth certificate required an application, a notarised affidavit and a physician letter confirming appropriate clinical treatment, without surgery or sterilisation being required.

Adult medical access carries Florida-specific barriers. The state medical board imposed a 24-hour waiting period for adults before sexual reassignment surgery on 31 October 2022, and Senate Bill 254 restricted gender-affirming care to physicians, barring nurse practitioners and physician assistants; the Human Rights Campaign estimates this disrupted care for more than 80 percent of transgender clinic patients, with temporary or permanent suspensions after signing. Insurance coverage for such treatment is banned and a physician rather than a nurse practitioner must administer it.

State statutes do not address gender identity discrimination in employment, housing or public accommodations. Nursing home and hospital protections in force since 2000 and amended in 2007 cover sexual orientation but not gender identity, and the state hate-crime law provides harsher penalties based on sexual orientation but not gender identity. Counties and cities comprising about 55 percent of the population do prohibit discrimination on gender identity in private and public employment, housing and public accommodations, and since February 2021 the Florida Commission on Human Relations has enforced Bostock v. Clayton County (2020) across employment, housing and public accommodations.

Equality Florida took the unprecedented step on 12 April 2023 of issuing a travel advisory warning of risks to the health, safety and freedom of those considering short or long-term travel or relocation to Florida, citing laws hostile to LGBTQ people alongside reproductive-health restrictions, gun-safety rollbacks and book bans; the Human Rights Campaign joined the advisory in May 2023. Equality Florida reports events and conferences cancelling in response.

The advisory followed a wave of visitor safety inquiries; EQFL reports events and conferences cancelling and notes the US military considering redeployment for service members' families.

sources.title: LGBTQ rights in Florida (Wikipedia)
sources.summary: Since 2021 the state has seen significant erosion especially in transgender rights: on June 1, 2021 a law excluded transgender girls and women defined as students of the male sex based on sex assigned at birth from female school sports, in early 2023 the Florida High School Athletics Association recommended female athletes supply menstrual cycle information to a school-accessible database speculated to enforce abortion restrictions and detect trans women, and the Attorney General threatened competitions including an Irish step dancing competition and Miss America for allowing transgender competitors as deceptive and depriving women of fair competition. Since July 1, 2023 under the Facility Requirements Based on Sex Act it is illegal for a trans person at any state school, state university, or government building e.g. beach or airport to use a bathroom or changing facility consistent with gender identity, requiring gender labels and internal disciplinary procedures where an authority figure may order departure and a non-member who does not depart can be charged with criminal trespass; on August 23 the Board of Education approved firing employees of 28 public community and state colleges who enter the forbidden bathroom, and on October 18, 2023 voted to apply similar restriction to private college and university buildings including student housing with compliance proof by April 1, 2024, after an August 2020 Eleventh Circuit ruling that Ponte Vedra Beach high school violated the law by refusing transgender student Andrew Adams consistent restroom use was reversed in January 2023 when the Eleventh Circuit sided with the district to uphold the ban, codified May 17, 2023. For identity documents, in January 2024 the Department of Highway Services and Motor Vehicles unilaterally banned issuing any driver's license with a gender marker different from assigned sex at birth, treating holders/users or applicants as criminally guilty of fraud with suspension and revocation, and in July 2024 transgender individuals born in Florida could not update or change sex on birth certificates despite explicit legislation permitting it; previously an amended birth certificate required an Application to Amend a Florida Birth Record, notarized Affidavit, physician letter confirming appropriate clinical treatment for gender transition without requiring surgery or sterilization, and after 2011 driver's license/ID changes required a court order for name and physician statement of appropriate clinical treatment, while in January 2022 the first sex-unknown birth certificate was reported. For healthcare, after August 2022 rule-change citing state guidance against gender-affirming care, on October 31, 2022 the Medical Board required a 24-hour waiting period for adults before sexual reassignment surgery and banned minors from gender-affirming healthcare approved November 4, 2022 and effective March 16, 2023, codified May 17, 2023 to prohibit hormone replacement therapy for transgender minors and create adult barriers including banning insurance coverage and requiring a physician rather than nurse practitioner to administer treatment; minors under 18 cannot receive puberty blockers, hormone therapy, or confirming surgeries unless intersex and a memo stated social transition should not be a treatment option, opposed by HHS, the Endocrine Society and other major medical organizations. On custody, May 17, 2023 Senate Bill 254 allows child custody modifications on the basis the child received or might receive gender-affirming care, and April 2023 legislation allowed modifying or nullifying out-of-state parental custody agreements if the child is allowed or threatened with access, described by opponents as allowing kidnapping across state lines amid protests where trans children were detained and one arrested for disturbing the peace; three plaintiffs obtained a June 6 preliminary injunction limited to them, stayed August 26, 2024 by the 11th Circuit, before a federal judge in June 2024 permanently blocked provisions banning care for minors and adults. On discrimination and protection, statutes do not address gender identity discrimination in employment, housing or other areas and nursing home/hospital protections since 2000 amended 2007 cover sexual orientation but not gender identity, but counties and cities comprising about 55 percent of population prohibit private and public employment, housing and public accommodations discrimination on sexual orientation and gender identity, the February 2021 Commission on Human Relations announced enforcement of Bostock v. Clayton County June 15, 2020 holding workplace discrimination on sexual orientation or gender identity is sex discrimination under Title VII to investigate employment, housing and public accommodations, and Glenn v. Brumby December 2011 held employment discrimination based on transgender status is sex discrimination, while hate-crime law provides harsher penalties based on sexual orientation but not gender identity. In May 2023 a medical practitioner law allows discrimination in doctors surgery, medicine and hospitals on conscience, religion or belief effective immediately by emergency clause criticized as preventing PrEP, gender-affirming care and abortion access, a May 2023 law bans adult live performances anywhere a minor might view under criminal penalty which DeSantis said was about drag shows but was preliminarily enjoined June 23 as not all drag is obscene, and on April 23, 2026 HB 1001/SB 1134 effective January 2027 prohibits state and local funding or promoting diversity, equity and inclusion defined to include gender identity with suits and removal of officials, interpreted as banning government support to LGBTQ organizations/events as in Palm Beach County denying a HUD grant to repair Compass headquarters air conditioning; in April 2023 Equality Florida issued a travel advisory to avoid visiting or moving to the state joined in May by the Human Rights Campaign citing DeSantis-signed legislation. Same-sex sexual activity became legal after Lawrence v. Texas June 26, 2003 striking all sodomy laws, though the 1868 felony crime against nature law punishable up to 20 years and 1917 misdemeanor unnatural and lascivious act law punishable by up to $500 or 6 months remained unenforced and unrepealed as of 2020, with the 1955 psychopathic offender law labeling sodomy convicts criminal sexual psychopathic persons for periodic examination repealed in 1979; in 2026 the legislature passed CS/CS/HB 1525 repealing §800.02, House 108-0 March 3, 2026 and Senate 38-0 March 10, 2026, signed June 16, 2026 effective October 1, 2026, and in October 2018 during a gay sex sting a judge ruled gay sex is not illegal in a public space so long as within a room. On enforcement, in September 2020 Hillsborough County arrested 11 men on misdemeanor non-sex charges after agreeing to consensual sex in a park and published names and mugshots, with critics accusing deliberate targeting of gay men and asking if a man and woman meeting similarly would have been arrested. Same-sex marriage has been legal since January 6, 2015 after Brenner v. Scott August 21, 2014 held Florida's ban violated the U.S. Constitution as marriage is a fundamental right under Fourteenth Amendment Due Process and Equal Protection subject to strict scrutiny, superseding the 1977 same-sex marriage ban law and November 2008 Amendment 2 adding Article I Section 27 banning same-sex marriage, civil unions and substantial equivalents; nine counties, thirty cities and one town offer domestic partnership benefits, and a 2016 repeal of the 1868 unmarried cohabitation ban passed House 112-5 and Senate 38-0, signed April 6, 2016 effective July 1, 2016. On protection, Bostock v. Clayton County June 15, 2020 outlawed workplace discrimination on sexual orientation as sex discrimination under Title VII, which the Florida Commission on Human Relations announced in February 2021 it will enforce for employment, housing and public accommodations, though statutes otherwise do not address sexual orientation discrimination; counties and cities comprising about 55 percent of population including Jacksonville, Miami, Tampa, Orlando, St. Petersburg, Tallahassee and West Palm Beach prohibit private and public employment, housing and public accommodations discrimination on sexual orientation, nursing homes and hospitals since 2000 amended 2007 cannot discriminate on sexual orientation, the Department of Agriculture added sexual orientation to workplace policy in January 2019, and hate-crime law provides harsher penalties for crimes based on sexual orientation. Conversion therapy is banned in a number of cities mainly in the Miami metropolitan area but has been struck down by the 11th Circuit Court of Appeals, in September 2023 Lake Worth Beach became an official LGBTQ sanctuary city to protect and defend LGBTQ rights, and in April 2023 Equality Florida issued a travel advisory to avoid visiting or moving to the state joined in May by the Human Rights Campaign citing recently signed legislation while stopping short of boycott.

66186276B65591139260314.outOfScopeNotes:
Whether the Facility Requirements Based on Sex Act would survive a merits challenge is unresolved: the only known prosecution was dismissed on standing grounds on 20 June 2025, so no court has ruled on the statute's constitutionality or its precise reach.

The scope of the statute across private schools is asserted by the law's text but has not been tested in the reported litigation, and ACLU Florida's guidance that each situation requires fact-specific judgement and counsel indicates the boundary between covered and uncovered locations is not settled in practice.

The claim that the Florida High School Athletics Association menstrual-cycle database was intended to detect trans women is reported as speculation rather than documented purpose; the recommendation itself is sourced, the motive is not.

The status of the Eleventh Circuit stay of the Senate Bill 254 custody injunction, entered 26 August 2024, and of the June 2024 permanent block on the care-ban provisions, is not resolved in the available sources; which provision governs at any given date should be confirmed.

Enforcement of HB 1001/SB 1134, effective January 2027, rests on an interpretation rather than on adjudicated cases; the Palm Beach County grant denial is reported as an application of that interpretation, not as a court ruling.

Estimates of the share of transgender clinic patients affected by the physicians-only requirement come from the Human Rights Campaign and are not independently corroborated in the inventory.

66186276B73402293045483.summary:
Nebraska's state-level framework for trans visitors is set by Executive Order No. 23-16, signed by Governor Jim Pillen on 30 August 2023. The order establishes a Women's Bill of Rights and defines sex, female, male, woman, girl, man, boy, mother and father for use by state agencies, stating that biological sex is determined at birth and that biological differences between males and females in athletic ability and safety warrant sex-based segregation in some athletic, social and educational spaces. The order backs single-sex spaces for women's sports, bathrooms and changing rooms. Pillen was the second U.S. governor to sign such an order. Opponents questioned the order's scope and legality.

State documents are correspondingly restrictive. A legal gender marker change on a Nebraska birth certificate requires a notarized affidavit from the physician who performed sex reassignment surgery together with a certified copy of a court order changing the applicant's name. A driver's licence or state ID change requires a court order certifying the change and/or a physician-signed form confirming sex reassignment surgery. A name change requires district court paperwork, a court date, and publication for four consecutive weeks, or two weeks for minors. These requirements apply to state-issued documents; a visitor holding an out-of-state or foreign passport is not directly governed by them, but a trans person resident in Nebraska or seeking Nebraska-issued identification faces them.

Participation rules for trans students in Nebraska athletics have tightened in stages. The Nebraska School Activities Association requires transgender students to show evidence of hormone replacement therapy and/or sex reassignment surgery. In June 2025 Legislative Bill 89, banning transgender athletes from any sports, passed the unicameral legislature by a two-thirds majority and was signed by Governor Pillen; ten transgender athletes were identified as affected.

Gender-affirming healthcare for people under 19 is barred in Nebraska. The legislature passed the ban 33-15 in May 2023 and Governor Pillen signed it effective immediately. The Nebraska Supreme Court upheld it 6-1 in July 2024. A trans visitor under 19 cannot obtain this care in the state, and a visitor of any age cannot obtain it for a minor in their care.

Custody is a documented site of harm specific to Nebraska. A transgender woman diagnosed with gender dysphoria and transitioning while held in Nebraska's men's prison sued prison officials and workers; on 10 August 2022 U.S. District Judge Brian C. Buescher ruled for the defendants, dismissing her claims of failure to treat her dysphoria, denial of gender-conforming surgery, and failure to protect her. Nebraska had housed her by assigned sex at birth among male prisoners and placed her in a cell with a convicted male sex offender who sexually assaulted her. The judge had earlier dismissed the failure-to-protect claim over that placement, wrote that without medical evidence no reasonable jury could conclude the providers were deliberately indifferent to her serious medical need, and said she had not plausibly alleged more than de minimis injuries from the assault. He found no support for inferring a substantial risk from a prospective cellmate's sexual-offence conviction coupled with the alleged vulnerability of a transgender inmate transitioning to a woman in a men's prison. The placement followed her within the system.

Protection machinery is uneven. Nebraska's 1997 hate crime law guarantees the right to live free from violence or intimidation by threat of violence and enhances sentences for manslaughter, assault, terroristic threats, stalking, kidnapping and false imprisonment, rape and sexual assault, arson, criminal mischief and trespassing. It does not address gender identity. Federal law has covered gender identity under the Matthew Shepard and James Byrd Jr. Hate Crimes Prevention Act since 2009. The state Supreme Court upheld the hate crime law in April 2016, in a case protecting even a straight victim in the company of gay friends.

Discrimination protection for trans people in Nebraska rests on federal rulings and municipal ordinances rather than statewide statute. Employment discrimination on the basis of gender identity became illegal under Bostock v. Clayton County, decided 15 June 2020. In August 2020 the Nebraska Equal Opportunity Commission announced it would investigate and resolve housing discrimination claims on account of sexual orientation or gender identity, applying the same ruling to housing. Federal enforcement followed: from 11 February 2021 the Fair Housing Act prohibition on discrimination because of sex was enforced to include sexual orientation and gender identity, with HUD accepting, investigating and enforcing complaints of anti-trans housing discrimination covering sale, rental, terms, conditions and services. Omaha has prohibited discrimination on the basis of gender identity in employment and public accommodations in both the public and private sectors since 2012, when the City Council voted 4-3 on 13 March to amend the city's anti-discrimination laws to add sexual orientation and gender identity as protected classes, with an exemption for religious institutions. Lincoln passed a 5-0 ordinance in February 2022 covering employment, accommodation and housing, but the protections were removed in June 2022 after a petition drive. In November 2021 the Nebraska State College System voted 4-2 to include gender identity in its policy.

Conversion therapy aimed at changing gender identity is outlawed in Lincoln under a 2021 ordinance and remains lawful in the rest of Nebraska. Statewide ban bills were reintroduced in 2021 and 2025 but have not passed.

Marriage and family recognition are settled in Nebraska as a matter of federal law. Same-sex marriage has been legal since Obergefell v. Hodges on 26 June 2015, with then Attorney General Doug Peterson directing compliance and non-enforcement of contrary Nebraska laws. That replaced a constitutional ban adopted in November 2000 by 70 per cent to 30 per cent defining marriage as the union of a man and a woman. A trans visitor in what would be locally classed as a same-sex relationship can marry and have that marriage recognised. Nebraska permits adoption by same-sex couples and single LGBT individuals: the Lancaster County District Court ruled for the plaintiffs in Stewart v. Heineman on 5 August 2015, the Nebraska Supreme Court upheld that ruling in April 2017 striking down the ban on same-sex foster parents, and in March 2021 it held that state adoption law clearly allows a same-sex married couple to adopt.

Sodomy prohibitions in Nebraska were repealed by a revised criminal code enacted in June 1977, effective 1 July 1978, by a veto override of 32-15 against Governor J. James Exon.

The practical weight of Nebraska's state measures depends on how long a visitor stays and what they need from state institutions. A short-stay visitor using only federal documents and private accommodation encounters the state framework mainly through facilities practice and the absence of a statewide gender-identity discrimination statute. A trans person resident in Nebraska, or a visitor needing Nebraska-issued identification or care, meets the marker requirements, the under-19 care ban and the athletics rules directly.

A trans visitor in a relationship that Nebraska authorities would read as same-sex under birth-sex status has full marriage and adoption recognition, so the usual concern about partner recognition in hostile jurisdictions does not arise here. The exposure lies elsewhere: in facilities, in custody if arrested and held in state or county detention, and in the absence of a statewide hate-crime or anti-discrimination provision naming gender identity.

Enforcement of the 1997 hate crime law is documented in a case the state Supreme Court decided in April 2016 protecting a straight victim in the company of gay friends, which indicates the statute is applied to perceived-association bias, but nothing in the state's own law extends that to gender identity. Federal protection under the Matthew Shepard and James Byrd Jr. Hate Crimes Prevention Act covers gender identity, so a bias-motivated offence against a trans person can be charged federally even where state law is silent.

66186276B22971435435932.summary:
Senate Bill 150, enacted on 29 March 2023 after the General Assembly overrode Governor Andy Beshear's veto, carries Kentucky's restriction on which bathrooms transgender students may use in public schools alongside its ban on gender-affirming medical care for transgender minors. It is the single 2023 statute containing the K-12 facility restriction, and the Movement Advancement Project's equality map lists it among state-level bans on transgender people using public facilities according to gender identity. The facility provision is written for public school students; the sources reviewed identify no statewide rule governing adult use of bathrooms or other sex-segregated facilities.

Responsibility for carrying out the school restriction sits with local districts. The Kentucky Department of Education issued guidance in April 2023 for districts implementing the state's 2023 rules, advising them to remove sex education from the fifth-grade curriculum and to proceed cautiously with the bathroom provisions.

The care ban took effect on 14 July 2023, when U.S. District Judge David Hale lifted the injunction he had issued the previous month, barring transgender minors from puberty blockers and hormone therapy. Seven transgender children and their parents had sued to block the law, and the ACLU of Kentucky described the ruling as a temporary setback. On 28 September 2023 a federal appeals panel allowed the ban to remain in force while challenges proceed. Minors already receiving care were given no phase-out.

Birth certificates can be amended only for post-operative applicants: a doctor's letter stating that gender-affirming surgery has been performed goes directly to the Department of Vital Statistics in Frankfort. A court order was previously required for a Kentucky-born person.

School sport is closed to transgender girls under Senate Bill 83, which passed the General Assembly in March 2022, was vetoed by Governor Beshear in April 2022 on constitutionality and vagueness grounds, and was enacted over that veto the same month with immediate effect. House Bill 470, carrying the minors' care ban among other provisions, advanced on 2 March 2023 and passed on 17 March 2023, was vetoed, and was overridden on 29 March 2023 by simple majority votes; police arrested 19 capitol protesters for criminal trespassing that day.

Employment protection derives from federal appellate and executive sources rather than from statute. On 7 March 2018 the U.S. Court of Appeals for the Sixth Circuit, which covers Kentucky, held in EEOC v. R.G. & G.R. Harris Funeral Homes that Title VII of the Civil Rights Act of 1964 bars firing an employee for being transgender or for transitioning, because it penalises failure to conform to birth-assigned sex stereotypes, and that the Religious Freedom Restoration Act does not permit a private employer to dismiss a transgender worker on religious grounds. The case arose from funeral director Aimee Stephens, dismissed in 2013 after disclosing her planned transition. A June 2008 executive order barred hiring or firing state employees on the basis of sexual orientation or gender identity, restoring protections first issued in 2003 and removed in 2006. Nineteen cities maintain Fairness Ordinances covering gender identity in employment, housing and public accommodations.

Kentucky's hate-crime statutes cover sexual orientation and expressly exclude gender identity, so bias-motivated violence against a transgender person falls outside the state's hate-crime enhancement. The sexual-orientation provision was used in the April 2011 beating of Kevin Pennington at Kingdom Come State Park near Cumberland, which produced arrests on 15 March 2012 by Kentucky State Police working with the FBI and guilty pleas from two defendants after advocacy by the Kentucky Equality Federation.

Conversion therapy on minors has been illegal statewide since Governor Beshear's executive order of 18 September 2024, following city bans in Covington (March 2020, 5-0), Louisville (September 2020, 24-1) and Lexington (May 2021, unanimous).

Consensual same-sex sexual activity has been lawful since the Kentucky Supreme Court struck down KRS 510.100 in Kentucky v. Wasson in 1992 on state constitutional grounds, a result reinforced by Lawrence v. Texas in 2003. The unenforceable statute remains on the books; it formerly punished specified sexual acts as a misdemeanour carrying up to 12 months in jail and a $500 fine, with solicitation punishable by up to 90 days and $250.

Religious-exemption and service-access rules cut against those protections. The 2013 Religious Freedom Act requires the state to show clear and convincing evidence before burdening a sincerely held religious belief; Governor Beshear vetoed it over vagueness and the risk of overriding local non-discrimination ordinances, and the General Assembly overrode him 79-15 in the House and 32-6 in the Senate. Senate Bill 17, signed by Governor Matt Bevin in March 2017, allows religious student organisations use of school facilities and control of their internal affairs. In August 2020 a district court held that a Christian photographer, as a public business, could not be compelled to photograph same-sex weddings because the photographs are art and speech protected against compulsion.

66186276B6801956407400.name: North Carolina
66186276B6801956407400.summary:
North Carolina stands under the United States framework, and national rules on passports, entry screening, federal custody and federal health funding apply in the state as they do elsewhere in the country. The state layer is where the facility, identification, care and bias-crime questions are decided.

Facility rules are the subject of live legislative conflict rather than settled prohibition. House Bill 2, passed in an emergency 2016 session after the Charlotte city council allowed transgender people to use facilities matching their gender identity, required public bathroom use according to the sex listed on a birth certificate and barred cities from enacting anti-discrimination ordinances covering gay and transgender people. The birth-certificate bathroom provision was repealed by the General Assembly on 30 March 2017, and no state statute now bars a trans person from using the facility matching their gender identity, nor criminalises facility use. Republican legislators revived a bathroom bill in the 2025 session, so the position remains open and could change within a legislative term.

Identification documents are narrowing. A federal ruling of 26 June 2022 removed the undefined sex-reassignment-surgery requirement from the state's birth-certificate amendment process after Lambda Legal's November 2021 suit. House Bill 805, enacted over veto on 29 July 2025 and effective 1 January 2026, recognises only male and female sexes and requires an amended certificate to keep displaying the sex originally assigned alongside any change, which means a corrected state document still carries the original marker.

Care for minors is closed. Three veto-overridden laws effective 16 August 2023 ended the prescription of puberty blockers and hormone therapy and the provision of gender-affirming surgery to people under 18, and House Bill 574 barred individuals assigned male at birth from female sports and athletic teams. House Bill 805 additionally bars state funds for gender-transition care for minors and for people in prison, so a trans visitor held in state custody would not obtain transition care at state expense. A trans athlete visiting or competing in the state falls under the sports restriction.

Recourse after violence is limited. The state hate-crime statute covers neither gender identity nor sexual orientation, so an assault on a trans visitor may not be charged as a bias crime under state law even where bias is evident.

Non-discrimination coverage outside public employment is municipal and county-level. A state prohibition on local ordinances covering gender identity expired on 1 December 2020; Charlotte and Wake County ordinances explicitly covering gender identity took effect 1 January 2022, and roughly 30 per cent of the state's population lives under a local ordinance covering sexual orientation and gender identity. A trans visitor therefore has no statewide protection in private employment, housing or public accommodations, and the answer depends on the particular city or county.

sources.title: LGBTQ rights in North Carolina (Wikipedia)
sources.summary: In March 2016 the Public Facilities Privacy & Security Act (HB2) barred local governments from enacting contrary hiring and bathroom-facility policies and required bathroom use according to gender listed on birth certificate, with the birth-certificate bathroom-use portion repealed by the legislature March 30, 2017. A prior state ban on local non-public-employment ordinances prohibiting discrimination based on gender identity expired December 1, 2020, and Charlotte (August 2021) and Wake County (October 2021) ordinances explicitly covering gender identity took effect January 1, 2022, with the article reporting about 30% of the state population covered by local sexual-orientation and gender-identity ordinances. For public employment, an April 12, 2016 executive order barred LGBT discrimination including gender identity and an October 2017 extension applied protection to state contractors, while the University of North Carolina system and most listed campuses maintain gender-identity non-discrimination policies for employment and students. On August 16, 2023 three veto-overridden laws took effect requiring educators to notify parents if a student requests a different name or pronouns, banning trans girls from team sports, and banning gender-affirming care for transgender minors, with House Bill 574 specifically banning individuals assigned male at birth from female sports and athletic teams. Since August 2023 minors cannot be prescribed puberty blockers or hormone therapy or receive gender-affirming surgery, and under HB 805 veto-overridden July 29, 2025, effective January 1, 2026 the state recognizes only male and female sexes and disallows state funds for gender transition care for minors and people in prison. On gender-marker documents, a June 26, 2022 federal ruling removed the undefined sex-reassignment-surgery requirement for North Carolina birth-certificate changes following a November 2021 Lambda Legal suit, but the July 29, 2025 HB 805 override requires amended certificates to continue displaying originally assigned sex alongside any change. Effective August 15, 2023 SB49 Parents' Bill of Rights bans K-4 instruction on gender identity, requires parental notification if a child requests a different name or pronoun in records or by personnel, and grants inspection and objection rights over instructional materials, while the state hate-crime statute does not cover gender identity. Private consensual same-sex sexual activity was decriminalized by Lawrence v. Texas (2003), but N.C. G.S. section 14-177 remains unrepealed and unenforceable for that conduct after State v. Whiteley (2005) upheld it facially only for minors, non-consensual or coercive conduct, public conduct, and prostitution. A prior state ban on local municipalities prohibiting sexual-orientation discrimination outside public employment expired December 1, 2020, while Durham and Guilford counties and Bessemer City, Durham, and High Point prohibit sexual-orientation discrimination in local public employment or discrimination and Charlotte and Wake County ordinances effective January 1, 2022 explicitly ban sexual-orientation discrimination. In public employment, the April 12, 2016 executive order and October 2017 extension bar sexual-orientation discrimination for state employees and contractors, with University of North Carolina campuses and the Housing Finance Agency maintaining sexual-orientation non-discrimination policies. The state hate-crime statute does not cover sexual orientation. In January 2021 a federal judge struck down North Carolina's exclusion of same-sex couples from domestic-violence protection, extending protections to them, and a 2008 Patients' Bill of Rights provision granted hospital visitation via designated visitor statute. In November 2021 a law banning sexual-orientation discrimination in foster-parenting placements was signed effective January 1, 2022, and on August 3, 2019 an executive order banned state funding of conversion therapy on minors.

66186276B80192890672447.name: Montana
66186276B80192890672447.summary:
Montana stands under the legal framework of the United States, and separately under a state constitution whose equal-protection and dignity guarantees have repeatedly defeated anti-trans legislation in its courts. Legislation that would otherwise place Montana among the most restrictive states has not taken full effect, and in the July 2026 anti-trans national risk assessment Montana is the only state whose standing improved, on the strength of that court record. Adult restrictions that were enacted remain unenforced pending litigation, while the youth-side picture stays unsettled through continuing federal policy shifts and court challenges.

Senate Bill 458, signed in May 2023, codified sex as an immutable male-female binary determined at birth and unchangeable. District Judge Leslie Halligan struck it down in February 2025 for violating the equal-protection clauses of the Montana Constitution, finding that it left a gap in sex-discrimination protection. Senate Bill 437, signed on 24 March 2026, re-enacted biological definitions of sex, gender, male, female, man, woman, mother and father keyed to primary sexual anatomy and reproductive system, and provides that gender means sex and not gender identity, experienced gender, expression or role. Those definitions reach more than 60 sections of state law, including driver's licences, marriage licences and anti-discrimination protections, and applicants for driver's and marriage licences must list sex as so defined. Representative Zooey Zephyr stated that the bill erases transgender, intersex and Two-Spirit recognition, and in April 2026 plaintiffs sought to add it to the ongoing litigation as fundamentally identical to SB 458.

Identity-document changes have been restricted and blocked in alternating waves. On 9 September 2022 Montana prohibited changing sex identification on birth certificates absent proof of a data-entry error or a DNA test; a court order on 15 September 2022 blocked the rule and the Department of Public Health and Human Services complied. A bill signed on 19 May 2023 prohibited gender-marker changes on all identity documents and was blocked by a December 2024 injunction from District Judge Mike Menahan. Following an April 2024 suit by two trans women unable to update their driver's licences and birth certificates, Judge Menahan issued a preliminary block on 16 December 2024 on sex-discrimination grounds, which the Montana Supreme Court upheld on 15 April 2026, holding that the constitution requires treating individuals with dignity.

A Helena district court reached the same position in December 2024, preliminarily enjoining enforcement of the 2022 health department rule barring gender-identity-based changes to birth-certificate sex, the Motor Vehicle Division policy requiring a birth certificate before a driver's-licence sex change, and portions of SB 458, on finding that the plaintiffs were likely to succeed on claims that the restrictions constitute sex discrimination violating the Montana Constitution's fundamental right to be free from sex discrimination. Enforcement is paused while that litigation continues. The prior sequence ran the other way: sex-reassignment surgery and clinical treatment were required until December 2017, when the surgery requirement was replaced by a correction affidavit, gender designation form, court order and doctor's letter for licences; an April 2021 law reintroducing surgical procedures and a court order, signed with immediate effect by Governor Greg Gianforte, was blocked in April 2022 for lack of clear legal definitions, after which the department imposed a temporary emergency rule in May 2022 banning updates and later made it permanent.

Facility use is governed by House Bill 121, passed in February 2025, which requires bathrooms, locker rooms and sleeping areas in publicly funded facilities to be segregated by biological sex assigned at birth. The ACLU of Montana sued immediately, and on 2 April 2025 District Judge Shane Vannatta temporarily restrained the law, ruling that it is motivated by animus and supported by no evidence that the restrictions advance women's safety and privacy. Two earlier attempts failed: a 2018 Montana Family Foundation initiative to require public bathroom use matching birth-certificate gender did not gather enough signatures for the ballot, and on 3 December 2024 the Montana House voted down a proposal to bar trans people from using Capitol bathrooms aligned with their gender.

Gender-affirming care for trans minors is not banned in Montana. Senate Bill 99, signed on 28 April 2023 and described as the most comprehensive such prohibition in the United States, was preliminarily enjoined on 27 September 2023 by District Judge Jason Marks, who held that discrimination against a person for being transgender is inherently sex discrimination under Bostock v. Clayton County and served no compelling governmental interest in protecting minors. The Montana Supreme Court kept the injunction in place on 11 December 2024 on privacy grounds, with Justice Laurie McKinnon adding that transgender status should be treated as a suspect class, and Judge Marks permanently struck the law down on 14 May 2025 for failure to establish a bona fide health risk clearly and convincingly or a change in the stance of major United States medical organizations.

A 2021 law barring transgender athletes from public school sports, contingent on continued federal education funding and signed the following month by Governor Gianforte, was struck down in September 2022 by District Judge Rienne McElyea as unconstitutional on administrative grounds for infringing the authority of the Regents of the Montana University System.

Protection against discrimination is split across layers. By executive order Montana prohibits gender-identity discrimination in state employment and by state contractors and subcontractors, a policy originating in 2000 personnel rules from Governor Marc Racicot, broadened in November 2008 by Governor Brian Schweitzer's Executive Order 41-2008 and extended to gender identity and contractors in January 2016 by Governor Steve Bullock. Federal Title VII protection for gender identity under Bostock v. Clayton County applies in Montana, and ordinances in Bozeman, Butte-Silver Bow County, Helena, Missoula and Whitefish prohibit gender-identity discrimination in public and private employment, housing and public accommodations, with Missoula County covering county employees only. Montana's hate-crime statutes do not include gender identity, so prosecution falls to federal courts under the Matthew Shepard and James Byrd Jr. Hate Crimes Prevention Act of October 2009. In April 2021 Governor Gianforte signed legislation granting a right to discriminate where religious beliefs are substantially burdened, widely viewed as a licence to discriminate against LGBTQ people.

Same-sex marriage has been recognised in Montana since 19 November 2014, when Judge Brian Morris enjoined the state ban effective immediately; the U.S. Supreme Court's decision in Obergefell v. Hodges on 26 June 2015 mooted the question, and the Montana Supreme Court recognised a common-law same-sex marriage as retroactively valid in Adami v. Nelson on 10 December 2019.

sources.summary: Montana has passed laws that would normally place it among the worst states, but state courts have repeatedly blocked or enjoined them under the state constitution. That court record improves Montana's standing in the July 2026 anti-trans national risk assessment.

sources.title: Montana House Bill 819 (May 2025) - government flag 'neutrality' law

66186276B13694661525286.name: Missouri
66186276B13694661525286.summary:
Missouri law makes state identity documents effectively unavailable to a transgender visitor who has not had surgery. Under Mo. Ann. Stat. § 193.215(9), changing the sex on a Missouri birth certificate requires a court order supported by certified proof on hospital letterhead, including the attending physician's licensing and contact information, stating that the petitioner's physical sex has been altered and the surgical changes are irreversible. The original certificate has the old name and gender struck through and the abstract marked amended. Two earlier cases, 13AR-CV00157 and 13AR-CV00240, which had allowed exceptions, were reversed in May 2022, leaving no route around the surgical requirement.

Driver's licences and state identification follow a separate and unstable path. Between 2016 and 2024 the Department of Revenue accepted Form 5532 to change the gender designation after a policy review; the department then reverted to requiring surgery documentation or a court order, a change the sources attribute to an unspecified incident.

Health care for minors is banned. The Save Adolescents from Experimentation (SAFE) Act, Senate Bill 49, took effect on 28 August 2023 and bars under-18s from starting hormones or puberty blockers, permits those already in treatment to continue, and prohibits all transition-related surgery for minors. The same law bars MO HealthNet, the state Medicaid programme, from paying for gender-affirming care for a patient of any age, and it restricts treatment access in prisons, jails and correctional centres. Providers who violate it can lose their Missouri medical licence and can be sued by patients up to 15 years after treatment. The ban carries a sunset of 28 August 2027.

The ban has survived every court test so far. A preliminary injunction was denied and the law took effect as scheduled; after a September 2024 trial in the 44th Judicial Circuit Court, Judge Robert Craig Carter upheld it as constitutional on 25 November 2024, and the Missouri Supreme Court unanimously affirmed on 13 January 2026, citing the 2025 U.S. Supreme Court ruling that upheld Tennessee's equivalent ban. The plaintiffs, represented by Lambda Legal and the ACLU of Missouri, said they would appeal. Lawmakers have introduced legislation to make the ban permanent, and a November 2026 ballot initiative seeks to ban the care indefinitely.

Adults are not covered by the minor ban, but the state has attempted to restrict adult care. In April 2023 the attorney general issued an emergency order declaring adult gender-affirming care experimental and requiring three years of documented intense dysphoria, at least 15 psychiatric sessions over 18 months with at least 10 with the same therapist, full treatment of comorbidities, autism screening, 15-year adverse-effect tracking, annual dysphoria assessment, screening for social contagion, written consent every three months for three years and then every six months, and detailed compliance records. A judge temporarily blocked the order and the attorney general withdrew it in May 2023, along with separate March and April 2023 emergency orders on youth care that had imposed social media addiction screening, consent and dysphoria assessment requirements.

Custody is a documented site of exposure. The SAFE Act restricts treatment access in prisons, jails and correctional centres, and an appropriations law signed by Governor Mike Kehoe, HB 2009, took effect on 2 July 2026, barring state funds from paying for cross-sex hormones or gender-transition surgery for transgender people in Missouri prisons, with no taper plan for inmates already receiving care.

The state operates a tipline for anonymous reporting of suspected violations and of complaints about a "gender transition intervention," which gives residents and staff a channel to report transgender people and their providers.

Statewide protections are thin. Missouri's non-discrimination legislation does not address gender identity, so there is no statewide protection in employment, housing or public accommodations; a 2010 executive order extends sexual orientation protections to state government employees only. The hate crime statute does explicitly cover gender identity, defined as "having a self-image or identity not traditionally associated with one's gender." Kansas City declared itself a sanctuary city for transgender individuals and rights in May 2023, and Columbia voted in February 2024 to add LGBT protections to its sanctuary ordinance.

Missouri recognises marriages between people of the same sex. Out-of-state marriages were recognised from November 2013 under an executive order on joint tax filing upheld in Barrier v. Vasterling on 3 October 2014; St. Louis city and county and Jackson County began licensing such marriages after State of Missouri v. Florida and Lawson v. Kelly in November 2014, and a July 2015 executive order directed state agencies to comply.

sources.summary: Missouri Gov. Mike Kehoe signed an appropriations law, effective July 2, 2026, barring state funds from paying for cross-sex hormones or gender-transition surgery for transgender people in Missouri prisons, with no taper plan for inmates already receiving care. sources.title: Missouri Supreme Court upholds ban on minor transgender care

66186276B62688952876525.summary:
Alaska falls in the Moderate-Risk group of Erin In The Morning's July 2026 legal-risk assessment, alongside Kentucky and North Carolina.
