sources.title: LGBTQ rights in Alaska (Wikipedia)
sources.summary: Alaska state law provides no protection against discrimination based on gender identity in employment, housing, or public accommodations, and the 2002 executive order covering state employment addresses sexual orientation only with no gender identity provision. Four municipalities — Anchorage, Juneau, Sitka and Ketchikan, covering about 46% of the state population — ban discrimination based on gender identity in public and private employment, public accommodations and housing, with Ketchikan's unanimous ordinance passed in July 2020 effective in mid-August, and Anchorage's September 2015 ordinance (9-2) retained after voters rejected Proposition 1 to strip protections from transgender individuals on April 3, 2018 by 53% to 47%. In Fairbanks, a February 2019 City Council ordinance banning discrimination on gender identity in employment, housing and public accommodations was vetoed by Mayor Jim Matherly. Under federal law, the June 15, 2020 U.S. Supreme Court ruling in Bostock v. Clayton County holds workplace discrimination on gender identity is sex discrimination prohibited by Title VII, and the October 2009 Matthew Shepard and James Byrd, Jr. Hate Crimes Prevention Act provides federal penalty enhancements for crimes motivated by actual or perceived gender identity prosecutable in federal court, while Alaska state hate-crime law does not cover gender identity. Transgender persons may obtain an amended birth certificate with corrected name and gender marker by submitting a Birth Certificate Request Form, ID photocopy, letter from a medical or mental health provider attesting appropriate clinical treatment for gender transition or certified copy of a court-ordered change of sex, plus fee, but the amended certificate retains the previous legal name at the bottom with notation it was originally issued under the former name and amended due to change of name. Changing the gender marker on a driver's license requires a letter from a licensed provider attesting clinical treatment or an already-updated birth certificate or court order for gender change. In September 2023 the Alaska Board of Education voted 7-1 to ban transgender individuals from participating in female sports and athletics statewide, while in August 2020 Anchorage voted 9-2 to ban conversion therapy on minors, the first such city ban in Alaska. Same-sex sexual conduct has been allowed since January 1, 1980 when Alaska repealed its sodomy law, which under the 1899 Alaska-specific statute had punished crime against nature with up to ten years in jail. Same-sex marriage has been legal since October 12, 2014 via the Hamby v. Parnell district court ruling declaring statutory and constitutional bans unconstitutional, with licenses accepted from October 13, 2014, following a 1996 statutory ban allowed to become law without Governor Tony Knowles' signature on May 6, 1996 and a constitutional amendment approved November 3, 1998. Alaska law does not address discrimination on the basis of sexual orientation in employment, housing, or public accommodations, except for a 2002 executive order prohibiting sexual orientation discrimination in state employment and a 1975 Human Rights Commission stance; a 2015 bill banning discrimination based on sexual orientation died without a vote. Anchorage, Juneau, Sitka and Ketchikan, representing about 46% of the population, ban sexual orientation discrimination in employment, housing and public accommodations; Anchorage first passed an ordinance 7-4 in 2009 vetoed by Mayor Dan Sullivan, voters rejected Proposition 5 in April 2012 with 57% opposed, then passed an ordinance 9-2 in September 2015, and Ketchikan passed an ordinance unanimously in July 2020 effective mid-August, while Fairbanks limits protection to sexual orientation discrimination against city employees after mayoral veto of a broader 2019 ordinance. Federal protections apply via Bostock on June 15, 2020 holding workplace discrimination on sexual orientation violates Title VII, and the October 2009 Matthew Shepard Act providing federal penalty enhancements for crimes motivated by actual or perceived sexual orientation prosecutable in federal court, while Alaska state hate-crime law does not cover sexual orientation. Alaska permits adoption by married same-sex couples and recognizes the non-genetic, non-gestational mother as legal parent for a child born via donor insemination only if the parents are married, with lesbian couples having access to in vitro fertilization and courts generally favorable to surrogacy despite no surrogacy laws; Anchorage banned conversion therapy on minors in August 2020 by a 9-2 vote.

Georgia's own law and practice diverge from the national layer in ways a trans visitor should weigh. Care for minors is banned by statute, the state employee health plan is under a court settlement requiring it to pay for gender-affirming care, and access to adult surgery narrowed abruptly in Savannah in 2025. Documented violence against transgender women in the state has centred on Atlanta.

Senate Bill 140, signed by Governor Brian Kemp on 23 March 2023 and in force since 1 July 2023, bars licensed medical professionals from providing hormone therapy or surgery for gender transition to patients under 18. Licence revocation is a possible penalty. Minors who began hormone replacement therapy before 1 July 2023 may continue under the law. The ACLU of Georgia said it would sue.

A settlement announced in October 2023 in federal court in Atlanta requires Georgia's State Health Benefit Plan to pay for medically necessary gender-affirming care for employees, their spouses and their dependents, after a December 2022 lawsuit alleged the plan illegally discriminated by refusing to pay. The plan's coverage of minors' care can extend to treatment obtained outside Georgia, even though that care is prohibited inside the state. The settlement keeps public-employee coverage in place alongside the 2023 ban.

Atlanta police said in April 2023 that they were investigating three violent crimes against transgender women in the city that year, after two Black transgender women were fatally shot a week apart; a January 2023 shooting that left a transgender woman in critical condition also remained open. The department described the violence against Black and Brown transgender women as epidemic-level. The sourcing gives raw counts without a denominator for the city's general homicide rate, so the figures establish that these attacks occurred and were under investigation, not that transgender residents face a risk measurably above the background rate of violence in the city.

Memorial Health University Medical Center in Savannah cancelled all gender-affirming surgeries on 13 February 2025, including a pre-approved double mastectomy for a 24-year-old transgender man. The hospital cited a responsibility to follow state and federal laws and regulations, and the cancellation came in the weeks after a January 2025 federal order denying Medicare and Medicaid funding to providers of youth gender-transition care. Savannah Pride Center said at least two other area residents were also denied care.

66186276B86627915353587.name: New Hampshire
66186276B86627915353587.summary:
New Hampshire is a state of the United States. Passports, visas, entry screening and federal facilities are governed by federal law; the findings below concern the state layer.

State anti-discrimination law has covered gender identity in housing, employment and public accommodations since June 2018. Coverage was extended to health care, public accommodations and jury selection effective 1 January 2020, and to public schools effective 17 September 2019, with the anti-bullying statute reaching gender identity and expression, including cyberbullying. Sexual orientation has been protected in public accommodations, housing and private and public employment since 1998.

Hate-crime penalty enhancements for offences motivated by gender identity took effect on 15 October 2019; sexual orientation has been covered since 1991. The gay and trans panic defence was abolished effective 1 January 2024, following passage in June 2023.

Enforcement of the state civil rights statute is documented. On 17 July 2026 the Merrimack County Superior Court found that a Concord man had violated the New Hampshire Civil Rights Act by striking a transgender woman.

GLAAD's 2025 national incident census recorded 72 anti-LGBTQ incidents in New Hampshire, the second-highest raw count of any state after California (198) and ahead of Texas (66), Ohio (50) and Washington (50). The census ranks by raw count and publishes no per-capita denominator, so the figure does not by itself establish New Hampshire's incident rate relative to larger states.

Identity documents are asymmetric. A New Hampshire birth certificate can be changed to reflect a different gender only on proof of sex reassignment surgery, legal in the state since 1990, together with a certified court order stating a "sex change," an application form, a photograph and fees. A reform bill was vetoed in July 2019 and the surgical requirement remains. Driver's licences have offered male, female and X markers since 1 January 2020, implemented in August 2021; the X marker is not available on birth certificates.

Care rules for minors have tightened. Laws passed on 18 July 2024 banned gender-affirming medicine for minors and, from 1 January 2025, banned reassignment surgery for transgender minors while retaining it for intersex people and circumcisions. House Bill 377 and House Bill 712, passed in August 2025 and effective January 2026, ban puberty blockers, hormone therapy and chest surgery for under-18 gender-affirming care, with a grandfather clause for treatment already under way as of 1 January 2026, disciplinary action against providers who violate the ban, and a right to sue. Those August 2025 laws removed access to gender-affirming care for transgender youth even where a physician judged it medically necessary.

The same July 2024 package barred transgender girls from girls' sports in grades 5 to 12 from 19 August 2024, with a birth certificate required to establish eligibility. A fourth bill in that package, which would have permitted discrimination against transgender people including adults, was vetoed. In August 2024 the state Supreme Court ruled 3-1 to protect transgender students in schools on privacy and autonomy grounds, and a judge granted a temporary stay of the sports ban pending investigation and appeals.

Marriage between two people of the same sex has been legal since 1 January 2010, following civil unions from 1 January 2008. An April 2021 Supreme Court ruling recognised adultery in such marriages, reversing the 2003 Blanchflower rule.

Same-sex sexual activity has been legal since the sodomy repeal of June 1975. The age of consent is 16 regardless of sexual orientation, and 18 where one party is under the care, guardianship or authority of the other.

66186276B89395128410123.name: Arizona
66186276B89395128410123.summary:
Arizona has not enacted restrictions on transgender adults' use of public facilities or on their participation in public life. A July 2026 national legal risk assessment placed it in a low-risk group of eight states and the District of Columbia, described as jurisdictions that have largely refrained from targeting transgender adults, and named Arizona with Virginia as a state whose youth-targeting policies were judged unlikely to be extended to adults.

Bathroom and school measures have been stopped at the executive stage rather than enacted. In June 2023 the governor vetoed legislature-passed bills on bathroom use and on classroom pronoun use, and in April 2023 vetoed a bill aimed at LGBT safe spaces in schools. No state law bars a trans visitor from using a restroom or changing facility that matches their gender.

Statewide non-discrimination protection rests on executive action rather than statute. A January 2023 gubernatorial executive order bars discrimination based on gender identity in state employment and state contracts, and a June 2023 attorney general opinion treats gender identity as within the state's sex-discrimination prohibition. Municipal ordinances in Phoenix, Flagstaff, Tempe, Sedona, Winslow, Mesa, Scottsdale, Glendale and Tolleson prohibit gender-identity discrimination in employment, housing and public accommodations, with exemptions for religious organisations, expressive groups, government agencies, private clubs and small businesses. Outside those municipalities and the state employment context, a trans visitor has no state statutory remedy for discrimination in a shop, hotel or restaurant.

The state hate-crime statute does not list gender identity among its protected categories, so bias-motivated violence against a trans person is neither recorded nor sentenced as a hate crime under Arizona law. A panic defence resting on a victim's sexuality or gender identity remains available at common law, and reform bills have lapsed without a vote.

Identity documents can be changed, on conditions. A driver's licence or state identification change requires a signed physician statement attesting that the applicant is irrevocably committed to the gender-change process; surgery is not required. Birth-certificate changes were permitted without surgery by a federal court order in August 2024, following a November 2020 suit brought by three families against the Department of Health Services.

Adult health coverage is uneven. A 1982 state regulation excludes sex reassignment surgery from Medicaid, and two transgender teenagers challenged it as unconstitutional in August 2020. A June 2023 executive order extended full Medicaid access and insurance coverage for gender-affirming health care to state government employees over the age of 21.

For younger trans people the state has legislated. A March 2022 law, effective March 2023, bans surgery on transgender minors while permitting it on intersex children. A second March 2022 law bars transgender girls from female school sports. In March 2023 the Department of Education opened a hotline for reporting schools that expose children to topics including gender ideology.

Partner recognition is settled in practice. Marriages between people of the same sex have been recognised since a federal district court ruling on 17 October 2014; the statutory and constitutional bans remain on the books and are unenforceable under Obergefell v. Hodges and, for marriages entered elsewhere, the Respect for Marriage Act. Phoenix, Bisbee, Tucson and Flagstaff have enacted domestic-partnership or civil-union registries. The Arizona Supreme Court ruled unanimously in September 2017 that married same-sex spouses hold equal parental rights and may both be listed on a birth certificate.

The article describes thousands of years of indigenous inhabitation with traditions of cross-dressing and gender variance and perceptions of gender and sexuality different from the Western world with no legal or social punishments for same-sex activity, including Navajo recognition of four roles asdzáán (feminine female), hastiin (masculine male), dilbaa (masculine female) and nádleehi defined as a male-bodied person with a feminine nature whose identity is fluid. It states today LGBT Navajo may find it difficult being accepted by family with 70% of LGBT Navajo youth reportedly attempting suicide. It notes Phoenix and Tucson are home to prominent LGBTQ communities with Tucson Pride founded 1977 as first in the state and first Phoenix Pride parade in 1981 now attracting thousands yearly, and cites 2019 Public Religion Research Institute polling that 71% of Arizona residents supported LGBTQ non-discrimination legislation, with 2017 PRRI finding 63% supported same-sex marriage, 73% supported anti-discrimination law covering sexual orientation and gender identity, and 59% opposed religious refusals to serve LGBTQ people.

66186276B53580985925186.name: Virginia
66186276B53580985925186.summary:
Virginia operates within the federal framework of the United States, and the national layer of exposure is carried in the country assessment. State law protects gender identity across several areas a visitor encounters directly, while the state's transgender-related restrictions are concentrated in schools and in rules covering minors.

The Virginia Values Act, passed 6 February 2020, signed 11 April 2020 and effective 1 July 2020, prohibits discrimination on the basis of gender identity in employment, housing, public accommodations and credit. It covers sexual orientation on the same terms and replaced earlier protections limited to state employment. A law signed 4 March 2020 with the same effective date authorises localities to enact their own sexual-orientation and gender-identity protections.

Violence motivated by gender identity falls within Virginia's hate crime law under legislation signed 4 March 2020 and effective 1 July 2020, which also added sexual orientation. HB 2132, repealing the gay and trans panic defence, passed in March 2021, was signed by Governor Northam, and took effect on 1 July 2021.

State identity documents are comparatively accessible. Virginia has offered an X gender marker on driver's licences since 1 July 2020, and since 1 September 2020 changing the sex designation on a birth certificate requires only "appropriate clinical treatment", replacing a surgery requirement that had been in force since 1979.

The state's criminal provisions on private sexual conduct no longer stand. §18.2-361 was struck down on 12 March 2013 and revised to remove the criminalisation of consensual same-sex relations, by a Senate vote of 40-0 on 7 February 2014 and a House vote of 100-0 on 6 March 2014, signed into immediate effect. §18.2-345 on lewd cohabitation was repealed in 2013 and §18.2-344 on fornication was repealed on 4 March 2020. The sodomy statutes had already been rendered unenforceable by Lawrence v. Texas in 2003.

Marriage between people of the same sex is recognised in Virginia and has been performed since 6 October 2014, when the U.S. Supreme Court declined to hear the appeal in Bostic v. Rainey/Schaefer and marriages began at 1 p.m. that day. The statutory ban was repealed on 3 March 2020, and a codifying protection was signed in March 2024, effective 1 July. The 2006 constitutional amendment banning such marriages remains in the constitution, with repeal resolutions approved in January 2025 and January 2026 awaiting a voter referendum. A designated-visitor statute signed 26 March 2007 and effective 1 July 2007 extended hospital visitation rights to same-sex couples.

On schools, in 2014 a Gloucester County school board was held to have acted unlawfully in denying a transgender high school student use of the boys' bathroom, a ruling the U.S. Supreme Court allowed to stand in 2021. In July 2023 the state Department of Education adopted policies banning bathroom access and pronoun usage for transgender students, which were intended to be reversed in 2026. The Virginia High School League barred transgender athletes from girls' sports in February 2025. Virginia prohibits health care providers from attempting to change the gender identity of minors.

Official posture toward transgender students has moved in both directions through the courts. In September 2021 the Virginia Supreme Court upheld the reinstatement of a teacher suspended for speaking against transgender children and declining to use their pronouns on grounds of Christian belief. In May 2024 Governor Youngkin vetoed a bullying-definition bill that would have included gender identity.

A July 2026 legal risk assessment places Virginia in its Low-Risk States group alongside Arizona, Delaware, Maine, Michigan, Nevada, Pennsylvania, Wisconsin and the District of Columbia, and names Virginia and Arizona as states that have enacted youth-targeting anti-trans policies which, on that assessment's reading of state-specific factors, appear unlikely to extend to adults.

66186276B94082813086253.name: District of Columbia
66186276B94082813086253.summary:
The District of Columbia stands under the national framework of the United States. It is the federal seat rather than a state, so national law applies directly within its boundaries and Congress retains authority over its local legislation and budget.

The District has no bathroom ban of its own. The facilities restriction in force there was attached by Congress, and on 5 December 2024 transgender-rights activists protesting that measure at the Capitol were arrested. The ban originates with Congress rather than with the District's elected legislature, so it is not something the local council can repeal.

A July 2026 legal risk assessment places the District of Columbia on its low-risk list alongside Arizona, Delaware, Maine, Michigan, Nevada, Pennsylvania, Virginia and Wisconsin, while cautioning that the District may no longer warrant its reputation as the most protective jurisdiction, because its law can be overridden by congressional action and by executive orders.

66186276B78821008370123.name: Maine
66186276B78821008370123.summary:
Maine law prohibits discrimination on the basis of actual or perceived gender identity or expression in employment, housing, credit, public accommodations and education opportunity. The protections were added in 2005 and retained after a veto referendum on 8 November 2005, and LD 1688, signed on 17 June 2021, wrote gender identity explicitly into state statutes. The state hate-crime law provides penalty enhancements for offences motivated by actual or perceived gender identity, and the gay and trans panic defence was abolished by legislation passed in June 2019 by 132-1 in the House and 35-0 in the Senate, effective 1 July 2019.

Gender markers on Maine driver's licences and state identification cards can be changed without medical provider certification, a rule in place since November 2019, on a completed Gender Designation Form offering male, female and X options. Birth certificates reflecting gender identity, including an X marker, have been issued since July 2020 on notarized affidavit. The X marker on a birth certificate requires a declaration from a licensed physician or mental health provider, and applicants who are minors require parental consent.

Maine has no state law restricting transgender people's use of sex-segregated facilities. The Maine Supreme Court ruled in January 2014 in Doe v. Regional School Unit 26 against a school district that had denied a student use of the bathroom aligned with her gender identity.

A law effective since July 2023 allows 16 and 17 year olds to obtain hormone therapy as gender-affirming care, and an April 2024 law explicitly protects, defends and safeguards gender-affirming healthcare. From 1 October 2026 healthcare facilities in Maine must mandate and include sexual orientation and gender identity data.

In June 2025 the Maine Senate rejected Legislative Document 233, which would have barred transgender women from competing in women's sports in state-funded schools. It was the only one of eight anti-trans bills introduced in the state in 2025 to pass the House.

The University of Maine System announced on 21 March 2025, with an update on 24 March, that it would comply with federal restrictions on transgender sports participation. The announcement followed the US Department of Agriculture's suspension of federal funding for research and programmes while it investigated possible sex-based discrimination in federally funded education programmes.

A July 2026 national anti-trans legal risk assessment places Maine in its Low-Risk States group. The same assessment separately flags that Maine's risk has increased because of the University of Maine System's capitulation on sports participation.

66186276B31549545599635.summary:
Delaware is a state of the United States and stands under the national framework, which governs entry, visas, passports and federal screening; the national record carries that layer. What follows is Delaware's own law and practice.

A July 2026 risk assessment places Delaware in its Low-Risk group, described as states that largely refrain from targeting transgender adults without specialising in their protection.

Delaware imposes no ban on transgender people using public bathrooms and facilities according to their gender identity, per the Movement Advancement Project equality map. The archived page for that map returned HTTP 404 when checked, so the finding rests on the map's recorded data rather than a retrievable page.

Since 2013, SB 97 prohibits discrimination on the basis of actual or perceived gender identity in employment, housing, public accommodations and other areas. The bill passed the Senate 11-7 on 6 June 2013 and the House 24-17 with amendments, returned to the Senate where it passed on amendments 11-9 on 18 June, was signed the next day and took effect immediately. Since 2013 the state also imposes additional penalties for violent crimes motivated by the victim's actual or perceived gender identity.

Changing the gender marker on state-issued identification requires only the signed statement of a licensed medical provider. Since 11 February 2017 sex reassignment surgery is no longer an explicit requirement for an amended birth certificate, which instead requires a signed affidavit of surgical, hormonal, psychological or other treatment appropriate for gender transition. As of April 2020 Delaware does not offer a gender X option on driver's licences.

Conversion therapy is restricted by SB 65, introduced on 26 April 2017, passed by the Senate 12-3 on 17 May 2017 and by the House 24-14 on 7 June 2018, and signed and effective on 23 July 2018 as Laws of Delaware 81:340. The statute defines conversion therapy to include practices seeking to change gender identity, behaviours or gender expressions, makes performing it on a minor, or referring a minor out of state for it, unprofessional conduct subject to discipline for physicians, nurses, mental health and chemical dependency professionals, psychologists and clinical social workers, and bars the Department of Services for Children, Youth and Their Families from performing or recommending it for a minor.

Since 26 March 2016 Delaware has prohibited discrimination based on gender identity within insurance contracts, including coverage of sex reassignment surgery.

Delaware has recognised marriages between partners of the same sex since 1 July 2013, with civil unions that had been available from 1 January 2012 converted into marriages.

HB142, which would formally repeal the common-law gay and trans panic defence and bar its use, was introduced in May 2023 and passed both chambers in June 2023. The source records no signature or veto, so the current status of the defence is unresolved.

No Delaware-specific policy on housing transgender inmates in state custody appears in the sources.

No Delaware-specific placement policy is documented.

66186276B6628180846672.name: Pennsylvania
66186276B6628180846672.summary:
Pennsylvania's law operates inside the United States framework, which governs passports, visas, entry screening, federal custody and federally funded programmes; those national rules sit above the state layer and are not restated here. An independent anti-trans legal-risk assessment placed Pennsylvania in its low-risk tier in a July 2026 update, the category covering states that largely refrain from targeting trans adults without extending them specific protection.

Statewide discrimination protection is explicit. Since June 2023 discrimination on the basis of gender identity has been banned across Pennsylvania, with sexual orientation covered from the same date, and municipalities including Philadelphia, Pittsburgh, Allentown, Erie and Reading maintain their own bans. The Pennsylvania Human Relations Commission has interpreted the Human Relations Act's prohibition on sex discrimination to cover gender identity since August 2018, investigating complaints and awarding remedies that include stop orders, training and economic damages. Legally binding regulations signed in December 2022 define sex to include gender identity. State employees have held executive-order protection since 2003 and state contractors since 7 April 2016. A bill to write gender identity and sexual orientation protection into statute, House Bill 300, passed the House 102-98 in April 2023 and awaits a Senate vote, so the current statewide guarantee rests on commission interpretation and regulation rather than legislation.

State identity documents are comparatively open. Since August 2016 a transgender person can change the gender on a Pennsylvania birth certificate on a physician's note of appropriate clinical treatment, with no requirement for surgery and a parental request required below age 18; birth certificates carry no X option. Driver's licences and state IDs have offered X alongside M and F since 23 July 2020.

Philadelphia has built a local layer on top of the state rules. Ordinances adopted in November 2019 bar youth-serving organisations from discriminating against trans, nonbinary and gender-nonconforming youth, require at least one gender-neutral bathroom in every city-owned building, and confirm that the Fair Practice Ordinance protects nonbinary and gender-fluid people; in December 2021 X was added alongside male and female in all virtual public schools. On 17 October 2023 Mayor Jim Kenney declared Philadelphia a sanctuary for gender-affirming care by executive order, prohibiting the use of city resources to investigate or punish in-state or out-of-state residents seeking such care in the city, deprioritising enforcement of any future state or federal restriction, and shielding travellers from out-of-state enforcement.

Gender-affirming surgery is lawful in Pennsylvania, and no statewide prohibition on gender-affirming care for adults appears in the sources reviewed.

Violence motivated by anti-LGBTQ bias sits outside the state hate-crime statute. A 2002 hate-crime law covering LGBTQ people was struck down in 2008 on the constitutional ground that its content had been inserted into an agricultural terrorism bill; bills to reinstate it have never left committee, leaving no statewide hate-crime provision that reaches anti-LGBTQ violence. In April 2021 a Pittsburgh mayoral proposal sought a city ordinance explicitly naming gender identity; no enactment followed.

Restrictions on transgender participation in sport have moved through the legislature without becoming law. A June 2022 bill that would have required public K-12 schools and colleges to designate sports as male, female or coed, with female-designated teams restricted to athletes assigned female at birth, passed both chambers but was vetoed on 11 July 2022 by Governor Tom Wolf. On 6 May 2025 the Senate approved Senate Bill 9, the Save Women's Sports Act, reserving women's teams for "biological females" in K-12 and collegiate sport, and sent it to the House. On 22 April 2026 the Senate passed Senate Bill 1293 under the same title; Governor Josh Shapiro called supportive lawmakers "extremists", and it was unclear whether the House would take the bill up. All of these measures concern youth school sport rather than transgender adults or public facility access.

Consensual same-sex sexual activity is legal in Pennsylvania. The sodomy statute was held unconstitutional by the state Supreme Court in the 1980 ruling Commonwealth v. Bonadio on equal protection grounds, and the remaining sodomy laws were repealed in 1995. Marriage between two people of the same sex has been recognised statewide since Whitewood v. Wolf struck down the statutory ban on 20 May 2014; before that ruling the state recognised no marriages, civil unions or domestic partnerships. Philadelphia offers life partnerships for long-term committed couples with a city nexus, Pittsburgh provides domestic partnerships, and Luzerne County defines domestic partnership as between people of the same gender.

66186276B91272823970344.summary:
Wisconsin is a state of the United States and stands under the national framework carried by the national record; the findings below are the Wisconsin-specific layer. A July 2026 national legal-risk assessment places Wisconsin in its low-risk group, alongside Arizona, Delaware, Maine, Michigan, Nevada, Pennsylvania, Virginia and the District of Columbia, describing jurisdictions that have largely refrained from targeting transgender adults while not taking extraordinary steps to protect them.

No statewide law prohibits discrimination on the basis of gender identity, and gender identity is not a protected class under the state hate-crime statute, though sexual orientation is. Prosecutors have sometimes used perceived sexual orientation as the route to charge crimes motivated by a victim's gender identity. Local protection is patchwork: as of 29 May 2025, 21 per cent of the state's population lived in the ten cities with full employment, housing and public-accommodation ordinances covering gender identity, and 12 per cent in cities with partial ordinances. Dane and Milwaukee counties and the cities of Appleton, Cudahy, De Pere, Janesville, Madison, Milwaukee and Racine ban gender-identity discrimination; Oshkosh and Stevens Point extend protection only to transgender city employees. Executive Order #1, issued 7 January 2019, prohibits discrimination on the basis of sexual orientation, gender identity and gender expression in state employment, state contracting and the provision of state services, and directs state agencies to adopt and enforce nondiscrimination policies.

Wisconsin has no law barring transgender people from using government-building bathrooms or facilities consistent with their gender identity, no law defining sex to exclude transgender people, and no restriction on drag performance. The state's equality-map profile, current to 29 May 2025, records no ban on best-practice medical care for transgender youth and no shield law protecting providers or patients from out-of-state action.

Identity documents are the main friction point. Gender-marker change on a Wisconsin driver's licence is permitted only in limited circumstances, and change on a birth certificate is restricted: a person born in the state who has completed sex reassignment surgery may amend the birth certificate on documentation of the surgery and a name change. Neither licence nor birth certificate offers an X gender-neutral option, and the name-change process is restrictive.

State law does not ban gender-affirming care for minors. Governor Tony Evers vetoed Assembly Bill 465 on 6 December 2023, blocking a legislature-passed ban on gender-affirming health care for people under 18; he had earlier vetoed a June 2023 budget provision that would have barred Medicaid coverage of sexual reassignment surgery and other gender-affirming care for all individuals regardless of age. Care access nonetheless contracted under federal funding pressure: UW Health and Children's Wisconsin each announced on 13 January 2026 that they would pause gender-affirming pharmacologic care for patients under 18 after the U.S. Department of Health and Human Services said it would deny Medicaid and Medicare payments to hospitals providing such care to minors. Mental and behavioural health services continued. Wisconsin Attorney General Josh Kaul joined a multistate coalition seeking to block the HHS declaration. The pause follows federal funding pressure on Wisconsin hospitals rather than any state ban.

Marriage between two people regardless of sex has been recognised since 6 October 2014, when the Supreme Court declined the appeal in Wolf v. Walker and the district court's stay was lifted. A trans visitor whose relationship would be read as same-sex under birth-sex status can expect that marriage to be recognised. Parenting rules allow individuals to adopt without regard to sexual orientation and married couples to adopt; access to IVF and artificial insemination is permitted, with state recognition of the non-genetic, non-gestational mother only if she is married. A September 2016 federal ruling required both parents to be recorded on birth certificates, and since 1 July 2021 birth certificates offer gender-neutral 'spouse' and 'parent 1'/'parent 2' options.

Private, non-commercial sexual conduct between consenting adults has been legal since 1983, when the state's sodomy provisions were repealed; the repealing legislation stated that Wisconsin did not approve of sexual conduct outside marriage.

The Milwaukee Police Department stopped listing the gender of crime victims in September 2023, alongside race, in order to avoid misgendering transgender people.

sources.title: LGBTQ rights in Wisconsin (Wikipedia)
sources.summary: Wisconsin has no statewide anti-discrimination law covering gender identity and gender identity is not covered in the state's hate crime law, though perceived sexual orientation is often used as a medium to prosecute crimes based on the victim's gender identity; Executive Order #1 in January 2019 prohibited gender-identity discrimination in government employment, while Dane and Milwaukee counties and the cities of Appleton, Cudahy, De Pere, Janesville, Madison, Milwaukee and Racine ban gender-identity discrimination and Oshkosh and Stevens Point ban discrimination against transgender city employees only. A person born in the state who has completed sex reassignment surgery may amend their birth certificate upon documentation of surgery and name change, while persons on Wisconsin's sex offender registry are not allowed to change their names with no exception if the person is transgender. Sex reassignment surgery had to be explicitly included in Wisconsin Medicaid for government employees from January 2019 and was ordered extended to non-government employees in May 2019 under the Equal Protection Clause of the 14th Amendment, while a June 2023 budget bill passed by both houses banning Medicaid coverage of sexual reassignment surgery and other gender-affirming healthcare to all individuals regardless of age was vetoed under line-item veto power. People in prison are entitled to hormone therapy after the 2005 Inmate Sex Change Prevention Act denying hormone therapy to prisoners undergoing sex reassignment was ruled unconstitutional unanimously in Fields v. Smith by the Seventh Circuit on August 5, 2011, with Supreme Court denial of the state's appeal on March 26, 2012. Since September 2023 the Milwaukee Police Department no longer lists gender as well as race of victims to avoid misgendering transgender individuals in the future. On sports, a 2021 Republican bill banning transgender women from teams aligning with their gender passed the Assembly on party lines but was never voted in the Senate, was re-introduced in 2023, and a 2024 legislature-passed bill banning transgender individuals from female sports and athletics teams was vetoed by the Governor. On medical care, a 2021 Republican bill prohibiting insurers from covering gender-affirming care procedures for minors failed in committee, a re-introduced bill passed the Assembly October 12, 2023 and Senate October 17, 2023 and was vetoed December 6, 2023, and in December 2023 the Governor also vetoed a legislature-passed bill explicitly banning gender-affirming healthcare to individuals under 18. Consensual sodomy prohibitions originating in Michigan Territory in 1836 and retained at 1848 statehood, expanded to fellatio in 1897 and to cunnilingus with five-year penalties for sexual perversion in the 1950s, were reclassified as a misdemeanor punishable by nine months jail and/or 10,000 dollars in 1977 and legalized for private, non-commercial acts between consenting adults in 1983 with a statement that Wisconsin did not approve of any sexual conduct outside marriage. Same-sex marriage has been legal since October 6, 2014 when the Supreme Court refused appeal in Wolf v. Walker, lifting Judge Crabb's stay, while the Chapter 770 domestic partnership registry established in 2009 providing 43 of 200-plus spousal rights without stepchild adoptions was upheld unanimously in Appling v. Walker on July 31, 2014 and ended April 1, 2018, with same-sex partner benefits for state employees since 2009. Discrimination based on sexual orientation has been banned statewide in employment, housing, education, credit and all public accommodations since 1982, making Wisconsin the first U.S. state to do so, and sexual orientation is a protected class in hate crime law and under a 2001 law prohibiting sexual-orientation discrimination in schools. Parenting provisions allow individuals to adopt without respect to sexual orientation and married same-sex couples to adopt, allow lesbian access to IVF and artificial insemination with state recognition of the non-genetic, non-gestational mother only if married, required recording of both same-sex parents on birth certificates under a September 2016 federal ruling, and from July 1, 2021 provide gender-neutral spouse and spouse or parent 1 and parent 2 birth certificate options for children of same-sex couples. Conversion therapy on minors is banned in 14 communities including Milwaukee in March 2018, Madison in July 2018, Eau Claire in October 2018, plus Cudahy, Shorewood, Racine, Glendale, Sheboygan, Superior, West Allis by 6-3 in September 2020, Kenosha by 14-1 in October 2020 with maximum 1,000 dollar fine plus costs and 90 days in Kenosha County Jail and possible suspension of driving privileges up to five years, Sun Prairie, Appleton and La Crosse, while a June 2021 executive order banned state taxpayer dollars funding conversion therapy on LGBT minors, statewide ban efforts were blocked in June 2020 and January 2023, and in July 2025 the Wisconsin Supreme Court ruled 4-3 that bans can be enacted by regulation and executive order. A 2017 PRRI poll found 73% supported an anti-discrimination law covering sexual orientation and gender identity with 20% opposed, distinct from 66% support for same-sex marriage with 26% opposed and 8% unsure. In October 2023 Governor Evers, speaking to "LGBTQ folks — especially our trans kids", said he would "veto any bill that makes Wisconsin a less welcoming, less inclusive, and less safe place for you to be who you are". Since September 2023 the Milwaukee Police Department has omitted victim gender to avoid misgendering transgender individuals in the future. Introductions of the transgender athlete and medical-care bills sparked significant backlash from organizational and community advocates, including Fair Wisconsin, GSAFE, and the ACLU of Wisconsin.

The July 2026 anti-trans legal risk assessment map places Michigan in its 'Low-Risk States' tier, describing the state as having enacted fairly robust non-discrimination policies while falling short on healthcare equity and on protections for incarcerated transgender people.

Discrimination on the basis of gender identity is unlawful in Michigan under the Elliott-Larsen Civil Rights Act, following a July 2022 Michigan Supreme Court ruling that affirmed the Attorney General's appeal; the legislature codified the protection in a bill passed in March 2023 and signed by Governor Gretchen Whitmer on 8 March 2023. The ruling built on a 21 May 2018 Civil Rights Commission interpretation adopted 5-0 and on the 7 March 2018 Sixth Circuit decision in EEOC v. R.G. & G.R. Harris Funeral Homes holding that Title VII prohibits employment discrimination against transgender people. Sexual-orientation protection followed the same route, from a December 2003 executive order and a March 2013 marina-loan non-discrimination provision through the May 2018 commission interpretation to the March 2023 codification.

Hate-crime law covers gender identity implicitly within Michigan's 1992 hate-crime statute under the category 'gender', per an August 2021 court declaration. A hate-crime package adding 'gender identity or expression' explicitly passed the House in June 2023 and the Senate in December 2024, was signed in January 2025 and took effect 90 days after signature. Sexual orientation has been recognised for hate-crime data collection since 1992.

The gay and trans panic defence was abolished by a law passed, signed and implemented in July 2024.

Conversion therapy is banned statewide under a bill passed by both chambers in June 2023 and signed in July 2023, following a June 2021 executive order barring taxpayer dollars or funding for conversion therapy on minors.

Sex on a Michigan birth certificate can be changed without sexual reassignment surgery under a 30 June 2021 court ruling that declared the 1978 surgery and physician-statement requirement unconstitutional; the position was certified and codified by a bill passed in December 2024. Changing sex on a driver's licence or state ID requires a signed statutory declaration and a fee under the system in place since November 2019.

Marriage between two people of the same sex is legal in Michigan under Obergefell v. Hodges (26 June 2015). Michigan had barred it by a 1995 statute signed by Governor Engler and by the 2004 constitutional amendment Proposal 04-2, approved with 58.6% of the vote, which also barred civil unions. In DeBoer v. Snyder the district court held the ban unconstitutional on 21 March 2014; more than 300 licences were issued on 22 March 2014 before Sixth Circuit stays, and the Sixth Circuit reversed on 6 November 2014.

Michigan's sodomy statute has not been repealed by the legislature even though same-sex sexual activity is legal under Lawrence v. Texas (2003). The statute as written applied to both homosexual and heterosexual conduct, and Michigan and Massachusetts are the only northern states without statutory codification.

The Michigan Supreme Court announced a September 2023 decision on respecting an individual's pronouns for judges.

66186276B98615608994420.name: Nevada
66186276B98615608994420.summary:
Nevada stands under the United States federal framework, which governs passports, entry screening, federal custody and federal care measures; those apply within the state and are carried by the national record. The findings below are those specific to Nevada.

A national legal risk assessment published in July 2026 places Nevada in its Low-Risk group, directly below the most-protective tier, crediting the state with fairly robust non-discrimination policies while finding it falls short on healthcare equity and on protections for incarcerated transgender people.

State anti-discrimination law covers gender identity or expression in employment, housing and public accommodations, effective 1 October 2011 and extended throughout the state statutes effective 1 July 2017. Protections covering sexual orientation alone came earlier: in public and private employment and in public accommodations from the 1999 legislative session, and in housing from the 2011 laws. In November 2022 voters approved Question 1 by 58%, adding sexual orientation and gender identity or expression to the state constitution's equal protection clause.

Hate-crime law provides additional penalties for offences motivated by listed actual or perceived characteristics; gender identity or expression was added by amendment effective 1 October 2013. A hate-crime reporting hotline was established in January 2025. The gay panic defence was repealed by legislation signed 14 May 2019, effective 1 October 2019, and the state's 1983 HIV-specific offences were repealed by SB 275, signed in May 2021 and effective immediately, following a 2019 law creating an HIV task force.

State identity documents are comparatively open. Since 2016 the state vital records office has issued a birth certificate with a corrected gender on two affidavits, with no requirement for sex reassignment surgery, and driver's licences and state IDs can be changed on the same basis. An X third-gender designation is available on driver's licences, birth certificates and state IDs with no medical documentation, introduced in 2019. Legislation passed in May 2017 and signed on 22 June 2017 abolished the 1988 requirement that transgender people publish their names in newspapers before obtaining a legal sex change on government documents. These rules govern Nevada documents; federal travel documents follow the rules set out in the national record.

On public bathrooms and facilities, Nevada's position is assessed against the Movement Advancement Project's Equality Map, which tracks state-by-state rules on whether transgender people may use public bathrooms and facilities according to their gender identity.

Marriage and partner recognition: a federal appellate court struck down the state's constitutional ban on same-sex marriage on 8 October 2014 in Sevcik v. Sandoval. The marriage statute has used gender-neutral language since 1 July 2017, and in November 2020 voters removed the constitutional ban with 62% support. In December 2020 the Nevada Supreme Court required retroactive recognition of out-of-state same-sex marriages performed before 2014. The Nevada Domestic Partnership Act, effective 1 October 2009 after a veto override, grants many of the rights of marriage but exempts private and public employers from providing medical coverage to domestic partners, leaves parental rights less well defined and carries uncertain recognition outside the state.

The Movement Advancement Project's Equality Map records state-by-state rules on whether transgender people may use public bathrooms and facilities according to their gender identity, and is the source used to situate Nevada within that comparison.

66186276B21291522594454.name: Maryland
66186276B21291522594454.summary:
Maryland's gender-identity law is protective. The Fairness for All Marylanders Act of 2014, effective 1 October 2014, prohibits discrimination based on gender identity in employment, housing and public accommodations statewide; before that date protection existed only in Baltimore City, Baltimore County, Howard County, Hyattsville and Montgomery County. Discrimination based on sexual orientation has been prohibited statewide since the Antidiscrimination Act of 2001 took effect on 21 November 2001.

The hate-crime statute adds penalties for crimes motivated by actual or perceived gender identity, listed as a separate category by an amendment effective 1 October 2021. HB231, effective the same date, abolished the common-law gay and trans panic defence.

A 2024 law declaring Maryland a sanctuary state for the protection and defence of transgender individuals passed the Senate 33-13 and the House 97-38 and was signed by Governor Wes Moore, effective 1 October 2024. It followed a June 2023 executive order protecting unimpeded access to gender-affirming healthcare and an insurance law effective 1 January 2024 described in state-by-state rights research as the most transgender healthcare friendly in the United States.

Maryland stands under the United States federal framework. Passport and visa sex markers, federal facility rules, immigration detention and federal custody are governed nationally, not by the state.

State-level identity documents are accessible but not complete. Since 1 October 2015 a birth-certificate gender marker can be changed without surgery or sterilisation on certification from a licensed healthcare provider confirming gender identity; the X marker remained unavailable on Maryland birth certificates as of 2023. Motor Vehicle Administration IDs and voter registration have allowed X since 1 October 2019 without legal or medical documentation, and the University of Maryland will add X in 2026. HB39, effective 1 October 2021, repealed the 1971 requirement to publish a name in a newspaper before a legal change on a birth certificate.

Facilities and student access run in favour of transgender people. In March 2018 a federal court ruled that transgender students may use restrooms and locker rooms consistent with gender identity, striking down a Talbot County policy; Montgomery County adopted gender-neutral bathroom requirements by a 9-0 vote in July 2022 and Baltimore does so by ordinance. A February 2022 county report records that transgender athletes may participate according to gender identity without proof, documentation, or medical or legal transition, after bills in 2022 and 2023 that would have restricted teams by biological sex failed.

Violence against transgender people in Maryland is documented. On 11 September 2026 Sophie Lee, a 27-year-old Black trans woman, was found shot in Baltimore's Charles Village and died; she was the second Black trans woman shot to death in Baltimore within ten weeks.

Protection machinery includes Montgomery County's unanimous October 2020 LGBTIQ+ bill of rights ordinance, a 15-member Commission on LGBTIQ+ Affairs created by HB130 effective October 2021 and expanded to 21 members in April 2023, and HB1380, effective 1 October 2022, which automatically restores honorable discharges retrospectively to LGBT individuals who lived in Maryland at the time.

Marriage between people of the same sex has been legal in Maryland since 1 January 2013 under the Civil Marriage Protection Act, approved 72-67 in the House on 17 February 2012 and 25-22 in the Senate on 23 February 2012, signed 1 March 2012 and approved by 52.4% of voters on 6 November 2012, after a 1973 ban; domestic partnerships have existed since 2008 and out-of-state marriages have been recognised since 2010. A trans visitor whose relationship Maryland law reads as same-sex under birth-sex status can marry here.

sources.title: Transgender legal history in the United States (Wikipedia)
sources.summary: Federal policy on housing transgender prisoners moved in both directions between 2015 and 2018. A January 2015 ICE memo directed that transgender immigration detainees be housed according to gender identity, and in 2016 the US Department of Justice released guidelines forbidding corrections agencies from assigning trans inmates to men's or women's units solely on birth anatomy. In 2018 the Federal Bureau of Prisons revised its Transgender Offender Manual, deleting the sentence that the Transgender Executive Council 'will recommend housing by gender identity when appropriate' and replacing it with placement on 'a case-by-case basis' in which 'biological sex' is 'the initial determination' and gender identity is used only 'in rare cases'. No Delaware- or Maryland-specific placement policy is covered.

sources.title: Transgender rights in the United States (Wikipedia)
sources.summary: Trans women held in men's facilities are subjected to V-coding, the assignment of trans women to aggressive cisgender male cellmates, characterized as 'a central part of a trans woman's sentence'. Trans women who physically resist sexual assault are often criminally charged with assault and placed in solitary confinement, with the charge then used to extend the sentence and deny parole. A 2021 California study found that 69% of surveyed trans women prisoners reported being made to perform unwanted sexual acts, 58.5% reported violent sexual assault, and 88% reported a 'marriage-like relationship'. Maryland has no documented placement rule, special unit, or named case.

66186276B43071933723331.name: California
66186276B43071933723331.summary:
California's own care-access law is the most protective element of its record. SB 107, signed by Governor Gavin Newsom in September 2022, made California the first state to declare itself a sanctuary for transgender young people seeking medical care. Young people from other states can obtain hormones and puberty blockers in California, and the law shields families from child-abuse investigations or criminal prosecution for seeking gender-affirming care. The shield covers families who travel to California for that care.

Recorded anti-LGBTQ hostility in California is the highest raw count of any state. The GLAAD ALERT Desk documented more than 1,000 anti-LGBTQ incidents nationwide in 2025, of which California accounted for 198; the next highest state recorded 72. California is the most populous state and no per-capita denominator accompanies the ranking, so the figure is a raw count only and does not establish that a trans visitor faces more risk in California than in a smaller state.

Law-enforcement data show a dramatic increase in anti-LGBTQ hate-crime reports in Los Angeles over the same period.

A July 2026 analysis places California in its "Safest States" law band with a score of 4.1 and 1.9 recorded incidents, and argues that even the most protective law floors do not eliminate recorded hostility.

66186276B35012827062242.name: Colorado
66186276B35012827062242.summary:
Colorado's Anti-Discrimination Act prohibits discrimination on the basis of gender identity and gender expression in employment, housing, public accommodations, education and credit, a coverage in force since 2008 and expanded again by the 2025 legislature, as documented in the Colorado Legislature's own 2025 summary of gender-affirming-care and transgender legislation. As of 12 October 2026 the state's gender-identity policy score stands at 23.25 of 25 within an overall score of 44.5 of 47, and a July 2026 national legal-risk assessment lists Colorado among the most protective states for transgender people.

House Bill 1312, the Kelly Loving Act, was signed by Governor Jared Polis on 16 May 2025 after passing on 6 May. It requires employers and schools to use a person's chosen name and pronouns, prohibits deadnaming and misgendering in workplaces and schools with immediate effect, and requires schools with dress codes to allow a student to choose from any uniform option. Its provisions simplifying changes of gender identity on birth certificates and driver's licences, and changes of name on marriage licences, take effect on 1 October 2026.

Gender markers on state documents are changeable without surgery. The Board of the Colorado Department of Public Health and Environment removed the surgical requirement unanimously in February 2019, ending a rule that had applied since 1 January 1984. A change is made by request, using a Change of Sex Designation form to the Division of Motor Vehicles for licences and IDs and Birth Certificate Correction and Sex Designation forms to the Department of Health for birth certificates. Birth certificates offer M, F, Intersex and X markers; IDs and licences offer male, female and X. Minors need parent or guardian consent plus confirmation from a medical or mental health professional.

Facilities access is protected. In 2013 the Colorado Civil Rights Division ruled that transgender six-year-old Coy Mathis could use the girls' restroom at her elementary school in Fountain, and in 2023 Colorado implemented a law granting full access to bathroom facilities for all genders. The state anti-bullying law prohibits bullying on the basis of gender identity and requires school districts to adopt prevention policies.

Colorado's hate-crime law has covered gender identity or expression since 2001, with penalty enhancements for bias-motivated crimes. In 2009 a Greeley jury convicted a man of first-degree murder with a hate-crime finding in a case described as the first murder trial applying a hate-crime law where the victim was transgender. The gay panic defence was abolished by a bipartisan bill passed in June 2020 and signed in July 2020, effective immediately.

Gender-affirming care is protected at state level but is under direct pressure. Legislation signed in April 2023 was enacted to protect, defend and guarantee gender-affirming healthcare services and to guarantee safe passage of transgender individuals from other states. Since the beginning of 2023 basic health insurance coverage in Colorado must explicitly include sexual reassignment surgery as a basic policy, and a July 2026 assessment counts Colorado among the states with comprehensive health-insurance laws covering facial-hair removal and expanded gender-related coverage. On 18 May 2026 the Colorado Supreme Court ruled 5-2 that Children's Hospital Colorado violated state anti-discrimination law when it suspended gender-affirming care for transgender youth under federal pressure, and ordered a lower court to issue an injunction requiring the hospital to resume puberty blockers and hormone therapy. Justice William Hood wrote that continuing such treatment for cisgender children while stopping it for transgender youth meant the decision denies the petitioners the full and equal enjoyment of services based on gender identity; two justices dissented, citing federal threats that could shut the hospital system.

Conversion therapy has been banned statewide on minors since a bill signed on 31 May 2019. After the Colorado Supreme Court's 8-1 ruling of 31 March 2026 in Chiles v. Salazar requiring strict scrutiny of that ban, House Bill 26-1322, passed on 8 May 2026, redefines conversion therapy as direction toward a pre-determined gender identity or sexual orientation outcome and removes the statute of limitations for claims.

Custody is governed by litigation rather than statute. A 2019 class action on behalf of transgender women held in men's prisons alleged that the Colorado Department of Corrections subjected them to sexual and physical violence and denied medically necessary care. The court-approved 2024 consent decree in Raven v. Polis, entered in Denver District Court, required the department to expand health care, create voluntary specialised housing comprising a 100-bed unit at the men's Sterling facility and an integration unit at the women's prison, and pay about $2.1 million to roughly 400 class members without admitting liability. A separate 2019 settlement paid Lindsay Saunders-Velez $170,000 over the safety of a transgender inmate held in a men's prison. No identity-based-housing statute governs placement in Colorado; trans women were historically held in men's prisons, with relief won through consent decree rather than a baseline housing rule.

66186276B10610315112087.summary:
Minnesota sets its own civil, health-care and criminal law within the federal framework of the United States; federal rules on passports, visas, entry screening and federal custody are fixed nationally and are not restated here. On the matters a trans visitor encounters at state level, Minnesota law runs in a protective direction.

Minnesota Session Law 2023 ch. 29 (HF 146) declares that gender-affirming health care as defined in the Act "is against the public policy of this state and must not be enforced or applied" in pending cases, and amends state provisions on warrants, arrests and extraditions that arise from other states' laws on gender-affirming health care. The House passed the bill 68-62 on 24 March 2023 after a late-night debate, and Governor Tim Walz signed it. It followed a March 2023 executive order directing the Minnesota Department of Health to summarise the scientific literature on the safety and effectiveness of gender-affirming care and confirming that providers could bill insurance for such care.

The shield reaches out-of-state process. Minnesota authorities may not enforce subpoenas, arrest warrants or extradition requests issued elsewhere over gender-affirming care that is legal in Minnesota, and may not comply with out-of-state court orders to remove children from parental custody for having obtained such care. 66186276B83663796884405.name: Connecticut
66186276B83663796884405.summary:
Connecticut sits in the fifteen-state 'Most Protective' tier of a July 2026 national legal-risk ranking, an assessment built from a rubric covering thousands of tracked anti-trans bills, including youth-care bans, bathroom bans, birth-certificate and driver's-licence restrictions and the withdrawal of legal recognition. The ranking finds the state's laws have gone above and beyond in safeguarding trans rights.

A 2022 shield law protects patients and providers from civil or criminal charges when care that is lawful in Connecticut was banned in the patient's home state. That protection is directly relevant to a visitor arriving from a state that has criminalised gender-affirming care.

State law bans discrimination on the basis of gender identity or expression in public places, in public and private employment, in governmental services and in the receipt of goods and services; gender identity and expression were added to the statute in 2011. The state hate-crime law covers gender identity or expression and carries additional penalties, consolidated and strengthened by legislation signed in June 2026 and effective 1 October 2026.

Identity documents are comparatively open. Since 1 October 2015, under H.B. No. 7006, a birth-certificate sex marker can be changed without surgery on a notarised affidavit from the applicant plus a notarised affidavit from a licensed physician, advanced practice registered nurse or psychologist stating that the person has received appropriate clinical treatment such as hormone therapy. That change replaced an earlier surgery requirement, which the Senate voted 32-3 to remove on 1 June 2015. Driver's licences and state identification can be changed on request, and birth certificates, IDs and licences offer M, F and X options.

Since 1 July 2018, people in Connecticut custody are treated consistent with their gender identity, including in strip searches and in access to clothing, commissary items and educational materials, and in housing based on recognised gender.

The state anti-bullying law prohibits bullying on the basis of gender identity and expression, explicitly covering cyberbullying and harassment, and applies to all school premises. In April 2021 a federal judge dismissed the lawsuits seeking to block transgender female athletes from competing in Connecticut girls' high-school sports, leaving their eligibility intact.

Conversion therapy on minors was banned with immediate effect after signing in May 2017, following House passage 141-8 on 2 May and Senate passage 36-0 on 10 May. The gay panic defence was repealed after unanimous passage in June 2019, signed by Governor Ned Lamont and effective 1 October 2019. Consensual same-sex sexual activity was decriminalised with effect from 1971, and the age of consent is 16 regardless of gender or sexual orientation, having been lowered to 15 in 1975.

66186276B99594608635082.summary:
Hawaii is a state of the United States and stands under the US federal framework; the national record carries federal law, passport rules and entry screening. The findings below concern Hawaii's own statutes and their application.

A July 2026 national legal-risk assessment, built from a rubric applied to thousands of tracked anti-trans bills covering youth-care bans, bathroom bans, birth-certificate and driver-licence restrictions and the withdrawal of legal recognition, places Hawaii in a fifteen-state Most Protective tier and describes the laws of that tier as having gone above and beyond in safeguarding transgender rights. The assessment is a rubric-based ranking of legislation rather than a measure of enforcement.

Hawaii holds a healthcare shield law or executive order, recorded as current on 27 September 2026, which protects patients and providers from civil or criminal charges where care that is lawful in Hawaii was banned in the patient's home state. For a trans visitor travelling from a state with a youth-care ban or another care restriction, this is the provision most directly relevant to obtaining care while in Hawaii.

State law prohibits discrimination on the basis of gender identity or expression in housing and public accommodations since 2005 and 2006, in employment since 2011, in insurance contracts since 1 July 2016, and in jury selection under legislation signed in June 2022 and effective 1 January 2023. The same 2022 legislation created a state LGBTIQ+ commission and mandated state health insurance coverage for sexual reassignment surgery.

The hate-crime statute covers actual or perceived gender identity or expression, defined to include a person's actual or perceived gender, gender identity, gender-related self image, appearance or expression, whether or not it differs from that traditionally associated with the person's sex at birth. The gay and trans panic defences were abolished by a bill passed in April 2019, signed on 26 June 2019 and effective immediately.

Changing a gender marker on state documents does not require surgery. Since a law passed on 5 May 2015, signed 14 July 2015 and effective immediately, transgender people may change the marker by request; an updated birth certificate requires a completed Application for Amendment to Birth Record and an affidavit from a licensed physician, and an updated driver's licence or state ID requires a Gender Designation Form completed by a medical or social professional confirming gender identity. An X sex option on driver's licences and birth certificates, passed in May 2019, signed 26 June 2019 and effective 1 July 2020, is available by request with no medical documentation required.

Health insurance provisions include coverage of sex reassignment surgeries under the 2016 insurance nondiscrimination rule, mandatory coverage effective 1 January 2023, and the inclusion of transgender individuals in health insurance planning under a bill passed in May 2022 with an emergency clause signed a month later and effective immediately, replacing male-only and female-only planning in place since 1980. Conversion therapy on minors has been banned since 1 July 2018.

Marriage is open to couples regardless of gender under the Hawaii Marriage Equality Act, passed by the Senate 20-4 on 30 October 2013 and by the House 30-19 on 8 November 2013, given final Senate approval 19-4 on 12 November 2013 and signed on 13 November 2013, with marriages beginning 2 December 2013. The 1998 constitutional amendment that authorised the legislature to reserve marriage to opposite-sex couples was repealed by referendum on 5 November 2024, with 55.94 per cent voting to delete the opposite-sex limitation from Article I Section 23. Reciprocal beneficiary relationships have existed since 1997, civil unions were signed on 23 February 2011 and effective 1 January 2012, and benefits for the partners of state employees have been provided since 1997.

Parentage rules have moved toward gender neutrality. A bill passed in April 2021 and signed in July 2021 recognised unmarried same-sex parentage with immediate effect, and Act 298, effective 1 January 2026, implements gender-neutral parentage by voluntary acknowledgment or court adjudication.

Consensual same-sex sexual activity has been lawful since the 1972 repeal took effect in 1973, replacing an 1850 anti-sodomy statute; the age of consent has been 16 regardless of gender or sexual orientation since 2001.

The national inventory of bathroom restrictions does not list Hawaii among the nine states and one territory that bar transgender people from sex-segregated facilities in schools or government buildings.

66186276B11383391196245.name: Illinois
66186276B11383391196245.summary:
Illinois is placed in the fifteen-state "Most Protective" tier of a July 2026 national legal-risk ranking compiled from a rubric over thousands of tracked anti-trans bills, which describes the tier's laws as having gone above and beyond in safeguarding trans rights.

Discrimination on the basis of gender identity has been banned in employment, housing, credit and public accommodations since 1 June 2006, with "sexual orientation" defined to include gender-related identity whether or not traditionally associated with the sex assigned at birth. The exemption for employers with fewer than 15 employees was removed by legislation signed in August 2019 and effective 1 July 2020, following a 2018 veto, and discrimination on the basis of sexual orientation in jury selection was banned effective 1 January 2020.

Hate-crime penalties were extended to gender identity by HB 3930, passed unanimously on 16 April and 20 May 2015, signed by Governor Bruce Rauner on 20 July 2015 and effective 1 January 2016; before that, such offences were covered only as perceived sexual orientation. The state's hate-crime statute has provided enhanced penalties for crimes motivated by actual or perceived sexual orientation since 1991. The gay and trans panic defence was repealed by SB1761, passed unanimously in June 2017, signed on 25 August 2017 and effective 1 January 2018.

Gender-affirming care is protected by legislation signed on 13 January 2023 and effective immediately, covering care provided within Illinois, including for people who travel from outside the state to obtain it. Under the shield law, patients and providers are protected from civil or criminal charges where care lawful in Illinois was banned in the patient's home state. Conversion therapy on minors under 18 by mental health providers has been banned under the Youth Mental Health Protection Act since 1 January 2016; a federal court dismissed a challenge brought by pastors on 15 February 2017, holding that private religious counselling is not trade or commerce.

Birth-certificate gender-marker changes no longer require surgery, under legislation passed on 31 May 2017 by 63-43 in the House and 32-22 in the Senate, signed on 25 August 2017 and effective 1 January 2018. An X option has been available since July 2020, and a self-attestation reform passed in January and February 2023 took effect on 1 July. Since 1 July 2024, people born outside Illinois can change the sex designation on an Illinois birth certificate. Driver's licences and state identification are corrected on a Gender Designation Change Form, with an X option available from 2024.

Single-occupancy public restrooms were designated gender-neutral by legislation passed 109-5 in the House and 53-0 in the Senate, signed in July 2019 and effective 1 January 2020. Chicago's Human Rights Ordinance, as amended in 2016, provides that each person determines their own gender identity, with no proof required beyond expression for bathroom access, and all Chicago public schools have had all-gender bathrooms by signage since December 2021. A May 2023 bill permitting use of multi-occupancy facilities consistent with a person's gender identity passed both chambers but had not been signed or vetoed.

Marriage equality was enacted by statute signed by Governor Pat Quinn on 20 November 2013 and effective 1 June 2014, after House approval 61-54 and Senate approval 32-21, superseding a 1996 statutory ban. Gender-neutral marriage certificates have been available under a July 2021 law, and 2023 legislation repealing out-of-jurisdiction null-and-void provisions took effect in 2024. Civil unions have been recognised since 1 June 2011 under a law signed on 31 January 2011, with out-of-state marriages of same-sex couples recognised as civil unions. The Illinois Domestic Violence Act is written in gender-neutral terms and applies to partners who share or have shared a dwelling or a dating relationship.

Private consensual same-sex sexual activity has been lawful since 1 January 1962, when a new criminal code eliminated the state's sodomy law, making Illinois the first state to do so. The age of consent is 17, raised from 16 effective 1 January 2012.

Discrimination on sexual orientation has been banned in employment, housing, public accommodations and credit since June 1, 2006, expanded by removal of the 15-employee loophole signed August 2019 effective July 1, 2020 after a 2018 veto, jury-selection discrimination on sexual orientation banned effective January 1, 2020 after unanimous passage in May 2019, and anti-bullying law expanded in 2014 to include sexual orientation. Hate-crime legislation since 1991 provides harsher penalties for crimes based on actual or perceived sexual orientation alongside race, religion, sex and other categories. Conversion therapy on minors under 18 by mental health providers was banned under the Youth Mental Health Protection Act passed 68-43 in the House on May 19, 2015 and 34-19 in the Senate on May 29, 2015 and signed August 20, 2015 effective January 1, 2016 after a 2014 bill failed 44-51, with a federal court dismissing pastors' suit on February 15, 2017 as private religious counseling is not trade or commerce.
