66186276B15934532614691.name: Massachusetts
66186276B15934532614691.summary:
Massachusetts prohibits discrimination on the basis of gender identity and expression in credit, public and private employment, union practices and housing under legislation enacted on 23 November 2011 and in force from 1 July 2012, following an executive order of 17 February 2011 that barred state government and its contractors from discriminating against transgender state employees. Public-accommodation coverage was added by a Senate vote of 33-4 on 12 May 2016 and a House vote of 117-36 on 7 July 2016, signed by Governor Charlie Baker and effective 1 October 2016, and was retained at the ballot on 6 November 2018 by 67.8 per cent to 32.2 per cent, the first statewide popular vote of its kind in the United States. For a visitor these are the operative rules in hotels, restaurants, shops, transport and other places open to the public.

Gender identity was written into the hate-crime statute with effect from 1 July 2012. The framework defines a hate crime as a criminal act accompanied by overt actions motivated at least in part by prejudice, including on grounds of gender and sexual orientation, and requires incidents to be collected, summarised and publicly reported through the Crime Reporting Unit created by the 1990 Hate Crimes Reporting Act, involving the State Police, the Attorney General and legislative committees, alongside a Governor's Task Force on Hate Crimes established in 1991.

The state issues its own identity documents on self-declared terms. Birth certificates may be amended to reflect gender identity without sex reassignment surgery. Non-binary X markers on driver's licences and state identification cards have been available since November 2019 under a Registry of Motor Vehicles regulation, and non-binary X birth certificates and amendment of gender on marriage certificates were authorised by law signed on 29 July 2024 in the FY25 budget. Marriage licence forms in Boston have carried no gender or sex field since August 2023. Name changes can be obtained confidentially without public notice under An Act Protecting Personal Security, signed on 25 November 2025.

Health care is protected in two directions. A shield law in place since 2022 protects patients and providers from civil or criminal charges where care lawful in Massachusetts was banned in the patient's home state; this is the provision most likely to matter to a visitor travelling from a state that has banned the care. In July 2022 both chambers passed and the Governor signed a bill codifying gender-affirming healthcare protections, which took effect immediately under an emergency clause rather than after the usual 90-day period. Conversion-therapy practices on minors were banned by legislation passed 147-8 in the House on 13 March 2019 and 34-0 in the Senate on 28 March 2019, enacted on 4 April 2019 and signed on 8 April 2019 with immediate effect, making Massachusetts the sixteenth state with such a ban.

Marriage is open to same-sex couples following the Supreme Judicial Court's ruling of 18 November 2003, with licences issued from 17 May 2004 after the 180-day legislative window; attempts at a constitutional amendment failed and ended in 2007. The 1913 bar on non-resident marriages was repealed on 31 July 2008, so a couple travelling to Massachusetts can marry there, and 2012 rulings treat out-of-jurisdiction civil unions and California registered domestic partnerships as equivalent to marriage.

Two provisions of the criminal code remain on the books unrepealed: section 34, criminalising the abominable and detestable crime against nature, and section 35, covering any unnatural and lascivious act. Private consensual adult conduct has been outside their reach since the Supreme Judicial Court's 1974 decision in Commonwealth v. Balthazar, and the provisions are unenforceable as applied to such conduct. Repeal attempts repeatedly stalled in committee, including through the 2018 session that removed the abortion, adultery and fornication laws but left the sodomy, anal-sex and oral-sex provisions; the Senate passed repeal unanimously in January 2024, the House advanced it in June 2025, and a Senate committee scheduled it for floor consideration on 24 July 2025. Massachusetts is the only New England state, and one of two northern states, that still carries legislative criminalisation of same-sex conduct. A trans visitor in a relationship that local law would read as same-sex under birth-sex status falls nominally within the statute's wording, though it is not enforced against private consensual conduct.

In a national legal-risk ranking published in July 2026, built from a rubric applied to thousands of tracked anti-trans bills covering youth-care bans, bathroom bans, birth-certificate and driver's-licence restrictions and removal of legal recognition, Massachusetts sits in the fifteen-state Most Protective tier.

66186276B2592965416524.summary:
New Mexico sits inside the United States framework, which governs passports, visas, entry screening and federal facilities; the state's own law is among the most protective in the country for transgender people. A July 2026 national legal-risk ranking, compiled by applying a rubric to thousands of tracked anti-trans bills covering youth care, bathroom access, birth-certificate and driver's-licence restrictions and the withdrawal of legal recognition, placed New Mexico in a fifteen-jurisdiction "most protective" tier.

State law has prohibited discrimination on the basis of gender identity in employment, housing, credit, public accommodations and union membership since 1 July 2003. The exemption for employers with fewer than fifteen employees was repealed effective 1 July 2019, legislation passed in 2023 extended coverage explicitly to local entities, counties, schools, universities and government-run agencies under an emergency clause, and Albuquerque aligned its Human Rights Ordinance with the state scheme in May 2024.

Violence committed on the basis of actual or perceived gender identity has been covered by the state hate-crime law since 2003, and the common-law gay and trans panic defence was repealed by HB68, signed on 9 March 2022. School-bullying legislation passed in March 2019 and effective 1 July 2019 requires districts to protect students on the basis of gender identity, with policies covering prohibition, reporting, investigation, discipline, prevention and staff training.

No statewide measure restricts trans people's use of sex-segregated facilities, and since 1 July 2019 single-occupancy restrooms in businesses and public facilities must be marked gender-neutral and be available to any person regardless of gender identity or sex.

Since 1 November 2019, trans people may change their legal gender without surgery. The legislation repealed a 1984 surgery requirement and provides male, female and X designations on birth certificates, driver's licences and state identification. A birth-certificate change requires a completed Request to Change Gender Designation on a Birth Certificate form and fees, with parental consent for minors; licences and state IDs require a Request for Sex Designation Change form filed with the Motor Vehicles Division. Those forms replaced an earlier requirement for a perjury statement from an institution or physician confirming surgical change plus a certified name-change order. State-issued documents carry no weight in federal passport and visa processing, which is set nationally.

Health care is protected by statute. HB7, adopted in March 2023, codified protection for gender-affirming care and sexual reassignment surgery for adults on request without restrictions, expressly including interstate travellers, and the state is recorded as holding a shield law or executive order dated 2023 by the MAP Transgender Healthcare Equality Map (data as of 27 September 2026). The shield protects patients and providers from civil or criminal charges where care that is lawful in New Mexico was banned in the patient's home state, which is the provision that matters most to a visitor travelling from a ban state. Gender-affirming care for minors is not banned here and the state is described as a sanctuary for transgender young people travelling from states that prohibit it. In 2026 the state health care authority announced it would use state funds to maintain Medicaid coverage for gender-affirming care after a federal rule to exclude it.

No state law bars transgender girls from school sports. Eligibility is determined by the original or amended birth certificate, and the New Mexico Activities Association has issued no further guidance on the question.

sources.summary: State law effective July 1, 2003 prohibits discrimination based on gender identity in employment, housing, credit, public accommodations and union membership, later expanded by repeal of the 15-or-more-employees exemption effective July 1, 2019 and by 2023 legislation explicitly covering local entities, counties, schools, universities and government-run agencies under emergency clause, with Albuquerque amending its Human Rights Ordinance in May 2024 to align. Since 2003 hate-crime law explicitly covers violence committed based on actual or perceived gender identity, and March 2019 school-bullying legislation protects students on the basis of gender identity and requires districts to adopt prohibition, reporting, investigation, disciplinary, prevention and staff-training policies effective July 1, 2019. Since November 1, 2019 transgender people may change legal gender without surgery under legislation repealing the 1984 surgery requirement and providing male, female and X neutral designation on birth certificates, driver's licenses and state IDs, passed 26-13 in the House and 33-14 in the Senate and signed by Governor Michelle Lujan Grisham. Applicants need only submit a completed Request to Change Gender Designation on a Birth Certificate form with fees, with parental consent for minors, and a Request for Sex Designation Change form to the Motor Vehicles Division for licenses and IDs, replacing the prior requirement for a perjury statement from an institution or physician of surgical change plus certified name-change order. Since July 1, 2019 businesses and public facilities with single-occupancy restrooms must mark them gender-neutral available to any person regardless of gender identity or sex under legislation passed 54-12 in the House and 23-15 in the Senate and signed by the Governor. In March 2023 HB7 codified protection for gender-affirming care and sexual reassignment surgery for adults on request without restrictions even for interstate travellers, making New Mexico a sanctuary state for transgender youths, while HB31 repealed the requirement to publish a legal name change in a newspaper that risked privacy, safety and lives of transgender individuals, and in 2026 the health care authority announced use of state funds to maintain Medicaid coverage for gender-affirming care after a federal rule to exclude it. In February 2022 the Legislature passed omnibus crime bill HB68 repealing the common-law gay and trans panic defence, signed March 9, 2022, and there is no state law prohibiting transgender girls' sports participation with eligibility determined by birth certificate original or amended and no further guidance from the New Mexico Activities Association. Consensual same-sex sexual activity has been legal since repeal of the anti-sodomy law in 1975, with a 1986 attempt to reinstate it failing. Same-sex couples have had the same marriage rights as different-sex couples since the December 19, 2013 state Supreme Court ruling requiring equal marriage rights, making New Mexico the 17th state to recognize same-sex marriage, with benefits for same-sex partners of state employees since 2003 and statutory codification passed 62-0 in the House and 39-0 in the Senate in March 2019, signed in April by Governor Michelle Lujan Grisham effective July 1, 2019. Single persons, same-sex couples and second-parent adoptions are permitted with no prohibition, lesbian couples may access in vitro fertilization and donor insemination regardless of sexual orientation or marital status with the non-genetic, non-gestational mother recognized as legal parent, and no statute or case law prohibits gestational or traditional surrogacy which courts generally recognize. State law effective July 1, 2003 prohibits discrimination based on sexual orientation in employment, housing, credit, public accommodations and union membership, supplemented by a 1985 executive order barring sexual-orientation discrimination in public employment, with enforcement upheld unanimously in Elane Photography v. Willock in 2013 for refusal to photograph a same-sex commitment ceremony. Since 2003 hate-crime law explicitly covers violence based on actual or perceived sexual orientation, and March 2019 school-bullying legislation protects students on the basis of sexual orientation effective July 1, 2019. Sexual orientation change efforts on minors are prohibited under SB121 passed 32-6 in the Senate and 44-23 in the House, signed April 7, 2017 by Governor Susana Martinez effective July 6, 2017. The common-law gay panic defence was repealed through omnibus crime bill HB68 passed in February 2022 and signed March 9, 2022 after unanimous Senate-only passages in 2019 and 2021 that died without House action. Historically the Navajo recognized four gender roles including nadleehi defined as a male-bodied person with a feminine nature, who due to perceived balance between sexes were typically chosen for certain societal and communal roles such as spiritual healers. They would traditionally wear female clothes and do female work, and some would have sexual relations with men which was accepted by the tribe, with similar recognized roles including Zuni lhamana and katsotse and equivalents among Mescalero Apache, Tiwa, Tewa and pueblos. As a result of colonization much of this cultural acceptance has disappeared, Navajo nadleehi became the subject of ridicule, and Christian converts among the Hopi were prohibited from attending the traditional snake dance because male cross-dressing could be observed. Will Roscoe is documented as writing about the "tolerance or even respect of transgender people" as fueling Spanish explorers' argument for colonization of native peoples and their lands in the name of Christianity. Today LGBTQ Navajo may find it difficult being accepted by family, with 70% of LGBT Navajo youth reportedly attempting suicide. Statewide polling showed 73% supported anti-discrimination legislation protecting LGBTQ people in 2018 and 64% supported a law covering sexual orientation and gender identity in 2017, while Santa Fe is cited as a gay capital and Albuquerque including its metropolitan area as a gay-friendly city.

66186276B43575054209436.name: New York
66186276B43575054209436.summary:
New York sits in the fifteen-state "Most Protective" tier of a July 2026 national legal-risk ranking built from a rubric applied to thousands of tracked anti-trans bills, covering youth-care bans, bathroom bans, birth-certificate and driver's-licence restrictions and the withdrawal of legal recognition. The same ranking places the least protective states at the opposite end, with prison terms of up to five years for youth-care provision and arrest policies for gender-identity bathroom use.

Gender identity and expression have been protected statewide in credit, housing, employment, education and public accommodations since the Gender Expression Non-Discrimination Act took effect in February 2019. That statute built on a 16 December 2009 executive order barring state agencies from gender-identity discrimination across hiring, termination, retention, appointment, promotion, tenure, recruitment and compensation, and on Division of Human Rights regulations issued 4 November 2015 and effective 20 January 2016 prohibiting transgender harassment and discrimination in those domains. A 2024 constitutional amendment explicitly bans discrimination on the basis of gender identity.

The Hate Crimes Act has covered gender identity and expression since 1 November 2019, with further anti-bias reform bills signed in November 2022. The gay and transgender panic defence was repealed in June 2019 with immediate effect, and conversion therapy on minors has been banned since 25 January 2019.

New York operates a shield or refuge law for gender-affirming care, listed as in force in equality-mapping data as of 27 September 2026. It protects patients and providers from civil or criminal charges when care that is legal in New York has been banned in the patient's home state, which bears directly on visitors travelling from states with youth-care bans.

Custody exposure is addressed by a shield statute of 25 June 2023, which bars New York courts from enforcing out-of-state orders that remove custody over youth gender-affirming care, bars treating that care as child abuse, and bars law-enforcement cooperation with out-of-state agencies. A New York City executive order of 12 June 2023 bars city resources from being used to detain, prosecute or investigate the provision or receipt of gender-affirming care; an Ithaca ordinance followed in September 2023 and City Council bills expanding provider protections were introduced in April 2025.

Identity documents are comparatively open. Since 2014 transgender adults have been able to change the gender on a New York birth certificate by notarized medical affidavit verifying surgery or a gender dysphoria diagnosis; a 2020 revision allows self-affirmation at 17 or older and change with parental consent below that age. The June 2021 Gender Recognition Act allowed an X marker on driver's licences and eased sealing of name and gender-change records. An X marker took effect on New York City birth certificates on 1 January 2019, on death certificates from 2 January 2020, was reported for state court and jury documents in November 2019 and in healthcare data from August 2020, and was approved for all state forms in April 2022 for 2023.

A law signed in December 2020 and effective 23 March 2021 mandates gender-neutral bathrooms. New York operates no state bathroom ban of the kind in force in nine states and one territory elsewhere, where trans use of facilities is restricted in schools or government buildings and in some cases made a criminal offence.

Nassau County is the one local exception: it bans transgender athletes from women's sports on county-run facilities. A 2025 ruling found no clear violation of anti-discrimination law in that ban, and a civil-liberties lawsuit seeking inclusion remains the mechanism challenging it.

Enforcement machinery has been reformed rather than turned against trans people. Former Penal Law Section 240.37, in force since 1976 and used by police to harass and arrest transgender individuals, was repealed in February 2021 with immediate effect. The 2009 executive order defines gender identity to include having or being perceived as having a gender identity, self-image, appearance, behaviour or expression whether or not different from sex assigned at birth, and requires equal-opportunity efforts, consistent guidelines and swift confidential investigation of complaints.

Sector-specific protections round out the position: the state anti-bullying law covers gender including gender identity and expression, including cyberbullying, in all public elementary and secondary schools, with a loophole closed in 2019; a June 2023 law explicitly includes gender identity in drug treatment and addiction programs; a November 2020 law requires annual judiciary statistics broken down by gender identity; and a November 2021 law effective 1 January 2022 requires utilities and municipalities to use residents' preferred names and pronouns.

Marriages are recognised without regard to the partners' sex under the Marriage Equality Act, in effect since 24 July 2011, so a trans visitor in a relationship that would be locally classed as same-sex can marry in New York and have that marriage recognised.

Mincolla on May 30, 2012 holds labeling someone gay or homosexual is no longer defamation, St. Patrick's Day parade bans ended September 2014 in New York City and November 2024 in Staten Island, and the 1985 law enabling municipalities to close gay bathhouses and saunas where high-risk sexual activities occur remains in effect as of August 2026. 66186276B97229519707655.summary:
Oregon sits in the fifteen-jurisdiction "Most Protective" tier of a July 2026 national legal-risk ranking compiled from a rubric covering thousands of tracked anti-trans bills, among them youth care bans, bathroom bans, birth-certificate and driver's licence restrictions, and measures removing legal recognition. The rubric describes the laws in this tier as having gone beyond baseline safeguarding of trans rights.

Statewide anti-discrimination law covers the settings a visitor uses daily. The Oregon Equality Act, signed 9 May 2007 as Senate Bill 2 and in force since 1 January 2008, prohibits discrimination in employment, housing, public accommodation, public education and public services on the ground of gender identity. Sexual orientation is defined to include gender identity regardless of whether a person's identity, appearance, expression or behaviour differs from what is traditionally associated with sex assigned at birth. The protections apply uniformly across the state and do not depend on the locality; religious employers, organisations and institutions are exempt.

Bias-motivated violence carries enhanced penalties: state hate-crime statutes add punishment for crimes committed because of the victim's gender identity. SB704, passed and signed in May 2021 and effective 1 January 2022, abolishes the gay panic and trans panic defences in murder, manslaughter and hate-crime cases.

Identity documents are comparatively accessible. Sex reassignment surgery has not been required to change the gender marker on a birth certificate by request since 2014. Legislation in May 2017 abolished the 1991 requirement that transgender people publish their names in newspapers before a legal change of sex. A circuit court ruling on 10 June 2016 allowed a resident to change gender to non-binary, which the Transgender Law Center believed was the first ruling of its kind in the country. An October 2019 executive order added gender identity to a 1987 policy barring state agencies from unlawful discrimination and required a third gender option X; legislation signed in June 2021 updated the 2008 definition of gender identity.

Care is shielded for people arriving from states that have banned it. Oregon's shield law, signed by Governor Tina Kotek on 13 July 2023, protects patients and providers from civil or criminal charges or investigation when care that is legal in Oregon was prohibited in the patient's home state. The House passed the bill in May 2023; the Senate passed a version with amendments after a Republican boycott.

Partner recognition does not turn on the parties' birth sex. Federal district judge Michael McShane struck down the 2004 constitutional amendment banning marriage for same-sex couples on 19 May 2014, marriages of same-sex couples performed elsewhere have been recognised since 16 October 2013, and gender-neutral marriage was codified effective 1 January 2016. Domestic partnerships have been available since 4 February 2008.

sources.summary: Since January 1, 2008 Oregon has banned unfair discrimination in employment, housing and public accommodations based on gender identity under the Oregon Equality Act signed May 9, 2007, where sexual orientation is defined to include gender identity regardless of whether identity, appearance, expression or behavior differs from that traditionally associated with assigned sex at birth, with an October 2019 executive order adding gender identity to a 1987 policy prohibiting state agencies from unlawful discrimination and requiring a third gender option X, and June 2021 legislation updating the 2008 definition of gender identity signed effective immediately. State hate crime statutes provide additional penalties for crimes committed based on the victim's gender identity, and SB704 passed and signed in May 2021 effective January 1, 2022 abolishes the gay panic and trans panic defenses in murder, manslaughter and hate crime cases. Since 2014 sex reassignment surgery has not been a requirement to change the gender marker on a birth certificate solely by request, a June 10, 2016 circuit court ruled a resident could legally change gender to non-binary in what the Transgender Law Center believed was the first ruling of its kind in the U.S., and since July 1, 2017 the Department of Motor Vehicles has offered X designating neutral or non-binary identity on licenses and IDs with X also available for birth certificates, while May 2017 legislation abolished the 1991 requirement for transgender people to publish names in newspapers before legal change of sex. In January 2013 as part of a discrimination settlement the state agreed to provide full medical insurance coverage for gender-affirming surgeries, drugs and related treatments for individuals on public employee health plans, and in August 2014 officials announced Medicaid would shortly begin covering gender-affirming hormone therapy and other gender-affirming healthcare. In May 2023 amid national backlash the House passed a bill to protect and defend gender-affirming healthcare especially for those entering Oregon from other states, frozen then passed in the Senate with watered-down amendments after a Republican boycott, signed July 13, 2023 by Governor Tina Kotek. A transgender-inclusive public schools policy survived challenge after the District Court ruled against plaintiffs July 24, 2018, the Ninth Circuit upheld February 12, 2020, and the Supreme Court denied certiorari in December 2020 in Parents for Privacy v. Barr, while April 2019 legislation signed May 6 amended a 1951 mental health law that equated transvestites with pedophilia after 58-2 House and 29-0 Senate votes. In July 2025 the 9th Circuit ruled the State adoption requirement to respect, accept and support a child's gender expression and sexual orientation was unconstitutional after the Department of Human Services prevented a woman seeking to adopt, and in June 2025 the U.S. Department of Education announced a Title IX investigation into the Oregon Department of Education for allowing transgender women to compete in women's sports. Oregon decriminalized same-sex sexual activity in 1972 after the 1971 repeal of the consensual sodomy law with an age of consent of 18, and a controversial lewd solicitation provision making it criminal to invite a person in a public place to have sexual intercourse was declared unconstitutional on free speech grounds in a unanimous 1981 Oregon Supreme Court decision. Same-sex marriage was legalized May 19, 2014 after Judge Michael McShane ruled the 2004 constitutional amendment banning such marriages via Ballot Measure 36 unconstitutional under the Equal Protection Clause, with same-sex marriages from other jurisdictions recognized since October 16, 2013 per Department of Justice opinion and gender-neutral marriage codified effective January 1, 2016, while domestic partnerships have been available since February 4, 2008 under the Family Fairness Act and benefits to same-sex partners of state employees have been provided since 1998. Since January 1, 2008 Oregon has banned unfair discrimination in employment, housing and public accommodations based on sexual orientation under the Equality Act signed May 9, 2007, and the anti-bullying law prohibits bullying including cyberbullying and harassment on the basis of sexual orientation among other categories in all public schools. State hate crime statutes provide additional penalties for crimes based on the victim's sexual orientation, and SB704 passed and signed in May 2021 effective January 1, 2022 abolishes the gay panic defense in murder, manslaughter and hate crime cases. Oregon became the third state to ban conversion therapy on minors after House 41-18 on March 17, 2015 and Senate 21-8 on May 7, 2015 votes, signed May 18, 2015 by Governor Kate Brown effective July 1, 2015. Same-sex couples whether unmarried or married may apply to adopt and lesbian couples have access to assisted reproduction such as in vitro fertilization with the non-genetic, non-gestational mother recognized as legal parent if married, while surrogacy is neither expressly prohibited nor permitted but courts are generally favorable including for same-sex couples.

66186276B98073251815399.name: Rhode Island
66186276B98073251815399.summary:
A July 2026 legal risk assessment map places Rhode Island in its most protective tier for gender-identity nondiscrimination. The map states that its top tier can no longer be considered most protective nationwide, so the ranking describes the state's own law rather than conditions a visitor will meet at every point of the journey.

Gender identity or expression has been protected against discrimination since 2001 in employment, credit, housing and public accommodations under R.I. Gen. Laws §§ 28-5-3, 28-5-7, 34-37-4, 34-37-4.3 and 11-24-2. Sexual orientation has been protected in the same fields since 1995. A bill signed in June 2023 added explicit bans on discrimination in patient care, nursing and related healthcare, and the exemption that had permitted discrimination in owner-occupied housing with three or fewer occupants was repealed with effect from 1 January 2023.

Hate-crime law under R.I. Gen. Laws § 42-28-46 provides penalty enhancements for crimes motivated by a victim's actual or perceived gender identity or expression. The gay and trans panic defence was repealed in June 2018 by votes of 68-2 in the House and 27-0 in the Senate, signed by Governor Gina Raimondo a month later and effective immediately.

State-issued identity documents are comparatively open. Since 23 October 2014 a birth certificate gender change has required a Birth Certificate Request Form and an affidavit from a physician, certified nurse practitioner or physician's assistant confirming transgender status, replacing an earlier surgery requirement. The Division of Motor Vehicles issues a corrected driver's licence on a Gender Designation Form signed by the applicant. An X option on driver's licences and birth certificates was announced in August 2019 and available from July 2020. A June 2018 law requires transgender people to be correctly recorded on death certificates. Passports and visas are issued under national rules and are not covered by this record.

Single-occupancy toilets may legally be designated gender-neutral from 1 January 2022 under a bill signed in July 2021.

Rhode Island is covered by shield laws or executive orders from the 2023 and 2024 batches, which make protections enforceable against out-of-state action.

Conversion therapy on minors and state funding for such practices were prohibited by a law signed on 19 July 2017 by Governor Raimondo and effective immediately, after House votes of 69-0 and 62-0 and a Senate vote of 29-0.

In March 2025 the Rhode Island Interscholastic League updated its transgender athletes policy. Transgender athletes remain able to compete, but member schools are responsible for ensuring compliance with all applicable state and federal law when determining gender-based eligibility, replacing a policy that allowed participation consistent with gender identity.

As of July 2026 Vermont is listed among the most protective states on gender-identity nondiscrimination. State law bans discrimination based on gender identity in employment, public accommodations, education, housing, credit, insurance and union practices. The provision was added after a 2006 veto, passed again in 2007, was signed by Governor Jim Douglas on 22 May 2007 and took effect on 1 July 2007. For a visitor the public-accommodations coverage is the operative part: hotels, restaurants, shops and service providers fall under it.

The gay and trans panic defence was abolished and repealed by legislation that passed the House 144-1 in March 2021 and the Senate 29-0 in April 2021, was signed by Governor Phil Scott on 5 May 2021 and took effect on 1 July 2021.

Single-user public bathrooms have had to be marked gender-neutral since 1 July 2018, under a bill signed in May 2018.

Vermont's shield laws, enacted in 2023 and 2024, are enforceable against out-of-state action and place the state among those protecting transgender and non-binary people who travel in for gender-affirming healthcare; the 2023 measure took effect immediately by emergency clause.

Partner recognition is settled. Civil unions were introduced in July 2000 as the first state status identical to marriage, following a 1999 Vermont Supreme Court ruling on equal marriage benefits, and marriage for same-sex couples has been legal since 1 September 2009, the first state to adopt it through the legislature and governor rather than a court decision.

Texas. 66186276B98555229882405.name: Washington
66186276B98555229882405.summary:
Washington operates under the United States framework on passports, entry screening, federal facilities and federal custody, which are set nationally. State law and state institutions govern health care, insurance, the state prison system and state ballot measures.

A July 2026 legal-risk assessment of United States anti-trans measures places Washington among the most protective states in the country. The same assessment flags two Washington ballot initiatives, I-001 and I-638, due for a November vote, as targeting transgender residents; whether they pass decides whether that protective posture holds.

Washington has shield laws or executive orders from the 2023 and 2024 batches that are enforceable against out-of-state action, and a nationwide tracker of such measures lists the state among those covered. For a trans visitor who travels to Washington for gender-affirming care, these measures bear on whether another state's action can reach care provided in Washington.

State correctional practice carries a documented reversal. Washington state prisons have been legally required since October 2023, under court order and rulings, to provide gender-affirming healthcare and, where indicated, sex-reassignment surgery to inmates. In July 2024 a transgender woman prisoner was transferred out of a women's prison back to a men's prison as punishment for consensual sex with a cisgender inmate of the women's prison, so housing assigned by birth sex functioned as the disciplinary sanction.

64170238B96397749018979.name: Monaco
64170238B96397749018979.summary:
Same-sex intimacy has been lawful in Monaco since the 18th century, and the age of consent is 15 for same-sex and opposite-sex relationships alike. Hate crime and hate speech on the ground of sexual orientation are criminalised. Discrimination on the grounds of sexual orientation and gender identity is not banned, and reported discrimination is described as rare; one travel guide states that such discrimination is illegal only in certain contexts, which conflicts with the country overviews reporting no general prohibition.

Loi n° 1.299 of 15 July 2005 on public freedom of expression bans hate speech and incitement to hatred and violence based on sexual orientation. Article 234-2 of the Civil Code, amended by Loi n° 1.435 of 8 November 2016, punishes threats based on sexual orientation with 2 to 5 years' imprisonment and related offences with 6 months to 3 years. Law n° 1.478 of 12 November 2019 added sexual orientation to Civil Code articles 238-1, 239 and 421, covering violent acts not causing total incapacity (6 months to 1 year), attacks on a partner or co-resident (10 years), and unprovoked attacks on a person or group (5 years).

The provisions cited in the sources name sexual orientation; none of them names gender identity. A trans visitor has no equivalent statutory protection on the face of the text.

Enforcement is documented. In July 2010 a Monegasque court jailed a man for five days and fined him €5,000 for openly homophobic rhetoric against a gay man.

Legal gender recognition is not available. Transgender people cannot alter their legal gender in Monaco, and ILGA-Europe's 2019 ranking placed Monaco 45th of 49 European countries. A trans visitor's identity documents will not correspond to any Monegasque recognition procedure, because none exists.

Partner recognition is limited. Monaco does not recognise same-sex marriage and same-sex couples have no right to adopt. Since 27 June 2020 same-sex couples may sign a contrat de vie commune, signed before a notary and deposited at a public registry; cohabiting couples are treated like siblings for inheritance tax rather than like married couples, and the arrangement is also open to siblings and to parents and children. Same-sex partners have no equal succession rights, survivor pensions or parental leave. For a trans visitor whose relationship would be read as same-sex under Monegasque law, none of these routes produces spousal recognition.

Anti-discrimination legislation has repeatedly failed. The 2011 anti-discrimination bill's article 44 would have required a school programme in every year of the primary and secondary cycles to sensitise pupils against racism and the other article 1 discriminations, including sexual orientation. The Council of Government did not approve the bill, and the replacement introduced on 18 December 2012 dropped the sexual-orientation provisions.

Visibility is low. Roughly ten people are openly out in Monaco, and LGBTIQ visibility in the principality is described as limited. Most Monegasques affiliate with the Catholic Church, which regards homosexuality and transgender identity as immoral. Béatrice Fresko-Rolfo, a Council of Europe rapporteur, described the position as the sad record of Monaco.

There is no Pride in Monaco and no official gay bars, clubs or events; visitors travel to France or Italy for Pride, and the nearest comparable scenes are in Marseille, Nice and Lyon. Some gay-friendly establishments operate with community support.

The US State Department's 2023 human rights report for Monaco recorded no significant changes and no reports of torture, arbitrary detention or other abuses. The significant issues it identified were the libel and lèse-majesté laws, which it described as not enforced.

sources.summary: Outright International country overview (last updated 12 March 2026): same-sex intimacy legal but very few protections — hate crimes and hate speech on sexual orientation are penalised, while discrimination on grounds of sexual orientation and gender identity is not banned (reported discrimination is described as rare); same-sex couples have no marriage or adoption, and LGBTIQ visibility in the principality is limited.

French gay travel guide Monaco page: no gay Pride is held anywhere in Monaco (visitors are sent to France or Italy for one); the ~200-hectare state is pitched as a luxury/relaxation destination with an LGBTQ+-welcoming accommodation directory but no discernible local scene.

US State Department 2023 Human Rights Report for Monaco: no significant changes; significant issues limited to libel and lèse-majesté laws (not enforced); no torture, arbitrary detention or other abuses reported.

Nice-Matin via Monaco Haut Commissariat (March 2025, French): homosexuality decriminalised since the 18th century, yet Monaco ranks near the bottom of European LGBT-rights rankings — no equal succession, survivor pensions or parental leave for same-sex partners; roughly 10 people dare to be openly out; Council of Europe rapporteur Béatrice Fresko-Rolfo: "C’est le triste bilan de Monaco".

Queer In The World Monaco guide (updated 3 December 2023): homosexuality legal and SOGI discrimination illegal only in certain contexts — limited protections with room for improvement; advises visitors to stay current with local laws and customs.

sources.summary: Wikipedia country coverage: Hate-speech protection rests on Loi n° 1.299 of 15 July 2005 on public freedom of expression, which bans hate speech and incitement to hatred and violence based on sexual orientation. Article 234-2 of the Civil Code, amended by Loi n° 1.435 of 8 November 2016 (technological crime law), punishes threats based on sexual orientation with 2–5 years' imprisonment and related offences with 6 months–3 years. In July 2010 a Monegasque court jailed a man for 5 days and fined him €5,000 for openly homophobic rhetoric against a gay man. Law n° 1.478 of 12 November 2019 added 'sexual orientation' to Civil Code articles 238-1 (6 months–1 year for violent acts not causing total incapacity), 239 (10 years for attacking a partner or co-resident) and 421 (5 years' probation for unprovoked attacks on a person or group). Monaco does not recognize same-sex marriage, and ILGA-Europe's 2019 ranking (45th of 49 European countries) notes that transgender people cannot alter their legal gender. Since 27 June 2020 same-sex couples may sign a cohabitation agreement (contrat de vie commune), introduced in Parliament on 16 April 2018, unanimously approved by the National Council on 4 December 2019 and in force six months after publication in the Journal de Monaco; it is signed before a notary and deposited at a public registry. Cohabiting couples are treated like siblings for inheritance tax, not like married couples, and the arrangement is also open to siblings and parents/children. Same-sex couples have no right to adopt children. The LGBT community supports some gay-friendly establishments inside Monaco, but there are no official gay bars, clubs or events in the country, unlike nearby French cities Marseille, Nice and Lyon. Monaco is not an EU member, so EU LGBT-rights protections do not bind it, though it has strong cultural and economic ties with France. Monaco has no armed forces, only a National Guard; France handles defence and allows openly gay, lesbian, bisexual and transgender people to serve. The age of consent is 15 for both same-sex and opposite-sex relationships. The 2011 anti-discrimination bill's article 44 would have required a school programme every year of primary and secondary cycles to sensitise against racism and all article 1 discriminations (including sexual orientation), but the Council of Government did not approve the bill and its 18 December 2012 replacement dropped the sexual-orientation provisions. Same-sex couples' inability to adopt children directly affects family formation for youth, and most Monegasques affiliate with the Catholic Church, which regards homosexuality and transgender identity as immoral.

Anti-discrimination protection for sexual orientation and gender identity is not in force. The 2011 bill's article 44 school-sensitisation requirement was not approved by the government, and the 18 December 2012 replacement dropped the sexual-orientation provisions.

Most residents affiliate with the Catholic Church, which regards homosexuality and transgender identity as immoral.

No enforcement data is available for the 2019 amendments to the civil code, and no trans-specific violence figures for the country were identified in the sources.

SYN-ABW.name: Aruba
SYN-ABW.summary:
Aruba is a constituent territory within the Kingdom of the Netherlands. Its own Criminal Code (Wetboek van Strafrecht / Kódigo Penal), enacted in 2012, carries the anti-discrimination provisions that apply on the island.

Same-sex sexual activity is legal for both male and female forms, and the age of consent is 16, equal for heterosexual and homosexual intercourse.

Article 1:221 of the Criminal Code defines discrimination as any form of discrimination, exclusion, restriction or preference that has the purpose or effect of affecting recognition, enjoyment or the exercise of human rights and fundamental liberties in political, economic, social or cultural fields or in other areas of social life. Articles 2:61 and 2:62 provide penalties ranging from fines to one year of imprisonment. The enumerated grounds cover sexual orientation only; gender identity and gender expression are not addressed anywhere in the provision. A trans visitor therefore has no statutory ground of protection against discrimination in Aruba.

On 12 July 2024 the Supreme Court of the Netherlands upheld the Appeals Court decision barring discrimination based on sexual orientation, in the ruling that made same-sex marriage legal in Aruba. Since the Dutch Supreme Court ruling of 13 April 2007, Aruba must recognise same-sex marriages registered in the Netherlands and in Bonaire, Sint Eustatius and Saba.

On 8 September 2016 the Staten of Aruba passed a civil-code amendment opening registered unions to same-sex couples by 11 votes to 5, with four abstentions, after a 2.5-year campaign sponsored by openly gay MP Desirée de Sousa-Croes and an Igualdad Aruba petition of nearly 20,000 signatures. The amendment extends the marriage articles of the civil code to those registered unions and grants spousal pension succession and emergency medical decision-making rights. Aruba's own news service reported the vote as making the island the first in the Caribbean to act. A same-sex marriage bill introduced in June 2022 was rejected after tied parliamentary votes in May and June 2024.

Marriages performed in the Netherlands were already recognised throughout the Kingdom, and the bill's sponsor had used exactly that route. The Associated Press reported that religious and cultural opposition to the measure was strong, and that neither Sint Maarten nor Curaçao allowed such unions at the time.

Charlene and Esther Oduber-Lamer reported frequent harassment and having rocks thrown at them during their court challenge of 2004 to 2007, which forced Aruba and the other Dutch Caribbean islands to recognise same-sex marriage. The Aruban government was particularly vocal in opposing same-sex marriage during that court challenge, and the Roman Catholic Church, the island's largest denomination, contributed to mainstream societal opposition.

On 22 April 2015 representatives of all Kingdom governments endorsed prompt equal rights for LGBT persons expressly including transgender persons on Aruba, Curaçao and Sint Maarten. Aruba's own representation at that endorsement acknowledged that strict conservative norms made coming out difficult for LGBT youth on the island, who were stigmatised as disordered.

The official Aruba tourism board markets the island as an established LGBT destination, positioning feeling safe, secure and welcome as the foundation of the offering and quoting a repeat visitor of nearly 20 years who reports never encountering mistreatment or discrimination based on sexual orientation. This is the destination's own marketer speaking, not independent evidence, but it documents mainstream tourism positioning.

GlobalGayz describes Aruba as tolerant and mostly open with a smaller, quieter out-and-proud LGBT population than Curaçao, and notes that same-sex adoption is legal. Several gay bars and clubs operate in the capital city of Oranjestad, and various venues, hotels and restaurants cater to or advertise as LGBT-friendly. Numerous LGBT associations operate, including Equality Aruba (Igualdad Aruba), Equal Rights Aruba and Alternative Lifestyle Federation Aruba; the last is quoted: 'Aruba has always been accepting, as long as it's not in their face. People are out, but discreetly out. There has never been anything official.'

sources.summary: On 22 April 2015 representatives of all Kingdom governments endorsed prompt equal rights for LGBT persons expressly including transgender persons on Aruba, Curaçao and Sint Maarten, and Aruba's representation acknowledged that strict conservative norms made coming out difficult for LGBT youth in Aruba who were stigmatized as disordered.

SYN-ABW.tangentialFactors:
Aruba is frequently described as one of the Caribbean's most LGBT-friendly islands, and the Associated Press noted that at the time of the 2016 vote neither Sint Maarten nor Curaçao allowed same-sex unions. That comparison concerns sexual-orientation rights; it does not establish any differential treatment of trans visitors, and Aruba's anti-discrimination statute still omits gender identity.

The Kingdom-level endorsement of 22 April 2015 expressly named transgender persons among those due equal rights, but it is a statement of intent by Kingdom governments rather than an enforceable provision in Aruba's Criminal Code. The gap between that endorsement and the sexual-orientation-only wording of Articles 1:221, 2:61 and 2:62 is unresolved in the sources.

Public hostility documented on the island has been directed at visible same-sex couples rather than at trans people specifically. The Oduber-Lamer harassment of 2004 to 2007 and the Catholic Church's role in opposing the 2016 amendment indicate that visibility, not legal status alone, has driven risk.
SYN-ABW.localsOnly:
Aruba's own representation at the 22 April 2015 Kingdom endorsement acknowledged that strict conservative norms made coming out difficult for LGBT youth on the island, who were stigmatised as disordered. That statement is a local admission about resident conditions, not a visitor-facing finding.

Residents who are read as gender-nonconforming have no enumerated ground of protection under Articles 1:221, 2:61 and 2:62 of the Criminal Code, which name sexual orientation only. Local advocacy organisations, including Equality Aruba (Igualdad Aruba), Equal Rights Aruba and Alternative Lifestyle Federation Aruba, operate on the island, but the sources do not document any of them providing trans-specific legal representation.

Same-sex adoption is legal in Aruba, and registered unions open to both opposite-sex and same-sex couples have been available since the 8 September 2016 vote. A same-sex marriage bill introduced in June 2022 was rejected after tied parliamentary votes in May and June 2024, before the 12 July 2024 Supreme Court ruling made same-sex marriage legal.
SYN-ABW.outOfScopeNotes:
No source in this inventory documents airport or border screening practice in Aruba that treats binders, packers, breast forms or gender presentation differently from other travellers, and no source addresses gender markers on passports or identity documents as issued or read in Aruba. Whether Aruban authorities inspect or question documents whose gender marker does not match the holder's presentation is unresolved.

No source addresses access to gender-affirming healthcare, hormone prescriptions or their customs treatment for visitors, and none addresses bathroom or facility access rules on the island. These remain not sourced rather than absent.

No source records any hate-crime or violence incident in Aruba against a trans person specifically. The documented harassment (the Oduber-Lamer case, 2004 to 2007) concerns a same-sex couple; whether comparable conduct against a trans resident or visitor would be prosecuted is unresolved.

The 22 April 2015 Kingdom endorsement naming transgender persons is a political statement by Kingdom governments. Whether it has been implemented in Aruban statute or practice is not sourced here.

SYN-AIA.name: Anguilla
SYN-AIA.summary:
Anguilla is a British Overseas Territory and the law that governs a visitor is local law; United Kingdom legislation reaches the island only where an Order in Council extends it, so no United Kingdom-level anti-discrimination floor applies of its own force.

Private consensual same-sex conduct was decriminalised by order of the Privy Council on 5 January 2001, in a decision that also covered the Cayman Islands, the British Virgin Islands, Montserrat and the Turks and Caicos Islands. The order was issued unilaterally after the local legislatures refused to repeal their statutes, and religious leaders protested the decision. Anguilla had never carried the prohibition in exactly the same statutory form as those other territories.

Anguillian law provides no protection against discrimination on grounds of sexual orientation or gender identity. The Constitution's anti-discrimination clause reaches race, political opinions, colour, creed, sex and place of origin, so gender identity sits outside the protected categories and a trans visitor has no statutory non-discrimination footing in local law.

The age of consent is 18 for same-sex conduct and 16 for different-sex conduct. A trans visitor in what would be locally classed as a same-sex relationship therefore carries legal exposure that a different-sex couple does not face.

The Marriage Act defines marriage as the union of a man and a woman as husband and wife. Same-sex marriage and civil unions are not legal, and Anguilla is among the British overseas territories that have not legislated for civil partnerships. A commercial destination-wedding service marketing ceremonies on the island states that same-sex marriage is not recognised under Anguillan law, so a trans visitor in what would be locally classed as a same-sex relationship has access only to a symbolic, non-legal ceremony. Non-legal ceremonies of same-sex couples have taken place there.

Public LGBT life is highly constrained. A subdued and subtle climate of homophobia has pushed local LGBT people toward secrecy. The island has no pride events, gay organisations, venues, bars or clubs and no community infrastructure, which the source attributes to a population of about 15,000. The only recorded public event is a small protest on 17 May 2011 in The Valley marking the International Day Against Homophobia, Transphobia and Biphobia.

Visiting same-sex couples have described the island as gay-friendly and reported that nobody was discriminatory in any way, though the same source cautions that the position of local people may differ. A 2023 first-person account by a queer family found same-sex conduct legal under the British order but the scene muted rather than openly visible, an outcome that account attributes to decriminalisation imposed from outside rather than to local initiative.

SYN-BES.name: Bonaire Sint Eustatius and Saba
SYN-BES.summary:
Bonaire, Sint Eustatius and Saba are three special municipalities within the Kingdom of the Netherlands. The civil-status and anti-discrimination law in force on the islands is Dutch national law, applied there in the same form as in the European Netherlands, with no separate island legislation on marriage or discrimination operating alongside it.

No source in the inventory describes any provision that addresses trans visitors directly. The protection that exists is carried by marriage registration and general anti-discrimination law, not by text naming gender identity, gender markers or facilities.

Travel coverage published by GayCities on 14 December 2022 and updated 1 September 2023 places Bonaire fifth among destinations in the Caribbean and Latin America that celebrate marriage equality, citing its standing as part of the Netherlands, under whose strict anti-discrimination laws it says citizens and visitors are protected, and describing same-sex couples as warmly welcomed.

Registered unions for same-sex couples have been available in the islands since 2012. The first was recorded by the Census Office in Saba on 4 December 2012: Cedeno Xiomar Gonzalez, an Aruban national aged 26, and Israel Ernesto Ruiz Pinto, a Venezuelan national aged 27. Neither man was resident on Saba and both were visiting, which establishes that the island registry performs ceremonies for couples who are only passing through.

Saba Tourism's weddings page states that civil ceremonies run routinely through the island registry, that the Court Room in the Administrative Building is the simplest venue for an efficient ceremony, and that registrar Julieta Woods is flexible with couples' wishes. Caterers, florists and accommodation serving destination weddings operate on the island.

SYN-BLM.name: Saint Barthélemy
SYN-BLM.summary:
Saint Barthélemy is a French overseas collectivity, and the national framework of France applies here as it does in metropolitan France: its criminal law, identity documents, anti-discrimination statute and marriage regime govern the island.

Medical capacity is the sharpest practical constraint. The island covers about 8 square miles and holds roughly 10,000 residents, and the single red flag recorded against it in an aggregate travel-safety rating is limited healthcare access. Prescriptions and ongoing gender-affirming treatment cannot be assumed to be available locally, and a visitor who depends on either should carry supplies and confirm provision before arrival.

The same aggregate index rates Saint Barthélemy 7.7 out of 10, counting nine positive rights against the one healthcare red flag.

Anyone detained in Saint Barthélemy falls under the French prison administration, whose placement policy recognises only biological sex; trans detainees, overwhelmingly women, are held under birth sex. The controller-general of detention places, in an opinion of 25 May 2021 drawing on about 40 referrals received since 2010, found that serious violations of fundamental rights persist across places of detention, with recommendations that also cover intersex and non-binary persons.

Socially the island is discreet rather than permissive. It has no LGBTQ venues, no Pride events and no visible scene; same-sex couples attract no attention, crime is low, and the sources record no hostility toward gay or trans visitors. The luxury-yacht economy has long welcomed gay couples, and hospitality staff are described as trained for a diverse clientele.

Politically, Saint Barthélemy's joint deputy with Saint Martin was among 11 overseas deputies who voted against the 2013 law opening marriage to same-sex couples.

sources.summary: French prison-system reporting: the controller-general of detention places finds trans detainees — overwhelmingly women held under birth-sex placement — suffer the most in prison; administration policy recognises only biological sex (a 2011 Nantes case placed a trans woman in a men's prison). BLM detainees fall under this French system.

France's Contrôleur général des lieux de privation de liberté opinion of 25 May 2021 on transgender persons in places of deprivation of liberty draws on about 40 referrals since 2010. It finds serious violations of fundamental rights persist across places of detention, with recommendations applicable also to intersex and non-binary persons.

The French framework applies in Saint Barthélemy: legal gender-marker change without surgery or sterilisation, hormone therapy and surgery available since 1975, anti-discrimination coverage; non-binary recognition limited.

Full equality under French law applies across about 8 square miles and about 10,000 residents. The luxury-yacht economy has long welcomed gay couples, with no visible scene; discretion is the norm and same-sex couples attract no attention.

Aggregate rating 7.7/10, with 9 positive rights and 1 red flag: legal gender change without surgery, anti-discrimination law in place but limited healthcare access. No government LGBT+ travel advice exists; FCDO shows no warnings. No trans-specific visitor tips have been submitted.

Low crime, an open and accepting culture, no Pride-specific events, and staff trained for diverse guests. Visitors are high-end and discreet; there are no LGBTQ venues or scene, and no hostility is noted.

sources.title: LGBTQ rights in Saint Barthélemy (Wikipedia)
sources.summary: French law banned discrimination on the basis of "sexual identity" in July 2012 and replaced that term with "gender identity" by the law of 18 November 2016 amending article 225-1 of the Penal Code; Chapter 2 of the Labour Code prohibits exclusion from recruitment, internships or training and sanction, dismissal or discriminatory measures on account of gender identity. Since 1 January 2017 transgender people have been allowed to change legal gender without sex reassignment surgery, sterilisation, psychiatrist certificates or medical diagnosis under the law signed 18 November 2016 after Constitutional Council approval on 17 November 2016, but they must go before a court to change the gender marker while first-name change can be done at the registry office. France legalised gender affirmative surgery domestically in 1979, removed gender identity disorder as a diagnosis by decree in 2010 as the first country to declassify gender dysphoria, with transsexualism remaining under ALD 31 with treatment funded by Sécurité Sociale, though transgender rights organizations stated nothing changed beyond the announcement. A 2022 ILGA-Europe report found lack of self-determination, extended waiting times and inequitable access by location for gender affirming healthcare and recommended informed consent and self-determination, while the National Academy of Medicine characterized increased demand as an "epidemic-like phenomenon" advising extreme caution without changing practice, and in late 2024 the French Society of Pediatric Endocrinology and Diabetology issued first guidelines recommending puberty blockers plus calcium and vitamin D from at least Tanner stage 2. In 2017 transphobia became an aggravating circumstance for all crimes punishable by prison, and police identified around 1,870 victims of transphobic and homophobic attacks in 2019, up 36% from around 1,380 in 2018. Conversion therapy was legally banned by a bill passed by the Senate on 7 December 2020, concurred by the National Assembly on 25 January 2022 and published 1 February 2022, with proposed punishments of two years' imprisonment and/or a 30,000 euro fine. A Senate-passed bill of May 2024 to ban medical transition under age 18, following a March 2024 Senate-commissioned report criticizing youth care, is opposed by the Macron government, unlikely to pass the National Assembly and had no update since 23 July 2024. All sodomy laws were repealed in 1791 during the French Revolution with no mention of private same-sex relations in the Penal Codes of 1791 and 1810, while a 1960 ordinance inserting article 330 alinea 2 doubling the penalty for indecent exposure for homosexual activity, adopted via the Mirguet amendment, was repealed in 1980, and the discriminatory age of consent raised to 21 for homosexual relations versus 15 for heterosexual in 1942 and lowered to 18 in 1974 was equalised at 15 on 4 August 1982 under President François Mitterrand. In March 2024 the National Assembly unanimously passed a bill for compensation to gay men arrested under Article 330 prior to 1980, still awaiting Senate vote. National legislation since 1985 prohibits sexual orientation discrimination in employment, housing and public and private goods and services, and the law of 31 December 2004 criminalised homophobic comments with a maximum penalty of 45,000 euro fine and/or 12 months' imprisonment and increased penalties when physical assault or murder is motivated by sexual orientation, enforced with the first conviction in January 2006 later cancelled by the Court of Cassation. Civil solidarity pacts (PACS) were enacted in 1999 for same-sex and unmarried opposite-sex couples, and same-sex marriage became legal nationwide including all overseas departments and territories after National Assembly approval 12 February 2013 by 329-229, Senate approval 12 April, Constitutional Council validation 17 May 2013, presidential signature 18 May 2013 and first ceremony 29 May in Montpellier, with joint adoption legal since May 2013. The historic MSM blood-donation ban dating to 20 June 1983 was recalled 12 January 2009, replaced by one-year abstinence from 10 July 2016, reduced to four months from 2 April 2020, and fully removed 16 March 2022 so policy applies regardless of sexual orientation. Same-sex marriage is legal in Saint Barthélemy but its joint deputy with Saint Martin was among 11 overseas deputies voting against, while Guadeloupe, Martinique, Saint Martin and Saint Barthélemy are noted for gay bars, discos, saunas and beaches, and Saint Barthélemy's reputation as an international celebrity tourist destination is stated to have produced a more open and relaxed social climate for LGBTQ people than other French Caribbean territories. President Emmanuel Macron in October 2018 denounced homophobic violence as "unworthy of France" and announced future concrete measures after a rise in attacks.

SYN-BLM.tangentialFactors:
Among the French Caribbean territories, Saint Barthélemy's standing as an international celebrity destination is credited with a more open and relaxed social climate for LGBTQ people than Guadeloupe, Martinique or Saint Martin.

The island's small size and its dependence on a luxury-tourism economy shape both the absence of an organised scene and the discretion expected of visitors, in contrast to the larger French Caribbean territories.
SYN-BLM.localsOnly:
Residents who need ongoing gender-affirming care face the same capacity limit that constrains visitors: the island's small size and population support only limited medical services, and specialist provision is not assured locally.

The collectivity's representation in the national legislature voted against the 2013 marriage law, and the island has no LGBTQ venue, Pride event or visible organising of its own.
SYN-BLM.outOfScopeNotes:
No government LGBT+ travel advice specific to Saint Barthélemy exists, and the UK FCDO records no warnings for the collectivity. No trans-specific visitor tips have been submitted to the aggregate index.

The aggregate rating of 7.7 out of 10, with nine positive rights and one red flag, is a composite score rather than a legal finding, and its components are not itemised in the source.

Accounts of the island's LGBTQ infrastructure conflict: one source lists gay bars, discos, saunas and beaches among the French Caribbean territories including Saint Barthélemy, while island-level guides report no LGBTQ venue or scene. The discrepancy is unresolved.

SYN-BMU.name: Bermuda
SYN-BMU.summary:
Bermuda is a British Overseas Territory where local legislation governs. United Kingdom law, including the Equality Act 2010 and its 2025 single-sex services code, does not extend automatically and could be applied only by Order in Council.

Bermuda has no legal recognition of transgender people. The Human Rights Act has prohibited discrimination on grounds of sexual orientation since 2013, when the Senate passed the Human Rights Amendment Act, which also banned age discrimination; gender identity is not covered, leaving trans people without statutory protection against discrimination. The sources identify no transgender-specific provisions on documents, screening, facilities, custody, healthcare, penalties or protection machinery.

Expression of gender identity is described as often difficult. In 2006 the Government attempted to bar Mark Anderson, the drag performer known as "Queen of Bermuda" Sybil, from a parade, stating that he contradicted local mores and sensitivities.

Consensual sex between adult men is legal. The House of Assembly voted 22–16 on 14 May 1994 to decriminalise it, striking two sections of the Criminal Code; the debate divided the island, with religious leaders split and the Christian Coalition staging marches against the change. Prior liability carried up to ten years' imprisonment for anal and oral sex. Lesbian activity has never been illegal, and the gross indecency provision between men was repealed in 2019.

The age of consent is unequal: 18 for consensual anal intercourse under the law effective 1 November 2019, against 16 for other sexual activity. A prior higher age of 18 for gay male conduct had been found in violation of the European Convention on Human Rights.

Same-sex marriage is not legally available as of 2022. The Supreme Court legalised it in May 2017 in the Godwin and DeRoche case under the Marriage Act 1944 and the Human Rights Act. The Governor gave assent to the Domestic Partnership Act on 7 February 2018, effective 1 June 2018, replacing marriage with domestic partnerships open to same-sex and opposite-sex couples and making Bermuda the first jurisdiction to revoke marriage equality. The Supreme Court restored marriage on 6 June 2018 and the Court of Appeal on 23 November 2018, but the Judicial Committee of the Privy Council banned it again on 14 March 2022, with July 2022 laws retrospectively backdating prior legality. Recognition of a partner therefore rests on the partnership register.

sources.summary: Bernews (Feb 2018): Bermuda's Governor gave assent to the Domestic Partnership Act 2017, replacing same-sex marriage with domestic partnerships for both same-sex and heterosexual couples - the reversal that made Bermuda the first jurisdiction to revoke marriage equality.

Bermuda's AME and other churches protested a gay cruise (Norwegian Dawn, New York–Bermuda, July 12) as 'incompatible with the word of God and the Christian moral fibre', an instance of organised religious hostility toward visible same-sex couples.

LGBTQ Nation/AP (July 2013): Bermuda's Senate passed the Human Rights Amendment Act outlawing discrimination on grounds of sexual orientation (also banning age discrimination); same-sex marriage not then permitted.

Royal Gazette (14 May 1994): the House of Assembly voted 22–16 to decriminalise consensual sex between adult men, removing two Criminal Code sections. The debate split the island, with religious leaders divided and the Christian Coalition staging marches against it.

SYN-COK.name: Cook Islands
SYN-COK.summary:
The Cook Islands is self-governing in free association with New Zealand, which supplies nationality and passport rules; criminal and marriage law on the islands is made and applied locally.

Sex between men was decriminalised by the Crimes Amendment Bill, which Parliament passed on 14 April 2023 and which took effect on 1 June 2023. The provisions removed were sections 154 and 155 of the Crimes Act 1969, covering sexual activity between men and any indecent act with or upon another male, with consent expressly excluded as a defence. Sources disagree on the maximum penalties: coverage from 2017 records up to seven years for sex between men and five years for an indecent act, while reporting on the repeal cites up to ten years for indecent acts between males. No source records a prosecution under these sections in living memory, and the note attached to the amending bill cited growing acceptance of LGBT people in the Cook Islands.

The same bill added protections for victims of sexual abuse and assault. It did not change the marriage law.

Marriage is defined by the Marriage Amendment Act 2000 as between a man and a woman. A trans visitor in what would be locally classed as a same-sex relationship has no spousal standing in the Cook Islands, and a marriage entered into abroad on that basis is not recognised locally.

sources.summary: PinkNews (14 Apr 2023): Cook Islands parliament voted on Friday to remove the never-enforced 'indecent acts between males' law — exposure of up to 10 years under the 1969 Crimes Act — through the Crimes Amendment Bill, effective 1 June 2023; a note in the bill cited growing acceptance of LGBTQ+ people, and the bill also adds protections for victims of sexual abuse and assault. Same-sex marriage remains outlawed under the Marriage Amendment Act 2000.

PinkNews (1 Oct 2020): decriminalisation stalled again — MPs deferred the Crimes Bill report by three months. Traces the full path: colonial-era 1969 sections 154/155 (up to 7 years for sex between men) criminalise; a 2017 select committee recommended removing them and 'indecent acts between men'/sodomy were struck from the draft, but MPs later backtracked and the kick-down-the-road continued; notes colonisation introduced the taboo into a historically accepting society.

PinkNews (3 Aug 2017): draft Crimes Bill, written with New Zealand help, would remove sections 154/155 of the 1969 Crimes Act — up to 7 years for gay sex and 5 years for 'any indecent act with or upon any other male', with consent explicitly not a defence. Population 21,000; the country's only LGBTI community group, Te Tiare Association, welcomed the move (member Valentino Wichman quoted on the law's homophobia).

RNZ Pacific (10 Aug 2017): public submissions opened in parliament on the Cook Islands Crimes Bill intended to replace the widely considered outdated 1969 Crimes Act. The clerk of Parliament, John Tangi, confirmed a submission from the Te Tiare Association representing the country's LGBTI community was already before the select committee; at least three lawyers expected to speak on penalties and sentencing.

SYN-COK.tangentialFactors: The repeal concluded a reform process that had run since 2017, when a draft Crimes Bill written with New Zealand legal assistance would have removed sections 154 and 155; a select committee recommended deletion and the offences were struck from the draft, after which members reversed that decision and, in October 2020, deferred the bill's report by a further three months. Public submissions on the 2017 bill were taken by a parliamentary select committee in a country of roughly 21,000 people, and at least three lawyers were expected to address penalties and sentencing.
SYN-COK.localsOnly:
Te Tiare Association is the country's LGBTI community organisation, and its submission was before the select committee examining the 2017 draft Crimes Bill. The offences struck from the draft at that stage were restored by members before the 2023 amendment finally removed them.

The Marriage Amendment Act 2000 continues to govern who may marry locally, so same-sex marriages cannot be entered into in the Cook Islands.
SYN-COK.outOfScopeNotes:
No sourced material in the inventory addresses gender-marker or passport policy for trans travellers, gender-recognition procedures, healthcare access, facility use, hate-crime or anti-discrimination protection, or police practice in the Cook Islands. Nothing in the available sources documents a trans-specific prosecution, enforcement action or violent incident.

The maximum penalties recorded for the repealed sections 154 and 155 are inconsistent across sources: seven years and five years in the 2017 reporting, up to ten years in reporting on the repeal. The discrepancy is unresolved, and whether the offences were ever applied before living memory is not established either.

SYN-CUW.name: Curaçao
SYN-CUW.summary:
Curaçao is an autonomous constituent country of the Kingdom of the Netherlands, with full autonomy except in defence, foreign affairs and matters reserved to the Supreme Court of the Netherlands.

Both male and female same-sex sexual activity is legal, with an equal age of consent of 16 for heterosexual and homosexual intercourse. A trans visitor in a relationship read locally as same-sex faces no conduct offence on that basis.

Same-sex marriage has been legal in Curaçao since 12 July 2024, when the Supreme Court of the Netherlands upheld an Appeals Court decision barring discrimination based on sexual orientation. Before that ruling, Curaçao recognised as valid same-sex marriages registered in the Netherlands and in Bonaire, Sint Eustatius and Saba, but offered no in-island marriage, civil union or other form of recognition.

Recognition arrived by court order rather than by statute. A limited-rights proposal was put to the Estates of Curaçao in 2017, and a marriage bill submitted on 4 June 2019 was withdrawn in September 2020 for lack of support. In April 2015 representatives of all Kingdom governments agreed that LGBT people on Aruba, Curaçao and Sint Maarten should receive equal rights quickly, and the August 2015 Oliari and Others v. Italy judgment of the European Court of Human Rights, applicable to Curaçao, required legal recognition.

The Criminal Code enacted in 2011 prohibits unfair discrimination and incitement to hatred and violence on grounds that include heterosexual or homosexual orientation. Article 1:221 defines discrimination as any distinction affecting the recognition, enjoyment or exercise of human rights in political, economic, social, cultural or other social life, and Articles 2:61 and 2:62 set penalties ranging from fines to one year of imprisonment. The protected grounds named in the source material do not include gender identity, and no Curaçao-specific authority on gender-identity coverage was identified.

Official rhetoric has not consistently governed practice. In April 2015 commissioner Marvelyne Wiels of Pueblo Soberano publicly backed equal rights for everyone in the local press, while her party colleague Winifred Raveneau opposed the rights push fiercely and used a last-minute, exceptionally strict permit requirement to force Curaçao's 2013 Gay Pride to relocate to a hotel premises. Public LGBT assembly on the island can be obstructed through administrative permitting at short notice.

Curaçao opened an LGBT community centre, the Pink House, in 2010, and alongside Aruba and Sint Maarten has acted as a driver of equal-rights moves across the Kingdom. Curaçao Gay Pride's Frank Holtslag cites an IGLTA award naming the island the most gay welcoming in the region, and a rights wishes-package was delivered to ministers in The Hague.

No Curaçao-specific sourcing was found on gender markers in locally issued identity documents, entry or border screening triggered by gender presentation, access to gender-affirming care, or the designation of facilities. Those areas are unassessed rather than cleared.

Aruba passed same-sex civil partnerships 8 Sept 2016 — comparator context, not Curaçao law.

SYN-CYM.name: Cayman Islands
SYN-CYM.summary:
The Cayman Islands' constitutional discrimination grounds were drafted in 2009 without sexual-orientation protection. The omission drew criticism from the United Kingdom parliament's Foreign Affairs Committee, which called it deplorable and warned that Cayman courts could afford less protection than Article 14 of the European Convention on Human Rights requires; the Foreign and Commonwealth Office answered that the list of grounds was open-ended. No enumerated constitutional ground anchors a discrimination claim, and no trans-specific ground is listed.

No domestic route to marriage exists. In March 2019 Grand Court Chief Justice Anthony Smellie struck down the statutory prohibition on same-sex marriage; the Court of Appeal overturned that ruling in August 2019 and restored the ban. Recognition survives at the level of immigration administration: in December 2020 immigration authorities recognised the overseas marriage of Paul Pearson and Randall Pinder, who had wed in Ireland, and the Court of Appeal held that refusing recognition would treat persons unequally on sexual-orientation grounds. For a trans visitor whose relationship would be locally classed as same-sex, an overseas marriage therefore carries immigration effects even though the territory offers no domestic route to marry.

Public visibility in the tourist-facing environment is high. Around 600 people, among them the premier, the governor, ministers and members of the Legislative Assembly, joined the Cayman LGBTQ Foundation's first Pride parade on 7 August 2021, with broad official participation.

No trans-specific legal provision is documented for the Cayman Islands. Nothing in the available sources addresses gender recognition, identity documents, single-sex facilities, healthcare access or hate-crime protection, and no trans-specific incident or enforcement action is recorded.
