SYN-ESH.name: Western Sahara
SYN-ESH.summary:
Western Sahara is a disputed territory with no single legal order running through it. Morocco controls most of the ground and Moroccan security services, courts and detention facilities operate there; the Sahrawi Arab Democratic Republic claims sovereignty and governs through exile institutions and refugee camps in Algeria. Which framework a visitor stands under depends on which part of the territory they are in.

Moroccan jurisdiction reaches into the territory in practice. On 9 December 2005 Human Rights Watch reported the trial of seven human-rights defenders from Moroccan-controlled Western Sahara on charges of fomenting illegal protests, called the charges dubious and demanded a fair trial. The case shows Moroccan courts and detention operating on Sahrawi political cases, not only on paper.

Same-sex intimacy is criminalised under both frameworks. Moroccan law carries six months to three years of imprisonment. For the Sahrawi Arab Democratic Republic, the Council for Global Equality, Equaldex and ILGA record same-sex sexual activity as illegal for both men and women, punishable by up to three years, and a July 2017 PinkNews roundup listed the SADR among jurisdictions where homosexuality is illegal for men and women and had been for decades. A trans visitor in a relationship that local law would read as same-sex under birth-sex status therefore stands inside a criminal prohibition in either part of the territory.

The SADR's own position is contested. In 2010 Ahmed Mulay Alli, the SADR's diplomatic representative in Mexico, said the Constitution 'does not refer to homosexuality or any other sexual practice... it does not punish it'. The Spanish Commission for Refugee Aid (CEAR) reads the same silence as leaving LGBTQ people with no legal protection against discrimination or violence. Constitutional silence is not decriminalisation, and no statute in the inventory decriminalises anything.

The only documented account of the Sahrawi authorities applying such charges comes from a 2009 USCRI report: officials running the refugee camps in Algeria said they were holding some prisoners on 'homosexuality' charges while alleging facts that would more fittingly describe rape. The charge sits in the hands of camp administration rather than a court.

Social exposure is high. Most residents are Muslim, and relationships between people of the same sex are widely read as a foreign phenomenon.

No source in the inventory records a trans-specific statute, a protection mechanism, or a documented case of a trans visitor being processed under either framework.

SYN-FLK.name: Falkland Islands (Malvinas)
SYN-FLK.summary:
The Falkland Islands are a British Overseas Territory with their own Legislative Assembly, which legislates locally; the United Kingdom is responsible for the territory's defence. The United Kingdom's Equality Act 2010 and Gender Recognition Act 2004 do not extend to the Islands, so legal protection and gender recognition depend on the territory's own ordinances.

Same-sex activity has been legal since 1989 and the age of consent has been equal since 2005.

Marriage and civil partnerships have been available since 29 April 2017. The Legislative Assembly passed the bill in March 2017 by 7 votes to 1, and the registrar general confirmed by reply in June 2017 that it is law. Civil partnerships are open to opposite-sex as well as same-sex couples, and a trans visitor whose relationship would be classed as same-sex under local birth-sex status can marry or register a civil partnership on the same terms. A public consultation ahead of the bill recorded 90% support for same-sex marriage and 94% for civil partnerships in a territory of roughly 3,000 residents.

Legal gender change has been possible since 2014 under the CPE Ordinance 2014. There is no self-identification route and no recognition of non-binary status. Holders of a UK Gender Recognition Certificate are recognised in their acquired gender under that ordinance.

The Constitution Order 2008, at Article 16, bans discrimination on grounds of sexual orientation. The provision covers sexual orientation only; no gender-identity ground is identified in it.

Two ordinances frame the criminal-justice treatment of bias. The Crimes Ordinance 2014 provides for hate-stirring on grounds of sexual orientation, and the CPE Ordinance 2014 makes sexual orientation an aggravating factor in sentencing. On the sources available, neither ground extends to gender identity.

Rob Salerno blog (22 Jun 2017): the Falklands registrar general confirmed by reply that the same-sex marriage and civil partnership bill passed in March is law, resolving the outstanding question of its assent; the same registrar confirmed that same-sex marriage is not legal in the South Georgia and South Sandwich Islands dependency.

SYN-FRO.name: Faroe Islands
SYN-FRO.summary:
The Faroe Islands is a self-governing territory within the Realm of Denmark. Danish national criminal law and document rules apply here; equality and family law are set locally.

Same-sex sexual activity has been legal in the Faroe Islands since 1933, when it was decriminalised across the Kingdom of Denmark. The age of consent for male same-sex relations was set at 18 and stayed there until 1988, when the Faroes adopted Denmark's gender-neutral age of 15, eleven years after Denmark made that change.

In November 2006 activists gathered around 20,000 online signatures in a population of about 47,000, demanding an end to discrimination on grounds of sexual orientation and a registered-partnership law matching the other Nordic countries. Neither existed at that date, and homophobic conduct was legally unaddressed. A separate petition against same-sex marriage gathered 1,262 signatures. After the 2006 assault on Rasmus Rasmussen an internet petition collected 20,000 signatures, and eight women in Tórshavn added a further 2,000 by email and from collection points in shops, tourist centres and petrol stations.

The anti-discrimination provision took effect on 1 January 2007, making the Faroe Islands the last country in Northern Europe to ban discrimination and harassment on grounds of sexual orientation. Anyone who publicly makes a statement threatening, insulting or degrading a group on account of race, colour, national or ethnic origin, religion or sexual orientation is liable to a fine or up to two years' imprisonment. Gender identity is not among the enumerated grounds, so a trans visitor or resident targeted as a member of a group falls outside the article as written, and no separate gender-identity hate-crime provision appears in the sources.

The most fully documented anti-LGBT attack is the 2006 assault on Rasmus Rasmussen, an openly gay singer, songwriter and radio host, who was severely beaten by five men in Tórshavn and hospitalised shortly after coming out; he and his family then received threatening telephone calls. Police declined to handle the case because no Faroese law at the time banned discrimination against sexual minorities. The source records that he was later admitted to a psychiatric hospital with severe depression worsened by the beating, never recovered, and died by suicide in 2012. In 2005 the Norwegian drag group Great Garlic Girls had to run from a gang of young men in Tórshavn intent on physically assaulting them; the group noted that nowhere else had it been attacked.

Public visibility has drawn sustained opposition. The first gay pride march, in 2005, provoked much controversy. In June 2015 the Speaker of the Løgting, Jógvan á Lakjuni, published a letter to the editor attacking the national broadcaster Kringvarp Føroya for the space it gave LGBT Føroyar and condemning a drag show at the Nordic House as "non-culture". Centre Party leader Jenis av Rana repeatedly compared LGBT Føroyar to the Sea Shepherd whale-hunting protesters and suggested the Tórshavn pride parade be moved out of the centre. In July 2015, two days before the national holiday, he demanded that Pride be banned, and the singer Eivor Pálsdóttir publicly urged people to ignore him. His party remains formally opposed to homosexuality. In September 2010 av Rana refused to attend a state banquet for the visiting Icelandic prime minister Johanna Sigurdardóttir and her partner, citing his religion.

For a trans visitor the recorded hostility is political and rhetorical rather than physical. The named targets are openly gay public figures, a visiting drag performance group and Pride events, and the documented actions are a refusal to sit at an official table, a letter to a newspaper and calls for a ban. No prosecution, conviction or official sanction under the 2007 provision appears in the sources. The two assaults on record date from 2005 and 2006; in the one case where the police response is documented, officers declined to act, and the legal footing that exists today covers sexual orientation and not gender identity.

sources.summary: PinkNews (9 Nov 2006): LGBT activists gathered around 20,000 online signatures demanding an end to sexual-orientation discrimination and a registered-partnership law aligned with the rest of the Nordics; at the time the Faroes (population ~47,000, self-governing within Denmark) had neither protection, leaving homophobia legally unaddressed.

PinkNews (7 Sep 2010): Centre Party leader Jenis av Rana refused to attend a state banquet for visiting Icelandic PM Johanna Sigurdardottir and her partner, citing his religion — signals the prominence of religiously motivated opposition to openly gay public figures in Faroese politics.

SYN-GGY.name: Guernsey
SYN-GGY.summary:
Guernsey is a self-governing Crown Dependency with its own parliament, the States of Guernsey, and its own statute book. The United Kingdom's Equality Act 2010 and the single-sex services code issued under it in 2025 do not apply here automatically; United Kingdom measures reach Guernsey only by Order in Council.

Same-sex sexual activity is lawful for men and women. Criminalisation ended before 1983, when the age of consent was set at 21 in line with the United Kingdom; the male same-sex age of consent fell to 18 in 2000 and was equalised at 16 by legislation approved in 2011 that took effect on 5 November 2012. Guernsey retains specific male homosexual offences, including a ban on homosexual sexual acts not conducted in private. A trans visitor in what would be locally classed as a same-sex relationship can therefore face prosecution for conduct that is lawful in the United Kingdom.

Transgender people have been able to change their legal gender since 2007, including obtaining a new birth certificate. The law permits only the issue of a new certificate and does not amend or remove entries from the existing record, so prior gender markers remain visible on the original document. A visitor carrying both records, or documents issued at different times, should expect the earlier marker to remain on file.

The States of Guernsey approved same-sex marriage on 10 December 2015 by 37 votes to 7, rejecting a civil-partnership-only scheme and a single secular status called Union Civile as insufficient. The enabling legislation was left to a separate bill and commenced in 2018. Guernsey is the only part of the British Isles never to have enacted its own civil partnership legislation; United Kingdom civil partnerships have been recognised for succession purposes since 2 April 2012.

A review of the Adoption Law, recorded at page 1170 of the Billet d'État of 24 June 2015, ended a fifty-year bar on unmarried couples adopting. The States agreed that same-sex couples may adopt, that civil partnerships are recognised in adoption proceedings, and that both partners hold equal parental responsibility.

Discrimination protections were built in stages. A 2004 law enabled the States to pass Ordinances banning discrimination, and the Sex Discrimination (Employment) (Guernsey) Ordinance, 2005 prohibited discrimination based on gender identity in employment. As of 2020 no equivalent Ordinance had outlawed discrimination on the basis of sexual orientation. Protections covering sexual orientation and gender identity have applied in child welfare proceedings in Guernsey and Alderney since 2008 and in Sark since 2016. In September 2022 the States passed a comprehensive anti-discrimination bill unanimously, 33 votes to 0, explicitly including sexual orientation and rejecting proposed exemptions for businesses of five employees or fewer and for religious affiliations. It took effect on 1 October 2023.

Les Nicolles, Guernsey's only prison, opened in 1989 and holds male, female and vulnerable prisoners of juvenile and adult ages across 11 wings, with a capacity of 139 and about 99 prisoners in November 2024. No rule on housing prisoners by birth sex versus gender identity, no separate unit for trans prisoners, and no solitary or segregation practice for them is recorded in the available sources, so a trans visitor has no sourced assurance about placement if detained.

SYN-GIB.name: Gibraltar
SYN-GIB.summary:
Gibraltar is a self-governing British Overseas Territory with its own Parliament and its own Supreme Court, which make and interpret its civil and criminal law. Measures enacted by the United Kingdom do not apply of their own force: the Equality Act 2010 and the single-sex-services code issued in 2025 bind Gibraltar only if extended by Order in Council, and no such extension appears in the sourced material.

The principal legal gap facing a trans visitor is gender recognition. No process exists in Gibraltar for changing a legal gender marker, and the sourced material records that transgender persons are not permitted to change legal gender. A trans visitor therefore travels on a document whose marker cannot be altered by any local route, and can expect to be read at the border and in public under that marker.

Statutory discrimination protection covering gender reassignment has been in place since the Equal Opportunities Act 2006 took effect on 1 March 2007. The Act prohibits discrimination in employment and in the provision of goods and services on the ground of gender reassignment, defined as a process for the purpose of reassigning a person's sex by changing physiological or other attributes of sex. Sexual orientation is a protected ground under the same Act.

Hate-crime coverage extends to trans people. Parliament amended the Crimes Act 2011 in September 2013 to criminalise hatred and harassment on grounds of sexual orientation, with approval on 19 September, royal assent on 25 September and effect from 10 October 2013. In July 2026 Parliament passed a bill amending hate crime and hate speech legislation to include protections for transgender identity.

In July 2021 the Ministry for Justice and Equality said it would urgently consider legislation to tackle what the Chief Minister, Fabian Picardo, called "disgusting lurking homophobia" on social media during Pride month, following an incident of anti-gay abuse. The proposal at that stage concerned sexual orientation; the trans-inclusive amendment came in July 2026.

In July 2026 Parliament also passed a bill making it an offence to offer or practise conversion therapy. The sourced excerpt states the offence generally without specifying whether its scope covers sexual orientation, transgender identity, or both.

Partner recognition is established locally. Civil partnerships have been available since March 2014, and same-sex marriage since 15 December 2016, after the Civil Marriage Amendment Act passed unanimously on 26 October 2016, received royal assent on 1 November and took effect on 15 December, with the first marriage the following day. A deputy registrar may opt out, requiring assignment of an alternative registrar. Because no gender-recognition route exists, a trans visitor's legal sex for marriage purposes remains that recorded at birth; a relationship locally read as same-sex can be registered.

Adoption is open to same-sex couples. The Supreme Court ruled on 10 April 2013 that section 5(2) of the Adoption Act 1951 violated the Gibraltar Constitution, and the Adoption Act 2023 took full effect on 18 April 2024, expressly allowing same-sex couples to adopt without discrimination.

The age of consent is 16 for all sexual activity regardless of sexuality or gender. The Supreme Court ruled on 8 April 2011 that the previous age of 18 for gay sex was unconstitutional, and the gender-neutral Crimes Act 2011, approved in August 2011, set the equal age of 16 with effect from 23 November 2012.

sources.summary: The UK House of Commons Foreign Affairs Committee's Seventh Report (2007-08) on Overseas Territories sets accountability and good-governance expectations that apply to Gibraltar as an overseas territory; it also records corruption concerns raised in Turks and Caicos.

El País in English (15 Aug 2016): Gibraltar put a draft bill amending the Civil Marriage Act for same-sex marriage before Parliament after a December 2015 consultation that left Gibraltarians polarized; a government minister presided over an inter-ministerial committee weighing all viewpoints, with popular consultation and main parties suggesting support for the change.

Gibraltar Chronicle (22 Jul 2021): the Ministry for Justice and Equality said it would 'urgently' consider legislation to tackle 'disgusting lurking homophobia' following an incident of anti-gay abuse.

Wikiwand (Wikipedia mirror): LGBTQ rights in Gibraltar - legal since 1993, equal age of consent since 2012, adoption right by Supreme Court ruling 2013, civil partnerships since 2014, same-sex marriage since Dec 2016 (passed unanimously), discrimination protections for sexual orientation and 'gender reassignment' since 2007; transgender persons not allowed to change legal gender.

sources.summary: Wikipedia country coverage: Gibraltar's Parliament passed a bill on 19 September 2013, given royal assent on 25 September and in force on 10 October, amending the Crimes Act 2011 to criminalise hatred and harassment on grounds of sexual orientation as a hate crime. In July 2021 the Justice Ministry began investigating a further proposal to make denigration of a person on the basis of sexual orientation a specific criminal offence, prompted by what Chief Minister Fabian Picardo called 'disgusting lurking homophobia' on social media during Pride month. In July 2026 Parliament passed a bill amending hate crime and hate speech legislation to include protections for 'transgender identity'. The Supreme Court of Gibraltar ruled on 10 April 2013 that section 5(2) of the Adoption Act 1951 violated the Gibraltar Constitution, de jure legalising LGBT adoption, after a long-term lesbian couple denied adoption for lack of legal recognition of their relationship challenged the law; the government amended the law through the 2014 civil partnership legislation. The Adoption Act 2023 took full effect on 18 April 2024 and explicitly allows same-sex couples to adopt children without discrimination. In February 2021 Gibraltar enacted a surrogacy law permitting non-commercial, altruistic surrogacy for married couples or civil partners unable to conceive, with automatic recognition of children of same-sex couples conceived through artificial insemination. In June 2017 the Gibraltar Health Authority approved an amendment to its in vitro fertilisation policy allowing lesbian couples to access assisted reproductive technology. In July 2026 Parliament passed a bill making it an offence to offer or practice conversion therapy. The age of consent for all sexual activity regardless of sexuality or gender was equalised at 16. The Supreme Court of Gibraltar ruled on 8 April 2011 that the higher age of 18 for gay sex was unconstitutional, and the gender-neutral Crimes Act 2011, approved in August 2011, set an equal age of consent of 16 that took effect on 23 November 2012. Before that, gay male minors faced a discriminatory age of 18, and a private member's bill to equalise consent was defeated in Parliament on 18 May 2009. The Foreign Affairs Committee's 2008 enquiry into overseas territories recommended making discrimination on the basis of sexual orientation or gender status illegal in all overseas territories.

Civil partnerships have been available since March 2014 granting most rights of marriage including adoption as mandated by the 2013 ruling, and same-sex marriage was legalised by the Civil Marriage Amendment Act 2016 passed unanimously on 26 October 2016, receiving royal assent on 1 November and taking effect on 15 December 2016 with the first marriage the next day, requiring assignment of an alternative registrar where a deputy registrar opts out. The Supreme Court ruled on 10 April 2013 that section 5(2) of the Adoption Act 1951 violated the Constitution, in effect de jure legalising LGBT adoption, followed by civil partnership law amendments and effective 18 April 2024 the Adoption Act 2023 explicitly allowing same-sex couples to adopt without discrimination. In June 2017 the Gibraltar Health Authority amended IVF policy to allow lesbian couples access to assisted reproductive technology, and in February 2021 surrogacy law allowed non-commercial altruistic surrogacy for individuals and married or civil-partnered couples unable to conceive with automatic recognition for children of same-sex couples conceived through artificial insemination. The 2006 Constitution does not mention sexual orientation after 2002 proposals omitted it, but the Equal Opportunities Act 2006 effective 1 March 2007 prohibits discrimination in employment and goods and services on grounds including sexual orientation defined as orientation towards persons of the same sex, opposite sex, or both. Amendments to the Crimes Act 2011 approved 19 September 2013, assented 25 September and effective 10 October 2013 criminalised hatred and harassment on the ground of sexual orientation, while in July 2021 the Justice Ministry was investigating proposals against lurking homophobia including a possible specific offence of denigrating a person as a result of sexual orientation.

SYN-GIB.blindSummary:

The principal legal gap facing a trans visitor is gender recognition. No process exists in the state/province for changing a legal gender marker, and the sourced material records that transgender persons are not permitted to change legal gender. SYN-GLP.name: Guadeloupe
SYN-GLP.summary:
Guadeloupe is a French overseas department. Criminal law, identity-document rules, custodial conditions and the national preventive mechanism are set at the national level and carried by the parent record; this assessment covers what is specific to the island.

Guadeloupe's first LGBT+ centre, the Maison des Diversités et de l'Inclusion, opened on 24 April 2024, run by a federation of Guadeloupean associations. It offers reception, support and orientation for people of diverse identity, sexual, bodily and gender diversities.

The opening was attended by the visiting national minister Aurore Bergé, who announced measures to strengthen the fight against gender-based violence and discrimination in Guadeloupe, with structures adapted for the overseas territories. The centre's opening was presented as a concrete step toward inclusion and safety.

Community organisations Secret's Out, Queer Gang and Lovo Nova partnered on a year of LGBT-friendly social events across Guadeloupe in 2025, described locally as a potential 'annus mirabilis' for the island's community.

A September 2023 interview with Leïla of Secret's Out reported that community members increasingly reconcile their lives with their orientation, and described activism on the island as advancing after neighbouring Martinique; the interview also featured Prisca Melyon-Reinette of Amalgame Humani's.

sources.title: Wikipedia country coverage
sources.summary: French law applicable in Guadeloupe decriminalised same-sex relations in the Penal Code of 1791 and retained this in the 1810 Code, while public morality laws continued to be used against LGBTQ people; in Alsace and Lorraine, annexed in 1940, men were interned in Nazi camps and persecuted under Vichy despite the absence of a sodomy law. Vichy's article 334 of 6 August 1942 (later 331) set consent at 21 for homosexual relations against 15 for heterosexual, lowered to 18 in 1974 and equalised at 15 on 4 August 1982. The Mirguet amendment of 1960 doubled penalties for indecent exposure in homosexual activity (art. 330, 2nd alinea), repealed in 1980. In March 2024 the National Assembly unanimously passed a compensation bill for men arrested under article 330 before 1980; the Senate has yet to vote. A conversion therapy ban passed the Senate on 7 December 2020 and was published on 1 February 2022, carrying two years' imprisonment and/or €30,000. The law of December 2004, passed 31 December 2004, made homophobic, sexist, racist and xenophobic comments illegal, with a maximum penalty of a €45,000 fine and/or 12 months' imprisonment; civil liberties groups including Reporters Without Borders called it a serious infringement of free speech. It created the Haute autorité de lutte contre les discriminations et pour l'égalité and amended the 1881 Freedom of the Press Law to cover injury, defamation, insult, incitement to hatred or violence or discrimination on grounds of gender, sexual orientation or disability. Christian Vanneste, an MP from the ruling UMP party, became the first person convicted under it in January 2006, though that conviction was later cancelled by the Court of Cassation. Pride has been held in Paris since 4 April 1981 (Place Maubert, about 10,000 people), reaching 500,000 participants in 2019, with events in dozens of other cities. Transgender people have changed legal gender without surgery or medical diagnosis since 1 January 2017 (law signed 18 November 2016), but must still appear before a court to change the gender marker; a first name change can be done at the registry office. Self-certification of gender and proof of medical treatment were both dropped from the final bill. Until 2015 France refused to recognise surrogate children as French citizens, leaving many in legal limbo; the Court of Cassation ruled on 5 July 2017 that a child born to a surrogate abroad can be adopted by the partner of the biological father, the Court of Appeal of Paris held in May 2019 that a Canadian birth certificate must be recognised, and in December 2019 the Court of Cassation ruled that foreign birth certificates recognising same-sex partners must be fully recognised in France. In 2022 a court of appeal ruled that a transgender woman should be considered the mother of the child she conceived before her sex change, while a 2017 legal bid for 'neutral sex' classification was rejected by the Court of Cassation. In 2010 France became the first country to declassify gender dysphoria as a mental illness, removing gender identity disorder by decree, though French trans rights organisations said nothing changed beyond the announcement; transsexualism remains under ALD 31 with treatment funded by Sécurité Sociale, and gender-affirming surgery has been legal domestically since 1979. A 2022 ILGA-Europe report found significant problems in gender-affirming healthcare: lack of self-determination, extended waiting times and inequitable access depending on location, recommending an informed-consent, self-determination model. In March 2024 centre-right senators commissioned the Little Mermaid Observatory, a group opposed to all gender transition for minors, to report on youth gender care, which called transition a 'health scandal' and transness a 'social contagion'; a bill to ban medical transition under 18 passed the Senate in May 2024, opposed by the Macron government, with no update since 23 July 2024, while in late 2024 the French Society of Pediatric Endocrinology and Diabetology issued the country's first trans youth guidelines recommending puberty blockers from Tanner stage 2. Blood donation deferrals for gay and bi men were cut to four months in April 2020 and abolished entirely on 16 March 2022. The French Académie Nationale de Médecine characterised the rise in trans people seeking treatment as an 'epidemic-like phenomenon' and 'a primarily social problem', advising extreme caution on access, though this did not change actual practice. In October 2018 President Macron denounced homophobic violence as 'unworthy of France' after a rise in attacks, and a report released 16 May 2020 showed homophobic and transphobic attacks and insults rose 36% in 2019, with police identifying around 1,870 victims against about 1,380 in 2018. In 2022 it emerged that the president of the scientific committee of DILCRAH, France's interministerial body against racism, anti-Semitism and anti-LGBT hatred, was a member of The Little Mermaid Observatory; one member resigned and the president stepped away. In March 2008 Education Minister Xavier Darcos announced a policy fighting all forms of discrimination including homophobia in schools as one of 15 national education priorities for 2008–2009. In January 2019 the Ministry of Education launched the campaign 'Tous égaux, tous alliés' to tackle anti-LGBTQ bullying, providing reporting services, a helpline for students and staff, and requiring all French schools to give guidance on LGBTQ issues, with 17 May as a special sensitisation day. In March 2019 Higher Education Minister Frédérique Vidal announced all higher education institutions should use transgender people's preferred names, including on student cards and exam forms; in February 2019 the use of 'parent 1' and 'parent 2' on school enrolment forms caused widespread conservative outrage. Legislation to ban medical transition for under-18s passed the Senate in May 2024, prompting large-scale protests, making trans minors a direct legislative target.

SYN-GUF.name: French Guiana
SYN-GUF.summary:
French Guiana is an overseas department of France and has no gender-identity legislation of its own. Criminal law, identity documents, anti-discrimination provisions and the marriage regime that operate here are the French national ones, applied without local variation.

Detention carries the most serious documented risk. No local protocol governs the custody of transgender detainees, so placement in French Guiana's facilities follows the national practice: assignment to a men's or women's wing is based on the detainee's legal gender and decided case by case, without a consistent protective standard.

Specialist gender-affirming care is not provided locally on the same basis as in metropolitan France. Patients travel to the mainland for surgery and specialist assessment, and the journey adds cost and delay to every medical step, including any undertaken during a stay in the department.

Transphobia and cultural taboos discourage visibility in the department, and abuse is less likely to be reported, including to the police. Under-reporting is a feature of the local situation rather than evidence that abuse is rare.

sources.title: LGBTQ rights in French Guiana (Wikipedia)
sources.summary: France removed gender identity disorder as a diagnosis by decree in 2010, becoming the first country to declassify gender dysphoria as mental illness, with transsexualism remaining under ALD 31 with treatment funded by Sécurité Sociale. Since 1 January 2017 under the law signed 18 November 2016 after the Constitutional Council ruling of 17 November, transgender people may change legal gender marker by court order without sex reassignment surgery, sterilisation, psychiatrist certificate or medical diagnosis, with first-name change available at the registry office. This followed a decades-long legislative ban on legal gender change despite the 1959 change for Coccinelle and 1979 legalisation of gender-affirming surgery inside France, overturned only after the 1992 B. v France case at the European Court of Human Rights. Discrimination on the ground of "sexual identity" was prohibited from July 2012, with the term replaced by "gender identity" on 18 November 2016 amending Penal Code article 225-1 and Labour Code protections covering recruitment, internships, training, sanction and dismissal. Since 2017 transphobia is an aggravating circumstance for all crimes punishable by prison, and police identified around 1,870 victims of homophobic and transphobic attacks and insults in 2019, up 36% from around 1,380 in 2018. Gender-affirming healthcare was found by a 2022 ILGA-Europe report to lack self-determination with extended waiting times and location-dependent inequitable access recommending informed consent and self-determination, while the National Academy of Medicine advises extreme caution and actual practice is unchanged. For youth, the French Society of Pediatric Endocrinology and Diabetology issued the first national guidelines in late 2024 recommending puberty blockers from at least Tanner stage 2 with calcium and vitamin D supplements, while a Senate-passed May 2024 bill to ban medical transition under age 18 following the March 2024 Little Mermaid Observatory report has had no update since 23 July 2024 and is opposed by the Macron government. Private same-sex sexual activity was decriminalised by the Penal Code of 1791 and retained in the Penal Code of 1810 applied to nations and French colonies, ending ancien régime capital punishments including castration, dismemberment and burning with the last burning on 6 July 1750. A discriminatory age of consent of 21 for homosexual relations versus 15 for heterosexual relations introduced 6 August 1942 as article 334, moved to article 331 in 1945 and lowered to 18 in 1974, was equalised at 15 on 4 August 1982 under President Mitterrand, while the discriminatory 1960 Mirguet amendment to Penal Code article 330 alinea 2 doubling penalty for homosexual indecent exposure was repealed in 1980 with a March 2024 National Assembly unanimous compensation bill for pre-1980 Article 330 victims pending Senate vote. Discrimination based on sexual orientation has been prohibited since 1985 in employment, housing and public and private provision of goods and services, codified in the Labour Code. The law of 31 December 2004 criminalised homophobic, sexist, racist and xenophobic comments with a maximum penalty of 45,000 euro fine and/or 12 months imprisonment and amended the Law on Freedom of the Press of 29 July 1881 to cover injury, defamation, insult, incitement to hatred or violence or discrimination based on gender, sexual orientation or disability, while physical assault or murder motivated by victim sexual orientation carries increased penalties, and created the Haute autorité de lutte contre les discriminations et pour l'égalité. Same-sex marriage following civil solidarity pacts in 1999 was legalised in 2013 with the law signed 18 May 2013 after the 17 May Constitutional Council ruling and first ceremony 29 May in Montpellier, and is legal in all overseas departments and territories, with French Guiana's two deputies recording one vote in favour and one abstention. Lesbian, gay and bisexual people may serve openly in the Armed Forces, men who have sex with men blood-donation abstinence requirements of one year from 10 July 2016 and four months from 2 April 2020 were fully removed 16 March 2022 to an orientation-neutral policy, and the conversion therapy ban passed the Senate 7 December 2020, the National Assembly 25 January 2022 and was published 1 February 2022.

SYN-IMN.name: Isle of Man
SYN-IMN.summary:
The Isle of Man is a self-legislating Crown Dependency. Its parliament, Tynwald, legislates on these questions itself, and United Kingdom statutes reach the island only by Order in Council rather than automatically.

The Gender Recognition Act 2009 (c.11) allows transgender people to change their legal gender and have the new gender recognised.

The Equality Act 2017, which received royal assent on 18 July 2017 and was largely brought into force on 1 January 2019, lists gender reassignment as a protected characteristic and as a ground on which discrimination is prohibited. A ban on conversion therapy covering sexual orientation and gender identity was passed in 2020 as an amendment to the sexual offences bill in the Legislative Council and took effect in 2024; the Isle of Man was the first part of the British Isles to prohibit the practice.

Partner recognition is established. Civil partnerships became available to same-sex couples under the Civil Partnership Act 2011 (c.2) on 6 April 2011, and same-sex marriage took effect on 22 July 2016 after royal assent on 19 July 2016. A civil partnership converts into a marriage without a second ceremony, and the first conversion was completed within days of entry into force, which indicates routine registration rather than discretionary approval.

Parental recognition is narrower than the marriage position. Full joint and stepchild adoption has been open to same-sex couples since 6 April 2011 and lesbian couples have access to artificial insemination, but as of an August 2023 consultation same-sex couples are not recognised as parents on birth certificates for children born through IVF or surrogacy, and no Manx law acknowledges surrogacy. A trans visitor whose relationship is read as same-sex under local law would meet that gap.

Sexual-conduct law on the island has been gender-neutral since the Sexual Offences (Amendment) Act 2006 (c.3), which set a single age of consent of sixteen for all sexual conduct regardless of gender and sexual orientation.

A hate crime bill that would explicitly include gender reassignment alongside sexual orientation and marital or civil partnership status was put to community consultation in July 2022. The sources reviewed do not record its enactment.

sources.summary: Tynwald Hansard (26 April 2016): Legislative Council proceedings - Third Reading of the Marriage and Civil Partnership (Amendment) Bill 2016 (same-sex marriage) and consideration of the Equality Bill 2016 - the primary legislative record of the Isle of Man's marriage-equality debate.

BBC (28 Jul 2016): same-sex marriage took effect on the island after Royal Assent of the Marriage and Civil Partnership Act (2015-16 law reform); the first civil-partnership-to-marriage conversion was completed days after entry into force, with civil partnerships (legal since 2011) convertible without a second ceremony — confirming a smooth, routine registration process for couples.

BBC (30 Nov 2005): the House of Keys adopted an Employment Bill amendment protecting gay and lesbian employees from dismissal on sexual-orientation grounds (tabling by Onchan MHK Peter Karran) — the island's employment non-discrimination milestone, aligned with UK human-rights law.

3FM (9 Jun 2015): Chief Minister Allan Bell publicly backed same-sex marriage and said he would formulate a bill to repeal the island's marriage prohibition — the political commitment that preceded the 2016 Marriage and Civil Partnership Act.

Separate units exist for remand and convicted prisoners, female prisoners, young offenders and vulnerable prisoners, plus a segregation unit. No birth-sex-vs-identity placement rule, no trans-specific unit, and no trans-specific solitary or segregation practice are documented: no usable finding on the prison-housing axis.

sources.title: LGBTQ rights in Isle of Man (Wikipedia)
sources.summary: The Gender Recognition Act 2009 (c.11) allows transgender persons to change their legal gender and to have their new gender recognised. The Equality Act 2017, granted royal assent on 18 July 2017 with much of the law in force from 1 January 2019, lists gender reassignment as a protected characteristic and ground of non-discrimination. A ban covering sexual orientation and gender identity conversion therapy was passed in 2020 as an amendment to the extensive sexual offences bill in the Legislative Council and came into effect in 2024. In 2024 the Isle of Man became the first British territory and the first part of the British Isles to ban conversion therapy. In July 2022 community consultation progressed on a hate crime bill that would explicitly include gender reassignment alongside sexual orientation and marital or civil partnership status. Private and consensual male homosexual acts were decriminalised in September 1992 with age of consent set at 21, lowered to eighteen by the Criminal Justice Act 2001 (c.4), then lowered to sixteen and made gender-neutral for all sexual conduct regardless of gender and sexual orientation by the Sexual Offences (Amendment) Act 2006 (c.3). Until 2021 Section 9 of the Sexual Offences Act 1992 retained offences of buggery and gross indecency between men if under sixteen or committed elsewhere than in private, defined in Section 10 as more than two persons present or in a public-access place, and in 2021 the more-than-two-persons specification was deleted and language on indecent exposure and sexual activity in a public place was made gender-neutral. The Sexual Offences and Obscene Publications Act 2021 passed with royal assent in July 2021 and took effect 1 July 2022 by proclamation, pardoning historical gay sex offences committed prior to 1992 explicitly based on the UK Alan Turing law of 2017. Chief Minister Howard Quayle issued an unqualified apology to gay men convicted under previous laws, and in August 2022 on the 30th anniversary of decriminalisation the police commissioner formally apologised for enforcement of anti-gay laws up to 1992. Same-sex couples were granted civil partnerships by the Civil Partnership Act 2011 (c.2) effective 6 April 2011, and same-sex marriage effective 22 July 2016 after royal assent 19 July 2016. By the Civil Partnership Act 2011 same-sex couples have had equal access to full joint or stepchild adoption since 6 April 2011, lesbian couples have access to artificial insemination, but as of August 2023 consultation same-sex couples are not recognised as parents on birth certificates from IVF and surrogacy and no laws acknowledge surrogacy. Under the Employment Act 2006 (c.21) effective 1 September 2006 dismissal on grounds of sexual orientation was made unlawful, and the Equality Act 2017 lists sexual orientation, defined to include attraction to same, opposite, either sex and lack of attraction to either sex, as a protected characteristic.

SYN-IMN.tangentialFactors:
Tynwald Hansard for 26 April 2016 records the Legislative Council's third reading of the Marriage and Civil Partnership (Amendment) Bill 2016 alongside consideration of the Equality Bill 2016, the primary legislative record of the island's marriage reform. Chief Minister Allan Bell had publicly backed same-sex marriage on 9 June 2015 and said he would formulate a bill to repeal the island's marriage prohibition, a commitment that preceded the 2016 Act.

The criminal-law record runs from decriminalisation of private consensual acts between men in September 1992, when the age of consent was set at twenty-one, through the Criminal Justice Act 2001 (c.4), which lowered it to eighteen, to the Sexual Offences (Amendment) Act 2006 (c.3), which lowered it to sixteen and made the law gender-neutral for all sexual conduct regardless of gender and sexual orientation. Until 2021, Section 9 of the Sexual Offences Act 1992 retained offences of buggery and gross indecency between men where a participant was under sixteen or the act was committed other than in private, with Section 10 defining other than in private as more than two people present or a place to which the public had access. The Sexual Offences and Obscene Publications Act 2021 deleted the more-than-two-people specification and made the language on indecent exposure and sexual activity in a public place gender-neutral.

The Sexual Offences and Obscene Publications Act 2021 received royal assent in July 2021 and took effect on 1 July 2022 by proclamation. It pardoned historical convictions for gay sex offences committed before 1992, following the United Kingdom's 2017 Turing law. Chief Minister Howard Quayle issued an unqualified apology to men convicted under the earlier laws, and in August 2022, on the thirtieth anniversary of decriminalisation, the police commissioner formally apologised for enforcement of anti-gay laws up to 1992.
SYN-IMN.localsOnly:

The Employment Act 2006 (c.21) took effect on 1 September 2006. The Equality Act 2017 lists sexual orientation, defined to include attraction to the same sex, the opposite sex or either sex as well as lack of attraction to either sex, as a protected characteristic alongside gender reassignment.

The island's only functioning prison is at Jurby, a GBP 41.7m facility on the site of the former RAF Jurby that became fully operational on 14 August 2008 and is run by the Isle of Man Prison Service. It has separate units for remand and convicted prisoners, for female prisoners, for young offenders and for vulnerable prisoners, plus a segregation unit. No rule on placement by birth sex against gender identity, no trans-specific unit and no trans-specific segregation practice are documented.
SYN-IMN.outOfScopeNotes:
No rule on identity-document markers for trans residents or visitors is documented in the sources reviewed, and no entry, visa or border-screening procedure is recorded that would require disclosure of a trans visitor's status.

Whether the legal gender recognition process under the Gender Recognition Act 2009 is open to people who are not resident on the island is not established by the sources reviewed.

Hate-crime protection covering gender identity rests on a July 2022 consultation proposal; the sources reviewed do not show an enacted provision, or how such a provision would be enforced.

No trans-specific violence figures, prosecutions or documented incidents on the island appear in the sources reviewed.

SYN-MSR.name: Montserrat
SYN-MSR.summary:
Montserrat is a British Overseas Territory and stands under the United Kingdom's framework, including the European Convention on Human Rights and its non-discrimination and equality obligations.

Same-sex sexual activity between consenting adults in private has been lawful since 2001, when the prohibitions were swept away retrospectively by an Order in Council under Sections 3(1) and 3(7) of the Caribbean Territories (Criminal Law) Order, 2000. Lesbian conduct was never an offence. Group sex and sex in public remain criminal offences for all persons.

The age of consent is 18 for homosexual activity and 16 for heterosexual activity. A trans visitor whose relationship would be read locally as same-sex therefore falls under the higher threshold of 18.

Same-sex marriage and civil unions are not legal. Article 10(1) of the Constitution protects only opposite-sex marriage, providing that every man and woman of marriageable age has the right to marry a person of the opposite sex and to found a family. A trans visitor's partner would not be recognised as a spouse or civil partner.

Article 16 of the Montserrat Constitution and Article 79 of the Labour Code prohibit discrimination on grounds including sexual orientation, defining 'discriminatory' as affording different treatment on grounds such as sex, sexual orientation, race, colour, language, religion or other status. Neither provision names gender identity among the enumerated grounds, which end with an open-ended 'other status'.

There are no gay bars, nightclubs or other dedicated venues on the island. Several hotels welcome gay tourists and operate non-discrimination policies, which is the main documented point of entry for a visitor seeking a welcoming environment.

sources.summary: GlobalGayz 'Gay Life in Montserrat' (Sept 2012): a 104 km2 island reshaped by Hurricane Hugo (1989) and the 1995 Soufriere Hills eruption, which wastelanded the south and displaced over half the population north. Gay life barely exists locally: 'gays are everywhere but hardly here,' and the social scene is decimated.

Associated Press report (Jan 2001, via GLAPN): Britain scrapped the anti-gay statutes in five Caribbean territories including Montserrat and Turks & Caicos, saying they violated signed international human rights agreements — the legal basis on which Montserrat's prohibitions were eventually swept away; local politicians and religious leaders opposed, framed as a cultural rift with London.

SYN-MTQ.name: Martinique
SYN-MTQ.summary:
Martinique is an overseas department of France and stands under the French national framework in full: Article 73 of the Constitution applies French law to the island, so the identity documents, criminal law, anti-discrimination provisions and marriage regime a visitor would rely on are national law operating locally. A trans visitor is subject to the same substantive rules as in metropolitan France, administered through the department's own courts, administrative services and registry offices, and no island-specific procedure or exemption applies.

Martinique's correctional establishments are French prisons, so the national placement rules and the national detention watchdog's findings on transgender detainees apply to them by virtue of being French places of deprivation of liberty; no rule specific to the department governs placement, isolation or safety there. The watchdog's on-site interviews were conducted at establishments outside the department, so that finding rests on referrals and inspections elsewhere while still binding Martinique's prisons.

Same-sex conduct has been lawful in Martinique since 1815. The 2013 marriage-equality law applies in the department, discrimination on grounds of sexual orientation has been prohibited in goods and services since Law No. 2001-1066 (Penal Code articles 225-1 and 225-2) and in employment since 2008 (Labour Code article L1132-1), and gender-identity discrimination has been prohibited since Article 4 of the 2012 sexual-harassment law, with the term "sexual identity" replaced by "gender identity" in 2016.

Community infrastructure operates on the island. JM Concept 972 runs information, meetings and services for Martinique's LGBT community, and LGBTQ organisations listed for the overseas departments include AIDES Territoire Martinique, KAP Caraïbe, Tjenbé Rèd Prévention and SAFE SXM.

sources.summary: BuzzFeed News feature (12 Jan 2018): trans women in France are held in prisons matching the gender marker on their identity documents (Article D248 of the French criminal procedure code) — most end up in all-male facilities where other detainees threaten them ('we don't want any women here'), placement following the ID marker rather than anatomy. The French prison framework applies to the department's establishments as French law.

Opinion of the CGLPL, France's detention-places watchdog (25 May 2021): finds 'the persistence of serious violations' of the fundamental rights of transgender detainees across ALL French places of deprivation of liberty, based on referrals since 2010 concerning some forty transgender persons plus on-site inspections (eight trans women and one trans man interviewed at Fleury-Mérogis, Caen, Saint-Martin-de-Ré and Toulouse sites). Covers placement, isolation, safety and staff-training recommendations. Binds the department's prisons as French establishments.

Rights in Exile (AsyLex) Martinique resource page: same-sex acts decriminalised in 1815; Article 73 of the Constitution applies French law to the department; 2013 marriage-equality law applies; discrimination on grounds of sexual orientation prohibited in goods/services since Law No. 2001-1066 (Penal Code arts. 225-1/225-2) and in employment since Labour Code art. L1132-1 (2008); gender-identity discrimination prohibited since Article 4 of the 2012 sexual-harassment law, with 'sexual identity' replaced by 'gender identity' in 2016. Also lists local support organisations, case law and country-of-origin experts.

JM Concept 972 is a Martinique lesbian, gay, bi and trans network that provides information, meetings and services to the island's LGBT community and runs private parties and garden parties, with 2025 events listed for 4 July, 15 August and 5 September, supported by gay-friendly heterosexual supporters. Its active, dated operation evidences local community infrastructure on the island.

sources.title: Wikipedia country coverage
sources.summary: French law governs Martinique, and the following national provisions apply in the department. Homophobic, sexist, racist and xenophobic public comments were made illegal by a National Assembly amendment approved 31 December 2004, carrying a maximum penalty of a €45,000 fine and/or 12 months' imprisonment; the same law amended the 1881 Law on the Freedom of the Press to cover injury, defamation, insult, incitement to hatred or violence, and discrimination on grounds including sexual orientation. Christian Vanneste, an MP in Chirac's UMP party, became the first person convicted under it in January 2006, though the conviction was later cancelled by the Court of Cassation. Since 1 January 2017 transgender people can change their legal gender without surgery or a medical diagnosis, but must still go before a court to change the gender marker, while a first name change can be done at the registry office. The bill was signed 18 November 2016 after passing the Senate on 6 November 2015 and the National Assembly, with the Constitutional Council ruling it constitutional on 17 November 2016 and dropping the original self-certification provision; before that, legal gender change had been banned for decades until the 1992 European Court of Human Rights case B. v. France. A report released 16 May 2020 showed homophobic and transphobic attacks and insults rose by 36% in 2019, with police identifying around 1,870 victims, up from about 1,380 in 2018. Penalties increase where physical assault or murder is motivated by the victim's sexual orientation, and since 2017 transphobia has been an aggravating cause for all crimes punishable by prison. Conversion therapy was banned by a bill published 1 February 2022. Assisted reproduction for lesbian couples and single women took effect in September 2021 with state cover for women under 43, and the MSM blood donation deferral was removed on 16 March 2022. A 2022 ILGA-Europe report found significant problems with gender-affirming healthcare, including extended waiting times and inequitable access depending on location, with treatment covered by Sécurité Sociale under ALD 31. In March 2024 centre-right Republican senators commissioned The Little Mermaid Observatory to report on youth gender care, after which legislation to ban medical transition under 18 passed the Senate in May 2024, opposed by the Macron government with no update since 23 July 2024; in late 2024 the French Society of Pediatric Endocrinology and Diabetology issued the country's first guidelines for trans youth, recommending puberty blockers from Tanner stage 2 with calcium and vitamin D. The Académie Nationale de Médecine characterised the rise in trans people seeking treatment as an 'epidemic-like phenomenon' and a 'primarily social problem', advising extreme caution on access. Earlier state hostility includes the 1960 Mirguet amendment treating homosexuality as a 'national scourge' alongside alcoholism and the Vichy age-of-consent law of 6 August 1942 setting 21 for homosexual relations against 15 for heterosexual ones, lowered to 18 in 1974 and equalised at 15 on 4 August 1982. In January 2019 the Ministry of Education launched the Tous égaux, tous alliés campaign against anti-LGBTQ bullying, with 17 May as a special sensitisation day, and in March 2019 Higher Education Minister Frédérique Vidal announced that all higher education institutions should use transgender people's preferred names, including on student cards and exam forms. LGBTQ organisations listed for the overseas departments include AIDES Territoire Martinique, KAP Caraïbe, Tjenbé Rèd Prévention and SAFE SXM.

SYN-MTQ.tangentialFactors:
The support network that names Martinique sits alongside organisations listed for the wider group of overseas departments. A visitor moving between these French Caribbean departments encounters the same national legal rules and a community network that crosses administrative borders.

Conditions inside the department's prisons are documented through national rather than island sources: inspections and press reporting on transgender detainees in French custody were produced for the national prison estate as a whole, and Martinique's establishments fall within their scope because they are French prisons.

The Rights in Exile listing places Martinique inside a country-by-country directory of sexual orientation and gender identity resources, so some of the legal material indexed under the entry concerns France as a whole rather than the department alone.
SYN-MTQ.localsOnly:
Residents' legal business is handled locally: the department's courts, registry offices and administrative services process identity documents, marriage and discrimination complaints under national rules, with no island-specific variant of the procedure.

JM Concept 972 provides information, meetings and services to Martinique's LGBT community and runs private parties and garden parties, with 2025 events listed for 4 July, 15 August and 5 September, supported by gay-friendly heterosexual supporters.

The Rights in Exile (AsyLex) Martinique page gathers local support organisations, case law and country-of-origin experts alongside the provisions in force on the island; the case law and expert material it indexes is the locally grounded record available to residents and to anyone preparing a claim about the department.
SYN-MTQ.outOfScopeNotes:
No figures specific to Martinique on anti-trans violence, and no enforcement record specific to the island, were located in the sources consulted. National hate-crime statistics exist but cover France as a whole and are documented at national level rather than as findings about the department.

The resource page records 1815 as the date same-sex conduct was decriminalised in the department; it gives no account of enforcement or of local practice in the intervening period.

Details of legal gender recognition procedure, gender-affirming care provision and the status of youth transition care are national matters under the framework in force in the department; they are not sourced here as island-specific findings.

SYN-MYT.name: Mayotte
SYN-MYT.summary:
Mayotte is a French overseas department in the Indian Ocean and stands under the French national framework. The national rules on identity documents, criminal law, anti-discrimination, marriage and custody placement extend to the island, including its places of deprivation of liberty.

Formal entitlement and lived experience diverge. A teacher at the university centre of Mayotte and his Malagasy partner married at Sada town hall in 2023, after what reporting described as a long and complicated path, on a predominantly Muslim island where the written law is not the whole of what a couple faces.

Legal representation is thinly available locally. A French-language directory of LGBT-friendly lawyers returns no referenced practitioner for Mayotte's towns, including Mamoudzou, Koungou, Dzaoudzi and Sada, while listing a Paris-based lawyer admitted to the Conseil d'État and Cour de cassation, working in persons and family law, as available.

sources.summary: BuzzFeed News feature (12 January 2018): trans women in France are incarcerated per their identity-document gender (Article D248 of the French criminal procedure code), typically in all-male facilities where other detainees threaten them, placement following the ID marker rather than anatomy. The French prison framework binds this department's establishments as French law.

Opinion of France's detention-places watchdog CGLPL (25 May 2021): 'persistence of serious violations' of transgender detainees' fundamental rights across all French places of deprivation of liberty — based on referrals since 2010 concerning some forty transgender persons and on-site inspections (eight trans women and one trans man interviewed at Fleury-Mérogis, Caen, Saint-Martin-de-Ré, Toulouse). Extends to local jails as French establishments.

LINFO.re (French-language report): the French National Assembly voted the simplification of legal gender change (civil-status change for trans people). French law applies to the department, bringing the simplified procedure here.

Erasing 76 Crimes (23 May 2023, Moïse Manoël-Florisse): Bruno Agar, a teacher at the university centre of Mayotte, and his Malagasy partner (pseudonym Abdallah) married at Sada Town Hall after a 'long and complicated' path — showing the gap between formal French rights and lived reality on this predominantly Muslim island. Same-sex marriage is legal here — a rarity in Africa and the Islamic world — since Mayotte voted to remain part of France in 1975.

Avocat Gay-Friendly directory (French): no LGBT-friendly lawyer is yet referenced in Mayotte — the town list (Mamoudzou, Koungou, Dzaoudzi, Sada and others) returns 'we do not yet have a lawyer referenced in your region' — while Paris-based Maître Isabelle Zribi (lawyer at the Conseil d'État and Cour de cassation, including persons and family law) is listed as available. Evidence of thin local legal-access infrastructure for anyone needing counsel on the island.

sources.title: LGBTQ rights in Mayotte (Wikipedia)
sources.summary: French law bans discrimination on the basis of 'sexual identity' since July 2012, with article 225-1 of the Penal Code amended on 18 November 2016 to replace 'sexual identity' with 'gender identity', and the Labour Code prohibits exclusion from recruitment, internships or training and sanction, dismissal or discriminatory measures on account of gender identity. France removed gender identity disorder as a diagnosis by decree in 2010, though transgender rights organizations stated nothing changed beyond the announcement, while transsexualism remains under ALD 31 with treatment funded by Sécurité Sociale, and gender affirmative surgery performed in-country was legalised in 1979 after previously only accessible abroad. Legal gender change without sex reassignment surgery, forced sterilisation, psychiatrist certificates or proof of medical interventions was approved by the Senate on 6 November 2015 and the National Assembly on 24 May 2016, modified on 12 July 2016 to drop self-certification, re-approved on 12 October after rejecting Senate amendments requiring medical treatment, ruled constitutional on 17 November, signed 18 November 2016 and effective 1 January 2017, but still requires going before a court for the gender marker while first-name change can be done at the registry office. In 2017 transphobia became an aggravating factor for all crimes punishable by prison, and hate-crime provisions cover injury, defamation, insult, incitement to hatred or violence or discrimination, with a 16 May 2020 report recording a 36% rise in homophobic and transphobic attacks and insults in 2019 with around 1,870 victims identified by police compared to around 1,380 in 2018. Healthcare provision was found by a 2022 ILGA-Europe report to suffer lack of self-determination, extended waiting times and inequitable access by location, with a recommendation for informed consent and self-determination, while the National Academy of Medicine has characterized increased demand as an 'epidemic-like phenomenon' and 'primarily social problem' advising extreme caution without changing actual practice. In March 2024 centre-right senators commissioned a report critical of youth gender-affirming care, after which legislation to ban medical transition under age 18 passed the Senate in May 2024 but is opposed by the Macron government with no update since 23 July 2024, while in late 2024 the French Society of Pediatric Endocrinology and Diabetology issued first national youth guidelines recommending puberty blockers with calcium and vitamin D supplements from at least Tanner stage 2. Transgender individuals are allowed to serve openly in the French Armed Forces, conversion therapy was banned by Senate vote 7 December 2020, National Assembly concurrence 25 January 2022 and publication 1 February 2022 with proposed punishments of two years' imprisonment and/or 30,000 euros fine, and in March 2019 the Minister of Higher Education sought use of transgender people's preferred names on student cards and exam forms. Same-sex sexual activity in private was decriminalised by the Penal Code of 1791 with no mention of same-sex relations, retained in the Penal Code of 1810 and followed in nations and French colonies adopting the Code, while a discriminatory age of consent under Vichy article 334 moved to article 331 on 8 February 1945 set 21 years for homosexual relations versus 15 for heterosexual, lowered to 18 in 1974, and repealed 4 August 1982 under President François Mitterrand to equalise at 15. A 1960 Mirguet amendment inserting article 330 alinea 2 doubled the penalty for indecent exposure for homosexual activity to repress pimping and other national scourges, was repealed in 1980 as part of an act redefining sexual offenses, and in March 2024 the National Assembly unanimously passed a compensation bill for gay men arrested under Article 330 prior to 1980 with Senate vote still pending. Discrimination on the basis of sexual orientation has been banned since 1985 in employment, housing and public and private provision of services and goods, and the law of 31 December 2004 made homophobic, sexist, racist and xenophobic comments illegal with maximum penalty of 45,000 euros fine and/or 12 months' imprisonment, created the Haute autorité de lutte contre les discriminations et pour l'égalité, and amended the Press Law of 29 July 1881 for injury, defamation, insult, incitement to hatred or violence or discrimination with increased penalties when assault or murder is motivated by sexual orientation. Civil solidarity pacts (PACS) were enacted in 1999 for same-sex and unmarried opposite-sex couples with most marriage protections, and same-sex marriage was approved by the National Assembly 12 February 2013 by 329-229, by the Senate 12 April with amendments accepted 23 April, ruled constitutional 17 May 2013, signed 18 May 2013 and published next day, with first ceremony 29 May in Montpellier and joint adoption legal since May 2013. Lesbian, gay and bisexual people are allowed to serve openly in the Armed Forces, conversion therapy was banned by Senate 7 December 2020, Assembly 25 January 2022 and publication 1 February 2022, and the 20 June 1983 ban on men who have sex with men donating blood recalled 12 January 2009 was replaced by one-year abstinence effective 10 July 2016, four-month abstinence from 2 April 2020, and removal of deferral 16 March 2022 for all regardless of orientation. Same-sex marriage is legal in all overseas departments and territories under French law, with 11 of 27 overseas deputies voting for and 11 against, 1 abstaining and 3 absent.

SYN-NCL.name: New Caledonia
SYN-NCL.summary:
New Caledonia is a French collectivity. It stands under the French national framework: France retains responsibility for penal law, civil-status documents and the justice system, while the collectivity legislates locally on many domestic matters. The protections a trans visitor would rely on are French national provisions, applying here because French law governs.

The inventory records no New Caledonia-specific law, enforcement action, incident, institution or statistic bearing on trans visitors, and no local ordinance narrowing the national protections. No region-specific signal was identified, and the national assessment for France applies.

Same-sex marriage has been available in this collectivity since France's 2013 marriage-equality law, which applies here as French law. CNN reported on 29 May 2013 on France's first same-sex wedding under that law.

French law extends marriage equality to this collectivity. PinkNews reported on 26 August 2012 that the government would introduce its same-sex marriage and adoption bill into Parliament in October 2012, fulfilling President Hollande's campaign pledge.

Yagg (July 2012, French): 'identité sexuelle' (sexual identity) became a ground of discrimination in the French Penal Code via the sexual-harassment law — enabling prosecution of discrimination and transphobia as discrimination. French law applies to the collectivity, and the same provision was updated to read 'gender identity' in 2016.

SYN-PCN.name: Pitcairn Islands
SYN-PCN.summary:
The Pitcairn Islands are a British Overseas Territory. Defence and external affairs are reserved to the United Kingdom, and United Kingdom domestic measures do not extend to Pitcairn of their own force; local ordinance governs.

Same-sex sexual activity has been legal in the Pitcairn Islands since 2001, so a visitor faces no criminalisation exposure on that ground.

The Pitcairn Constitution Order 2010 prohibits discrimination on grounds of sexual orientation, in force since 2010. The guarantee is constitutional rather than an offence provision, and it names sexual orientation and not gender identity, so a trans visitor has no express constitutional protection on gender-identity grounds.

Same-sex marriage has been legal since 14 May 2015. The Same Sex Marriage and Civil Partnerships Ordinance 2015 defines marriage as the union of two people regardless of sex, sexual orientation or gender identity, so the local definition of marriage carries no birth-sex or gender-identity bar.

The same ordinance recognises civil partnerships performed outside Pitcairn, which supports recognition of a visitor's existing foreign partnership.

The permanent population is roughly 50 and no resident is known to be in a same-sex relationship. There is no documented trans or LGB community presence, and a visitor cannot be anonymous in a population that small.

No trans-specific violence has been reported in the Pitcairn Islands, and no sourced reporting documents hostility toward visitors on these grounds.

Military service falls under UK responsibility.

SYN-PYF.name: French Polynesia
SYN-PYF.summary:
French Polynesia is an overseas collectivity of France, and French law governs justice and civil status in the territory while territorial institutions in Papeete regulate much of daily life.

Gender-diverse healthcare in the territory is limited by the small number of specialists available locally. Under Vice-President Eliane Tevahitua, the territorial government tabled a social-security bill that would have fully reimbursed hormonal treatment with progesterone and testosterone, matching mainland France; after heated debate in the Territorial Assembly the bill did not obtain sufficient support and lapsed. For a trans visitor staying any length of time, the gap between the law on paper and the care actually reachable in the archipelago is the most concrete material constraint.

The mahu role, a traditional Polynesian recognition of gender diversity in which individuals embody both male and female qualities and hold recognised standing, predates colonisation, and mahu and rae-rae are visible across the islands in daily life. Reporting from OutTraveler in July 2025 described this openness as ingrained in the culture rather than secured by law, noting that a visiting gay couple checked online whether the destination was safe before travelling and found mainstream inclusivity and acceptance operating without pride flags or organised protest. The 118-island territory has no Pride movement to speak of, which visitors read either as reassurance or as evidence that visibility is tolerated rather than defended.

sources.summary: BuzzFeed News feature (Jan 2018): in France, detention follows the gender marked on an ID, and Article D248 requires separate men's and women's establishments, so trans women holding male markers are held with men. The article treats this as a legal grey area. France's framework governs French Polynesia as an overseas collectivity subject to French law.

CGLPL opinion (25 May 2021) on transgender persons in places of deprivation of liberty: since France's Law 2016-1547 civil-status gender change no longer requires medical transition/surgery, yet no norms were added on how to house detainees accordingly - serious violations persist across French detention. French-framework treatment applicable in French Polynesia's prisons.

The mahu is a traditional Polynesian social role in which mahu embody both male and female qualities and hold cultural standing.

OutTraveler (4 Jul 2025): 'French Polynesia doesn't need Pride flags' describes openness as ingrained in the culture, with mahu and rae-rae visible in daily life across the 118 islands. A visiting gay couple reports first checking whether the destination is safe, and describes mainstream LGBTQ+ inclusivity and acceptance without Pride displays.

RNZ Pacific: French Polynesia LGBTQIA reflection - churches round table with University of French Polynesia; Vice-President Eliane Tevahitua's government tabled a social-security Bill to fully reimburse hormonal treatment (progesterone/testosterone) like mainland France, but after heated Territorial Assembly debate the Bill failed to gain sufficient support. sources.summary: French national law, drawn from Wikipedia country coverage, with no stated bearing on French Polynesia: sodomy provisions were repealed by the Penal Code of 1791 and the Penal Code of 1810 retained that silence; an indecent-exposure clause (article 330, 2nd alinea) inserted in 1960 by the Mirguet amendment doubled penalties where the act was homosexual and was repealed in 1980, and in March 2024 the National Assembly unanimously passed a compensation bill for men arrested under it, with the Senate yet to vote. A Vichy law of 6 August 1942 set consent at 21 for homosexual relations against 15 for heterosexual ones, lowered to 18 in 1974 and equalised at 15 in 1982; LGBTQ people in Alsace and Lorraine were interned in Nazi camps after 1940. The law of 31 December 2004 made homophobic, sexist, racist and xenophobic comments illegal, punishable by up to €45,000 and/or 12 months' imprisonment, criticised by Reporters Without Borders and defended by the Chirac government; Christian Vanneste was convicted under it in January 2006 and that conviction was later cancelled by the Court of Cassation. Sexual orientation became a protected ground in employment and services in 1985, 'sexual identity' was added in July 2012, and on 18 November 2016 'gender identity' replaced it in article 225-1 of the Penal Code, with the Labour Code covering sexual orientation and gender identity in recruitment and training. Assaults motivated by the victim's sexual orientation attract heavier penalties, and in 2017 transphobia became an aggravating circumstance for all crimes punishable by prison. A report of 16 May 2020 recorded a 36% rise in homophobic and transphobic attacks in 2019, with police identifying around 1,870 victims against roughly 1,380 in 2018. The conversion-therapy ban passed the Senate on 7 December 2020 and took effect on 1 February 2022; Le Refuge estimated 3-4% of its helpline calls concerned conversion therapy. The Académie Nationale de Médecine described the rise in trans people seeking treatment as an 'epidemic-like phenomenon' and a 'primarily social problem'; a March 2024 report commissioned from The Little Mermaid Observatory called gender-affirming care a 'health scandal' and youth transness a 'social contagion', and a bill banning medical transition under 18 passed the Senate in May 2024 without National Assembly action since 23 July 2024. Late-2024 guidelines from the French Society of Pediatric Endocrinology and Diabetology recommend puberty blockers from Tanner stage 2. Civil solidarity pacts (PACS) date from 1999; same-sex marriage passed the National Assembly 329-229 on 12 February 2013 and was signed on 18 May 2013, with joint adoption rare thereafter and assisted reproduction extended to lesbian couples from September 2021. Schools observe 17 May under the 2019 Tous égaux, tous alliés campaign, enrolment forms use 'parent 1' and 'parent 2', and since March 2019 higher education institutions should use trans students' preferred names. Mayotte reports frequent family rejection and discrimination, and in 2014 only about 20% of overseas residents viewed homosexuality as a sexuality like any other, against 77% in metropolitan France.
