SYN-REU.name: Réunion
SYN-REU.summary: Réunion is a department of France and stands under French national law without local variation. No Réunion-specific signal on transgender visitors was identified in the source inventory: the criminal law, identity-document rules, anti-discrimination statute, marriage regime and custodial-placement rules that govern the island are the French national rules, and the national assessment applies here unchanged.

sources.summary: BuzzFeed News feature (12 Jan 2018): in France, where prisoners are placed by the sex on their ID under Article D248 of the criminal procedure code, transgender women held in male prisons fall into a legal grey area and are 'punished for a lot more than their alleged crimes' — the piece follows cases including a trans woman held at Lille in 2014 amid inmate threats. French framework applying to Réunion as a department.

Opinion of 25 May 2021 of the French places-of-deprivation-of-liberty watchdog (CGLPL): finds 'the persistence of serious violations' of transgender detainees' fundamental rights across French custody facilities, based on referrals since 2010 covering some forty transgender persons, interviews with associations and experts, and on-site/document inspections, with recommendations to the Interior, Justice and Health ministries. National framework covering Réunion.

PinkNews (26 Aug 2012): PM Jean-Marc Ayrault announced the same-sex marriage and adoption bill would go to the National Assembly and Senate in October 2012, fulfilling President Hollande's campaign pledge; both houses had to approve, and the Catholic Bishops Conference came out against adoption. The marriage statute that subsequently applied to Réunion with the 2013 metropolitan law.

Yagg (25 Jul 2012, French): the harassment bill adopted by the National Assembly amended Penal Code article L225-1 to add 'identité sexuelle' as a discrimination ground, making transphobia prosecutable; deputies Sergio Coronado (EELV) and Elisabeth Pochon (PS) intervened in the debate. This is the discrimination-protection basis in force in Réunion.

Yagg (19 May 2016, French): the National Assembly adopted amendment 282 — tabled by about forty Socialist deputies — inserting a Civil Code section to facilitate legal gender change for trans people, though the government's three sub-amendments could limit its scope. The gender-change framework applying to Réunion as state law.

sources.title: LGBTQ rights in Réunion (Wikipedia)
sources.summary: In 2010 France became the first country to declassify gender dysphoria as a mental illness by decree, though transgender rights organizations stated nothing changed beyond the announcement, with transsexualism remaining under ALD 31 with treatment funded by Sécurité Sociale. Discrimination on the basis of "sexual identity" was banned in 2012, with the term replaced by "gender identity" in 2016 including amendment of article 225-1 of the Penal Code on 18 November 2016 and protection in the Labour Code, and since 2017 transgender people have been allowed to change legal gender without surgery or medical diagnosis. The legal gender-change regime took effect 1 January 2017 after Senate approval 6 November 2015, Assembly approvals 24 May 2016 and 12 July 2016 and 12 October 2016, Constitutional Council ruling of constitutionality 17 November 2016, signature 18 November 2016 and publication the next day, requiring application before a court without psychiatrist certificates or proof of reassignment surgery while first-name change can be done at the registry office. In 2017 transphobia became an aggravating factor for all crimes punishable by prison, and a 16 May 2020 report recorded police identification of around 1,870 victims of transphobic and homophobic attacks in 2019, up 36% from around 1,380 in 2018. Gender-affirming surgery within France was legalised in 1979, and a 2022 ILGA-Europe report found lack of self-determination, extended waiting times and inequitable access by location and recommended informed consent and self-determination. The National Academy of Medicine has characterized increased treatment-seeking as an "epidemic-like phenomenon" and "primarily social problem" advising extreme caution without changing actual practice, while a March 2024 Senate-commissioned report led to a Senate-passed May 2024 bill to ban medical transition under 18 opposed by the Macron government and unlikely to pass the Assembly with no update since 23 July 2024, and in late 2024 the French Society of Pediatric Endocrinology and Diabetology recommended puberty blockers from at least Tanner stage 2 with calcium and vitamin D supplements. Transgender individuals are allowed to serve openly in the French Armed Forces, conversion therapy was banned by a bill passed by the Senate 7 December 2020, concurred by the Assembly 25 January 2022 and published 1 February 2022 with proposed punishments of two years' imprisonment and/or 30,000 euro fine, and in March 2019 the Minister of Higher Education announced institutions should use transgender people's preferred names including on student cards and exam forms. Same-sex sexual activity was decriminalised by the Penal Code of 1791 with no mention of same-sex relations in private, retained in the Penal Code of 1810 and followed in French colonies adopting the Code, while a discriminatory age of consent of 21 for homosexual relations versus 15 for heterosexual introduced 6 August 1942 and lowered to 18 in 1974 was repealed 4 August 1982 to equalise at 15, and a 1960 provision doubling penalty for homosexual indecent exposure under article 330 alinea 2 was repealed in 1980. Civil solidarity pacts (PACS) were enacted in 1999 for same-sex and unmarried opposite-sex couples affording most marriage protections, and France became the thirteenth country to legalise same-sex marriage through a bill approved by the Assembly 12 February 2013 by 329-229 and Senate 12 April 2013, ruled constitutional 17 May 2013, signed 18 May 2013 with first ceremony 29 May in Montpellier, with joint adoption legal since May 2013. National legislation prohibiting sexual orientation discrimination in employment, housing and goods/services was enacted in 1985 and incorporated in the Labour Code, and the law of 31 December 2004 made homophobic comments illegal punishable by up to 45,000 euro fine and/or 12 months' imprisonment and amended the Press Law of 29 July 1881 to cover injury, defamation, insult, incitement to hatred/violence or discrimination based on gender, sexual orientation or disability, while physical assault or murder motivated by sexual orientation carries increased penalties. The December 2004 law created the High Authority against Discrimination and for Equality, the Ministry of Education announced anti-discrimination including homophobia as a 2008-2009 priority and launched the January 2019 Tous égaux, tous alliés campaign with reporting services, helpline and LGBTQ guidance plus observance of 17 May, and lesbian, gay and bisexual individuals are allowed to serve openly in the Armed Forces. A ban on men who have sex with men donating blood dating to 20 June 1983 was recalled 12 January 2009, replaced by one-year abstinence effective 10 July 2016, reduced to four months from 2 April 2020, then removed 16 March 2022 applying the same policy regardless of sexual orientation, and in March 2024 the Assembly unanimously passed a bill for compensation to gay men arrested under Article 330 prior to 1980 pending Senate vote.

SYN-SHN.name: Saint Helena
SYN-SHN.summary:
Saint Helena is a British Overseas Territory. United Kingdom legislation reaches it only where extended by order, so the territory's own ordinances and institutions, not United Kingdom law, determine what a visitor encounters. No transgender-specific criminal, documentation, screening, facilities, custody, care or violence provision is documented in territory law.

Consensual same-sex activity has been lawful since 2001, and the age of consent is equalised at 16 across Saint Helena, Ascension Island and Tristan da Cunha. No penalty provision specific to transgender people is documented.

The St Helena, Ascension and Tristan da Cunha Constitution Order 2009 bans discrimination on grounds including sexual orientation and has been in force since 2009. It defines "discriminatory" as affording different treatment to different persons on any ground such as sex, sexual orientation, race, colour, language, religion, political or other opinion, national or social origin, association with a national minority, property, age, disability, birth or other status. The enumerated grounds do not include gender reassignment, and no extension of the ban to gender reassignment is documented.

The Commission for Equality and Human Rights Ordinance 2015 defines "gender reassignment" as an intended, current or past process, or part of such a process, for reassigning a person's sex by changing physiological or other attributes of sex, or the state of mind whereby a person psychologically identifies with a gender inconsistent with, or not culturally associated with, their assigned sex at birth. The same ordinance defines sexual orientation as a person's orientation towards persons of the same sex, the opposite sex, or either sex.

The Equality and Human Rights Commission in Saint Helena monitors human rights laws, promotes understanding of the importance of equality, and works towards the elimination of unlawful discrimination. It may conduct inquiries and investigations into persons suspected of having committed an unlawful act, including unlawful discrimination on the basis of sexual orientation or gender reassignment.

Same-sex marriage is legal on Ascension Island under the Marriage (Ascension) Ordinance 2016, approved by the Ascension Island Council on 31 May 2016 by 5 votes to 0, signed and gazetted on 20 June 2016, and commenced on 1 January 2017. On Tristan da Cunha it has been legal since 4 August 2017 under the Marriages (Tristan da Cunha) Ordinance 2017, which defines marriage as the union of two persons regardless of sex and extends eligibility, formalities, rights and recognition to same-sex couples on equal terms with opposite-sex couples. On Saint Helena it has been legal since 20 December 2017 under the Marriage Ordinance 2017; the first same-sex marriage there took place on 31 December 2018. No marriage provision specific to transgender people is documented.

Adoption by same-sex couples has been permitted since 2017. Under the Saint Helena Welfare of Children Ordinance 2010, covering Saint Helena and Tristan da Cunha, and the Ascension Island Child Welfare Ordinance 2011, single and married people may adopt regardless of sexual orientation. No adoption provision specific to transgender people is documented.

sources.summary: As of 25 Apr 2026, same-sex sexual activity is legal in the territory, discrimination protections have been in force since 2009, and same-sex marriage has been legal on Ascension Island since 2017 (Alchetron).

Consensual same-sex relations became lawful in 2001. The age of consent is equalised at 16 territory-wide. The territory is an Overseas Country or Territory of the EU, with EU Charter applicability (GayLawNet, accessed 23 Jun 2013, citing ILGA State-sponsored Homophobia).

sources.title: LGBTQ rights in Saint Helena (Wikipedia)
sources.summary: No transgender-specific criminal, documentation, screening, facilities, custody, care, or violence provisions are documented. The Equality and Human Rights Commission in Saint Helena monitors human rights laws, promotes understanding of the importance of equality, and works towards elimination of unlawful discrimination. The Commission may conduct inquiries and investigations on persons suspected of having committed an unlawful act, including unlawful discrimination on the basis of sexual orientation or "gender reassignment". Under the Commission for Equality and Human Rights Ordinance 2015, "gender reassignment" means "an intended, current or past process (or part of such a process) for the purpose of reassigning a person's sex by changing physiological or other attributes of sex or the state of mind whereby a person psychologically identifies with a gender inconsistent or not culturally associated with their assigned sex at birth". No extension of the Constitution Order 2009 sexual-orientation discrimination ban to gender reassignment, and no transgender-specific marriage, adoption, or penalty provisions, are documented. Homosexuality is legal in Saint Helena, Ascension and Tristan da Cunha. The St Helena, Ascension and Tristan da Cunha Constitution Order 2009 bans discrimination based on sexual orientation, defining "discriminatory" as "affording different treatment to different persons on any ground such as sex, sexual orientation, race, colour, language, religion, political or other opinion, national or social origin, association with a national minority, property, age, disability, birth or other status." The Equality and Human Rights Commission in Saint Helena monitors human rights laws, promotes "understanding of the importance of equality" and works towards elimination of unlawful discrimination, with power to conduct inquiries and investigations into suspected unlawful discrimination on the basis of sexual orientation. Under the Commission for Equality and Human Rights Ordinance 2015, sexual orientation means "a person's sexual orientation towards— (a) persons of the same sex; (b) persons of the opposite sex; or (c) persons of either sex". Same-sex marriage has been legal on Ascension Island since 1 January 2017 under the Marriage (Ascension) Ordinance, 2016, on Tristan da Cunha since 4 August 2017 under the Marriages (Tristan da Cunha) Ordinance, 2017, and on Saint Helena since 20 December 2017 under the Marriage Ordinance 2017, with the first same-sex marriage in Saint Helena occurring on 31 December 2018. Under the Saint Helena Welfare of Children Ordinance 2010 for Saint Helena and Tristan da Cunha and the Ascension Island Child Welfare Ordinance 2011 for Ascension Island, single and married people may adopt regardless of sexual orientation, while a 2006 UK Government report recorded no adoptions in Saint Helena or Ascension Island for many years.

SYN-TCA.name: Turks and Caicos Islands
SYN-TCA.summary:
The Turks and Caicos Islands is a British Overseas Territory standing under the United Kingdom framework, and its own ordinances and courts govern immigration status, family recognition and non-discrimination. Same-sex sexual activity has been legal there since 2001, and the constitution prohibits discrimination on the ground of sexual orientation.

In a Court of Appeal ruling, the Director of Immigration was ordered to issue a residence permit to Timothy Haymon as the spouse of Richard Sankar. The court read "spouse" in the Immigration Ordinance to include a spouse lawfully married in another jurisdiction, and held that refusing the permit on sexual-orientation grounds contravened the constitution's equality, non-discrimination and private-and-family-life guarantees. The statutory definition of marriage was left untouched, so the decision creates no local right to marry. A trans visitor whose relationship local law would read as same-sex under birth-sex status can rely on a marriage lawfully entered elsewhere to support residence in the territory, in the same way as the spouses of residents.

Document handling for trans people runs through United Kingdom channels. The HM Passport Office knowledge-base profile for the Turks and Caicos Islands, official operational guidance published in 2025, states that transgender citizens are recognised in the territory and that the passport office processes gender-recognised documents for this jurisdiction. A visitor presenting a United Kingdom passport with a changed gender marker can expect it to be treated as valid in the territory. No local statute or instrument giving effect to that recognition is identified in the available sources.

Visibility is low. A resident account published in 2009 described virtually no information about gay life in the territory and no visible social scene, with privacy as the everyday norm; the account attributed this partly to a population in which roughly two-thirds of residents are not originally from the islands, leaving full-citizen Belongers a demographic minority. That account is dated and impressionistic, and does not establish anything about current violence risk.

SYN-VAT.name: Holy See
SYN-VAT.summary:
No criminal provision in Vatican City law reaches consensual same-sex sexual activity between adults in private and non-commercial. The territory's legal code derives from the Italian Zanardelli Code of 1889 and has carried no such offence since 1890, including through the founding of the sovereign state in 1929. Nothing in the criminal law addresses being transgender.

The age of consent is 18 for all persons regardless of gender. A lower age of 14 applies to sexual relations within a marriage recognised as valid by the Catholic Church and by Vatican City law.

Vatican City has no legal mechanism for changing a gender marker on identity documents, and no anti-discrimination law covering sexual orientation or gender identity applies in the territory. No rule governs access to single-sex facilities for a trans visitor, and no document-amendment route exists for a resident or a visitor.

Vatican City operates no prison system. It maintains a few cells for pre-trial detention, and a person sentenced to imprisonment by Vatican City serves the term in Italian prisons at Vatican expense. There is no trans-specific prisoner-placement policy and no documented case of a trans prisoner held under Vatican City's authority.

The Congregation for Catholic Education's 2019 document 'Male and Female He Created Them' frames 'gender theory' as denying the difference and reciprocity of man and woman and as eliminating the anthropological basis of the family. It is an educational instruction addressed to Catholic institutions rather than a rule binding visitors, but it states the governing institution's position on gender identity.

A 2023 declaration by the Dicastery for the Doctrine of the Faith permitted spontaneous blessings for same-sex couples while forbidding any rite resembling marriage. A January 2024 press release reiterated that blessings never extend to the unions themselves.

Vatican City has consistently rejected civil recognition of same-sex unions, same-sex marriage, and the granting of adoption rights to same-sex couples. Pope Francis in 2023 expressed support for same-sex civil unions outside the Catholic Church while maintaining that the Sacrament of Marriage is between a man and a woman as instituted by God.

In 2021 Vatican foreign minister Archbishop Paul Richard Gallagher wrote to the Italian ambassador to the Holy See objecting to an Italian parliamentary bill meant to protect LGBTQ Italians against violence and discrimination. The objection targeted the provision prohibiting incitement of hatred on the basis of sexual orientation and gender identity, which the letter described as a violation of freedom of speech and of religion, and asked for the draft law's text to be reformulated.

On 13 January 1998 the activist Alfredo Ormando set himself on fire on St. Peter's Square, under Vatican jurisdiction, in protest at the Catholic religion's refusal of homosexuality. He died days later in hospital from severe burns.

The objection specifically targeted the section prohibiting incitement of hatred on the basis of sexual orientation and gender identity. The letter claimed that prohibition constituted a violation of freedom of speech and of religion. It asked for the draft law's text to be reformulated. Since 1890 the territory of what is now Vatican City has had no criminal laws against non-commercial, private, adult and consensual same-sex sexual activity under a legal code based on the Italian Zanardelli Code of 1889 in force since the founding of the sovereign state in 1929. The age of consent is set at 18 years for all persons regardless of gender, except for sexual relations within marriage recognized as valid by the Catholic Church and Vatican City laws where the legal age is 14. Foreign diplomats must not be part of a same-sex family and must not be divorced to be accredited, with openly gay French nominee Jean-Loup Kuhn-Delforge in a civil pact rejected in 2008 and openly gay practising Catholic single nominee Laurent Stefanini rejected in 2015, leading France to leave the post vacant from March 2015 to May 2016 before nominating another diplomat in May 2016. Vatican City has always expressed disagreement with any civil recognition of same-sex unions, same-sex marriage, and granting of adoption rights to same-sex couples, and while Pope Francis in 2023 expressed support for same-sex civil unions outside the Catholic Church he remained firm that the Sacrament of Marriage is between a man and a woman as instituted by God. The Vatican reserves the right to remove, suspend and dismiss immediately any official and employee who publicly admits to being gay or questions the general policy of the Vatican towards homosexuals. SYN-VGB.name: British Virgin Islands
SYN-VGB.summary:
Same-sex intimacy has not been a criminal offence in the British Virgin Islands since January 2001, when the United Kingdom's Privy Council ordered the repeal of the sodomy laws across the territory and four other remaining British Caribbean territories after the local legislatures declined to act. The change came by order of the United Kingdom's highest court of appeal rather than by enactment of the local House of Assembly; local legislator Orlando Smith said at the time that "there is nothing we can do."

The British Virgin Islands stands under the United Kingdom's constitutional framework, and measures of the United Kingdom's Parliament extend to it only when brought into force by Order in Council. A trans visitor should not assume that United Kingdom discrimination and service-access protections, including the Equality Act 2010 and its 2025 single-sex-services code, are available in the territory by default; any such protection must be traced to British Virgin Islands legislation or to a specific extension order.

Whether a marriage between two people of the same sex validly contracted elsewhere is recognised under British Virgin Islands law remains contested rather than settled. The case testing whether the United Kingdom marriage of Kinisha Forbes and Kirsten Lettsome is valid locally was still running when, on 29 July 2022, the BVI Christian Council lost its bid to appeal the case-management orders of Justice Adrian Jack, as reported by BVI News. That refusal cleared a procedural obstacle and left the proceedings in place; it is not a ruling on recognition. A trans visitor in a relationship that would be classed locally as same-sex cannot rely on recognition being settled.

No criminalisation of trans people, and no trans-specific protection machinery, appears in the sources for the territory. The visitor-relevant legal questions are the framework relationship with the United Kingdom and the unsettled recognition of marriages contracted elsewhere.

SYN-WLF.name: Wallis and Futuna Islands
SYN-WLF.summary:
Wallis and Futuna is a territorial collectivity of the French Republic. French civil and criminal law applies locally unless a local measure overrides it, and no provision of that framework criminalises transgender people or same-sex relations. Discrimination on grounds of gender identity has been prohibited since 2012, when the statute covering employment, housing and access to services was extended to Wallis and Futuna; the term used was "sexual identity" until a 2016 amendment replaced it with "gender identity" in article 225-1 of the Penal Code. The Labour Code bars exclusion from recruitment, internships, sanctions, dismissal and other discriminatory measures on account of gender identity.

Legal change of gender marker is available under the French reforms that took effect on 1 January 2017, following the Constitutional Council ruling of 17 November 2016, signature on 18 November and publication the next day. Applicants no longer need sex-reassignment surgery, forced sterilisation, a psychiatrist's certificate or medical proof, but must still go before a court. Change of first name can be handled at a registry office, after the self-certification provision was dropped. French law recognises no non-binary status, so a third-gender or X marker cannot be obtained. Gender identity disorder was removed as a diagnosis by decree in 2010, while transsexualism remains classified under the long-term illness category ALD 31, funded by the national health insurance scheme; gender-affirming surgery has been lawful domestically since 1979.

Since 2017 transphobia is an aggravating circumstance for every crime punishable by imprisonment. Conversion therapy was banned by a law published on 1 February 2022, after passage by the Senate on 7 December 2020 and concurrence by the National Assembly on 25 January 2022; the offence carries two years' imprisonment and a 30,000 euro fine.

Marriage between two people of the same legal sex has been lawful since 2013, following Constitutional Council approval on 17 May 2013, signature on 18 May and the first ceremony on 29 May in Montpellier, and is stated to be legal in all French overseas departments and territories; registered partnerships (PACS) have been available since 1999 and joint adoption since May 2013. A trans visitor whose relationship would be read as same-sex under birth-sex status can expect it to be recognised.

Detention is governed by the French framework. The national preventive mechanism's opinion of 25 May 2021, extending an earlier opinion of 30 June 2010, found that serious violations of fundamental rights persist in French places of deprivation of liberty, drawing on referrals concerning about 40 transgender detainees since 2010 and on interviews with associations and experts. Trans women whose legal gender is recorded as male, largely those who have not had surgery, are held in all-male establishments, a documented legal grey area; one such case involved a transfer to a men's facility in Lille in 2014.

Access to gender-affirming healthcare is uneven. A 2022 ILGA-Europe report found a lack of self-determination, extended waiting times and location-dependent inequitable access, and recommended informed consent and self-determination. The National Academy of Medicine has characterised the rise in demand as epidemic-like and primarily social, urging extreme caution without changing practice. After a March 2024 Senate-commissioned report critical of youth gender-affirming care, a bill to ban medical transition under the age of 18 passed the Senate in May 2024; it is opposed by the government and has been stalled since 23 July 2024. Guidelines issued in late 2024 by the French Society of Pediatric Endocrinology and Diabetology recommended puberty blockers with calcium and vitamin D supplements from at least Tanner stage 2.

Locally, the collectivity has a population of about 11,000, and its isolation and dominant Catholic and Polynesian norms leave practical barriers to healthcare and social acceptance. Roles comparable to fakafafine coexist with stigma and concealment.

sources.title: LGBTQ rights in Wallis and Futuna (Wikipedia)
sources.summary: Discrimination on the basis of 'sexual identity' has been banned since 2012, with the term replaced by 'gender identity' in 2016 amending article 225-1 of the Penal Code, and the Labour Code prohibits exclusion from recruitment, internships, sanctions, dismissal or discriminatory measures on account of gender identity. Effective 1 January 2017 after a Constitutional Council ruling on 17 November 2016, signature on 18 November 2016 and publication the next day, transgender people can legally change gender without sex reassignment surgery, forced sterilisation, psychiatrist certificates or medical proof, but must go before a court, while first-name change can be done by registry office after the self-certification provision was dropped. Gender identity disorder was removed as a diagnosis by decree in 2010 with transsexualism remaining under ALD 31 funded by Sécurité Sociale, and gender affirmative surgery has been legal domestically since 1979. Since 2017 transphobia is an aggravating circumstance for all crimes punishable by prison, and police identified around 1,870 victims of homophobic and transphobic attacks and insults in 2019, up 36% from around 1,380 in 2018. Transgender individuals are allowed to serve openly in the French Armed Forces, and in March 2019 the Minister of Higher Education sought use of transgender people's preferred names including on student cards and exam forms. A 2022 ILGA-Europe report found lack of self-determination, extended waiting times and location-dependent inequitable access to gender-affirming healthcare and recommended informed consent and self-determination, while the National Academy of Medicine characterized the rise as an epidemic-like and primarily social phenomenon urging extreme caution without changing practice. After a March 2024 Senate-commissioned report critical of youth gender-affirming care, a bill to ban medical transition under age 18 passed the Senate in May 2024 but is opposed by the Macron government and stalled since 23 July 2024, while late-2024 guidelines from the French Society of Pediatric Endocrinology and Diabetology recommended puberty blockers with calcium and vitamin D supplements from at least Tanner stage 2. Private same-sex sexual activity was decriminalised by the Penal Code of 1791 retained in the Penal Code of 1810 for colonies, while the 1960 Mirguet amendment doubling the penalty for homosexual indecent exposure under article 330 alinea 2 was repealed in 1980 and the discriminatory age of consent of 21 then 18 for homosexual relations versus 15 for heterosexual relations was equalised at 15 on 4 August 1982. In March 2024 the National Assembly unanimously passed a compensation bill for gay men arrested under Article 330 prior to 1980, still pending Senate vote. Sexual orientation discrimination in employment, housing and public and private goods and services has been banned since 1985 with Labour Code protection, and same-sex marriage signed 18 May 2013 after Constitutional Council approval 17 May 2013 with first ceremony 29 May in Montpellier following PACS partnerships from 1999 and joint adoption since May 2013 is stated as legal in all overseas departments and territories. The law of 31 December 2004 criminalised homophobic comments punishable by up to 45,000 euro fine and/or 12 months imprisonment and amended the Press Law of 29 July 1881 to cover injury, defamation, insult, incitement to hatred or violence or discrimination based on sexual orientation, with increased penalties when assault or murder is motivated by sexual orientation, creating the High Authority against Discrimination and for Equality. Police identified around 1,870 victims of homophobic and transphobic attacks in 2019 versus around 1,380 in 2018, after President Macron in October 2018 denounced homophobic violence as unworthy of France. Conversion therapy was banned by law published 1 February 2022 after Senate passage 7 December 2020 and Assembly concurrence 25 January 2022 carrying two years imprisonment and/or 30,000 euro fine, and the MSM blood-donation ban from 20 June 1983 recalled in 2009 moved from one-year abstinence effective 10 July 2016 to four months from 2 April 2020 to removal on 16 March 2022 for all regardless of orientation, with lesbian, gay and bisexual individuals allowed to serve openly in the Armed Forces.

SYN-WLF.tangentialFactors:
Wallis and Futuna has no local legislature producing trans-specific law; the legal position is the French one, and no local measure overriding the national framework was identified in the sources. The practical constraints are geographic and social rather than statutory: a small, isolated population with limited specialist services.

Provisions of French law that are not specific to Wallis and Futuna, among them the older criminal-code history, the employment discrimination provisions dating from 1985, the press-law offences created in 2004, the blood-donation rules and the position of transgender service members, are documented at the national level.
SYN-WLF.localsOnly:
Residents seeking a gender-marker change must still appear before a court, and first-name changes are handled at the registry office. Transsexualism remains classified under ALD 31, so related care is funded through the national health insurance scheme.

Specialist gender-affirming care is not available locally; residents travel to metropolitan France or rely on limited local services. Social acceptance is constrained by the dominant Catholic and Polynesian norms, and roles comparable to fakafafine coexist with stigma and concealment.
SYN-WLF.outOfScopeNotes:
No source in the inventory documents entry or airport screening practice specific to transgender travellers in Wallis and Futuna, or local enforcement of the discrimination and hate-crime provisions. Local hate-crime statistics for the collectivity are not sourced; the French figures cited in the national material are raw counts without a population denominator.

The 2024 Senate bill on medical transition under 18 remains stalled and its application to the collectivity is unresolved. Provisions of French law that are not specific to Wallis and Futuna are documented at the national level.
SYN-WLF.blindSummary:
The country is a dependent state/province of the parent nation. The parent nation's civil and criminal law applies locally unless a local measure overrides it, and no provision of that framework criminalises transgender people or same-sex relations. Discrimination on grounds of gender identity has been prohibited since 2012, when the statute covering employment, housing and access to services was extended to the country; the term used was "sexual identity" until a 2016 amendment replaced it with "gender identity" in the criminal code. The labour code bars exclusion from recruitment, internships, sanctions, dismissal and other discriminatory measures on account of gender identity.

Legal change of gender marker is available under the reforms that took effect on 1 January 2017, following the constitutional court's ruling of 17 November 2016, signature on 18 November and publication the next day. Applicants no longer need sex-reassignment surgery, forced sterilisation, a psychiatrist's certificate or medical proof, but must still go before a court. Change of first name can be handled at a registry office, after the self-certification provision was dropped. The law recognises no non-binary status, so a third-gender or X marker cannot be obtained. Gender identity disorder was removed as a diagnosis by decree in 2010, while transsexualism remains classified under a long-term illness category funded by the national health insurance scheme; gender-affirming surgery has been lawful domestically since 1979.

Since 2017 transphobia is an aggravating circumstance for every crime punishable by imprisonment. Conversion therapy was banned by a law published on 1 February 2022, after passage by the upper house on 7 December 2020 and concurrence by the lower house on 25 January 2022; the offence carries two years' imprisonment and a 30,000 euro fine.

Marriage between two people of the same legal sex has been lawful since 2013, following the constitutional court's approval on 17 May 2013, signature on 18 May and the first ceremony on 29 May in a city, and is stated to be legal in all outlying jurisdictions of the parent nation; registered partnerships have been available since 1999 and joint adoption since May 2013. A trans visitor whose relationship would be read as same-sex under birth-sex status can expect it to be recognised.

Detention is governed by the parent nation's framework. The national preventive mechanism's opinion of 25 May 2021, extending an earlier opinion of 30 June 2010, found that serious violations of fundamental rights persist in places of deprivation of liberty, drawing on referrals concerning about 40 transgender detainees since 2010 and on interviews with associations and experts. Trans women whose legal gender is recorded as male, largely those who have not had surgery, are held in all-male establishments, a documented legal grey area; one such case involved a transfer to a men's facility in a city in 2014.

Access to gender-affirming healthcare is uneven. A 2022 report by a regional rights organisation found a lack of self-determination, extended waiting times and location-dependent inequitable access, and recommended informed consent and self-determination. The national medical academy has characterised the rise in demand as epidemic-like and primarily social, urging extreme caution without changing practice. After a March 2024 upper-house-commissioned report critical of youth gender-affirming care, a bill to ban medical transition under the age of 18 passed the upper house in May 2024; it is opposed by the government and has been stalled since 23 July 2024. Guidelines issued in late 2024 by a national paediatric endocrinology society recommended puberty blockers with calcium and vitamin D supplements from at least Tanner stage 2.

Locally, the country has a small population, and its isolation and dominant religious and local cultural norms leave practical barriers to healthcare and social acceptance. Gender-variant roles recognised in local custom coexist with stigma and concealment.

72843720B863019116732.name: Centro
72843720B863019116732.summary:
Centro stands under Italy's national framework on legal gender recognition, discrimination and asylum. The findings specific to this region are judicial and documentary: a regional distribution of recorded anti-LGBT violence, an administrative ruling in Rome, and a homicide acquittal in Perugia.

Progetto Gionata's region-by-region study of anti-LGBT hate-motivated violence, covering 2012 to 2025, ranks six Italian regions at the top by victim count. Lazio and Toscana, both within Centro, are two of the six, alongside Lombardia and Piemonte in the north-west and Campania and Puglia in the south. The ranking is by raw victim counts, which track population, and the study supplies no per-capita denominator, so it does not establish that any one of these regions carries a higher rate of violence than another.

In Rome, the municipal administration announced on 30 August 2025 that the Consiglio di Stato, the country's highest administrative court, had upheld the city's 2022 removal of Pro Vita & Famiglia posters attacking "gender" ideology in schools. The court found the images discriminatory, one of them showing a boy being handed a red hairbow, and held that public spaces may not be used for messages that generate alarmism, fear or serious disturbance, particularly where minors are concerned. The campaign behind the posters had collected 105,000 online signatures. The outcome confirms that anti-trans public messaging can be restricted in the region's largest city.

In Perugia, the Court of Cassation confirmed on 5 March 2026 the appeal acquittal of a trans woman, Pinheiro Reis Duarte Hudson, known as Patrizia, over the death of Samuele De Paoli on 27 April 2021. The court held that the death resulted from cardiac arrhythmia caused by accidental compression during a scuffle that De Paoli started, making the acquittal on the homicide charge final. The case was a national anti-trans media flashpoint, and the definitive judicial outcome favoured the trans defendant in the region's main university city.

sources.summary: On 24 January 2025 a Bologna first-instance court recognised a transphobic motive in the punitive rape of a trans sex worker, sentenced the perpetrator, awarded damages to the victim and to the trans-movement association that helps sex workers, and for the first time admitted the Movimento Identita Trans (MIT) as civil party. This is the strongest judicial recognition of transphobic aggravation recorded in Italy.

Progetto Gionata's region-by-region study of anti-LGBT hate-motivated violence, covering 2012 to 2025, names the Italian regions with the highest victim counts, six regions ranking at the top. Lazio and Toscana, both in Centro, are two of the six highest-victim regions, alongside Lombardia, Piemonte (Nord-Ovest), Campania and Puglia (Sud). The study supplies the per-region distribution of violence.

72843720B99597932318450.name: Nord-Ovest
72843720B99597932318450.summary:
Nord-Ovest stands under the national framework of Italy; the findings below are specific to this region. Milan operates Italy's first gender registry, the registro di genere, which allows transgender people to use their chosen name on civic and municipal documents. Turin runs a parallel practice, Identita Alias, at municipal offices and libraries. Both are city-level instruments, and no regional statute governs gender recognition or anti-discrimination in Nord-Ovest.

Progetto Gionata's breakdown of anti-LGBT aggressions by region and city for 2012–2025 places two of Nord-Ovest's constituent regions among the six highest-victim regions in the country. The ranking is by raw count and the source provides no per-capita denominator, so it does not establish that an individual in Nord-Ovest faces higher risk than in a smaller, less populous region.

sources.summary: LifeGate: Milan inaugurated Italy's first gender registry ('registro di genere'), letting transgender people use their chosen name on civic and municipal documents — presented as a milestone for transgender rights in the country; the record ties it to a 2022 council motion by the country's first elected transgender councillor, with Turin's parallel 'Identita Alias' practice at municipality and libraries.

Progetto Gionata's breakdown of aggressions by region and city, 2012-2025, shows that the region's two constituent regions rank among the country's six highest-victim regions for anti-LGBT hate-motivated violence.

sources.title: Italy 'to open first prison for transgender inmates' | BBC News
sources.summary: BBC News (12 Jan 2010): Italy announced plans for one of the world's first dedicated transgender prisons at Pozzale, near Florence - converting a nearly empty medium-security women's prison into a specially equipped detention centre for about 30 of Italy's roughly 60 transgender prisoners (mostly convicted of drug or prostitution offences); gay-rights groups welcomed the dedicated space and its psychological support. The report states that until then transgender prisoners had been located in women's prisons 'where they are often segregated for their own safety' - the documented 2010 baseline for placement practice in Italy. Repubblica (2013) later reported the Pozzale project was abandoned.

sources.title: La doppia sofferenza delle trans in carcere | La Repubblica (Inchieste)
sources.summary: La Repubblica investigative report 'La doppia sofferenza delle trans in carcere' (28 Aug 2013): at that date the prison administration counted 69 transsexual prisoners spread across ten Italian facilities, with placement tracking legal sex - female hormones could not be prescribed to prisoners who 'according to their identity card, count as men,' trans women were held in men's sections, and those who had already undergone sex-change surgery were 'destined for the women's sections.' Segregation practice: in some prisons trans prisoners were put in isolation when cells were lacking - described as the most inhumane way to preserve their safety - and protected sections such as the G8 section at Rebibbia (Rome) and the protected section at Poggioreale (Naples) imposed limitations, including on partner visits. Documented ruling: the 2011 Terni case in which the Spoleto surveillance magistrate ordered the local health authority to pay for the prisoner's hormone therapy 'to guarantee psychophysical integrity'; the ruling was appealed and followed by a July 2012 appellate decision. The dedicated Pozzale transgender prison project (2008-2010), which would have drawn trans women from the special wing of Sollicciano (Florence), was shelved.

72843720B59566147937015.name: Nord-Est
72843720B59566147937015.summary:
Visitors to Nord-Est fall under the national framework of Italy. Rules on entry, identity documents, legal gender recognition and criminal law are national and are set out in the country record for Italy; the region-level material identified for Nord-Est concerns Veneto.

The Veneto Regional Council passed motion n.340 at its 178th public session in Venice on 3 July. Deliberation n.92 of 14 October 2014 approved that motion, committing the regional government to a mandatory 'Natural Family Day' observance on the last school day before Christmas and rejecting the aims of gender-awareness content.

The full text of the motion is carried in the official bulletin of the Veneto regional government, which is the primary source for the act; the deliberation is the instrument through which the regional administration was committed.

The measure is educational in scope. It governs a school observance and the regional government's stated position on gender-awareness teaching inside Veneto, and creates no requirement for visitors. No Veneto or other Nord-Est provision on documents, facilities or health-care access appears in this inventory.

The inventory holds no region-specific material for other parts of Nord-Est, and none on regional policing or enforcement practice. For those areas the national assessment for Italy applies without regional qualification.

82249235B5553315981608.name: Alberta
82249235B5553315981608.summary:
Alberta stands under the Canadian national framework for human rights, criminal law, entry and federal custody. The province's own trans-specific lawmaking is a 2024 package of three statutes that passed final legislative stage on 4 December 2024. The Education Amendment Act, 2024 introduced parental opt-in for classroom instruction on sexuality and rules on students' preferred names, pronouns and participation in school sport. The Health Statutes Amendment Act, 2024 bars certain gender-affirming care for minors. The Fairness and Safety in Sport Act bars trans women from women's sport. All three operate on minors, schools and organised sport rather than on adult visitors.

The Protecting Alberta's Children Statutes Amendment Act, 2025 invoked the Charter's notwithstanding clause to shield the three statutes from Charter challenge. Egale Canada, the Skipping Stone Foundation and five families stated that their court challenge continues regardless. The three statutes are in force and the constitutional litigation is pending, so the restrictions apply while their validity is contested.

The package deliberately excluded custodial and facility settings. Premier Danielle Smith's 12 February 2024 announcement stated that the measures would not extend to women's shelters, women's prisons or women's changing rooms. No provincial rule requiring placement by birth sex in Alberta correctional institutions was enacted, and no Alberta-specific trans-prisoner placement, special unit or segregation case is documented. For a visitor, no provincial rule restricts restroom or changing-room use, and no provincial custodial placement rule is on the books.

Alberta's human rights legislation prohibits discrimination on the grounds of gender identity and gender expression in employment, housing and public and private accommodation, giving a visitor or resident a provincial complaint route against an employer, landlord or service provider.

On partner and family recognition, Alberta's 2000 Marriage Act, which defined marriage as between a man and a woman and invoked the notwithstanding clause, was invalid: the capacity to marry is exclusive federal jurisdiction and the Act's five-year exemption expired in 2005. Alberta legalised stepchild adoption in 1999 and joint adoption in 2007.

The practical reach of the 2024 package for a visitor is narrow. A trans adult travelling to Alberta faces no restriction on facilities or on adult care under these statutes. A trans minor, or a family travelling with one, would be in a province where certain gender-affirming care for minors is prohibited by statute, and a trans woman entering competition in Alberta would be barred from women's categories.

sources.summary: CBC (4 Dec 2024): Alberta's trio of trans-youth bills passed final legislative stage — the Education Amendment Act 2024 (parental opt-in for classroom instruction, student pronoun and sport rules), a health-statutes act barring certain gender-affirming care for minors, plus sports policy. Egale Canada and the Skipping Stone Foundation announced constitutional litigation, calling the package discriminatory.

CBC (Dec 2024): Bill 9, the Protecting Alberta's Children Statutes Amendment Act, passed at the tail of the fall sitting, invoking the Charter's notwithstanding clause to shield the three trans-youth laws from legal challenge for years; Egale Canada, Skipping Stone Foundation and five families said their court challenge to Bill 26 continues regardless. Result: laws in force, constitutional litigation pending.

sources.title: Transgender rights in Canada (Wikipedia)
sources.summary: Federal placement mechanics governing trans prisoners in federal custody inside Alberta: since 2018, federal corrections operations accommodate offenders based on gender identity rather than sex assigned at birth, and the Correctional Service of Canada (CSC) permits gender-diverse offenders to request placement or transfer to a men's or women's institution aligned with their gender identity or expression, regardless of anatomy or the sex/gender marker on identity documents, with requests refused only where CSC finds unresolvable 'overriding health or safety concerns'. As of 2025 CSC reported 90 self-identified transgender women in federal institutions, 73 housed in men's institutions and 17 in women's. The Office of the Correctional Investigator called CSC's 2022 gender-diversity policy an important change but flagged the lack of clear parameters for what counts as an 'overriding health or safety concern' and the absence of a dedicated mechanism for gender-diverse prisoners to report abuse. Provincial correctional policies vary; no Alberta-specific rule is documented.

sources.title: Danielle Smith (Wikipedia)
sources.summary: Alberta's statutory trans package deliberately excluded jail and prison settings. Premier Danielle Smith's 12 February 2024 announcement covered a ban on gender-affirming care for minors, parental-consent rules for school pronouns and sexuality instruction, and a ban on trans women in women's sports, and stated the bans 'would not include a ban on women's shelters, women's prisons or women's changing rooms' (Wikipedia biography of Danielle Smith, citing CBC's Lily Dupuis, 12 April 2024, that Alberta's proposed transgender rules won't include public change rooms or jails). No provincial placement-by-birth-sex rule for trans prisoners was enacted, and no Alberta-specific trans-prisoner placement, special unit or segregation case is documented.

sources.title: LGBTQ rights in Alberta (Wikipedia)
sources.summary: Federal, provincial and territorial human rights acts prohibit discrimination on the basis of gender identity or expression in employment, housing and public and private accommodations, with all jurisdictions explicitly including gender identity as a prohibited ground as of 2017. Supreme Court jurisprudence has interpreted the concepts of sex and physical disability in section 15 of the Charter to include transsexuality and HIV/STDs, and section 15 applies to all laws and government institutions including law enforcement authorities, while private-sector complaints proceed under applicable federal or provincial human rights statutes. Transgender people are able to change their legal gender in all provinces and territories under varying rules, with vital statistics including identity documents such as birth certificates falling under provincial jurisdiction. In 2023 Saskatchewan passed The Education (Parents’ Bill of Rights) Amendment Act, 2023 invoking the notwithstanding clause, which requires schools to obtain parental consent for students under age 16 who request use of their gender-related preferred name or gender identity and has prompted calls for repeal and legal action. In 2024 Alberta passed the Health Statutes Amendment Act, 2024, the Education Amendment Act, 2024 and the Fairness and Safety in Sport Act, which faced legal challenges in Alberta courts, and in 2025 Alberta passed Bill 9: Protecting Alberta’s Children Statutes Amendment Act, 2025 using the notwithstanding clause to block those Charter challenges. In December 2020 the Canadian Association of Chiefs of Police apologized for harm to Two-Spirit, Lesbian, Gay, Bisexual, Transgender and Queer Communities, acknowledged contribution to institutional bias, intolerance and violation of human rights and personal suffering, shame, trauma and distrust, stated “We must stand together against homophobia, transphobia, and any other kind of marginalization, shaming, disrespect or hate,” and created an Equity, Diversity and Inclusion Committee to identify, mitigate and eliminate implicit bias and systemic barriers. Since 2022 the Criminal Code statutorily bans conversion therapy nationwide for both minors and adults and makes it a crime to subject anyone to it as defined by statutory law. British Columbia, Ontario and Saskatchewan grant parental status to three or more intentional parents, allowing for a wider range of queer and trans families in addition to or in place of the birth parent. Same-sex sexual activity in private between consenting adults was decriminalized June 27, 1969 by the Criminal Law Amendment Act, 1968–69 (Bill C-150), and the remaining anal-intercourse offence in section 159 was repealed June 21, 2019 by Bill C-75 after courts in Ontario, Quebec, British Columbia, Nova Scotia and Alberta each declared it unconstitutional under Charter equality provisions, leaving a general age of consent of 16 since June 2019 and 18 where there is trust, authority, dependency or exploitation. In Egan v Canada (1995) the Supreme Court held sexual orientation is constitutionally protected under section 15 as an analogous ground, and in Vriend v Alberta (1998) held failure to include sexual orientation in human rights law itself violated section 15, with all provinces, territories and the federal government explicitly including sexual orientation as a prohibited ground of discrimination in employment, housing and public and private accommodations as of 2017. Same-sex marriage became legal nationwide July 20, 2005 by the federal Civil Marriage Act, making Canada the fourth country worldwide and first in the Americas to do so with no residency requirement, following court rulings in several provinces and one territory between 2002-2005, while Alberta’s 2000 Marriage Act defining marriage as between a man and a woman and invoking the notwithstanding clause was invalid because capacity to marry is exclusive federal jurisdiction and its five-year exemption expired in 2005. Same-sex adoption was legalized province by province from British Columbia in 1996 to Nunavut in 2011 as the last jurisdiction, with Alberta legalizing stepchild adoption in 1999 and joint adoption in 2007. In 2022 Canada became the third country worldwide and first in North America to statutorily ban conversion therapy nationwide for both minors and adults, making it a crime under the Criminal Code to subject anyone to it as statutorily defined. On November 28, 2017 the Prime Minister issued a formal parliamentary apology for oppression of lesbian, gay, bisexual, transgender, queer and two-spirit communities, and on June 21, 2018 the Expungement of Historically Unjust Convictions Act received royal assent allowing RCMP and federal departments to destroy or remove judicial records for pre-1969 homosexual acts or section 159 convictions, requiring notification to involved provincial or municipal police and courts, available to living and deceased persons and distinct from pardon or record suspension as recognition the act should never have been a crime. In December 2020 Canada’s police chiefs apologized for decades of oppression and opposition from the 1960s to the present, acknowledging institutional bias, intolerance and human rights violations. In a poll commissioned by the Privy Council Office reported for 2020, 91.8% of those surveyed said they would be “comfortable” if a next-door neighbour was gay, lesbian or bisexual, a sexuality-tolerance finding distinct from transgender tolerance. In that same 2020 Privy Council Office poll, 87.6% said they would be “comfortable” if a neighbour was a transgender person, the article’s documented transgender-specific tolerance statement. 2020 Pew Research showed 85% of Canada’s general population (92% among Canadians aged 18-29) favoured social acceptance of homosexuality, up from 80% in 2013, and June 2013 polls showed majority support for same-sex marriage available since 2005, with 70% agreeing same-sex couples should have same adoption rights and 76% agreeing they are just as likely to successfully raise children, all sexuality-specific findings. The article notes Canada was ranked first indicating least dangerous in Asher & Lyric’s LGBTQ+ Danger Index in 2023, first in the Gay Travel Index in 2024, and ninth in the Equaldex Equality Index in 2024, general LGBTQ rankings not disaggregated for transgender people.

Transgender people are now able to change their legal gender in all provinces and territories under varying rules. In 2023, Saskatchewan passed The Education (Parents’ Bill of Rights) Amendment Act, 2023 while invoking the notwithstanding clause, requiring schools to obtain parental consent for students under age 16 who request use of their gender-related preferred name or gender identity, and calls by human rights groups to repeal the law led to legal action that the clause may prevent from succeeding on Charter grounds. Saskatchewan is one of three provinces, with British Columbia and Ontario, that will grant parental status to three or more intentional parents, allowing for a wider range of queer and trans families. In December 2020, the Canadian Association of Chiefs of Police apologized for harm to Two-Spirit, Lesbian, Gay, Bisexual, Transgender and Queer communities, stated police must stand together against homophobia, transphobia and other marginalization, and created an Equity, Diversity and Inclusion Committee to address implicit bias and systemic barriers. Same-sex sexual activity in private between consenting adults was decriminalized on June 27, 1969 when the Criminal Law Amendment Act, 1968-69 (Bill C-150) was brought into force on royal assent. 82249235B4167839012994.name: New Brunswick
82249235B4167839012994.summary:
New Brunswick sets its own school and provincial human rights rules inside the Canadian legal framework; criminal law and the national human rights statute sit with the federal government. Its schools operate under a sexual orientation and gender identity policy issued by the Department of Education and Early Childhood Development. The policy's application clause covers the school environment as a whole, and alongside students and school personnel it names contract and casual employees, visiting professionals, student teachers, parents, volunteers and visitors. A trans visitor who enters a New Brunswick classroom as a visiting professional, student teacher or volunteer falls inside a rule set written to govern sexual orientation and gender identity.

The policy's current text took effect on 1 January 2025 under the Holt government. It allows students of any age to choose the names and pronouns used for them in informal school settings; parental consent is encouraged but not required. For students under 16, the name and gender recorded in formal school records still requires parental consent. The revision goes beyond the recommendations of child advocate Kelly Lamrock and reverses the consent rule the previous Progressive Conservative government introduced.

Under that earlier rule, in force from 1 July 2023, teachers were barred from using the preferred names and pronouns of students under 16 without parental consent, and explicit wording that allowed students to take part in extracurricular activities, including sports teams, in line with their gender identity was dropped. Premier Blaine Higgs's government made the change without a legislative vote. Two ministers resigned in protest and two more were pushed out; dissidents in the party called for a leadership review. When the change was proposed in June 2023, eight Progressive Conservative members, six of them cabinet ministers, sat out question period over the lack of process and transparency. A constitutional challenge to the rule was brought by the Canadian Civil Liberties Association.

The policy it replaced, adopted in 2020, required schools to respect students' chosen names and pronouns and to provide gender-neutral bathrooms, and required teachers to obtain a student's informed consent before discussing names and pronouns with parents. About 350 people rallied at the New Brunswick legislature on 14 May 2023 against the review of that policy; Gail Costello of Pride in Education, who helped write it, said the policy saves lives and that changing or removing it would lose children. Education Minister Bill Hogan confirmed the review. The federal prime minister said trans children in New Brunswick needed to feel safe and not targeted by politicians.

Outside schools, gender identity and gender expression are listed as prohibited grounds of discrimination in New Brunswick's human rights legislation, covering employment, housing and public and private accommodations; every province and territory lists the same two grounds as of 2017. Complaints about discrimination in areas of provincial responsibility are brought under the provincial human rights statute.

A constitutional challenge to the rule was brought by a civil liberties organisation.

The policy it replaced, adopted in 2020, required schools to respect students' chosen names and pronouns and to provide gender-neutral bathrooms, and required teachers to obtain a student's informed consent before discussing names and pronouns with parents. About 350 people rallied at the state/province legislature on 14 May 2023 against the review of that policy; an organiser with the education group that helped write it said the policy saves lives and that changing or removing it would lose children. The state/province's education minister confirmed the review. The national prime minister said trans children in the state/province needed to feel safe and not targeted by politicians.

Outside schools, gender identity and gender expression are listed as prohibited grounds of discrimination in the state/province's human rights legislation, covering employment, housing and public and private accommodations; every state/province lists the same two grounds as of 2017. Complaints about discrimination in areas of state/province responsibility are brought under the state/province human rights statute.

14339913B23556801435424.name: Scotland
14339913B23556801435424.summary:
Scotland is a constituent nation of the United Kingdom. Criminal law, policing, prisons and family law are devolved to the Scottish Parliament, while legal gender recognition and equality law are set at United Kingdom level; the findings set out here are those specific to Scotland.

Hate crime in Scotland is governed by the Hate Crime and Public Order (Scotland) Act 2021, passed by the Scottish Parliament in March 2021 by 82 votes to 32, given royal assent a month later and brought into force on 1 April 2024. It lists gender identity as a protected characteristic. Earlier Scottish legislation from 2009 provides for penalty enhancements where an offence is motivated by the victim's gender identity, alongside sexual orientation.

The Crown Office and Procurator Fiscal Service recorded 7,115 hate-crime charges in 2025-26, 17 per cent more than in 2024-25 and the highest total since 2003-04. Charges with a sexual-orientation aggravation numbered 2,062, the second most common category. Charges with a transgender-identity aggravation numbered 104, up 21 per cent from 86 and the highest figure since the 2021 Act took effect. Transgender-identity aggravations remain a small share of the total, and the increase is measured in raw counts.

Police-recorded hate crime for 2024-25, the first annual report under the 2021 Act, totalled 8,538 offences. Race was the aggravator in 62 per cent of them and sexual orientation in just over a quarter. The highest rates per 10,000 residents were in Glasgow City and the City of Edinburgh, at about 32.25 each.

Reform of gender recognition in Scotland has not taken effect. The Scottish Government announced in 2018 that it would add an "X" sex descriptor to identity documents and lower the minimum age of transition to 16. A Gender Recognition Reform (Scotland) Bill, applying only to Scotland, was introduced in March 2022 and passed by the Scottish Parliament in December 2022 by 86 votes to 39. The United Kingdom government blocked it under section 35 of the Scotland Act 1998, the first use of that power to overturn Scottish legislation, and it did not receive royal assent.

Same-sex marriage has been lawful in Scotland since 16 December 2014 under the Marriage and Civil Partnership (Scotland) Act 2014, passed on 4 February 2014 by 108 votes to 15, with royal assent on 12 March 2014 and first ceremonies on 31 December 2014. No religious organisation or celebrant is obliged to solemnise such a marriage. Civil partnerships have been available since 2005 under the Civil Partnership Act 2004.

sources.title: LGBTQ rights in Scotland (Wikipedia)
sources.summary: Under the Gender Recognition Act 2004, transgender people in Scotland may change their legal gender. In 2018 the Scottish Government announced plans to provide an "X" sex descriptor on identity documents and to lower the minimum age of transition to 16. A Gender Recognition Reform (Scotland) Bill to reform the 2004 Act was introduced in March 2022 and passed in December 2022 by 86-39, applying only to Scotland. The Bill was blocked by the UK government under section 35 of the Scotland Act 1998, the first use of that power to overturn Scottish legislation, while awaiting royal assent. The Equality Act 2010 covers gender reassignment and outlaws discrimination, harassment and victimisation because a person belongs to, is thought to belong to, or is associated with a protected group. Scotland enacted 2009 legislation providing penalty enhancements where crime is motivated by the victim's gender identity, and hate-crime legislation passed in March 2021 by 82-32, receiving royal assent a month later and taking effect 1 April 2024, explicitly includes gender identity. Same-sex sexual activity was legalised in Scotland by Section 80 of the Criminal Justice (Scotland) Act 1980, in force 1 February 1981, and the age of consent was equalised at 16 in 2001. Section 2A prohibiting promotion of homosexuality was repealed in Scotland by the Ethical Standards in Public Life etc. (Scotland) Act 2000. The Historical Sexual Offences (Pardons and Disregards) (Scotland) Act 2018, passed in June 2018 and effective in October 2019, issued symbolic pardons to men convicted of consensual same-sex activity before decriminalisation and allows an accepted disregard application to prevent inclusion in disclosure checks and treat the offence as not occurred. Civil partnerships for same-sex couples have been available since 2005 under the Civil Partnership Act 2004, conferring property, inheritance tax, social security, pension, parental responsibility, maintenance, tenancy, insurance and next-of-kin rights with formal dissolution akin to divorce. Same-sex marriage has been legal since 16 December 2014 under the Marriage and Civil Partnership (Scotland) Act 2014, passed 4 February 2014 by 108-15 with royal assent 12 March 2014, with first ceremonies 31 December 2014 and no obligation on religious organisations or celebrants to perform them. Same-sex couples obtained joint and stepchild adoption rights from 28 September 2009, with the Looked After Children (Scotland) Regulations 2009 allowing consideration as foster parents on the same basis as others. The Equality Act 2010 outlaws discrimination, harassment and victimisation based on sexual orientation, and 2009 legislation provides penalty enhancements for crimes motivated by sexual orientation, with sexual orientation explicitly included in the 2021 hate-crime law effective 1 April 2024.

31927357B79016588373767.name: Distrito Federal
31927357B79016588373767.summary:
Mexico City recorded 17 homicides of LGBT+ people in 2024, 11 of them trans women, the highest raw state count in the country that year and the first time the city has led the count, according to annual monitoring published in May 2025 by a Mexican LGBT+ news collective. These are raw counts. The sources supply no per-capita denominator and no general homicide rate for the city, so the figure cannot be presented as a rate or as a measure of risk relative to other jurisdictions.

The city's congress approved transfeminicidio as a distinct offence in the local penal code in July 2024, reported as 18 July and 19 July in different sources. The reform is known as the Ley Paola Buenrostro, after a trans woman murdered in 2016, and made Mexico City the second state to create the offence. Article 148-Ter, added to the code on 23 August 2024, defines transfeminicidio as the killing of a trans woman or feminine-spectrum person by reason of gender identity or expression.

In December 2024 the city created a dedicated Transfeminicide Investigation Unit. Its investigators may no longer demand legal name or gender change or medical documentation from trans people.

The prosecution-service agreement FGJCDMX/04/2025 sets initial-response protocol rules for transfeminicide cases alongside feminicide investigations.

On 25 August 2025 the mayor launched a Gender Police with 30 patrol units to handle cases of violence against women and girls in the city. The sources do not state whether its remit covers trans women.

31927357B30741484985331.name: Nuevo Leon
31927357B30741484985331.summary:
Nuevo León sits under Mexico's national framework; the findings below are specific to the state. Its penal code does not typify transfeminicidio. A bill to add the offence was filed, ignored for a year and allowed to lapse, so a fresh filing was required. A trans visitor assaulted in Nuevo León has no state-level aggravated homicide category for anti-trans violence.

Three trans women were killed in Nuevo León in under a week in July 2024. One was Arantza Castillo, 23, killed while doing sex work; another was found dead in a motel on 27 June 2024 and had not been identified. The state justice ministry issued no case information on any of them.

Civil-society tallies for 2024 record four transfeminicides in Nuevo León. Asamblea Nacional Trans No Binarie counted at least four in the state that year; Verificado recorded four transfeminicides alongside seven attacks on LGBT people and three forced disappearances. These are raw counts, not rates, and the sources supply no per-capita denominator or comparison with the state's general homicide rate, so they do not by themselves establish how much of the risk is trans-specific.

31927357B49073316106075.name: Michoacan de Ocampo
31927357B49073316106075.summary:
Michoacán, one of Mexico's states, has not typified the killing of LGBT people as a hate crime under state law, and the majority of attacks on the community concentrate in Tierra Caliente, the subregion under armed-group influence.

Six LGBT+ homicides were recorded in the state in the first four and a half months of 2026, among them the killing of Daniela, a trans woman found beaten to death in a drainage channel in Morelia on 2 April 2026; a suspect was arrested in April 2026. Civil-society groups place the six cases in Morelia (three), Uruapan, Ocampo and Maravatío, and count at least 56 registered aggressions against the community in the state since 2014.

The Observatorio Nacional de Crímenes contra Personas LGBT recorded 46 LGBT+ homicides in Michoacán between 2015 and 2024. Morelia accounts for the largest number at 11, followed by Lázaro Cárdenas with 6, Apatzingán and Uruapan with 5 each and Zamora with 4; 2015 was the deadliest year with 10 victims. Trans women were the most affected group, 27 of the 46, and people aged 25 to 39 the most affected age bracket. Thirteen disappearances of LGBT+ people were reported between 2022 and 2024. These are raw counts without a population denominator, so ranking municipalities by number of cases reflects population size as much as risk.

Enforcement is minimal. Of the 46 hate-crime cases recorded by civil society in the state since 2015, only one was being processed for judicialization, the murder of Meredith Escarlet, a trans woman killed in Tarímbaro, and the state prosecutor's office keeps no disaggregated data on such crimes.

31927357B5337219705256.name: Veracruz de Ignacio de la Llave
31927357B5337219705256.summary:
Veracruz was among the last Mexican states to legislate legal gender recognition. Its Congress reformed the Civil Code in 2025 to create an administrative procedure for legal gender recognition, with no age requirement. Human Rights Watch's state-by-state survey covers Veracruz only in relation to identity documents held by the civil registry; it documents no prison-placement rule for the state and no information on where transgender prisoners are housed.

Violence against LGBT+ people is recorded in high raw numbers. Diario de Xalapa reported that Veracruz closed 2025 with 15 recorded hate crimes against the LGBT community. The Letra S annual impunity report published on 7 May 2026 counts six of the 60 LGBT+ murders recorded nationwide in 2025 as occurring in Veracruz, level with Guanajuato and behind Puebla's seven; the same tally includes the November 2025 killing of a trans woman at a motel in Oluta. These are raw counts published without a per-capita denominator, so the state ranking is by raw count only and does not by itself establish that a visitor faces higher risk in Veracruz than in a less populous state.

Earlier counts run the same direction. Letra S's 2021 report found that Veracruz led the national count of violent deaths of LGBT+ people for the fourth consecutive year, with 10 recorded cases, ahead of Guanajuato (9), Estado de México (7) and Chihuahua (6); 19 of the 32 states recorded victims that year. The same report documents systematic under-counting: in a third of the 2021 cases no name was published, and in 43 percent the sex was recorded as male with no attention to gender identity. State figures are compiled for the LGBT+ category as a whole, so no trans-specific homicide rate for Veracruz is published.

Prosecution is the weak point. The state prosecutor's office holds several open files on LGBT murders, according to the activist Leonardo Ruiz of Orgullo Xalapa, among them the case of Edhibaldo Presa Parra, a Universidad Veracruzana professor found dead on 7 January. Activists argue that hate-crime classification in these cases rests on inference from motive patterns and aggravating circumstances rather than direct evidence, and place responsibility for the absence of outcomes on the FGE. Not every monitoring source points the same way: data from the group Soy Humano put Veracruz's 2024 figures below the national average.

The report notes under-reporting: in a third of 2021 cases no name was published, and in 43 percent the sex recorded was male without attention to gender identity.

31927357B6525686063804.name: Oaxaca
31927357B6525686063804.summary:
Oaxaca stands under Mexico's national framework on legal gender recognition; the findings below are specific to the state. Oaxaca created an administrative procedure for legal gender recognition through a 2019 reform to its civil code. A 2021 decree extended the procedure to people aged 12 and over, and a June 2023 Supreme Court ruling reopened access for children under 12, leaving the route open across age groups.

Oaxaca's only documented gender-identity legislation governs identity documents.

Violence against LGBTIQ+ people and against muxes is documented at state level. Oaxaca's human-rights ombudsperson opened 34 investigations into attacks on LGBTIQ+ people between 2015 and 2022. Muxe teacher Marimar 'Estrellita' Santiago was killed in 2022 on the road to Huilotepec, in the Istmo de Tehuantepec, prompting community demands for justice.

A profile published by Trendencias in April 2025 describes Oaxaca as Mexico's fastest-growing tourist destination and, at the same time, the country's most dangerous state for the LGBT+ community. It reports violent incidents under investigation with possible municipal-police involvement in municipalities where armed groups operate, and names two victims: muxe Cristian Hernández Cutino, 31, and stylist Zulma Hernández Mendoza, 43. The ranking is stated without per-capita figures, so it cannot be weighed against the state's general homicide rate.

The state's response has concentrated on visitor security rather than institutional reform, according to the same profile.
