1811400B57209440839078.name: Tripura
1811400B57209440839078.summary:
Tripura stands under India's national framework, and the national assessment of legal recognition, identity documents, entry, facilities and healthcare applies to visitors here without regional modification. The region's own sources contain no Tripura statute, court order or state policy on any of those questions.

What the region's sources document is checkpoint and transport-hub enforcement in which gender presentation is treated as a possible concealment method. On 2 August 2024, police at the Panisagar check post in North Tripura district stopped a bus on the Assam-Agartala highway bound for Mumbai via Guwahati and detained seven Bangladeshi nationals, two of them transgender and five described by police as disguised as third gender; the case was registered as one of fraudulent documents and border crossing.

A separate report of the same period records 15 Bangladeshi nationals, seven of them transgender, apprehended in separate incidents within 24 hours, carrying fake Aadhaar and PAN cards. The two accounts differ on the number detained at Panisagar and on how many of them were transgender.

On 9 November 2024 a joint 24-hour operation detained 12 Bangladeshi nationals, among them minors and transgender people. Six, including three transgender persons, were held after midnight while travelling to Mumbai; a second group of six, including three children from Khulna, was held at Udaipur Railway Station. A local facilitator was arrested for moving them.

Tripura shares an 856-km border with Bangladesh, and these checkpoints sit on the highway and rail routes running from that border towards the rest of the country. Police in the operations treated third-gender presentation as a disguise, and transgender people were among those detained. The operations were immigration enforcement directed at Bangladeshi nationals, and the sources do not record whether the same scrutiny falls on transgender residents or on visitors whose documents and appearance diverge. The figures are raw counts from individual operations, with no denominator for the number of people passing through these checkpoints.

1811400B32673734874058.name: West Bengal
1811400B32673734874058.summary:
West Bengal is a state of India and stands under the national framework on transgender recognition, identity documents and healthcare, which the national record carries. This record covers enforcement, institutions and documented incidents specific to the state.

In August 2024 a group of trans women travelling to RG Kar Medical College in Kolkata filed an FIR alleging that a Railway Protection Force constable at Rabindra Sadan metro station groped one of them while checking her gender and made inappropriate remarks. Metro Railway and the RPF denied the allegation and filed a counter-FIR against the group; video footage showed the complainant in tears. The episode records gender-checking conduct by uniformed personnel in the state.

West Bengal accounted for three of the seven cases registered nationally under the Transgender Persons Act in 2021, the joint highest count that year alongside Assam and Kerala. The national total is small: 20 cases between 2019 and 2023, which the reporting attributes to police-registration bias rather than to low levels of violence. Official case counts in the state therefore understate what trans people there experience.

On border enforcement, South Dinajpur police arrested a transgender woman from Sirajganj district in Bangladesh on allegations of infiltrating India, together with the e-rickshaw driver who had brought her across. The person arrested was a foreign national entering without authorisation, not a visitor on a visa, and the single case does not establish a pattern of targeting trans travellers at the state's land border.

West Bengal is among the 12 states and union territories that notified a transgender welfare board. A Right to Information investigation published in November 2024 found the state's board operating without a functioning policy framework, and that most boards nationally have met less than once a year since being constituted, with several lacking a compliance mechanism or any decision-making power.

sources.title: LGBT rights in India - Wikipedia
sources.summary: On September 6, 2018 a five-judge bench of the Supreme Court ruled unanimously in Navtej Singh Johar v. Union of India, striking down Section 377 of the Indian Penal Code insofar as it criminalised consensual same-sex acts, holding that discrimination based on sexual orientation violates the Constitution, and preserving the provision for non-consensual acts. In July 2024 the Indian Penal Code was replaced by the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023, which omits Section 377 entirely. The 2014 NALSA judgment recognised a legal third gender and the right to self-identified gender identity, codified by the Transgender Persons (Protection of Rights) Act, 2019, which bans discrimination in education, employment, healthcare and housing. All of these determinations bind Punjab. No Punjab-specific statute or institution targeting trans people exists.

sources.title: Transgender Persons (Protection of Rights) Act, 2019 - Wikipedia
sources.summary: The Transgender Persons (Protection of Rights) Act, 2019 (Act No. 40 of 2019) is the national statute governing transgender people in Punjab. It was passed by the Lok Sabha on August 5, 2019 and the Rajya Sabha on November 26, 2019, received presidential assent on December 5, 2019, and has been in force since January 10, 2020. Following the Supreme Court's 2014 NALSA ruling, it grants transgender people the right to declare self-perceived gender identity without undergoing sex reassignment surgery, bans discrimination, creates a National Council for Transgender Persons, and prescribes imprisonment of not less than six months up to two years plus a fine for crimes against transgender people; criticism holds that it omits mandatory reservations in jobs and education. On January 27, 2020 the Supreme Court issued notice in a petition challenging the Act's constitutionality. No statute in Punjab targets trans people, and this is the framework a trans visitor to Amritsar stands under.

1811400B21167269026319.name: Tamil Nādu
1811400B21167269026319.summary:
Tamil Nadu stands under India's national framework for legal gender recognition, identity documents and criminal law. The state layer governs welfare provision, healthcare access and the administrative categories used in state records and services.

Tamil Nadu was the first Indian state to adopt a transgender welfare policy. Its transgender welfare portal publishes the operative paperwork for changing gender in state records: an affidavit form, a certificate of identity for change of gender, relaxation of membership identification requirements, and user manuals. The thirunangai and thirunambi categories are embedded in state governance rather than sitting outside it.

State provision includes free sex-reassignment surgery in government hospitals, and access to housing and citizenship schemes through the state regime.

The Madras High Court, in its order of 4 August 2025 in WP 7284 of 2021, recorded that the government had brought the Tamil Nadu State Policy for Transgender Persons 2025 into effect. The court described the policy as a victory for transgender and intersex persons after a long struggle and commended the government for it.

Prosecution data place Tamil Nadu ahead of other states in reaching court on transgender offences. A civil-society crime-data analysis published on 30 January 2026 records Tamil Nadu as the only state with a case under the Transgender Persons Act in 2020 (one of one nationally) and in 2022 (one), and as the source of seven of the eleven national cases in 2023. The same analysis warns that registration bias shapes these figures, so the counts measure reporting and prosecution reachability rather than the incidence of violence. The 2023 figure is a share of the national total, not a per-capita rate; no population denominator is given.

1811400B45534780755480.name: Kerala
1811400B45534780755480.summary:
Kerala maintains a state-level transgender policy and welfare architecture that predates and runs alongside the national framework. In November 2015 it adopted India's first government transgender policy, providing for identification as male, female or TG (third gender), equal access to social and economic resources, equal treatment under law, and non-discrimination on grounds of sex. Kerala was reported to Parliament in December 2021 as one of the states and union territories that had constituted a Transgender Welfare Board under Section 10(1) of the 2019 Rules.

Transition-related care is nominally subsidised but unevenly available. In March 2016 the Social Justice Department proposed free sex-reassignment surgery in government hospitals, at least in medical colleges, from the following financial year; the state later provided reimbursement for gender-affirming surgeries. Training gaps mean many government hospitals cannot perform the procedures, pushing patients toward costlier private institutions, and reimbursement requires patients to raise funds before they are refunded. The Government Medical College Hospital in Kottayam opened a clinic exclusively for transgender patients in 2017, operating twice a month with a specialist panel and also serving sex workers, after a District Legal Services Authority proposal prompted by reports that transgender people feared approaching hospitals and relied on self-medication; the same authority proposed separate public toilets for transgender people to the district collector. The Government Medical College Hospital in Thiruvananthapuram completed its first sex reassignment surgery in January 2017. The suicide of Anannyah Kumari Alex after alleging a botched gender-affirmation procedure prompted protests and led the state to appoint an expert committee on transgender health-sector issues and to begin steps toward free surgeries in government hospitals.

Kottayam's clinic issues health cards denoting transgender status, a documentation practice a visitor should expect to encounter at state facilities. Welfare measures include scholarships for transgender students in classes 7 to 10, a Kannur district budget allocation for employment and skill training, and a 2017 Social Justice Department workshop in Kozhikode with around 30 transgender representatives covering identity cards, pensions for those over 60, skill development, scholarships, educational loans and driving lessons for employment as Uber drivers. A transgender-owned and operated G Taxi service was launched to provide livelihood and public visibility. A transgender school opened in Kochi in 2016 to prepare students for 10th and 12th board examinations and vocational training for ten students aged 25 to 50; it ceased operating as a school after three months and became a hostel for transgender Kochi Metro staff. A Gender Park opened in Kozhikode in February 2016.

Policing is the sharpest risk area. Reports describe a spate of killings of transgender people with inadequate police investigation, and a rise in police harassment when transgender people approach stations to file complaints, which produced a Director General of Police direction that grievances be received without delay. In October 2023 the annual pride march in Malappuram was attacked by a mob and police carried out a lathicharge. In December 2023 the High Court of Kerala described cyber attacks against the LGBT+ community as a serious issue and directed authorities to act. The suicide of Praveen Nath, described by Minister R. Bindu as a martyr, drew attention to transphobic groups rooted in religious fundamentalism, with the minister attributing it to cyberbullying and media transphobia.

Recorded cases under the Transgender Persons Act are few nationally and concentrated in a small number of states. Kerala accounted for 2 of the 7 national cases in 2021 and 4 of the 11 in 2023, joint-highest with Tamil Nadu. These are raw counts against very small national totals, and the reporting itself attributes the low figures to bias in police registration rather than to low incidence; they are not a per-capita measure of risk and do not establish that Kerala is more dangerous than a less populous state.

Community infrastructure is comparatively developed. Queerala campaigns on sensitisation of healthcare, curricula and workplace policy; Queerythm runs a 24-hour helpline for members in distress; Sahayathrika serves female-born LGBTIQA+ members. Kerala Queer Pride has been held since July 2010 in Thrissur, and Queerythm has run annual walks since 2017 focused on sensitising police and media. An estimated 25,000 transgender people live in the state, around 81 per cent of whom wish to transition and 76 per cent of whom conceal their identity for fear of non-acceptance; societal discrimination in employment and housing and implementation gaps in state schemes remain documented problems.

sources.summary: Queerbeat crime-data report (30 Jan 2026), Kerala rows: 2 of the 7 national Transgender Persons Act cases in 2021 and 4 of the 11 in 2023 (joint-highest with Tamil Nadu) — among the highest sub-national totals, with the report's caveat that national counts are tiny from police-registration bias.
PIB federal reply (Dec 2021): Kerala is among the 12 states/UTs reported to parliament as having constituted Transgender Welfare Boards under Section 10(1) of the 2019 Rules.

sources.title: LGBTQ rights in Kerala (Wikipedia)
sources.summary: In National Legal Services Authority v. Union of India (2014) the Supreme Court recognized a "third gender," affirming freedom from discrimination and right to equality, and Kerala became the first state to follow up with a government transgender policy in 2015 addressing the right to identify as "male", "female" or "TG" (Third Gender) with provisions for equal access to social and economic resources, equal treatment under law, life, liberty and justice, and non-discrimination based on sex. The Transgender Persons (Protection of Rights) Act, 2019 bans unfair discrimination against transgender people in educational establishments and services, employment, healthcare, use of goods, accommodation, services, facilities, benefits, privileges or opportunities available to the public, right to movement, right to reside, purchase, rent or occupy property, opportunity to stand for or hold public or private office, and in government or private establishments. In 2016 the State Government proposed free sex reassignment surgeries in government hospitals, Kannur district allocated budget for employment and skill training, and the government later provided reimbursement for gender affirming surgeries plus scholarships for transgender students in classes 7 to 10, but lack of training means many government hospitals cannot offer surgery forcing reliance on costlier private institutions with stigma, lack of care standards and fund-disbursement problems because patients must raise funds before refund. The Government Medical College Hospital in Kottayam opened in 2017 a clinic exclusively attending to the transgender community with a specialized panel, described as the first government clinic of its kind and also open to sex workers after a DLSA proposal following health-concerns campaigning, while a February 2016 Gender Park in Kozhikode opened by President Pranab Mukherjee was dedicated to gender equality and LGBT issues. A 2017 Social Justice Department workshop in Kozhikode with around 30 transgender representatives discussed identity cards, pension for those over 60, skill development training, scholarships and educational loans, and driving lessons for employment as Uber drivers, and Kochi's 2016 first transgender school for 10th and 12th board exams and vocational training for 10 students aged 25-50 ceased functioning as a school after three months and became a hostel for transgender Kochi Metro staff. A recent spate of killings of transgender people with lack of responsible police investigation raised security concerns, alongside a rise in police harassment when transgender people approach stations to file complaints that resulted in a DGP direction to address grievances without delay. The suicide of Anannyah Kumari Alex alleging botched gender affirmation surgery triggered protests and discussion of irregularities and absence of specific protocol in private hospitals, leading the state to appoint an expert committee on transgender health-sector issues and initiate steps for free surgeries in government hospitals, while the suicide of Praveen Nath drew attention to mushrooming transphobic groups rooted in religious fundamentalism. Homosexual intercourse was criminalized under Section 377 of the Indian Penal Code in 1861 as voluntarily having "carnal intercourse against the order of nature." In 2009 the Delhi High Court in Naz Foundation v. Govt. of NCT of Delhi found Section 377 prohibitions on private, adult, consensual, non-commercial same-sex conduct violated fundamental rights, but on 11 December 2013 the Supreme Court overturned that order while noting Parliament should debate the matter, followed by protests, and on 28 January 2014 dismissed review petitions by the Central Government, Naz Foundation and others. On 2 February 2016 the Supreme Court agreed to review criminalisation and on 6 September 2018 unanimously struck down Section 377 as unconstitutional for infringing autonomy, intimacy and identity, legalising same-sex sexual activity in India including Kerala. Same-sex marriages are not recognised or performed in India, though movements for recognition have emerged in Kerala and nationally. In line with Navtej Singh Johar v. Union of India, discrimination on the basis of sexual orientation is prohibited via Article 15 of the Constitution, but this extends only to discrimination by state or government bodies. Gay conversion therapy is widely practised by both licensed psychiatrists/psychologists and quacks despite position statements by multiple psychiatrist/psychologist organisations condemning the practice as unscientific and illegal. For transgender-specific conditions, the article reports "societal discrimination, particularly in employment and housing, and various implementation issues remain major problems" despite Kerala's early policy lead. Transgender activist Vijayarajamallika, head of Kochi's transgender school, stated "the school aims at making transgender people eligible for taking decent jobs and living a dignified life," reflecting employment barriers, while Minister R. Bindu blamed cyber bullying and transphobia in the media for the suicide of Praveen Nath, Kerala's first transgender bodybuilder, describing him as a martyr amid mushrooming transphobic groups rooted in religious fundamentalism. More broadly for LGBT visitors, the article notes historical and contemporary opposition especially due to meninist groups, conservative political groups, religious organizations and social conservatism, with increasing recent opposition including hate-speech allegations against mainstream politicians and all-time-high cyberbullying linked to suicides of at least two LGBTQ persons. In December 2023 the High Court of Kerala described cyber attacks against the LGBT+ community as a 'serious issue' and asked authorities to take necessary action. The October 2023 annual pride march in Malappuram was attacked by a homophobic mob leading to lathicharge by police, while Kerala Queer Pride since July 2010 in Thrissur and annual walks by Queerythm since 2017 focus on sensitisation of police and media to prevent violence and discrimination. Community protection resources noted are Queerala campaigning for sensitisation of healthcare, curriculum and workplace policies, Queerythm running a 24X7 helpline for members in distress, and Sahayathrika for female-born LGBTIQA+ members, amid an easing climate from prior invisibility where few opted to come out for fear family would "take them to a psychiatrist or file a police complaint against friends."

sources.title: National Legal Services Authority v. Union of India (2014)
sources.summary: On 15 April 2014 the Supreme Court recognized hijras/transgenders as a third gender who could no longer be forced to identify as male or female and required their treatment as socially and economically backward with OBC reservation in educational admission and employment, Centre and state social welfare schemes, public awareness to erase stigma, construction of special public toilets and provision for special medical needs, legal entitlement to affirmed sex after surgical change without discrimination, and protection from harassment and discrimination including misuse of IPC section 377, with the ruling limited to eunuchs/hijras/transgenders and not to gay, lesbian and bisexual persons.

sources.title: Kerala Government proposal for free gender affirmation surgery (2016) and reimbursement/scholarship scheme
sources.summary: In November 2015 Kerala adopted India's first transgender policy to improve living conditions, and in March 2016 the social justice department proposed free sex-reassignment surgery in government hospitals, at least in medical colleges, from the next financial year, addressing the absence of any SRS facility in-state that forced travel to Chennai/Bengaluru for procedures costing Rs 2-5 lakh for male-to-female and Rs 4-8 lakh for female-to-male plus 6 months-2 years counselling, 1+ year hormone therapy and post-surgery observation, with implementation pending health ministry approval and training of multidisciplinary urology, endocrinology, sexology and psychology teams, alongside a transgender-owned and operated G Taxi equality-taxi service for all passengers to provide livelihood and public visibility, in a context where ~25,000 transgender persons were estimated in-state with ~81% wishing to transition and 76% concealing identity for fear of non-acceptance.

sources.title: Government Medical College Hospital, Kottayam transgender clinic and District Legal Services Authority (DLSA) proposal (2017)
sources.summary: By mid-February 2017 the Government Medical College Hospital in Kottayam was to open Kerala's first government clinic exclusively for transgender persons, operating twice a month with specialist doctors and also serving sex workers, with distribution of health cards denoting transgender status after a District Legal Services Authority proposal prompted by transgender persons' reported apprehension about approaching hospitals and reliance on self-medication, while DLSA also proposed separate public toilets for transgender persons to the district collector, and in January 2017 the Government Medical College Hospital in Thiruvananthapuram had completed its first sex reassignment surgery through staged procedures over three years.

Assam's complaint machinery under the Transgender Persons Act has been reachable. Of the seven cases registered nationally under the Act in 2021, two were in Assam; the 2023 national tally recorded none in the state. A Queerbeat crime-data report of 30 January 2026 cautions that national counts are tiny (20 cases across 2019 to 2023) because of police-registration bias, so low counts do not indicate low incidence. The same report's 2025 survey puts prevalence of physical violence against trans people at 27.2% and sexual violence at 22.3%.

As of December 2021, Assam had not constituted a Transgender Welfare Board under the 2019 Rules; a Parliamentary reply from the Ministry of Social Justice and Empowerment listed 12 states and union territories that had done so, and Assam was not among them. No state welfare machinery coordinating housing, surgery or pensions therefore existed in Assam at that date.

Transgender persons arrested by the Railway Protection Force in Assam have recounted degrading treatment in custody, a state-specific instance of the police-conduct concerns documented elsewhere in India.

14911670B7632012573600.name: Ceara
14911670B7632012573600.summary:
Ceará stands under Brazil's national framework; the national record carries the federal law, passport and marker rules, health-system rules and custodial resolutions. What follows is the state-level layer.

Ceará recorded 11 killings of trans people in 2024, the highest count of any state in the Northeast and the third highest nationally, according to the ANTRA dossier reported on 28 January 2025. The state has about 9.2 million residents, which the source puts at roughly 0.12 killings per 100,000 residents. Ceará's general homicide rate is not in the source inventory, so the two cannot be compared here, and the national ranking is by raw count, which tracks population size rather than risk. The ninth ANTRA dossier, reported on 26 January 2026, recorded 8 killings in Ceará in 2025, level with Minas Gerais at the top of the state ranking, or about 0.09 per 100,000 residents on the source's own figures. Both counts come from a dossier that compiles media-reported killings.

Law No. 17,480, sanctioned by Governor Camilo Santana and published on 19 May 2021, requires public and private establishments in Ceará, from 90 days after publication, to display a notice of at least 50 cm by 50 cm on the exterior or at an entrance stating that discrimination on grounds of sexual orientation or gender identity is expressly prohibited, and listing the phone number of the Special Coordination for LGBT Public Policies for complaints, clarifications and reports. No enforcement actions, penalties or compliance data under the law are sourced.

On 7 March 2013 the state general attorney, Francisco Sales Neto, issued decision 02/2013 obligating all notaries in Ceará to accept same-sex marriages, effective 15 March 2013. For a trans visitor whose relationship or identity documents are read under birth-sex status, that notarial obligation is the operative state-level guarantee; no Ceará-specific rule on how a notary handles a trans partner's documents is sourced.

On 22 May 2024 the Court of Justice of Ceará authorized Brune Bonassi to rectify documents to reflect a neutral gender, the first non-binary person in the state to obtain such a rectification. On 29 May 2024 the state was reported to be issuing its first birth certificate recognising a person as non-binary. Whether the two concern the same person is not stated.

On 16 November 2006 Governor Lúcio Alcântara signed a law requiring educational material on sexual orientation to be included in the training of Ceará's Civil and Military Police, published in the Official Gazette on 26 November 2006. How the requirement is applied today is not recorded.

On 12 December 2017 the Sobral municipal chamber approved Bill No. 2154/17, introduced by Councillor Adauto Izidoro Arruda, prohibiting pedagogical activities that reproduce the concept of "gender ideology" or any discussion of gender diversity in all municipal and private schools in Sobral. It passed by majority with the sole opposing vote from Councillor Maria Socorro Brasileiro Magalhães and was sent to Mayor Ivo Gomes. Whether it was signed or vetoed is not recorded.

sources.summary: G1/Globo report (28 Jan 2025), citing the ANTRA dossier: Ceará was the Northeast state with the most killings of trans people in 2024, with 11 killings, third highest nationally — in a state of some 9.2 million people, about 0.12 killings per 100,000 residents, so the raw-count ranking says little about per-capita risk.

Igbá Agência (26 Jan 2026): per the 9th ANTRA dossier, Ceará was among the states with most trans killings in 2025 with 8 cases (in a state of some 9.2 million people, about 0.09 per 100,000 residents); Brazil totalled 80 (18th year as world's highest). Among 57 victims with race data, 70% were Black (avg 77% over 2017-2025).

SBT News (26 Jan 2026): ANTRA 9th dossier — Ceará and Minas Gerais topped the 2025 state ranking with 8 killings each; Brazil's 80 total down 34% vs 2024, still 1st worldwide; 1,261 killings 2017-2025 (avg 140/yr).

sources.title: LGBTQ people in prison
sources.summary: Wikipedia's general overview article (28 Sep 2026) reports no codified Brazil-specific trans-prisoner housing policy. Its Brazil paragraph states only that traumatic social vulnerability and stigma facing travestis and transgender people shape rehabilitation. For comparison, the article sets out international placement norms: Scotland's 2022 inspection standards admit trans and intersex prisoners to facilities matching their lived or experienced gender, and Canada places prisoners by gender identity.

sources.title: LGBT rights in Brazil
sources.summary: Wikipedia's 'LGBT rights in Brazil' article (28 Sep 2026), in its Politics section, states that LGBTQ people have a special place in Brazilian prisons, separate from other prisoners; that transgender people ('transsexuals') have the right to be called by their social name and not their birth name and to be forwarded to women's prisons; and that LGBTQ prisoners may choose male or female clothing. The statement is footnoted (ref. 253) to a Mix Brasil (UOL) article, 'Vivemos uma inercia no congresso...', archived 18 Jan 2012.

sources.title: Supreme Federal Court ruling on gender identity
sources.summary: In 2018 in ADI 4275 Brazil's Supreme Federal Court recognized gender identity/expression as protected under equality and allowed alteration of name and gender in the civil registry without sex-reassignment surgery or judicial authorization; in ADO 26 and MI 4733 it equated transfobia and homofobia to the crime of racism until Congress enacts specific criminal legislation; in 2024 in ADI 5668 interpreting the National Education Plan (Law 13.005/2014) it imposed on public and private schools a duty to combat discrimination based on gender, gender identity and sexual orientation; in ADPF 787 it required the Unified Health System (SUS) to guarantee transsexual and travesti persons full access to health services matching their biological apparatus and physiological needs; in precautionary decision in ADPF 527 it ordered transfer of transsexual women inmates to women's prisons, followed by a National Justice Council resolution requiring a judge to set detention location after asking the detained person's preference, in a context where Brazil leads global violence against transgender persons with average life expectancy around 30 years versus ~75 nationally.

14911670B91095571793858.name: Rio Granda do Norte
14911670B91095571793858.summary:
Lethal violence against trans women in Rio Grande do Norte continued into 2026, after a year in which the state was recorded with no such killings at all. Two deaths are documented in the first half of the year, both of women killed inside their own homes.

In the early hours of 4 May 2026 Emanuelle Samira Fernandes Neta, 27, was shot dead while she slept in the rented house she lived in on Rua Vivaldo Dantas, in the Dom Jaime Câmara neighbourhood of Mossoró, in western Rio Grande do Norte. Five men broke in. Military police found the body on a routine patrol. One suspect was arrested carrying a pistol and booked for illegal firearms discharge and armed criminal association. The state trans-rights association ATTRANSPARÊNCIA/RN publicly mourned her as an artist killed by the transphobia she faced.

A transgender woman known as Naomi was found dead in her own home in Praia da Pipa, in the municipality of Tibau do Sul on the state's southern coast, in late February 2026. She had been stabbed. The Civil Police opened an investigation, and ATTRANSPARÊNCIA/RN called for justice.

The state's recorded count has moved sharply. Rio Grande do Norte appeared with no recorded trans killings in 2024 in the ANTRA dossier and with four in the 2025 tabulation, the largest deterioration recorded for any state in that dataset. Both are raw counts, no per-capita figure for the state accompanies them, and a change of that size from a zero base therefore establishes no rate.

The zero counts carry limited weight on their own. The dossier behind them records systematic under-counting because official bodies do not record LGBTQIA+ victims properly, and one reproduction of the 2025 figures records no trans killings in Rio Grande do Norte for that year at all, contradicting the count of four given elsewhere. The two 2026 deaths post-date both tallies and are not yet reflected in any count for the state.

Sources document no rule of Rio Grande do Norte's own on the housing of trans prisoners. Custodial placement of LGBTI people arrested or imprisoned in the state stands under Brazil's federal framework, and no placement policy at state level appears in the sources consulted.

14911670B97385369352280.name: Paraiba
14911670B97385369352280.summary:
Paraíba's own documented signal on trans safety consists of lethal attacks recorded by civil-society monitoring. The ANTRA dossier for 2025, reported by SBT News on 26 January 2026, records 4 trans killings in the state that year; CNN Brasil's dossier for 2024 recorded 5. Both are raw counts published without a per-capita denominator, so they do not establish the state's relative risk; the 2025 dossier's national total was 80 killings.

Custody in Paraíba's state prison system is governed by a federal portaria issued in April 2014 by the Secretariat for Human Rights of the Presidency of the Republic, which sets where LGBT prisoners are housed. No Paraíba-specific implementation, dedicated wing, segregation practice or individual case under that order is documented.

sources.summary: G1 (17 Apr 2014) reported a federal portaria issued by the Secretaria de Direitos Humanos da Presidência da República that sets where LGBT prisoners are housed across Brazil's prison system and applies in Paraíba's state system. Transsexual men and women must be forwarded to female prison units. Gay and travesti prisoners held in male prisons must be offered specific conviviality spaces. LGBT inmates may use their social name, which must appear in the admission record, and choose male or female clothing. Non-compliance carries no sanction. No Paraíba-specific implementation, wing, segregation practice or case is documented.

14911670B44044837234259.name: Minas Gerais
14911670B44044837234259.summary:
Minas Gerais is a state of Brazil and stands under the national framework set out for that country; the findings below are those specific to the state.

Recorded lethal violence against trans people and travestis places Minas Gerais among the highest-counting states. The 2024 dossier compiled by the national trans association ANTRA recorded 12 trans killings in Minas Gerais, second nationally behind São Paulo's 16 and ahead of Ceará's 11, with a cumulative total of 100 for the state between 2017 and 2024. The 2025 dossier recorded 8 killings in Minas Gerais, tied with Ceará for the highest count, within a national total of 80. Both sets of figures are raw counts published without a per-capita denominator, so they rank states by volume rather than by rate.

A study published on 1 July 2024 by the Federal University of Minas Gerais and the state Public Prosecutor's Office found that 60% of deaths involving trans people and travestis in the state resulted from violence, and that 74% of the victims were Black or Pardo.

On 15 July 2026 the Court of Justice of Minas Gerais, working with the National Council of Justice, launched an incident-reporting mechanism for LGBTQ violence in Belo Horizonte.

Bathroom access has been fought out in the courts rather than settled by statute. Uberaba's municipal ban on unisex restrooms, approved on 12 September 2022 and enacted on 7 October 2022, was declared unconstitutional by the Court of Justice in 2024, after a 2023 lawsuit by the state Public Defender's Office. A Belo Horizonte law signed on 20 November 2023, which authorised religious institutions to bar transgender people from restrooms matching their gender identity, was suspended by preliminary injunction in August 2025. In August 2026 the Court of Justice ordered a shopping mall in Contagem to pay 2,000 reais in compensation to a trans woman denied access to a women's restroom in a 2019 incident in which a guard demanded proof of "sex change"; the ruling reversed a Contagem court decision that had denied the claim for insufficient evidence.

Prison housing for trans people in Minas Gerais is governed by a 2014 federal portaria of the national human-rights secretariat, which applies to the state prison system: transsexual men and women are to be sent to female units, gay and travesti prisoners held in male prisons are to be offered specific conviviality spaces, and LGBT inmates may use their social name, recorded at admission, and choose male or female clothing. The instrument provides no sanctions for non-compliance, and no Minas Gerais-specific implementation, wing, segregation practice or individual case is documented.

SBT News (26 Jan 2026): the ANTRA 2025 dossier records Minas Gerais tied with Ceará in 1st place at 8 trans killings in 2025, within a national total of 80.

14911670B2612452665424.name: Pernambuco
14911670B2612452665424.summary:
Pernambuco recorded 7 killings of trans and travesti people in 2025, the second-highest raw count of any Brazilian state in the ANTRA dossier released on 26 January 2026, behind Ceará and Minas Gerais at 8 each, against a national total of 80. In a state of some 9.1 million people that is roughly 0.08 per 100,000 residents. SBT News reported the figures on 26 January 2026, Valor Internacional on 27 January 2026, and Diario de Pernambuco carried the state ranking on the same date. The ranking is by raw count alone; the sources provide no per-capita comparison between states.

The 2025 figure is Pernambuco's lowest annual count since 2022, when 13 trans and travesti people were killed, after 9 in 2023 and 8 in 2024. The same dossier records 83 violent deaths of trans people in Pernambuco over six years, the sixth-highest state total for that period, and 349 killings across the Northeast from 2017 to 2025.

Killings are concentrated outside the Recife capital region. On 2 October 2025 a trans woman was shot dead inside her home in Belo Jardim, in the Agreste interior; the Civil Police opened an inquiry to identify the author and motive and no arrests had been reported at publication. On 7 July 2021 Fabiana da Silva Lucas, a 30-year-old Black trans woman, was found dead along highway PE-160 in Santa Cruz do Capibaribe, killed by several knife strikes, the third recorded killing of a trans or travesti person in the state that month. Pernambuco's Civil Police told press that a 22-year-old suspect was lynched by locals at the scene.

Pernambuco stands under Brazil's national legal framework, which the Brazil record carries; the state layer adds its own instruments. The Legislative Assembly of Pernambuco's president signed Law No. 18,634 on 13 July 2024, instituting the State Policy for Combating Violence against LGBTQIA+ People, approved on 4 July 2024. It treats violence based on gender identity, sexual orientation and sex characteristics as structural and incompatible with democratic rule, and requires the state to monitor violence data with a compiled methodology, build protection and reception services, map and train public and civil-society reception facilities, and prioritise victims facing rupture of family or community ties and compounded vulnerabilities.

Municipal hostility has been documented and reversed. On 13 December 2017 Garanhuns enacted Municipal Law No. 4432/2017 banning discussion of gender theory or identity in municipal schools, passed 11-to-1 despite a state prosecution recommendation to reject it as reinforcing stereotypes and prejudice. On 15 October 2025 the Supreme Federal Court struck the law down, lifting the ban on gender-related instruction in the city's schools.

The state judiciary has applied national document-recognition rules locally. In 2023, following a 2022 lawsuit by the Public Defender's Office of Pernambuco, the Court of Justice of Pernambuco authorised Tarlazza Messina to rectify their birth certificate to register gender as non-binary, the first such recognition in the state.

In June 2026 state deputy João Paulo (PT) presented Bill No. 4.092/2026 to create a State Policy for Integral Health Promotion of the LGBTQIAPN+ population within the Unified Health System. It would reinforce the right to a social name in registration and care, address travestis and transexuais who delay or avoid care for fear of mistreatment, and require training of health professionals and publication of LGBT health indicators under data-protection rules. The bill's status is unresolved in the sources.

sources.title: LGBTQ rights in Pernambuco (Wikipedia)
sources.summary: Since 2019, discrimination based on gender identity has been prohibited nationwide in Brazil through a decision by the Supreme Federal Court, a broad provision covering gender identity alongside sexual orientation. On 13 July 2024, the president of the Legislative Assembly of Pernambuco signed Law No. 18,634, which establishes the State Policy for Combating Violence against LGBTQIA+ People, a broad LGBTQIA+ protection measure not transgender-specific alone. In June 2026, state representative João Paulo (PT) presented a bill to prohibit discrimination based on sexual orientation and gender identity in the Unified Health System, covering gender identity alongside sexual orientation in care. On 1 March 2018, the Supreme Federal Court ruled that a transgender person has the right to change official name and sex without surgery or professional evaluation, by self-declaration of psychosocial identity. In 2023, following a lawsuit filed in 2022 by the Public Defender's Office of Pernambuco, the Court of Justice of Pernambuco authorized Tarlazza Messina to change documents to reflect gender identity, making them the first non-binary person to do so in the state. On 15 October 2025, the Supreme Federal Court struck down a 13 December 2017 Garanhuns municipal law signed by Mayor Izaías Régis prohibiting "gender ideology" in city schools, following lawsuits by the Prosecutor General of the Republic and the Socialism and Liberty Party. Same-sex sexual activity has been legal in Brazil since 1830, and homosexuality is legal in Pernambuco. Same-sex marriage has been legal in Pernambuco since 2013 via a National Council of Justice decision implementing a 2011 Supreme Federal Court decision. Since 2010, same-sex adoption has been officially permitted in the state through a Supreme Federal Court decision. On 9 October 2008, Judge Élio Braz of the 2nd Court of Childhood and Adolescence in Recife permitted a male homosexual couple to adopt two sisters from a shelter with new birth certificates listing two parents, with the Public Prosecutor agreeing and declining further action. On 2 March 2012, a Recife court authorized adoption of a baby by a gay couple, the first in the country to register a child with both fathers' names. Since 2019, discrimination based on sexual orientation has been prohibited nationwide in Brazil through a Supreme Federal Court decision. On 13 July 2024, the president of the Legislative Assembly of Pernambuco signed Law No. 18,634 establishing the State Policy for Combating Violence against LGBTQIA+ People, a broad measure covering sexual orientation alongside gender identity. In June 2026, state representative João Paulo (PT) presented a bill to prohibit discrimination based on sexual orientation and gender identity in the Unified Health System.

sources.title: Law No. 18,634 - State Policy for Combating Violence against LGBTQIA+ People, Legislative Assembly of Pernambuco
sources.summary: On 4 July 2024 Pernambuco instituted the State Policy for Combating Violence against LGBTQIA+ People to confront discrimination and violence based on gender identity, sexual orientation and sex characteristics and promote full citizenship, with objectives to monitor violence data with compiled methodology, strengthen and implement protection, promotion and defense services and reception for those in vulnerability and social risk, build a governmental and non-governmental response network, and expand protection statewide, recognizing such identity-based violence as structural, historical and incompatible with democratic rule and human rights and requiring consideration of intersecting race, territory, class, gender, age, religion and disability vulnerabilities, to be implemented transversally through reception-service guidelines, emergency support to civil-society services respecting individual liberty and citizenship, and government reception policies focused on assistance, health, citizenship, culture, public security and justice including mapping and training of public and civil-society reception facilities, data collection and knowledge production with research bodies and universities, partnerships with municipalities and public-private entities, and support for aligned civil-society initiatives, prioritizing victims of identity-based violence/discrimination, those with actual or imminent rupture of family/community ties, and those with compounded vulnerabilities, with regulation by the Executive and entry into force on publication.

sources.title: Supreme Federal Court of Brazil ruling of 1 March 2018 on gender identity
sources.summary: On 1 March 2018 in ADI 4275 the Brazilian Supreme Federal Court, applicable in Pernambuco, held that the right to equality without discrimination encompasses gender identity and expression and authorized alteration of name and gender in the civil registry without sex-reassignment surgery or judicial authorization, on the basis that gender identity is a manifestation of personality that the State must recognize.

sources.title: Court of Justice of Pernambuco 2023 ruling authorizing Tarlazza Messina document change
sources.summary: In 2023 in Pernambuco the judiciary for the first time recognized non-binary gender and authorized rectification of Tarlazza Messina's birth certificate to register gender as 'não binárie'.

sources.title: Supreme Federal Court decision of 2019 prohibiting discrimination based on sexual orientation and gender identity
sources.summary: On 24 May 2019 a majority of Brazil's Supreme Federal Court (6 of 11 justices) voted to treat transphobia and homophobia as crimes equivalent to racism, punishable under Brazil's racism law until Congress adopts specific LGBT-protection legislation.

sources.title: Municipal law of Garanhuns signed 13 December 2017 by mayor Izaías Régis prohibiting 'gender ideology' in schools
sources.summary: On 13 December 2017 Garanhuns, Pernambuco enacted Municipal Law No. 4432/2017 prohibiting direct or indirect discussion and pedagogical including extracurricular activities on gender theory, questions, identity or ideology in municipal schools effective upon publication after 11-to-1 council approval despite a late-November 2017 state prosecution recommendation to reject it as reinforcing stereotypes and prejudice against those not conforming to dominant standards.

sources.title: Supreme Federal Court decision of 15 October 2025 striking down Garanhuns 'gender ideology' law
sources.summary: On 15 October 2025 the Supreme Federal Court struck down Garanhuns, Pernambuco's municipal law prohibiting teaching about gender, thereby lifting the ban on gender-related instruction in local schools.

sources.title: Bill presented June 2026 by state representative João Paulo (PT) on non-discrimination in Unified Health System
sources.summary: In June 2026 Pernambuco state deputy João Paulo (PT) presented Bill No. 4.092/2026 to create the State Policy for Integral Health Promotion of the LGBTQIAPN+ population in the SUS, reinforcing the right to use the social name in registrations and care and respect for gender identities, setting as objectives expanded SUS access with special attention to travestis and transexuais who avoid or delay seeking care for fear of mistreatment plus mental health, violence prevention and vulnerability reduction, and setting as directives combating LGBTphobia and institutional discrimination in health services, continuous training of public health professionals for humanized respectful care, and production, segmentation and publication of LGBT health data and indicators subject to data-protection laws.

14911670B19428866735507.name: Bahia
14911670B19428866735507.summary:
Bahia is a state in north-east Brazil; the national framework applies, and the findings below are specific to the state.

The ANTRA 2025 dossier records 7 trans killings in Bahia during 2025, placing the state immediately behind the leading states, which recorded 8; a second report identifies those as Ceará and Minas Gerais. Across 1,261 killings recorded nationwide between 2017 and 2025, Bahia ranks third with 97, after São Paulo (151) and Ceará (107). These are raw counts with no per-capita denominator, and Bahia is one of Brazil's most populous states, so the ranking reflects population size as well as incidence and does not establish that the state is more dangerous per resident than smaller ones.

The pattern is not new. The ANTRA dossier for 2022 ranked Bahia seventh nationally for killings of trans people, with 7 killings of travestis in the state that year, when Pernambuco led the ranking.

On the weekend of 6-7 December 2025, Rhianna, an 18-year-old trans woman, was choked to death in Luís Eduardo Magalhães, in the west of the state. The Civil Police opened a feminicide investigation, treating the killing as gender-based. The suspect, a 19-year-old app driver, drove the victim's body to the police station, confessed and claimed self-defence, and was released.

Bahia was the first Brazilian state to enact an anti-discrimination ordinance, in 1997. On 1 June 2022 the Legislative Assembly passed, and on 30 June 2022 Assembly President Adolfo Menezes signed, the Millena Passos Law banning discrimination on grounds of gender identity; a parallel measure covering sexual orientation was signed the same day.

Transgender people in Bahia have been able to change their name and legal gender since 2008, with gender self-determination permitted since 2018, and the Bahia Public Defender's Office works with other agencies on joint efforts to facilitate document rectification. A decree signed by Governor Rui Costa on 23 May 2017 gave travesti and transexual people the right to use their social name and have their gender identity recognised across the state's direct and indirect public administration; the social name must appear alongside the legal name on official documents, and minors require guardian authorisation. On 11 May 2022 the Court of Justice of Bahia allowed a third gender option on documents, and on 26 December 2024 Governor Jerônimo Rodrigues sanctioned Law 14,806, exempting the cost of protest certificates so that document rectification is free of charge for transgender people.

In 2008 Léo Kret, a travesti club dancer, won a seat on the Salvador city council with 12,861 votes and, on taking office, insisted on a feminine wardrobe and on using the women's restroom.

Against these protections, on 17 December 2025 the Salvador City Council approved a bill banning the teaching of gender identity in schools, signed into law on 26 March 2026 by Mayor Bruno Soares Reis.

14911670B85657526756793.name: Rio de Jeneiro
14911670B85657526756793.summary:
Rio de Janeiro state courts and police have acted in cases involving trans women. In February 2026 the state court (TJ-RJ) ordered preventive detention of a man accused of exploiting trans women in Niterói; the suspect had been a Niterói city-hall employee until January 2026, and pre-trial custody was confirmed in the extortion case. In April 2025 the state tourism police (DEAT) arrested two trans women in flagrante for extorting a Norwegian tourist in Copacabana, in the Zona Sul beach strip.

A peer-reviewed census study of travestis and transgender women in the Rio de Janeiro state prison system interviewed 138 self-declared travesti or trans-woman inmates across eleven units classified as masculine in the metropolitan region between April and June 2021, drawing on the state prison administration's own database. It documents that travestis and trans women in that system are housed in units treated as masculine, with some held in so-called neutral or security units, and characterises placement in male units as a double punishment compounded by recurring violations of basic rights. A 2015 Rio de Janeiro state law grants them parity of treatment with cisgender women in women's units, covering hair length, feminine clothing, accessories and cosmetics.

14911670B48776179681147.name: Para
14911670B48776179681147.summary:
Pará stands under Brazil's national framework; the national provisions on identity documents, marriage and partner recognition, hate-crime law and custodial placement apply in the state and are set out in the national record.

Facilities access is the sharpest state-level change. On 14 July 2026 the governor of Pará signed a state law authorising religious temples and schools to restrict bathroom use on the basis of biological sex. Before enactment the Federal Public Prosecutor's Office recommended a veto, arguing that the measure would violate the rights of transgender people and the principle of secularism. On 15 July 2026 the Socialism and Liberty Party announced it had filed a lawsuit against the law.

Documentation. On 21 June 2025 Ember Alves Oliveira became the first person in Pará to obtain a birth certificate carrying an X sex marker, through an action brought by the Public Defender's Office of Pará after the registry office in Ananindeua refused rectification. The registry relied on Provision 73 of the National Council of Justice, which does not provide for a third gender option, and refused a first-name change without stated legal justification. The Public Defender's Office argued that documentation which does not reflect a person's gender identity is a source of suffering and anguish and a violation of human dignity.

State law layer. A 2007 amendment to the Constitution of the State of Pará prohibits discrimination on grounds of sexual orientation, and Decree No. 3831 of 8 April 2024 created a State Council for Sexual Diversity within the State Secretariat for Racial Equality and Human Rights.

Violence. The national ANTRA dossier for 2025 records five of that year's killings of trans and travesti people in Pará. The figure is a raw count taken from a national tally and is not accompanied by a state population denominator, so it does not by itself establish the state's rate or rank it against other states.

sources.summary: SBT News (26 Jan 2026) reports ANTRA's 9th annual dossier: 80 trans and travesti people were killed in Brazil in 2025, a fall of about 34% year-on-year, and Brazil ranks first in world rankings. The victims were overwhelmingly travestis and trans women, killed with extreme violence. This national dossier supplies this record's 2025 count of 5 of 80.

Sergipe Em Debate (27 Jan 2025) reports ANTRA's dossier recording 122 trans and travesti killings in Brazil in 2024, 16% below 2023, with five of the victims rights defenders. The dossier is the source for this record's 2024 comparison year, and Pará's 2024 position cannot be fixed from the audited sources.

sources.title: LGBTQ rights in Para (Wikipedia)
sources.summary: In 2019 discrimination based on gender identity was banned through a decision by the Supreme Federal Court. In 2008 the State Department of Education published Decree 016 which guarantees the right of transgender people to use their social name in schools. On 21 June 2025 Ember Alves Oliveira became the first person in the state to obtain a birth certificate with an X sex marker through an action by the Public Defender's Office of the State of Para after the registry office in Ananindeua denied rectification. The registry denied the gender change based on Provision Number 73 of the National Council of Justice which does not provide for a third gender option and denied the first name change without any legal justification, leading the Public Defender's Office to file a lawsuit to obtain rectification. The Public Defender's Office emphasized that maintaining documentation that does not reflect gender identity represents 'a source of suffering and anguish, which constitutes a violation of human dignity'. On 14 July 2026 Governor Hana Ghassan signed a law authorizing religious temples and schools to restrict bathroom use based on biological sex. Before enactment the Federal Public Prosecutor's Office had recommended a veto arguing that it would violate the rights of transgender people and the principle of secularism, and on 15 July 2026 the Socialism and Liberty Party announced that it had filed a lawsuit against the law. Homosexuality has been legal in the state since 1830 when Emperor Pedro I sanctioned the Imperial Penal Code removing all references to sodomy from Brazilian law. Since 2007 a constitutional amendment to the Constitution of the State of Para prohibits discrimination based on sexual orientation. On 21 April 2009 the Governor signed Law Number 7261 which establishes the State Day to Combat Homophobia. On 11 June 2024 the Governor signed Law Number 10570 which establishes the State Day of Bisexual Visibility. On 8 April 2024 the Governor signed Decree Number 3831 which establishes the State Council for Sexual Diversity as part of the State Secretariat for Racial Equality and Human Rights. On 21 December 2011 a court in Belem authorized the adoption of a two-year-old child by a lesbian couple and on 28 June 2012 28 same-sex couples got married in a ceremony in Belem.

sources.title: Supreme Federal Court decision (2019)
sources.summary: On 13 June 2019 Brazil's Supreme Federal Court voted eight to three to criminalize homophobia under Brazil's existing racism law until Congress enacts specific legislation, holding that sexual orientation and gender identity are essential to self-determination.

14911670B9724590061217.name: Alagoas
14911670B9724590061217.summary:
The state's own statutory protection dates to Constitutional Amendment No. 23, enacted by the Legislative Assembly of Alagoas on 22 March 2001, which prohibits discrimination on grounds of sexual orientation.

Alagoas moved ahead of the rest of the country on relationship recognition. On 7 December 2011 the Court of Alagoas opened marriage to same-sex couples throughout the state, the first Brazilian state to do so, and couples do not need a judge's approval to obtain a marriage licence. For a trans visitor whose relationship would be read as same-sex under local birth-sex status, a marriage contracted in Alagoas is therefore available without a judicial step.

On 3 March 2026 the Legislative Assembly of Alagoas enacted a law prohibiting the participation of children and adolescents in pride parades in the state. LGBTQ rights organisations challenged it at the Supreme Federal Court; no ruling is recorded in the sources.

Violence data for the state come from the annual dossiers of ANTRA. The ninth dossier, reported on 26 January 2026, counted 80 trans and travesti people killed in Brazil during 2025, of whom 2 were in Alagoas. The 2024 dossier, reported by CNN Brasil on 27 January 2025, counted 122 killings nationally, of whom 6 were in Alagoas. Both are raw counts. The sources give no population denominator for Alagoas and no general homicide rate for the state, so its share cannot be converted into a per-capita comparison and the figures are not a measure of relative risk. The national dossier recorded that victims were mostly young Black women, many from the Northeast, the region that includes Alagoas.

The victims were overwhelmingly travestis and trans women, killed with extreme violence. Alagoas accounted for 2 of those 80 killings.

CNN Brasil (27 Jan 2025) reports ANTRA's 2024 dossier. Brazil ranked first in the world for the killing of trans people for a 16th consecutive year, with 122 people killed in 2024, a figure 16% below 2023. The victims were mostly young Black women, many from the Northeast, and the crimes were marked by extreme violence. Alagoas accounted for 6 of those 122 killings.

sources.title: LGBTQ rights in Alagoas (Wikipedia)
sources.summary: In March 2018 the Brazilian Supreme Federal Court unanimously ruled that transgender people may change their legal gender without undergoing surgery or hormonal therapy, which were previously requirements. A transgender individual seeking to change gender to reflect gender identity can now simply apply to do so at a registry post in the country. No judicial document is required for the change. No medical report is required for the change. Since 2019 discrimination based on gender identity has been prohibited nationwide in Brazil through a decision by the Supreme Federal Court. On October 15, 2021 Fênix da Silva Leite became the first non-binary person to change their documents in the state, through a court decision. On December 7, 2011 the Court of Alagoas legalized same-sex marriage throughout the state of Alagoas, being the first Brazilian state to do so. Same-sex couples do not need to have judge's approval to have a marriage license. On March 22, 2001 the Legislative Assembly of Alagoas enacted Constitutional Amendment No. 23 prohibiting discrimination based on sexual orientation. On May 5, 2016 Alagoas enacted a law establishing the Escola Livre program prohibiting "ideological and political indoctrination" in the state's schools. On March 21, 2017 Supreme Court Justice Luís Roberto Barroso suspended that law through a preliminary injunction. On March 3, 2026 the Legislative Assembly of Alagoas enacted a law prohibiting the participation of children and adolescents in pride parades in the state. That law was challenged in the Supreme Federal Court by LGBTQ rights organizations.

14911670B2082355341666.name: Mato Grosso
14911670B2082355341666.summary:
Mato Grosso's 1989 Constitution, Article 10, item III, prohibits discrimination on grounds that include sexual orientation and obliges the state to implement measures ensuring no one is harmed or privileged on account of birth, race, colour, sex, marital status, nature of work, age, religion, sexual orientation, political or philosophical belief, disability, or any other particularity or condition. Gender identity is not named in that enumeration. A state decree published in the official gazette on 12 March 2021 guarantees travestis and trans people in Mato Grosso the right to use their social name before state public offices. The name is accepted on badges, cards and identification documents, state employees may register it in internal records and systems, and official publications are barred from using a person's civil name without consent.

Mato Grosso recorded 3 killings of trans and travesti people in 2025, the twelfth-highest raw count among Brazilian states in a national dossier that tallied 80 such killings across the country, and 43 killings of travestis, trans women, trans men, transmasculine and non-binary people in the state since 2017. These are raw counts. The source supplies no per-capita rate for Mato Grosso and no state homicide denominator, so the ranking reflects the size of the count rather than a measured level of risk against other states.

A jury in Mato Grosso sentenced businessman Jorlan Cristiano Ferreira, 44, to 13 years and 6 months in prison for the feminicide of trans woman Mayla, who was found dead with knife wounds in January 2024 on a farm beside MT-485 in Sorriso. He was also convicted of procedural fraud and concealment of a corpse. The jury found the killing was motivated by gender-based contempt and discrimination.

On 1 November 2025 a 39-year-old trans woman was expelled from a pizzeria in Feliz Natal after using the women's restroom, following complaints from staff and customers. The owner was taken to a police station for gender-identity discrimination and released on 2 November 2025 after a custody hearing subject to precautionary measures. The case was under judicial secrecy and Civil Police investigation, monitored by the Mato Grosso Public Prosecutor's Office, as of 16 September 2026.

Cuiabá prohibits trans athletes from women's sports. Councilman Beal Ranalli introduced a bill on 4 February 2025 to make biological sex the sole criterion for participation in city competitions; the City Council passed the prohibition on 19 August 2025, Mayor Abilio Brunini signed it, and it was published in the Official Gazette on 15 September 2025. The Mato Grosso LGBTQIA+ Pride Parade Association and the state Public Defender's Office sued to overturn it and sought 600,000 reais in damages for moral harm; the Court for Collective Actions dismissed the action on 30 October 2025, and the Association said it would appeal to the Court of Justice of Mato Grosso.

On 30 July 2025 Professor Maria Inês da Silva left the Municipal Conference of the Unified Health System in Cuiabá after Mayor Abilio Brunini interrupted her for using gender-neutral language. Health organisations, women's rights groups and Black rights organisations condemned the interruption.

The decree is a Mato Grosso state-government measure recognizing trans identity in documents and name usage.

sources.title: LGBTQ rights in Mato Grosso (Wikipedia)
sources.summary: On 1 March 2018 the Supreme Federal Court ruled that a transgender person has the right to change official name and sex by self-declaration of psychosocial identity without surgery or professional evaluation. In 2019 discrimination based on gender identity was banned through a Supreme Federal Court decision. On 4 February 2025 Cuiabá Councilman Beal Ranalli introduced a bill to establish biological sex as the sole criterion for athlete participation in city competitions, stating that trans women should compete in men's sports. On 19 August 2025 the Cuiabá City Council passed a law banning trans athletes from competing in women's sports, signed by Mayor Abilio Brunini and published in the Official Gazette on 15 September 2025. The Mato Grosso LGBTQIA+ Pride Parade Association and the state Public Defender's Office filed a lawsuit seeking to overturn the law and obtain 600,000 reais in damages for moral harm, which was dismissed by the Court for Collective Actions on 30 October 2025, with the Association stating it would appeal to the Court of Justice of Mato Grosso. On 1 November 2025 a trans woman was expelled from a pizzeria in Feliz Natal after using the women's restroom, the owner was taken to the police station for gender identity discrimination and released on 2 November following a custody hearing, with the case under investigation by the Civil Police as of 16 September 2026. On 30 July 2025 Professor Maria Inês da Silva left the Municipal Conference of the Unified Health System in Cuiabá after being interrupted by Mayor Abilio Brunini for using gender-neutral language, an action condemned by health organizations, women's rights groups, and Black rights organizations. Same-sex sexual activity has been legal in Brazil since 1830 and homosexuality is legal in Mato Grosso. Same-sex marriage has been legal in Mato Grosso since 2013 via a National Council of Justice decision in compliance with a 2011 Supreme Federal Court decision. Same-sex adoption has been officially permitted in the state since 2015 through a Supreme Federal Court decision. The 1989 Constitution of Mato Grosso Article 10, item III prohibits discrimination based on sexual orientation and requires implementation of measures to ensure no one will be harmed or privileged on account of birth, race, color, sex, marital status, nature of work, age, religion, sexual orientation, political or philosophical beliefs, physical or mental disability, and any other particularity or condition. On 4 February 2025 Councilman Beal Ranalli introduced a bill to ban participation of minors in Cuiabá's Pride events.

sources.title: Supreme Federal Court ruling of 1 March 2018
sources.summary: On 1 March 2018 in ADI 4275 the STF held that equality without discrimination encompasses gender identity and expression and that trans persons may change name and gender on the civil registry without sex-reassignment surgery or judicial authorization because gender identity is a manifestation of personality that the State must recognize.

sources.title: Court of Justice of Mato Grosso - Sinop 'gender ideology' law struck down
sources.summary: On 10 November 2022 the Mato Grosso Court of Justice granted preliminary relief holding unconstitutional Sinop's March 2022 municipal law prohibiting distribution, exhibition and dissemination of didactic material containing "gender ideology" in the city's public and private schools, on grounds of violation of the Federal Constitution and Mato Grosso Constitution and excess of municipal legislative competence, in an action brought by the Procuradoria-Geral de Justiça against the Sinop City Council with participation of OAB-MT.

sources.title: Court of Justice of Mato Grosso - state 'gender ideology' teaching ban struck down
sources.summary: On 21 August 2026 the Órgão Especial of the Mato Grosso Court of Justice unanimously declared unconstitutional the state law sanctioned in April 2026 that prohibited teaching and dissemination in state public schools of content on so-called "gender ideology," gender identity and sexual orientation, including films, music, paintings and other artistic materials, thereby voiding the ban and restoring schools' pedagogical autonomy to address gender identity and sexual orientation on grounds of formal usurpation of the Union's exclusive competence over education guidelines under Article 22 of the Federal Constitution and violation of academic freedom, pluralism of ideas, and protection against bullying and discrimination.

10402087B89016843004490.summary:
Sachsen is a state within Germany and stands under the German national framework: legal gender recognition, identity documents and equality protections are set nationally and cannot be disapplied at state level. The findings below are those specific to Sachsen itself.

On 31 May 2025 thousands marched through Dresden for Christopher Street Day while neo-Nazi counter-demonstrators mounted a protest aimed at disrupting the march; the march went ahead. That far-right attempt to stop Dresden Pride is the documented basis for the elevated risk rating Sachsen carries.

Sachsen is a co-sponsor, with Sachsen-Anhalt and Thuringia, of a joint state initiative to tighten the federal Self-Determination Act, launched after the case of Marla-Svenja Liebich and directed at what the sponsoring states describe as misuse of self-identification. The state government is therefore working to narrow the self-identification route at federal level; it cannot amend the national statute alone, and the initiative is a push on the federal legislature.

25490228B14384488423733.name: Comunitat Valenciana
25490228B14384488423733.summary:
The Comunitat Valenciana has its own two-statute framework for trans and LGTBI people: Ley 8/2017 of 7 April, the integral law on the right to gender identity and expression, and Ley 23/2018 of 29 November on LGTBI equality. Both sit under the Spanish national framework on legal gender recognition carried by the national record; what follows is the regional layer.

Article 1 of Ley 8/2017 sets the law's purpose as guaranteeing an adequate normative framework for gender self-determination for people whose felt gender identity differs from that assigned at birth, and public bodies of the Comunitat Valenciana must treat people according to their felt gender identity. The duty reaches the regional administration, health and education services a visitor may deal with.

Ley 23/2018 prohibits discrimination on grounds of sexual orientation and gender identity and expression, provides access and admission rights (article 56), reverses the burden of proof (article 57), and establishes a Title V regime of administrative infringements and sanctions for discrimination against LGTBI people (articles 58 to 66). A complaint about being refused service or admission in the region can shift the evidential burden onto the respondent, and the regional administration can fine discriminators.

Regional courts have handled gender-identity-motivated offences. The Audiencia Provincial de Valencia, Section 5, convicted over a June 2022 incident in a Valencia park in Patraix, where an 18-year-old and several minors insulted, chased, filmed and mocked a trans woman solely because of her gender identity. The adult accepted six months' imprisonment, suspended for two years on condition of committing no offence, plus a 720-euro fine and 1,000 euros in moral damages to the victim; two minors had already been sentenced to supervision measures. The specialised hate-crime prosecutor (fiscal coordinadora de delitos de odio) handled the case.

Other communities in the same inventory carry a single statute, among them Cataluña (Ley 11/2014) and Aragón (Ley 4/2018).

LGTBI federation's 2025 radiography of public educational policies across Spain's autonomous communities, covering gender-identity protocols and education legislation in each, places the Comunidad Valenciana with Madrid, Extremadura, Murcia and Navarra among the leaders on educational policy coverage, and records that the Valencian parliament completed its gender legislation.

19177384B97722443848736.name: Buenos Aires
19177384B97722443848736.summary:
Buenos Aires province stands under Argentina's national framework for gender recognition and implements that regime through its own civil registry. The provincial ombudsman published a guide in September 2024 setting out the steps for rectifying the gender marker of people born in the province, including provisions for people born in Buenos Aires province who now live elsewhere.

The provincial ombudsman's Gender Violence Office, created by Resolución Nº 100/10, submitted evidence to the UN Human Rights Committee for its June and July 2016 review documenting violence, persecution and harassment of trans and travesti people in Buenos Aires province by provincial police and by third parties acting under police cover. The submission carries a dedicated section on violence by judicial, state and police agents.

Academic and legal research records the criminalisation of trans and travesti women in the province through drug-offence prosecutions brought under microtrafficking enforcement, concentrated in La Plata's Zona Roja. After the 2012 Gender Identity Law formally decriminalised trans presence, security-led street-offence policing became the operative instrument of indirect criminalisation in the province.

That instrument rests on a jurisdictional transfer: in 2005 Buenos Aires province assumed jurisdiction over drug sale and possession offences, the devolution that allowed provincial street-offence and drug-law prosecution to function as the enforcement route.

No trans-specific placement rule for prisoners is recorded for the province. Buenos Aires province operates no separate trans housing unit and no province-level rule on where trans women are held; placement is governed by the national prison-housing framework.

17162690B44985096553766.name: Subcarpathian Voivodeship
17162690B44985096553766.summary:
Subcarpathian Voivodeship stands under the national framework of Poland, which carries the country's entry rules, custody conditions, document and marker rules, and hate-crime measures; the findings below are those specific to the voivodeship.

On 20 September 2021 the Podkarpackie voivodeship council repealed its 'LGBT-free' resolution and replaced the ordinance with a generic anti-discrimination statement. The county-level layer ended later: on 27 April 2025 the county of Łańcut, in the voivodeship's southeast, repealed its anti-LGBT resolution at an extraordinary councillors' session, the last local authority in Poland to do so.

No region-specific enforcement action, prosecution, healthcare restriction, facility rule or trans-specific incident in Subcarpathian Voivodeship is documented in the available sources. For those matters the national assessment applies.

sources.summary: Notes from Poland (27 Apr 2025): the county of Łańcut in southeast Poland (Podkarpackie), the last local authority in the country with an anti-LGBT resolution, repealed the measure at an extraordinary councillors' session. At the wave's peak about one third of Poland's territory was covered by such documents, per the Atlas of Hate mapping project. This sets the dated end-point for the county-level resolution era.

The Them (23 Sep 2021, updated 29 Sep): Podkarpackie's voivodeship council repealed its 'LGBT-free' resolution on Monday 20 September 2021, alongside Małopolska and Lubelskie, after the European Commission threatened to withhold regional development funds. Podkarpackie replaced its ordinance with a generic anti-discrimination statement.

17162690B69262761487853.name: Lublin Voivodeship
17162690B69262761487853.summary:
Lublin Voivodeship, in south-eastern Poland, stands under the Polish national framework: passport and marker rules, conditions in custody, and hate-crime provisions are set nationally and are carried by the national assessment. What is specific to the voivodeship is its own record of official hostility.

Świdnik, a town in the voivodeship, was the first place in Poland to adopt an "LGBT-free" declaration. Its county council passed the resolution in March 2019, pledging to shield children from "homosexual propaganda" and to refrain from actions encouraging "tolerance of LGBT people". The text is non-binding; it does not itself restrict a visitor's movement or access to services, and it records the posture of a local authority rather than a rule enforceable against anyone.

The voivodeship legislature adopted a comparable declaration of its own and, when the matter was revisited, voted to keep it in place. It repealed the resolution on 20 September 2021, after the European Commission threatened to withhold funding from voivodeships that retained such declarations. The repeal changed the regional assembly's formal position. Whether the county-level declarations, including Świdnik's, were withdrawn is not established by these sources.

The Spotlight places this first such resolution within global anti-gender campaigning.

The Them (23 September 2021, updated 29 September): on Monday 20 September 2021 the provinces of Podkarpackie, Małopolska and Lubelskie repealed their 'LGBT-free' resolutions. Lubelskie had previously voted to keep its resolution. All three repeals followed European Commission funding threats, dating the Lublin voivodeship repeal to 20 September 2021.
