17162690B86810837764805.summary:
Łódź Voivodeship sits inside Poland's national legal framework. The country's entry rules, its custody and detention findings, and its hate-speech legislation are carried by the national record and are not restated here. What is specific to the voivodeship is its own anti-LGBT declaration and the court action that ended it.

The Supreme Administrative Court revoked the Łódź Voivodeship council's anti-LGBT resolution on 12 October 2023. The invalidation rested on equal-treatment grounds under Article 32 of the constitution, the reasoning Polish administrative courts applied to these instruments. Łódź was one of five voivodeships the European Commission wrote to on 2 June 2020, asking their governors to withdraw the declarations.

The resolution was declaratory rather than penal. It created no offence, attached no penalty, and physically barred no one from any place. Its effect was institutional: it signalled to local bureaucracies and schools which families and identities the voivodeship's leadership considered legitimate.

No record specific to Łódź Voivodeship of enforcement action, police conduct, prosecution, violence, or facility and healthcare practice was identified. 27671186B7584771598694.name: Bauchi
27671186B7584771598694.summary:
Bauchi's Sharia Penal Code remains in force. The UK Home Office country policy and information note of June 2025 confirms it, and death by stoning is the penalty provided under Section 133 of the Bauchi Sharia Penal Code Law 2001 and Section 134 of the Bauchi State Penal Law of 2001.

On 28 June 2022 a Sharia court sitting in Ningi local government area sentenced three men to death by stoning for homosexuality, among them 70-year-old Malam Haruna. The prosecution was brought by members of the Hisbah Vanguard through Adamu Dan Kafi, who told the court the three were arrested at Gwada village, Ningi LGA, on 14 June 2022. Presiding judge Munka'ilu Sabo-Ningi held that they had violated Section 134 of the Bauchi State Penal Law of 2001 and granted a 30-day appeal window. Relatives of the convicted men said the judgment had not been carried out at the time of reporting. Reuters described the sentence as the first time the death penalty had actually been imposed for homosexuality in Nigeria.

The UK Home Office note records that the 2022 Bauchi sentence could not be carried out until ratified by the state governor, and that a further report placed a death-by-stoning sentence for homosexuality from a Sharia court in Bauchi in May 2024.

Earlier convictions in the state were reversed on appeal. Jubrin Babaji was convicted on 25 September 2003 under Section 133 of the Bauchi Sharia Penal Code Law 2001 and sentenced to death by stoning; the Upper Sharia Court of Bauchi State quashed the sentence for denial of counsel and a defective confession. Yunusa Rafin Chiyawa's conviction was quashed on 14 November 2003. Amnesty International recorded a number of cases in which convictions and sentences to death were quashed on appeal.

In 2007 Bauchi state police arrested eighteen men and charged them with sodomy for dressing as women, an offence under the Shari'a penal code. The charges were later reduced to vagrancy, and the men were held in jail for several years awaiting trial; the pre-trial detention dissolved by the end of 2011.

Persons perceived as trans-feminine in Bauchi have been arrested and held in custody under Shari'a charges for years.

27671186B50148357657004.name: Kano
27671186B50148357657004.summary:
Kano stands under Nigeria's national legal framework and operates its own Sharia Penal Code Law 2000, in force since 26 November 2000. Consensual same-sex activity under that code carries 100 lashes and up to one year's imprisonment where the person is unmarried, and stoning to death (rajm) where the person is or has been married.

The capital maximum is not confined to men. The UK Home Office country policy and information note of June 2025 records Kano's maximum penalty for what the note terms lesbianism as death, and records the Sharia codes as remaining in force.

A separate state statute, the Prostitution and Immoral Acts (Prohibition) Law, criminalises cross-dressing by men, so a trans visitor's appearance is a point of legal exposure in its own right, distinct from conduct. Enforcement of dress is documented: eight people convicted of wearing female clothing at a wedding were reportedly flogged in public on hisbah premises in Kano in 2023.

The Hisbah, the state religious police, is the most active command among the states examined in the USCIRF 2019 study of Sharia criminal-law implementation, which drew on 173 Sharia-court cases from 2017 in Kano, Sokoto and Zamfara.

27671186B99510750195830.name: Sokoto
27671186B99510750195830.summary:
Sokoto State stands under Nigeria's national legal framework and layers its own religious penal code on top of it. The Sokoto State Sharia Penal Code Laws took effect across the state on 31 January 2001. Under the code, male same-sex activity is punished by stoning to death where the offender is or has been married, and by 100 lashes where he is not. Sexual acts between women, recorded in the code as wsafa, draw ta'azir punishment of up to 100 lashes and imprisonment.

Sokoto's Shari'a criminal code applies to Muslims in the state, one of twelve northern states whose codes carry a maximum penalty of death for men and whipping or imprisonment for women for same-sex acts.

Sokoto's Sharia courts apply the code in practice, including its capital provisions. On 9 October 2001 the Upper Sharia Court at Gwadabawa convicted Safiyatu Hussaini Tungar Tudu of zina under sections 128 and 129 of the Sokoto State Sharia Penal Code and sentenced her to death by stoning; the co-accused was discharged and acquitted. She filed an appeal on 26 October 2001, and the Sharia Court of Appeal of Sokoto State quashed the conviction and discharged and acquitted her on 25 March 2002. The conviction was for zina rather than same-sex conduct, but it establishes that the state's religious courts impose the code's capital sentences and that an appellate tier reviews them.

The groundwork for the code within the state is documented. An interim committee report was submitted to Sokoto Governor Attahiru Dalhatu Bafarawa on 13 October 1999, and a final report followed on 16 December 1999 with an annexe draft bill to establish Sharia courts applying Sharia law in the state.

27671186B69054806776702.name: Yobe
27671186B69054806776702.summary:
Yobe adopted Shari'a into its criminal legislation in 2000, under Governor Bukar Abba Ibrahim, as part of the 1999-2002 wave of northern states that created a parallel religious-criminal jurisdiction. Human Rights Watch's 2004 report lists Yobe among the twelve states that had done so by 2002, the only states whose Shari'a courts try Muslim criminal cases beyond federal law. The state's inhabitants are mainly Muslims, so the Shari'a penal code's personal scope covers most people in the state, residents and visitors alike; a visitor who is not Muslim falls outside that code's application to Muslims.

The UK Home Office country policy and information note on sexual orientation and gender identity in Nigeria (version 4.0, June 2025) records that the Sharia penal codes of the twelve northern states apply to Muslims, that death is the maximum penalty for men in all twelve, and that penalties for acts between women range from death in a minority of states to flogging and imprisonment. Yobe is one of the twelve, so death is the maximum penalty for men here; the note does not identify which scale Yobe applies to acts between women.

Enforcement in the northern Sharia states includes public flogging. The same note's enforcement and Hisbah section records public flogging of persons cross-dressing in 2023. The source does not identify the state in which that flogging took place.

27671186B21163522287660.name: Zamfara
27671186B21163522287660.summary:
Zamfara operates its own Sharia criminal-law layer in addition to Nigeria's national framework. The state's governor was the first in Nigeria to move, promulgating the Sharia Establishment Law on 27 October 1999, in force 27 January 2000. The enabling legislation, the Sharia Courts (Administration of Justice and Certain Consequential Changes) Law 1999, was enacted under section 6 of the 1999 Constitution; it established Sharia courts with criminal jurisdiction in Islamic law and enabled the codification of a Sharia Penal Code.

The codification of offences and punishments produced a penal-code architecture applied by the Sharia courts of the twelve northern states, a framework Zamfara pioneered. By 2002 twelve northern states had adopted some form of Sharia into their criminal legislation, and those states remain the only ones in Nigeria where Sharia courts hold jurisdiction to try criminal cases.

For a visitor, the operative consequence is that criminal cases in Zamfara can be heard by Sharia courts applying codified Islamic criminal law, a track separate from the national statute. The state's courts are the venue in which Sharia criminal penalties would be imposed locally.

sources.summary: Alh. Ahmed Bello Mahmud, then Attorney-General and Commissioner for Justice of Zamfara State, set out the state's account of its Sharia adoption at a JNI-sponsored seminar on 6 July 2000. He details Zamfara's enabling legislation, the Sharia Courts (Administration of Justice and Certain Consequential Changes) Law 1999, enacted under section 6 of the 1999 Constitution, which established Sharia courts with criminal jurisdiction in Islamic law and enabled the codification of a Sharia Penal Code. The Grand Kadi took over court administration on 29 June 2000, alongside policy moves against prostitution and gambling. The account documents the adoption process that began Nigeria's Sharia criminal-law wave in Zamfara.

By the end of 2000 eleven other northern states had adopted the application of Sharia. The codification of offences and punishments produced a penal-code architecture that the Sharia courts of the twelve states apply, a framework Zamfara pioneered across the northern bloc.

27671186B753479316714.name: Borno
27671186B753479316714.summary:
Borno stands under the national framework of Nigeria, and its criminalisation of same-sex conduct rests on Borno's own legislation as well as that framework. The state's statute on prostitution, homosexuality, brothels and other sexual immoralities (2000) was signed by Governor Kachalla on 10 December 2000 and gazetted in Borno State Gazette No. 42 Vol. 26 on 18 October 2001. Section 3 makes prostitution, lesbianism, a homosexual act and pimping offences in the state. Section 7 provides that any person who 'engages in sexual intercourse with another person of the same gender' shall upon conviction be punished with death. Section 4 deems all brothels closed on commencement, and Section 9 assigns jurisdiction to the Upper Sharia Courts, Area Courts and Magistrate Courts. The death penalty for same-sex intercourse is enacted in Borno's own statute, so the state's criminalisation does not depend on the federal framework for its severity.

Borno is among the twelve northern states that had adopted Shari'a into criminal legislation by 2002, according to Human Rights Watch's 2004 report, with Shari'a courts holding criminal jurisdiction over Muslims beyond federal law. Borno enacted a separate Sharia Penal Code Law 2001, signed into law on 3 March 2003. The parallel Shari'a layer in Borno therefore rests on a Borno-specific enactment rather than on federal or umbrella coverage.

The Shari'a provisions that apply to Muslims in Borno, as one of the twelve northern states, criminalise same-sex sexual acts between men and between women. The UK Home Office country policy and information note on sexual orientation and gender identity in Nigeria (June 2025) records the maximum penalty for sodomy for men as death in all twelve states, and penalties for lesbianism ranging from death to flogging and imprisonment. The note devotes a section to enforcement of the Shari'a provisions and the posture of the hisbah morality police.

Exposure differs by religion and by court. Shari'a courts hold criminal jurisdiction over Muslims beyond federal law, while the 2000 state statute assigns cases to the Upper Sharia Courts, Area Courts and Magistrate Courts. A Muslim visitor in Borno is exposed through the Shari'a track; other visitors are exposed through the state morality statute and its courts.

27671186B90305463766462.name: Gombe
27671186B90305463766462.summary:
Gombe State criminalises same-sex conduct under its own Sharia Penal Code Law 2001, signed into law on 23 November 2001, which operates alongside federal law. Human Rights Watch's 2004 survey of Shari'a implementation lists Gombe among the twelve northern states that had adopted Shari'a into criminal legislation by 2002, with Shari'a courts holding criminal jurisdiction over Muslims beyond the federal code.

The penalties are severe and gendered. Gombe, Jigawa, Kano and Zamfara share a sodomy offence that punishes unmarried men with 100 lashes plus one year's imprisonment and married men with stoning to death (rajm). The offence covering same-sex conduct between women carries up to 50 lashes plus up to six months' imprisonment. Gombe defines gross indecency in its own formulation as 'any sexual offence against the normal or usual standards of behaviour'. The enacted statutory text reaches same-sex conduct by men and women beyond the federal code.

Gombe enforces its moral-crimes layer on the ground. In October 2023 the Gombe State Command of the Nigeria Security and Civil Defence Corps raided a birthday gathering at Duwa Plaza along the Bauchi-Gombe Expressway where a same-sex wedding was being prepared, arresting 76 people. State PRO Buhari Sa'ad told reporters that 59 males were detained, 21 of whom confessed to being homosexuals, with 17 females present at the scene, and that those arrested would be charged to court for 'a crime in Gombe State'.

The Guardian of Lagos, in a report bylined James Agberebi and archived on 4 December 2023, independently confirms the raid: about 76 people were arrested after a tip-off about a same-sex birthday party and planned marriage. Gombe NSCDC Commandant Mohammed Muazu confirmed the arrests; spokesperson Buhari Saad said 21 of the 59 detained males were involved in gay activities while the remaining males and the 17 females were invited guests and onlookers, and officers voiced concern over the participants' ages.

The Sharia layer within which Gombe's statute sits is assessed in the UK Home Office country policy and information note of June 2025, which records that Islamic law applies to Muslims in the twelve northern states and includes a dedicated section on enforcement of Sharia provisions and the attitude of the hisbah (morality police).

27671186B1226853346294.name: Jigawa
27671186B1226853346294.summary:
Jigawa State's own criminal layer is the Sharia Penal Code Law 2000, Law No. 12 of 2000, signed on 18 December 2000 and brought into operation on 27 December 2000 (Jigawa State Gazette Vol. 1 No. 12). It operates alongside the national framework rather than replacing it: the UK Home Office country policy and information note on Nigeria (June 2025) treats the Sharia penal layer as the operative criminal frame for Muslims in Jigawa. A trans visitor who is Muslim by the state's reckoning is therefore exposed to the state code's offences and penalties, not only to the national statute.

The Home Office's Sharia penalties table covering twelve northern states records Jigawa's penalties under the Sharia Penal Code (2000): married men face death by stoning; unmarried men face 100 lashes and imprisonment of up to one year; same-sex acts between women carry up to 50 lashes and imprisonment of up to six months. The sourcebook on Sharia implementation in northern Nigeria records the same structure and places Jigawa among four states whose sodomy offence punishes unmarried men with 100 lashes plus one year's imprisonment and married men with stoning to death (rajm), with lesbianism carrying up to 50 lashes plus up to six months' imprisonment. Exposure turns on the sex and marital status a Sharia court applies to the person before it. A trans visitor in what would be locally classed as a same-sex relationship sits in the women's tier where that is how the court reads the conduct, and in the heavier tier where the conduct is classified as sodomy between men, reaching rajm where the court treats the person as a married man.

The Jigawa code reaches conduct the national statute does not cover, including same-sex conduct between women, and its own explanation of the offence includes the "unnatural fusion of the female sexual organs".

Jigawa is among twelve northern states that had adopted some form of Sharia into their criminal legislation by 2002, and those states remain the only ones where Sharia courts hold jurisdiction to try criminal cases, as recorded by Human Rights Watch in 2004.

27671186B54051914323789.name: Kaduna
27671186B54051914323789.summary:
Kaduna is a state in northern Nigeria and stands under the national framework; its own criminal law adds two further layers that a visitor must read together. The UK Home Office country policy and information note on sexual orientation and gender identity (June 2025) records a Kaduna secular Penal Code adopted in 2017 whose Section 259 punishes 'unnatural offences' (sodomy, lesbianism and bestiality) with up to 21 years' imprisonment and a fine. Running in parallel is the Kaduna Sharia Penal Code Law 2002 (Law No. 4 of 2002), which applies to Muslims.

The Sharia layer is Kaduna's own promulgated code, not a federal instrument. Ostien's annotated compilation of northern Sharia legislation gives the Sharia Penal Code Law 2002 as Law No. 4 of 2002, signed and brought into operation on 21 June 2002, published in Kaduna State Gazette No. 17 Vol. 36 of 4 July 2002 at pp. A15-A108, and bound together with the Sharia Criminal Procedure Code.

27671186B99661334382691.name: Katsina
27671186B99661334382691.summary:
Katsina stands under Nigeria's national framework and additionally operates its own Sharia criminal layer. Katsina is among the northern states that adopted Sharia criminal codes from 1999 onward, and the provisions cited remain in force.

Katsina's own statute is the Sharia Penal Code Law 2001, Law No. 2 of 2001, which came into operation on 20 June 2001 and was gazetted in Katsina State Gazette Vol. 12 No. 23 on 27 August 2001.

The code's sodomy provision reads: "Whoever commits the offence of sodomy shall be punished with stoning to death (rajm)". Katsina is one of three states, with Kaduna and Kebbi, whose sodomy text carries that wording.

Katsina's lesbianism provision is among the harshest in the northern block. Only Kano and Katsina reach stoning to death as the maximum for the lesbianism offence, against the harmonised code's base penalty of 50 lashes and up to six months. Katsina is one of only two states whose law carries death as the maximum for same-sex acts between women as well as men.

For a trans person held in Katsina, the penalty structure runs from lashing or caning to capital punishment. Lesbianism, defined as carnal acts or stimulation between women, is punishable by imprisonment or caning in most northern states, with death penalties applied in Kano and Katsina.

The Sharia layer in Katsina reaches women as well as men. Arrest data for these offences is limited, so the recorded enforcement picture is incomplete.

Presentation is separately exposed. Sources describe a cross-dressing layer in the northern states under which men who dress or behave as women face prison or a fine.

It traces the process from Zamfara's Shari'a Establishment Law, promulgated 27 October 1999 and in force 27 January 2000. The provisions cited remain in force.

27671186B53868438251790.name: Kebbi
27671186B53868438251790.summary:
Kebbi is one of twelve northern Nigerian states that adopted criminal Shari'a in the wave running from 1999 to 2002, and it is among the only states in the country whose Shari'a courts hold criminal jurisdiction over Muslims. The state's own penal layer is the Penal Code (Amendment) Law, Law No. 21 of 2000, signed and brought into operation on 1 December 2000 and published in the Kebbi State Gazette Vol. 2 No. 1 (Supplement, 31 December 2000).

Under that statute, sodomy (liwat) carries death by stoning (rajm), and same-sex acts between women carry up to 50 lashes and imprisonment of up to six months. Kebbi's enacted text states the stoning formula explicitly rather than leaving the penalty to judicial construction. The penalty for conduct between women sits at the standard northern tier of lashing and imprisonment, not at a capital maximum.

The state code reaches further than the federal statute. It criminalises acts between women as well as between men, and for Muslim defendants it is both broader in scope and harsher in penalty than the national law. A trans visitor in Kebbi therefore faces a state-level capital exposure for conduct the federal statute punishes with a term of years, and a state-level prohibition on conduct between women that the federal statute does not reach.

Application is by religion. The Shari'a criminal jurisdiction in Kebbi runs over Muslims, so a Muslim trans visitor or resident is exposed to the state's Shari'a penalties while a non-Muslim is not.

27671186B79778155682183.name: Niger
27671186B79778155682183.summary:
Niger State stands under Nigeria's national framework, which applies here as it does elsewhere in the country. The findings below are specific to Niger State.

Niger State is one of the states that adopted Sharia criminal provisions in the wave that began with Zamfara's Shari'a Establishment Law, promulgated on 27 October 1999 and in force from 27 January 2000. Human Rights Watch's 2004 survey of that wave names Niger State among the states concerned. Those provisions remain in force.

The state's own instrument is the Penal Code (Amendment) Law 2000. It was signed on 22 February 2000, came into operation on 4 May 2000, and was gazetted in the Niger State of Nigeria Gazette, volume 25, number 8, of 9 March 2000, at pages B29 to B36. It amends Penal Code Law Cap 94, Laws of Niger State (the 1960 Penal Code), to revise the punishments set out in it.

The amendment defines adultery to include sodomy and inserts section 68A. Under that section a Muslim convicted of a listed offence, where the offence is proved against him to the Islamic evidentiary standard, receives the harsher punishment specified under Sharia; the amendment also adds amputation to the caning paragraph of section 68. Where that standard is not met, the ordinary Penal Code punishment applies. The law is not a complete Sharia penal code: it leaves the 1960 code in place and makes certain sections carry different burdens of proof and different punishments when applied to Muslims than when applied to non-Muslims.

For a visitor, the consequence is that a Muslim traveller whose conduct falls within the listed offences and who is identified to the authorities stands under a harsher parallel legal frame in Niger State than the national law alone would impose. Travellers who are not Muslim remain under the ordinary Penal Code provisions.

No arrest, prosecution, conviction or sentencing in Niger State under the 2000 amendment appears in the sources reviewed. The state-level exposure documented here is statutory rather than evidenced by enforcement.

It traces the wave from Zamfara's Shari'a Establishment Law, promulgated 27 October 1999 and in force 27 January 2000. sources.title: LGBTQ rights in Niger (Wikipedia)
sources.summary: Article 25 of the Refoundation Charter, adopted in March 2025, criminalizes all lesbian, gay, bisexual, transgender, queer, intersex, asexual acts or practices, expressly including transgender acts or practices. The February 2026 penal code punishes LGBTQIA+ acts or practices with 5 to 10 years in prison and a fine up to 100 million CFA francs (€152,448.94; US$176,604.56). The punishable practices expressly include changing or attempting to change one's birth sex. Creating, managing, financing, or participating in LGBTQIA+ organizations, clubs and social venues, directly or indirectly, is punished with 10 to 20 years in prison and a fine up to 500 million CFA francs (€762,244.71; US$882,829). Mitigating circumstances and suspended sentences cannot be applied to these penalties. There are no broad legal protections against discrimination based on gender identity. After the 2026 code took effect, dozens of people were arrested across the country and some imprisoned, including military officials, and LGBTQ people went into hiding. Same-sex sexual activity was explicitly outlawed in 2025 and penalized in 2026, and before that change the age of consent was 13 for heterosexual acts and 21 for homosexual acts. Article 25 of the March 2025 Refoundation Charter criminalizes same-sex sexual relations and LGBTQIA+ acts or practices. The February 2026 penal code punishes same-sex sexual relations with 5 to 10 years in prison and a fine up to 100 million CFA francs, covering same-sex sexual activity and public announcement of one's romantic relationship with a person of the same sex. Creating, managing, financing, or participating in LGBTQIA+ organizations, clubs and social venues, directly or indirectly, is punished with 10 to 20 years in prison and a fine up to 500 million CFA francs, with no mitigating circumstances or suspended sentences allowed. Since March 2025 under Article 24 marriage is defined as a union between a man and a woman, and since June 2026 getting married to a person of the same sex and officiating, organizing or bearing official witness to same-sex weddings is punished with 10 to 20 years in prison. There are no broad protections against discrimination based on sexual orientation, but Article 95 of Law 2022-59 punishes collecting and processing data revealing sexual life or sexual orientation with three months to five years imprisonment and a fine of 5,000,000 to 50,000,000 CFA francs, while Law 2015-36 which had prohibited discrimination including sexual orientation was repealed in 2023 with convictions expunged. Enforcement included two men caught naked in a parked car arrested for public indecency and fined a small fee, two young women in Maradi in 2022 prosecuted for lesbianism and acquitted for lack of legislation but imprisoned for two years for posting nude videos allegedly portraying a lesbian act, and two young women reported as lesbians in Niamey in 2025 prosecuted for public indecency but acquitted because the facts did not pertain to the public sphere with the judge allegedly sanctioned for leniency. After the 2026 code, dozens were arrested across the country and some imprisoned, LGBTQ people went into hiding, and organizations providing HIV prevention services to MSM stopped working, ending access to condoms, HIV testing and PrEP. Gay men and lesbians experienced societal discrimination with strong pressure to conform to societal norms, leading many to lead socially acceptable lives in public while seeking LGBT relationships privately. No violence based on sexual orientation or gender identity was reported and no documented cases of discrimination in employment, housing, education, health care or statelessness based on sexual orientation were recorded, though stigma or intimidation probably prevented incidents from being reported. Two gay rights organizations operated in secret partly because they were not formally registered. Asylum seekers from Cameroon, Liberia and Côte d'Ivoire who held LGBTQ public demonstrations in Niamey in 2022 were denied refugee recognition hindering relocation and faced shops refusing to serve them and verbal or physical violence from strangers. Niger's attitude toward LGBTQ issues is described as usually discreet, even though male prostitution was prevalent in Niamey and effeminate men were known for having always been part of Niger's culture by organizing traditional wedding ceremonies and supporting themselves that way. The 2025 acquittal of two women prosecuted for public indecency caused widespread debate ranging from approval to outrage. The article documents no statement about societal tolerance of transgender people specifically; the only official cultural-values statement concerns LGBTQ practices generally: "all LGBTQ practices, whatever they may be (...) are not in line with our social and cultural values".

sources.title: Statement by Minister of Justice and Human Rights Alio Daouda
sources.summary: Niger criminalizes LGBTQIA+ practice.

sources.title: 2022 Maradi prosecution and parliamentary proposal by lawmaker Nana Djibou Harouna
sources.summary: As of 8-9 December 2022 Niger had no specific law criminalising same-sex relationships, while Maradi lawmaker Nana Djibou Harouna presented to the Speaker of Parliament a proposal backed by nearly all MPs to criminalise same-sex relationships with punishment unspecified and no scheduled debate, following weeks earlier a Maradi court acquitting two young women of lesbianism-related charges for lack of clear legislation but sentencing them to two years imprisonment for posting nude social-media videos allegedly showing a lesbian act.

27671186B8148656125930.name: Imo
27671186B8148656125930.summary:
Imo is a state in south-eastern Nigeria and stands under the national legal framework. Its own record covers enforcement action taken inside the state against private gatherings and against people accused of same-sex conduct in public.

On 26 April 2018 two men in Imo State were stripped, beaten and paraded through the streets after being accused of gay sex. An inquiry by NoStringsNG found that the victims were then arrested by the police themselves, and that they might need legal support. The state's role in the episode was to detain the people who had been attacked, not the crowd that attacked them.

Enforcement continued into 2025. On 19 February the Imo Police Command broke up a party at Graziella Hotels in Orogwe, Owerri West, arrested many of those present, described as gay and lesbian suspects, and placed attendees who fled on a police search list. The event was a private hotel gathering, and the police treated it as an operation with names attached to people who were not detained.

Seven years separate the two documented episodes, and they occurred in different parts of the state: a street in 2018, a hotel in Owerri West in 2025. Police action in Imo is therefore not confined to a single locality, and it has not been limited to public conduct. Both a public street and a closed private venue appear in the record as points of exposure, and leaving before an arrest did not remove people from the search.

27671186B63712480376187.name: Edo
27671186B63712480376187.summary:
Edo State stands under Nigeria's national legal framework. Its own documented record is one of mob violence against people accused of same-sex conduct, and it contains no instance in which police protected the person accused.

In February 2008, in a remote community in Edo State, police declared Ugbogbo Ovbukhan wanted over 'gay practice' after he and his partner Jerry were found together. A mob beat both men for desecrating the community; Ovbukhan escaped before police arrived and police arrested Jerry for interrogation. The Nigerian Observer reported the wanted declaration on 15 August 2008.

On 10 June 2010, The Nigerian Observer reported from Benin City, in Oredo local government area, that Mark Osato Edomwonyi narrowly escaped being killed by a mob after he was found with his partner Paddy in Paddy's rented apartment. A neighbour raised the alarm; Edomwonyi fled through the backyard before the mob arrived, and the crowd then, in the newspaper's words, 'unleashed terror' on Paddy. No police intervention, arrest or prosecution appears in the report, and Edomwonyi's whereabouts were still unknown when it was filed.

In May 2018, at Ekpoma, a mob lynched one of two men found together while the other escaped. The report presented the killing as an 'abominable act' against traditional heritage, treating it as community redress.

For a visitor, the documented exposure in Edo comes from community perception rather than from a prosecution: in these accounts it is neighbours, not patrols, who raise the alarm, and the single police action documented across the three cases was taken against the couple rather than against those who beat them. The cases reported involve men accused of same-sex conduct, and the inventory holds no Edo case in which a report identifies the victim of violence as a transgender person. Risk to a trans visitor therefore has to be read from the way accusations of sexual and gender nonconformity mobilise a crowd, not from a documented attack on a trans person in the state.

sources.summary: Nigerian Observer (May 2018): in Ekpoma a mob lynched one of two men caught together and the other escaped, framed as an 'abominable act' under traditional heritage. Documents fatal community violence in Edo State.

The Initiative for Equal Rights (TIERs) '2024 Human Rights Violations Report', published January 2025, records 556 violations affecting 850 victims based on real or perceived SOGIESC across Nigeria during the reporting period. The figures are national in scope, with no Edo-specific breakdown, and TIERs states they represent only a fraction of the true scale.

65028918B93184959873838.name: Aceh
65028918B93184959873838.summary:
Aceh operates a provincial sharia criminal code alongside the national criminal code. Special autonomy granted in 2005 authorised the introduction of Islamic criminal law for Muslim residents, and Qanun Aceh Nomor 6 Tahun 2014 tentang Hukum Jinayat has been enforced since 23 October 2015. The code's provisions are applied to anyone present in the province, including foreign visitors, so a trans traveller's exposure does not depend on religion or residency.

Article 63 of the Qanun defines liwath as sexual acts between males and Article 64 defines musahaqah as sexual acts between females, each determined by birth sex. Both offences carry up to 100 lashes, up to 100 months' imprisonment, or a fine of up to 1,000 grams of gold. Because the definitions turn on birth sex rather than current presentation or documents, a trans visitor whose identity papers, appearance or partner are read as same-sex conduct falls inside the offence.

The provisions were first applied on 23 May 2017, when an Islamic court in Banda Aceh had two men publicly caned with 82 lashes each for gay sex before hundreds of spectators outside a mosque. Two men aged 20 and 23 were sentenced to public caning for same-sex relations the same year, and several further cases of men publicly caned after guilty findings followed.

On 11 August 2025 a sharia court sentenced two men aged 20 and 21 to public caning for kissing, following an April arrest in which police broke into a toilet. The caning was reported on 26 August 2025. Public caning is the province's standing punishment for sharia offences.

Enforcement against transgender women in Aceh has taken a different form. In January 2018 police in North Aceh arrested twelve transgender women, forcibly cut their hair, compelled them to wear men's clothing and closed their beauty salons. Accounts of a January 2018 parlour raid in the province describe officers shaving the heads of transgender women, stripping their shirts and bras and parading them in the street while forcing them to shout that they would become men.

Legal scholarship from Aceh's Islamic university analyses a rising number of waria cases in Banda Aceh through the lens of sharia law enforcement, indicating that enforcement against transgender women in the province is an ongoing subject of local legal study rather than an isolated episode.

Aceh legal scholarship analysing the rise of waria cases through a sharia-law-enforcement lens.

CBS News/AP (26 Aug 2025): two men were publicly caned in conservative Aceh province after a sharia court convicted them of hugging and kissing. Public caning is the province's standing punishment for sharia offences.

iNews Aceh (undated local report, Feb-2025 round-up context): Satpol PP and Wilayatul Hisbah Banda Aceh secured an alleged gay couple in a boarding house; a local advocate urged police to investigate and boarding-house owners to monitor tenants. The report concerns a gay couple, and no trans person is identified in it.

UNSW Human Rights Research Centre reports that transgender women face the highest rates of violence among LGBTIQ Indonesians, with survey data on relative social hostility. The report covers the January 2018 detention of twelve transwomen. Its scope is Indonesia-wide rather than Aceh-specific.

sources.title: LGBTQ rights in Aceh (Wikipedia)
sources.summary: Cross-dressing is not per se illegal in Indonesia, and transgender identity (also called waria) has long been part of Indonesian culture and society. Transgender people are allowed to change their legal gender on official documents after undergoing sex reassignment surgery and receiving a judge's approval, after which they can marry a person of the opposite legal gender, exemplified by Vivian Rubiyanti Iskandar as the first trans Indonesian legally recognized as female and by Aprilio Manganang in 2021 as the first service member to legally change gender from female to male although his case was intersex assigned female at birth. Since June 2021 the Ministry of Home Affairs has conducted outreach to issue transgender Indonesians with identification papers including Kartu Tanda Penduduk for residents of Banten, West Java, Central Java, East Java, North Sumatra, South Sumatra, South Sulawesi, Lampung and Papua, recognizing only male and female descriptors with no third gender/X option and printing gender at birth unless court recognition was already obtained, on the stated reasoning that many were undocumented where families did not approve. Indonesian law does not explicitly protect transgender people from discrimination or harassment, and transgender people who do not hide their gender identity often find it challenging to maintain legitimate employment and are thus often forced into prostitution and other illegal activities to survive. In Aceh transgender people have faced targeted enforcement: in January 2018 police in North Aceh arrested twelve transgender women, forcibly cut their hair, compelled them to wear men's clothing, and closed their beauty salons, and in a January 2018 parlour raid in Aceh police tortured LGBTQ citizens, shaved the heads of transgender women, stripped their shirts and bras, and paraded them in the street forcing them to shout "to become men". In Jakarta the Social Agency declared waria to be socially dysfunctional and regularly conducts raids against transgender women, taking detained individuals to city-owned rehabilitation centres where they are incarcerated with homeless people, beggars and street buskers and only released upon documentation of lack of homelessness and a signed promise not to repeat the offence, with officials stating this is to create a deterrent against being transgender and continued violations will result in jail time. The Indonesian Ulama Council ruled transgender persons must live in the gender they were born with, stating if not willing to cure themselves medically and religiously they must accept their fate to be ridiculed and harassed, while the judicial system takes the contrary position recognizing actual genders and authorities have in some cases arrested and prosecuted perpetrators of hate crimes against the transgender community. Aceh has special autonomous status implementing Islamic Sharia-based criminal law (Qanun Jinayat), with authority granted in 2005 to introduce Sharia law for Muslim residents and the 2014 Qanun Jinayat providing that consensual same-sex sexual acts between adults are punishable by up to 100 lashes or up to 100 months (8 years) imprisonment, set for enforcement by the end of 2015. Enforcement outcomes in Aceh include the 2017 sentencing of two young gay men aged 20 and 23 to public caning, several high-profile cases of men publicly caned after guilty findings for same-sex relations, and the 11 August 2025 sentencing of two men aged 20 and 21 to public caning for kissing after April arrest when police broke into a toilet. Nationally Indonesia has allowed private consensual same-sex activity since 1993 at age 18, has no explicit sodomy law unlike Malaysia, and the Penal Code does not prohibit non-commercial private consensual activity between consenting same-sex adults. In December 2022 Parliament passed a Penal Code criminalizing sex outside marriage upon complaint by immediate family, set to take force on 2 January 2026 with up to one year imprisonment for unmarried partners, with the spokesperson stating the draft will not criminalize private sexual orientation including LGBTQ persons and Coordinating Minister Mahfud MD stating it did not criminalize an LGBTQ person and only targets adults committing sexual violence or rape of underage same-sex children and immoral acts in public, while Article 421(1) punishes obscene acts against a same-sex person in public with maximum 1 year and six months imprisonment or maximum fine category III. Indonesian law does not recognise same-sex marriage, civil unions or domestic partnerships, households headed by same-sex couples lack the same legal protections as opposite-sex couples, and same-sex couples are ineligible to adopt as only married husband-wife couples can adopt. As of 2019 no specific law protects from discrimination or harassment based on sexual orientation or gender identity nor prohibits hate crimes based on sexual orientation and gender identity, though a 2015 police circular states processing of hate speech related to sexual orientations and gender identity and Head of National Police Regulation No. 8 of 2009 stipulates the duty to protect special rights of minority groups including sexual orientation. Police have conducted repeated raids and detentions for gay parties and saunas under pornography-related offences, including the November 2016 Jakarta raid after an Islamic Defenders Front tip-off, May 2017 arrest of 141 men for a gay sex party with ten charged and detention of 144 in the Atlantis Gym raid, October 2017 arrest of 51 in a Central Jakarta sauna with six charged including the owner, and 2025 raids detaining 56 on 1 February, nine on 24 May, and arresting 75 on 22 June near Jakarta. The article states: "While transgender people in Indonesia are generally more accepted than gays, lesbians and bisexuals, they have, in recent years, faced growing discrimination and rejection, mostly from sharia-supporting Muslim groups, which have become more and more popular in Indonesia." The article states "some public tolerance is given to some transgender people working in beauty salons or the entertainment industry, most notably the celebrity talk show host Dorce Gamalama." The article states transgender identity (also called waria) has long been part of Indonesian culture and society. The article states discrimination and harassments directed at transgender people is not uncommon, though violence is quite rare, and transgender people who do not hide their gender identity often face employment exclusion forcing reliance on prostitution and other illegal activities. The article reports officials justify rehabilitation detention as creating a deterrent against being transgender and cites the Ulama Council position that those unwilling to cure themselves medically and religiously must accept their fate to be ridiculed and harassed, evidencing institutional rejection despite noted cultural presence.

65028918B88589358118692.name: Lampung
65028918B88589358118692.summary:
Lampung stands under Indonesia's national legal framework, which the parent record carries in full. The province's own documented record of official conduct toward transgender people is a November 2018 operation in which the Satpol PP, the regional morals-and-order force, raided three trans women, detained them at the Satpol PP office and hosed them down at the firefighter building while an officer recorded the incident.

OutRight International's Creeping Criminalisation study names Lampung as one of eight Indonesian provinces whose discriminatory regional regulations it analyses, and it examines those rules at both province and district level. Restrictive rules in Lampung therefore operate below the national tier as well as at it, and enforcement of morals and order in the province rests with a regional force rather than solely with the national police.

For a trans visitor, the exposure documented in Lampung is sub-national: regulations analysed at province and district level, and a regional morals-and-order force with a documented raid and degrading treatment of trans women, sit alongside the national provisions that apply throughout Indonesia.

65028918B84835514626455.name: West Papua
65028918B84835514626455.summary:
West Papua operates no provincial criminal law reaching sexual conduct or gender expression; the national framework applies in the province without local additions. No regency-level regulation on dress, public morality or gender presentation is documented.

Security-force conduct is the province's defining risk. A human rights report published in July 2025 recorded 138 acts of torture or other ill-treatment against people in detention in Maybrat and the Central Highlands through early 2025, with near-total impunity. Most victims were men under 24; seven were women and seven were minors aged 15 to 17. The figure is a recorded count rather than a rate, and the report's finding of impunity and silence indicates the true number is higher.

Military deployments and operations in the highland regions increased from August 2025. Police in Sorong arrested more than a dozen participants in a protest that month. On 27 September 2025 a military task force opened fire on civilians in Agats, Asmat Regency, in a context of displacement and racial tension affecting indigenous Papuans.

None of these monitors records a trans-specific incident, and no raid, prosecution or assault directed at a trans person in West Papua is documented. The exposure is indirect: a visitor whose appearance or documents draw attention at a checkpoint, a protest or a detention facility meets the same security apparatus described above. Detention, rather than street-level violence, is the acute risk.

Trans residents of Papua are reached by the interior ministry's identity-card outreach, which prints the sex recorded at birth unless a court has granted recognition and offers no third descriptor. A card that does not match presentation can obstruct employment and access to services.

Police have repeatedly raided private "gay parties" and gay saunas under national pornography law in the 2010s-2020s, including November 2016 Jakarta raid, May 2017 arrest of 141 men with ten charged and detention of 144 at Atlantis Gym Jakarta, October 2017 arrest of 51 with six charged, February/May/June 2025 South Jakarta hotel/villa raids detaining 56, nine and 75, August 2025 arrest of three for creating LGBTQ Facebook page facing up to 12 years and 6 billion rupiah fines, and 22 May 2026 sentencing of 25 to prison for violating anti-pornography law. Indonesian law does not recognise same-sex marriage, civil unions, domestic partnerships or adoption by same-sex couples, limiting adoption to husband-wife married couples, and as of 2019 provides no specific anti-discrimination protection nor hate-crime prohibition based on sexual orientation and gender identity. Limited protection machinery cited is a 2015 police circular to process hate speech related to sexual orientations and gender identity, Regulation of Head of National Police No. 8 of 2009 duty to protect special rights of minority groups including sexual orientation, and theoretical constitutional and Human Rights Law No. 39/1999 guarantee against employment discrimination on any ground. The article states "While transgender people in Indonesia are generally more accepted than gays, lesbians and bisexuals, they have, in recent years, faced growing discrimination and rejection, mostly from sharia-supporting Muslim groups, which have become more and more popular in Indonesia." It further states "some public tolerance is given to some transgender people working in beauty salons or the entertainment industry, most notably the celebrity talk show host Dorce Gamalama," noting transgender identity (also called waria) has long been part of Indonesian culture and society. For trans visitors, the article reports discrimination and harassments directed at transgender people is not uncommon though violence is quite rare, but those not hiding gender identity often cannot maintain legitimate employment and are forced into prostitution and other illegal activities, while gays in jails are often sexually abused due to orientation and do not report due to trauma and fear of return. Documented violence includes the January 2018 Aceh parlour ransacking where police tortured all LGBTQ citizens, shaved transgender women's heads, stripped shirts and bras and paraded them forcing them to shout "to become men," criticised by human rights organisations. Care context notes the 2012 Health Ministry estimate of around 31 thousand transgender women and Yayasan Srikandi Sejati founded 1998 focusing on transgender health providing HIV/AIDS counselling and free condoms to transgender sex workers at a free health clinic, amid lack of school sex education and early movement focus leading public to believe AIDS was a "gay disease." Control environment includes the 2006 Law Against Pornography and Pornoaction prohibiting presentations suggesting same-sex relations punishable by fine or up to seven years, March 2016 broadcasting commission policy banning programs making LGBTQ behaviour appear "normal" discouraging effeminate, transgender or cross-dressing figures, bans on sites/apps with "gay" or LGBTQ terms including Grindr, and widely practiced openly advertised conversion therapy including rehabilitation centre treatment with de facto legalization by some city governments after the "RUU Ketahanan Keluarga" Family Resilience draft was rejected by 5 of 9 factions.

Security-force conduct is the state/province's defining risk. A human rights report published in July 2025 recorded 138 acts of torture or other ill-treatment against people in detention in a highland district and the central highlands through early 2025, with near-total impunity. Most victims were men under 24; seven were women and seven were minors aged 15 to 17. The figure is a recorded count rather than a rate, and the report's finding of impunity and silence indicates the true number is higher.

Military deployments and operations in the highland regions increased from August 2025. Police in a coastal city arrested more than a dozen participants in a protest that month. On 27 September 2025 a military task force opened fire on civilians in a district in the south, in a context of displacement and racial tension affecting indigenous residents.

None of these monitors records a trans-specific incident, and no raid, prosecution or assault directed at a trans person in the state/province is documented. The exposure is indirect: a visitor whose appearance or documents draw attention at a checkpoint, a protest or a detention facility meets the same security apparatus described above. Detention, rather than street-level violence, is the acute risk.

Trans residents of the state/province are reached by the national interior ministry's identity-card outreach, which prints the sex recorded at birth unless a court has granted recognition and offers no third descriptor. A card that does not match presentation can obstruct employment and access to services.

Central Kalimantan stands under Indonesia's national framework, and the sources reviewed identify no provincial-level legal divergence. OutRight Action International's 2022 mapping of Indonesian laws and regional regulations that violate the rights of women and LGBTIQ people lists eight provinces with discriminatory regional regulations; Central Kalimantan is not among them. No provincial enforcement action, police operation, prosecution or incident directed at trans or LGBTIQ people in Central Kalimantan appears in the sources reviewed. Absence from a list of discriminatory regulations is a legal finding only. It does not establish how provincial police, local officials or communities treat trans visitors in practice, and nothing in the sources reviewed addresses that question.

sources.title: 2023 Indonesian Penal Code – Wikipedia
sources.summary: Indonesia's 2023 Penal Code (RUU KUHP) was passed on 6 December 2022 and took effect on 2 January 2026, three years after enactment. It criminalises sexual activity outside marriage, with unmarried partners facing up to one year in prison if an immediate family member lodges a complaint. The code does not explicitly criminalise same-sex relationships, and because Indonesia does not recognise same-sex marriage, all sexual activity by same-sex couples falls under that outside-marriage restriction. This is the national criminal baseline applying to a visitor in Central Kalimantan, whose risk follows the country's national framework rather than any local divergence.

65028918B37605681672150.name: North Sumatra
65028918B37605681672150.summary:
North Sumatra is a province of Indonesia and stands under the national legal framework, which applies here as it does nationwide.

North Sumatra is one of eight provinces covered by OutRight Action International's mapping of national laws and discriminatory regional regulations. That mapping documents regional rules imposing dress codes, curfews and restrictions on where transgender people may appear, with significant variation between regions; the report states its findings hold for areas beyond the provinces it examined directly.

Medan, the provincial capital, is the site of the only documented legal-process case for a transgender person in North Sumatra. Dimas Cahya became the first transgender man in the city to change his name legally to match his identity, and the Medan District Court granted the application after a six-week process. The judge warned that the change would 'erase my identity' but declined to engage with LGBTI issues, and no enforcement action against the couple is recorded.

UNAIDS reporting describes Medan as conservative, with LGBTI people regarded locally as 'immoral'.

sources.summary: OutRight Action International's 'Creeping Criminalisation: Mapping of Indonesia's National Laws and Regional Regulations That Violate Human Rights of Women and LGBTIQ People' (Katjasungkana & Wieringa; 2022 file copy) maps national laws and discriminatory regional regulations across eight focus provinces: Aceh, DKI Jakarta, East Kalimantan, Lampung, North Sumatra, South Sulawesi, South Sulawesi, South Sumatra and Yogyakarta. It finds much overlap but significant regional variation in dress codes, curfews and restrictions on where transgender people may appear, and states that its findings are valid for regions beyond the focus set.

sources.title: The first but not the last: Indonesian transgender man fights for recognition | UNAIDS
sources.summary: Dimas Cahya, a transgender man from Medan, North Sumatra's capital, told UNAIDS how he became the first transgender man in Medan to legally change his name to match his identity. After a six-week process the Medan District Court granted the application; the judge warned that the change would 'erase my identity' but stayed out of LGBTI issues completely. The article frames Medan as conservative, with LGBTI people deemed 'immoral', and reports that a Medan legal-aid organisation asked the couple invasive questions before the case. This is the only documented legal-process case for North Sumatra: a local court handled a trans person's application neutrally, and the article records no enforcement action against the couple.

65028918B26897900130576.name: North Sulawesi
65028918B26897900130576.summary:
North Sulawesi stands under Indonesia's national framework, and the national laws described in the Indonesia record apply to visitors here. No North Sulawesi-specific regulation appears in the sources reviewed.

The mapping of Indonesia's discriminatory regional regulations published by OutRight Action International examined eight provinces and did not include North Sulawesi, so no provincial dress code, curfew or restriction on where transgender people may appear is documented for this province.

Local enforcement has a documented record of harassment during raids. SALUT (Sanubari Sulawesi Utara), the Manado LGBT organisation, reported that police raids in the city have included harassment of LGBT people, including a butch lesbian who was groped during a raid. The account records no arrests or prosecutions.

Official posture has not been uniformly hostile. On 10 November 2012 a waria beach-queen pageant was held at Malalayang beach in Manado, organised by the sitting national legislator Paula Sinjal together with the National Narcotics Agency of North Sulawesi as an outreach event on drugs and HIV/AIDS; Sinjal said waria are part of the local population and deserve attention. No adverse official action was recorded.

Public LGBT organising is visible in Manado. On 11 June 2016 LGBT groups joined the city's women's movement in a street action against sexual violence at Bundaran Zero Point, running from 08.00 to 10.00 WITA, with SALUT taking part.

Visibility carries a social cost. Alexa, elected Ratu Waria Sulawesi Utara for 2016 to 2018 at the Sahid Kawanua Hotel in Manado, said that after taking the title she faced discrimination from sensationalist media and from the public, with her personal crisis peaking around 25 March 2019. No legal or police action appears in her account.

Reporting by victims is limited. SALUT told Suara Kita that victims often do not report because they fear their families will not accept their orientation.

65028918B6070530336190.name: Special Region of Yogyakarta
65028918B6070530336190.summary:
The Special Region of Yogyakarta carries its own layer of discriminatory regional regulation. A 2022 mapping of Indonesia's national laws and regional regulations that violate the rights of women and LGBTIQ people examined eight focus provinces, Yogyakarta among them, and found substantial overlap alongside significant regional variation. The regulations it documents include dress codes, curfews and restrictions on where transgender people may appear. The mapping states that its findings are valid for regions beyond the eight it examined, so the categories it identifies are not confined to the provinces it names.

The most fully documented enforcement action against a trans institution in Yogyakarta is the February 2016 closure of Pondok Pesantren Waria Al-Fatah, a religious school where trans women study Islam. The hardline Front Jihad Islam threatened to seal the school, and on the night of 24 February 2016 a two-hour meeting at the Jagalan ward office in Yogyakarta ended with an agreement to shut it. Those present included ward and residents' officials, the lurah and the local military district commander; an earlier session on 19 February was attended by the Banguntapan camat and the local police sector chief. The district head justified the closure on the grounds that the pesantren lacked a permit, conflicted with Islamic values and had once had alcohol found on site. Its founder, Shinta Ratri, said about 20 waria attended the weekly weekend classes, which taught ordinary Islamic instruction.

A waria witness at the meeting said a Front Jihad Islam leader delivered anti-LGBT remarks to shouts of "Allahu Akbar" and vowed the group would keep hunting LGBTI people wherever they gather. The Governor of the Special Region of Yogyakarta, Sultan Hamengku Buwono X, publicly urged restraint on both sides, called LGBT people "sama-sama anak bangsa" (fellow children of the nation) and said the regional government would study the issue. The shutdown concluded on administrative and community grounds; no provincial anti-trans statute was cited.

The pesantren and the Yogyakarta waria community were operating again years after the closure, and economic and social marginalisation of trans people in the province persists.

76434192B26311534340602.name: KwaZulu-Natal
76434192B26311534340602.summary:
KwaZulu-Natal is a province of South Africa and stands under the national framework: the constitutional equality guarantee, the Equality Court under the Promotion of Equality and Prevention of Unfair Discrimination Act, legal gender recognition, the 2024 hate-crime statute and the national correctional rules for transgender inmates apply here as they do elsewhere in the country. No provincial law, by-law or provincial institution departing from that layer is documented in the sources.

The provincial evidence on violence and victimisation is a 2024 masters thesis in criminology at the University of KwaZulu-Natal in Durban. It interviewed 15 self-identifying queer participants recruited through the Imvelo Yesizwe Organisation in KwaMashu township and reports substantial queerphobic violence and victimisation in that township setting. The study also examines whether the support and interventions available to those residents were adequate, and what safety strategies they used.

The study is small and its participants were purposively recruited, so it records the experiences of that group rather than a measured rate of violence. It does not disaggregate transgender participants from other sexual minorities, and no source gives a KwaZulu-Natal figure for violence against transgender people. A trans visitor to the province has no validated local victimisation figure to work from.

Region-specific evidence of top traditional authority hostility toward gay people in the province.

sources.title: Transgender prisoners challenge prison authorities (GroundUp)
sources.summary: GroundUp news feature (6 Aug 2025, Elna Schutz) documenting where transgender prisoners are held in South Africa: Jade September, a transgender woman, was imprisoned in the male section of Pollsmoor and won her 2019 Equality Court case against the Minister of Correctional Services, which ruled that not allowing her to express her gender identity was unfair discrimination. Reports that the resulting Department of Correctional Services standard operating procedure (SOP) for LGBT+ prisoners requires a safety-risk assessment within the first six hours of admission and stipulates that transgender men and transgender women are to be detained or transported only with other transgender men or transgender women respectively, alongside respectful-search and communication rules. Also notes Lawyers for Human Rights representation of 'NM', a transgender woman serving a long-term sentence at Johannesburg Correctional Centre, in litigation against DCS over gender-affirming healthcare, and rights organisations' concern about implementation of the SOP.

sources.title: Nthabiseng Mokoena v Head of Johannesburg Correctional Centre - Lawyers for Human Rights
sources.summary: Lawyers for Human Rights case page (14 Nov 2025): the South African High Court, sitting as an Equality Court, ruled in favour of transgender inmate Nthabiseng Mokoena against the Department of Correctional Services (DCS), finding unfair discrimination and harassment because DCS refused to allow her to express her gender identity (feminizing attire, she/her pronouns) and failed to provide appropriate accommodation. The court held that the constitutional right to adequate medical treatment includes gender-affirming hormonal therapy at State expense, rejected DCS's contrary argument, and ordered DCS to immediately implement accommodations, enforce its own SOPs relating to transgender inmates, and provide the prescribed medical care. Subject-verified: documents that trans inmates are accommodated inside the standard national corrections system (here Johannesburg Correctional Centre) and that placement/accommodation obligations rest on DCS SOPs enforced through litigation.

sources.title: Media Statement: National Preventive Mechanism welcomes the High Court ruling affirming the rights of transgender persons in correctional facilities (SAHRC)
sources.summary: South African Human Rights Commission, acting as the National Preventive Mechanism under OPCAT (designated 4 Dec 2024), media statement (14 Nov 2025) welcoming the Gauteng Division of the High Court, Johannesburg, judgment (delivered 10 Nov 2025) in Nthabiseng Beverly Mokoena v Head of Johannesburg Correctional Centre and Others (Case No. 2024/070075). Describes Mokoena, assigned male at birth and identifying as female from early childhood, being restricted from wearing feminine clothing and makeup and misgendered while in a correctional facility. Subject-verified: an official state human-rights body confirming that transgender persons are held in the ordinary correctional system and that the 2025 ruling affirms their rights in correctional facilities, including accommodation.

76434192B92524600968894.name: Mpumalanga
76434192B92524600968894.summary:
Mpumalanga is a province of South Africa and stands under the national framework; the constitutional guarantees, the criminal-law position on consensual conduct, the gender-recognition statute, the hate-crime provisions and the national correctional rulings are carried by the national record. The findings below are those specific to the province.

Traditional-authority structures have been openly opposed to legal recognition of same-sex relationships. A published letter of June 2010, issued by the National House of Traditional Leaders together with its provincial houses after a meeting held at Hazyview in Mpumalanga, stated that traditional leaders were disappointed that the Constitutional Court's marriage judgment had given what the letter called an immoral practice a lifeline, declared that they did not support legalisation of same-sex marriage, warned of ostracism and violence, and committed to a five-year campaign against it. The same structure asked Parliament in 2016 to review the constitutional clause protecting people against discrimination on the basis of sexual orientation.

Violence against people read as sexuality- or gender-nonconforming has produced both a killing and a mass response inside the province. Portia Mtsweni, a 25-year-old lesbian, was found dead near Zamani Primary School in Tweefontein, in Thembisile Hani Local Municipality, in the early hours of Sunday 29 December 2019; she was half naked and had stab wounds. On 2 January 2020 about 800 people marched in the same municipality in protest, in a demonstration organised by Lasiphumakhona LGBTI, the ANC Women's League and others. Thembisile Hani mayor Nomsa Mtsweni called on parents, leaders and churches to stand united against gender-based violence.

Public LGBTIQ+ presence has also drawn official cooperation. Mpumalanga's first Pride march and celebration was held on Saturday 9 August 2014 in the provincial capital, then Nelspruit and now Mbombela, under the theme 'Moving Forward, Proud, Strong & United'. Around 1,000 participants marched from the SABC offices to Nelspruit Plaza, followed by a picnic at Oorwesig Garden Park. The organiser, Joy Kunene, said police were visible and supportive and supplied about 20 police and traffic officers; the event launched the LGBTI Mpumalanga Movement, an umbrella body for the province's LGBTI organisations.

Police conduct is the most consistently reported grievance. At a Pride Flag Tour event held at the eMbalenhle Sasol Club on 18 August 2026, LGBTIQ+ community members led by the Rainbow Seed Institute raised concerns about discrimination and stigmatisation at government institutions, particularly police stations. Participants said they were ridiculed, questioned or treated unfairly when seeking assistance, and one member alleged that after she was sexually assaulted in eMbalenhle months earlier, an officer at eMbalenhle Police Station asked why she had not fought back. Attendees said they fear reporting crimes because of stigmatisation.

The documented pattern is community-level violence and police mistreatment inside a protective national legal framework. Enforcement appears to turn on the individual station, municipality or venue rather than on any province-wide practice, and the sources identify no Mpumalanga-specific court ruling, provincial policy or facilities rule.

Limpopo is a province of the Republic of South Africa and stands under the national legal framework; the province-specific material in the source inventory concerns the reach of customary law and traditional authority in rural districts that formed part of the former Bantustans.

76434192B85643022077130.name: North West
76434192B85643022077130.summary:
North West is a province of South Africa and its law sits inside the national framework; the South Africa record carries the constitutional protections, legal gender recognition, marriage law and hate-crime statute. The findings below are those specific to the province.

The clearest practical obstacle for a trans visitor who depends on prescribed hormone treatment is the provincial health system. No public health facility in North West provides hormone replacement therapy for transgender people, and the North West Department of Health confirmed that position to the South African Human Rights Commission in response to a complaint lodged by Action for Social Justice International. Residents travel sometimes hundreds of kilometres, most often to Soweto in Gauteng, to obtain treatment. A visitor whose supply runs out in the province cannot expect a public clinic or hospital to fill or continue the prescription.

Institutional enforcement of gendered appearance is documented in the province. In March 2016 an 18-year-old, Zinzi Manini Molema, was barred from attending school at Maphoitsile village after refusing to wear a skirt; the principal sent her home on the stated ground that she must wear a skirt because she was a girl, and she missed three weeks of classes. The case concerns a pupil rather than a visitor, but it records a North West school applying a dress rule against a gender-nonconforming person rather than accommodating her.

The province's quantitative evidence on anti-LGBT discrimination rests on a single survey. Conducted during 2009 and 2010 under the auspices of the UNISA Centre for Applied Psychology with OUT LGBT Well-being, OUT North-West and Gay Umbrella, it surveyed 319 LGBT people, most of them from rural backgrounds in one of the country's poorest and least populated provinces, and asked about openness about same-sex sexuality, how LGBT people perceive their environment, and experiences of sexual abuse and discrimination. Campaign research published in 2016 lists that North West study alongside only two others as the quantitative South African studies of anti-LGBT hate crime conducted up to that point.

sources.summary: HRW (29 May 2012) reported that the Traditional Courts Bill then before parliament threatened LGBT South Africans by creating a parallel customary-law justice system covering people in the former Bantustans. HRW reported that rural LGBT people already face discrimination, violence and poor police cooperation, that chiefs' courts punish lesbians in rural areas, and that the bill offered no opt-out from customary jurisdiction.

Love Not Hate campaign research (GALA-hosted, conducted by OUT LGBT Well-being, 2016) records that only three quantitative studies of hate crimes against LGBT people have been done in South Africa: the 2003 empowerment study across Gauteng, KwaZulu-Natal and Western Cape, a 2010 North West province study, and this national campaign study, which measures levels of discrimination against LGBT people nationally.

Documents the province-level absence of trans-specific healthcare that a trans visitor reliant on prescribed HRT would confront on the ground.

76434192B98113213215773.name: Eastern Cape
76434192B98113213215773.summary:
Eastern Cape stands under the national framework of South Africa. The province's trans-relevant law is the national layer: the constitutional prohibition on unfair discrimination, the Promotion of Equality and Prevention of Unfair Discrimination Act and its Equality Court, the Hate Crimes and Hate Speech Act of 2024, and legal gender recognition under the Alteration of Sex Description and Sex Status Act of 2003.

Transgender prisoners held in Eastern Cape correctional centres, among them St Albans, Mthatha and East London, are governed by the national placement standard rather than any provincial rule. Under the regulations to the Correctional Services Act on the accommodation of vulnerable inmates, and the Department of Correctional Services' standard operating procedures, inmates are to be housed in cells appropriate to their gender identity where that is feasible and safe, and transgender inmates are to be held in single cells. No Eastern Cape-specific transgender placement case is on record, so the province's custody practice is read entirely from the national instruments.

Rural districts under customary jurisdiction carry a risk that does not apply in the metropolitan centres. A bill before the national parliament in 2012 would have created a parallel customary-law justice system covering people in the former Bantustan areas, with no opt-out from customary jurisdiction. Human Rights Watch reported at the time that rural LGBT people already faced discrimination, violence and poor cooperation from police, and that chiefs' courts punished lesbians in rural areas.

Gender-affirming care in the province runs through the public hospital system and is documented as slow. In December 2024 LGBT activists in East London delivered a memorandum to Frere Hospital over year-long delays in transgender healthcare. A trans visitor who depends on the public system in the Eastern Cape should plan for waiting times rather than immediate access.

Supports the province's framing of traditional-court rural jurisdiction as the defining risk factor for LGBT travellers off the main cities.

76434192B69392740373411.name: Gauteng
76434192B69392740373411.summary:
Gauteng's documented record of violence against transgender people rests on a single recent case. Aobakwe Mahlobo, a 23-year-old transgender woman from Soshanguve who was living in Winterveld (both in Tshwane), was attacked at about 1:30 am on 26 December 2024 in a tavern in Tshwane. A man had been saying that gay and lesbian people 'don't deserve to live'; he smashed a bottle into her face as she lit a cigarette and told her 'I told you I'm gonna kill you'. The cuts to her mouth, lips, nose, cheek and forehead were stitched after treatment at Kgabo Clinic. She opened an assault case at Dube Police Station, which had shown no progress when MambaOnline reported on 6 January 2025. The incident is the province's most recent documented trans-specific hate crime on record.

On 10 November 2025 the Gauteng Division of the High Court, Johannesburg, sitting as an Equality Court under the Promotion of Equality and Prevention of Unfair Discrimination Act, delivered judgment in Nthabiseng Beverly Mokoena v Head of Johannesburg Correctional Centre and Others (Case No. 2024/070075). The court found that the Department of Correctional Services had engaged in unfair discrimination and harassment of a transgender woman inmate by refusing to allow her to express her gender identity and by denying her prescribed gender-affirming hormone therapy. It held that the right to adequate medical treatment includes gender-affirming hormonal therapy at state expense, and ordered the Department to implement the required accommodations and to enforce its own standard operating procedures for transgender inmates. The South African Human Rights Commission's National Preventive Mechanism welcomed the ruling on 14 November 2025. The orders are enforceable against the Department in the province, giving trans people in Gauteng an operational equality-court remedy for discrimination of this kind.

The same judgment records the only documented determination of how transgender prisoners are housed in Gauteng. Mokoena, a transgender woman serving a life sentence at Johannesburg Correctional Centre, was initially held in the Medium A section, where she could express her gender identity through long hair, makeup and women's clothing. sources.title: Transgender Woman in Brutal Hate Crime Attack in Tshwane Tavern
sources.summary: Aobakwe Mahlobo, a 23-year-old transgender woman originally from Soshanguve and living in Winterveld (both in Tshwane, Gauteng), was assaulted at a local tavern at about 1:30 am on 26 December 2024 after a man began saying gay and lesbian people 'don't deserve to live'; he smashed a bottle into her face as she lit a cigarette, saying 'I told you I'm gonna kill you', leaving deep cuts to her mouth, lips, nose, cheek and forehead that were stitched after treatment at Kgabo Clinic. 76434192B56312278962278.name: Western Cape
76434192B56312278962278.summary:
The Western Cape has no provincial law or municipal by-law that bars transgender people from gender-segregated facilities; access is decided venue by venue, by the operator's own rules and by the staff enforcing them. On 19 February 2025 Taswald Ruiters, a transgender woman from Eerste River, was threatened with removal from the Green Point Athletic Stadium in Cape Town after using the women's bathroom. A security guard told her "Look at you, you're a man", directed her to the men's bathroom and said he had the final say. Police were called four times and had not arrived after nearly three hours. The stadium is a public facility operated by the City of Cape Town; on the day it was rented by Western Province Athletics, which was responsible for the security services on site.

The incident records a gap between the absence of any provincial restriction on facility access and the response a visibly trans person actually received in the province's best-resourced metro. The Western Cape stands under the national framework of South Africa; the constitutional guarantees, the criminal-law position, the hate-crime statute, legal gender recognition and gender-affirming care are national provisions carried by the national record, and the provincial layer neither adds to nor subtracts from them.
