19338628B22645672383103.name: Île-de-France
19338628B22645672383103.summary:
Île-de-France stands under the French national framework: identity documents, anti-discrimination law, criminal law and marriage are set nationally and apply uniformly across the region, and no separate regional regime governs transgender visitors. What is specific to the region is where recorded anti-LGBT+ offending falls and how the Paris agglomeration's LGBT venues and events are policed.

The Interior Ministry's statistics service records that anti-LGBT+ offences concentrate in urban units of more than 200,000 inhabitants, notably Paris. The Paris rate of 22 recorded offences per 100,000 inhabitants is roughly three times the national figure of 7.

Paris Pride, held on 28 June 2025, was classified a sensitive event by the Interior Ministry. National police reinforcements were deployed after a far-right homo-patriotes group announced it would join the march, with officers positioned to separate opposing groups.

Paris holds the country's densest LGBT commercial and social infrastructure and its only officially organised gaybourhoods, and hosts the annual Marche des Fiertés. A 2004 count recorded 140 LGBT bars, clubs, hotels, restaurants and shops in the city.

As of 2004 the city had 140 LGBT bars, clubs, hotels, restaurants and shops, and it hosts France's only officially organised gaybourhoods, along with the annual Paris Pride parade (La Marche des Fiertés). The article also records that Bertrand Delanoë became France's first openly gay mayor of Paris in 2002 and was stabbed that same year during the Nuit Blanche festival by an assailant who told police he hated politicians, the Socialist Party and homosexuals. 19338628B95725112529620.name: Provence-Alpes-Côte d'Azur
19338628B95725112529620.summary:
Provence-Alpes-Côte d'Azur's only documented item bearing on how a visibly non-conforming visitor may be policed in public space is a municipal swimwear order in Fréjus (Var). On 1 August 2023 the town's mayor, of the Rassemblement National, banned "covering and baggy clothing" while swimming from its sea beaches, in force until 17 September 2023, with a €135 fine.

The administrative court of Toulon suspended the order's execution on 5 August 2023 and ordered the commune to pay €3,000. In freedom-of-relief order n° 2302537, brought by the Ligue des droits de l'homme, the court held the arrêté to be a grave and manifestly unlawful attack on fundamental freedoms: the manifestation of religious conviction, freedom of movement, and freedom of dress in public space.

The mayor's communiqué justified the ban by laïcité while public statements cited safety, and observers read the measure as aimed at religiously marked swimwear. The suspension is interim relief; it prevents enforcement of the order.

No other region-specific measure, enforcement practice or incident affecting transgender visitors appears in the inventory, and the national assessment applies to the region.

The article quotes observers noting the mayor justified the ban on laïcité in the communiqué while citing safety publicly — framing religiously-marked swimwear as the target. 28173009B98838729156012.name: Chechnya
28173009B98838729156012.summary:
Chechnya is a republic of Russia and stands under the Russian national framework; the national assessment applies here, but the practical exposure a visitor faces is materially harsher than the national baseline.

Human Rights Watch documented a February 2017 police purge in which men believed to be gay were rounded up and held in unofficial detention facilities for days, humiliated, starved and tortured. Some were forcibly disappeared; others were returned to their families barely alive from beatings, with captors outing them and urging honour killings. The same reporting establishes that top regional officials knew of the operation despite Ramzan Kadyrov's denial. In late March and early April 2017, Human Rights Watch recorded security forces under Kadyrov rounding up dozens of men suspected of being gay and subjecting them to detention, torture, humiliation, enforced disappearance and severe beatings, with at least three deaths.

Novaya Gazeta reported that more than 100 men were detained across Grozny and other settlements in late March 2017, among them muftiate religious figures and television presenters who had concealed their orientation; at least three detainees were killed and further killings were alleged. Detainees were held in a secret prison in Argun and in multiple detention centres, where they were beaten and tortured with electric shocks; at least three and reportedly up to 20 were beaten to death. Men who were released fled the republic, and users abandoned LGBT messenger groups and closed social-media accounts.

The purge reactivated within two years. A renewed campaign beginning in December 2018 detained around 40 people, including gay men and women, with two killed; by May 2019 police had resumed unlawful detentions, beatings and humiliation of men presumed to be gay or bisexual. In January 2019 Novaya Gazeta learned that warnings were circulating through VKontakte LGBT-group administrators telling those still at large to leave the republic; Kadyrov's press secretary Alvi Karimov denied the reports. The paper's April 2017 investigation into the torture and killings produced no criminal case.

Detention has been converted into a conscription channel. The Insider reported in September 2024, citing the monitoring project SK SOS, that Chechen security forces were coercing detained gay men into military service, with at least seven sent to the frontlines in Ukraine and one already killed; the practice began before the 21 September 2022 mobilisation order. In early September 2022 six men were detained on suspicion of homosexuality, threatened with fabricated charges and warned they would be sent to the front. A Memorial Human Rights Centre investigation recorded a mass wave of unlawful detentions in which people were seized over minor pretexts such as missing insurance documents, taken to police departments, subjected to psychological pressure and physical abuse and forced to sign contracts; families sometimes had to recruit two "volunteers" to secure a detained relative's release.

A UK Home Office country policy note of June 2025 records systematic anti-LGBT campaigns across Chechnya and the wider North Caucasus between 2017 and 2024, including abductions, torture and extrajudicial killings, and assesses that in the North Caucasus trans people and publicly active LGBT+ advocates are likely to face treatment amounting to persecution.

Russian law formally applies in Chechnya, but in practice there are no protections for LGBT residents and visitors, and authorities are alleged to encourage families to kill those suspected of homosexuality. Human Rights Watch found no safe route of complaint or judicial recourse, because retaliation against a complainant was practically inevitable.

A renewed purge beginning December 2018 detained around 40 persons including gay men and women with two killed, and by May 2019 police renewed unlawful detentions, beatings and humiliation of men presumed gay or bisexual. In March 2021 the EU imposed sanctions on two Chechen government officials for government-sponsored violence against LGBTQIA+ individuals.

28173009B24428243574749.name: Dagestan
28173009B24428243574749.summary:
Dagestan is a republic within the Russian Federation. National legislation and national enforcement practice apply throughout the republic; that layer is carried in Russia's own record rather than restated here.

The UK Home Office country policy note on sexual orientation and gender identity and expression, version 2.0 of June 2025, names the North Caucasus, Dagestan among it, as an area where LGBT+ people are likely to face treatment amounting to persecution. The note documents systematic campaigns by Chechen and North Caucasus authorities between 2017 and 2024 involving abduction, torture and extrajudicial killing, and it assesses trans people and visible advocates as specifically exposed.

Global Affairs Canada advises against all travel to Russia and warns of violence targeting 2SLGBTQI+ persons, naming the North Caucasus republics of Chechnya and Dagestan in particular.

North Caucasus SOS, an organisation that works from exile, states that there is no safe life for LGBTIQ+ people in the North Caucasus and that even private existence can trigger violence, detention or forced return to families; it describes the situation worsening year on year.

A trans visitor who is read as trans or LGBT meets the same enforcement environment as residents: detention, assault or extrajudicial violence, and coercion through family or community, with public expression or visible advocacy raising the likelihood of action by the authorities. The sources identify no republic-level protection mechanism in Dagestan that would supplement the national framework.

It documents systematic campaigns by Chechen and North-Caucasus authorities from 2017 to 2024, involving abductions, torture and extrajudicial killings, and assesses trans people and visible advocates specifically.

Global Affairs Canada advises against all travel to Russia. It flags frequent terrorist attacks in the republics of Chechnya, Dagestan, Ingushetia and Stavropol Krai. Entry to certain areas and regions requires special permission from the Ministry of the Interior. The advisory also warns of violence targeting 2SLGBTQI+ persons, particularly in the North Caucasus republics of Chechnya and Dagestan.

David Isteev of North Caucasus SOS, who works in exile, told the Human Rights House Foundation: 'There is no safe life for LGBTIQ+ people in the North Caucasus, and even private existence can trigger violence, detention, or forced return to families.' He said the situation worsens year on year.

sources.title: LGBTQ rights in Dagestan (Wikipedia)
sources.summary: In July 2023 Russia enacted a law banning gender transition that prohibited both gender-affirming surgery and legal gender recognition outright, and transgender people are not allowed to change their legal gender and gender-affirming care is banned. In April-May 2023 proposals sought to rule out the possibility of changing a person's gender purely by changing the documents and to ban gender reassignment without surgery, with the Duma Speaker claiming 2,700 such document changes had been made in recent times amid claims men sought changes to avoid conscription for the special operation. The 2022 expansion of the propaganda law applies to anyone regardless of age group and prohibits distribution of materials that make minors interested in gender transitions. A 2024 law bans adoption of Russian children by citizens or permanent residents of countries that allow gender transitions, and a single person living in a foreign country may adopt only if that country neither recognises same-sex marriage nor gender transition. The 1 July 2003 military medical expertise statute provides that people who have problems with their identity and sexual preferences can only be drafted during war times, while officials stated different sexual orientation should not be considered a deviation and non-standard orientation does not forbid service but should not be revealed to avoid beating. On 30 September 2022 President Putin stated teaching children that instead of men and women there are supposedly some other genders and offering sex-change surgeries is unacceptable. Consensual sexual activity between adults of the same sex is legal after 1993 removal of Article 121, with age of consent at 16 since 2003 regardless of sexual orientation, but neither same-sex marriages nor civil unions are allowed and July 2020 constitutional amendment bans same-sex marriage with no legal recognition offered. Russia provides no anti-discrimination protections for LGBTQ people and has no hate-crime designation based on sexual orientation and gender identity, and does not officially record hate crimes against the LGBTQ community, with an estimated 1,056 hate crimes against 853 individuals between 2010 and 2020 including 365 fatalities and annual crimes tripling from 46 in 2010 to 138 in 2015. The 2013 federal law criminalised distribution of propaganda promoting non-traditional sexual relationships among minors and was expanded in 2022 to apply to anyone regardless of age group. In November 2023 the Supreme Court designated the international LGBT public movement as an extremist organisation, formally added on 22 March 2024 to the unified list of terrorist and extremist organizations, where leading, participating in, financially supporting, or repeatedly displaying its symbols is a criminal offense punishable by prison time, leading to arrests of gay bar and club owners with at least one dying in custody as of April 2025 and fines or jail for displaying the rainbow flag including earrings. Between March and May 2026 city courts outlawed nine LGBTQ organisations as extremist with founders convicted for leading an extremist organisation, including Centre T, Coming Out, LGBT Resource Centre, Irida, Kallisto movement, Moscow Community Center for LGBT+ Initiatives, Parni Plus, Russian LGBT Network, and T9 NSK. In Chechnya since February 2017 authorities conducted forced disappearances including secret abductions, imprisonment and torture targeting persons based on perceived sexual orientation with over 100 men detained and tortured and at least three dead in extrajudicial killing, followed by a December 2018 purge with around 40 detained and two killed, confirmed by a December 2018 OSCE report as ignored by authorities and leading to EU economic sanctions in March 2021 on two officials. In 2010 the European Court of Human Rights fined Russia for discriminating by systemically refusing permits for pride parades, and in August 2012 the Moscow City Court upheld blocking Moscow Pride permits yearly through 2012 citing possibility of public disorder.

sources.title: LGBTQ rights in Ingushetia (Wikipedia)
sources.summary: In July 2023 Russia enacted a law banning gender transition which prohibited both gender-affirming surgery and legal gender recognition outright, following April-May 2023 proposals to rule out changing gender purely by changing documents and to ban reassignment without surgery. Transgender people are not allowed to change their legal gender and gender-affirming care is banned. The 2022 expansion of the propaganda law applies to anyone regardless of age group and prohibits distribution of materials that make minors interested in gender transitions. A 2024 law bans adoption of Russian children by citizens or permanent residents of countries that allow gender transitions, and a single person living abroad may adopt only if that country neither recognises same-sex marriage nor gender transition. Russia provides no anti-discrimination protections for LGBTQ people and has no hate-crime designation based on gender identity. In November 2023 the Supreme Court designated the international LGBT public movement as an extremist organisation, formally added on 22 March 2024 to the unified list of terrorist and extremist organizations and persons, making leading, participating in, financially supporting, or repeatedly displaying its symbols a criminal offense punishable by prison time. Enforcement has included arrests of gay club owners with at least one dying in custody as of April 2025, fines or jail for displaying the rainbow flag including earrings, addition of activist Karèn Shainyan to the terrorist and extremist list with a 5-year prison sentence in absentia, and March-May 2026 court outlawing of nine LGBTQ organisations including Centre T with convictions of founders for leading an extremist organisation. Consensual sexual activity between adults of the same sex is legal after 1993 re-legalisation removing Article 121, which had punished consensual sex between men with three to five years imprisonment and a maximum five years under the 1961 revision, and the age of consent stands at 16 since 2003 regardless of sexual orientation. Neither same-sex marriages nor civil unions are allowed, marriage is defined as between a man and a woman with a July 2020 constitutional amendment banning same-sex marriage, and in the 2021 Fedotova and Others v. Russia case the European Court of Human Rights ruled failure to offer any legal recognition violated rights, though Russia left the court in 2022. The 2013 federal law criminalised distribution of propaganda promoting non-traditional sexual relationships among minors and was expanded in 2022 to apply to anyone regardless of age. Russia provides no anti-discrimination protections for LGBTQ people, does not officially record hate crimes against the community, and has no hate-crime designation based on sexual orientation. Adoption is allowed for single persons regardless of sexual orientation but for couples jointly only if a married heterosexual couple, and foreign single adopters are barred if their country recognises same-sex marriage. Authorities refuse to register LGBTQ organisations and to authorize pride parades, with a 2010 European Court of Human Rights fine for discrimination over pride bans and an August 2012 Moscow City Court ruling upholding a yearly ban through 2012 citing public disorder, while pro-LGBTQ groups have been declared extremist and prohibited. Documented violence includes an estimated 1,056 hate crimes against 853 individuals between 2010-2020 with 365 fatalities, tripling from 46 in 2010 to 138 in 2015 with premeditated group hunts via dating apps, and Chechnya purges involving forced disappearances, secret abductions, imprisonment and torture with over 100 men detained and tortured and at least three extrajudicial killings from February 2017 and around 40 detained and two killed in the December 2018-January 2019 purge, confirmed by a December 2018 OSCE report and followed by March 2021 EU sanctions on two Chechen officials.

28173009B76603557910928.name: Orenburg Oblast
28173009B76603557910928.summary:
Orenburg Oblast stands inside the national framework of the Russian Federation, and the federal statutes and enforcement machinery described in the national record apply to visitors here. What is specific to the region is criminal enforcement of the extremism designation against an LGBTQ venue and its staff, in the only such prosecution brought so far.

Orenburg's Central District Court registered the materials in Russia's first criminal case under the Supreme Court's designation of the "international LGBT movement" as extremist. The file had been opened in March 2024 and was sent to the court on 9 July 2025; it concerned staff of the Pose club in the city of Orenburg.

The proceedings concluded in the region in June 2026 with the first known "LGBT extremism" convictions recorded in the country. Pose owner Vyacheslav Khasanov was sentenced to seven years' imprisonment with forfeiture of 1 million rubles, manager Diana Kamilyanova to six years and three months, and art director Alexander Klimov to two years and three months.

36201628B69282955287113.name: NCR
36201628B69282955287113.summary:
The National Capital Region stands under the national framework of the Philippines: national law on legal gender recognition, anti-discrimination, detention placement and marriage applies here as it does elsewhere in the country. The layer specific to this region is municipal.

Quezon City has enacted an ordinance, sponsored by Councilor Bernard Herrera and colleagues, requiring every city public health facility to provide gender-affirming consultations and counselling, mental health support, and medical guidance and referrals irrespective of a patient's gender identity or expression. Mayor Joy Belmonte said the measure removes longstanding healthcare barriers for gender-diverse and transgender residents. The obligation attaches to city-run facilities, so its reach is municipal rather than regional.

Trans-specific violence in the region is documented. Shaina Bayabay, 29, was killed in Pasig City on 1 March 2024; the recorded cause is strangulation, and the underlying report states she was killed during a drinking session. The inventory records this as a single case and supplies no regional count or rate against which to read it.

36201628B76469343449086.name: Soccsksargen
36201628B76469343449086.summary:
Soccsksargen stands under the national framework of the Philippines. Criminalisation, legal gender recognition, anti-discrimination protection, custody rules and hate-crime machinery are set nationally, and the sources identify no regional ordinance, court ruling or enforcement practice that departs from them. What the region carries on its own record is one killing, described in the sourcing as an apparent targeted attack.

On 23 June 2025 an unidentified gunman shot and killed Ali Macalintal inside an acupuncture clinic in General Santos City. Macalintal was a trans woman who had worked as a journalist and activist; she was a former deputy secretary general of Karapatan-Soccsksargen Region and a former anchor-reporter for Radio Philippines Network DXDX-General Santos City.

Human Rights Watch described the General Santos shooting as an apparent targeted killing, and police examined her activism as a possible motive.

The Commission on Human Rights condemned the June 2025 killings of transgender women as marked by cruelty and impunity and named Macalintal's death among them; the commission counted her killing within the series of deaths of trans women it has described as a disturbing pattern of transfemicide.

Bahaghari and other advocates cited the General Santos killing in renewed calls for national anti-discrimination and gender-recognition legislation. Commission on Human Rights official Fayda M. Dumarpa pledged the commission's support for the Simplified Legal Gender Recognition Bill during Pride Month.

The sources record no region-specific rule on identity documents, entry, health care, public facilities, partner recognition or hate-crime protection applying in Soccsksargen, and no region-specific protective institution or ordinance. Those matters follow the national position.

36201628B63748016552864.name: Cagayan Valley
36201628B63748016552864.summary:
Cagayan Valley is one of the Philippines' regions. The national legal position on trans identity, identity documents, custody and entry applies here and is set out in the national record; what follows is what the sources document inside the region.

Two killings of trans women are documented in the region within a single national monitoring series. On 31 July 2024 a trans person named Cabansag was stabbed to death in Ilagan City, Isabela, after an alleged kidnapping and rape; three suspects were identified. On 23 June 2025 Kierra Apostol, 18, was found dead in a river in Cagayan province. She lived in Zone 7, Centro, Peñablanca, was an incoming first-year Business Management student at Cagayan State University's Caritan campus, and worked as a hair-and-makeup artist on the local pageant circuit. She had been reported missing days earlier; her body was found floating in the river between Amulung and Iguig on the morning of 23 June, and her mother told local media she saw visible signs of physical assault.

A criminology student at the University of Cagayan Valley, named online as 'Menco de Guzman' or 'Sherwin Kyqle', surrendered voluntarily at the Peñablanca police station. He admitted picking Kierra up on the Saturday night and denied involvement in her death. No outcome of the case appears in the sources.

LGBTQIA+ groups responded with demands for a full investigation and for justice, and renewed their call for the pending SOGIESC Equality Bill. Among those pressing the demand were the Cagayan State University-Andrew campus student organisation CSU Crystal, LGBT Pilipinas Taguig City Inc., and Bahaghari chairperson Reyna Valmores Salinas, who said the killing showed LGBTQ+ people remain unsafe.

Both killings are raw counts drawn from a monitoring project's national series. The sources give no homicide rate for Cagayan Valley, so trans-specific violence in the region cannot be compared against its background rate of violence, and the monitoring project's tally is a documented floor rather than a measured magnitude.

36201628B91065962446027.name: Western Visayas
36201628B91065962446027.summary:
No law, ordinance, or enforcement practice specific to Western Visayas and aimed at trans visitors appears in the available sources for this region. Criminalisation, documentation, and entry rules are set at national level and are carried by the Philippines record; nothing in the regional inventory adds a Western Visayas restriction on entry, movement, or public conduct.

The material specific to this region that is documented concerns a publicly funded institution. Students perceived as trans women were excluded at Capiz State University under an October 2022 directive on hair and uniforms. A legal non-governmental organisation's case study dated December 2025 examines that exclusion, the advocacy campaign that followed it, and the university's later valedictorian milestone.

The outcome is reported on 7 August 2025, when Capiz State University's 21st commencement exercises produced its first openly trans woman to graduate summa cum laude. Khaz-JP Padilla was batch valedictorian of the social work class, taking the highest Latin honour, and the result is attributed to the Capiz State advocacy campaign that followed the 2022 hair-and-uniform directive. Padilla described the binary haircut rules she faced in earlier years, saying that each time she cut her hair it felt like losing self-confidence, and described her transition beginning once pandemic-era online classes removed her from the haircut rule.

36201628B64564033926366.name: Ilocos Region
36201628B64564033926366.summary:
The Ilocos Region stands under the national framework of the Philippines.

Bayambang, a municipality in Pangasinan, enforces Municipal Ordinance No. 15, s-2023, which protects lesbians, gay, bisexual, transgender, queer and intersex people in the municipality against discrimination solely on the basis of sexual orientation, gender identity, expression and sex characteristics. The penalty ladder runs from a fine of at least 1,000 pesos or one month's imprisonment for a first offence, to at least 2,000 pesos or between one month and a day and six months for a second, to at least 2,500 pesos or between six months and a day and eight months for a third. A subsequent violation carries one year's imprisonment and a fine of at least 2,500 pesos. Every violator must also complete mandatory human rights education.

Complaints are filed through the barangay Katarungang Pambarangay mechanism established by the Local Government Code, Republic Act 7160. A trans visitor discriminated against inside Bayambang therefore has a local complaint route that does not depend on a national anti-discrimination statute.

The Sangguniang Panlalawigan of Pangasinan adopted Resolution No. 799-2024 at its session of 19 August 2024 in Lingayen, declaring the Bayambang ordinance conformant with the Bill of Rights and Section 16 of Republic Act 7160. The resolution is a provincial-level endorsement of the municipal instrument; it does not extend the ordinance's protections to other municipalities in Pangasinan.

The municipality's official ordinance registry records the instrument as dated 16 October 2023, authored by Coun. Benjamin Francisco S. De Vera, and publishes a certified copy for public view.

The ordinance's reach stops at the municipal boundary. The source inventory contains no region-specific legal instrument, enforcement record or incident for Ilocos Norte, Ilocos Sur or La Union, so for those provinces the national assessment applies without local modification.

36201628B49646111072560.name: ARMM
36201628B49646111072560.summary:
The Bangsamoro Autonomous Region in Muslim Mindanao stands under the national framework of the Philippines. Bangsamoro Autonomy Act No. 13, the Bangsamoro Administrative Code, begun 29 March 2019, sets out the region's structures and rules of governance and guarantees religious freedom. Its justice-dispensation clause directs that justice be dispensed "in consonance with the Constitution, Shari'ah, traditional or tribal laws". Nothing in the regional code addresses gender identity or gender non-conformity.

A Shari'ah Justice Code proposed in the Bangsamoro Parliament on 14 July 2026 would widen Shari'ah jurisdiction beyond the personal-status field it has occupied since the Code of Muslim Personal Laws (Presidential Decree 1083, 1977), reaching into civil actions, Islamic commercial transactions, ta'tir offences and alternative dispute resolution. The proposal rests on the region's organic-law authority and on the 1977 Code of Personal and Family Relations. For a visitor, the practical consequence is that a dispute can be routed to a Shari'ah forum rather than a civil court, and the applicable law follows the forum.

Marriage, divorce, succession and family relations for Muslim residents remain governed by Shari'ah forums, with written opt-in clauses allowing civil entities to take on matters otherwise within that jurisdiction. A visitor married to a Muslim spouse therefore enters a legal-pluralist marriage regime in which the forum that hears a matter determines which body of personal law applies.

Bangsamoro Parliament (2026-07-14) proposed a Shari'ah Justice Code of 10 books extending Shari'ah jurisdiction beyond the personal-status law confined since PD 1083 (1977) into civil actions, Islamic commercial transactions, ta'tir offences and ADR, resting on BOL authority and the 1977 Code of Personal and Family Relations. Marriage, divorce, succession and family relations for Muslim residents remain governed by Shari'ah forums with written-opt-in clauses for civil entities, the legal-pluralist marriage regime that applies to a visitor married to a Muslim spouse.

In August 2024 President Marcos Jr. signed a law creating three new Shari'ah judicial districts and 12 circuit courts, expanding the Shari'ah court system beyond the Bangsamoro into majority-Christian northern Mindanao, Davao-region provinces, parts of the Visayas, Luzon and Metro Manila; parliament passed it unanimously. Christianity Today reported it in 2024-11 with local Christian-leader reaction. The measure carries Bangsamoro's Shari'ah personal-law regime onto a national footing.

sources.title: LGBTQ rights in CAR (Wikipedia)
sources.summary: There is no legal gender recognition. There are no laws protecting LGBTQ people from discrimination in health, employment, education, and access to goods and services. Openly LGBTQ people cannot serve in the military. There are no laws against psychology or medical practices being used as conversion therapy on LGBTQ people. Law 24-001 on the Protection of Personal Data protects sexual orientation as sensitive data, with Article 17 stating "Any processing of sensitive data is prohibited due to risks of discrimination or infringement of personal freedoms"; the article describes this protection only for sexual orientation and does not state coverage for gender identity. The Central African Republic signed a joint statement on ending acts of violence and related human rights violations based on sexual orientation and gender identity at the United Nations condemning violence and discrimination against LGBTQ people. Male and female same-sex sexual activity are legal. The penal code criminalizes public expression of love between persons of the same sex with imprisonment for six months to two years or a fine of between 150,000 and 600,000 CFA francs ($300 and $1,200). When one participant is a child, the adult may be sentenced to two to five years imprisonment or a fine of 100,000 to 800,000 CFA francs ($200 and $1,600). In 2012 there were no reports that police arrested or detained persons under these provisions. There is no legal recognition of same-sex couples, and same-sex marriage is constitutionally banned under Article 7 which defines marriage as the union between one man and one woman with family and marriage under protection of the State. Alternatives Centrafrique has documented cases of people being arrested due to false accusations of same-sex intercourse. "societal discrimination against lesbian, gay, bisexual and transgender persons was entrenched, and many citizens attributed the existence of homosexuality to undue Western influence." Cultural stigma continues to persist, and due to criminalization of public same-sex affection along with cultural stigma the LGBTQ community has to conceal itself. LGBTQ people face discrimination in education, healthcare, and employment. Religious preach conversion, but this is rarely enacted since people keep their LGBTQ identities hidden. While there were no reports of violence against LGBTQ people, it is unclear if this is due to lack of incidents or victims not reporting it. Alternatives Centrafrique states that LGBTQ people have experienced mistreatment and torture by law enforcement. Being diagnosed with HIV is used as a source of stigmatization in the workplace leading to harassment, blackmail, and firings.

68945753B94077674833362.name: Daegu
68945753B94077674833362.summary:
Daegu's visitor-relevant signal is concentrated in the Daegu Queer Culture Festival, held every June since 2009 without interruption and described as the country's second-largest LGBT event: a pride parade and film festival running a week or two, usually in late June. The city stands under the national framework of South Korea for criminal law, legal gender recognition, documents and healthcare; the findings below are those specific to Daegu.

Opposition is organised, annual and large. A Daegu-Gyeongbuk conservative-Protestant umbrella body convened its 17th annual "National Assembly Against Queer" in response to the festival, gathering roughly 3,500 believers from about 1,600 churches at Banwoldang station and along a 450 m stretch toward Gyesan intersection under anti-homosexuality slogans. An estimated 28 religious and right-wing groups have formed a "gay issue countermeasure committee" in Daegu to block LGBT events, and that opposition has kept the festival off an outdoor stage on a popular central Daegu street.

Court bids to stop the festival have failed each year. The Daegu Queer Opposition Countermeasure Committee sought an injunction against the 2025 edition; the court dismissed it, as it had dismissed the bids for 2022, 2023 and 2024. In 2023, under then-Mayor Hong Joon-pyo, municipal officials physically blocked the road. Police again restricted the 2025 march to a single bus-only lane. Organisers framed the event as resistance to "hate and discriminatory politics".

The dispute continued into the 2026 edition. The Daegu Queer Opposition Countermeasures Headquarters, made up of the Daegu-Gyeongbuk Parents' Alliance for Protecting the Next Generation, the Daegu Christian Council and the Dongseong-ro Merchants' Association, filed a collective petition with the National Human Rights Commission of Korea demanding a change of venue, arguing the event is likely to infringe public welfare. The group says about 34,000 people signed, which it calls unusually large for a single commission petition. The petition cites the Daegu District Court's dismissal of the festival committee's injunction request, a ruling that found the police notice restricting the event legitimate because Jungang-ro is a key urban traffic artery and one lane must be secured for public welfare. It responds to the festival committee's January petition against the National Police Agency Commissioner General and the National Assembly Speaker over Article 12(1) of the Assembly and Demonstration Act.

68945753B85435209225479.name: Daejeon
68945753B85435209225479.summary:
Daejeon has no separate legal regime of its own; the national law of South Korea governs transgender residents and visitors in the city. What is documented here runs through a court seated in Daejeon and through a cemetery. On 7 October 2021 the Daejeon District Court ordered the cancellation of the Army's discharge of Staff Sergeant Byun Hee-soo, the first known legal case involving a transgender soldier. The court held that the military should have treated her as female following her legal sex change, that the loss of genitalia was not a valid ground for dismissal, and that a fitness-for-service review must weigh basic rights. The decision upheld the appeal pursued on her behalf after her death.

On 24 June 2024 Byun Hee-soo was buried at the National Cemetery in Daejeon; she was Korea's first transgender soldier. Around 60 activists protested at the burial, arguing that it was marred by discriminatory treatment. The ceremony was conducted as an official state honour in the city.

Decision vindicated the posthumous appeal. For the record: dated, court-level proof that a Daejeon court delivered a pro-recognition ruling on trans military status.

Her state burial in Daejeon stands as official honouring while institutional stance remains conservative.

68945753B59172752195743.summary:
North Chungcheong stands under the national framework of South Korea. The province has no separate law on gender identity or gender expression; the national provisions on criminalisation, legal gender recognition, marriage and anti-discrimination apply here as they do elsewhere in the country.

The province's documented trans-specific event is the death of Byun Hui-su, a 23-year-old transgender woman and the country's first transgender soldier, found dead at her home in Cheongju on 3 March 2021. A counsellor raised the alarm after 28 February. She had been discharged over gender-affirming surgery, and her challenge to that discharge had been rejected in July 2020. The death became the reference point for national debate on the treatment of transgender service members.

Public grief and demands for LGBT protections followed the death. The National Human Rights Commission honoured her, and prosecutors and activists called for an anti-discrimination bill, its eighth introduction since 2007; the June 2020 draft had included gender-identity provisions. A society-wide discourse of responsibility followed. No new provincial law resulted from the incident.

68945753B70752081047384.name: South Chungcheong
68945753B70752081047384.summary:
South Chungcheong Province stands under South Korea's national framework, which carries the country's criminal law, legal gender recognition rules, document policy and protection machinery. The province's own documented signal concerns students rather than visitors. Its student human-rights ordinance, enacted on 10 July 2020, contains Article 15, covering gender identity and sexual orientation. The provincial council voted to repeal the ordinance on 24 April 2024. The Chungcheongnam-do Office of Education, which enforces the ordinance, challenged the repeal at the Supreme Court on 13 May 2024 and obtained suspension of execution on 30 May 2024, so the ordinance remains in force while the case proceeds. The office argues that the repeal violates the Constitution and international human-rights treaties.

The ordinance's status is contested between sources. A reference article records that the province's ordinance was revoked in 2024, matching the 24 April 2024 council vote, while the Republic of Korea's submission to UN Special Procedures, dated 21 February 2025, states that the suspension of execution keeps it in effect. No region-specific rule on restroom access, healthcare, policing, hate-crime enforcement or violence in South Chungcheong was identified; for those matters the national assessment applies.

68945753B43731078897969.name: Gyeonggi
68945753B43731078897969.summary:
Gyeonggi Province's region-specific record concerns student protections rather than visitor-facing rules. Gyeonggi-do enacted South Korea's first student human rights ordinance in 2010, and the ordinance bars discrimination on grounds of sexual orientation and gender identity, the clauses that religious groups and parents targeted in the repeal campaign they mounted from August 2022. When the Seoul Metropolitan Council abolished its own ordinance in April 2024, Gyeonggi was one of six regional education offices still enforcing a comparable instrument, together with Gwangju, North Jeolla, South Chungcheong, Incheon and Jeju. A Gyeonggi-based teacher quoted in the coverage argued against wholesale abolition.

Gyeonggi and Seoul are the only two jurisdictions whose ordinances include a right not to be discriminated against on the basis of pregnancy. The provincial Superintendent of Public Instruction conducts an annual survey on student human rights, and the province marks a Student Human Rights Day.

No Gyeonggi-specific rule on criminal exposure, entry, identity documents, airport or security screening, restroom access or healthcare access was identified. Visitors in the province fall under the national framework carried by the South Korea record.

Región del Bío-Bío stands under Chile's national framework for trans people; the findings below are those specific to the region.

Movilh's XXIII annual human rights report, covering 2024 data and published in March 2025, attributes 5.89% of Chile's documented cases of discrimination and violence on grounds of sexual orientation and gender identity to Bío-Bío, the third-highest share of any region. Jiménez Carrasco was interned from 28 September to 3 October 2016 and was placed and treated as male, despite the legal duty to use a trans patient's chosen name and social sex. The complaint described the staff conduct as brutal and illegal discriminatory acts.

La Araucanía has no legal regime of its own. Criminal law, policing, the courts, identity registration and legal gender recognition all operate under Chile's national framework, and the available sources identify no regional law, ordinance or institutional practice that departs from the national position on identity documents, facilities, care access or partner recognition. The regional signal in those sources concerns recorded anti-LGBT incidents rather than law.

Movilh's XXIV annual human rights report, published in March 2026 with 2025 data, names La Araucanía as the Chilean region where recorded homophobic and transphobic cases and complaints rose most, at 150% year on year. No other region recorded a larger increase.

The same report places La Araucanía at 1.96% of the national case total, so the 150% rise is measured on a small base and represents a small number of additional recorded complaints. The region ranks first by rate of increase, not by volume of cases, and neither source gives a per-capita rate for it.

The regional figure aggregates homophobia and transphobia and is not disaggregated for trans people, so it establishes no trans-specific rate of violence or discrimination in La Araucanía. What a trans visitor can take from it is a documented upward trend in complaints in the region relative to the rest of Chile, from a low base, with no region-specific enforcement, protection or documentation rule attached.

47653553B1207481020383.name: RegiÃ³n de Arica y Parinacota
47653553B1207481020383.summary:
Arica y Parinacota is a region of Chile and stands under the national legal framework; the country-level law is carried by Chile's national record. The findings below are specific to this region.

Movilh's XXIII annual human-rights report on sexual and gender diversity, covering 2024 data and published in March 2025, recorded 2,847 cases nationally, a rise of 78.7 per cent, with Arica y Parinacota accounting for 0.84 per cent of the national total, among the lowest shares of any region. Increases were recorded in 11 of the 16 regions. A share that small means a single additional case moves the region's position, and the report itself notes that in regions with such small shares one case can dominate.

An earlier Movilh report covering 2021, published in April 2022, recorded national homophobia and transphobia complaints and cases falling 12 per cent, the first decline in eight years, while complaints rose in five regions. Arica y Parinacota was one of them, with reports up around 300 per cent against 2020. The report attributes the national decline to the visibility won by the sexual-diversity movement in the year equal marriage was approved; the region's complaint trajectory ran against that national direction. The 300 per cent figure rests on the region's small complaint base.

47653553B78904739401519.summary:
The Región Metropolitana de Santiago is a region of Chile and stands under the national framework, which supplies the gender-recognition, anti-discrimination and migration protections that apply within it. The municipal-level facts below are specific to the region.

Municipal practice in the region is not uniform. On 15 April 2026 the council of Ñuñoa approved an anti-discrimination ordinance by nine votes to one, the first adopted anywhere in Chile. The ordinance bans hate speech, requires non-discrimination clauses in municipal tenders and contracts, establishes a communal good-practice seal, and requires notices against exclusion in municipal buildings. It was drafted by María Fernanda Ulloa, head of the comuna's Diversity and Non-Discrimination Department, and endorsed by mayor Sebastián Sichel.

Elsewhere in the region the posture runs the other way. Vitacura had committed to Movilh to fly the LGBT flag for the 17 May anti-homophobia date, then withdrew under pressure from its councillors and declined to raise it; Santiago and Ñuñoa took part. Movilh records the refusal as a municipal-level retreat in the capital's wealthier comunas.

For a trans visitor, official recognition inside the region is set comuna by comuna rather than uniformly. The rights a visitor holds derive from national law; what a municipality does on its own premises and in its own contracts depends on which comuna they are in, and the two documented cases point in opposite directions.

10402087B60477050509260.name: Bayern
10402087B60477050509260.summary:
Bayern stands under Germany's national framework on legal gender recognition, identity documents, relationship recognition and anti-discrimination, and that layer is carried by the national record. What follows is specific to the Free State.

A prohibition on gender-inclusive German took effect in Bavaria on 1 April 2024. It bars gender-neutral word forms in schools, universities and all state administration, implementing a government declaration of December 2023 together with a cabinet decision amending the language rules that govern public authorities. Critics dismiss the measure as symbol politics while pointing out that it reaches every public counter, registry office and classroom in the state. A trans visitor dealing with a Bavarian registry office, town hall or university therefore deals with offices operating under an official register from which gender-neutral wording has been excluded.

Bavaria has co-sponsored a Bundesrat initiative with Sachsen, Thüringen and Sachsen-Anhalt to tighten the federal Self-Determination Act, an organised Land-level attempt to make the nationwide self-declaration route stricter. The contested ground behind the initiative was the Act's treatment of children's gender entry: the Bundesrat's criticism of 20 October 2023 held that the draft allowed parents to decide changes for under-14s "without any counselling, examination and investigation of the child's welfare". The Free State government's posture toward self-declaration is therefore openly restrictive, even though the procedure itself remains the national one.

The Self-Determination Act was approved by the cabinet in August 2023 and passed the Bundestag 374-251 on 12 April 2024; it lets adults over 18 change first name and gender by self-determination with three months' notice, in force since 1 November 2024. Same-sex marriage and adoption have been legal since 2017, and discrimination on sexual orientation and gender identity is banned nationwide in employment and goods and services, with some protections varying by region. This is the federal baseline within which Bavaria's gender-language ban and the Länder push to tighten the SBGG operate.

Adults declare the change themselves before the registry office. Those aged 14-17 need a guardian's consent or the family court's; for under-14s only the guardian can declare. 10402087B20892132820961.name: Berlin
10402087B20892132820961.summary:
Berlin is a Land of the Federal Republic of Germany; legal gender recognition, identity documents, border screening and anti-discrimination law are set at national level and are carried by the parent record.

MANEO, Berlin's anti-violence documentation project, recorded 723 LGBTIQ+-hostile incidents in the city in 2025, slightly fewer than the 738 documented in 2024, drawn from 1,014 new reports, which is a new high for incoming reports. The recorded incidents include insults, threats and physical attacks on public transport, in parks and on the street. Schöneberg, Neukölln, Kreuzberg, Friedrichshain and Tiergarten are the most affected districts, and 58 attacks targeted LGBTIQ+ venues, memorials and events. MANEO states that its figures capture only part of what occurs because of a high dark figure, and reports that its own counselling centre was attacked several times in 2025. Neukölln is named among the worst-hit districts.

At the 48th Berlin Christopher Street Day, a vehicle was driven into a crowd in the Tiergarten area, killing one woman and injuring several people; the event was cancelled. MANEO offers victim counselling and an anonymous reporting line on 030-2163336, open daily from 17:00 to 19:00.

Ahead of the 2025 parade season, Berlin CSD organisers urged vigilance with hundreds of thousands of participants expected. A queer café owner in Berlin-Neukölln reported 45 police complaints over homophobic attacks in 18 months.

sources.title: LGBTQ rights in Berlin (Wikipedia)
sources.summary: Hirschfeld's Institute for Sexual Science held studies of the first gender-affirming surgeries among decades of research, destroyed when the institute at In den Zelten was sacked on May 6, 1933 and burned. The article states there were no explicit laws against exhibiting non-gender-conforming behavior, so enforcers criminalized queer women through other provisions with incarceration for so-called anti-social behavior under an extremely vague definition and no reliable numbers. Contemporary Berlin is described as having a rise of queer spaces catering to marginalized groups within the LGBTQ community such as transgender individuals. FLINTA spaces are defined as "Frauen, Lesben, Intergeschlechtliche, Nichtbinäre, Trans und Agender Personen," meaning those who do not fit into a cis male gender identity, motivated by discomfort around cis men and male-domination of many queer spaces. Male-exclusive venues Lab.Oratory and Boiler historically catered exclusively to male patrons with cases of feminine men and gender queer individuals rejected, with entry policy evolving since the 2000s to include more types of non-female gender expressions though instances of exclusion still occur, while a concept of queer masculinities including gay, bi, trans and queer men reshapes selection. Cited studies indicate gay, lesbian, and trans individuals especially may engage in drug use as a means of coping with societal marginalization and discrimination, exacerbated by multiple minority stress including gender identity. Several thousand men were sentenced under Section 175 of the Reich Criminal Code between 1933 and 1945, with about 6,000 actually interned to camps with a presumed high death rate, and upon liberation inmates feared re-incarceration with fears justified. In 1950 East Germany returned to the pre-Nazi version of Section 175 while Section 175a continued to be applied, from the late 1950s homosexual acts among adults were no longer punishable, and in 1968 a new penal code made same-sex sexual acts with minors punishable for both women and men in §151, deleted with effect from July 1, 1989. West Germany retained the Nazi-era versions of Sections 175 and 175a for two decades, convicting 50,000 men from 1945 to 1969, roughly the same amount as during the Nazi era. Reforms in 1969 and 1973 effectively made only sexual acts with males under age 18 punishable, while the age of consent for lesbian and heterosexual acts was 14 years. Section 175 was completely repealed in 1994, four years after unification, for the territory of the old Federal Republic. Those punished under the broader version in effect until 1969, many suffering imprisonment and entry in the national criminal record with life-long employment and housing consequences, were not rehabilitated until 2017. Compensation, only for actually convicted men still alive and eligible, was 3,000 euros and an additional 1,500 euros for each year of detention suffered, described as negligible.

10402087B85226028911536.name: Hessen
10402087B85226028911536.summary:
Queer-hostile offences recorded by Hessen police have risen in each year since 2022: 33 offences that year, 83 in 2023, 135 in 2024 and 141 in 2025, a more than fourfold increase across four years. Interior Minister Roman Poseck (CDU) called the development alarming in answers to Landtag inquiries from Grüne members and attributed part of the responsibility to far-right forces.

The 2024 figure, given in the interior ministry's answer to an August 2025 inquiry, was 52 higher than the previous year and comprised 16 cases of dangerous grievous bodily harm, seven of bodily harm, 13 of property damage and 26 of insult. Suspects were identified in 46 of the 2024 proceedings, and six convictions resulted.

Physical attacks form part of the record. Poseck cited a January 2026 incident on a Kassel tram in which a male couple was insulted, threatened and spat on for homophobic motives.

Frankfurt Airport produced a documented complaint by a trans traveller. On 23 November 2024 the DJ and producer BASHKKA was refused a search by a female officer during screening, and the male officer handling her told her she was 'not a woman'. She filed a complaint under the General Act on Equal Treatment. The airport apologised by email, said the security service provider had been instructed to investigate, and committed to training security staff on dealing with transgender and gender non-conforming travellers.

Federal Criminal Police Office (BKA) situation report on the security of LSBTIQ* people in Germany, published with the Interior Ministry: a multi-year rise in police-registered queer-hostile offences and the new federal reporting category that makes Land-by-Land comparison possible; classification changes can inflate Land counts, so cross-Land numbers need caution.

10402087B23625801106445.name: Sachsen-Anhalt
10402087B23625801106445.summary:
Sachsen-Anhalt is a Land of Germany. Identity documents, equality law and the self-declaration route for legal gender change are set at federal level; what is specific to this Land is a political record and one prosecution.

Sachsen-Anhalt is one of three sponsors, with Sachsen and Thüringen, of a Bundesrat initiative to tighten the federal Self-Determination Act, reported by dpa on 2 June 2026. The proposal would create an "abuse review" mechanism allowing registry offices to intervene on objective, documentable grounds. It is backed by Union MPs and resisted by the SPD, while the federal family ministry runs a scheduled evaluation of the Self-Determination Act.

The case the initiative cites is a Sachsen-Anhalt prosecution. In July 2023 the Halle District Court sentenced Marla-Svenja Liebich, then registered as male, to one year and six months' imprisonment without parole for incitement to hatred, defamation and insult. At the end of 2024 she changed her legal gender from male to female by declaration at a registry office. The chief public prosecutor in Halle told MDR Sachsen-Anhalt that she would begin the term at Chemnitz women's prison, and German outlets including Der Spiegel questioned whether the change was serious. That case is the trigger for the Land's Bundesrat initiative.

For a trans visitor, the Land's registry offices are the point of contact with the federal self-declaration route, and the Land government is on record seeking to add a review layer to it. Nothing in the sources documents Land-level police, prison, health-service or venue practice bearing on trans people.

14339913B89763821047858.name: Wales
14339913B89763821047858.summary:
Wales stands under the United Kingdom framework for legal gender recognition, equality law and sex-based segregation in custody. The Senedd's devolved competence runs through health, education and equality delivery, so a visitor's legal status is set nationally while Welsh institutions determine which services and protections are actually available.

Devolved policy does not extend to legal gender recognition, equality legislation or prisons. The marker rules, single-sex space enforcement and custody segregation a visitor encounters in Wales are set by the national framework rather than by Welsh ministers.

The Welsh Government's LGBTQ+ Action Plan for Wales, published in February 2023, states the aim of making Wales the most LGBTQ+ friendly nation in Europe. It commits the devolved administration to pursue a Welsh-specific ban on conversion practices; a Working Group on Banning Conversion Practices was formed in December 2022 and the government published its banning conversion practices document in May 2024.

Transgender healthcare in Wales was historically delivered by referral to clinics in London. The first Welsh gender identity clinic opened in September 2019, ending the default referral of Welsh adults outside Wales.

The Welsh Government's LGBTQ+ Action Plan document for young people, posted in January 2026, forms part of the standing devolved inclusion programme. The programme's update page addresses the For Women Scotland judgment of 19 December 2025.

sources.title: LGBTQ+ Action Plan for Wales
sources.summary: The Welsh Government's February 2023 LGBTQ+ Action Plan for Wales aims to make Wales 'the most LGBTQ+ friendly nation in Europe'. Deputy Minister Hannah Blythyn announced it in the Senedd on 21 June 2022 under the 2021 Welsh Labour–Plaid Cymru agreement. It was built on 61 recommendations from the Independent LGBTQ+ Expert Panel (March 2021) and a 12-week public consultation with 1,328 responses, and it funds a Grassroots Pride Fund. The government pursued a Welsh-specific ban on conversion practices, forming a Working Group on Banning Conversion Practices in December 2022 (gov.wales 'Banning conversion practices in Wales', May 2024). The plan records the UK Government's blocking of the Gender Recognition Reform (Scotland) Bill in January 2023. Welsh NHS commissioners stated in March 2024 they had no plans to develop a children's gender service, and parents of transgender children called for more help (BBC, March 2024).

Trans adults in Wales were historically referred to London clinics for transgender healthcare until the first Welsh gender identity clinic opened in September 2019 (BBC).

14339913B6930312138089.name: Northern Ireland
14339913B6930312138089.summary:
Northern Ireland's equality legislation is separate from that of England, Wales and Scotland, and as of August 2026 the regional authorities were still assessing how the United Kingdom Supreme Court's ruling on the meaning of sex applies there. The position on single-sex facilities and services should be treated as unsettled rather than as a settled extension of the framework operating elsewhere in the United Kingdom.

Legal gender recognition in Northern Ireland runs on the Gender Recognition Act 2004. A May 2021 judgment of the Northern Ireland courts made a binding ruling in the region that gender dysphoria based on an individual's mental dynamic is no longer legally required, following the World Health Organization's 2019 decision to stop treating gender identity disorder as a mental illness or mental disorder. That ruling applies in Northern Ireland only and has not been extended to the rest of the United Kingdom.

In December 2025 other executive parties blocked justice minister Naomi Long's plan to add transgender people as a protected characteristic in Northern Ireland's new hate-crime legislation. Long had sought executive approval in early November 2025 with a response deadline in mid-November; the bill had held executive agreement since December 2024. She cited Police Service of Northern Ireland statistics recording close to 100 transgender-identity incidents or hate crimes. That figure is a raw count without a population denominator.

In September 2025 guidance supporting transgender pupils was withdrawn from the Northern Ireland Education Authority's website after Education Minister Paul Givan requested its removal, arguing it conflicted with departmental policy and the law in Northern Ireland. The guidance had recommended that trans pupils be allowed to use changing rooms matching their gender identity. Teachers' representatives warned that the removal ignores the practical realities.

Same-sex marriage took effect in Northern Ireland on 13 January 2020, under regulations signed on 19 December 2019 after UK Parliament legislation receiving royal assent on 24 July 2019 required extension if the Assembly did not reconvene by 21 October 2019. The first wedding followed on 11 February 2020 after a 28-day notice period, and religious and church same-sex weddings have been permitted since 1 September 2020. Civil partnerships have been available to same-sex couples since 2005 under the Civil Partnership Act 2004.

sources.title: LGBTQ rights in Northern Ireland (Wikipedia)
sources.summary: The Gender Recognition Act 2004 applies to Northern Ireland and provides for a person's change of gender to be officially recognised, introduced after the 2002 case of Goodwin v United Kingdom in which the European Court of Human Rights ruled the United Kingdom's failure violated articles 8 and 12 of the European Convention on Human Rights. To change gender, a person must demonstrate gender dysphoria and have lived in the relevant gender for two years before applying for a gender recognition certificate. Before the 2020 introduction of same-sex marriage, a person had to be unmarried before changing legal gender. In May 2021 a Northern Ireland court judgment on a challenge to the UK gender recognition law made a binding ruling that gender dysphoria based on an individual's mental dynamic is no longer legally required, due to the WHO decision in 2019 no longer treating gender identity disorder under DMD-IV as a mental illness or mental disorder. That ruling applies only to Northern Ireland so far and not the rest of the UK, but sets up a legal precedent for the rest of the UK in the future. The Sex Discrimination (Gender Reassignment) Regulations (Northern Ireland) 1999 provides a degree of protection for transgender people who are undergoing gender reassignment in employment and vocational training. Same-sex sexual activity has been legal since 1982 under the Homosexual Offences (Northern Ireland) Order 1982 which came into force on 8 December 1982, following the 22 October 1981 European Court of Human Rights 15-4 ruling in Dudgeon v United Kingdom that criminalisation of male homosexual acts under the Offences Against the Person Act 1861 violated Article 8. Anti-LGBT criminal provisions were removed throughout Northern Ireland by section 9 of the Sexual Offences Act 2003 abolishing buggery and gross indecency, with private gay sex between more than two people legalised but cottaging remaining illegal, and the age of consent equalised at 17 by the Sexual Offences (Amendment) Act 2000 effective in 2001 then reduced to 16 by the Sexual Offences (Northern Ireland) Order 2008. Civil partnerships have been available to same-sex couples since 2005 under the Civil Partnership Act 2004, and same-sex marriage took effect on 13 January 2020 under regulations signed 19 December 2019 after UK Parliament legislation receiving royal assent on 24 July 2019 required extension if the Assembly did not reconvene by 21 October 2019, with the first wedding on 11 February 2020 after a 28-day notice period and religious and church same-sex weddings permitted since 1 September 2020. Same-sex couples were granted full adoption rights in 2013 after High Court 2012 and Court of Appeal 2013 rulings that the ban was discriminatory and a breach of human rights and rejection of a further Supreme Court appeal. Section 75 of the Northern Ireland Act 1998 requires public authorities to have due regard to promoting equality of opportunity between persons of different sexual orientation through Equality Schemes monitored by the Equality Commission for Northern Ireland. The Employment Equality (Sexual Orientation) Regulations (NI) 2003 effective 2 December 2003 prohibit discrimination and harassment in employment, higher education and vocational training, and the Equality Act (Sexual Orientation) Regulations (NI) 2006 effective 1 January 2007 prohibit discrimination in goods and services, premises, education and public functions. The permanent blood donation ban on men who had sex with men moved to a one-year deferral effective 1 September 2016, to a 3-month deferral effective 1 June 2020, and from August 2021 monogamous gay and bi men may donate without a waiting period while non-monogamous gay and bi men must wait 3 months, and historic convictions became eligible for pardon under the Policing and Crime Act 2017 Alan Turing Law extended by a November 2016 Legislative Consent Motion, though by June 2019 only two men had sought pardons and both failed.

82085004B70364588595557.name: Northern Territory
82085004B70364588595557.summary:
The Northern Territory legislates its own anti-discrimination regime beneath the Australian national framework, which carries the federal gender-identity protections. The territory's own layer narrowed in 2025.

The Anti-Discrimination Amendment Act 2025 (No. 27 of 2025) was assented on 30 October 2025, with Part 3 commencing on 27 July 2026. It removes the civil prohibition on conduct that offends, insults, humiliates or intimidates a person in public because of a protected attribute, gender identity among them. From that commencement date a trans visitor or resident cannot found a vilification complaint on that ground before the Northern Territory Anti-Discrimination Commission.

The repeal was announced in March 2025 by the Country Liberal Party government, which framed it as restoring freedom of speech and religious freedom. The government had earlier retreated from scrapping the vilification section outright before the bill passed parliament on 17 October 2025.

NT Anti-Discrimination Commissioner Jeswynn Yogaratnam publicly rebuked the change, warning that the government may be opening the doors for a very dangerous stream of hate speech.

The territory's hate-crime statute does not list sexual orientation or gender identity among the motives it covers. Coverage of those motives in the Northern Territory therefore rests on the national layer alone.

Territory discrimination protections covering gender identity date from 2022, when the vilification provision was added to the Anti-Discrimination Act. That provision is the one now being removed.

Changing the sex marker on a Northern Territory birth certificate has required clinical treatment since 2018.

The territory government issued a policy directive in December 2025 banning gender-affirming healthcare for minors. In February 2025 it banned rainbow pride flags in public hospitals.

The practical exposure for a trans visitor to the Northern Territory is a shrinking civil remedy rather than a criminal or entry risk: the conduct that will cease to be actionable from 27 July 2026 is harassment and vilification on the ground of gender identity, and no territory provision replaces it.

82085004B60194602145168.name: Victoria
82085004B60194602145168.summary:
Victoria's anti-vilification law, the Justice Legislation Amendment (Anti-Vilification and Social Cohesion) Act 2025, passed in April 2025. It inserts civil vilification protections into the Equal Opportunity Act 2010 and criminal protections into the Crimes Act 1958, and repeals the Racial and Religious Tolerance Act. The stated aims are equal participation and public safety. The criminal provisions take effect on 30 June 2026 and cover vilification on the grounds of gender identity, sex, sex characteristics and sexual orientation, with a maximum penalty of five years' imprisonment. Political, religious and academic exemptions apply, along with a further provision reported as the "Sam Kerr clause".

Gender identity has been a prohibited discrimination ground in Victoria since 2000, when the Equal Opportunity (Gender Identity and Sexual Orientation) Act 2000 amended the Equal Opportunity Act 1995; the ground was retained in the replacement Equal Opportunity Act 2010. Sex characteristics were added with effect from 2021. The Justice Legislation Amendment (Police and Other Matters) Bill 2022, passed in September 2022, extended protection on sexual orientation and gender identity grounds to on-duty Victoria Police officers.

Religious exemptions remain in the Equal Opportunity Act 2010. They allow religious organisations, including adoption and fostering agencies and charities that receive no government funding, to discriminate against and reject LGBT employees and clients. The Equal Opportunity (Religious Exceptions) Amendment Bill 2021, passed in December 2021 and effective 15 June 2022, bars religious schools and organisations from discriminating against employees because of sexual orientation, gender identity or marital status, and bars government-funded bodies from refusing services on those grounds except where conformity with doctrine is an inherent requirement, such as hiring a religious studies teacher.

Victoria recognises gender transition. Birth certificates are issued by the state Registry of Births, Deaths and Marriages, and driver licences carry no recorded gender marker. Updated regulations in November 2025 removed all fees and costs for applications to change the sex recorded on a birth certificate. Earlier law required an applicant to be unmarried and to have undergone sexual reassignment surgery. Parliament removed the unmarried requirement early, in May 2018, ahead of its scheduled lapse in December 2018. An August 2016 bill that would have removed both requirements and allowed parents to alter a child's gender descriptor with the child's informed consent did not pass.

Conversion practices are prohibited. The Change or Suppression (Conversion) Practices Prohibition Bill passed the lower house 55-0 in December 2020 and the Legislative Council 27-9 on 5 February 2021, with penalties of up to approximately A$200,000 or up to 10 years' imprisonment, effective February 2022, one year after royal assent. The prohibition was preceded by the Health Complaints Act, from the Health Complaints Bill 2016 and effective 1 February 2017, which empowers the Health Complaints Commissioner to issue warnings and temporary or permanent bans; the commissioner opened an investigation in May 2018.

In August 2024 the Supreme Court of Victoria upheld the provision of puberty blockers to transgender children with stress and anxiety. In the same month a Victorian coroner investigating the suicides of five young transgender women recommended urgent investment in health care for trans and gender-diverse people. The state government says it is reviewing the recommendations, and local advocacy groups will press for their implementation.

Victoria is the only state with an LGBTIQA+ Commissioner. The inaugural Gender and Sexuality Commissioner, Ro Allen, was appointed in July 2015 to streamline federal and state laws so that passports and birth certificates align with affirmed gender and to strengthen workplace protections for transgender workers; the office was later renamed Commissioner for LGBTIQ+ Communities. Joe Ball, a transgender man, was appointed on 23 September 2024 for a three-year term to advise government on safe and inclusive policies, services and programmes and to lead implementation of Pride in our Future, Victoria's ten-year LGBTIQA+ equality plan.

Reported funding cuts risk a backlog at the Victorian Equal Opportunity and Human Rights Commission, established in 1975.

82085004B21656044714531.name: New South Wales
82085004B21656044714531.summary:
New South Wales sets its own discrimination, document, facilities and custody rules inside Australia's national framework; federal law, passports and marriage are carried by the national record. The Anti-Discrimination Act 1977 has covered transgender status since 1996 and prohibits discrimination in work, public education, goods and services, banking, health care, property and nightclubs. Section 16 of the Mental Health Act 2007 states that sexual orientation and gender identity are not mental illnesses.

Birth certificates and driver licences are issued by the state, while passports and marriage are Commonwealth matters. Since 1 July 2025 a change of sex on a New South Wales birth certificate no longer requires surgery: the applicant files a form, supplies a good-faith witness who is an unrelated adult known for at least a year, and pays a $73 fee. The replacement certificate does not disclose that the record was changed.

The Conversion Practices Ban Act 2024 took effect on 4 April 2025. Practices causing substantial mental or physical harm carry up to five years' imprisonment, and taking a person out of New South Wales for conversion therapy carries up to three years. Anti-Discrimination NSW can investigate complaints from that date and refer matters into civil pathways. The bill passed unamended on 22 March 2024 by 22 votes to 4 in the upper house, with limited religious and parental exemptions that include sermons preaching against homosexuality.

Fatal violence against a trans visitor is on record. Mhelody Bruno, a 25-year-old transgender woman from the Philippines visiting Australia, was killed in Wagga Wagga; the perpetrator pleaded guilty to manslaughter and received a 22-month term.

Hate-crime law is narrower than the discrimination statute. The Crimes Amendment (Publicly Threatening and Inciting Violence) Act 2018, passed unanimously by both houses in June 2018, repealed the earlier vilification provisions and created a criminal offence effective 13 August 2018 carrying up to three years' imprisonment; the grounds covered remain limited to sexual orientation, so gender identity sits outside New South Wales vilification law. Nazi symbols were banned under the Crimes Act 1900 by unanimous vote, assented on 19 August 2022 and effective immediately, with the LGBTIQ community named among those the provision protects.

Exemptions in the Anti-Discrimination Act permit discrimination on grounds of sex, gender, pregnancy and homosexuality in sport and in non-public religious schools. Transgender people can be excluded from female sports categories on that basis, and religiously run adoption agencies may refuse same-sex couples.

Facilities are covered at local government level rather than by state statute: Sydney City Council adopted a gender-neutral bathrooms policy in April 2023.
