82085004B93533858076668.name: Western Australia
82085004B93533858076668.summary:
Western Australia's Equal Opportunity Act 1984 protects one attribute relevant to trans people: "gender history", defined in the statute and in state government guidance as living, or seeking to live, as a member of the opposite sex. Guidance published by the state government and updated on 12 February 2026 states that direct and indirect discrimination on this ground are unlawful, and that treating a person as their former sex is a form of direct discrimination. The attribute is not framed as gender identity, so the state's protection is worded more narrowly than the gender-identity grounds used in several other Australian jurisdictions.

Eligibility to complain is tied to legal recognition. Gender history is established through a recognition certificate or a recorded change of sex or gender under the births, deaths and marriages framework, which means a trans person who has not amended Western Australian identity documents may sit outside the complaint mechanism even where the treatment described is discriminatory. The Equal Opportunity Commission's fact sheet records that the 2024 recognition reforms amend section 4(1) of the Act to delete the "gender reassigned person" definition and insert one keyed to certificates or registration, that the amendment does not operate retrospectively, and that complaints will have to satisfy the new registration requirements once it commences.

The Births, Deaths and Marriages Registration Amendment (Sex or Gender Changes) Act 2024 was assented to on 26 September 2024 and took effect on 30 May 2025. It repeals the Gender Reassignment Act 2000 and abolishes the Gender Reassignment Board, which the Premier and Attorney-General described at introduction on 16 April 2024 as the last body of its kind in the country. Medical and surgical reassignment are no longer prerequisites; a statement from a medical practitioner or psychologist certifying appropriate clinical treatment, which may include counselling, replaces the board process. Male, female, indeterminate/intersex and non-binary descriptors are available, a change may be made once a year, the fee is A$195 and non-refundable, and processing takes up to four weeks. Applicants under 18 need parental consent or the permission of the Family Court of Western Australia. The Act carries a statutory review clause after three years.

The removal of surgical prerequisites has a longer history in the state. Sterilisation was required before 2012, until the High Court held on 6 October 2011 in AB v Western Australia that two trans men who had undergone bilateral mastectomies and androgen therapy were entitled to male recognition certificates without hysterectomy, oophorectomy or genital reconstructive surgery. The requirement that an applicant be unmarried was repealed by legislation that passed both chambers in early 2019 and commenced on 19 March 2019.

Complaints go to the state Commissioner of Equal Opportunity, with a 12-month lodgement window, acknowledgment of receipt within one week and a free conciliation conference as the next step. A complainant may instead use the federal route to the Australian Human Rights Commission under national sex discrimination law within 24 months, or 12 months for employment matters, but only one route may be chosen. TransFolk of WA and the Freedom Centre, the latter for people under 26, provide trans-specific support in the state.

Prison policy reported in November 2020 allows transgender prisoners to be housed according to their gender identity for health and safety reasons, provided their criminal record carries no sexual offences. Placement turns on that record check rather than operating as an unconditional entitlement.

No law in Western Australia prohibits conversion practices. The government said a bill would be introduced only after the March 2025 state election; as of September 2026 Western Australia and Tasmania were the only Australian jurisdictions without an explicit criminal prohibition, leaving Western Australia the only mainland state where the practices remain lawful. A Public Order Bill that would criminally ban harassment on grounds of sex, sexual orientation, gender identity and sex characteristics passed the lower house but had not passed the upper house. Announced reforms to the Equal Opportunity Act would add gender identity and sex characteristics as protected attributes and repeal the exemption allowing religious schools to discriminate; neither change had been enacted.

In October 2021 the Western Australia Supreme Court removed a transgender child from parental custody entirely over continuing abuse, the first order of its kind in the country, following the April 2021 death of a 15-year-old trans teenager in Perth that prompted calls to reform the birth-certificate law.

sources.summary: Western Australian law recognises a transgender person's change of sex, with sterilisation required before 2012 until the High Court in AB v Western Australia (2012) held two transgender men who had undergone mastectomies and hormone treatment did not need sterilisation to obtain a gender recognition certificate. Legislation introduced in August 2018 repealed the requirement to be unmarried for a change of sex on a birth certificate, passing the lower house on 20 November 2018 and the upper house on 12 February 2019, receiving royal assent on 19 February 2019 and commencing on 19 March 2019. The Births, Deaths, Marriages Registration Amendment (Sex or Gender Changes) Act 2024 passed both chambers in September 2024 to formally abolish and repeal the WA Gender Reassignment Board, receiving assent on 26 September 2024 and taking effect on 30 May 2025. That Act permits male, female, indeterminate/intersex and nonbinary options and allows change of sex on a birth certificate once a year on appropriate clinical treatment signed off by a doctor, nurse or psychologist with no sexual reassignment surgery required, subject to a $195 non-refundable fee and up to 4 weeks waiting. Reported November 2020 policy allows transgender prisoners to be housed according to their own gender identity for strict health and safety reasons so long as they have no sexual offences on their criminal record. In October 2021 a Western Australia Supreme Court order in an Australian legal first removed custody entirely from a family for continuing abuse of their transgender child, following the April 2021 suicide of a 15-year-old transgender teenager in Perth that prompted calls to immediately reform archaic birth-certificate sex or gender legislation. Private same-sex acts were decriminalised by the Law Reform (Decriminalisation of Sodomy) Act 1989 effective 23 March 1990, but the Act set the age of consent at 21 for homosexual male acts versus 16 for heterosexual acts and created offences of promoting or encouraging homosexual behaviour in primary or secondary teaching or public policy. Historical homosexual convictions became expungeable under the Historical Homosexual Convictions Expungement Bill 2017, passed by the Assembly on 22 February 2018 and the Council with amendments on 23 August 2018, approved on 11 September 2018, assented on 18 September 2018 and effective 15 October 2018, requiring a mandatory test of historical homosexual offence considering consent and ages and allowing family members of deceased persons to apply, accompanied by the Premier's formal parliamentary apology to the LGBTIQ community. The Equal Opportunity Act 1984 was amended in 2002 to prohibit sexual-orientation discrimination in employment, education, accommodation and provision of goods, services and facilities, supplemented federally by the Sex Discrimination Amendment (Sexual Orientation, Gender Identity and Intersex Status) Act 2013. No law in Western Australia currently bans conversion therapy, with the government stating a bill would only be introduced after the March 2025 state election, leaving WA as the only mainland state to legally allow the practices and, as of September 2026 with Tasmania, the only Australian places without explicit criminal prohibition. A 2026 Public Order Bill to explicitly criminally ban harassment based on sex, sexual orientation, gender identity and sex characteristics passed the lower house but had yet to pass the upper house.

82085004B40257551482390.name: Australian Capital Territory
82085004B40257551482390.summary:
Visitors in every state stand under the national framework: gender identity is a protected ground under the federal Sex Discrimination Act, and marriage and federal documents are uniform nationwide.

The territory's Human Rights Act 2004 requires public authorities to act compatibly with human rights and enables courts to issue declarations of inconsistency, giving a visitor who encounters discriminatory conduct by a police officer, public servant or public facility a legal review mechanism that common-law states without a charter lack. The territory is also one of four jurisdictions with an explicit self-identification basis for prison placement, reducing the risk of inappropriate custody for a detained gender-nonconforming visitor.

No region-specific incident series, enforcement pattern or institutional-failure finding was identified in the dossier for this territory; the absence of negative evidence, combined with the structural rights protection and the self-identification custody rule, places it modestly above the national average.

A conversion-practices ban has been in force since early 2021, with offending practices attracting up to a 12-month custodial term or a fine, alongside civil penalties giving a tribunal power to issue orders and order redress; practices supporting someone undergoing or considering a gender transition are explicitly not banned. No visitor documents or border-screening practice specific to this territory is recorded in the dossier.

sources.summary: ABC News, 3 Jul 2020: national survey of trans prisoners — experts estimate up to 400 trans and gender-diverse people in Australian cells, often inappropriately housed and at elevated risk of physical and sexual violence; NSW, Victoria, the ACT and Tasmania run explicit self-identification policies while QLD/NT/SA are unclear. ACT-relevant: names the ACT's explicit self-ID prison policy.

The Human Rights Law Centre report 'Ending Strip Searching in Australian prisons' (2026), produced with the trans-community groups Flat Out and FIGJAM, documents strip-searching practice in Australian prisons, including those in the ACT, and its disproportionate harms for trans, gender-diverse and Indigenous prisoners.

sources.title: Human Rights Act 2004 | Acts | ACT Legislation Register
sources.summary: The official ACT Legislation Register lists the Human Rights Act 2004 (A2004-5) as In Force, with the current republished version and a full republication history back to 1 July 2004. Section 31 provides that interpreters may consider international law and the judgments of foreign and international courts and tribunals relevant to a human right. The register also records uncommenced amendments by the Human Rights (Housing) Amendment Act 2025. The Act is the statutory rights framework that ACT public authorities must operate within.

sources.title: Serious barriers in accessing health care for Canberra's transgender community highlighted in new study - ABC News
sources.summary: ABC News reported on 16 April 2022 that the ACT government's LGBTIQ+ Health Scoping Study found serious barriers for transgender and gender-diverse Canberrans: a shortage of primary-care professionals, including GPs, mental-health supports and paediatric specialists with LGBTIQ+ health understanding, resulting in 'excessive wait times, delays from referrals and high costs associated with interstate and international travel'. The article records 20 young transgender people on the waitlist of Canberra's only paediatric endocrinologist, some patients waiting a year for an appointment, GP demand rising 20-40 per cent a year, and the study calling the ACT 'the only jurisdiction not to have a comprehensive gender-focused health service' in private practice or through a publicly-funded gender clinic. The study documents a shortfall of institutional capacity for transgender health care in the ACT.

sources.title: LGBTQ conversion therapy banned in Canberra as Sexuality and Gender Identity Conversion Practices Bill passes - ABC News
sources.summary: ABC News reported on 27 August 2020 that the ACT Legislative Assembly passed the Sexuality and Gender Identity Conversion Practices Bill, so that from early 2021 conversion practices used on protected persons attract up to a 12-month jail term or a $24,000 fine, alongside civil penalties giving the ACT Civil and Administrative Tribunal power to issue orders and order redress. The bill was amended before passage after the Association of Christian Schools and the ACT Law Society argued the definition of conversion practice was 'too broad and vague', while practices supporting someone undergoing or considering a gender transition were explicitly not banned. The statute is an ACT criminal and civil protection measure.

25490228B8471183517505.name: Castilla y León
25490228B8471183517505.summary:
Castilla y León operates under Spain's national legal framework on gender recognition and anti-discrimination. Its own regional protection layer has been the subject of legislative activity rather than settled law: in December 2024 the PSOE parliamentary group registered a bill for the real and effective equality of LGBTI+ people in Castilla y León, one of three bills the group tabled that week. The bill's stated purpose includes ending the out-migration of LGBTI people from the region, and the group's leader, Tudanca, called for the fastest possible processing.

On 11 June 2025 the Cortes de Castilla y León voted to take the PSOE-sponsored LGTBI+ bill into consideration. The text runs to 76 articles and answers long-standing demands of the region's LGBTI+ collectives. The motion carried; the Partido Popular abstained and Vox voted against. Taking the bill into consideration opens debate, and LGBTI advocates have said they fear the process could stall in committee, which would leave the initiative without effect.

No regional LGBTI equality statute in force in Castilla y León appears in the material reviewed, and no region-specific rules on identity documents, facility access, health care or hate-crime enforcement were identified for the region. A trans visitor to Castilla y León encounters no documented regional-layer rule that departs from the national framework; the open question is whether the pending bill becomes law.

Diario de Castilla y Leon (11 Jun 2025): the plenary approved taking the LGTBI equality bill into debate with opposition support except Vox and PP abstention; LGBTI advocates fear the process could stall in committee.

25490228B48808997991554.name: Ciudad Autónoma de Ceuta
25490228B48808997991554.summary:
Ceuta is an autonomous city of Spain with no LGTBI or gender-identity statute of its own. It stands under the national framework of Ley 4/2023 and central-government policy, and no regional ordinance supplements them, so a trans visitor deals directly with Spanish law and Spanish institutions rather than with any local statute.

FELGTBI+'s September 2025 radiography of LGTBI+ public policy, prepared with the Universidad de Salamanca, names Asturias, Castilla y León, Ceuta and Melilla as the only Spanish territories still without a specific law on the promotion of LGTBI+ rights. The report records legislative progress in Castilla y León and Asturias in June 2025 and no equivalent step for Ceuta or Melilla.

The gap is not new. A 2020 precedent study cited in the same body of work placed Ceuta and Melilla at the tail of rankings for the recognition and protection of trans students.

Protection questions in Ceuta also run through migration. Europa Press reported on 17 September 2026 that the LGTBI+ association Arcópoli wrote to the Secretary of State for Migration, Pilar Cancela, demanding the urgent transfer to the peninsula of LGTBI+ migrants remaining in Ceuta after thousands entered irregularly on 30 and 31 July. Arcópoli described transfer as the only effective measure to guarantee their protection and inclusion, cited the extreme vulnerability of people fleeing criminalisation and persecution in countries including Morocco, and launched a free remote social, psychological and legal support service for those in Ceuta.

For a visitor, the practical consequence is that no regional layer of LGTBI+ policy exists to consult or appeal to: recognition, anti-discrimination and criminal-law protection operate through the national framework, and the documented deficit is one of regional legislation and regional-level provision rather than of a hostile local statute.

25490228B18225280299410.name: Ciudad Autónoma de Melilla
25490228B18225280299410.summary:
Ciudad Autónoma de Melilla has no autonomous LGTBI or gender-identity statute. An index of Spain's regional LGTBI legislation states expressly that Melilla and Ceuta have no laws of this kind and rely instead on the national framework and on central-government equality policies. The city therefore stands entirely under Spanish national law for legal gender recognition, anti-discrimination protection, criminal aggravating circumstances and access to facilities, and no city-level rule either adds to or subtracts from those guarantees.

The only city-level instrument touching partnership recognition is a registry for unmarried couples, created in Melilla in 2008. Comparable registries exist in Ceuta and across the mainland communities, and the benefits they confer on unmarried couples are regarded as mainly symbolic. The Melilla registry is not an LGTBI or gender-identity statute and does not modify the national rules on marriage or adoption, so a trans visitor's recognition as a partner or spouse rests on the national framework rather than on anything the city has enacted.

15666254B53975248776023.name: Kelantan
15666254B53975248776023.summary:
Kelantan is a state of Malaysia, and its Syariah criminal jurisdiction operates within the national legal framework; the provisions set out below are specific to Kelantan. The state assembly passed the Syariah Criminal Offences (Kelantan) Bill 2026 on 13 August 2026, legislating decency, the covering of aurat, and gender change as matters of Islamic criminal law. The enactment replaces 16 provisions of the Kelantan Syariah Criminal Code Enactment 2019 that the Federal Court struck down in February 2024, so the state's regulation of dress, modesty and gender presentation has been rebuilt on a new statutory basis rather than withdrawn. Clause 15 requires Muslims to safeguard the sanctity and modesty of their private parts in accordance with Islamic law.

The state legislature has placed gender change expressly inside the criminal jurisdiction of Islamic law, and the new decency and gender-change provisions are in force and being applied by the Syariah courts from 2026. For a trans visitor in Kelantan, a presentation or a document that raises a gender-change question therefore falls under provisions drafted for that subject, with the operative boundaries set by the state's religious courts rather than by anything the Federal Court's 2024 ruling settled.

A February 2026 case, decided before the bill was tabled, was the first Kelantan Syariah Court matter involving gender change. Judicial practice on the question was already running in the state in the months before the replacement enactment came into force.

15666254B71460903090065.name: Terengganu
15666254B71460903090065.summary:
Terengganu is a state of Malaysia and stands under the national framework; the federal Penal Code and the national rules on identity documents, entry and enforcement apply here as they do elsewhere in the country. The findings below are specific to Terengganu.

Official state-level hostility toward LGBTQ people is stated openly. In May 2025 a Terengganu state executive councillor confirmed that warning signboards against homosexual practices, installed at strategic locations in the state, are intended to instil hatred of those acts, and said the state wants people to regard them as "dirty, wrong, and to be avoided". The statement is an endorsement of hostility by a serving member of the state government rather than a remark by a private individual, and it sets the posture a visibly gender-nonconforming visitor moves through in the state.

The signboards drew a public challenge. In May 2025 thirteen civil-society organisations, among them Justice for Sisters, called on the Kuala Terengganu City Council to take the signboards down, describing them as discriminatory and as a violation of international human rights law, and criticising the executive councillor's defence of them as incitement to hatred and discrimination against LGBTQ people. The appeal was directed at the municipal authority associated with the signboards' placement.

Terengganu's own Sharia enactment carries a longer institutional-rehabilitation term than the six months recorded in some other states. A 2022 amendment extended to one year the period for which a person convicted under the state enactment may be ordered into counselling or rehabilitation at a religious institution, a custodial and institutional alternative to imprisonment available to the state's Sharia courts.

For this record: official state-level endorsement of anti-homosexual messaging — a direct indicator of the hostile official stance a transgender visitor faces in Terengganu.

Thirteen civil-society organisations including Justice for Sisters (May 2025) urged the Kuala Terengganu City Council to remove anti-LGBT signboards, condemning them as discriminatory and a violation of international human rights law; they criticised the Terengganu state executive councillor's defence of the signboards as inciting hatred and discrimination against LGBTQ individuals. For this record: corroborates the official anti-LGBT campaign in Terengganu and documents civil-society pushback with named actors.

15666254B71428205180864.name: Kedah
15666254B71428205180864.summary:
Kedah's own criminal law is set out in the Syariah Criminal Offences (Kedah Darul Aman) Enactment 2014 (En.18/2014). Sections 23 and 24 criminalise liwat and musahaqah, punishable by a fine of up to RM5,000, up to three years' imprisonment, up to six strokes of whipping, or any combination of those penalties. Section 26 criminalises a male posing as a woman in public, carrying a fine of up to RM1,000 or up to one year's imprisonment. Female cross-dressing is not an offence under the enactment, so the state's public-presentation offence falls asymmetrically on trans women and on anyone read as male presenting as a woman. Section 52 allows a woman convicted of musahaqah to be committed to an approved home for up to six months in addition to the sentence imposed.

Enforcement in Kedah has reached private gatherings. In October 2020 a private birthday party was raided and 30 trans women were singled out and arrested, while the event organiser was placed under investigation for "encouraging vice". A coalition of Malaysian human-rights groups publicly objected to the probe, describing a pattern in which organisers and allies of transgender people are pursued alongside those who attend.

65028918B28366581005022.summary:
West Java stands under the national framework of Indonesia; the findings below are those specific to the province.

On 22 June 2025 the West Java Regional Police detained 75 people at a privately rented villa in the Puncak area of Bogor Regency, acting on a tip from local residents. Police described the gathering as an LGBT "family gathering" held "to avoid detection".

Amnesty International condemned the arrests on 24 June 2025 as a discriminatory raid and "a blatant violation of human rights and privacy", stated that the gathering violated no law, and demanded the release of those held and accountability for the operation.

In August 2026 men doused a trans woman with what appeared to be urine on a street in Bogor, one of a wave of attacks on trans women in the province.

Activists link that violence to a 2025 presidential regulation classifying the spread of LGBTQ culture as a non-military threat and to discriminatory regional regulations, arguing that official language of this kind legitimises violence against trans women.

A trans woman quoted in the reporting said that people who previously appeared in public now live in fear.

65028918B4119458748300.name: West Sumatra
65028918B4119458748300.summary:
West Sumatra stands under Indonesia's national legal framework, which carries the criminal provisions, document rules and entry regime; what follows is specific to the province.

Two local instruments in West Sumatra restrict LGBT people. Bukittinggi City's Regional Regulation No. 2 of 2024 on Public Order targets LGBT people and is framed as an expression of local religious values and Minangkabau customary norms. In Limapuluh Kota regency the regional legislature finalised a draft anti-LGBT regulation on 13 May 2026, folded into a Public Order and Tranquillity (Trantibum) regulation; the chair of the drafting body said the drafting stages had reached finalisation.

The Limapuluh Kota text provides for administrative fines and rehabilitation for LGBT people. Neither instrument is recorded as carrying criminal penalties; the sanctions documented are administrative fines and mandated rehabilitation, which directs LGBT people into a corrective programme rather than a fine alone.

Both instruments operate through public-order powers rather than the criminal code, so their reach is conduct in public space in the two named localities. No West Sumatra-specific enforcement action, arrest or prosecution appears in the source inventory, so a trans visitor's exposure in the province rests on these two instruments and on the national framework.

For this record: documents a 2024 local anti-LGBT public-order regulation in a West Sumatra city, showing formal municipal-level restrictions.

Peer-reviewed study (2025) of LGBT cases in Bukittinggi City, West Sumatra: recorded cases rose from 56 individuals in 2023 to 272 in 2024; the Kurai Customary Law Community (Masyarakat Hukum Adat Kurai) acts as a non-state actor, initiating the customary sanction 'dibuang sepanjang adat' (expulsion under adat), proposing village regulations on social deviance, and implementing barcode monitoring in boarding houses to police LGBT presence. For this record: documents rising state-and-adat surveillance and customary sanctions against LGBT people within a West Sumatra city.

Mimbarsumbar.id (13 May 2026): the DPRD (regional legislature) of Limapuluh Kota regency, West Sumatra, finalised a draft anti-LGBT regional regulation (Ranperda) within a Public Order and Tranquility (Trantibum) regulation, including administrative fines and rehabilitation for LGBT people; the drafting body chair stated the stages have reached finalisation. For this record: a 2026 draft regency-level regulation introducing fines and 'rehabilitation' targeting LGBT people in West Sumatra.

OutRight Action International, 'Creeping Criminalisation' (Katjasungkana & Wieringa; cached copy): maps discriminatory national laws and regional regulations across eight Indonesian provinces (Aceh, DKI Jakarta, East Kalimantan, Lampung, North Sumatra, South Sulawesi, South Sumatra, Yogyakarta) - the reference for Indonesia's regional-bylaw mechanism; West Sumatra's newer Bukittinggi regulation postdates the mapping.

65028918B6690755070061.name: Bali
65028918B6690755070061.summary:
Bali stands under Indonesia's national framework, and that framework is where the legal risk sits. The national penal code signed in December 2022 took effect on 2 January 2026 and penalises consensual extra-marital sex between adults with up to two years' imprisonment. Because same-sex marriage is not permitted anywhere in Indonesia, that provision reaches consensual relations involving a trans visitor that would be locally classed as same-sex; reporting indicates prosecutions are selective rather than systematic. Same-sex marriage remains unrecognised for visitors and residents alike.

Bali's own social environment differs from the national legal picture. Peer-reviewed ethnographic fieldwork published in 2025, drawing on four case studies in Bali, documents a visible transpuan (trans feminine) community living with precarity, discrimination and informal resistance, challenging narratives of pure victimhood while confirming real material insecurity.

Traveller-facing guidance rates Bali 6.3 out of 10 overall but gives it a legal score of 2.0, warning that LGBTQ+ travellers face legal risk under Indonesian law and advising visitors to keep affection quiet despite the island's tolerant reputation. A March 2026 guide describes Bali as broadly welcoming on a 'live and let live' basis, while noting that the new Criminal Code in effect from January 2026 adds complexity to the legal backdrop. Same-sex relationships are not separately criminalised under a Bali-specific provision; the exposure runs through the national code.

Same-sex marriage is not legally recognised anywhere in Indonesia. Seminyak (Eat Street and Batu Belig), Canggu and Ubud are named as the most consistently LGBTQ+-friendly areas with active venues, and public displays of affection warrant discretion across the island.

For this record: academic ground-truth that Bali hosts a visible trans community living with precarity, discrimination, and informal resistance.

65028918B16658067687714.summary:

65028918B17554737605304.name: South Sulawesi
65028918B17554737605304.summary:
South Sulawesi is a province of Indonesia and stands under the national legal framework, which applies here in full.

OutRight Action International's 2022 report Creeping Criminalisation, by Katjasungkana and Wieringa, lists South Sulawesi among the eight Indonesian provinces it covers and records that provincial and city bylaws in these jurisdictions criminalise same-sex conduct and gender nonconformity, adopted under the regional-autonomy powers that let local legislatures pass their own regulations.

In Makassar, the mayor reaffirmed in April 2025 a commitment to push an anti-LGBT regional regulation (Perda) after a same-sex act at a night-entertainment venue circulated online. The deputy chair of the city legislature's law-drafting body (Bapemperda) backed the move, saying the regulation was needed to preserve moral and religious norms.

The proposal is not new. It entered the 2023 local legislative programme (prolegda) as a priority for discussion, and two city legislature members, including Azwar ST of the PKS faction, said it was modelled on regulations already passed elsewhere, such as Bogor. As of April 2026 the Makassar rule remained a draft (Ranperda) rather than an enacted regulation.

Official posture in the city has hardened independently of the draft's status. The Makassar city government's women's-empowerment and child-protection agency (DP3A) is running an LGBT "prevention" programme, and a city legislature member, Muchlis Misbah, backs the pending Ranperda on HIV/AIDS and LGBT as legal reinforcement.

31927357B17004778023462.name: Aguascalientes
31927357B17004778023462.summary:
Aguascalientes stands under Mexico's national framework, and legal gender recognition in Mexico is settled state by state. Human Rights Watch's state-by-state survey of 11 March 2025 records that Aguascalientes 'has not reformed its legislation to create a legal gender recognition procedure for transgender people'; its reporting of 31 March 2025 places the state among those that have not legislated such a procedure. The state therefore operates no administrative mechanism of its own for changing name or gender markers on official records.

The March 2024 Human Rights Watch report on the cost of absent recognition names Aguascalientes among the non-reforming states whose trans residents have no lawful marker procedure. Its documented consequence is that trans people carry documents contradicting their lived identity, which amplifies discrimination in banking, health care and dealings with police.

A court-ordered route now exists. Infobae reported on 9 April 2026 that the Supreme Court, in Amparo en Revisión 430/2025 on a draft by Minister Giovanni Figueroa Mejía, held that the state Civil Code's requirements for changing the gender on a birth certificate, namely judicial or ministerial intervention, civil trials, probative proof of identity and marginal annotations, are discriminatory and violate privacy. The Court ordered the Civil Registry to grant recognition through a simple, confidential administrative procedure honouring self-perception, issuing a new birth certificate with no marginal note revealing a prior gender. The immediate effect is confined to the persons represented by the civil association that brought the case, so the ruling establishes a recognition route in the absence of legislative reform without yet establishing one for the state's trans population generally.

No trans-specific homicide offence covers the state. The Guardian reported on 24 July 2024 that Mexico City criminalised transfemicide; Aguascalientes is among the states that have adopted no comparable reform.

Violence and coercive practice persist according to local accounts. La Jornada Aguascalientes reported on 23 August 2026 that activists Alicia Cruz, Kevin Cruz and Hened Musalem of Diversx Laboratorio Cultural Disidente say conversion-therapy operations continue in the state under the guise of addiction-treatment annexes despite the legal prohibition, and that a person who escaped one such space reached the group the previous year. The same activists state that trans women continue to suffer prejudice-motivated aggression.

31927357B35339934753022.name: Baja California
31927357B35339934753022.summary:
Baja California is among the Mexican states that have legislated an administrative procedure for legal gender recognition. The state congress created the procedure through a 2022 reform to the Civil Code, initially limited to adults. In June 2023 the Supreme Court of Justice of the Nation invalidated the 18-years requirement, holding that the law failed to recognise the rights of transgender children and adolescents, and the state congress responded with a further reform in 2024 establishing a procedure for individuals under 18 and extending legal gender recognition to non-binary people.

No criminalisation of trans presence applies. The national framework, as Human Rights Watch set out on 31 March 2025, leaves legal gender recognition to the states and records a patchwork of procedures whose implementation differs sharply; where recognition is absent or obstructed, requests for identity documents expose trans people to discrimination, violence and humiliation. Baja California sits on the reformed side of that patchwork, but the gap between statute and practice documented across Mexico applies here as elsewhere: Caroline Beer's analysis for LSE USAPP (22 November 2024) concludes that Mexico's progressive LGBTQ+ legislation is rarely enforced fairly or uniformly.

Lethal violence against women in the state is under-classified. Zeta Tijuana reported on 8 March 2025 that under Governor Marina del Pilar Ávila 1,179 women have been killed in Baja California while only 110 cases were typified as feminicide. The same reporting places female economic participation in the state at roughly 46-47%, 14th of 32 states.

Extradition machinery has been used in feminicide cases. Zeta Tijuana reported on 8 July 2023 that Brayan Rivera was presented on 6 July 2023 before US Judge Karen L. Stevenson in provisional detention for extradition, accused by Mexico of the feminicide of Ángela Carolina Acosta, killed on 24 January 2022 in room 404 of Hotel Cascadas beside Bar Hong Kong in Tijuana's tolerance zone. A US federal court determined probable cause on 29 June 2023; he was arrested at his parents' Downey, California home, where officers found the Hotel Cascadas rent receipt and rope and gloves. At a 7 July 2023 press conference the Baja California attorney general called the 30-year-old a serial perpetrator, said extradition could take from 15 days to two years, and that nearly a decade of open case files were being reviewed; the investigation had linked him to at least three feminicides: Ángela (January 2022), Elizabeth (14 February), and Karen, 28 (30 August 2021, Motel Hacienda Soler).

Partnership recognition is settled at the national level: same-sex marriage has been legal across Mexico since 2009.

31927357B33389180120223.name: Baja California Sur
31927357B33389180120223.summary:

31927357B65177449444732.name: Chiapas
31927357B65177449444732.summary:
Chiapas is a state of Mexico and sits under the national framework that governs identity documents and criminal law. Its legislature has not created a legal gender recognition procedure. As of March 2025, no administrative route existed in the state for changing the name or gender marker recorded on identity documents, and Human Rights Watch's state-by-state assessment places Chiapas among the states that have not reformed their legislation on this point.

Recognition therefore runs through the courts alone. A trans person in Chiapas who needs documents matching their identity must bring an individual petition before a judge, with no administrative application to file and no published standard governing the result; the documents stay as issued until a ruling is handed down. Human Rights Watch describes the position of residents as mismatched documents combined with case-by-case judicial recourse. A visitor cannot obtain corrected documents from Chiapas either, since the state operates no such procedure; the papers a visitor carries are the papers presented.

Human Rights Watch has urged the states that lack a recognition procedure to adopt one, and promotes a simple self-identification mechanism as the remedy. No such mechanism has been adopted in Chiapas.

31927357B49801195703560.name: Chihuahua
31927357B49801195703560.summary:
Chihuahua stands under Mexico's national framework; the national legal-gender-recognition and anti-violence layer is carried by the Mexico record. What is specific to the state is procedural. As of March 2025 the state congress had enacted no legislative reform recognising gender identity, and the state's civil registry operates an administrative practice of recognition instead. Human Rights Watch's state-by-state review of 31 March 2025 places Chihuahua among 22 of Mexico's 32 states whose procedure runs on administrative practice rather than statute, following the 2019 Supreme Court ruling that struck down the requirement to obtain recognition through a court process.

A trans visitor or resident dealing with the Chihuahua civil registry is therefore relying on an administrative procedure rather than on an entitlement written into state law. The procedure exists and was counted as operative as of March 2025. Its criteria, its cost, the documents it demands and its availability to minors are not described in the sourcing.

No Chihuahua-specific finding appears in the available sourcing on enforcement of the recognition procedure, on trans-specific violence in the state, on hate-crime protection, on police or custodial treatment, on health-care access, or on access to facilities. Those questions are answered, where they can be, by the national record for Mexico.

31927357B32124965101143.name: Coahuila de Zaragoza
31927357B32124965101143.summary:
Coahuila de Zaragoza, one of Mexico's states, runs its own administrative procedure for legal gender recognition. The congress of Coahuila passed the Ley del Registro Civil del Estado de Coahuila in 2018; articles 124 to 128 of that law establish the administrative procedure by which a person's self-identified gender identity is recognised. Human Rights Watch's March 2025 tracker of legal gender recognition across Mexico's states records Coahuila among those that have legislated such a procedure and links the official gazette text of the reform at articles 124 to 128.

The law defines the concept it administers. Article 2, fraction XI, of the Civil Registry law defines gender identity as a personal and internal conviction. The 2018 reform also amended article 133 of the Ley para la Familia de Coahuila de Zaragoza, so the change reached the state's family law alongside the registry.

Use of the procedure is documented. The director of Coahuila's Civil Registry, Ricardo Malacara, said that between early 2019 and March 2023 around 1,500 people in the state completed the legal gender-identity change before the registry, in both directions, male to female and female to male.

Human Rights Watch's state-by-state tracker on legal gender recognition in Mexico (March 2025) records this among the 32 states that have legislated such a procedure, alongside the Supreme Court rulings that drove the expansion.

Human Rights Watch report 'I Just Want to Contribute to Society' (6 March 2024) on Tabasco, cited as a baseline for how a state without a legal gender-recognition procedure behaves: no administrative procedure exists there, the August 2023 killing of activist Karina Gomez remained unsolved, hate-motivation provisions are absent from Tabasco's criminal code, and healthcare staff out patients by calling legal names.

Tangential to Coahuila: Mexico City made transfemicide a crime on 18 July 2024, with sentences up to 70 years under the Paola Buenrostro law, in one of Latin America's deadliest settings for trans people, the Guardian reported on 24 July 2024. More than 95% of homicides nationally went unpunished in 2022.

sources.summary: National framework (HRW, 31 Mar 2025): legal gender recognition in Mexico is set state by state. As of March 2025, 22 of the 32 states had legislated an administrative recognition procedure, two more run one in practice without enactment, six legislatures have enacted none, and only seven states extend recognition to children. Mexico's Supreme Court set binding guidelines for the states and extended the right to minors in 2022; the Inter-American Court requires a simple, accessible procedure. HRW documents the consequences where no procedure exists: identity-document mismatch drives discrimination in schools, medical clinics and the labour market, incidents recorded in Guanajuato and Tabasco. The operative framework for Colima is this national picture, not any locally enacted certainty.

HRW and the Community Center for Inclusion reported on 6 Mar 2024 from Tabasco, a Mexican state with no legal gender-recognition procedure: without identity documents matching a trans person's gender, every document request or appearance scrutiny carries risk of violence, harassment and humiliation, excluding trans people from employment, health services, education and financial transactions. The context includes the Aug 2023 murder of trans woman Karina Gomez in Villahermosa and more than 95% of homicides nationally going unpunished in 2022. The account shows what an absent state procedure means for trans people, and bears on Colima.

The Guardian (24 Jul 2024): Mexico City passed the 'Paola Buenrostro law' in July 2024, making transfemicide a crime punishable by up to 70 years, the second of Mexico's 32 states to criminalise it after Nayarit (up to 60 years). In 2022 more than 95% of homicides in Mexico went unpunished, with transfemicide impunity thought higher still. sources.title: LGBTQ rights in Mexico (Wikipedia)
sources.summary: On 13 March 2004 amendments to the Mexico City Civil Code took effect allowing transgender people to change gender and name on their birth certificates. In September 2008 the Mexico City Legislative Assembly passed a law making it easier for transgender people to change their gender on birth certificates. On 13 November 2014 the Legislative Assembly of Mexico City approved a gender identity law making the process for transgender people to change gender much quicker and simpler. On 13 July 2017 the Michoacan Congress approved a gender identity law and on 20 July 2017 a gender identity law was approved in Nayarit. On 17 October 2018 the Supreme Court held that a transgender person could change name and gender marker on official documents through a simple administrative process based solely on their own declaration of gender identity. On 13 November 2018 Coahuila passed a gender identity bill allowing transgender individuals easier access to birth certificates reflecting their new legal gender. On 25 April 2019 the Hidalgo Congress approved a gender identity law and on 17 May 2019 San Luis Potosi began authorizing legal gender changes for transgender people. Private same-sex sexual conduct between adults ceased to be a criminal matter in 1871 through adoption of the Napoleonic Code. On 2 September 1999 Mexico City passed an ordinance banning discrimination based on sexual orientation, the first of its kind in the country. A federal anti-discrimination law took effect on 11 June 2003 creating a national council to enforce it. Article 1 of the Federal Constitution was amended in 2001 to prohibit discrimination under the term preferences and in June 2011 the more precise term sexual orientation was inserted. Mexico City passed same-sex marriage on 21 December 2009 with effect on 4 March 2010 and the Supreme Court upheld its constitutionality on 5 August 2010 by 9 to 2. On 3 June 2015 the Supreme Court released a jurisprudential thesis deeming laws restricting marriage to a man and a woman unconstitutional and requiring every judge to validate same-sex unions through amparo, with a nationwide adoption jurisprudence finalized on 23 September 2016. By 31 December 2022 every state had legalized same-sex marriage by legislation, executive order or judicial ruling though only twenty allowed those couples to adopt children. Civil unions for same-sex and opposite-sex couples are performed in Campeche, Coahuila, Mexico City, Michoacan, Sinaloa, Tlaxcala and Veracruz. Acceptance of transgender identities has been documented among Isthmus Zapotecs and Yucatan Mayas, with Zapotecs recognizing a traditional third gender known as muxe intermediate between male and female. Muxes are assigned male at birth but typically act and behave like women and do both women and men's work, and having a muxe in the family is perceived as good luck and a blessing. The article states: "Although they are perceived to be different from the general heterosexual male population, they are neither devalued nor discriminated against in their communities." It further states: "Mestizos, especially mestizo police, occasionally harass and even persecute muxe boys, but Zapotec parents, especially mothers and other women, are quick to defend them and their rights to \"be themselves\", because, as they put it, \"God made them that way.\"" It adds: "I have never heard an Isthmus Zapotec suggest that a muxe chose to become a muxe." Visible and well-attended LGBTQ marches and pride parades have occurred in Mexico City since 1979, in Guadalajara since 1996, and in Monterrey since 2001.

In late August 2008 the legislature passed 37-17 a law formalising the procedure for name changes and revised birth certificates reflecting gender identity, replacing a prior process without specific rules that could take years in court.

Gender identity laws followed in Michoacan on 13 July 2017, Nayarit on 20 July 2017, Coahuila on 13 November 2018, Hidalgo on 25 April 2019, and San Luis Potosi began authorising legal gender changes on 17 May 2019. On 17 October 2018 the Supreme Court held that a transgender person could change name and gender marker on official documents through a simple administrative process based solely on their own declaration of gender identity.

Mexico City legalised marriage for same-sex couples on 21 December 2009, effective 4 March 2010, and the Supreme Court upheld its constitutionality on 5 August 2010 by 9 to 2. On 3 June 2015 the Court released a jurisprudential thesis deeming laws restricting marriage to a man and a woman unconstitutional and requiring every judge to validate same-sex unions through amparo, with a nationwide adoption jurisprudence finalised on 23 September 2016. By 31 December 2022 every state had legalised same-sex marriage by legislation, executive order or judicial ruling, though only twenty allowed those couples to adopt children. Civil unions for same-sex and opposite-sex couples are performed in Campeche, Coahuila, Mexico City, Michoacan, Sinaloa, Tlaxcala and Veracruz.

31927357B15886886594254.name: Nayarit
31927357B15886886594254.summary:
Nayarit's gender-recognition and hate-violence rules operate inside Mexico's national legal framework. A 2017 reform of the state Civil Code established an administrative procedure for legal gender recognition, allowing adults to change identity documents to match their gender identity. Human Rights Watch's roundup of 31 March 2025 counts Nayarit among the states that have legislated such a procedure.

In 2024 Nayarit became the first of Mexico's 32 states to criminalise transfemicide, with a maximum sentence of 60 years. The offence is a distinct category in state law. No Nayarit-specific record of charges, prosecutions or convictions under it is available, so how the statute operates in practice is not established.

Nayarit is the first of Mexico's 32 states to criminalise transfemicide, introducing sentences of up to 60 years in 2024. 31927357B98648037880103.name: Queretaro de Arteaga
31927357B98648037880103.summary:
Querétaro de Arteaga is a state of Mexico and stands under the national framework; the legal gender recognition procedure and the penal code are matters for its own legislature. Querétaro has not reformed its legislation to create a legal gender recognition procedure for transgender people. Human Rights Watch's state-by-state table, current as of March 2025, lists Querétaro among the states that have never legislated any such procedure. A trans visitor has no state administrative route to align identity documents with lived identity, and the papers carried on arrival remain the only identification available.

Querétaro's Penal Code prohibits esfuerzos para corregir la orientación sexual y la identidad de género (ECOSIG), the practices commonly called conversion therapies. The reform was published and is in force. It carries a penalty of two to six years in prison, a fine of 20 to 2,000 times the UMA and 50 to 100 hours of community service, and treats the practices as discriminatory and torturous under articles 1 and 6 of the Inter-American Convention to Prevent and Punish Torture. Tribuna de Querétaro reported these terms on 20 September 2023, citing Walter López, spokesman for the Frente Queretano por el Derecho a la No Discriminación.

31927357B22618747134228.name: San Luis Potosi
31927357B22618747134228.summary:
San Luis Potosí sets its own rules on gender recognition, marriage and hate-crime aggravators within Mexico's national framework; the national layer is carried by the Mexico record. The state began authorising legal gender changes for transgender people on 17 May 2019, and is counted among the states that enacted a gender-identity law that year.

Partner recognition is settled at state level. The state Congress voted 14-12 on 16 May 2019 to approve same-sex marriage, which took effect on 21 May 2019, and joint adoption by same-sex couples became legal in the state in the same month. A trans visitor whose relationship would be read as same-sex under birth-sex status can therefore marry and be treated as a spouse here, and such couples can adopt jointly.

The state's hate-crime statute treats motivation by gender and sexual preference as an aggravating factor. On the source's wording the provision names gender and sexual preference rather than gender identity.

The state's anti-discrimination law bans discrimination on grounds of sexual orientation and gender, but not gender identity. Gender-identity discrimination therefore falls outside the state's own prohibition even though the hate-crime statute reaches gender-based motivation.

31927357B37261891092938.name: Sonora
31927357B37261891092938.summary:
Sonora is a state of Mexico and stands under the national framework of Mexico, which carries the country-level legal and enforcement picture; the findings below are those of the state itself.

Sonora's Congress approved the Ley de Identidad de Género on 1 October 2020, the Hermosillo daily El Sol de Hermosillo reported at the time, creating a state procedure for people who identify with the opposite gender to modify their official documentation. Wikipedia's LGBT rights in Mexico page lists Sonora among 25 Mexican states with a gender identity law dated to 2020 and describes the statute as giving trans people a statutory route to rectify gender on civil documents.

The state's protections extend past documents. On 6 December 2022 Sonora's Congress banned conversion therapies (ECOSIG). Sonora's hate-crime legislation recognises motivation by gender and sexual preference as an aggravating factor, and the state ratified the 2011 constitutional amendment prohibiting discrimination on grounds of sexual orientation.

Marriage between partners of the same legal sex is available in Sonora; by 31 December 2022 every Mexican state, Sonora included, had legalised it by legislation, executive order or judicial ruling. A trans visitor whose relationship would be locally classed as same-sex falls under the same recognition.

No source in the inventory records how these provisions are enforced in Sonora, and no trans-specific violence or incident data for the state was identified. The formal protections exist on the statute book; the state-level enforcement record is undocumented in these sources.

31927357B81008000569871.name: Tabasco
31927357B81008000569871.summary:
Tabasco is a state of Mexico. It has not reformed its legislation and operates no legal gender recognition procedure; Human Rights Watch reported on 31 March 2025 that the state is one of eight in Mexico with no such procedure.

Without a procedure, a trans person's identity documents never match their gender. Mismatched documents invite police stops and institutional mistreatment.

Human Rights Watch's Tabasco-dedicated report, published on 6 March 2024 and produced with a local community centre for inclusion, documents that the documentary mismatch curtails rights across four socio-economic areas.

The report sets those findings against the August 2023 murder of Karina Gómez, a trans woman killed in Tabasco.

31927357B88239390016047.name: Tamaulipas
31927357B88239390016047.summary:
Tamaulipas has not reformed its legislation to create a legal gender recognition procedure for transgender people, according to Human Rights Watch's state-by-state table dated 31 March 2025. The table places the state among eight Mexican states with no procedure at all. A trans person whose identity documents are issued in Tamaulipas therefore has no administrative route to change those documents to match their gender identity. Tamaulipas stands under Mexico's national framework, which governs passports, entry and federal enforcement.

On 18 June 2025 the Tamaulipas Congress unanimously approved reforms to the state Penal Code adding a chapter on crimes against sexual orientation, gender identity or gender expression. The reforms explicitly ban conversion therapies, with prison terms of two to six years and fines of up to 2,000 UMA. Penalties rise by half where victims are minors, disabled or elderly, or where the offence occurs in a subordinate setting such as the family, a medical context or the workplace. The state's criminal law thus protects gender identity even though no administrative gender-recognition procedure exists.

On 4 February 2026 deputies of Tamaulipas's 66th legislature and LGBT+ civil-society groups agreed a joint agenda to press for a Gender Identity Law and for anti-discrimination and health reforms. The initiatives have been pending since June 2025. The absent law continues to limit trans people's access to health care, education and employment. As of early 2026 no legal gender-recognition procedure exists in Tamaulipas and the Gender Identity Law remains unpassed.

31927357B35199150741361.name: Yucatan
31927357B35199150741361.summary:
Yucatán is one of Mexico's 32 states and stands under the national framework; the federal layer of law and enforcement is carried by the national record. The rules that govern a visitor's documents, marriage and access to conversion therapy inside the state are the state's own.

Legal gender recognition in Yucatán is administrative. In 2024 the state congress passed a reform to the Civil Registry Law creating a procedure through which transgender people can update the legal gender recorded on their documents without a court order. The reform was published in the state's official gazette, the Diario Oficial, on 26 April 2024. Human Rights Watch's state-by-state rundown of 11 March 2025 carries Yucatán on that basis. The operative fact for a visitor is that a Mexican identity document issued through Yucatán's registry can be corrected by application rather than litigation.

Marriage is open to same-sex couples in Yucatán, first through the courts and then by statute. On 1 July 2013 the Third District Court of the State of Yucatán ruled that two petitioners could marry, and the first same-sex marriage in the state was registered on 8 August 2013. The Yucatán Constitutional Court dismissed a challenge to the Civil Code's marriage provisions on 2 March 2015, and the federal Supreme Court dismissed the appeal on 31 May 2015. The Congress of Yucatán passed a constitutional amendment allowing same-sex marriage on 7 September 2021 and amended secondary legislation to permit it on 1 March 2022. A trans visitor whose relationship would be classed as same-sex under local law can marry here.

Yucatán enacted a conversion-therapy (ECOSIG) ban on 25 August 2021, making the practice unlawful for those who carry it out in the state.

31927357B22408340646138.name: Zacatecas
31927357B22408340646138.summary:
Zacatecas is a state of Mexico and stands under the national framework for passports, federal identity documents and federal criminal jurisdiction. The findings below are those specific to the state.

Zacatecas has a legislated administrative procedure for legal gender recognition. Deputies of the state's 64th Legislature approved a reform of the Family Code on gender identity on 23 December 2022 by 14 votes in favour to 7 against, after the Justice Committee issued a positive opinion on the measure. The reform establishes the possibility of issuing a new birth certificate recognising an applicant's gender identity, principally for the trans community. Zacatecas is not among the states identified as having no legislated gender-recognition procedure.

Implementation followed at the administrative level. In 2023 the director of the state Civil Registry issued guidelines giving effect to the law. Human Rights Watch's March 2025 state-by-state feature on legal gender recognition records both the 2022 Family Code reform and the 2023 Civil Registry guidelines for Zacatecas.

The state's criminal law carries its own protections. On 25 August 2021 the Congress of Zacatecas approved a prohibition and sanction on conversion therapies, known locally as ECOSIG, by adding fraction VI to article 182 Bis of the state Penal Code. Anyone who incites hatred or violence on grounds of sexual orientation, gender identity or expression, or who promotes such practices, faces one to three years' imprisonment or up to 300 days of community work. The same session typified hate crimes motivated by sexual orientation and gender identity in the state Penal Code.

Recognition came later than those protections. A gender-identity initiative debated in the same 2021 session, alongside a constitutional and family-code reform, failed to obtain enough votes and remained pending; the gender-identity reform passed in December 2022.

82249235B96958463903898.name: Newfoundland and Labrador
82249235B96958463903898.summary:
Police-reported hate crime in Newfoundland and Labrador ran at 5.3 per 100,000 in 2024, the joint-lowest provincial rate in the country alongside Manitoba. The figure rests on 29 incidents, up from 19 in 2023. At those volumes the 51 per cent increase is statistically fragile, and police counts record only incidents that were reported to police.

The province has not required surgery to change a gender marker since an amendment to the Vital Statistics Act, 2009 that received Royal Assent on 13 April 2016. That amendment followed a December 2015 ruling by a Board of Inquiry under the provincial Human Rights Commission on complaints brought by two trans women, and brought provincial law into line with the ruling.

A 2021 amendment extended change of sex designation to people who were not born in the province but have lived there at least three months. The resulting change certificate costs $25, counts as official provincial identification, and can be used by the holder to update records in other jurisdictions; for people born outside the country it serves as the identification document. The 2021 change followed earlier amendments that put a non-binary option on provincial birth certificates.

The province states that it cannot guarantee a birth certificate carrying an X gender marker will be accepted by authorities in other organisations, a caveat that matters for anyone relying on provincial documents after leaving Newfoundland and Labrador.

Gender identity is a prohibited ground of discrimination under the province's human rights legislation, covering employment, housing and public and private accommodations.

sources.summary: Statistics Canada (30 Mar 2026, police-reported hate crime 2024): 4,882 hate crimes reported nationally (+1% on 2023, after a +34% jump in 2023); national rate 12.1 per 100,000. Newfoundland and Labrador had the joint-lowest provincial rate at 5.3 per 100,000 (with Manitoba), while Ontario recorded the highest (16.0); the province's +51% rise reflects only 19 incidents in 2023 to 29 in 2024 — very small absolute numbers, so the rate change is statistically fragile. Federal criminal law and human-rights protections apply uniformly; police figures capture only reported incidents.

Egale Canada's 2024 hate-crime analysis report examines national police-reported hate-crime data, including offences motivated by sexual orientation and gender identity. Egale Canada is an LGBTIQ+ organisation.

sources.title: Changes to Vital Statistics Act Would Allow for Change of Sex Designation (Government of Newfoundland and Labrador news release)
sources.summary: Government of Newfoundland and Labrador news release, 17 June 2021: proposed changes to the Vital Statistics Act, 2009 would allow residents of the province who were not born there — but have lived there at least three months — to change their sex designation; the change certificate carries a $25 fee, counts as official provincial identification and 'could be leveraged by the applicant to update records in other jurisdictions,' serving as the identification document for people born outside the country. The release states the amendments align with earlier changes allowing a non-binary option on provincial birth certificates; the bill received second reading that day and Royal Assent on 23 June 2021. Gives the province a resident-based legal gender-change route (three-month residency) relevant to document enrolment for trans people in Newfoundland and Labrador.

sources.title: Legislative Amendment Respects Rights of Transgender Individuals (Government of Newfoundland and Labrador news release)
sources.summary: Government of Newfoundland and Labrador news release, 12 April 2016: an amendment to the Vital Statistics Act, 2009 removes the requirement to undergo sex-reassignment surgery before changing the gender marker on a birth or marriage registration, bringing provincial law into compliance with an order of a Board of Inquiry under the provincial Human Rights Commission (the December 2015 ruling on complaints from two trans women) and with LGBTQ advocates' requests. The province's gender-marker change on provincial records has therefore operated without a surgery requirement since the 2016 amendment (Royal Assent 13 April 2016).

sources.title: Changing Your Sex Designation (Government of Newfoundland and Labrador)
sources.summary: Current official Government of Newfoundland and Labrador page: applicants for a change of sex designation must be 16 or older, or be represented by a parent or legal guardian for under-16s (with consent of the other parent/guardian and written consent of individuals aged 12 to 15), and must be born in the province or have resided there at least three months; there is no fee for the change application, with charges applying only to official copies of updated documents (new birth certificate $35, or $30 online). The province states it cannot guarantee that a birth certificate with an 'X' gender marker will be accepted by authorities in other organisations — the documented cross-border document caveat relevant to carrying provincial records elsewhere.

sources.title: LGBTQ rights in Newfoundland and Labrador (Wikipedia)
sources.summary: Gender identity is explicitly included as a prohibited ground of discrimination in human rights acts in all provinces and territories and by the federal government as of 2017, prohibiting discrimination in employment, housing and public and private accommodations. Transgender people are able to change their legal gender in all provinces and territories under varying rules. The concepts of sex under section 15 of the Canadian Charter of Rights and Freedoms have been interpreted to include transsexuality, providing equality protection applicable to all laws and government institutions including law enforcement authorities. In Saskatchewan, The Education (Parents’ Bill of Rights) Amendment Act, 2023 invoked the notwithstanding clause to require schools to obtain parental consent for students under age 16 who request use of their gender-related preferred name or gender identity. In Alberta, the Health Statutes Amendment Act, 2024, Education Amendment Act, 2024, and Fairness and Safety in Sport Act were met with legal challenges, after which Bill 9: Protecting Alberta’s Children Statutes Amendment Act, 2025 invoked the notwithstanding clause. British Columbia, Ontario and Saskatchewan grant parental status to three or more intentional parents, allowing for a wider range of queer and trans families. Same-sex sexual activity in private between consenting adults was decriminalized on June 27, 1969 by the Criminal Law Amendment Act, 1968–69, with the general age of consent for all sexual activities 16 since June 2019, or 18 where there is a relationship of trust, authority or dependency. Section 159 of the Criminal Code on anal intercourse was declared unconstitutional by courts in Ontario, Quebec, British Columbia, Nova Scotia and Alberta, with repeal pursued through Bill C-32 incorporated into Bill C-75 receiving royal assent on June 21, 2019. The Expungement of Historically Unjust Convictions Act received royal assent on June 21, 2018, allowing the RCMP and federal departments or agencies to destroy or remove any judicial record of conviction for homosexual acts prior to being lawful in 1969 or anal intercourse under section 159. Sexual orientation was held constitutionally protected under section 15 in Egan v Canada in 1995, and failure to include it in human rights law was held a violation in Vriend v Alberta in 1998. Same-sex marriage was legalized nationwide on July 20, 2005 by the federal Civil Marriage Act, making Canada the fourth country in the world and first in the Americas to do so. Same-sex adoption was legalized in Newfoundland and Labrador in 2002, with joint adoption legalized in all provinces and territories by 2011, and conversion therapy was statutorily banned nationwide for minors and adults in 2022 and made a crime under the Criminal Code. A 2020 poll commissioned by the Privy Council Office found that 87.6% said they would be "comfortable" if a neighbour was a transgender person. The same poll separately measured sexuality tolerance, finding 91.8% said they would be "comfortable" if a next-door neighbour was gay, lesbian or bisexual, preserving a distinct result for transgender acceptance. 82249235B3191732862561.name: Prince Edward Island
82249235B3191732862561.summary:
Prince Edward Island stands under the national framework of Canada. The province's own rules govern gender-marker changes on provincial documents, driver's licence markers, and family law.

Prince Edward Island amended its Vital Statistics Act in 2016 so that a person can change the gender on provincial official documents by declaring the gender they identify with and providing a letter from a doctor. Sex-reassignment surgery is no longer required, and the province's gender-marker change has operated without a surgery requirement since that amendment.

The change of gender designation is not open to visitors. An adult applicant must have been born in Prince Edward Island and have lived in the province for at least three months, and must not be in the lawful custody of another person. A legal custodian may apply for a minor under 18 who was born on the island and has lived there at least three months, with the written consent of any other custodian or parent and of the child if the child is 12 or older.

Since 4 December 2018, provincial driver's licences can carry 'gender not listed' (shown as X) or 'prefer not to say' (shown as blank) alongside male and female, available at Access PEI locations.

The national police-reported hate-crime release for 2024 carries no Prince Edward Island-specific rate or incident count, and no provincially deviating pattern is documented for the province.

Prince Edward Island allowed joint adoption in 2009, extending the right to couples whose relationship is classed as same-sex under provincial law.

The release reports no Prince Edward Island-specific rate or incident count, and no provincially deviating pattern is documented for the province. sources.title: LGBTQ rights in Prince Edward Island (Wikipedia)
sources.summary: Discrimination on the basis of gender identity or expression in employment, housing and public and private accommodations is now prohibited by all provinces and territories as well as the federal government, with explicit inclusion as prohibited grounds in human rights acts as of 2017. The concepts of sex and physical disability in section 15(1) of the Canadian Charter of Rights and Freedoms have been interpreted to include transsexuality, extending equal protection guidance for interpreting human rights laws, although the Charter applies to laws and government institutions including law enforcement and not directly against the private sector. Transgender people are now able to change their legal gender in all provinces and territories under varying rules. Saskatchewan's Education (Parents' Bill of Rights) Amendment Act, 2023 requires schools to obtain parental consent for students under age 16 who request use of their gender-related preferred name or gender identity, enacted while invoking the section 33 notwithstanding clause. Alberta in 2024 passed the Health Statutes Amendment Act, 2024, Education Amendment Act, 2024, and Fairness and Safety in Sport Act, which faced legal challenges in Alberta courts, followed by Bill 9: Protecting Alberta's Children Statutes Amendment Act, 2025 which used the notwithstanding clause to prevent those challenges. In December 2020 the Canadian Association of Chiefs of Police apologized for harm to Two-Spirit, Lesbian, Gay, Bisexual, Transgender, Trans and Queer communities, stated police must stand against transphobia and marginalization, and created an Equity, Diversity and Inclusion Committee to identify, mitigate and eliminate implicit bias and systemic barriers. Same-sex sexual activity in private between consenting adults was decriminalized on June 27, 1969 when the Criminal Law Amendment Act, 1968-69 (Bill C-150) took effect upon royal assent, after an era when sex between men was a capital crime and gross indecency was enforced. Section 159 of the Criminal Code criminalizing anal intercourse was declared unconstitutional by courts in Ontario, Quebec, British Columbia, Nova Scotia and Alberta, and was repealed on June 21, 2019 through Bill C-75, setting the age of consent for anal intercourse at 16, matching the general age of consent of 16 since June 2019 and 18 where a relationship of trust, authority or dependency exists. In Egan v Canada in 1995 the Supreme Court held sexual orientation is constitutionally protected under the section 15 equality clause as an analogous ground, and in Vriend v Alberta in 1998 held failure to include sexual orientation in human rights law violated section 15. Parliament enacted the Civil Marriage Act on July 20, 2005 making Canada the fourth country in the world and first in the Americas to legalize same-sex marriage nationwide without a residency requirement, following court rulings from 2002 to 2005 and a Supreme Court reference in December 2004, while same-sex adoption was legalized province by province culminating with Nunavut in 2011 after Prince Edward Island allowed joint adoption in 2009. Discrimination on the basis of sexual orientation in employment, housing and public and private accommodations is now prohibited by all provinces and territories and the federal government, with explicit inclusion in human rights acts as of 2017. In 2022 Canada became the third country in the world and first in North America to statutorily ban conversion therapy nationwide for both minors and adults and make subjecting anyone to it a crime as defined in the Criminal Code. Prime Minister Justin Trudeau issued a formal apology on November 28, 2017 for oppression of lesbian, gay, bisexual, transgender, queer and two-spirit communities, and the Expungement of Historically Unjust Convictions Act received royal assent on June 21, 2018 allowing the RCMP and federal departments to destroy or remove judicial records for homosexual acts prior to 1969 and anal intercourse under former section 159 for living and deceased persons. In a 2020 poll commissioned by the Privy Council Office, respondents were asked about comfort with a transgender neighbour. In that poll, 87.6% of those surveyed said they would be "comfortable" if a neighbour was a transgender person. In the same poll, 91.8% said they would be "comfortable" if a next-door neighbour was gay, lesbian or bisexual. The article presents the 87.6% figure as the transgender-specific tolerance measure, separate from lesbian, gay or bisexual neighbour comfort and separate from general homosexuality acceptance polling.

82249235B69645938038492.name: Nova Scotia
82249235B69645938038492.summary:
Nova Scotia stands under the Canadian national framework: federal criminal law, human-rights protections and document rules apply uniformly across the province and are carried in the national record. Within provincial competence, Nova Scotia operates no restrictive trans-specific legislation. The provincial government released its first 2SLGBTQIA+ Action Plan on 8 January 2026, developed under the Dismantling Racism and Hate Act passed in 2022, which the province describes as the first Canadian law of its kind to explicitly acknowledge 2SLGBTQIA+ people. More than 600 community members took part through surveys, virtual meetings and consultations, and the plan maps actions to improve provincial programs and policies.

In the province's custodial system, a transgender woman from the Halifax region serving a two-year robbery sentence in a men's prison was given more time on 18 March 2025 to file an application for judicial review of the placement decision. The federal judge cited a lack of transparency and clear, timely communication in the institutional decision-making, and systemic barriers that restricted her access to her lawyer. The review application was pending at that date and no outcome is sourced.

82249235B52639524229375.name: Quebec
82249235B52639524229375.summary:
Quebec is a province of Canada and stands under the national framework carried in Canada's own record. Provincially, the Quebec Charter of Human Rights and Freedoms has prohibited discrimination on the grounds of gender identity and gender expression since 2016, reaching employment, housing and public and private accommodation.

Enforcement through the province's own tribunal is documented. On 10 June 2024 the Quebec Human Rights Tribunal found that a Montreal bar had discriminated against a trans woman in hiring because of her gender identity, and ordered the employer to pay $10,000 in moral damages, $4,000 in punitive damages and $118.40 for unpaid training.

The province's rules on legal sex designation were reshaped by litigation. In Centre for Gender Advocacy and al. v. Attorney General of Quebec the Quebec Superior Court declared provisions of the Civil Code of Quebec invalid because they violated the fundamental rights of trans, intersex and non-binary people (2021 QCCS 191, after a two-month trial with 29 witnesses). The Court of Appeal largely upheld that decision (2024 QCCA 348), and the ruling led to legislative reform of the Civil Code. The judgments are the controlling provincial authority on how sex designation and identity documents are handled in Quebec.

Correctional placement followed a different course. On 19 June 2025 Quebec's public security minister announced that transgender inmates will be incarcerated according to their anatomical sex rather than their gender identity, citing fairness and safety priorities. The directive was issued just after a trans woman convicted of murdering her partner and children sought transfer to a women's prison. Advocates say the policy violates the Quebec Charter of Human Rights and Freedoms. It reverses the previous provincial practice of taking gender identity into account in correctional placement, and it governs the treatment of anyone held in provincial custody.

No Quebec-specific rate figure appears in the release windows, so it supports the record's national-parity assessment. Federal criminal law and the federal human-rights framework apply uniformly in Quebec.
