sources.title: LGBTQ rights in Quebec (Wikipedia)
sources.summary: Federal, provincial and territorial human rights acts explicitly prohibit discrimination on the basis of gender identity or expression in employment, housing and public and private accommodations as of 2017, and section 15 concepts of sex have been interpreted to include transsexuality. Transgender people are able to change their legal gender in all provinces and territories under varying rules. In 2023 Saskatchewan passed The Education (Parents’ Bill of Rights) Amendment Act, 2023 invoking the notwithstanding clause, requiring schools to obtain parental consent for students under age 16 who request use of their gender-related preferred name or gender identity. In 2024 Alberta passed the Health Statutes Amendment Act, 2024, Education Amendment Act, 2024, and Fairness and Safety in Sport Act, then blocked court challenges by passing Bill 9: Protecting Alberta’s Children Statutes Amendment Act, 2025 using the notwithstanding clause. The Canadian Association of Chiefs of Police in December 2020 apologized for harm to Two-spirit, Lesbian, Gay, Bisexual, Transgender, and Queer Communities, stated “We must stand together against homophobia, transphobia, and any other kind of marginalization,” and created an Equity, Diversity and Inclusion Committee to address implicit bias and systemic barriers. British Columbia, Ontario and Saskatchewan grant parental status to three or more intentional parents, allowing for a wider range of queer and trans families. Same-sex sexual activity in private between consenting adults was decriminalized June 27, 1969 by the Criminal Law Amendment Act, 1968-69 (Bill C-150), and the discriminatory anal-intercourse offence in section 159 was repealed June 21, 2019 by Bill C-75, leaving a general age of consent of 16, or 18 where there is trust, authority, dependency or exploitation. In Egan v Canada (1995) sexual orientation was held protected under section 15 of the Charter as an analogous ground, and in Vriend v Alberta (1998) omission of sexual orientation from a human rights act was itself a section 15 violation. Same-sex marriage was legalized nationwide July 20, 2005 by the federal Civil Marriage Act, while Quebec in 2002 created civil unions by amending the Civil Code to give couples regardless of gender or sexual orientation the same effects as marriage for direction of family, parental authority, expenses, family residence, family patrimony and compensatory allowance, but valid only in Quebec. Same-sex adoption was legalized in Quebec in 2002 and in all provinces and territories by 2011, and discrimination on sexual orientation in employment, housing and accommodations is prohibited by all provinces, territories and the federal government. In 2022 Canada statutorily banned conversion therapy nationwide for minors and adults and made subjecting anyone to it a crime under the Criminal Code. The Expungement of Historically Unjust Convictions Act received royal assent June 21, 2018 to destroy or remove RCMP and federal records of pre-1969 homosexual convictions and section 159 convictions for living and deceased persons, following the Prime Minister’s November 28, 2017 apology and the December 2020 police chiefs apology for decades of oppression from the 1960s onward. For transgender tolerance specifically, a 2020 poll commissioned by the Privy Council Office found that “87.6% said they would be ‘comfortable’ if a neighbour was a transgender person,” compared to 91.8% who said they would be “comfortable” if a next-door neighbour was gay, lesbian or bisexual. Separate sexuality-attitude figures, not transgender-specific, showed 2020 Pew Research support for social acceptance of homosexuality at 85% of the general population and 92% among ages 18-29, up from 80% in 2013. June 2013 polls on sexuality attitudes found majority blessing for same-sex marriage, 70% agreeing same-sex couples should have the same adoption rights, and 76% agreeing they are just as likely to successfully raise children. Rankings cited are framed around gay-friendliness and sexuality, not transgender people specifically: first (least dangerous) in Asher & Lyric’s LGBTQ+ Danger Index in 2023, first in the Gay Travel Index in 2024, and ninth in the Equaldex Equality Index in 2024. Major cities maintain gay areas and communities including Toronto’s Church and Wellesley, Montreal’s Gay Village, Vancouver’s Davie Village and Ottawa’s Bank Street Gay Village, with Pride celebrated every summer in all major cities with federal, provincial and municipal political participation.

82249235B66370767641120.name: Ontario
82249235B66370767641120.summary:
Ontario stands under Canada's national framework, which carries federal criminal law and federal human-rights protections; the province's own layer is the Ontario Human Rights Code and the policy the Ontario Human Rights Commission publishes under it.

The Commission's policy on gender identity and gender expression states that the Code protects people from discrimination and harassment on those grounds in employment, housing, facilities and services, contracts, and membership in unions, trade or professional associations. It defines gender identity as a person's internal and individual experience of gender, and records that a chosen name and pronoun are common ways of expressing gender. The policy is the official provincial statement of the protections a trans person holds in Ontario's workplaces, housing and services.

Statistics Canada reported on 30 March 2026 that Ontario recorded the highest provincial rate of police-recorded hate crimes in 2024, 16.0 incidents per 100,000 population, against a national rate of 12.1 per 100,000. The figures count police-reported incidents only.

On 28 August 2023 Ontario's education minister, Stephen Lecce, said parents must be fully involved and fully aware of a child's decision to use a different name or pronoun at school. He said teachers and school boards already weigh exceptional circumstances and potential harm to the child. Ontario did not adopt legislation requiring parental consent for students under 16 who want to change names or pronouns at that time.

82249235B50381585000441.name: Manitoba
82249235B50381585000441.summary:
Manitoba is a province of Canada. Federal criminal law and federal human-rights protections apply here as they do elsewhere in the country, and the province's own human rights legislation and legislature operate alongside them.

The Manitoba Human Rights Code prohibits discrimination on the basis of gender identity. On 18 March 2025 the New Democratic Party government said it would amend the code to add gender expression as well. Justice Minister Matt Wiebe said the addition would bring Manitoba into line with most other provinces and would cover preferred pronouns and outward appearance such as clothing. The change sits in a government bill before the Legislative Assembly, with debate expected later in 2025, and Trans Manitoba executive director Charlie Eau welcomed it.

Police-reported hate crime in Manitoba stood at 5.3 incidents per 100,000 people in 2024, the joint-lowest provincial rate that year alongside Newfoundland and Labrador, one of eight provinces whose rates were stable or falling. Police figures count only incidents that are reported to and recorded by police.

The Manitoba legislature passed a bill on 30 May 2024 designating March 31 as Two-Spirit and Transgender Day of Visibility. It was brought forward by Logan Oxenham, a New Democratic backbench MLA for Kirkfield Park and a transgender man, who said the designation would show transgender, two-spirit and non-binary Manitobans that they are supported.

In November 2023 the province raised the transgender flag in Winnipeg's Memorial Park for the Transgender Day of Remembrance, an observance it had first marked eight years earlier. The flag was raised by Oxenham, the first openly transgender man elected to the Manitoba legislature. sources.summary: Discrimination on the basis of gender identity or expression in employment, housing and public and private accommodations is prohibited by all provinces and territories as well as the federal government, with explicit inclusion as a prohibited ground completed as of 2017. Transgender people are now able to change their legal gender in all provinces and territories under varying rules, while vital statistics including identity documents such as birth certificates fall under provincial jurisdiction. The concepts of sex under section 15(1) of the Canadian Charter of Rights and Freedoms have been interpreted to include transsexuality, and section 15 applies to all laws and government institutions including law enforcement authorities, with courts required to interpret human rights statutes consistently with the Charter. In 2023 Saskatchewan passed The Education (Parents' Bill of Rights) Amendment Act, 2023 invoking the notwithstanding clause, requiring schools to obtain parental consent for students under 16 who request use of their gender-related preferred name or gender identity, prompting human rights calls for repeal and legal action. In 2024 Alberta passed the Health Statutes Amendment Act, 2024, Education Amendment Act, 2024, and Fairness and Safety in Sport Act, then prevented Alberta court challenges by passing Bill 9: Protecting Alberta's Children Statutes Amendment Act, 2025, which used the notwithstanding clause. In December 2020 the Canadian Association of Chiefs of Police apologized for harm to Two-Spirit, Lesbian, Gay, Bisexual, Transgender, and Queer Communities, stated police must stand together against homophobia, transphobia and marginalization, and created the Equity, Diversity and Inclusion Committee to identify, mitigate and eliminate implicit bias and discrimination in practices and policies. Same-sex sexual activity between consenting adults in private was decriminalized June 27, 1969 by the Criminal Law Amendment Act, 1968-69 (Bill C-150), and the former section 159 anal-intercourse offence was declared unconstitutional by courts in Ontario, Quebec, British Columbia, Nova Scotia and Alberta and repealed by Bill C-75 receiving royal assent June 21, 2019, leaving a general age of consent of 16 since June 2019, 18 where there is trust, authority, dependency or exploitation, with close-in-age exceptions for ages 12-15. In Egan v Canada (1995) the Supreme Court held sexual orientation is constitutionally protected under section 15 as an analogous ground, and in Vriend v Alberta (1998) failure to include sexual orientation in a human rights law violated section 15; section 15 binds laws and government including law enforcement subject to section 1 reasonable limits under the Oakes Test and section 33 notwithstanding clause, which has never been used by federal Parliament. Same-sex marriage became legal nationwide July 20, 2005 by the federal Civil Marriage Act after 2002-2005 court rulings, making Canada the fourth country in the world and first in the Americas, while Alberta's 2000 Marriage Act opposite-sex definition invoking section 33 was invalid because capacity to marry is exclusive federal jurisdiction and the exemption expired in 2005. Adoption by same-sex couples was legalized in all provinces and territories between 1996 and 2011, from British Columbia in 1996 to Nunavut in 2011, with stepchild adoption in Alberta in 1999 and joint adoption in 2007. Discrimination on sexual orientation in employment, housing and public and private accommodations is now prohibited federally and in all provinces and territories. In 2022 Canada statutorily banned conversion therapy nationwide for minors and adults and made it a crime to subject anyone to it as defined in the Criminal Code. On November 28, 2017 the Prime Minister apologized for oppression of lesbian, gay, bisexual, transgender, queer and two-spirit communities, followed June 21, 2018 by the Expungement of Historically Unjust Convictions Act requiring RCMP and federal departments to destroy or remove judicial records for pre-1969 homosexual acts and section 159 convictions for living and deceased persons, and in December 2020 police chiefs apologized for decades of oppression from the 1960s onward. Transgender-specific tolerance finding: in a poll commissioned by the Privy Council Office reported for 2020, 87.6% said they would be "comfortable" if a neighbour was a transgender person. Broader sexuality-acceptance trend: 2020 Pew Research showed 85% of Canada's general population, 92% among ages 18-29, favoured social acceptance of homosexuality, up from 80% in 2013. June 2013 polls showed majority support for same-sex marriage available nationwide since 2005, with 70% agreeing same-sex couples should have the same adoption rights and 76% agreeing they are just as likely to successfully raise children. General LGBTQ climate indicators cited are ranking first indicating least dangerous in Asher & Lyric's LGBTQ+ Danger Index in 2023, first in the Gay Travel Index in 2024, and ninth in the Equaldex Equality Index in 2024.

82249235B82395866892480.name: Northwest Territories
82249235B82395866892480.summary:
The Northwest Territories is a territory of Canada. Criminal law, human rights protections and entry rules are set nationally rather than by the territory, and the territory's own legislative activity on transgender issues concerns vital statistics and name change.

In June 2026 the Legislative Assembly was taking feedback from police and from the Northern Mosaic Network on proposed amendments to the Vital Statistics Act and the Change of Name Act intended to make the legislation more inclusive for transgender, non-binary, gender-diverse and two-spirit people. The proposals include an option for trans and non-binary people to request that a name change not be published in the NWT Gazette. This is the first on-record territorial legislation in the Northwest Territories specifically addressing transgender and non-binary people. The amendments were under consultation and had not been enacted.

The RCMP has taken a position against part of the proposal. Chief Superintendent Dyson Smith asked MLAs to remove or amend the registrar general's option not to notify authorities, arguing that criminal records are tied to a person's legal name and that officers may put themselves in danger if records are not transferred to a new name. Yellowknife North MLA Shauna Morgan pressed the RCMP on how officers would verify legal names without identification. The police service is therefore on record opposing a measure designed to keep a trans person's former name out of public view.

Organised community support for trans and Two-Spirit young people is documented in the territory. In June 2023 the Beaufort Delta Education Council bused seventeen regional students into Inuvik for pride events centred on feeling comfortable in one's own gender and sexuality, with workshops led by Two-Spirit Anishinaabe/Metis musician G.R. 82249235B23927232378620.summary:
Nunavut is a territory of Canada and stands under the national human-rights and criminal law framework, which applies there as elsewhere in the country. Its own legislation adds a separate territorial layer.

The Nunavut Human Rights Act prohibits discrimination on the grounds of gender identity and gender expression. Bill 31, which added both grounds alongside sexual orientation, passed third and final reading in the Legislative Assembly on 13 March 2017 with unanimous support. Justice Minister Keith Peterson said the amendment would make clear that discrimination against transgender people is prohibited. Nine provinces and one territory already listed gender identity or expression in their human-rights legislation at that point, making Nunavut the first Canadian territory to do so.

Nunavut birth certificates carry a third, non-binary sex designation. On 18 September 2025 MLAs voted 12-8 in committee of the whole to restore that option through amendments to the Vital Statistics Act, after the standing committee had struck it from Health Minister John Main's May 2025 bill; the bill then passed third reading. Sponsor Adam Arreak Lightstone said the Government of Nunavut now joins the rest of Canada in recognizing non-binary and transgender individuals. The eight-vote minority against restoration shows the marker was contested in the legislature rather than adopted by consensus.

Transition-related surgical care funded by the territorial government is delivered through a contracted clinic in Montreal rather than at a Nunavut facility. A visitor who needs such care while in the territory would have to travel outside it.

sources.title: LGBTQ rights in Nunavut (Wikipedia)
sources.summary: As of 2017, all provinces, territories and the federal government explicitly include gender identity as a prohibited ground of discrimination in their human rights acts, prohibiting discrimination on the basis of gender identity or expression in employment, housing and public and private accommodations. The Supreme Court has interpreted the concepts of sex and physical disability in section 15(1) of the Charter to include transsexuality, and section 15 applies to all laws and government institutions in Canada including law enforcement authorities. Transgender people are now able to change their legal gender in all provinces and territories under varying rules. In 2023 Saskatchewan passed The Education (Parents’ Bill of Rights) Amendment Act, 2023 invoking the notwithstanding clause, with controversy over its requirement that schools obtain parental consent for students under age 16 who request the use of their gender-related preferred name or gender identity, prompting calls for repeal and legal action. In 2024 Alberta passed the Health Statutes Amendment Act, 2024, Education Amendment Act, 2024 and Fairness and Safety in Sport Act, which faced legal challenges in Alberta courts, but the government shielded them by passing Bill 9: Protecting Alberta’s Children Statutes Amendment Act, 2025 using the notwithstanding clause. In December 2020 the Canadian Association of Chiefs of Police apologized for harm, institutional bias and rights violations toward Two-Spirit, Lesbian, Gay, Bisexual, Transgender and Queer communities, stated police must stand together against transphobia and other marginalization, and created an Equity, Diversity and Inclusion Committee to identify, mitigate and eliminate implicit bias and systemic barriers. Same-sex sexual activity in private between consenting adults was decriminalized on June 27, 1969 when the Criminal Law Amendment Act, 1968–69 (Bill C-150) was brought into force upon royal assent. Since June 2019 the general age of consent for all sexual activities has been 16, with age 18 where there is a relationship of trust, authority or dependency and close-in-age exceptions for ages 12 through 15, after former section 159 criminalizing anal intercourse was repealed by Bill C-75 receiving royal assent on June 21, 2019. In Egan v Canada in 1995 the Supreme Court held sexual orientation is constitutionally protected under the equality clause of the Charter as an analogous ground under section 15, and in Vriend v Alberta in 1998 it found failure to include sexual orientation in human rights law itself violated section 15. Same-sex marriage became legal nationwide on July 20, 2005 with the federal Civil Marriage Act, making Canada the fourth country in the world and first in the Americas to legalize it, following court rulings between 2002 and 2005, while same-sex adoption was legalized in all provinces and territories with Nunavut last in 2011. In 2022 Canada statutorily banned conversion therapy nationwide for both minors and adults and made it a crime to subject anyone to it as defined in the Criminal Code, the third country in the world and first in North America to do so. On June 21, 2018 royal assent was granted to the Expungement of Historically Unjust Convictions Act allowing the RCMP and federal departments to destroy or remove judicial records of pre-1969 homosexual convictions and section 159 convictions, available to living and deceased persons and distinct from a pardon or record suspension, following the Prime Minister’s formal apology on November 28, 2017. On sexuality-specific tolerance, 2020 Pew Research showed that 85% of Canada’s general population (92% among Canadians aged 18 to 29) favoured social acceptance of homosexuality, up from 80% in 2013. June 2013 polls showed a vast majority blessing same-sex marriage available since 2005, with 70% agreeing that “same-sex couples should have the same rights to adopt children as heterosexual couples do” and 76% agreeing that “same-sex couples are just as likely as other parents to successfully raise children”. Canada was referred to as the most gay-friendly country when ranked first for least dangerous in Asher & Lyric’s LGBTQ+ Danger Index in 2023, first in the Gay Travel Index in 2024, and ninth in the Equaldex Equality Index in 2024. The largest cities feature gay areas including Toronto’s Church and Wellesley, Montreal’s Gay Village, Vancouver’s Davie Village and Ottawa’s Bank Street Gay Village, with Pride celebrated every summer in major cities with federal, provincial and municipal political figures. Distinct from sexuality tolerance, on transgender-specific tolerance the article documents that “87.6% said they would be ‘comfortable’ if a neighbour was a transgender person” in a 2020 poll commissioned by the Privy Council Office, compared to 91.8% saying they would be “comfortable” if a next-door neighbour was gay, lesbian or bisexual.

14339913B95766344400054.name: England
14339913B95766344400054.summary:
England stands under the United Kingdom's national framework, which the national record carries.

The Home Office's England-and-Wales hate-crime statistics, published 9 October 2025, record 115,990 police-recorded hate crimes in the year ending March 2025. The transgender strand fell 11% and the sexual-orientation strand 2% against the previous year. The bulletin states that recorded figures understate prevalence, with the Crime Survey for England and Wales estimating about 176,000 hate-crime incidents a year. A February 2024 change to the Metropolitan Police recording system means earlier years over-counted, so the year-on-year falls are measured against figures the Home Office treats as inflated.

The Equality and Human Rights Commission, which enforces the Equality Act 2010 in England and Wales, advises that services and businesses may ask for a person's birth certificate where there is genuine concern about biological sex, and that trans people may be excluded from single-sex sport when necessary for safety. This guidance is what a trans visitor meets at venues, transport and services.

sources.summary: BBC News (19 June 2026): Lady Ross of the Court of Session ruled unlawful Scottish Prison Service guidance that allowed some trans prisoners to be housed according to gender identity, holding that sex segregation in prisons must be based on biological sex, in line with the UK Supreme Court's April 2025 definition-of-a-woman ruling. The Supreme Court had already held that Article 8 confers no automatic right to accommodation with the opposite biological sex, and that UK-wide ruling governs England's prison and custody decisions. The first minister said the government will consider the judgment.

The UK Supreme Court's April 2025 ruling is the predicate for England's EHRC code and BTP strip-search policy, and a judicial review reported by BBC News on 5 February 2026 tests how far it reaches into prison accommodation UK-wide. In argument, government lawyers said a blanket rule housing trans prisoners by sex at birth would breach human rights and create an unacceptable suicide risk, while For Women Scotland called the identity-based policy 'Orwellian'.

The judgment fixes the definitions that govern services, searches and detention allocation in England.

sources.title: LGBTQ rights in England (Wikipedia)
sources.summary: In 1970 Corbett v Corbett barred transgender people from changing the sex marker on their birth certificate, which also prevented legal marriage to a person of the other gender as it would have been treated as an unrecognised same-sex marriage. In 1996 P v S and Cornwall County Council held that European anti-gender discrimination law applied to trans people, and in 2002 Goodwin v United Kingdom found the UK in breach of Articles 8 and 12 of the European Convention on Human Rights for maintaining that status quo, leading to the Gender Recognition Act 2004. A December 2002 Lord Chancellor's policy document categorically stated that transsexualism "is not a mental illness." Since 4 April 2005 the Gender Recognition Act 2004 has allowed transgender people to change legal gender and obtain a new birth certificate giving full recognition of acquired sex for all purposes. Applicants must present evidence to a Gender Recognition Panel for a Gender Recognition Certificate, must have transitioned for two years before issuance, and are not required to have undergone sex reassignment surgery though such surgery counts as supporting evidence, with formal approval for medical gender reassignment available on the NHS or privately. Under the Act as originally framed, a married transgender applicant was required to divorce or annul the marriage before issuance of a certificate, and a married couple including a transgender partner could not directly re-register but had to dissolve the marriage, obtain gender recognition, then register for civil partnership with associated paperwork and costs. ILGA-Europe's executive in 2020 expressed concern about a "hostile climate on trans rights fuelled by opposition groups" as the UK fell to ninth place with 66%, dropping further to 22nd place with 45% by 2025. The 1533 Buggery Act made male anal sex a civil offence punishable by death in England and Wales, later removed as capital by section 61 of the Offences Against the Person Act 1861 while male homosexual acts remained imprisonable, and lesbian acts were never criminalised as civilian offences. The Sexual Offences Act 1967, receiving royal assent 27 July 1967, provided limited decriminalisation in England and Wales only where the act was consensual, in private limited to two persons, and both were aged 21, a higher threshold than 16 for heterosexual acts and strictly interpreted to exclude hotel rooms or homes with a third person present. Equalisation came through the Sexual Offences (Amendment) Act 2000, in force 8 January 2001, lowering the age of consent to 16 throughout the UK and for the first time creating an age of consent for lesbian acts, followed by the Sexual Offences Act 2003 in force 1 May 2004 which removed privacy conditions and created sex-neutral offences. Section 28, introduced in the 1980s to prohibit "promotion of homosexuality" by schools and local authorities, was repealed in 2003, while discrimination protections in place since 1999 were extended to all areas by the Equality Act 2010 and the ban on open service by LGBT personnel was officially lifted in 2016 after non-enforcement since 2000. The Merchant Shipping (Homosexual Conduct) Act 2017 repealed sections 146(4) and 147(3) of the Criminal Justice and Public Order Act 1994, and the Policing and Crime Act 2017 in effect 31 January 2017 provided posthumous pardons and a disregard application process for historic convictions, with "disregards" available since 2012 under the Protection of Freedoms Act. Civil partnerships with most rights of marriage were legalised by the Civil Partnership Act 2004 effective 5 December 2005, adoption by same-sex couples in England and Wales took effect 30 December 2005 under the Adoption and Children Act 2002, and same-sex marriage in England and Wales was allowed by the Marriage (Same Sex Couples) Act 2013 in force 13 March 2014 with first marriages 29 March 2014. ILGA-Europe gave the UK the highest score in Europe in 2015 with 86% progress toward "respect of human rights and full equality" for LGBT people, but the score fell to 66% and ninth place by 2020.

82085004B13995298844162.name: Queensland
82085004B13995298844162.summary:
Queensland is a state of Australia and stands under the national framework; the national record carries the federal law, and this record covers the state layer.

Gender identity has been a protected attribute under Queensland's Anti-Discrimination Act since 2002. Amendments that commenced on 29 April 2024 moved serious vilification out of that Act and into the Criminal Code, with a maximum penalty of three years' imprisonment, raised from six months. The same amendments explicitly extend protection to non-binary and gender-diverse people and broaden the definition of gender identity. The Queensland Human Rights Commission described the Anti-Discrimination Bill 2024 as a rewrite that modernised the gender identity attribute and revised the vilification provisions.

Queensland was the first Australian state to criminalise conversion practices. The Health Legislation Amendment Bill 2019 passed the parliament on 13 August 2020, making practices including electro-shock, drug and hypnotherapy aimed at changing a person's sexuality or gender identity offences carrying fines and imprisonment for practitioners, with a maximum of 18 months. Survivors report that the ban does not reach conversion practices in informal, non-healthcare settings.

Access to gender-affirming care for minors has been restricted since January 2025. The health minister, Tim Nicholls, halted puberty blockers and hormone therapy for new public-system patients under 18 with gender dysphoria, formalised by a Queensland Health directive of 28 January 2025. The restriction remains in force and is legally contested. Patients already enrolled with the Queensland Children's Gender Service are exempt, so the practical effect falls on new patients and their families.

Queensland documents have carried an X non-binary option alongside male and female since 1 September 2021, including marriage certificates and official forms. Transgender and intersex residents can update government records and their birth certificate; the requirement to divorce before changing a record was repealed in 2018 and the surgery requirement was repealed in 2024.

State law recognises relationships through civil partnership registration or an unregistered de facto relationship, recognised since 2002. A trans visitor whose relationship would be read as same-sex under birth-sex status can register a civil partnership or rely on de facto recognition in the same way as any other couple.

The state's criminal-law regime has been progressively liberalised. Private consensual sex between men has been legal since 1991, and lesbian sexual acts were never criminalised. The age of consent was equalised at 16 for all sexual acts in 2016, Queensland being the last Australian jurisdiction to do so; the former section 208 carried up to 14 years' imprisonment for anal sex involving a person under 18. The gay panic defence was abolished from the criminal law in 2017.

82085004B14973555098025.name: South Australia
82085004B14973555098025.summary:
South Australia stands under the Australian national framework: federal law, federal courts and national entry rules apply here and are carried by the national assessment. The findings below are the state's own.

State anti-discrimination law protects gender identity and sexual orientation. The Equal Opportunity Act 1984 was amended in 2016 to add both grounds, giving trans residents and visitors a state-level remedy alongside the federal one.

Hate-crime sentencing laws that explicitly cover sexual orientation, gender identity and intersex characteristics passed and were implemented in November 2021, so offences motivated by a victim's gender identity fall within the state's sentencing aggravation provisions.

The gay-panic defence was abolished on 1 December 2020 and ceased to operate on 1 April 2021. A defendant can no longer rely on a claimed non-heterosexual advance by the victim as a partial defence.

The Conversion Practices Prohibition Act 2024 is in legal effect from 1 April 2025, prohibiting conversion practices in the state.

Birth certificate changes have been available since 23 May 2017 under the Births, Deaths and Marriages Registration (Gender Identity) Amendment Act 2016, which received royal assent on 15 December 2016. A change of sex descriptor requires appropriate clinical treatment but not sex-reassignment surgery, and a marriage does not have to be ended first. Non-binary and indeterminate sex descriptors are also available on state birth certificates.

Registered domestic relationships have been available since 1 August 2017. Marriage is recognised under the federal Act that took effect in December 2017; 62.5% of South Australian respondents voted Yes in the 2017 postal survey.

Tasmania's own statutory layer sits on top of the national framework. The Anti-Discrimination Act 1998 prohibits discrimination on the grounds of gender identity, gender expression, sex characteristics and variations of sex characteristics. A September 2013 amendment extended protection to transgender and intersex people and prohibited conduct that offends, humiliates, intimidates, insults or ridicules a person on the basis of actual or perceived gender, sexual orientation or gender identity. Later amendments added gender expression, gender identity (including being transgender or transsexual and identifying or living as another gender), and sex characteristics and variations of sex characteristics as grounds, and brought those grounds within the incitement-of-hatred prohibition.

A hate crimes bill passed the lower house in September 2025 that explicitly includes gender identity and sexual orientation within the 1997 sentencing act. The upper house had not voted at the time of the source.

The age of consent is 17 and is equal for all forms of sexual activity, a threshold Tasmania shares only with South Australia.

Conversion therapy practices remained legally permitted in Tasmania as of September 2026.

No state-specific incident series or enforcement pattern is documented for Tasmania.

Same-sex couples can enter registered domestic partnerships in Tasmania with an optional official ceremony, and adoption rights for same-sex couples applied in all states and territories from April 2018.

sources.title: LGBT rights in Australia – Wikipedia
sources.summary: The equality timeline for Tasmania is dated precisely. After the Commonwealth Human Rights (Sexual Conduct) Act 1994 commenced on 19 December 1994, Tasmania still refused to repeal its anti-gay Criminal Code provisions and, faced with a likely High Court loss in Croome v Tasmania, decriminalised male homosexuality with effect from 14 May 1997, the final Australian jurisdiction to do so. The age of consent in Tasmania is 17, shared only with South Australia. Same-sex couples can enter registered domestic partnerships in Tasmania with an optional official ceremony. Equality of adoption rights for same-sex couples applied in all states and territories from April 2018. As of 2019 Tasmania issues 'X' sex descriptors on birth certificates. No state-specific incident series or enforcement pattern is documented. The standing statutory particularity a trans visitor should know is the age of consent of 17.

sources.title: Tasmania makes gender optional on birth certificates after Liberal crosses floor – ABC News
sources.summary: ABC News reported on 11 April 2019 that Tasmania's House of Assembly passed the Marriage Amendments Bill the previous day, 10 April 2019, after Liberal Speaker Sue Hickey crossed the floor to vote with the Opposition; the legislation had already passed the Legislative Council. The reforms make gender on birth certificates optional, remove the requirement that transgender people undergo surgery for their gender to be recognised, and let people aged 16 or older change their registered gender without parental approval. The Tasmanian Government opposed the amendments and declined to rule out later repeal. This is enactment-level evidence of the equal-status finding for trans visitors in Tasmania, secured against government resistance rather than against any criminalisation or incident series.

sources.title: LGBTQ rights in Tasmania (Wikipedia)
sources.summary: Cross-dressing was an offence under the Police Offences Act 1935 until repealed in 2001, with Tasmania described as the only Australian state to have criminalised cross-dressing. Convictions for cross-dressing prior to 2001 and homosexual sexual offences prior to 1997 are eligible for expungement under the Expungement of Historical Offences Act 2017 effective 9 April 2018 and for up to $75,000 compensation payments effective 2 August 2026. Legal gender change is governed by 2019 amendments to the Births, Deaths and Marriages Registration Act 1999 receiving royal assent 8 May 2019 and taking effect 5 September 2019, requiring only a simple declaration with no forced divorce, sex reassignment surgery or other medical requirement. The same laws allow parents to choose whether a child's gender is recorded, allow individuals to remove a gender descriptor entirely, lower the age to change legal gender without parental permission to sixteen, allow parents to change the legal gender of their children, and extend the registration period for parents of intersex children to 120 days after birth. The Anti-Discrimination Act 1998 (Tas) prohibits discrimination on gender identity and was amended in September 2013 to extend protections to transgender and intersex people and to prohibit offending, humiliating, intimidating, insulting or ridiculing on the basis of actual or perceived gender, sexual orientation and/or gender identity, with state law also updated to incorporate gender expression. A hate crimes bill passed the lower house in September 2025 that explicitly includes gender identity within the 1997 sentencing act, with the upper house yet to vote. Consensual homosexual activity was decriminalised by the Criminal Code Amendment Act 1997 passed 1 May 1997 with royal assent 13 May 1997 and effect the next day, after penalties of up to 21 years described as the harshest in the Western world and following the United Nations Human Rights Committee decision in Toonen on 31 March 1994 and the federal Human Rights (Sexual Conduct) Act 1994 section 4 legalising adult consensual sexual activity in private nationally. The age of consent in Tasmania is 17 years and is equal for all forms of sexual activity. The Anti-Discrimination Act 1998 (Tas) prohibits discrimination on lawful sexual activity and actual or perceived sexual orientation, amended in September 2013 to prohibit offending, humiliating, intimidating, insulting or ridiculing on that basis, with additional federal protection under the Sex Discrimination Amendment (Sexual Orientation, Gender Identity and Intersex Status) Act 2013. A hate crimes bill passed the lower house in September 2025 explicitly includes sexual orientation within the 1997 sentencing act, with the upper house yet to vote. As of September 2026 conversion therapy practices remain legally permitted within Tasmania. Historic convictions for consensual homosexual activity prior to 1997 are eligible for expungement from 9 April 2018 under the Expungement of Historical Offences Act 2017 and for up to $75,000 compensation effective 2 August 2026, following an official parliamentary apology on 13 April 2017.

sources.title: Expungement of Historical Offences Act 2017 (Tas)

sources.summary: From 8 May 2019 Tasmania permits self-declared gender registration for Tasmanian-registered births with no medical certificate or medical document required, allowing persons aged 16+ to register male, female, indeterminate gender, non-binary or other self-described neither-entirely-male-nor-female gender via statutory gender declaration of identity and lived/seeking-to-live gender subject to Registrar refusal power for non-prescribed terms, allowing parents/guardians to register a gender for under-16s supported by the child's gender declaration where able or statements of consistency with will and preference plus optional counselling evidence where under 18, while birth sex registration remains male-or-female only and unchangeable except to correct initial error but ceases upon gender registration, and expands Anti-Discrimination Act 1998 protections to gender expression, gender identity including being transgender/transsexual and identifying/living as another gender, sex characteristics and variations of sex characteristics including as a ground for incitement-of-hatred prohibition.

Convictions for homosexual sexual offences prior to 1997 are also eligible. 82085004B12086860067424.name: Other Territories
82085004B12086860067424.summary:
Norfolk Island, Christmas Island, the Cocos (Keeling) Islands and Jervis Bay Territory have no territory-specific law on gender identity, sexual orientation or intersex status. Each stands under Australia's national framework, which the national record carries; the territory-specific question is which body of law attaches to each.

Norfolk Island was incorporated into New South Wales legislation from 1 July 2016 under the Norfolk Island Legislation Amendment Act 2015 and the Territories Legislation Amendment Act 2016. A visitor there meets New South Wales law rather than a Norfolk Island enactment.

Christmas Island and the Cocos (Keeling) Islands, administered together as the Australian Indian Ocean Territories, are jurisdictions in which Western Australian law applies.

Jervis Bay Territory is governed directly under Commonwealth law, and the Commonwealth Sex Discrimination Act 1984, as amended in 2013, applies throughout Australia including the external territories governed directly by Commonwealth law. That statute is the anti-discrimination framework a visitor to Jervis Bay stands under.

Availability of the 'X' sex descriptor and anti-discrimination protection on the grounds of sexual orientation and gender identity or expression extend across the states and territories alongside concurrent federal protection. No territory-specific provision on markers or on discrimination diverges from that position in the four territories.

No territory-specific rule on facilities, care access, entry or screening was located for any of the four, and no territory-specific enforcement action or incident involving a trans visitor was found.

14911670B45290909693812.name: Roraima
14911670B45290909693812.summary:
Roraima stands under Brazil's national framework, which the parent record carries in full. Two instruments specific to this state appear in the sources. State Ordinance No. 1,797/2023 addresses homophobia. On 9 August 2023 a law published in the Official Gazette of Boa Vista, approved by Mayor Genilson Costa of the Solidarity party, prohibited transgender athletes from competing in sports according to their gender identity.

No further region-specific signal on policing, custody placement, health-care access or violence against trans people was identified. On those questions the national assessment applies unchanged.

sources.summary: Brazil's national framework: same-sex marriage legal nationwide via CNJ Resolution of 14 May 2013 (14-1 vote), adoption since 2010 (full rights 2015), and gender-marker change without surgery, hormones or diagnosis since the STF ruling of 1 March 2018. On 13 June 2019 the Supreme Federal Court held discrimination and violence on grounds of sexual orientation or gender identity a crime equivalent to racism under Law 7.716/1989, punishable by imprisonment and fines. No third-gender option nationwide, though civil-registry 'non-binary/unspecified' entries have been possible since 2020 and a 6 May 2025 Superior Court of Justice ruling allows neutral-gender registry rectification as precedent. First transgender federal legislators (Salabert, Hilton) were elected in 2022.

OutRight International reports that Brazil's LGBTIQ legal advances are significant but face repeal pressure in a conservative Congress. Brazil retains one of the world's highest rates of violence against sexual and gender minorities, particularly trans people. Gender-marker change proceeds by self-determination, and trans voters may register under lived name and identity even before documents are updated. Over 3,000 openly LGBTQ candidates ran in the 2024 municipal elections.

An OAB/SP guide for expatriates states that Brazil has among the most progressive LGBTQ+ protections in Latin America on paper: same-sex marriage (CNJ Resolution 175/2013), joint adoption, name and gender-marker change without surgery, and homophobia and transphobia criminalised as equivalent to racism (ADO 26 and MI 4733, 13 June 2019, imprisonment 1-5 years). Enforcement is uneven in practice. Major cities including Sao Paulo, Rio de Janeiro, Brasilia, Belo Horizonte, Curitiba and Florianopolis are broadly welcoming with established legal infrastructure, while smaller cities and rural areas may present more social friction despite identical legal rights.

sources.title: LGBTQ rights in Roraima (Wikipedia)
sources.summary: On 1 March 2018 the Supreme Federal Court of Brazil ruled that a transgender person has the right to change their official name and sex. The change requires only self-declaration of their psychosocial identity. No surgery is required for the change. No professional evaluation is required for the change. In 2019 discrimination based on gender identity was banned through a decision by the Supreme Federal Court. On 9 August 2023 a law published in the Official Gazette of Boa Vista prohibited transgender athletes from participating in sports according to their gender identity. That law had been approved by Mayor Genilson Costa of the Solidarity party. Same-sex sexual activity has been legal in Brazil since 1830. Homosexuality is legal in Roraima. Same-sex marriage has been legal in Roraima since 2013 via a decision by the National Council of Justice. That 2013 decision was in compliance with a 2011 decision of the Supreme Federal Court. Since 2010 same-sex adoption has been officially permitted in the state through a decision by the Supreme Federal Court. In Roraima State Ordinance No. 1,797/2023 combats homophobia. In 2019 discrimination based on sexual orientation was banned through a decision by the Supreme Federal Court.

14911670B26412867168762.name: Amapa
14911670B26412867168762.summary:
Amapá's own legal layer sits on top of the national framework. Law No. 1,417/2009 provides administrative sanctions for discrimination motivated by gender identity or sexual orientation within the state public service. State Law No. 2,790/2022 makes discrimination on those grounds a crime, and Ordinary Law No. 2,710/2022 typifies anti-LGBTQ discrimination at state sports venues, football stadiums included, as an administrative offence. State Law No. 1,680/2012 established the State Day to Combat Homophobia, observed each 27 May.

Two state bodies carry the protection machinery: the State Council for Combating Discrimination and CELGBT, which run awareness campaigns and issue public repudiations of discriminatory acts against the LGBTQIAPN+ population. The source inventory contains no state-level enforcement statistics or case outcomes for these laws, so how they operate in practice cannot be assessed from the material available.

Civil-registry rectification is handled locally. On 19 February 2022 the Public Defender's Office of Amapá filed the state's first request for name and gender rectification on behalf of a non-binary person, treating the request as legally viable on the same self-determination basis as for transgender people and arguing that the registry should reflect social presentation. The procedure follows the ordinary civil-registry alteration process, and the Defender's Office assists applicants. Since 2022 the office has made legal gender change accessible to non-binary people in the state.

Gender-affirming care is available through the public system. On 13 February 2025 the Macapá municipal government opened the state's first Municipal Trans Outpatient Clinic, at the Papaléo Paes Specialties Center, running Monday to Friday from 08:00 to 17:00. It offers free multidisciplinary transition care to trans, travesti and non-binary people with no age restriction: general medicine, nursing, endocrinology, gynecology, dermatology, psychiatry, urology, cardiology, psychology, nutrition, social work, physiotherapy, speech therapy, dentistry, laboratory tests, ultrasound, mammography, densitometry, vaccination, rapid tests, Pap smear collection and dressings, with testosterone cypionate and estradiol supplied under clinical protocol. Entry is by referral from a basic health unit or by walking in; the first appointment is a general-practitioner evaluation with onward referral, and clinical demands unrelated to gender transition are excluded. Statewide gender-affirming services also run through the University Hospital of the Federal University of Amapá and the AMA-LBTI Center, which serves lesbian, bisexual, travesti, transsexual and intersex women.

Family formation has drawn judicial attention. In mid-2025 the Court of Justice of Amapá ran the campaign "Every form of love can also be family" under CNJ Resolution No. 532/2023, aimed at ensuring transgender people face no discrimination during the adoption qualification process. Adoption by same-sex couples has been recognised in the state since the national 2010 ruling; a couple from Santana obtained an adoption in 2016 after six years of proceedings, and in 2017 the Legislative Assembly considered a bill extending maternity or paternity leave to same-sex adoptive couples on the same terms as heterosexual families.

sources.summary: Same-sex marriage is legal nationwide via CNJ Resolution of 14 May 2013 (14-1 vote), with adoption since 2010 (full rights 2015), and gender-marker change without surgery, hormones or diagnosis since the STF ruling of 1 March 2018. On 13 June 2019 the Supreme Federal Court held discrimination and violence on grounds of sexual orientation or gender identity a crime equivalent to racism under Law 7.716/1989, punishable by imprisonment and fines. No third-gender option nationwide, but civil-registry 'non-binary/unspecified' entries have been possible since 2020 and a 6 May 2025 Superior Court of Justice ruling allows neutral-gender registry rectification as precedent. First transgender federal legislators (Salabert, Hilton) were elected in 2022.

Brazil's LGBTIQ legal advances face repeal pressure in a conservative Congress. The country retains one of the world's highest rates of violence against sexual and gender minorities, particularly trans people. Gender-marker change proceeds by self-determination, and trans voters may register under lived name and identity even before documents are updated. Over 3,000 openly LGBTQ candidates ran in the 2024 municipal elections, showing local political visibility.

Brazil has among the most progressive LGBTQ+ protections in Latin America on paper: same-sex marriage (CNJ Resolution 175/2013), joint adoption, name and gender-marker change without surgery, and homophobia and transphobia criminalised as equivalent to racism (ADO 26 and MI 4733, 13 June 2019, imprisonment 1-5 years). Enforcement is uneven in practice, and smaller cities and rural areas may present more social friction despite identical legal rights.

14911670B46798344041190.name: Amazonas
14911670B46798344041190.summary:
Amazonas stands under Brazil's national framework, and adds its own layer of protection. State Ordinary Law No. 3079 of 12 September 2006 prohibits discrimination on grounds of gender identity across employment, housing and other areas, and a provision in force since 2 August 2006 prohibits the manufacture, sale and distribution of symbols inciting discrimination, prejudice, hatred or violence on gender-identity grounds.

Non-binary recognition is not available in practice through Amazonas registries. In 2022 Alex Souza de Sa became the first non-binary person in the state to obtain recognition, doing so only after a rectification in Rio de Janeiro and an intervention by the Amazonas Public Defenders Office in Manaus, where no gender-neutral marker existed. Non-binary recognition in the state remains decided case by case.

Facilities are a live exposure in the state capital. On 18 October 2022 the mayor of Manaus signed a municipal law prohibiting unisex or multigender restrooms, and Equaldex records that bathroom access in Amazonas carries no explicit legal protection.

Access to gender-affirming care is contested on two fronts. On 10 June 2025 the governor of Amazonas signed Law 7552 banning gender-affirming care for minors under 18. In the opposite direction, in November 2023 the State Public Defenders Office opened a collective procedure to monitor public health services for trans and travesti people, covering hormone treatment, outpatient services and the refusal of authorisation for transsexualising surgeries including sexual reassignment surgery; after an October 2023 meeting, Manaus municipal health officials committed to dispensing standardised medications on Ambulatório Codajás prescriptions for hormone therapy and to designating reference primary-care units in each zone of the city, and the state health secretariat was required to report on gaps in equitable care and hormone therapy. In August 2024 the Federal Public Prosecutors Office recommended that Amazonas formally enable outpatient and hospital transsexualisation services, including sexual reassignment surgeries, with deadlines for approval and for presentation to the Ministry of Health.

Recorded violence against LGBTQ people in Amazonas is thin and structurally undercounted. Research published in the Brazilian Journal of Public Security finds that cases of violence against LGBTQ people in the state are underreported, and the Brazilian Public Security Forum has registered 43 cases. For 2021-2022, crimes reported in Manaus and the interior involving homosexual, lesbian, bisexual and transsexual persons accounted for 0.36% of all reports, with homophobia and transphobia motives and the categories of gender, sexuality, race and intersectionality absent from the records; LGBT victim data were few and poorly structured, victims were not infrequently recorded as perpetrators because of failures in police occurrence reports, and public agents were unprepared to handle these demands. On 5 July 2025 Fernando Vilaca de Souza was beaten and killed in Manaus after reacting to homophobic insults, with residents reporting that he had been bullied by other young people in the region.

State and municipal law also restricts LGBTQ expression and public presence. Amazonas Ordinary Law No. 6463, enacted 10 October 2023, expressly prohibits the use of neutral language, non-binary dialect or any expression departing from standard Portuguese in curricula and teaching materials of public and private educational institutions and in official documents of educational institutions and public agencies across the state. State Law 6469 of 2023 prohibits the participation of children and adolescents in pride parades, with fines of up to 10,000 reais for non-compliance. On 17 October 2024 the Legislative Assembly enacted a law prohibiting reproduction of digital media using children linked to homosexuality; it was amended on 13 December 2025 to remove the term homosexuality and instead prohibit reproduction of sexual content linked to children in cultural and artistic media.

Protection machinery exists at state level alongside those restrictions. In 2021 the State Public Defenders Office created the Sexual Diversity, Gender Identity and Citizenship Working Group, focused on human rights violations and on training security agents. In August 2024 the Amazonas State Court of Justice released the booklet Home is a Right, aimed at LGBTQ youth expelled from their homes, which states that conversion therapies are prohibited and ineffective and points readers to the Specialized Human Rights Public Defender's Office. In November 2012 a judge of the Amazonas Court of Justice authorised the state's first adoption by a same-sex couple.

No third-gender option nationwide, but civil-registry non-binary or unspecified entries have been possible since 2020, and a 6 May 2025 Superior Court of Justice ruling allows neutral-gender registry rectification as precedent. 14911670B32365136910534.name: Piaui
14911670B32365136910534.summary:
Piauí sits within Brazil's national framework for LGBTI people; national rules on marriage, legal gender recognition, anti-discrimination and custody placement apply in the state. The findings below are those specific to Piauí.

The state's own statutory layer is Ordinary Law No. 5,431, signed by the Governor on 29 December 2004, which bans discrimination based on sexual orientation. The source does not record gender identity among the grounds it covers.

Ordinary Law No. 5,916, enacted on 10 November 2009 and published on 12 November 2009, guarantees travestis and transexuais the right to be identified by their social name on registrations, forms, medical records and related documents when using the services of all direct and indirect state public administration bodies. The law defines the social name as the name by which they recognise themselves and are recognised socially, requires it to appear first and prominently with civil identification below, directs the Executive to designate within 60 days the body responsible for registration and issuance of social-name identification, and retains use of the civil name where public interest or third-party rights require.

On 20 July 2021 the Piauí judiciary granted civil registration as a non-binary person to a young person, the first recognition of a non-binary gender marker in the state.

On 14 December 2012 the Court of Justice of Piauí began granting marriage licences to same-sex couples through all notaries statewide, without the need for a judge's approval; the change was published in the Diário de Justiça on 17 December 2012. In 2012 Judge Maria Luiza de Moura de Melo e Freitas of the 1st Children and Youth Court granted adoption rights to a lesbian couple living together in a stable union since 2007.

Teresina restricts facilities. On 17 June 2026 the city council approved by 12 votes to 5, with one abstention, a bill prohibiting transgender women and travestis from using women's public restrooms, and on 30 July 2026 Mayor Sílvio Mendes signed it into law after LGBTQ rights activists protested that it is unconstitutional. The measure governs the capital only; no statewide facilities law is recorded.

Violence risk in the state is documented only in aggregate. A 2015 Grupo Gay da Bahia report listed Piauí as the second Brazilian state with the highest risk of LGBTQ people being murdered. That ranking is LGBTQ-wide rather than transgender-specific, and the source supplies no per-capita rate and no transgender-specific breakdown, so it does not establish a separate trans-specific risk level.

sources.summary: Same-sex marriage is legal nationwide via CNJ Resolution of 14 May 2013 (14-1 vote), adoption since 2010 (full rights 2015), and gender-marker change without surgery, hormones or diagnosis since the STF ruling of 1 March 2018. On 13 June 2019 the Supreme Federal Court held discrimination and violence on grounds of sexual orientation or gender identity a crime equivalent to racism under Law 7.716/1989, punishable by imprisonment and fines. No third-gender option nationwide, but civil-registry 'non-binary/unspecified' entries have been possible since 2020, and a 6 May 2025 Superior Court of Justice ruling allows neutral-gender registry rectification as precedent. The first transgender federal legislators, Salabert and Hilton, were elected in 2022.

OutRight International's report states that Brazil's LGBTIQ legal advances are significant but face repeal pressure in a conservative Congress. The country retains one of the world's highest rates of violence against sexual and gender minorities, particularly trans people. Gender-marker change proceeds by self-determination, and trans voters may register under lived name and identity even before documents are updated. Over 3,000 openly LGBTQ candidates ran in the 2024 municipal elections, evidencing local political visibility.

14911670B96632893955983.name: Acre
14911670B96632893955983.summary:
Acre is a state of Brazil and stands under the national framework carried in the Brazil record: nationwide marriage, gender-marker self-declaration and the 2019 criminalisation of transphobia on the same footing as racism apply here as elsewhere in the country. What Acre adds is a state and municipal layer of anti-discrimination, social-name and document-rectification instruments, and a documented pattern of social friction outside the capital.

Assessments of Brazil describe enforcement as uneven in practice. Smaller cities and rural areas, including those in Acre, may present more social friction than the major cities despite identical legal rights.

Violence data for the state is thin. The Associação de Homossexuais do Acre recorded 18 murders of homosexual people in the state between 2007 and 2018, 14 of them in Rio Branco. That is a raw count over eleven years with no per-capita denominator published, so it does not by itself establish Acre as more dangerous than a larger or smaller state. State government and Public Prosecutor's Office material issued in January 2025 states that no trans deaths were recorded in Acre in 2024.

Rio Branco Law 2389, enacted 30 December 2020 and in force from 5 January 2021, prohibits discrimination on grounds of sexual orientation or gender identity in the municipality and reaches conduct a visitor is likely to meet: refusing entry or stay in any public or private establishment open to the public, selective service not required by law, denying or surcharging hotel, motel or pension lodging, denying or surcharging the rental, purchase or lending of property, restricting access to buses and taxis, refusing school enrolment, and inciting discrimination or violence through any medium. Individuals and legal entities are liable. Penalties run from a warning and a fine set by municipal regulation to suspension of activities or operating licence for up to 30 days and interdiction or loss of licence, graded by gravity, recidivism and economic capacity. Any resident may complain, with confidentiality on request.

State Law 3,355 of 18 December 2017 guarantees the nome social in all acts, registrations, records and forms of the state's direct and indirect public administration. Registration and attendance must record both the civil-registry first name and the chosen social name; state servants must address the person by the indicated name in written acts, with the civil-registry name confined to internal use alongside the social name; pejorative expressions are prohibited; official letters, summons and notifications must carry both names; servant training is mandated; and non-compliance is a functional infraction carrying administrative liability and sanction. Dissemination is assigned to the State Secretariat of Justice and Human Rights.

State Decree 7311 of 3 August 2017 created the State Council for Combating Discrimination and Promoting the Rights of Lesbians, Gays, Bisexuals, Travestis and Transsexuals, charged with proposing public policy for the state's LGBTQ population.

Document rectification is free for those who cannot afford it. On 15 October 2024 the Court of Justice of Acre published Order 15/2024 requiring that legal change of name and gender on documents carry no charge for people without financial means.

Non-binary recognition is newer and slower. In 2025 a 46-year-old Sena Madureira resident became the first person in Acre to obtain a document marked with gender X, after a two-year process through the state public defender's office and a judicial grant by judge Luana Cláudia de Albuquerque Campos. The 48-hour compliance order to the Sena Madureira registry office was still pending transfer in late June 2025 and no physical rectified documents had been issued at that point. Non-binary document changes in Acre otherwise still require judicial action.

The public defender's office and the State Secretariat for Women ran a "Viver com meu nome" name-and-gender rectification mutirão on 28 June, with certificate issuance on 24-26 June, requiring RG and CPF, passport if held, voter title, proof of address, and negative state, federal, electoral, labour and, where registered male, military certificates, alongside health, social and electoral services.

On 29 January 2025 the State Secretariat for Social Assistance and Human Rights and the Public Prosecutor's Office of Acre signed a technical cooperation agreement on LGBTQIAPN+ rights and issued a booklet, "O que você precisa saber sobre os direitos da população LGBTQIAPN+: Mudança de nome e gênero de pessoas Trans e Travestis", covering rectification documents and steps and access to health, education and employment, with distribution through public bodies and civil society and prosecutor oversight of public policies including the trans outpatient clinic.

sources.summary: National framework applicable in Acre: same-sex marriage legal nationwide via CNJ Resolution of 14 May 2013 (14-1 vote), adoption since 2010 (full rights 2015), and gender-marker change without surgery, hormones or diagnosis since the STF ruling of 1 March 2018. On 13 June 2019 the Supreme Federal Court held discrimination and violence on grounds of sexual orientation or gender identity a crime equivalent to racism under Law 7.716/1989, punishable by imprisonment and fines. No third-gender option nationwide, but civil-registry 'non-binary/unspecified' entries have been possible since 2020 and a 6 May 2025 Superior Court of Justice ruling allows neutral-gender registry rectification as precedent. First transgender federal legislators (Salabert, Hilton) were elected in 2022.

OutRight International country report, last updated 12 March 2026: Brazil's LGBTIQ legal advances are significant but face repeal pressure in a conservative Congress. Brazil retains one of the world's highest rates of violence against sexual and gender minorities, particularly trans people. Gender-marker change proceeds by self-determination and trans voters may register under lived name and identity even before documents are updated. Over 3,000 openly LGBTQ candidates ran in the 2024 municipal elections, evidencing local political visibility.

Same-sex marriage (CNJ Resolution 175/2013), joint adoption, name and gender-marker change without surgery, and homophobia/transphobia criminalised as equivalent to racism (ADO 26 and MI 4733, 13 June 2019, imprisonment 1-5 years) are among the most progressive LGBTQ+ protections in Latin America on paper. Enforcement is uneven in practice: major cities (Sao Paulo, Rio de Janeiro, Brasilia, Belo Horizonte, Curitiba, Florianopolis) are broadly welcoming with established legal infrastructure, while smaller cities and rural areas, including those in Acre, may present more social friction despite identical legal rights.

sources.title: LGBTQ rights in Acre (Wikipedia)
sources.summary: On 3 August 2017 Decree 7311 established the State Council for Combating Discrimination and Promoting the Rights of Lesbians, Gays, Bisexuals, Travestis and Transsexuals to propose public policies for the LGBTQ community in the state. Discrimination based on gender identity became explicitly illegal through a 2019 Supreme Federal Court decision equating it to the crime of racism and through Rio Branco Law 2389 enacted 30 December 2020 prohibiting discrimination based on gender identity in the city. On 19 December 2017 Law 3355 guaranteed the use of social name by transgender people. On 1 March 2018 the Supreme Federal Court ruled that a transgender person has the right to change official name and sex by self-declaration of psychosocial identity without surgery or professional evaluation. On 15 October 2024 the Court of Justice of Acre published Order 15/2024 establishing that legal change of name and gender on documents must be free of charge for individuals lacking financial means. In 2025 Ariel Sebastos became the first person in the state to obtain a document marked with gender X, while non-binary document changes still require judicial actions. On 29 January 2025 the State Secretariat for Social Assistance and Human Rights and the Public Prosecutor's Office of Acre signed a cooperation agreement to promote LGBTQ rights and launched a booklet guiding Trans and Travesti people on rectifying name and gender on documents. Same-sex sexual activity has been legal since the 1830 Imperial Penal Code removed all references to sodomy. Same-sex marriage has been legal in Acre since 2013 via a National Council of Justice decision implementing a 2011 Supreme Federal Court decision. Same-sex adoption has been legal nationwide since 2015 through a Supreme Federal Court decision, following a 30 May 2008 ruling in Senador Guiomard allowing a gay couple in an eight-year stable relationship to adopt. Discrimination based on sexual orientation became explicitly illegal through a 2019 Supreme Federal Court decision equating it to the crime of racism and through Rio Branco Law 2389 enacted 30 December 2020 prohibiting discrimination based on sexual orientation in the city. On 13 November 2024 the Rio Branco City Council approved Bill 14/2024 by 10 votes to 1 to prohibit participation of children and adolescents in LGBTQ pride parades, which was criticized by the Federal Public Prosecutor's Office for perpetuating stereotypes about homosexual people and was vetoed by Mayor Tião Bocalom as unconstitutional. Between 2007 and 2018 the Associação de Homossexuais do Acre recorded 18 murders of homosexual people in the state, with 14 occurring in Rio Branco.

sources.title: Rio Branco Law No. 2389 (30 December 2020, Mayor Socorro Neri)

Assessments of the parent nation describe enforcement as uneven in practice. Smaller cities and rural areas, including those in the state/province, may present more social friction than the major cities despite identical legal rights.

Violence data for the state/province is thin. A local association recorded 18 murders of homosexual people in the state/province between 2007 and 2018, 14 of them in the state/province capital. State/province government and public prosecutor's office material issued in January 2025 states that no trans deaths were recorded in the state/province in 2024.

14911670B1613159902410.name: Rondonia
14911670B1613159902410.summary:
Rondônia is a state of Brazil and stands under the national framework; the state has no statute of its own prohibiting discrimination on grounds of sexual orientation or gender identity, so protection for trans visitors and residents rests on national law rather than on state legislation.

An ordinance signed on 28 August 2025 by appellate judge Daniel Ribeiro Lagos guarantees transgender people the use of their social name and the use of bathrooms and locker rooms in accordance with gender identity. It is the clearest region-specific rule on gendered facilities in the state.

In 2022 Hanier Miranda became the first person in Rondônia to obtain a birth certificate carrying an X sex marker. The civil registry had refused the entry for lack of a regulated third-gender procedure, and the marker was secured through a year-long lawsuit brought by the Center for Legal Practices, Research and Extensions at the Catholic Faculty of Porto Velho.

On 5 May 2025 the state prosecution service, the federal prosecution service, the labour prosecution service, the federal public defender's office and the state public defender's office jointly recommended that the state security secretariat and the state justice secretariat provide regular training for military police, civil police, firefighters, penitentiary and socio-educational agents on respect for LGBTQIA+ rights and improved service. The recommendation set a response deadline of 20 business days and required a training plan within 60 days covering 2025 and later years. It also requires gender identity, sexual orientation and social name to be recorded in police occurrence reports and prison records, with data protection and privacy safeguards, so that violence against transsexual women and travestis, including domestic and family violence, can be monitored.

Police records in the state logged 240 occurrences of anti-LGBTQIA+ violence across 2020 and 2021.

sources.summary: Same-sex marriage is legal nationwide under the CNJ Resolution of 14 May 2013 (14-1 vote), with adoption permitted since 2010 and full rights since 2015. Gender-marker change requires no surgery, hormones or diagnosis under the STF ruling of 1 March 2018. On 13 June 2019 the Supreme Federal Court held discrimination and violence on grounds of sexual orientation or gender identity a crime equivalent to racism under Law 7.716/1989, punishable by imprisonment and fines. No third-gender option exists nationwide, but civil-registry 'non-binary/unspecified' entries have been possible since 2020, and a 6 May 2025 Superior Court of Justice ruling allows neutral-gender registry rectification as precedent. The first transgender federal legislators, Salabert and Hilton, were elected in 2022.

Brazil's LGBTIQ legal advances are significant but face repeal pressure in a conservative Congress. The country retains one of the world's highest rates of violence against sexual and gender minorities, particularly trans people. Gender-marker change proceeds by self-determination, and trans voters may register under lived name and identity even before documents are updated. Over 3,000 openly LGBTQ candidates ran in the 2024 municipal elections, evidencing local political visibility.

Brazil has among the most progressive LGBTQ+ protections in Latin America: same-sex marriage (CNJ Resolution 175/2013), joint adoption, name and gender-marker change without surgery, and homophobia and transphobia criminalised as equivalent to racism (ADO 26 and MI 4733, 13 June 2019, imprisonment of 1-5 years). Enforcement is uneven in practice. Sao Paulo, Rio de Janeiro, Brasilia, Belo Horizonte, Curitiba and Florianopolis are broadly welcoming with established legal infrastructure. Smaller cities and rural areas may present more social friction despite identical legal rights.

sources.title: LGBTQ rights in Rondonia (Wikipedia)
sources.summary: Rondonia has no state law prohibiting discrimination based on gender identity, but since 2019 such discrimination is criminalized nationally by a Supreme Federal Court ruling equating it with the crime of racism. On 1 March 2018 the Supreme Federal Court ruled that a transgender person has the right to change official name and sex by self-declaration of psychosocial identity without surgery or professional evaluation. In July 2022 Hanier Miranda became the first person in the state to obtain a birth certificate with sex marker X after initial denial at the registry for lack of a regulated third-gender procedure and a year-long lawsuit by the Center for Legal Practices, Research and Extensions at the Catholic Faculty of Porto Velho. On 28 August 2025 an ordinance signed by Appellate Judge Daniel Ribeiro Lagos guarantees transgender people the use of their social name and the use of bathrooms and locker rooms in accordance with gender identity. Between 2017 and 2021 there were 12 murders of transgender people in the state, with Rondonia ranked as the 3rd state with the highest homicide rate in the North Region of Brazil. In 2025 federal and state prosecution and defender bodies recommended training on gender identity for police officers and firefighters and inclusion of LGBTQ population data in official reports. State Law no. 5123 banning gender-neutral language in schools, approved in October 2021 and signed on the 19th by Governor Marcos Rocha, was blocked in November 2021 by preliminary injunction and struck down on 10 February 2023, while a law passed on 10 July 2026 requiring parental authorization for classes on gender identity was struck down on 17 August by the Court of Justice of Rondonia. Homosexuality has been legal in Rondonia and throughout Brazil since 1830 when the Imperial Penal Code removed all references to sodomy. On 26 April 2013 the General Inspectorate of Justice published Provision 008/2013-CG providing for direct same-sex marriage and conversion of stable union into marriage in civil registration records. Rondonia has no state law prohibiting discrimination based on sexual orientation, but since 2019 such discrimination is criminalized nationally by a Supreme Federal Court ruling equating it with the crime of racism. In 2025 federal and state prosecution and defender bodies recommended training on sexual orientation for police officers and firefighters and inclusion of LGBTQ population data in official reports. A law passed on 10 July 2026 requiring parental authorization for students to attend classes on sexual orientation, sexual diversity and gender equality, enacted by Assembly President Alex Redano after Governor Marcos Rocha neither vetoed nor signed, was struck down on 17 August by the Court of Justice of Rondonia. Between 2020 and 2021 there were 240 police reports of violence against LGBTQ people recorded in the state. In 2022 Rondonia was named the worst Brazilian state in terms of public policies for the LGBTQ community.

sources.title: Brazilian Supreme Federal Court (STF) 2019 ruling on homophobia/transphobia
sources.summary: On 13 June 2019 the Supreme Federal Court criminalized transphobia throughout Brazil including Rondônia by applying Law 7.716/1989 Article 20 to anti-LGBTI discrimination and offenses, punishable by 1 to 3 years' imprisonment as a non-bailable and imprescriptible crime.

sources.title: 2025 Joint Recommendation - MPF, MPRO, MPT, DPU, DPE-RO
