14911670B86532577506919.name: Sergipe
14911670B86532577506919.summary:
Sergipe's own constitutional layer is older than most in Brazil: in 1989 the state, alongside Mato Grosso do Sul, was among the first to write a ban on sexual-orientation discrimination into its constitution. On 17 December 2025 Constitutional Amendment No. 59, proposed by state deputy Linda Brasil (PSOL), amended article 3(II) of the State Constitution to guarantee protection against discrimination based on sexual orientation and gender identity, with violators subject to punishment by law, effective on promulgation. Sergipe is the first Brazilian state to write gender-identity protection into its constitution.

The state judiciary has its own marriage provision. On 5 July 2012 the State Judiciary Power issued Provimento nº 06/2012, which regulated same-sex marriage throughout Sergipe. Since 2025 the state has allowed individuals to change their gender marker on documents to non-binary.

Court facilities in the state capital are explicitly gender-neutral. From 28 August 2025 the Court of Justice of Sergipe provides operating gender-neutral bathrooms on the ground, first and eighth floors of the Palácio da Justiça in Aracaju, usable by any person regardless of gender identity. The same measure directs that in all Sergipe judiciary units male and female bathrooms be used respecting each person's gender identity, under human-rights and non-discrimination principles, and requires that all new constructions and renovations be planned with gender-equity demands.

Institutional access has widened at the state's federal university. On 17 November 2025 the Federal University of Sergipe approved affirmative-action quotas for trans people in undergraduate courses.

A counter-current sits in the state legislature. On 1 December 2020 state deputy Rodrigo Valadares (UNIÃO) tabled a bill to prohibit the use and teaching of gender-neutral language in Sergipe's public and private schools and in state public offices, requiring traditional Portuguese in schools, official notices and public offices.

14911670B72497658138655.name: Tocantins
14911670B72497658138655.summary:
Tocantins has no state law prohibiting discrimination on grounds of sexual orientation or gender identity, a gap recorded by the state's own Public Defender's Office. A trans visitor in Palmas or in the interior depends on Brazil's national framework, which applies here without state-level variation, and on national enforcement machinery rather than any state statute.

The state bodies that have acted on trans documentation are the Public Defender's Office of Tocantins (Defensoria Pública do Estado do Tocantins) and the state judicial inspectorate, the Corregedoria-Geral da Justiça. On 29 January 2026 the Public Defender's Office published an article explaining how trans people change names and gender markers on documents.

Rectification in Tocantins is administrative and rests on self-declaration. A trans man, trans woman, travesti, non-binary or queer person may apply at the civil registry where the birth was recorded, with effect on the birth certificate and on all official documents, without medical or psychological reports and without proof of surgery or hormone treatment. The service is free where the applicant proves inability to pay, and a court is involved only if the registry refuses the request.

The exception is a change to a non-binary or unspecified marker, which the Public Defender's Office states requires a judicial decision. In August 2022 that office asked the Corregedoria-Geral da Justiça to allow "non-binary" entries in civil registry records, and in 2023 the inspectorate published a resolution authorising non-binary individuals to change their documents to include a third gender option. Whether an administrative route to a non-binary marker is open in practice is unresolved.

sources.summary: Same-sex marriage legal nationwide via CNJ Resolution of 14 May 2013 (14-1 vote), adoption since 2010 (full rights 2015), and gender-marker change without surgery, hormones or diagnosis since the STF ruling of 1 March 2018. On 13 June 2019 the Supreme Federal Court held discrimination and violence on grounds of sexual orientation or gender identity a crime equivalent to racism under Law 7.716/1989, punishable by imprisonment and fines. No third-gender option nationwide, but civil-registry 'non-binary/unspecified' entries have been possible since 2020 and a 6 May 2025 Superior Court of Justice ruling allows neutral-gender registry rectification as precedent. First transgender federal legislators (Salabert, Hilton) were elected in 2022.

OutRight International country report of 12 March 2026: Brazil's LGBTIQ legal advances are significant but face repeal pressure in a conservative Congress. Brazil retains one of the world's highest rates of violence against sexual and gender minorities, particularly trans people. Gender-marker change proceeds by self-determination, and trans voters may register under a lived name and identity even before documents are updated. Over 3,000 openly LGBTQ candidates ran in the 2024 municipal elections, evidencing local political visibility.

Brazilian law-firm guide for expatriates (OAB/SP, April 2026): Brazil has among the most progressive LGBTQ+ protections in Latin America on paper: same-sex marriage (CNJ Resolution 175/2013), joint adoption, name and gender-marker change without surgery, and homophobia and transphobia criminalised as equivalent to racism (ADO 26 and MI 4733, 13 June 2019, imprisonment of 1 to 5 years). Enforcement is uneven in practice. The guide contrasts major urban centers, broadly welcoming with established legal infrastructure, against smaller cities and rural areas, where identical legal rights may still meet more social friction.

14911670B28216513632935.name: Espirito Santo
14911670B28216513632935.summary:
Espirito Santo sits within Brazil's national framework for LGBTI rights; the national record carries the marriage, identity-marker and hate-crime provisions that apply here, and what follows is the state's own layer of law, institutions and enforcement.

Facilities are contested at municipal level. On 6 June 2022 the Vitoria City Council approved a bill banning the installation of unisex restrooms in the city. The source records the council vote but not whether the mayor signed or vetoed the measure, so its current legal force is unresolved.

On 14 April 2024 the Legislative Assembly of Espirito Santo approved a bill restricting athletes' participation in competitions according to biological sex. Governor Renato Casagrande vetoed it on 28 April 2024.

On 21 June 2025 the Legislative Assembly approved a law allowing parents to prohibit their children from participating in classes dealing with LGBTQ topics. LGBTQ rights organisations challenged it at the Supreme Federal Court, which began hearing the case on 21 November 2025 and struck the law down in May 2026 by 8 votes to 2; Justice Carmen Lucia stated that it violated the Brazilian Constitution.

Partner recognition was addressed in Espirito Santo before the national framework was settled. On 3 August 2012 a judge in Colatina authorised registration of the marriage of Ediana Calixto and Kamila Roccon, the first same-sex marriage recognised in the state. The State Public Prosecutor's Office appealed and the recognition was revoked on 15 August; on 20 September the state Court of Justice reversed that decision and authorised recognition. On 15 August 2012 the General Inspectorate of Justice issued a Circular Letter requiring all civil registries to treat same-sex marriages on the same terms as opposite-sex couples, making Espirito Santo the third Brazilian state to address the question statewide.

State institutions have also acted on document recognition. On 22 January 2025 the Public Defender's Office of Espirito Santo filed suit to secure name and gender rectification for a non-binary person from Vitoria, and the court granted the request and authorised the rectification. On 27 June 2025 the Legislative Assembly and the Public Defender's Office held a free event to help trans, non-binary and travesti people change their name and gender on official documents.

14911670B30315977547221.name: Parana
14911670B30315977547221.summary:
Paraná is a state of Brazil and stands under the national framework carried by the parent record; the findings below are those specific to the state and its municipalities.

Access to sex-separated facilities has been contested in Paraná's own legislature and municipal councils. In 2021 state representative Mara Lima introduced a bill prohibiting unisex bathrooms statewide and requiring separate male and female facilities. On 16 November 2021 the Curitiba City Council approved a municipal bill of the same kind introduced by councilman Ezequias Barros. Both measures target unisex provision and would require sex-separated bathrooms, which bears directly on how trans people use facilities.

On 4 October 2023 the Curitiba City Council approved a symbolic protest motion against Resolution 2/2023 of the Ministry of Human Rights and Citizenship, which recommended that educational institutions guarantee use of bathrooms, changing rooms and other gender-segregated spaces according to each student's gender identity and expression, with additional individual-use bathrooms recommended in public spaces. The ministry stated the resolution has no binding effect and that no school is obliged to adopt it. The Curitiba motion was to be converted into an official letter to the federal government.

The Court of Justice of the State of Paraná has moved in both directions on gender markers. In 2023 it published a provision guaranteeing inclusion of 'non-binary' in the civil registry gender marker, then revoked it in November 2023, limiting administrative replacement of first name and sex to 'male' and 'female' only. In 2025 the same court authorised a third gender option on documents.

On 26 April 2024 Londrina enacted a municipal law barring transgender people from competing in sports according to gender identity, with a fine of R$10,000 for non-compliance. In March 2026 LGBTQ rights organisations challenged the law at the Supreme Federal Court, and on 7 August 2026 rapporteur Justice Cristiano Zanin voted to strike it down.

On 26 February 2026 the Londrina City Council approved a motion to bar transgender athlete Tiffanny Abreu from the Brazilian Women's Volleyball Cup. The Brazilian Volleyball Confederation filed suit at the Supreme Federal Court, and Justice Cármen Lúcia issued a preliminary injunction the same day allowing her to compete.

Marriage and stable-union recognition in Paraná follow the ordinary procedures. On 26 March 2013 the General Inspector of Justice of Paraná ruled that same-sex marriage and the conversion of stable unions into marriage must use the normal marriage procedure and documentation in all registry offices statewide, without judicial authorisation. The first recognition of a same-sex union in Brazil was granted in Curitiba in 2004, when an English-Brazilian couple cohabiting for fourteen years was given common-law marriage status previously limited to opposite-sex couples.

sources.title: LGBTQ rights in Rio Grande do Sul (Wikipedia)
sources.summary: Since 2019, discrimination based on gender identity has been prohibited nationwide in Brazil through a Supreme Federal Court decision. On 1 March 2018, the Supreme Federal Court ruled that a transgender person may change official name and sex by self-declaration of psychosocial identity without surgery or professional evaluation. On 27 January 2020, the Rio Grande do Sul government installed signs in women's restrooms of state government offices stating use in accordance with gender identity and installed unisex restrooms. In August 2021, Special Secretary of Culture Mário Frias criticized those restroom measures as posing risks to children. On 22 April 2022, Rio Grande do Sul Justice allowed non-binary people to change first name and sex in the birth record to include 'non-binary' upon request to a notary without judicial authorization, but in December 2023 the Court of Justice revoked that provision. On 28 September 2025, a Porto Alegre court ordered a bar to pay 10,000 reais compensation for denying a trans man access to the men's restroom, and on 28 May 2026 an appellate court overturned that decision. Homosexuality is legal in Rio Grande do Sul. On 19 December 2002, the Legislative Assembly enacted State Law No. 14,896 prohibiting discrimination based on sexual orientation. On 29 May 2012, four of six notaries in Porto Alegre agreed to convert civil unions into marriages. On 11 November 2005, a Bagé judge permitted adoption of two brothers by a lesbian couple in a seven-year stable union, described as Brazil's first LGBTQ adoption. On 6 April 2006, same-sex couples in committed relationships were allowed to register at any notary office with rights to jointly own property, establish custody of children, and claim pensions and property on a partner's death. On 27 April 2010, the Superior Court of Justice recognized shared adoption of two sons by Bagé lesbian couple Lídia Brignol Guterres and Luciana Reis Maidana to secure pension, separation and inheritance rights. On 3 June 2011, Pelotas justice authorized adoption of a four-year-old by a gay couple with the biological mother's consent.

sources.title: Supreme Federal Court - 2019 nationwide gender identity discrimination ban
sources.summary: On 24 May 2019 a majority of Brazil's Supreme Federal Court (6 of 11 justices) voted to criminalize transphobia and homophobia as equivalent to racism, punishable under Brazil's racism law until Congress enacts specific LGBT-protection legislation.

sources.title: Supreme Federal Court ruling of 1 March 2018 on name and sex change
sources.summary: On 1 March 2018 in ADI 4275 the Federal Supreme Court held that the right to equality without discrimination encompasses gender identity and expression as a manifestation of personality that the State must recognize, and therefore authorized change of name and gender on the civil registry without sex-reassignment surgery or judicial authorization.

1811400B6111924962807.summary:
Goa is a state of India and stands under the national framework on transgender recognition, identity documents and criminal law. No Goan statute diverging from that national position is on file.

Marriage and partnership recognition in Goa is set by the Goa Civil Code, a state-level instrument that defines marriage as between a man and a woman and gives no legal recognition to same-sex marriage or civil union. A trans visitor whose relationship would be read as same-sex under birth-sex status cannot have that relationship recognised in Goa, and the code applies in this state rather than the personal-law system used elsewhere in India.

Goa has no state-level anti-discrimination law covering sexual orientation. Protection against discrimination on grounds of gender identity in Goa rests on the national Transgender Persons (Protection of Rights) Act, 2019, which applies in the state.

On 7 May 2025 the state government constituted a 14-member Model Transgender Welfare Board, chaired by the Chief Secretary, under the 2019 Act and the 2020 Rules, with a mandate covering implementation of welfare schemes and safeguarding transgender persons' rights in healthcare, education, employment and housing.

Administrative recognition in Goa lags the resident population. The 2011 census recorded 398 transgender people in Goa; by 2024 only 12 transgender people were registered on the state's electoral rolls, the first registrations having taken place in 2022. A trans visitor dealing with state offices should expect registration and documentation processes that have only recently begun to include transgender residents.

Harassment of transgender people in Goan institutions is documented. A 2018 study by the Goa Livelihoods Forum found that 87 per cent of transgender respondents had dropped out of school because of harassment. The figure describes the state's social climate for transgender residents rather than a specific risk to short-stay visitors, but it records a local pattern of harassment in schools and comparable settings.

No bill on relationship recognition has been introduced in the Goa legislature.

sources.title: LGBTQ rights in Goa (Wikipedia)
sources.summary: Federal law has recognized transgender identity since NALSA v. Union of India in 2014. The Transgender Persons (Protection of Rights) Act, 2019 prohibits discrimination based on gender identity. In 2025 Goa formed the Model Transgender Welfare Board under the provisions of that Act to facilitate welfare schemes for transgender people. The 2011 census counted 398 transgender people in Goa, but as of 2024 only 12 transgender people were registered in electoral rolls, with the first registrations occurring in 2022. A 2018 Goa Livelihoods Forum study found 87% of transgender respondents had dropped out of school due to harassment. Same-sex activity was decriminalized at federal level in 2018 by Navtej Singh Johar v. Union of India. In 16th century Goa, the Goa Inquisition criminalized same-sex activity with death penalty by burning to ashes and confiscation of property to the Crown, as applied in 1528 to a Muslim man and later to 16-year-old Portuguese army soldier Alberto Homem. Under the 1568 Constitutions of the Archbishopric of Goa, same-sex activity was classified as a serious sin punishable by deposition from office and lifelong penance in a religious institution for a clergyman and excommunication until repentance and required penance for a layman. In 1644 the Tribunal of Goa sought clarification on female same-sex acts and the majority concluded such acts generally did not constitute sodomy but sexual immorality rather than the crime of sodomy. Goa applies the Goa Civil Code defining marriage as between a man and a woman with no legal recognition for same-sex marriages or civil unions, though in 2023 the Supreme Court noted same-sex couples have the right to cohabit and enjoy some protections under law. Following the Supreme Court's 2023 decision not to legalize same-sex marriage, activists in Goa urged legislative steps but no bills have been introduced. There are currently no state-level anti-discrimination laws protecting sexual orientation in Goa.

10402087B44391416804171.name: Bremen
10402087B44391416804171.summary:
Bremen, as a German city-state, stands under the national framework set by the Self-Determination Act (Selbstbestimmungsgesetz). It has enacted no trans-specific statute of its own and no prison-placement rule of its own. Prison administration and the civil-registry offices are competences of the city-state, so the layer a trans person actually deals with in Bremen is run by Bremen authorities, applying the federal framework without local amendment.

Under the Self-Determination Act the legal gender entered in the civil registry is the reference point for prison placement in every Land, and § 6(1) SBGG permits Land law to override that entry. Bremen has not passed such an override. The placement of a trans person held in a Bremen facility therefore turns on the registered entry rather than on a Bremen exception clause; how intake review is conducted in Bremen's prisons is not documented in the available sources.

Legal gender changes for Bremen residents are processed through the city-state's own registry offices. Bremen maintains no separate rule on bathrooms, changing or leisure facilities, or identity documents of its own, so a visitor meets the national framework rather than a local variant.

The issue is framework-level for every Land, since prison administration and registry offices are Land competences.

Framework analysis (Verfassungsblog, 18 Mar 2026) of German state prison-placement rules under the Self-Determination Act: all Länder tie placement to the prisoner's legal gender; § 6(1) SBGG lets state law override the entry, and many Länder have enacted exception clauses — some abstract (all inmates), some criticised as trans-targeted. Bremen has no placement statute of its own, so this national framework is the operative standard for inmate-placement questions.

10402087B86022102756745.name: Nordrhein-Westfalen
10402087B86022102756745.summary:
North Rhine-Westphalia has enacted no trans-specific legislation of its own. A trans visitor's legal position in the state is set by the German national framework, and the state's correctional law contains no trans-specific placement provision, so a detained trans person in a North Rhine-Westphalia prison is placed under the national default rule that the legal gender entry governs, with no state exception clause to override it.

The closest thing to a regional assessment of trans people's situation is the study "Queer durch NRW – Lebenslagen und Erfahrungen von LSBTIQ*", published on 25 April 2025, the first comprehensive dataset on the living situations of lesbian, gay, bisexual, trans, inter, queer and non-binary people in the state. It combined quantitative online surveys of more than 5,000 LSBTIQ* respondents, 775 relatives and over 5,000 professionals with qualitative focus groups and expert interviews. Three thematic areas structure it: discrimination, violence and safety; health, care and ageing; and integration, migration and flight.

The study was commissioned under a Landtag resolution, Drucksache 18/6360, to give the state's "Aktionsplan für Vielfalt und gegen Homo- und Transfeindlichkeit" a broader data basis. The action plan is a policy programme of the state government rather than a statute, and it creates no rights a visitor can invoke. That discrimination, violence and safety are among the domains the state government measures indicates a recognised problem, but the figures for trans respondents are not in the reviewed sources, so no risk magnitude can be stated for the state.

10402087B42728698084544.name: Rheinland-Pfalz
10402087B42728698084544.summary:
Prison placement for people held in Rheinland-Pfalz is set by the state rather than the federal government: prison administration is a competence of the German Länder, so the placement rule for Rheinland-Pfalz prisoners sits in the state's own correctional act, while legal gender recognition and anti-discrimination law sit in the federal framework. Section 17 of the Landesjustizvollzugsgesetz Rheinland-Pfalz took effect on 1 March 2026 and anchors inmate placement to the legally recorded gender entry. The accompanying exception clause is drafted in general and abstract terms and is available to all prisoners; it is not written specifically for transgender prisoners. A trans visitor detained in Rheinland-Pfalz therefore has the placement decision taken at intake against the gender entry on their legal record, with the exception clause as the only route away from it.

A constitutional-law analysis published on 18 March 2026 reads the Rheinland-Pfalz drafting as the model preferable to the alternative used in other states, where exception clauses are written to target transgender prisoners specifically, and raises constitutional doubts about that alternative approach. The analysis is legal commentary on the statute and on the drafting choice; it is not a record of how the Rheinland-Pfalz clause has been applied.

10402087B83775792336645.name: Saarland
10402087B83775792336645.summary:
Saarland has no trans-specific statute of its own. Its state constitution was amended in 2011 so that its anti-discrimination provisions explicitly include sexual orientation and gender identity, one of five Länder constitutions to carry such a clause. The consequence for a visitor is that transphobic hate speech is prohibited under Saarland's constitution, while hate speech on the basis of sexual orientation and gender identity is not banned nationwide.

Prison placement in Saarland is governed by the national framework because the state has enacted no placement statute of its own; the legal gender entry is the default basis for placement unless a state law provides otherwise. A constitutional-law analysis published on 18 March 2026 cites Saarland's single-cell accommodation with en-suite shower as a positive practice model for trans inmates. The same analysis records that constitutional law does not oblige authorities to follow the legal gender entry, so the default in Saarland is a practice rather than an enforceable guarantee.

The case sits behind the state-level prison-placement law debate addressed in the accompanying analyses.

Verfassungsblog framework analysis (18 Mar 2026) of how German Länder place trans prisoners under the Self-Determination Act (SBGG, in force 1 Nov 2024): placement follows the legal gender entry unless a state law provides otherwise (§ 6(1) SBGG); no constitutional obligation to follow the entry. Cites Saarland's single-cell-with-en-suite-shower accommodation as a positive practice model for trans inmates; framework-relevant to Saarland, which has no separate placement statute.

sources.title: LGBTQ rights in Germany (Wikipedia)
sources.summary: The page records that Saarland's state constitution was amended in 2011 so that its anti-discrimination provisions explicitly include sexual orientation and gender identity, one of only five Lander constitutions to carry such a clause (Berlin since 1995, Brandenburg since 1992, Bremen since 2001, Saarland since 2011, Thuringia since 1993; Saxony-Anhalt in the public sector since 1997). It further records that Saarland, with Hesse, Berlin, Bremen and Schleswig-Holstein, tabled a joint Bundesrat motion for a ban on conversion therapy, presented in plenary on 12 April 2019, with Saxony, Saxony-Anhalt and Thuringia agreeing and Bavaria offering modified support. Gives the state-constitutional protection against discrimination on grounds of gender identity that a trans visitor stands under within Saarland.

sources.title: Transgender rights in Germany (Wikipedia)
sources.summary: The page states that hate speech on the basis of sexual orientation and gender identity is not banned nationwide in Germany, but that some states have laws banning all forms of discrimination in their constitutions - Berlin, Brandenburg, Bremen, Saarland and Thuringia - and that in those states hate speech based on both sexual orientation and gender identity is prohibited. For Saarland this is a jurisdiction-specific enforcement difference: transphobic hate speech is prohibited under the state constitution, unlike in most of Germany, and the federal General Act on Equal Treatment (in force since 18 August 2006) bans discrimination based on sexual orientation and gender identity in employment, education, health services and the provision of goods and services.

sources.title: Jens Spahn will Pseudotherapien gegen Homosexualität verbieten
sources.summary: Zeit Online (10 April 2019) reports that, parallel to Federal Health Minister Jens Spahn's announced plan to ban so-called conversion therapies, Hesse, Berlin, Bremen, Saarland and Schleswig-Holstein planned to present a joint Bundesrat motion (Entschließungsantrag) for a ban that same week. Saarland is one of the five tabling states in the run-up to the 12 April 2019 Bundesrat plenary presentation recorded on Wikipedia's LGBTQ rights in Germany page; the federal ban was subsequently approved by the Bundestag on 7 May 2020.

10402087B46069870964378.name: Schleswig-Holstein
10402087B46069870964378.summary:
Schleswig-Holstein stands under the German national framework. The state has enacted no statute or ordinance specific to trans people, and it has no provision of its own governing where a trans prisoner is held. Placement in a Schleswig-Holstein facility therefore follows the national rules, with no state-level variation layered on top of them.

No trans-specific exception clause of the kind that has drawn constitutional doubt in other states' prison acts exists in Schleswig-Holstein law.

The state's own trans-relevant legislative record is a co-sponsored initiative. Schleswig-Holstein, with Hesse, Berlin, Bremen and Saarland, tabled a joint motion in the Bundesrat for a ban on conversion therapy, presented in plenary on 12 April 2019.

sources.summary: A German court sent a person convicted of neo-Nazi incitement, whose legal gender had been changed to female under the Self-Determination Act, to a men's prison, prompting public outcry over women's-prison safety. Reported 16 July 2026; the case drove the state-level prison-placement law debate.

Under the Self-Determination Act (SBGG), in force 1 November 2024, a prisoner's placement tracks the legal gender entry unless state law excludes it. A Verfassungsblog analysis of 18 March 2026 raises constitutional doubts about trans-targeted exception clauses in Länder law. Schleswig-Holstein has no statute of its own on trans-prisoner placement; the July 2026 placement case and the SBGG mechanics are the operative rules.

Saxony, Saxony-Anhalt and Thuringia supported the motion, and Bavaria indicated potential support with modifications. The Bundestag approved the federal ban on 7 May 2020 with backing from every party except the AfD.

25490228B84620027724461.name: Canarias
25490228B84620027724461.summary:
Canarias is an autonomous community of Spain and stands under the national framework on legal gender recognition and LGTBI rights; its own statutory layer is a regional non-discrimination and self-identification regime.

Ley 8/2014 of 28 October 2014, on non-discrimination on grounds of gender identity and recognition of trans persons' rights (BOE-A-2014-11995), gives a trans visitor to the islands a region-specific statutory basis against discriminatory treatment.

Canarias has allowed trans people to self-declare their legal gender since 2021, one of 14 autonomous communities to do so before the national statute of 28 February 2023 took effect.

The community is listed among those that ban conversion therapies, and it created a registry for same-sex couples in 2003, giving partners a regional recognition instrument.

sources.summary: The Canary Islands created their same-sex couple registry in 2003 and banned discrimination on gender-identity grounds through Ley 8/2014 of 28 October 2014 (non-discrimination on gender-identity grounds and recognition of trans persons' rights, BOE-A-2014-11995). The community has allowed trans people to self-declare their legal gender since 2021, one of 14 communities to do so before the national Ley Trans of 28 February 2023. It is also listed among the communities banning conversion therapies, and Gran Canaria and Tenerife are named internationally known LGBT tourist destinations. A trans traveler therefore stands under a regional anti-discrimination and self-identification regime alongside the 2023 national law.

25490228B56567998760255.name: País Vasco/Euskadi
25490228B56567998760255.summary:
The Basque Country's own legal layer is a 2013 law passed by the Basque Parliament against discrimination on grounds of gender identity and recognising the rights of trans people. It brought an LGBTI perspective into gender-violence prevention in the Basque education system for the first time. The region's instruments sit under Spain's national framework, which carries legal gender recognition and the bias-motive aggravator in criminal law; the regional layer adds to that framework rather than displacing it.

No region-specific rules on facility access, identity documents, entry or screening appear in the sources. Those matters follow the national framework and are not set at regional level.

Attitudinal evidence specific to the region is dated. A 2017 survey by the Basque Youth Observatory reported that nine in ten Basque young people favour marriage between people of the same sex and legal change of sex.

sources.title: Historia LGBT en el País Vasco (Spanish Wikipedia)
sources.summary: The Basque Parliament passed a law against discrimination on grounds of gender identity and recognising the rights of trans people, dated 2013, which for the first time incorporated an LGTBI perspective into gender-violence prevention in the Basque education system. Institutional markers predating it include the first Basque Pride march in Bilbao in 1978, the legalisation of the activist collective EHGAM in 1983, and the creation of Emakunde, the Basque Women's Institute, in 1988. A 2017 survey by the Basque Youth Observatory reported that 9 in 10 Basque young people favour same-sex marriage and legal change of sex. Osakidetza, the Basque health service, provided assisted reproduction regardless of sexual orientation and reaffirmed that position in 2013. The Basque Country operates its own non-discrimination legal instruments and equality institutions, including Emakunde, within the national framework.

sources.summary: The earliest documented executions for same-sex acts in the Iberian peninsula occurred in the Kingdom of Navarra. In 1290 a Muslim man was burned in Arguedas for 'yacer con otros'. For the modern period, Diario de Navarra (12 May 2026) reports that Navarra planned to create an observatory against LGTBI-phobia, a measure placed at the planning stage by that date, which sits in tension with a 2025 observatory report. Ley Foral 8/2017 is not substantively covered in the material. Navarra's standing rests on the national framework, with no substantive regional divergence of its own.

25490228B27950689864224.name: Región de Murcia
25490228B27950689864224.summary:
Región de Murcia stands under Spain's national framework. The region's own layer is Ley 8/2016 of 27 May 2016 (BOE-A-2016-6170), which prohibits discrimination on grounds of sexual orientation, gender identity or expression, and sex characteristics across public and private activity in the region. Within its scope the statute bars any requirement that a person prove a declared gender identity by psychological or medical report, so a regional service, clinic or venue cannot demand documentation of a visitor's gender as a condition of service.

Article 5 creates the Observatorio regional contra la discriminación por orientación sexual e identidad de género, a participation and consultation body on which LGTBI entities are represented.

Title IV sets the sanctioning ladder. Minor breaches draw a warning or a fine of up to EUR 3,000. Serious breaches run EUR 3,001 to EUR 20,000 and cover degrading remarks or incitement to violence against LGBTI people or their families in the provision of services. Very serious breaches run EUR 20,001 to EUR 45,000, with accessory penalties that include exclusion from regional public aid for up to one year. Multiple discrimination raises the grade of the infraction.

Murcia was among eight autonomous regions that approved LGBTI and trans equality laws in the 2010s, and Ley 8/2016 remains the operative regional instrument. Implementation of the national trans-equality law falls to the regional government.

25490228B94236519555378.name: Galicia
25490228B94236519555378.summary:
Galicia is an autonomous community of Spain, and the national framework set by Ley 4/2023 of 28 February 2023, the organic law on real and effective equality for trans persons and the guarantee of LGBTI rights, governs legal gender recognition and protection against LGBTIphobic discrimination in the region as it does in the rest of the country.

The statute assigns implementation of its education-facing and administrative provisions to the autonomous communities. The Xunta de Galicia is one of the regional governments charged with carrying them out, and public authorities in Galicia act within their own competences when they do so. How the region's schools, administrative services and public bodies apply those provisions determines what trans residents and visitors meet in practice, and the sources reviewed do not describe Galicia's implementation record.

Galicia's courts have produced the first application of the discrimination aggravating circumstance for transfobia recorded in the country. In July 2026 the Tribunal de Instancia in Vigo fined the author of WhatsApp messages that threatened a trans woman EUR 300. The conviction was a misdemeanour, and it is the only documented regional enforcement of that aggravating circumstance in the sources reviewed.

Nothing in the sources reviewed documents region-specific legislation or practice in Galicia that restricts trans visitors. Recognition, document markers, facility access and healthcare access are governed by the national law, and no Galicia-level measure narrowing them appears.

sources.summary: Official gazette text (BOE-A-2023-5366) of State Law 4/2023 of 28 February 2023, the law for the real and effective equality of trans people and the guarantee of LGBTI rights. Title II regulates rectification of the registered sex entry by the person's freely expressed will, depathologizes the procedure (no medical diagnosis or treatment requirement) and removes the former age-majority requirement for requesting it, with corresponding document adaptation; Title III provides protection and reparation against LGBTIphobic discrimination and violence. The law mandates measures across administrative, workplace, health and education fields, with public authorities acting within their competences; the education-facing and administrative provisions are implemented by the autonomous communities, this region's government among them.

Human Rights Watch, 16 February 2023, reporting the Spanish Congress of Deputies' passage of the comprehensive LGBTI law known as the 'Trans Law': legal gender recognition by self-identification through a simple administrative process, replacing the prior requirements of a gender-dysphoria diagnosis and two years of medical treatment aligned to the sought marker. The law strengthens sexuality education, bans medically unnecessary normalising surgery on intersex children before their consent, enables parental recognition for unmarried same-sex couples and prohibits LGBTI discrimination in healthcare, employment and housing; children from age 12 may obtain recognition under certain conditions, a provision that provoked political conflict. HRW assesses the reform as upholding European and international standards against abusive, disproportionate requirements for legal gender recognition.

25490228B80227492032103.name: Cataluña/Catalunya
25490228B80227492032103.summary:
Catalunya stands under the national framework of Spain; the region-specific layer is set by Ley 11/2014 of 10 October 2014, published in the Diari Oficial de la Generalitat de Catalunya (DOGC núm. 6730) on 17 October 2014.

Ley 11/2014 defines direct discrimination, indirect discrimination and discrimination by association on grounds of sexual orientation, gender identity, gender expression or sex characteristics.

The statute obliges Catalan public administrations to establish mechanisms so that administrative documentation reflects a person's gender identity.

Its protections extend across education, health, employment and sport, and it broadens the mandate of the Observatori Català de l'Esport to act against violence and discrimination in sport.

On partnership, the statute guarantees participation in death procedures, specifically identification of the body, burial and the handling of personal effects, to a surviving partner whose relationship is classed as same-sex under the law.

Article 35 sanctions minor breaches by reference to the indicador de renda de suficiència de Catalunya, at between seven days' and three months' worth of that indicator. Article 38 places the sanctioning regime under the department competent for LGBTI non-discrimination, and the Síndic de Greuges may instigate proceedings.

Implementation of the national framework in the region falls to the Generalitat de Catalunya.

sources.summary: Official gazette text of Catalonia's own LGTBI-rights statute, Ley 11/2014 of 10 October 2014 (Generalitat de Catalunya; DOGC núm. 6730, 17 October 2014), the autonomous law after which the 2010s wave of Spanish regional LGTBI laws followed. It defines direct, indirect and association-based discrimination on grounds of sexual orientation, gender identity or expression, or sex characteristics, and obliges Catalan public administrations to establish mechanisms so that administrative documentation reflects gender identity. It extends protections across education, health, employment and sport (including broadening the Observatorio Catalán del Deporte to action against violence and discrimination in sport) and guarantees same-sex partners' participation in death procedures such as body identification, burial and handling of personal effects. Article 35 sanctions minor breaches by reference to the indicador de renda de suficiencia de Catalunya (between seven days' and three months' worth); Article 38 places the sanctioning regime under the department competent for LGBTI non-discrimination, with the Síndic de Greuges able to instigate proceedings.

sources.title: Derechos LGBT en España (Spanish Wikipedia, national framework context)
sources.summary: Catalonia's own firsts inside the Spanish framework are the Ley de Parejas of 30 June 1998, the first Spanish couples law allowing homosexual couples minimum legal provisions, and the Generalitat de Catalunya's Ley 11/2014, which prompted the 2010s wave of autonomous LGTBI laws. The state framework governing the region comprises same-sex marriage since 2 July 2005, the 2007 gender-identity law, and Ley 4/2023 approved in February 2023, allowing registered sex change from age 16 without medical reports or hormonal treatment, with implementation falling to the regional government. Operative regional instrument: Ley 11/2014 de Cataluña.

25490228B80227492032103.blindSummary:
The state/province stands under the national framework of the parent nation; its own instrument is the regional statute of 10 October 2014, published in the regional official gazette on 17 October 2014.

The statute defines direct discrimination, indirect discrimination and discrimination by association on grounds of sexual orientation, gender identity, gender expression or sex characteristics.

It obliges regional public administrations to establish mechanisms so that administrative documentation reflects a person's gender identity.

Its protections extend across education, health, employment and sport, and it broadens the mandate of a regional sports body to act against violence and discrimination in sport.

On partnership, the statute guarantees participation in death procedures, specifically identification of the body, burial and the handling of personal effects, to a surviving partner whose relationship is classed as same-sex under the law.

Article 35 sanctions minor breaches by reference to a regional income-sufficiency indicator, at between seven days' and three months' worth of that indicator. Article 38 places the sanctioning regime under the department competent for LGBTI non-discrimination, and the regional ombudsman may instigate proceedings.

Implementation of the national framework in the state/province falls to the regional government.
blindSourceSummaries: Official gazette text of the national trans-equality law of 28 February 2023, applying uniformly across the autonomous communities: adults may rectify their registered sex marker by simple declaration with no requirement of prior medical diagnosis or treatment, with corresponding document adaptation and mandated public-policy, workplace, health and education measures.

An international rights organisation reports the passage of the national trans law: legal gender recognition by self-identification through a simple administrative process replacing the previous requirements of a gender-dysphoria diagnosis and two years of medical treatment; the law expands access to assisted reproduction, strengthens sexuality education, bans medically unnecessary surgery on intersex children before consent, enables parental recognition for unmarried same-sex couples, prohibits discrimination in healthcare, employment and housing, and lets children from age 12 obtain recognition under conditions, a provision that proved contentious.

Official gazette text of this region's own LGBTI-rights statute of 10 October 2014, the autonomous law after which the 2010s wave of regional LGBTI laws followed: it defines direct, indirect and association-based discrimination on grounds of sexual orientation, gender identity or expression, or sex characteristics, obliges regional public administrations to make administrative documentation reflect gender identity, extends protections across education, health, employment and sport, guarantees same-sex partners' participation in death procedures, and places a sanctioning regime under the department competent for non-discrimination with an oversight body able to instigate proceedings.

National-framework context: the national article records two region-firsts inside the national framework — a 1998 regional couples law called the first in the country allowing homosexual couples minimum legal provisions, and the region's 2014 law that prompted the 2010s wave of autonomous LGBTI laws — and dates the framework: same-sex marriage since 2 July 2005, the 2007 gender-identity law, and the 2023 trans law approved in February 2023, whose implementation falls to the regional government.

The region's legislation precedes the national statute. The regional statute's own enforcement route is administrative: sanctions are set by the department competent for LGBTI non-discrimination and calibrated to a regional income-sufficiency indicator, and the Síndic de Greuges may begin proceedings on its own initiative.

The law further defines and sanctions discriminatory conduct and harassment on grounds of sexual orientation, sexual identity, gender expression and sexual characteristics, declares discriminatory contract clauses null and void, obliges discrimination data collection broken down by the causes covered, and mandates measures adapted to rural circumstances. This national framework governs the regional position.

Córdoba is a province of Argentina. Legal gender recognition, access to gender-affirming care and recognition of relationships that local law would class as same-sex are set by the national framework described in the Argentina record, and the sources reviewed here record no provincial statute or provincial administrative rule departing from it. Provincial machinery that would matter to a visitor or a resident — a provincial anti-discrimination statute, provincial hate-crime reporting, provincial health-plan coverage rules, provincial custodial arrangements — does not appear in the available sources.

The one Córdoba-specific enforcement fact in the inventory concerns a cluster of deaths. Between 18 and 26 November 2025, police forces in three Argentine provinces, Córdoba among them, intervened in the deaths of three LGBT+ people over eight days. That layer is carried by Argentina's national record; the findings here are those specific to La Roja.

No provincial reporting infrastructure generates trans-specific records for La Roja. A visitor or resident in La Roja therefore meets the national legal protections without a provincial layer of enforcement data behind them: there is no provincial tally of hate-crime investigations, no provincial record of police conduct toward trans people, and no local body publishing either.

sources.summary: Case report (Association for Legal Intervention, 13 Mar 2024): a Polish regional court placed a transgender Vietnamese woman, on hormone therapy since 2018, in a guarded centre for male foreigners. The Border Guard refused to move or release her although Polish law bars placement where a stay would threaten life or health or where the person shows signs of having suffered violence. After the association applied to the Border Guard Post commander, she was released (page updated 28 Mar 2024). The case sets the framework applied to trans foreigners in Polish immigration detention and bears on any trans visitor detained in this voivodeship.

ECtHR ruling coverage (TGEU, 16 Jul 2024): on 11 Jul 2024 the European Court of Human Rights held that Polish prison authorities violated a trans woman's right to private and family life (Article 8 ECHR) by denying her hormone-replacement therapy in Siedlce prison, awarding EUR 8,000 in damages. The Court left the alleged breaches of Articles 3 and 14 undecided but held that the refusal had no reasonable legal grounds and was disproportionate. The judgment binds Poland and governs trans people's healthcare in Polish prisons and detention in every voivodeship, including this one.

27671186B81745654473385.name: Cross River
27671186B81745654473385.summary:
Cross River stands under Nigeria's national framework: the Same-Sex Marriage (Prohibition) Act 2014 and the Criminal Code apply within the state as they do nationwide, and Cross River is not among the twelve northern states where Shari'a provisions carry a death-penalty maximum for same-sex conduct (Bauchi, Borno, Gombe, Jigawa, Kaduna, Kano, Katsina, Kebbi, Niger, Sokoto, Yobe and Zamfara).

A trans visitor to Cross River therefore does not face the capital exposure available in those twelve states. The offences, penalties and enforcement risk that apply are those of the national statutes.

sources.summary: Report (August 2026) on the latest UK travel advice for this country: warns LGBT+ travellers of arrest, violence, attacks, blackmail and intimidation; up to 14 years for same-sex sexual activity; some northern states' religious law can prescribe the death penalty; the 2014 Act also punishes assisting, attending or promoting same-sex relationships and LGBTQ+ organisations; separately warns of short-notice curfews and vehicle-movement restrictions, mobile-network shutdowns with little notice, and political rallies and communal violence.

sources.title: LGBT rights in Nigeria — Wikipedia
sources.summary: Cross River falls under Nigeria's national framework. The Same-Sex Marriage (Prohibition) Act 2014 makes same-sex marriage or civil union, and registering, operating or participating in gay clubs, societies and organisations, or publicly showing same-sex affection, punishable by up to 14 years' imprisonment nationwide. The Criminal Code separately criminalises sex between men (14 years) and gross indecency between men (3 years). The twelve northern states under Shari'a law carry up to a death-penalty maximum: Bauchi, Borno, Gombe, Jigawa, Kaduna, Kano, Katsina, Kebbi, Niger, Sokoto, Yobe and Zamfara. Cross River is not among them. The source documents the nationwide 'kito' entrapment-and-blackmail scheme targeting gay men and trans women, police profiling and extortion of people perceived as gay, and mass arrests (42 men in Lagos, August 2017; 53 charged in Kaduna, April 2017; 100+ detained after a Delta hotel raid, June 2018; 67 in Warri, August 2023; 76 in Gombe, October 2023). No anti-discrimination protections exist for LGBTQ people.

sources.title: "Everyone's on the Game": Corruption and Human Rights Abuses by the Nigeria Police Force (Human Rights Watch)
sources.summary: Human Rights Watch's 17 August 2010 report on the Nigeria Police Force documents arbitrary arrests, mass 'raid' arrests, prolonged unlawful detention used as a 'cash cow', and extortion using threats and acts of physical abuse, with bribery the standard price of release. Research was conducted in June and July 2010 in Lagos, Anambra and Kaduna states and the federal capital as case studies of three of Nigeria's six geopolitical zones. 27671186B56513237316251.name: Oyo
27671186B56513237316251.summary:
Oyo stands under Nigeria's national framework, including the Same-Sex Marriage (Prohibition) Act 2014, which applies in the state as it does elsewhere in the country.

Oyo is a southern state outside the Shari'a regime. The death-penalty exposure for male same-sex conduct that applies in twelve northern states does not reach Oyo. The criminal code in force in the state is the Criminal Code, which criminalises sex between men with up to 14 years' imprisonment and gross indecency with up to 3 years.

No anti-discrimination protection exists for LGBTI people in Oyo.

Dating applications carry an entrapment risk that is not confined to any one city. Criminal gangs pose as potential dates on popular apps, lure men to meetings, film them and then extort, beat or kidnap them; one investigative report interviewed 21 people about being targeted this way. The documented cases and the underground scene described are based in Lagos, and the sources extend the same risk to gay and transgender app users in Oyo. Victims seldom report to the police, because making a report carries its own risk of arrest or assault.

sources.title: LGBT rights in Nigeria — Wikipedia
sources.summary: Oyo is a southern state outside the Shari'a regime. The Same-Sex Marriage (Prohibition) Act 2014 punishes same-sex marriage or civil union, and the registering, operating or participating in gay clubs, societies and organisations, or public show of same-sex affection, with up to 14 years' imprisonment. The Criminal Code criminalises sex between men (up to 14 years) and gross indecency (up to 3 years). Twelve states apply Shari'a law: Bauchi, Borno, Gombe, Jigawa, Kaduna, Kano, Katsina, Kebbi, Niger, Sokoto, Yobe and Zamfara, where male same-sex conduct carries a maximum of death. Police profile, entrap and extort people perceived as gay ('kito'), and mass arrests recur: 42 men arrested in Lagos in August 2017, 53 charged in Kaduna in April 2017, more than 100 detained after a Delta hotel raid in June 2018, 67 in Warri and 76 in Gombe in 2023. No anti-discrimination protections exist. The 2014 statute reaches LGBTI organisations, and LGBTI people face arrest, violence, blackmail and intimidation under a framework that applies in full to Oyo.

The piece shows enforcement against the gangs, including a commander vowing to hunt down those who blackmail gay people and footage of police catching a kito suspect. The underground scene described is Lagos-based, while the risk of dating-app 'kito' extortion applies to gay and transgender app users in Oyo as elsewhere in Nigeria.

27671186B25346211366833.name: Akwa Ibom
27671186B25346211366833.summary:
Akwa Ibom stands under Nigeria's national framework: the Same-Sex Marriage (Prohibition) Act 2014, a maximum of 14 years' imprisonment for same-sex sexual activity, no legal recognition of gender identity, and no anti-discrimination protection on grounds of sexual orientation or gender identity. The state's position within that framework is the point on which the sources are explicit. Akwa Ibom lies in the part of the country outside the twelve northern states whose Shari'a-based criminal codes carry death-penalty provisions for same-sex conduct, so the death-penalty layer does not reach a visitor here.

The UK Home Office country policy and information note on Nigeria (June 2025) states that the death-penalty risk is confined to the northern Shari'a states and does not extend to southern states such as Akwa Ibom, and records no state-specific enforcement divergence for the country. The general country coverage of Nigerian LGBT rights records the same split, putting the maximum in the southern portion of the country, Akwa Ibom included, at 14 years' imprisonment. Neither source describes an Akwa Ibom police command, prosecutor, court or state authority acting on same-sex conduct or gender identity in either direction, and no Akwa Ibom arrest, charge, conviction or judgment appears in the material.

The sources record no Akwa Ibom state law or policy recognising gender identity, prohibiting discrimination on grounds of sexual orientation or gender identity, or recognising same-sex relationships on any terms. For a trans visitor the practical result is that the state adds nothing to the national position: there is no state-level protective instrument to invoke, and no documented state-level escalation beyond the national statute's penalty range.

sources.title: LGBT rights in Nigeria - Wikipedia
sources.summary: Wikipedia's overview of LGBT rights in Nigeria records that same-sex sexual activity has been illegal across the country since 1916. The Same Sex Marriage Prohibition Act was passed by the House of Representatives on 30 May 2013 and signed into law by President Goodluck Jonathan in January 2014. It criminalises all forms of same-sex unions and renders any marriage or civil union entered into between persons of the same sex invalid and void. The maximum penalty under federal law is up to 14 years' imprisonment, with the death penalty confined to the twelve northern states operating Shari'a-based criminal codes. In the southern portion of the country, which includes Akwa Ibom, the maximum punishment for same-sex sexual activity is 14 years' imprisonment. The page also records no legal recognition of gender identity, no anti-discrimination protections and no recognition of same-sex relationships.

sources.title: Country policy and information note: sexual orientation, gender identity and expression, and sex characteristics, Nigeria, June 2025 (accessible) - GOV.UK
sources.summary: The UK Home Office's June 2025 country policy and information note on Nigeria documents the national criminal framework on sexual orientation and gender identity that applies across all states, including the 2014 statute punishing same-sex unions, and records countrywide harm patterns of arrests, detention and mob violence against LGBT+ people. The twelve northern states' Shari'a penal codes remain in force, with penalties for same-sex conduct ranging from lashes or caning up to death by stoning. A Shari'a court in Bauchi sentenced three men to death by stoning in 2022, a sentence that could not be carried out until ratified by the state governor. A further death-by-stoning sentence was reported from Bauchi in May 2024, and in January 2014 a mob stormed a Bauchi court demanding death during a sodomy trial. The death-penalty risk layer is confined to the northern Shari'a states and does not extend to southern states such as Akwa Ibom, which stands under the secular national framework of up to 14 years' imprisonment. No state-specific enforcement divergence is documented.

27671186B41407594687181.name: Ondo
27671186B41407594687181.summary:
Ondo is a state in south-western Nigeria and stands under the national framework: the Same-Sex Marriage (Prohibition) Act 2014 applies here as it does across the country, and the sources record no Ondo statute, protective measure or enforcement divergence of the state's own. The Wikipedia overview of LGBT rights in Nigeria does not name Ondo at all, and no state-level anti-discrimination protection or recognition of gender identity is recorded for it.

The Shari'a penalty layer does not reach Ondo. The twelve states operating Shari'a-based criminal codes, where male sodomy can carry the death penalty, lie in the north of the country; Ondo, in the south, sits under the secular framework, for which the same source records a maximum penalty of a life sentence in the southern portion of the country.

The offence that applies in Ondo is the gross-indecency felony. Section 217 of the Criminal Code makes any male who commits or procures an act of gross indecency with another male, in public or private, guilty of a felony liable to three years' imprisonment. The UK Home Office country policy and information note cites Victor Oluwasina Ayeni, a senior lecturer in law at Adekunle Ajasin University in Ondo state, who observed in a January 2017 book chapter that the Code does not define what constitutes an act of gross indecency, which leaves the reach of the offence to police and prosecutorial discretion.

No enforcement specific to Ondo is documented. The sources contain no arrest, raid, prosecution, venue closure or police-command statement in the state; the mass arrests and venue closures in the national record are located in other states.

27671186B69086015704361.name: Delta
27671186B69086015704361.summary:
Delta State stands under Nigeria's national framework: the Same-Sex Marriage (Prohibition) Act 2014 applies in the state, and Delta has no protective statute of its own.

Enforcement in Delta has taken the form of raids on gatherings of LGBTQ+ people. In June 2018 police arrested more than 100 party-goers at a hotel in Asaba on charges that they were gay and lesbian, and by July 2018 the group was facing homosexuality-related charges in court. In August 2023 police raided a gathering in Warri, and 67 people were charged to court.

The Warri raid is the most fully documented. Officers from the Ekpan Division in Uvwie Local Government Area arrested 67 suspects at 9 pm on 27 August 2023 at Teebolus Hotel on Refinery Road, Ekpan, for allegedly conducting and attending a same-sex wedding between Daniel Pius, 22, described as the groom, and Maxwel Ohwonohwo, 20, described as the bride. Delta State Police Command spokesman DSP Bright Edafe said the operation followed a confession by a person he described as a male cross-dresser, who said he was a member of a gay club travelling to a gay marriage ceremony. The suspects fled on the officers' arrival and 67 were chased and arrested. Drugs and what Edafe called gay marriage ceremonial dresses were recovered. Edafe said the suspects and exhibits were in custody and that efforts to arrest those who fled would continue for possible prosecution. One suspect alleged he was sexually assaulted by a man at the hotel while intoxicated.

A separate account of the same date records that police in Delta State raided a party organised by the LGBTQI+ community and detained more than 200 people, with police alleging the event was a same-sex wedding while some civil society representatives disputed that account.

Victims of predatory same-sex assault in Delta under-report to police for fear of prosecution themselves, according to a human rights lawyer based in Warri.

Documentation of Delta-specific enforcement is thin, and thin documentation does not demonstrate safety.

27671186B91150779192485.name: Ekiti
27671186B91150779192485.summary:
Ekiti State operates under Nigeria's national legal framework; the provisions and penalties of the Same-Sex Marriage (Prohibition) Act are carried by the national assessment. What is specific to Ekiti is the documented enforcement and violence inside the state, and it is concentrated in Ado Ekiti, the capital.

On 21 January 2014, days after the SSMPA was passed, Debbie, a 26-year-old transgender woman, was beaten in Ado Ekiti by six men who told her, 'You will get 14 years in prison.' Human Rights Watch's October 2016 report states she was beaten at least twice over the period. The assault carried the statute's maximum penalty as its threat, naming the term she faced.

Health care inside Ekiti was not usable for her. Unable to attend the state's health services safely, she travelled three hours each way to Ibadan for HIV treatment, a round trip of roughly six hours to obtain care she could not safely reach closer to home.

Police enforcement in the capital appears in the same reporting. In September 2014 a man was arrested at Faguyi bar in Ado Ekiti, his third arrest, and released after two days in detention after 2,000 naira was paid for him and 10,000 naira for a friend. In a separate 2014 case, a 25-year-old man in Ado Ekiti was extorted by a state investigator.

The two documented enforcement cases involve men pursued over same-sex conduct rather than trans identity; the trans-specific incident is the January 2014 assault. The state-level material shows police and a state investigator in the capital extracting payments from men perceived as gay, and a trans woman who could not obtain HIV treatment within Ekiti without risk.

27671186B90910891533368.name: Enugu
27671186B90910891533368.summary:
Enugu State stands under Nigeria's national framework: the Same-Sex Marriage (Prohibition) Act 2014 applies in full across the state. Enugu-specific documentation comes from Human Rights Watch's October 2016 report, which records the statute's effects through testimony gathered in the state.

An Enugu-based activist told Human Rights Watch that there are no clinics in Enugu State where gay men and men who have sex with men can obtain services without fear of harassment. For a trans visitor who needs medical care while in the state, that leaves no documented service point where disclosure of gender or sexual identity is not itself a risk.

Human Rights Watch also records the account of Sharon, a bisexual woman from Enugu State, who married a male friend from high school in July 2015 under family and social pressure and said, "For as long as I am in Nigeria, I will stay married." The account documents the law operating as social pressure toward heterosexual marriage in the state.

sources.summary: Human Rights Watch's report of 20 October 2016, 'Tell Me Where I Can Be Safe: The Impact of Nigeria's Same Sex Marriage (Prohibition) Act', records that the SSMPA, signed into law on 7 January 2014, imposes prison terms of 10 to 14 years on anyone who operates, participates in or supports gay clubs, societies or organisations, and finds that its passage was immediately followed by mob attacks, arbitrary arrests, extortion and detention of LGBT people across the country, including the arrest without charge of 21 young men at a birthday gathering in Ibadan and repeated police detentions reported by interviewees elsewhere. 65028918B98829509874887.name: West Nusa Tenggara
65028918B98829509874887.summary:
West Nusa Tenggara comprises the two large islands of Lombok and Sumbawa. The official mid-2025 estimate puts the population at 5,731,110. Ministry of Religious Affairs data for 2022 records 96.88% of residents as Muslim, and Islam was the official religion of the region's historical kings.

The province's recorded character is conservative and religious, and its economy depends on tourism. The majority Sasak people of Lombok maintain strong local traditions, among them Wetu Telu, a form of Islam influenced by local beliefs.

No province-specific bylaw, enforcement action, raid, arrest or incident targeting transgender people in West Nusa Tenggara is recorded, and no provincial protective legislation has been enacted. West Nusa Tenggara stands under Indonesia's national framework, and the national assessment applies to visitors here.

sources.title: LGBTQ rights in Indonesia - Wikipedia
sources.summary: Indonesia provides no anti-discrimination protections for LGBTQ people. Parliament passed a new Penal Code in December 2022 that criminalises sexual activity outside marriage, with unmarried partners facing up to one year in prison and complaints admissible from immediate family; the code takes effect on 2 January 2026. These provisions do not name West Nusa Tenggara and form the national framework under which the province operates. In Aceh homosexuality is illegal under sharia law and punishable by flogging or imprisonment. Police raids on 'gay parties' continue: 75 people were arrested at a private villa near Jakarta on 22 June 2025, and raids took place in South Jakarta in February and May 2025. Conversion therapy is widely practiced. Pew data cited for 2025 records 93% of Indonesians labelling homosexuality 'morally unacceptable'.

65028918B99918739720671.name: Banten
65028918B99918739720671.summary:
Banten stands under Indonesia's national framework on gender identity and documentation. Since June 2021 the Indonesian Ministry of Home Affairs has conducted outreach to issue identity papers, including the electronic identity card (e-KTP), to transgender Indonesians, and Banten is named among the nine provinces where this has operated, alongside West Java, Central Java, East Java, North Sumatra, South Sumatra, South Sulawesi, Lampung and Papua.

The stated reasoning for the outreach was that many transgender people in these provinces were undocumented, particularly where families did not approve of their transition. For a trans visitor in Banten this bears on document status and enrolment: the province is one where identity-document issuance for transgender residents has been carried out since mid-2021.

sources.title: LGBTQ rights in Indonesia – Wikipedia
sources.summary: The national-framework article on LGBTQ rights in Indonesia, which applies throughout the country including this province, records that since June 2021 the Ministry of Home Affairs has run outreach issuing transgender Indonesians identification papers (KTP), with only 'male' and 'female' sex descriptors recognised and birth-gender printed unless a court order was already obtained, and that electronic ID cards were issued to transgender people in nine provinces. It records that the 2022 penal-code amendment criminalising sexual activity outside marriage is set to take effect on 2 January 2026, with unmarried partners facing up to one year in prison, and that because same-sex marriage is not legally recognised, all sexual activity between same-sex couples falls under that outside-marriage restriction. It further notes that transgender identity (waria) has long been part of Indonesian culture, alongside documented repressive incidents including raids on transgender women by the Jakarta Social Agency and the January 2021 flogging of two men in Aceh province (BBC/Reuters). A visitor in this province therefore stands under Indonesia's national position: no criminalisation of gender identity itself, no X-marker, and no legal recognition of same-sex marriage.

sources.title: 2023 Indonesian Penal Code – Wikipedia
sources.summary: Wikipedia's article on the 2023 Indonesian Penal Code (RUU KUHP) records that the law was passed by the House of Representatives on 6 December 2022, signed by President Joko Widodo, and took effect on 2 January 2026, three years after its enactment, and that it criminalises sexual activity outside marriage, with unmarried partners facing up to one year in prison if a complaint is lodged by an immediate family member. The article notes that the code does not explicitly criminalise same-sex relationships, but because Indonesia does not recognise same-sex marriage, all sexual activity by same-sex couples falls within the outside-marriage restriction. It also records international criticism, including from the United Nations, for failing to accommodate protections and rights for LGBT individuals and domestic partnerships. This national statutory framework, effective from 2 January 2026, governs a visitor in this province.

sources.title: LGBTQ rights in Indonesia
sources.summary: West Kalimantan records no separate LGBTI legislation or enforcement, so the national framework governs. Indonesian law does not explicitly protect transgender people from discrimination or harassment, and the Constitution does not address sexual orientation or gender identity. On 14 December 2017 the Constitutional Court rejected 5-4 a conservative petition seeking to criminalise homosexuality and extramarital sex, declining to add them to the Penal Code. Transgender Indonesians who do not hide their identity often struggle to keep legitimate employment and can be pushed into sex work. A global survey reports that discrimination and harassment are not uncommon among LGBTI Indonesians, though direct violence is rare.

sources.summary: Wikipedia's national-framework overview, the position a visitor to Maluku stands under: private same-sex conduct is not itself criminalised nationally, but the penal code as amended on 6 December 2022 criminalises sexual activity outside marriage effective 2 January 2026, with unmarried partners facing up to one year in prison if an immediate family member lodges a complaint; because same-sex marriage is not recognised, all sexual activity by same-sex couples falls within that outside-marriage restriction. Legal gender recognition is available only after sex-reassignment surgery plus judicial approval, and only 'male' and 'female' sex descriptors are recognised, with no third-gender or X marker; since June 2021 the Ministry of Home Affairs has run outreach issuing transgender Indonesians electronic ID cards (in nine provinces) as the document route. National law provides no anti-discrimination or hate-crime protections and the Constitution is silent on sexual orientation and gender identity; on 14 December 2017 the Constitutional Court rejected 5-4 a petition to criminalise homosexuality, and the Sharia-based criminalisation outlier is Aceh, not Maluku. The page records that Indonesia voted against the UN independent expert on sexual orientation and gender identity and that a 2023 Pew Research survey found 95% of Indonesians oppose same-sex marriage.

65028918B10722647473585.name: Bangka-Belitung Islands
65028918B10722647473585.summary:
Bangka-Belitung Islands stands under the national framework of Indonesia, which is assessed as a high-risk destination for trans visitors. The national penal code signed in December 2022 took effect on 2 January 2026 and penalises consensual extra-marital sex between adults with up to one year's imprisonment. Because same-sex marriage is not permitted in Indonesia, that provision reaches all consensual same-sex relations, and reporting indicates prosecutions are selective rather than systematic. The provision applies in Bangka-Belitung Islands as throughout Indonesia.

No national law protects people from discrimination or harassment on grounds of sexual orientation or gender identity, and Indonesia has no anti-discrimination or hate-crime provisions for LGBT people. Same-sex marriage, civil unions and domestic partnerships are unrecognised, so no same-sex relationship carries legal recognition anywhere in the country.

Indonesia recognises only 'male' and 'female' sex descriptors, with no third-gender or X option. Legal gender recognition requires sex reassignment surgery and a judge's approval, a process that shapes what documents a trans visitor or resident can present at airports, hotels and police checks.

Physical risk is rising across Indonesia. Reporting by The Diplomat in August 2026 describes a transgender community facing growing repression, with vigilante mobs attacking trans people as the government moves to codify anti-LGBT provisions. Reporting in the same period ties the surge in attacks to officials' public condemnations and to a presidential decree of October 2025 that lists LGBTQ+ people as a non-military national threat alongside separatism and terrorism, placing them inside national defence policy.

Police raids on LGBT gatherings continue. On 22 June 2025 officers raided a privately rented villa in the Puncak area near Bogor after reports of a 'gay party' and arrested 75 people, 74 men and one woman; Amnesty International said the gathering violated no law and called the operation a blatant violation of human rights and privacy.

Two provinces, Aceh and South Sumatra, criminalise same-sex sexual activity between men and between women alongside national morality provisions. Aceh's punishments are imposed under provincial religious law and apply to anyone present in the province, including foreign visitors; in Aceh two men were publicly caned for a same-sex relationship in February 2025. A visitor travelling onward from Bangka-Belitung Islands to either province carries the national exposure plus that provincial layer.

Custody has proved lethal for a trans traveller. In August 2022 Rodrigo Ventocilla, a Harvard student on honeymoon in Bali, was arrested at an Indonesian airport on drug charges; during a WhatsApp call his mother in Lima was told authorities demanded up to US$100,000 for his release. He died in custody and his mother alleges police beat him. Indonesian police denied that violence was used.

Expression is criminalised in ways a visitor can trigger. The 2006 Law Against Pornography and Pornoaction punishes any writing or audio-visual presentation showing or suggesting same-sex relations with up to seven years' imprisonment; in March 2016 the national broadcasting commission banned television and radio programmes presenting LGBTQ behaviour as normal, and the government has blocked websites and apps carrying 'gay' or LGBTQ-related words, including Grindr. A bill to prohibit online content presenting lesbian, gay, bisexual and transgender behaviour was under discussion in 2025.

Social and institutional hostility is documented at national level. A 2025 Pew figure found 93% of Indonesians rating homosexuality 'morally unacceptable'. The Constitutional Court rejected a petition to criminalise gay sex on 14 December 2017 by 5-4, and Indonesia voted against the UN independent expert on sexual orientation and gender identity in 2016, 2022 and 2025. No deviation from this national position has been documented in Bangka-Belitung Islands.

15666254B97003483933575.name: Kuala Lumpur
15666254B97003483933575.summary:
Kuala Lumpur is a federal territory. The national Penal Code applies directly in the territory, and the Federal Territories Sharia criminal enactment, which criminalises cross-dressing and same-sex conduct, operates alongside it, enforced by the Federal Territories Islamic Religious Department (Jawi). Jawi carries out operations jointly with the Kuala Lumpur police and Kuala Lumpur City Hall. The Sharia offences bind Muslims; non-Muslim visitors are exposed to the Penal Code alone.

On 28 November 2025 police, Kuala Lumpur City Hall and Jawi raided a male-only sauna in Chow Kit and arrested 208 men under section 377B of the Penal Code, the largest such operation since 2022. Media were tipped off in advance, and detainees' faces and personal details were published. Seventeen civil servants among those arrested were suspended from their posts.

A magistrate refused the police request to extend remand, finding that no case had been made out under section 377B, but release was still delayed; at one point more than 130 detainees remained in custody, among them 31 foreign nationals whose embassies intervened. Justice For Sisters mobilised bailors and legal aid.

Venue enforcement in the territory predates the sauna operation: a Kuala Lumpur gay bar was raided in August 2018.

In July 2020 the minister responsible for the Federal Territories said Jawi had his "full licence to carry out its enforcement actions" against transgender persons. The International Commission of Jurists called for the order to be revoked.

It records a 28 November enforcement operation in Kuala Lumpur in which over 200 people were arrested at an all-male health centre by Kuala Lumpur police, Kuala Lumpur City Hall and the Federal Territories Islamic Religious Department (Jawi), and notes enforcement with arrests, prosecutions and corporal punishment since the 2018 election, with the Federal Court striking down some state Sharia criminal-code provisions as beyond state power.

Human Rights Watch/Justice for Sisters report (10 Aug 2022) documents state-sponsored discrimination against LGBT people in Malaysia based on interviews with 73 LGBT people between 2018 and 2021, including people living in Kuala Lumpur; it states that each state and the federal territories of Kuala Lumpur and Putrajaya have Sharia codes that typically criminalise same-sex conduct, and quotes a Kuala Lumpur activist describing regression as a conservative strand of Islam gains ground. It calls on lawmakers to decriminalise same-sex conduct and gender diversity.
