15666254B60207109163985.name: Negeri Sembilan
15666254B60207109163985.summary:
Negeri Sembilan sits within the national framework of Malaysia, which carries the federal Penal Code offences, the identity-document rules and the entry position; those apply here as they do nationwide and are set out in the national record. The state's own layer is its Sharia criminal law. The Syariah Criminal Enactment 1992 contained at section 66 an offence of cross-dressing, and in November 2014 the Court of Appeal declared that provision unconstitutional for breaching rights guaranteed by the Federal Constitution.

Muslim visitors and residents in Negeri Sembilan are the people within reach of that enactment; non-Muslims are not. Section 66 was the operative state offence for a person whose dress or appearance was read as gender nonconforming, and whether an equivalent provision is in force or enforced in this state today is not established by the sources.

The Human Rights Watch and Justice for Sisters research published on 10 August 2022 is the only account in the inventory of how the state-level regime is experienced. It drew on interviews with 73 people conducted between 2018 and 2021, among them people living in Negeri Sembilan, and found state-backed discrimination against LGBT people; it calls on lawmakers to decriminalise same-sex conduct and gender diversity and to abandon rehabilitation programmes and the rhetoric attached to them.

Federal criminalisation of same-sex conduct persists under Penal Code 1936 Sections 377A/377B (up to 20 years' imprisonment with whipping), with a crackdown involving arrests, prosecutions and corporal punishment since the 2018 election.

Human Rights Watch/Justice for Sisters report (10 Aug 2022) documents state-sponsored discrimination and criminalisation of LGBT people in Malaysia, based on interviews with 73 people between 2018 and 2021 including people living in Negeri Sembilan; it states that every state and the federal territories of Kuala Lumpur and Putrajaya have Sharia codes that typically criminalise same-sex conduct. It calls on lawmakers to decriminalise same-sex conduct and gender diversity and to abandon 'rehabilitation' programs and rhetoric.

28173009B92397886288731.name: Sverdlovsk Oblast
28173009B92397886288731.summary:
Sverdlovsk Oblast has no legislation of its own on gender identity or sexual orientation and stands under the national framework of Russia, which applies in full; the oblast administration has added no protections of its own. What is documented at regional level is enforcement pressure and violence in Yekaterinburg, the oblast capital.

Reporting dated 21 October 2024 records that a gay man in Yekaterinburg was beaten and robbed after being lured into a fake date, and that a Yekaterinburg LGBTQ+ support group shut down after pressure. Together they show targeting in the oblast operating through private violence and through pressure on the organisations that would otherwise provide support.

sources.title: LGBTQ rights in Khakassia (Wikipedia)
sources.summary: Transgender people are not allowed to change their legal gender, and gender-affirming care is banned. In July 2023 Russia enacted a law banning gender transition which prohibited both gender-affirming surgery and legal gender recognition outright, after April-May 2023 proposals to rule out changing gender purely by changing documents and to ban reassignment without surgery. The propaganda law as expanded in 2022 applies to anyone regardless of age group and prohibits distribution of materials that make minors interested in gender transitions. A 2024 law bans adoption of Russian children by citizens or permanent residents of countries that allow gender transitions, and single-person foreign adoption is allowed only where the country neither recognises same-sex marriage nor allows gender transition. Russia provides no anti-discrimination protections for LGBTQ people and has no hate-crime designation based on gender identity. In a 30 September 2022 speech President Putin said teaching children about other genders and offering sex-change surgeries is unacceptable, linking opposition to transgender rights to willingness to use all means against Ukraine. Officials cited protection of family values and draft evasion, claiming about 2,700 recent legal-gender changes and that many young men turned to private clinics for sex change to avoid conscription in connection with the special operation. Consensual sexual activity between adults of the same sex is legal after 1993 re-legalisation removing Article 121 from the RSFSR Penal Code, which had punished consensual sex between men with three to five years imprisonment under Article 154-a and later Article 121, with age of consent at 16 since 2003 regardless of sexual orientation. Neither same-sex marriages nor civil unions are allowed, with a July 2020 constitutional amendment banning same-sex marriage, and same-sex couples are ineligible for legal protections available to opposite-sex couples with no legal recognition offered despite the 2021 Fedotova and Others v. Russia ruling. Russia provides no anti-discrimination protections for LGBTQ people and has no hate-crime designation based on sexual orientation, and refuses to register LGBTQ organisations. A 2013 federal law criminalised distribution of propaganda promoting non-traditional sexual relationships among minors, expanded in 2022 to apply to anyone regardless of age group. In November 2023 the Supreme Court designated the international LGBT public movement as an extremist organisation, formally added on 22 March 2024 to the unified list of terrorist and extremist organizations, making leading, participating in, financially supporting, or repeatedly displaying its symbols a criminal offense punishable by prison time. Enforcement includes arrests of gay bar owners, fines or jail for displaying the rainbow flag, a 2010 European Court of Human Rights fine for systemic refusal of pride parade permits and an August 2012 Moscow City Court decision upholding a ban on Moscow Pride through 2012, and Chechnya detentions, torture and killings targeting persons based on perceived sexual orientation since February 2017 with over 100 men detained and OSCE confirmation in December 2018. Adoption is limited domestically to single persons regardless of sexual orientation and jointly only to married heterosexual couples, with foreign single-person adoption barred where the country recognises same-sex marriage.

sources.title: LGBTQ rights in Tatarstan (Wikipedia)
sources.summary: Russia provides no anti-discrimination protections for LGBTQ people and has no hate-crime designation based on sexual orientation and gender identity. Transgender people are not allowed to change legal gender and gender-affirming care is banned under a bill passed in 2023 and a July 2023 law prohibiting both gender-affirming surgery and legal gender recognition outright. The 2022 expansion of the propaganda law applies to anyone regardless of age and prohibits distribution of materials that make minors interested in gender transitions. Russian children cannot be adopted by citizens or permanent residents of countries that allow gender transitions under a 2024 law, and a single foreign adopter is permitted only if their country neither recognises same-sex marriage nor gender transition. The military medical expertise statute provides that people 'who have problems with their identity and sexual preferences' can only be drafted during wartime, while authorities claimed about 2,700 legal gender-change decisions in recent times were sought to avoid conscription amid the special operation. On 30 September 2022 President Putin stated 'Do we want them to be taught that instead of men and women, there are supposedly some other genders and to be offered sex-change surgeries? This is unacceptable to us.' Consensual sexual activity between adults of the same sex is legal after homosexual acts between consenting males were re-legalised in 1993 with removal of Article 121, which had punished consensual sex between men with three to five years' imprisonment with an estimated 800 to 1000 men imprisoned per year in the Soviet era. The age of consent is 16 since 2003 regardless of sexual orientation, and homosexuality was removed from the list of mental illnesses in 1999 with ICD-10, though new laws introduced 1 July 2023 effectively reinstate the classification. Neither same-sex marriages nor civil unions are allowed, with a July 2020 constitutional amendment banning same-sex marriage and no legal recognition available despite the 2021 Fedotova and Others v. Russia ruling finding a human-rights violation. The 2013 law criminalising distribution of 'propaganda' promoting 'non-traditional sexual relationships' among minors was expanded in 2022 to apply to anyone regardless of age. In November 2023 the Supreme Court designated 'the international LGBT public movement' as an extremist organisation, formally listed 22 March 2024, making leading, participating in, financially supporting, or repeatedly displaying its symbols including the rainbow flag a criminal offense punishable by prison time, leading to arrests of gay club owners with at least one dying in custody as of April 2025 and fines or jail for displaying the rainbow flag, and between March and May 2026 city courts outlawed nine LGBTQ organisations as extremist. Russia provides no anti-discrimination protections, has no hate-crime designation based on sexual orientation, refuses to register LGBTQ organisations which are prohibited as extremist, and does not officially record hate crimes against the LGBTQ community. Anti-gay purges in Chechnya since February 2017 involved forced disappearances, secret abductions, imprisonment, torture and extrajudicial killings with over 100 men detained and tortured and at least three dead, a further purge from December 2018 with around 40 detained and two killed, confirmed by a December 2018 OSCE report and followed by EU economic sanctions on two Chechen officials in March 2021, while nationally an estimated 1,056 hate crimes against 853 individuals with 365 fatalities occurred between 2010 and 2020, tripling from 46 in 2010 to 138 in 2015 with hate groups using dating apps to hunt homosexuals.

28173009B68474107072963.name: Astrakhan Oblast
28173009B68474107072963.summary:
Astrakhan Oblast stands under the national framework of Russia, which applies in full across all the country's regions. Russia presents severe legal and physical risks for transgender visitors, and the position has hardened since 2022. Legal gender recognition and gender-affirming care were banned outright in 2023, when the law prohibiting gender reassignment surgery and legal gender changes on official documents was signed; the Supreme Court has designated the "international LGBT movement" an extremist organisation; and the expanded "propaganda" statute criminalises public expression that, explicitly, "justifies" gender transition. Foreigners who breach these provisions face arrest, up to 15 days' detention and deportation, and national government warnings state this directly to LGBT travellers.

The UK Home Office country policy and information note on sexual orientation and gender identity and expression (June 2025, assessment section updated 11 June 2025) records that same-sex activity is not criminalised in Russia, while same-sex marriage and gender transition are banned and trans-specific healthcare was effectively banned in 2023. No discrimination legislation based on sexual orientation or gender identity covers housing, healthcare or employment.

Penalties applicable in Astrakhan Oblast are substantial. 'Gay propaganda' offences carry fines up to 400,000 roubles (about £3,600) for individuals or up to 15 days' detention, and repeat offences can bring criminal prosecution with up to four years in prison. The November 2023 Supreme Court 'extremist' designation of the international LGBT+ movement makes participation punishable by two to six years and organising by six to ten years.

Enforcement volume is documented. Between December 2022 and March 2024 at least 139 people were affected by enforcement of anti-LGBT+ laws. Human Rights Watch reported on 30 June 2025 that Russian courts had issued 101 'extremism'-related convictions tied to the International Public LGBT Movement designation, approximately 98 administrative and three criminal. The Home Office assessment finds that trans people, publicly active LGBT+ advocates and those in the North Caucasus are likely to face treatment amounting to persecution, and affirms that LGBT+ people in Russia, including the autonomous republic of Chechnya, constitute a particular social group under the refugee convention.

Two foreign-government advisories bear on visitor exposure. The US State Department rates Russia Level 4, Do Not Travel, with warnings directed at LGBT travellers, and states that official support is 'very limited' in parts of the country.

sources.title: LGBTQ rights in Mari El (Wikipedia)
sources.summary: Transgender people are not allowed to change their legal gender, and gender-affirming care is banned. In July 2023 Russia enacted a law banning gender transition which prohibited both gender-affirming surgery and legal gender recognition outright, following April-May 2023 State Duma proposals to prevent trans women from changing legal gender from male to female without surgery and to rule out changing gender purely by changing documents. The 2022 expansion of the propaganda law applies to anyone regardless of age group and prohibits distribution of materials that make minors interested in gender transitions. A 2024 law bans adoption of Russian children by citizens or permanent residents of countries that allow gender transitions, and foreign single-person adoption is permitted only where the country neither recognises same-sex marriage nor gender transition. The article links legal gender change to conscription avoidance, stating that many young men have turned to private clinics to provide a sex change to avoid conscription in connection with the special operation and that Duma Speaker Vyacheslav Volodin claimed 2,700 such decisions in recent times. On 30 September 2022 President Putin stated "Do we want them to be taught that instead of men and women, there are supposedly some other genders and to be offered sex-change surgeries? This is unacceptable to us." while invoking transgender rights in justification for action against Ukraine and willingness to use all means at disposal. Consensual same-sex sexual activity between adults is legal after re-legalisation in 1993 removing Article 121, which had previously punished consensual sex between men with three to five years imprisonment under 1934 Article 154-a and up to five years under 1961 Article 121, with age of consent at 16 since 2003 regardless of sexual orientation. Neither same-sex marriages nor civil unions are allowed, voters approved a constitutional amendment banning same-sex marriage in July 2020, no legal recognition is offered despite the 2021 Fedotova and Others v. Russia ruling finding a human rights violation, and only married heterosexual couples may adopt jointly though single persons regardless of sexual orientation may adopt domestically. The 2013 federal law criminalised distribution of propaganda promoting non-traditional sexual relationships among minors and was expanded in 2022 to apply to anyone regardless of age. In November 2023 the Supreme Court designated the international LGBT public movement as an extremist organisation, formally added on 22 March 2024 to the unified list of terrorist and extremist organizations, making leading, participating in, financially supporting, or repeatedly displaying its symbols a criminal offense punishable by prison time. Enforcement includes arrests of gay bar owners, fines or jail for displaying the rainbow flag including earrings, at least one death in custody as of April 2025, and between March and May 2026 city courts outlawing nine organisations including Centre T, Coming Out, Russian LGBT Network and others with convictions of founders for leading an extremist organisation. Russia provides no anti-discrimination protections for LGBTQ people and has no hate-crime designation based on sexual orientation and gender identity and does not officially record hate crimes against the LGBTQ community, with estimates of 1,056 hate crimes against 853 individuals between 2010 and 2020 with 365 fatalities, annual crimes tripling from 46 in 2010 to 138 in 2015, and group-organised hunting via dating apps including Occupy Pedophilia active in 40 regions. In Chechnya, authorities targeted persons based on perceived sexual orientation with forced disappearances, secret abductions, imprisonment, torture and extrajudicial killing, with over 100 men detained and tortured and at least three dead from February 2017 and around 40 detained and two killed from December 2018, confirmed by a December 2018 OSCE report and followed by March 2021 EU sanctions on two officials.

28173009B27844369294009.name: Novosibirsk Oblast
28173009B27844369294009.summary:
Novosibirsk Oblast stands under the national framework of Russia. The federal ban on legal gender recognition, the expanded propaganda statutes and the November 2023 extremism designation of the "international LGBT movement" are carried by the national record; what follows is what is documented in the oblast itself.

A court in Novosibirsk fined the Elton John Bar 500,000 rubles (about £4,598) for "promoting LGBTI propaganda" through a rainbow flag. The case followed the venue's appearance in a video by the LGBT+ activist blogger Karen Shainyan. The fine shows the propaganda statutes reaching a commercial venue in the oblast, a step beyond enforcement against individuals posting online.

Coercive conversion practice has been documented in the oblast. A transgender woman was lured by relatives in summer 2021 to a centre near Novosibirsk and held for nine months, forced to take testosterone, pray and perform manual labour. She escaped only after police responded to a phone she had found.

A priest in a village in the Novosibirsk region told The Moscow Times that religion can correct "deviations", indicating that local religious authority frames gender variance as a defect to be corrected.

Human Rights Watch's tally of 101 extremism-related convictions nationally since the November 2023 designation records no case specific to Novosibirsk Oblast. The absence of a documented oblast case does not establish that none has been brought.

sources.title: Vitaly Milonov - Wikipedia
sources.summary: Wikipedia's biography of Vitaly Milonov documents the city-level origin of the anti-LGBT law a trans visitor to Saint Petersburg stands under. As a member of the Saint Petersburg Legislative Assembly (2007-2016), he is recorded as the principal sponsor of the legislation criminalising 'homosexual propaganda directed toward minors', the city ban enacted in 2012 that the New York Times report 'Anti-Gay Law Stirs Fears in Russia' (29 February 2012) covered. The page quotes his statement that he fully intended to catch Madonna committing a possible offence under it when she visited the city. It also records Milonov stating in 2013 that gay athletes could be arrested at the 2014 Sochi Winter Olympics if they promoted homosexuality to minors, and his protests against the city's Side by Side LGBT film festival in November 2013.

sources.title: LGBTQ rights in Russia - Wikipedia
sources.summary: Wikipedia's country overview of LGBTQ rights in Russia supplies the federal framework Saint Petersburg is assessed under: a 2013 law criminalises distributing 'propaganda' of 'non-traditional sexual relationships' among minors, with fines up to 5,000 roubles for citizens, 50,000 for officials, and 1 million roubles plus up to 90 days' suspension for organisations, while foreigners face up to 15 days' detention, a fine up to 100,000 roubles and deportation. Ten regions including Saint Petersburg (2012) enacted regional versions of the ban before the federal law, and Saint Petersburg removed its regional law in 2014, leaving the federal statute in force there. A July 2023 law bans gender transition outright, prohibiting both gender-affirming surgery and legal gender recognition. A 2010 European Court of Human Rights ruling fined Russia over the systematic refusal of pride-event permits.

sources.title: LGBTQ rights in Sakha Republic (Wikipedia)
sources.summary: Transgender people are not allowed to change their legal gender and gender-affirming care is banned. In 2022 the 'propaganda' law was expanded to apply to anyone regardless of age group and to prohibit distribution of materials that make minors interested in gender transitions. In July 2023 Russia enacted a law banning gender transition which prohibited both gender-affirming surgery and legal gender recognition outright, following April-May 2023 State Duma proposals to 'rule out the possibility of changing a person's gender purely by changing the documents' and to ban reassignment without surgery on 'family values' grounds. In 2024 Russia passed a law banning adoption of Russian children by citizens or permanent residents of countries that allow gender transitions; inside Russia single persons regardless of sexual orientation can adopt but a couple can adopt jointly only if a married heterosexual couple, and a foreign single adopter must live in a country that neither recognises same-sex marriage nor gender transition. In the draft-evasion context, authorities claimed many young men turned to private clinics for sex change to avoid conscription in connection with the special operation, with the Duma Speaker claiming some '2,700' such decisions, and Russian men were described as considering changing legal gender to avoid being drafted. On 30 September 2022 President Vladimir Putin said teaching children that 'instead of men and women, there are supposedly some other genders and to be offered sex-change surgeries' is 'unacceptable to us' while stating Russia would use 'all means at our disposal' against Ukraine. Russia provides no anti-discrimination protections for LGBTQ people and has no hate-crime designation based on gender identity, and authorities refuse to register LGBTQ organisations while pro-LGBTQ advocacy groups have been declared extremist and prohibited from operating. Consensual sexual activity between adults of the same sex is legal after re-legalisation in 1993 removing Article 121, which under Stalin from March 1934 as Article 154-a and from 1961 as Article 121 punished consensual sex between men with three to five years' imprisonment with a maximum of five years, with an estimated 800 to 1000 men imprisoned per year in the Soviet era; the age of consent is 16 since 2003 regardless of sexual orientation, and homosexuality was removed from the mental-illness list in 1999 with ICD-10 but new laws on 1 July 2023 effectively reinstated classification as mental illness. Neither same-sex marriages nor civil unions are allowed, the 2020 constitutional amendment bans same-sex marriage, marriage is defined as between a man and a woman, same-sex couples are ineligible for legal protections available to opposite-sex couples, and Russia did not implement the 2021 European Court of Human Rights Fedotova ruling requiring legal recognition after leaving the court in 2022. The 2013 federal law criminalised distribution of 'propaganda' promoting 'non-traditional sexual relationships' among minors and was expanded in 2022 to anyone regardless of age; in November 2023 the Supreme Court designated 'the international LGBT public movement' as extremist, formally added on 22 March 2024 to the unified list of terrorist and extremist organizations, where leading, participating in, financially supporting or repeatedly displaying symbols is a criminal offense punishable by prison time, leading to arrests of gay bar owners with at least one dying in custody as of April 2025 and fines or jail for displaying the rainbow flag including earrings. Enforcement includes refusal to register LGBTQ organisations, prohibition of advocacy groups as extremist and 'foreign agents,' systemic refusal of pride parade permits with Moscow never approving a request and Moscow City Court upholding a yearly ban through 2012 despite a 2010 European Court fine for discrimination, and Defence Ministry guidance recommending asking recruits about sexual history and examining genital or buttocks tattoos allegedly indicating homosexual orientation while openly gay men are formally not excluded from service but warned not to reveal orientation to avoid beating. Violence and custody include Chechen forced disappearances, secret abductions, imprisonment, torture and extrajudicial killings targeting perceived sexual orientation, with over 100 men detained and tortured since February 2017 and at least three dead, a December 2018 OSCE report confirming persecution ignored by authorities, another purge from December 2018 with around 40 detained and two killed, and March 2021 EU economic sanctions on two Chechen officials; nationally the government does not officially record hate crimes, with an estimated 1,056 hate crimes against 853 individuals between 2010 and 2020 including 365 fatalities, annual crimes tripling from 46 in 2010 to 138 in 2015, increased premeditated group attacks in 2017-2019 using dating apps to 'hunt' homosexuals, and 205 cases by homophobic hate groups including Occupy Pedophilia active in 40 regions. Protection machinery is absent with no anti-discrimination protections based on sexual orientation and no hate-crime designation, illustrated by the January 2013 firing of television anchor Anton Krasovsky after announcing he was gay and the September 2013 firing of Khabarovsk teacher Alexander Yermoshkin after attack by neo-Nazi group 'Shtolz Khabarovsk' amid a campaign by 'Movement against the propaganda of sexual perversions.'

sources.title: LGBTQ rights in Tuva (Wikipedia)
sources.summary: Transgender people are not allowed to change their legal gender, and gender-affirming care is banned. In 2022 the propaganda law was expanded to apply to anyone regardless of age group and to prohibit distribution of materials that make minors interested in gender transitions. In April and May 2023 the State Duma considered laws to prevent trans women from changing legal gender from male to female without surgery to rule out changing gender purely by changing documents, amid claims that men sought gender change to avoid conscription with Speaker Vyacheslav Volodin citing 2,700 such decisions. In July 2023 Russia enacted a law banning gender transition which prohibited both gender-affirming surgery and legal gender recognition outright. In 2024 Russia passed a law banning adoption of Russian children by citizens or permanent residents of countries that allow gender transitions, and single persons living abroad may adopt Russian children only if that country neither recognises same-sex marriage nor gender transition. On 30 September 2022 President Vladimir Putin said teaching children that instead of men and women there are supposedly other genders and offering sex-change surgeries is unacceptable to Russia. Consensual sexual activity between adults of the same sex is legal after re-legalisation in 1993 removing Article 121 from the RSFSR Penal Code, which had punished consensual sex between men with three to five years imprisonment under Article 154-a from 1934 and Article 121 from 1961 with an estimated 800 to 1000 men imprisoned per year, with age of consent at 16 since 2003 regardless of orientation and homosexuality removed from mental illness list in 1999 under ICD-10 though new laws on 1 July 2023 effectively reinstated the classification. Neither same-sex marriages nor civil unions are allowed, with a July 2020 constitutional amendment banning same-sex marriage, same-sex couples ineligible for protections available to opposite-sex couples, couples allowed to adopt only if married heterosexual, and no anti-discrimination protections or hate-crime designation based on sexual orientation and gender identity. In 2013 Russia passed a federal law criminalising distribution of propaganda promoting non-traditional sexual relationships among minors, expanded in 2022 to anyone regardless of age. In November 2023 the Supreme Court designated the international LGBT public movement as an extremist organisation, formally added on 22 March 2024 to the unified list of terrorist and extremist organizations, where leading, participating in, financially supporting or repeatedly displaying symbols is a criminal offense punishable by prison time, leading to arrests of gay bar owners and fines or jail for displaying the rainbow flag including earrings, and between March and May 2026 city courts outlawed nine LGBTQ organisations as extremist. Authorities in Moscow have never approved a gay pride rally, and in 2010 the European Court of Human Rights fined Russia for discriminating by refusing permits, while in 2012 the Moscow City Court upheld blocking permits yearly through 2012 citing public disorder. In Chechnya since February 2017 over 100 men were detained and tortured with at least three dead in extrajudicial killings in what witnesses called concentration camps, confirmed by a December 2018 Organization for Security and Cooperation in Europe report as ignored by authorities, with another purge reported in December 2018 with around 40 detained and two killed, and European Union sanctions imposed in March 2021 on two officials. The government does not officially record hate crimes against the LGBTQ community, with an estimated 1,056 hate crimes against 853 individuals between 2010 and 2020 with 365 fatalities, annual crimes tripling from 46 in 2010 to 138 in 2015 with increased premeditated group-organised crimes using dating apps to hunt homosexuals between 2017 and 2019, including 205 cases by homophobic hate groups such as Occupy Pedophilia present in 40 regions.

28173009B42697300509311.name: Ulyanovsk Oblast
28173009B42697300509311.summary:
Ulyanovsk Oblast stands under the Russian national framework, which applies in full. No regional law or policy deviates from it, and no regional authority is recorded as moderating enforcement.

Two prosecutions document how that framework operates locally. In August 2024 Ilya Zhuravlev, former head of the dialysis centre in Inza, was detained on charges of participating in the activities of the designated "international LGBT movement" under Part 2 of Article 282.2, alongside a charge of coercion of a person to act of a sexual nature under Part 1 of Article 133. The case is recorded in an October 2024 OVD-Info report cited in the UK Home Office country policy note on sexual orientation and gender identity and expression (June 2025).

In March 2025 a doctor in the region, already facing a maximum of one year's imprisonment over an allegation of sexual coercion, was additionally prosecuted for "involving" another man in the designated movement. He received a three-year sentence, as recorded by Human Rights Watch. The sentence exceeded the maximum available on the original allegation, so the extremism count drove its length.

A trans visitor to the region faces the national legal position without local relief, and the documented local cases show charges being brought against men in professional positions, a dialysis centre director and a doctor, rather than against people with any prior profile.

sources.summary: UK Home Office country policy and information note on Russia, SOGI (June 2025): same-sex sexual activity is not criminalised, while same-sex marriage and gender transition are banned, gender-marker changes on documents are prohibited, and trans-specific healthcare was effectively banned in 2023. The 2013 'gay propaganda' law carries administrative fines of up to 400,000 rubles for individuals or detention of up to 15 days, with repeated offences escalating to criminal prosecution and up to four years' imprisonment. Since the November 2023 Supreme Court 'extremist' designation of the international LGBT+ movement, participation carries 2-6 years and organising 6-10 years' imprisonment (Article 282.2). The note records at least 139 people in Russia impacted by anti-LGBT+ laws between 2022 and 2024 and assesses that openly LGBT+ people are likely to face discriminatory treatment that, by its nature or repetition, may amount to persecution, the state able but not willing to provide protection. Region-specific: citing an October 2024 OVD-Info report, the note records that Ilya Zhuravlev, former head of the dialysis centre in Inza in the Ulyanovsk region, was detained in August on charges of participating in the activities of the 'extremist' 'LGBT movement' (Part 2 of Article 282.2) and coercion of a person to act of a sexual nature (Part 1 of Article 133), enforcing the federal framework in this region.

Human Rights Watch (30 Jun 2025): Russian courts have issued 101 'extremism'-related convictions, about 98 administrative and 3 criminal, for alleged participation in the 'International LGBT Movement' or displaying its symbols since the 2023 Supreme Court 'extremist' designation. Between January 2024 and June 2025 at least 20 people faced criminal charges, including three publishing-house staff charged in May 2025 under Article 282.2 who each face up to 12 years' imprisonment, and 81 people were found guilty in 98 administrative cases under Article 20.3 for displaying banned symbols. Region-specific: in March, a Ulyanovsk-region doctor who faced a maximum of one year's imprisonment for alleged sexual coercion was also prosecuted for 'involving' another man in the 'LGBT movement' and received a three-year sentence, the federal enforcement pattern operating inside this region.

sources.title: LGBTQ rights in Kalmykia (Wikipedia)
sources.summary: Transgender people are not allowed to change their legal gender, and gender-affirming care is banned. In July 2023 Russia enacted a law banning gender transition that prohibited both gender-affirming surgery and legal gender recognition outright, after April-May 2023 proposals to rule out changing gender purely by changing documents and to ban reassignment without surgery. The 2022 expansion of the propaganda law prohibits distribution of materials that make minors interested in gender transitions and applies to anyone regardless of age group. A 2024 law bans adoption of Russian children by citizens or permanent residents of countries that allow gender transitions, and a single person living abroad may adopt only if their country neither recognises same-sex marriage nor allows gender transition. A 1 July 2003 military medical expertise statute provided that people "who have problems with their identity and sexual preferences" can only be drafted during war times, while Major-General Valery Kulikov stated the statute does not forbid people of non-standard sexual orientation from serving. Amid draft-avoidance claims, Duma Speaker Vyacheslav Volodin claimed some "2,700" gender-change decisions had been made in recent times, with reports that young men turned to private clinics for sex changes to avoid conscription in connection with the special operation. Russia provides no anti-discrimination protections for LGBTQ people and has no hate-crime designation based on gender identity. Sexual activity between consenting adults of the same sex is legal, after re-legalisation in 1993 removing Article 121; prior law punished consensual sex between men with three to five years imprisonment under 1934 Article 154-a and up to five years under 1961 Article 121, and the age of consent stands at 16 since 2003 regardless of sexual orientation. Neither same-sex marriages nor civil unions are allowed, same-sex couples and households headed by same-sex couples are ineligible for legal protections available to opposite-sex couples, and July 2020 voters approved a constitutional amendment banning same-sex marriage after the 2021 Fedotova ruling found failure to offer any recognition violated human rights, though Russia left the court in 2022. Russia provides no anti-discrimination protections for LGBTQ people and has no hate-crime designation based on sexual orientation, and authorities refuse to register LGBTQ organisations while pro-LGBTQ advocacy groups have been declared extremist and prohibited. A 2013 law criminalised distribution of "propaganda" promoting "non-traditional sexual relationships" among minors, expanded in 2022 to apply to anyone regardless of age group. In November 2023 the Supreme Court designated "the international LGBT public movement" as extremist, formally added on 22 March 2024 to the unified list of terrorist and extremist organizations and persons, making leading, participating in, financially supporting, or repeatedly displaying symbols a criminal offense punishable by prison time. Enforcement has included arrests of gay bar owners, fines or jailing for displaying the rainbow flag designated as the movement's symbol, at least one death in custody as of April 2025, and between March and May 2026 city courts outlawing nine LGBTQ organisations as extremist including Centre T, Coming Out, LGBT Resource Centre, Irida, Kallisto movement, Moscow Community Center for LGBT+ Initiatives, Parni Plus, Russian LGBT Network and T9 NSK with founders convicted for leading an extremist organisation. Authorities have never approved Moscow pride requests, and in 2010 the European Court of Human Rights fined Russia for discriminating by refusing permits, while in August 2012 Moscow City Court upheld blocking yearly permits through 2012 citing public disorder. Documented violence includes Chechnya detentions since February 2017 of over 100 men with torture and at least three extrajudicial killings, a further purge from December 2018 with around 40 detained and two killed, and an estimated 1,056 hate crimes against 853 individuals between 2010 and 2020 with 365 fatalities rising from 46 in 2010 to 138 in 2015, including 205 cases by homophobic hate groups such as Occupy Pedophilia using dating apps to hunt homosexuals.

Under the 'gay propaganda' law, public expression 'promising' non-heterosexual relationships or gender transition, including displaying rainbow symbols, is punishable by fines of up to 400,000 rubles (about £3,600) for individuals or detention of up to 15 days. A repeated offence can bring up to four years' imprisonment.

The Supreme Court designated the international LGBT+ movement an 'extremist' organisation in November 2023. Between 2022 and 2024, at least 139 individuals were impacted by anti-LGBT+ laws.

A national human-rights organisation reported on 30 June 2025 that courts had issued 101 'extremism'-related convictions for participating in the 'International LGBT Movement' or displaying its symbols since that designation, with penalties of up to 12 years in prison. The same organisation also identified 81 people in 98 cases found guilty since January 2024 of administrative offences under article 20.3 of the Code of Administrative Offenses for displaying banned LGBT symbols, mostly on social media. The 2013 'gay propaganda' law already made any positive or neutral depiction of non-heterosexual relations an administrative offence.

The national travel advisory advises against all travel regardless of personal characteristics. It warns that foreigners found guilty under the 'propaganda' law may be arrested, detained for up to 15 days and deported, and that displaying certain symbols including the rainbow flag is a crime.

76434192B57942368908249.name: Free State
76434192B57942368908249.summary:
Gender-affirming care in South Africa is concentrated in the major metropolitan centres, and the Free State has no documented concentration of its own. A trans visitor who needs hormone therapy or surgery while in the province should expect to travel outside it, paying private prices in the hundreds of thousands of rands or waiting on a long public list. No Free State-specific provider, waiting-time or funding data was identified.

No Free State-specific statute, provincial enforcement record, prosecution or documented incident involving a transgender person was identified. Policing, provincial hospitals, municipal facilities and the province's correctional centres operate under the national framework carried by the South Africa record, and for those matters the national assessment is the one a visitor should rely on.

sources.summary: Court record (High Court of South Africa, Gauteng Local Division sitting as an Equality Court, case 2024/070075, judgment 10 November 2025) in Mokoena v Head of Johannesburg Correctional Centre (Medium B): the landmark ruling for a trans inmate against the Department of Correctional Services - refusal of gender expression (feminine attire, she/her pronouns), inadequate accommodation and denial of state-funded gender-affirming hormone therapy held to be unfair discrimination; hormone therapy recognised as part of the constitutional right to adequate medical treatment under section 35(2)(e).

Human-rights commission / National Preventive Mechanism media statement (14 November 2025): welcomes the 10 November 2025 High Court ruling in Mokoena v Head of Johannesburg Correctional Centre (case 2024/070075); describes the OPCAT monitoring mandate over places of deprivation of liberty, the inmate's account (initially allowed to express her gender, later restricted from feminine clothing and make-up, misgendered, denied prescribed hormone therapy, DCS arguing it was cosmetic), and the court's finding that gender-affirming healthcare forms part of adequate medical treatment under section 35(2)(e) of the Constitution.

sources.title: LGBT rights in South Africa - Wikipedia
sources.summary: National framework applicable in the Free State: the 1996 Constitution was the world's first to expressly bar sexual-orientation discrimination, and the Constitutional Court's December 2005 judgment compelled Parliament to legalise same-sex marriage (Civil Union Act, National Assembly vote 229-41, November 2006). The Alteration of Sex Description and Sex Status Act 2003 allows a person to change sex status in the population registry, and therefore on identity documents and passports, on proof of medical treatment such as hormone therapy, without requiring surgery. Gender-affirming care is concentrated in the main cities, so transgender people in provinces like the Free State must travel long distances to reach it; private treatment costs hundreds of thousands of rands and public waiting lists are long. The Justice Department's National Task Team (2011) and 2014 National Intervention Strategy for LGBTI Communities address hate crimes against LGBT people. No Free State-specific trans source was surfaced, so this record rests on the national framework.

The feature also covers the well-publicised case of a US trans woman detained in poor conditions after a 2016 Paris protest case.

The CGLPL opinion of 25 May 2021, issued by the Contrôleur général des lieux de privation de liberté, examines the treatment of transgender persons in all places of deprivation of liberty. On legal gender recognition, a bill approved by the Senate on 6 November 2015 and by the National Assembly on 24 May 2016 was signed into law on 18 November 2016 and took effect on 1 January 2017. It abolished the sex-reassignment-surgery and forced-sterilisation requirements, rejected a Senate amendment that would have demanded proof of medical treatment, and requires going before a court rather than any medical intervention.

Transsexualism is classed under long-term-illness ALD 31, so gender-affirming treatment is funded by the Sécurité Sociale.

sources.summary: Outright International (IGLHRC) Philippines country overview (updated 2025): same-sex relations are legal and acceptance indices rank the country among the most accepting in Asia, but trans people cannot access legal gender recognition - the 2001 Clerical Error Law (RA 9048) blocks gender-marker correction - and national non-discrimination bills filed since 1999 remain unenacted, with two civil-union bills filed since 2022 facing religious-conservative opposition; non-discrimination ordinances exist at barangay, city, municipal and provincial levels. A 2018 SWS survey found only 22% of Filipinos supported same-sex civil unions and a majority opposed trans women's access to women's toilets. The Safe Spaces Act criminalises homophobic and transphobic slurs; the Anti-Bullying Act and the Gender-Responsive Basic Education Policy (reiterated 2022, June designated Pride Month) cover sexual orientation and gender identity in schools; Executive Orders No. 100 (2019) and No. 51 (2023) creating the national Diversity and Inclusion Program remain unimplemented as of 2025.

Bulatlat (26 Jun 2025): 18-year-old trans woman Kierra Apostol, a Cagayan State University business-management student, was found dead in a Cagayan province river on 23 June 2025, days after being reported missing, with signs of physical assault. A criminology student who admitted driving her surrendered to police while denying involvement. On the same day, trans woman and former activist-journalist Ali Macalintal was shot by an unidentified gunman inside an acupuncture clinic in General Santos. Bahaghari and other groups cite the cases in calling for passage of the SOGIESC Equality Bill, stuck in Congress for 25 years (latest version Senate Bill 1600), which would prohibit admission denial, denial of public and health services, and infliction of physical harm or verbal abuse based on SOGIE.

36201628B90061603712355.name: Davao Region
36201628B90061603712355.summary:
Davao Region has no regional statute or regional ordinance of its own governing sexual orientation or gender identity. A trans visitor to the region stands under the national framework of the Philippines, together with the municipal law of the particular city or municipality visited.

Davao City, the region's administrative center, is recorded among the Philippine localities that have a non-discrimination ordinance. Its council passed the measure in December 2012, banning discrimination against gays (LGBT people), minorities and differently-abled persons. Within Davao City, that ordinance is the only documented local layer of protection available beyond the national position.

Custody practice specific to the region is documented. The Bureau of Jail Management and Penology in Davao moves LGBT detainees in batches to the City Jail Annex, holding them alongside persons with disabilities, the sick and senior citizens as a stated measure to prevent abuse. Placement of trans detainees in Davao thus takes the form of administrative segregation rather than gender-matched accommodation.

The two legal standards it documents, the restroom-access damages ruling and the removal of the surgical prerequisite for a registered sex change, are national in scope and are recorded as applying in the province with no Gangwon-specific case attached to either. A trans visitor to Gangwon therefore faces the national legal position with no documented province-level variation.

sources.summary: Korea Times (22 July 2024): the Seoul appellate court dismissed the state's appeal and finalised a 300,000 won damages award against a 3 million won claim, ruling that police advice to a person transitioning from male to female, who had obtained court approval for a family-register gender change in 2020, to avoid women's public restrooms infringed personal rights. The appellate court held that comfortable restroom use is a fundamental and universal human right. A 2021 NHRCK survey of 591 transgender respondents found that 41% used a restroom of a different gender, 39% avoided food and drink and 36% forwent restroom use. A 2021 Daegu District Court (Pohang branch) award of 7 million won against a beauty academy that prohibited a transgender student from using its restroom forms part of the national standard applied in Gangwon, where no specific incident is documented.

Yonhap wire (8 May 2024): a regional court in Yeongdong approved changing the registered sex from male to female for five transgender applicants without sex-reassignment surgery, holding that it is against the law to determine gender change based on surgery and that court guidelines requiring surgery are now only reference, not criteria. 1875124B91024374055933.name: La Libertad
1875124B91024374055933.summary:
La Libertad stands under Peru's national framework, which governs identity documents, facility access and discrimination law; this assessment covers only what is specific to the region. Two documents carry the region-specific record: a national prosecution study that disaggregates homicides of LGTB people by prosecution district, and a 2024 regional ordinance on labour inclusion. Neither establishes a regional anti-discrimination enforcement mechanism, and no region-specific data on policing, restroom-law enforcement or service access appears in the sources.

The Public Prosecutor's Office published a study of intentional deaths of LGTB people between 2012 and 2021, drawn from 84 criminal complaints covering 88 victims and 72 identified suspects. Six fiscal districts accounted for 58% of the deaths. La Libertad recorded 10, second only to Lima's 12 and level with Lima Norte, ahead of Lima Este (7), Lima Sur (6) and Callao (6). The ranking is by raw count. La Libertad is one of Peru's more populous regions, and the study supplies no per-capita denominator, so the figure does not by itself show that a trans visitor faces higher risk in La Libertad than in a smaller district. The study was produced with the Justice Ministry's human-rights office and the Cayetano Heredia University LGTB-rights observatory with UNDP support.

Ordenanza Regional N.° 009-2024-GRLL-CR, approved in Trujillo on 6 September 2024 and published in El Peruano on 7 November 2024, promotes the labour inclusion of travesti, transsexual and transgender people in La Libertad. It declares their right to formal, dignified and productive work in equitable and satisfactory conditions without discrimination on grounds of gender identity or its expression, and recognises the trans community as a group in a situation of vulnerability in the region. It is a positive-action measure addressed to employment, not a protection a visitor can invoke against police, service providers or private venues, and it specifies no penalty or enforcement body.

The ordinance recommends that local governments issue municipal ordinances recognising gender identity and fundamental rights, and orders a working group (mesa de trabajo) to be convened. It cites constitutional equality guarantees and article 323 of the Penal Code on discrimination, and recalls a 2014 regional-council session that set a framework against discrimination on sexual orientation and gender identity. Whether any La Libertad municipality has acted on the recommendation is not documented in the sources.

sources.summary: Public Prosecutor's Office (Ministerio Público) news note of 23 March 2022 on its Observatory of Criminality study of intentional deaths of LGTB people in Peru 2012-2021: 84 criminal complaints involving 88 victims and 72 identified suspects; 58% of deaths concentrated in six fiscal districts - Lima (12), La Libertad (10), Lima Norte (10), Lima Este (7), Lima Sur (6) and Callao (6) - placing La Libertad second in absolute count (level with Lima Norte) behind Lima. The study was developed with the Justice Ministry human-rights office and the University Cayetano Heredia LGTB-rights observatory with UNDP support, and yielded recommendations including training criminal prosecutors on LGTB-victim identification and monitoring systems.

Ordenanza Regional N.° 009-2024-GRLL-CR of the Regional Government of La Libertad, dated 6 September 2024, approves promoting labour inclusion of travesti, transsexual and transgender persons in the region. It declares that every such person has the right to formal, dignified and productive work in equitable and satisfactory conditions without discrimination on grounds of gender identity and/or its expression, and recognises the trans community as a group in a situation of vulnerability in La Libertad.

Official-gazette record (El Peruano, publication date 07/11/2024) of Ordenanza Regional N.° 000009-2024-GRLL-CR, presented in the regional council's ordinary session of 3 September 2024, debated, approved and signed in Trujillo on 6 September 2024: Its object is positive-action measures for the effective labour inclusion of travesti, transsexual and transgender persons in La Libertad - the right to formal, dignified, productive work in equitable and satisfactory conditions. It cites constitutional equality guarantees and article 323 of the Penal Code (discrimination as a crime), recalls a 2014 regional-council session framework against discrimination on sexual orientation and gender identity, recommends local governments issue municipal ordinances recognising gender identity and fundamental rights, and orders a working group (mesa de trabajo); it enters into force the day after publication in El Peruano.

1875124B58976419670313.name: Tacna
1875124B58976419670313.summary:
Tacna stands under Peru's national framework; national law on criminalisation, anti-discrimination protection, identity documents and public-facility access applies here as it does across the country and is set out under Peru.

On 19 April 2025 Marcia Paucara Cora, a 48-year-old trans woman, was found dead in a room of the Los 5 Titos hostel on Arias y Aragüez street in central Tacna. The autopsy recorded death by mechanical asphyxia through compression of the airways. She had entered the hostel with a man who registered under a false identity and who left alone roughly two hours later carrying a white bag. Staff found the body when the rental time expired.

Tacna authorities are investigating the death as a possible hate crime, an offence motivated by prejudice and discrimination on grounds of the victim's sexual orientation or gender identity. No suspect had been identified in the reporting of 21 and 27 May 2025. The victim was initially processed as an unidentified body and was named through the hostel's cameras; police were analysing surveillance footage from inside and outside the premises to trace the suspect's escape route.

Family members and local LGTBIQ+ collectives held a vigil on Friday 23 May 2025 demanding justice, describing the killing as the reflection of a structural system of violence that silences trans lives. Relatives publicly denounced the killing and pressed for police action.

13589884B77991835419453.name: Atlántico
13589884B77991835419453.summary:
Atlántico department stands under Colombia's national framework. The department's own signal comes from the 2025 report "Un sistema que falla: prejuicio, violencia e impunidad contra personas LGBTIQ+ en Colombia", published by the regional LGBTI+ rights organisation Caribe Afirmativo and covered by Publimetro Colombia.

For Atlántico the report counts 54 cases of intrafamily violence, 41 sexual offences, 69 threats, 12 discrimination cases, 8 cases of digital violence, 8 cases of lethal violence, and 2 killings of LGBTIQ+ human-rights defenders during 2025. These are raw departmental totals; the report supplies no population or per-capita denominator, so they cannot be read as a ranking against other Colombian departments and no conclusion about relative danger follows from the counts alone.

The report designates Barranquilla and Soledad as territories carrying a "high" threat level for this population. Violence is described as expanding into territories with illegal-economy corridors and weak state presence, with the state response judged insufficient.

Threat cases recorded in the report show near-total impunity: 99.8% never advance past the investigation stage. Whether that percentage is calculated for the department or for the country as a whole is not stated in the material available here.

The department's development plan and Barranquilla's development plan commit the local authorities to coordinated action with the prosecutor's office, the police and the judiciary to strengthen reporting, investigation and prosecution of violence against LGBTIQ+ people.

For the Atlántico department it documents 54 intrafamily-violence cases, 41 sexual offences, 12 discrimination cases, 8 digital-violence cases, 69 threats, 2 killings of LGBTIQ+ human-rights defenders and 8 lethal-violence cases, and designates Barranquilla and Soledad as territories with 'high' threat levels for this population; it recalls the department's and Barranquilla's development plans commit coordinated action with the prosecutor's office, police and judiciary to strengthen reporting, investigation and prosecution of violence against LGBTIQ+ people. It also reports threats show near-total impunity, with 99.8% of cases never advancing past the investigation stage.

Caribe Afirmativo's 2025 report 'Un sistema que falla: prejuicio, violencia e impunidad contra personas LGBTIQ+ en Colombia' records that in 2025 one LGBTIQ+ person was killed every 32 hours, and describes violence as a continuum running from discrimination through intrafamily violence (1,531 cases), sexual violence (628 cases) and threats (1,184 victims) to homicide and impunity. It documents territorial expansion of the violence, including into territories with illegal-economy corridors and weak state presence, and criticises the insufficient state response.

13589884B96168520946689.name: Bolívar
13589884B96168520946689.summary:
Bolívar is a department of Colombia, and its trans-related law and enforcement sit within the national framework. The department's documented record on trans safety centres on the killing of Nawar Jiménez, a trans social leader, in Carmen de Bolívar on 22 May 2025. El Tiempo's data investigation classifies the case as a trans feminicide. Jiménez had campaigned with the 'No Es Hora De Callar' movement and had joined its sixth symbolic return march, which brought together more than 500 survivors of sexual violence. Her friend and fellow social leader Yirley Velasco remembers her as having taken up the fight for trans rights in the municipality.

More than 19 days after the killing, the circumstances remained unclear. No arrest, charge or explanation of the death is reported in that period, and the case is the department's documented instance of lethal violence against a trans person.

Caribe Afirmativo's 2025 report, 'Un sistema que falla: prejuicio, violencia e impunidad contra personas LGBTIQ+ en Colombia', does not name Bolívar. It documents violence against LGBTIQ+ people expanding toward territories with illegal-economy corridors and weak state presence, and places the department inside the Caribbean-coast cluster flagged for that expansion and for the weakest state response. The department's risk picture therefore rests on cluster-level findings rather than on monitoring specific to Bolívar.

The piece exposes the gap between official and NGO figures: the Fiscalía's own data base records 3,322 intentional homicides of people identified as LGBTIQ+ between January 2010 and May 2025, 431 for 2024 versus about 160 reported by the NGO (267 fewer), and 39 homicides in one Fiscalía dependency's 2025 data versus 156 in the policies-and-strategies base; experts cited describe the information system as neither unified nor reliable.

Caribe Afirmativo's 2025 report 'Un sistema que falla: prejuicio, violencia e impunidad contra personas LGBTIQ+ en Colombia' records one LGBTIQ+ person killed every 32 hours in 2025. Violence escalates along a continuum from discrimination to intrafamily violence (1,531 cases), sexual violence (628 cases), threats (1,184 victims), homicide and impunity, and the report documents its territorial expansion toward territories with illegal-economy corridors and weak state presence, together with insufficient state response. The report does not name Bolívar explicitly. The department nevertheless sits within the Caribbean-coast cluster flagged for that expansion and weakest response, and the killing in Carmen de Bolívar is covered by the El Tiempo investigation.

sources.title: LGBTQ rights in Amazonas (Wikipedia)
sources.summary: Since 2006 Amazonas state policies include discrimination based on gender identity, and since 2019 transphobia has been criminalized nationwide as equivalent to racism. Since the March 2018 unanimous Supreme Federal Court ruling, transgender people may change legal gender at a registry post without surgery, hormonal therapy, judicial authorization or medical report, with registry-office gender changes reported up 59% by 2024. Amazonas has no specific law recognizing non-binary gender; in 2022 Álex Souza de Sá became the first non-binary person recognized, requiring rectification in Rio de Janeiro and six months of insistence plus intervention by the Public Defender's Office to obtain recognition in Manaus where the registry lacked a gender-neutral marker. For facilities, on 18 October 2022 the mayor of Manaus signed a law banning unisex restrooms in the city. For care, in November 2023 the State Public Defender's Office opened monitoring of public health services for transgender and travesti people including hormones and surgeries, in August 2024 the Federal Public Prosecutor's Office recommended the state formally enable outpatient and hospital transsexualization services including sexual reassignment surgeries with deadlines for submission to the Ministry of Health, and on 10 June 2025 Governor Wilson Lima signed Law No. 7,552 banning gender-affirming care for minors under 18. For protection machinery, in 2021 the State Public Defender's Office created the Sexual Diversity, Gender Identity and Citizenship Working Group focused on human rights violations and training security agents, and in August 2024 the State Court of Justice released the booklet Home is a Right! for LGBTQ youth expelled from homes stating conversion therapies are "prohibited and ineffective." Cases of violence against LGBTQ people in the state are described as underreported, with 43 cases registered according to Brazilian Public Security Forum data cited in research. Same-sex sexual activity has been legal since 1830 when the Imperial Penal Code removed all references to sodomy. Same-sex marriage has been legal in Amazonas since 2013 via National Council of Justice decision following the 2011 Supreme Federal Court decision, with a 328% increase between 2020 and 2025, 287 unions registered in 2024 and 98 in the first five months of 2025. Same-sex adoption was first authorized in Amazonas in November 2012 by a state court judge, with nationwide legalization by the Supreme Federal Court in 2015. Since 2006 state policies include discrimination based on sexual orientation, and since 2019 homophobia has been criminalized nationwide as equivalent to racism. Assembly and expression restrictions include State Law 6,469/2023 prohibiting participation of children and adolescents in pride parades with fines up to R$10,000, and the 17 October 2024 law prohibiting reproduction of digital media using children linked to homosexuality, amended on 13 December 2025 to remove the term homosexuality and prohibit reproduction of sexual content linked to children in cultural and artistic media. On 5 July 2025 Fernando Vilaça de Souza was beaten and killed in Manaus after reacting to homophobic insults, with prior bullying reported by area residents.

sources.title: Manaus municipal law banning unisex restrooms - 18 October 2022

sources.title: Federal Public Prosecutor's Office (MPF) Recommendation - August 2024
sources.summary: In August 2024, the Federal Public Prosecutor's Office recommended that the state of Amazonas guarantee integral health care to the LGBTQIAPN+ population, including trans people.

sources.title: Amazonas Public Defender's Office (DPE-AM) monitoring process - November 2023
sources.summary: In Amazonas as of 1 November 2023 the State Public Defender's health unit opened a collective procedure to audit SUS care for trans people covering access to hormonization, outpatient services, and lack of accreditation for gender-affirming surgeries including sexual reassignment, and in October 2023 the Manaus Municipal Health Secretariat committed to dispense standardized medications to trans people on prescription from the Codajás Outpatient Clinic that handles hormonization and to designate reference UBS primary-care units in each city zone, while the State Health Secretariat was ordered to report on equitable integral care including remedying hormoniotherapy gaps guaranteed under Federal Council of Medicine Resolution No. 2,265 of 2019.

sources.title: Amazonas State Law No. 6,463/2023 - gender-neutral language ban in schools
sources.summary: On 10 October 2023 Amazonas State Law No. 6,463 expressly prohibited use of neutral language, non-binary dialect, or any expression departing from standard Portuguese in curricula and teaching materials of public and private educational institutions and in official documents of schools and public agencies statewide.

sources.title: Amazonas State Court of Justice (TJAM) booklet Lar e Direito! / Home is a Right! - August 2024
sources.summary: In Amazonas as of August 2024, LGBTQIAPN+ adolescents facing family discrimination and expulsion are guaranteed under ECA Article 17 physical, psychological and moral integrity including identity and autonomy and under Constitution/ECA duties of family, society and State to ensure health, food, education and protection from negligence and discrimination with equal treatment of children regardless of sexual orientation, with bullying criminalized under Law 14.811/2024 by fine to 4 years' imprisonment, homophobia criminalized per 2019 STF ruling as imprescriptible and non-bailable, conversion/"gay cure" therapy prohibited as illegal and ineffective, and legal support available through the Defensoria Especializada em Direitos Humanos.

sources.title: DPE-AM Working Group on Sexual Diversity, Gender Identity and Citizenship - 2021
sources.summary: On 28 June 2021 the Amazonas Public Defender's Office created the permanent Working Group on Sexual Diversity, Gender Identity and Citizenship to identify LGBTQIA+ human-rights violations in public security, train public-security agents for service to LGBTQIA+ people, and issue recommendations and extrajudicial measures, while LGBTQIA+ victims in Manaus can obtain assistance via Disk 129 Monday-Friday 8am-2pm through the Specialized Human Rights unit, in a context where Amazonas led North and Central-West states with 4.66 LGBTQIA+ persons murdered per million inhabitants in 2018.

sources.title: Nationwide criminalization of homophobia and transphobia - 2019
sources.summary: On 23 May 2019 a majority of Brazil's Supreme Federal Tribunal (6 of 11 justices) voted to criminalize transphobia under Brazil's 1989 racism law punishable by up to five years' imprisonment until Congress enacts specific LGBT-discrimination legislation, to take effect after all justices voted on 5 June 2019.

sources.title: Brazilian Public Security Forum / Brazilian Journal of Public Security data + Fernando Vilaca de Souza homicide 5 July 2025
sources.summary: In Amazonas during 2021-2022, crimes involving transsexual persons formed part of only 0.36% of total reported crimes in the capital and interior, police occurrence reports did not identify transfobia or gender, sexuality, race and intersectionality markers, trans victim data were few and badly structured with victims not infrequently inverted to accused through faulty BOs, and unprepared public agents and defective registration mechanisms left trans subjects invisibilized and without protection.

sources.title: LGBTQ rights in Colombia - Wikipedia
sources.summary: Wikipedia's 'LGBTQ rights in Colombia' page states the national framework a visitor stands under in Cundinamarca: since 1993 a person may change the gender marker on their Colombian birth certificate, with current options F, M, NB (no binario) and T (transgénero). On 9 July 2026 outgoing justice minister Jorge Iván Cuervo signed Decree 0732 of 2026, which obliges public notaries to complete the request within five business days, makes the first request (and a simultaneous name change) free of charge, and shields the change history from public disclosure. The Constitutional Court's 4 February 2022 ruling ordered the government to offer the nonbinary ('NB') option to everyone and to ask Congress to amend the relevant laws, and since August 2023 passports issued within Colombia offer three gender options (male, female, X). A 2016 report (Cartografía de derechos trans en Colombia, by OutRight Action International, El Aquelarre Trans and PAIIS) documented notaries refusing to process name changes and recommended ending the psychiatric pathologisation of transgender identity. Gender-marker change is a notarial/bureaucratic process with no surgery or court ruling required and applies equally in Cundinamarca.

The Constitutional Court's 4 February 2022 ruling ordered the government to offer the nonbinary ('NB') option to everyone and to ask Congress to amend the relevant laws, and since August 2023 passports issued within Colombia offer three gender options (male, female, X). A 2016 report (Cartografía de derechos trans en Colombia, by OutRight Action International, El Aquelarre Trans and PAIIS) documented notaries refusing to process name changes and recommended ending the psychiatric pathologisation of transgender identity. Gender-marker change is a notarial/bureaucratic process with no surgery or court ruling required and applies equally in Cesar.

sources.summary: EL PAÍS English, 14 April 2025, documents the killing of Sara Millerey, a trans woman, in Bello, Antioquia. She was attacked in broad daylight on 4 April 2025, the assault was filmed, and the video went viral on 5 April; she died of cardiac arrest that afternoon. Police interrogated local residents, and no one had been arrested even after the president ordered an urgent investigation. Nationally, 13 trans people were killed by hate in the first quarter of 2025, alongside earlier killings of gay men and the stabbing death of a trans rough-sleeper. No Córdoba-specific legal, enforcement or incident finding is documented. The national pattern is that lethal anti-trans violence can occur in daylight, be filmed, and leave the perpetrator unarrested.

The Guardian, 30 July 2024, documented armed groups in Caquetá department running a 'social cleansing' campaign: flyers on the streets and via WhatsApp named 'faggots, lesbians and men and women who destroy homes' as legitimate military targets. A trans woman and local election candidate was told by three armed men she had one week to leave town, hid for a week, then fled at night; a second trans woman said a friend was killed. Eight trans women were killed in Colombia between February and April 2024 and 41 in 2023, and discrimination limits trans women mainly to hairdressing or sex work. No Córdoba-specific finding is documented. The pattern is territorial violence and displacement of trans people by armed actors.

13589884B66570655136682.name: La Guajira
13589884B66570655136682.summary:
La Guajira stands under Colombia's national legal framework, which the national record sets out in full; the department's own documented signal is a campaign of written threats by armed groups. Since March 2024 armed groups operating in the department have circulated flyers carrying a kill list of named individuals, stating that "all will be military targets" and listing "homosexuals, lesbians, rapists, trans" among those designated. The wording places trans people in a category of persons marked for lethal violence, and it names individuals rather than issuing a general warning.

A trans visitor's exposure in La Guajira is therefore tied to where armed-group control is exercised rather than to the formal legal position, which is protective. The threat instrument is a written list distributed publicly, so visibility of a trans person to neighbours and to whoever posts the flyers is the operative risk factor in those areas.

Armed groups in Colombia's conflict-affected departments have used flyer campaigns of this kind to force trans women out of their homes and towns, and displacement rather than protection is the documented response available to those named. La Guajira has no separate legal regime of its own; the national protections apply here as elsewhere in the country.

sources.title: LGBT rights in Colombia
sources.summary: Colombia decriminalised homosexuality in 1981, and in 2011 Congress passed a law banning discrimination based on sexual orientation. The Constitutional Court legalised same-sex marriage in a 6-3 ruling of 28 April 2016, with the first wedding in Cali on 24 May 2016. Three rulings between February 2007 and April 2008 had granted same-sex couples property, social-security and pension rights, and a November 2015 ruling granted full adoption rights with dual-parent birth registration. Since August 2023 passports issued within Colombia offer three gender options: male, female and X. Adults can change legal gender before a notary without surgery, with a free simultaneous name change on first request. Gays, lesbians and bisexuals have served openly in the armed forces since a 1999 court ruling. Casanare adds no separate legal regime, so these national provisions define the formal legal exposure of a trans visitor to the department.

1875124B3772980127380.name: Puno
1875124B3772980127380.summary: No region-specific finding on trans visitor safety was identified for the department of Puno. The public restroom restrictions documented in the sources are national instruments applying across Peru, and no Puno ordinance, exemption, enforcement practice or regional institution of its own is recorded. The national assessment governs in the department without local modification.

sources.summary: Infobae Perú (20 Feb 2025) reports that the congressional Women and Family Commission unanimously approved a draft opinion merging bills 6506 and 8457, introduced by congressmen Jorge Montoya and Alejandro Muñante, barring trans people from public restrooms that do not correspond to their birth sex, with exceptions for custody, where medical attention is required, or accompanying an elderly person, a child under 12 or a person with disabilities, plus a ban on 'ambiguous' bathroom signage. The trigger was a July 2023 social-media complaint over the Jorge Chávez airport's gendered restroom labels. LGTBIQ activist Gianna Camacho calls the measure discriminatory, warning that bathroom access would come to depend on security staff's personal judgment, including ID checks, and notes there is no record of sexual assault by trans women in women's restrooms. The measure stood at committee stage in February 2025 and, as national law, binds Puno.

IDEHPUCP legal analysis by Miriam Tovar and Gonzalo Ugarte (15 Apr 2025) states that on Wednesday 2 April 2025 the congressional Plenary approved and exempted from second vote a bill whose article 5 bars any person from entering or using a public sanitary service that does not correspond to their 'biological sex', save for narrow listed exceptions, and argues this violates the equal-treatment and non-discrimination principle of article 2(2) of the Peruvian Constitution and article 1.1 of the American Convention on Human Rights. The authors say the law's stated aim of preventing child sexual abuse rests on a stigmatising stereotype presenting trans people as likely restroom harassers, while UN reporting shows trans people are more often victims than aggressors. The analysis addresses the national framework that governs Puno and records no Puno-specific finding.

sources.summary: Infobae Peru (20 Feb 2025): the congressional Comision de Mujer y Familia approved by unanimity a dictamen merging bills 6506 and 8457 (sponsored by Jorge Montoya and Alejandro Munante) that would prohibit any person from entering public sanitary facilities designated for the sex opposite to their birth sex, with narrow exceptions (custody, and cases where required, including accompanying minors, the elderly or people with disabilities), and would oblige venues not to post ambiguous restroom signs; the article notes the text still needed plenary backing and reports the trigger as the July 2023 complaint over gendered restroom labels at Lima's Jorge Chavez international airport. IDEHPUCP legal analysis (15 April 2025, Miriam Tovar and Gonzalo Ugarte): on Wednesday 2 April 2025 the plenary of Congress approved and waived a second vote on the dictamen of the 'Ley que fortalece el derecho a la indemnidad sexual de los ninos y adolescentes', whose Article 5.1 prohibits persons from entering or using public sanitary facilities designated for a sex other than their birth sex.
