sources.title: LGBTQ rights in Amazonas (Wikipedia)
sources.summary: Since 2006 Amazonas state policies prohibit discrimination based on gender identity, and since 2019 transphobia has been criminalized nationwide as equivalent to the crime of racism. In 2021 the Amazonas State Public Defender's Office created the Sexual Diversity, Gender Identity and Citizenship Working Group to address human rights violations and train security agents, and in November 2023 it opened a process to monitor public health services for transgender and travesti people including provision of hormones and surgeries. In March 2018 the Supreme Federal Court unanimously ruled transgender people may change legal gender at a registry post without surgery, hormonal therapy, judicial document or medical report, with registry gender changes reported up 59% by 2024. On 18 October 2022 the mayor of Manaus signed a law banning unisex restrooms in the city. In August 2024 the Federal Public Prosecutor's Office recommended Amazonas formally enable outpatient and hospital services for the transsexualization process including sexual reassignment surgeries, with deadlines for approval and presentation to the Ministry of Health. On 10 June 2025 Governor Wilson Lima signed Law No. 7,552 banning gender-affirming care for minors under age 18. Amazonas has no specific law recognizing non-binary gender, and in 2022 Alex Souza de Sa became the first non-binary person recognized in the state after rectification in Rio de Janeiro and intervention by the Public Defender's Office to secure recognition in Manaus after six months when the local notary lacked a gender-neutral marker. Homosexuality has been legal in Amazonas and Brazil since 1830 when the Imperial Penal Code removed all references to sodomy. Same-sex marriage has been legal since 2013 via National Council of Justice decision following the 2011 Supreme Federal Court decision, and same-sex adoption was first allowed in Amazonas in November 2012 by an Amazonas Court of Justice judge before nationwide legalization by the Supreme Federal Court in 2015. Since 2006 Amazonas state policies prohibit discrimination based on sexual orientation, and since 2019 homophobia has been criminalized nationwide as equivalent to the crime of racism. The August 2024 Amazonas Court of Justice booklet Home is a Right! for LGBTQ youth expelled from homes states that conversion therapies are "prohibited and ineffective." Research from the Brazilian Journal of Public Security states that cases of violence against LGBTQ people in Amazonas are underreported. Data from the Brazilian Public Security Forum indicates cases of violence against LGBTQ people have increased, with 43 cases registered. On 5 July 2025 Fernando Vilaca de Souza was beaten and killed in Manaus after reacting to homophobic insults, and residents reported he had previously been bullied by other young people in the region. The Ministry of Human Rights and Citizenship, the Order of Attorneys of Brazil and federal deputy Erika Hilton expressed regret over the incident. The article provides no documented statement about societal tolerance of transgender people specifically so no such quote can be reproduced, and the above violence figures refer to LGBTQ people generally not to transgender people specifically.

sources.title: Federal Public Prosecutor's Office (MPF) recommendation - August 2024
sources.summary: In August 2024 the Federal Public Prosecutor's Office recommended that the state of Amazonas guarantee comprehensive health care for the LGBTQIAPN+ population, including trans people.

sources.title: Public Defender's Office of the State of Amazonas (DPE-AM) monitoring process - November 2023
sources.summary: In Amazonas in October-November 2023, trans access to SUS was under enforcement review for primary care, outpatient services, hormonization, and lack of local authorization for transexualizing surgeries including sexual reassignment, with the municipal health authority committing to dispense standardized hormone medications on Ambulatório Codajás prescriptions and to designate a reference UBS in each city zone and the state health authority required to report on equitable integral care and hormoniotherapy gaps guaranteed under CFM Resolution No. 2.265/2019.

sources.title: Manaus municipal law banning unisex restrooms - 18 October 2022
sources.summary: On 18 October 2022 the municipality of Manaus sanctioned a law prohibiting multigender/unisex bathrooms.

sources.title: Amazonas State Law No. 6,463/2023 on gender-neutral language ban
sources.summary: On 10 October 2023 Amazonas Law No. 6,463 prohibited the use of gender-neutral language, non-binary dialect, or any expression deviating from standard Portuguese in the curricula and teaching materials of public and private educational institutions and in official documents of educational institutions and public offices throughout the state of Amazonas.

sources.title: Amazonas State Court of Justice (TJAM) booklet Lar e Direito! / Home is a Right! - August 2024
sources.summary: In Amazonas since August 2024, LGBTQIAPN+ adolescents facing family discrimination and expulsion from home are affirmed as protected by ECA Article 17 guaranteeing physical, psychological and moral integrity including identity, autonomy and beliefs, by Constitutional/ECA duties of family, society and State to ensure health, food, education and protection against negligence and discrimination with equal treatment of all children regardless of sexual orientation, by Law No. 14.811/2024 criminalizing bullying with penalties ranging from fine to 4 years' imprisonment, by the 2019 STF recognition of homophobia as an imprescriptible and unbailable crime, and by the prohibition of conversion/"cura gay" therapies as illegal and ineffective, with legal support available from the Defensoria Especializada em Direitos Humanos.

sources.title: Amazonas State Public Defender's Office (DPE-AM) Working Group - 2021
sources.summary: On 28 June 2021 the Amazonas Public Defender's Office (DPE-AM) created the permanent Working Group "Diversidade Sexual, Identidade de Gênero e Cidadania" to defend LGBTQIA+ rights and identify human rights violations in the area of public security. Its mandate includes training public security agents for service to LGBTQIA+ persons and issuing recommendations and other extrajudicial referrals. Victims of LGBTphobia are served by the Specialized Human Rights Defensoria via Disk 129 in Manaus Monday to Friday 8h-14h, in a context where Amazonas led North and Center-West states with an average of 4.66 LGBTQIA+ persons murdered per million inhabitants in 2018.

sources.title: Brazilian Public Security Forum / Brazilian Journal of Public Security + 5 July 2025 homicide case
sources.summary: In Amazonas during 2021-2022 trans persons faced persistent diverse violence intensifying each year while only 0.36% of crimes reported in the capital and interior involved homosexual, lesbian, bisexual and transsexual victims, police occurrence reports did not identify homophobia and transfobia motives or gender, sexuality, race and intersectionality markers, victim data were few and poorly structured with victims at times inverted to accused through faulty reports, and unprepared public agents and defective registration mechanisms produced invisibilization and lack of protection for trans victims.

1875124B5969368354394.name: Huánuco
1875124B5969368354394.summary: No Huánuco-specific signal was identified in the sources reviewed, and the national assessment for Peru applies to visitors to the department: the material available documents no departmental law, enforcement practice, recorded incident or institution bearing on trans visitors.

sources.summary: Infobae Peru (20 Feb 2025): the congressional Comision de Mujer y Familia approved by unanimity a dictamen merging bills 6506 and 8457 (sponsored by Jorge Montoya and Alejandro Munante) that would prohibit any person from entering public sanitary facilities designated for the sex opposite to their birth sex, with narrow exceptions (custody, and cases where required, including accompanying minors, the elderly or people with disabilities), and would oblige venues not to post ambiguous restroom signs; the article notes the text still needed plenary backing and reports the trigger as the July 2023 complaint over gendered restroom labels at Lima's Jorge Chavez international airport. Activist Gianna Camacho is quoted arguing the measure is discriminatory and that enforcement would rest on security staff checking the DNI to decide whether a woman entering a women's restroom is trans or cisgender. This is the national framework this department is scored against; the article contains no Huánuco-specific content.

IDEHPUCP legal analysis (15 April 2025, Miriam Tovar and Gonzalo Ugarte): on Wednesday 2 April 2025 the plenary of Congress approved and waived a second vote on the dictamen of the 'Ley que fortalece el derecho a la indemnidad sexual de los ninos y adolescentes', whose Article 5.1 prohibits persons from entering or using public sanitary facilities designated for a sex other than their birth sex. The institute reads Article 5 as a direct breach of equality and non-discrimination (Article 2(2) of the Peruvian Constitution and Article 1.1 of the American Convention on Human Rights), resting on the stereotype that trans people are more prone to enter restrooms to harass or sexually abuse minors, and recalls documented cases of trans people barred from public restrooms - including SPC-INDECOPI Resolution 0735-2022 dismissing a trans woman's discrimination complaint against SmartFit, where the company grounded bathroom assignment on the sex recorded in the DNI - and the fact that gender-identity recognition in Peru remains long, costly and invasive. This is the national framework this department is scored against; the article contains no Huánuco-specific content.

Agencia Presentes (22 July 2024), drawing on the annual report of the Observatorio de Derechos TLGBI of Universidad Peruana Cayetano Heredia: Peru recorded 54 assassinations of TLGBI people and 170 rights-violation cases in 2020-2023, the homicide victims being 30 trans women, 23 gay men and one lesbian; 19 killings occurred in 2023 alone (12 of them trans women), and killers were not identified in 26 of the 54 homicides (13 of 19 in 2023). The piece recounts the February 2023 murder of trans sex worker Rubi Torres Silvano (31), kidnapped from central Lima by a 'Los Gallegos' extortion gang and killed in Carabayllo with some 30 gunshots (Priscila Aguado Huatuco, 30, was shot days earlier), with two killers arrested in March 2023, and notes the state has not incorporated sexual orientation or gender identity into its crime-registration systems, so hate crimes cannot be prosecuted as such. This is the national violence baseline this department is scored against; the article contains no Huánuco-specific content.

sources.summary: Infobae Perú (20 Feb 2025) reports the congressional Women and Family Commission unanimously approved a draft opinion (dictamen) merging bills 6506 and 8457, introduced by congressmen Jorge Montoya and Alejandro Muñante, barring trans people from public restrooms that do not correspond to their birth sex, with exceptions for custody, where medical attention is required, or accompanying an elderly person, a child under 12 or a person with disabilities, plus a ban on 'ambiguous' bathroom signage; the trigger was a July 2023 social-media complaint over the Jorge Chávez airport's gendered restroom labels. LGTBIQ activist Gianna Camacho calls the measure discriminatory, warning that bathroom access would come to depend on security staff's personal judgment (including ID checks), and notes there is no record of sexual assault by trans women in women's restrooms. Ayacucho has no separate provision, enforcement action or incident on this point; the national ban on gender-matching restroom access, at committee stage in February 2025, applies to the region.

IDEHPUCP legal analysis by Miriam Tovar and Gonzalo Ugarte (15 Apr 2025) confirms that on Wednesday 2 April 2025 the congressional Plenary approved and exempted from second vote a bill whose article 5 bars any person from entering or using a public sanitary service that does not correspond to their 'biological sex', save for narrow listed exceptions, and argues this directly violates the equal-treatment and non-discrimination principle of article 2(2) of the Peruvian Constitution and article 1.1 of the American Convention on Human Rights. The authors say the law's stated aim of preventing child sexual abuse rests on a stigmatising stereotype implicitly presenting trans people as likely restroom harassers, while UN reporting shows trans people are more often victims than aggressors. Ayacucho has no separate provision, enforcement action or incident on this point; the analysis addresses the national framework in force in the region.

Agencia Presentes (22 Jul 2024), covering the Observatorio de Derechos TLGBI annual report, records 54 murders of TLGBI people and 170 rights-violation cases in Peru over 2020-2023, with trans women more than half the homicide victims (30), followed by 23 gay men and one lesbian; killings rose to 19 in 2023 (12 trans women) from 13 in 2022, 10 in 2021 and 12 in 2020, many committed with cruelty (multiple gunshots, stabbings), and the 170 violation cases include state violence and incitement to discrimination (61 denuncias in 2020). It recounts the February 2023 gang abduction of trans sex worker Rubí Torres Silvano, 31, in central Lima and her killing in Carabayllo with about 30 gunshots as part of an extortion scheme. It contains no Ayacucho-specific finding; for this record its value is the national hate-violence data the regional assessment relies on.

sources.summary: Infobae Perú (20 Feb 2025) reports that Congress' Commission on Women and Family unanimously approved a dictamen covering bills 6506 and 8457 that would bar entry to public sanitary facilities destined to the sex opposite to one's birth sex, with exceptions for custody, medical care, or accompanying an adult, a child under 12 or a disabled person, and would require unambiguous signage; as of publication it still awaited plenary backing. Trans-rights activist Gianna Camacho is quoted calling the measure discriminatory and warning that security staff would effectively judge people by personal criteria, such as requesting their DNI. IDEHPUCP analysis by Miriam Tovar and Gonzalo Ugarte (15 Apr 2025) reports that the Congress plenary on 2 April 2025 approved, exempt from second vote, the dictamen of the law 'fortaleciendo el derecho a la indemnidad sexual de los niños y adolescentes'. Its article 5 bars anyone whose biological sex does not match the facility's intended sex from public sanitary facilities, with exceptions limited to accompanying or assisting minors, patients or people with specific needs. The authors argue the measure implicitly brands trans people as more prone to entering bathrooms to harass or sexually abuse minors, conditions basic rights on verifiable 'biological sex', and violates equality, non-discrimination and gender self-determination; they note that Congress had already banned inclusive language and again rejected equal marriage. The analysis makes no Arequipa-specific finding.

sources.summary: National framework applying in Adana Province: same-sex sexual activity has been legal since 1858 under the Ottoman penal code, and transgender people have been able to change their legal gender since 1988, when gender reassignment surgery became legal. Türkiye has no comprehensive law prohibiting discrimination based on sexual orientation or gender identity, and LGBTQ people are barred from serving openly in the military. Same-sex relationships receive no legal recognition: marriage, civil unions and domestic partnerships are unavailable, and same-sex couples cannot adopt jointly or as individuals. Adana Province has no separate provisions, so this countrywide baseline governs visitors to the province.

Same-sex sexual activity has been legal since 1858 under the Ottoman penal code, and transgender people have been able to change their legal gender since 1988, when gender reassignment surgery became legal. Türkiye has no comprehensive law prohibiting discrimination based on sexual orientation or gender identity, and LGBTQ people are barred from serving openly in the military. Same-sex relationships receive no legal recognition: marriage, civil unions and domestic partnerships are unavailable, and same-sex couples cannot adopt jointly or as individuals. These provisions are countrywide, with no Adıyaman-specific content.

blindSourceSummaries: An international human-rights group's article (29 Oct 2025): a leaked draft omnibus justice reform would enable criminal charges against LGBT people — described by the group as one of the most alarming rollbacks of rights in decades; activists held a press conference against it (28 Oct 2025). It is national-level: it applies countrywide if adopted, and it has no state/province-specific provisions.

A national overview supplies the framework every visitor stands under: same-sex sexual activity has been legal since 1858 (a historic-era penal code), transgender people have been able to change their legal gender since 1988, there is no comprehensive law prohibiting discrimination based on sexual orientation or gender identity, LGBTQ people are barred from serving openly in the military, same-sex relationships receive no legal recognition — marriage, civil unions and domestic partnerships are unavailable — and same-sex couples cannot adopt jointly or as individuals. The page carries no state/province-specific content, so it supplies only the countrywide baseline against which this record's conservative estimate sits.
State/province page: thin: no usable finding.

25984515B26209284550223.name: Afyonkarahisar
25984515B26209284550223.summary: No provision, incident or enforcement practice specific to Afyonkarahisar was identified in the sources: the omnibus 11th Judicial Package reported by Human Rights Watch on 29 October 2025 carries no Afyonkarahisar-specific provision, and the Kaos GL 2025 human-rights report records no Afyonkarahisar-specific finding. The province stands under Turkey's national framework, and the national assessment applies to visitors here.

sources.summary: Human Rights Watch (29 Oct 2025) reports a leaked draft of Türkiye's omnibus 11th Judicial Package that would open the way to criminal charges against LGBT people, described as one of the most alarming rollbacks of rights in decades. Conduct deemed contrary to biological sex and general morality, including its so-called promotion, would bring up to three years in prison. Participation in same-sex engagement or marriage ceremonies would bring up to four years; since same-sex marriage is not legal, such ceremonies are by definition symbolic. Gender-affirming care would be restricted, with the surgery age raised from 18 to 25 and permanent infertility made mandatory. Medical professionals would face fines or up to seven years, and transgender patients up to three years for care outside the new limits, forcing treatment into underground settings. The package contains no Afyonkarahisar-specific provision and stands as national law over visitors in the province.

Kaos GL's 2025 report, A Major Siege against LGBTI+ People in 2025: Hostility Turned into State Policy, documents six right-to-life violations, three recorded as hate-motivated killings, with trans people the most affected. The counts come from media and civil-society reports because the state keeps no official hate-crime statistics. It records 89 torture or ill-treatment violations, up from 51, mostly linked to peaceful assembly, together with 336 assembly and 313 liberty violations, a roughly 2.5-fold liberty increase consisting mostly of detentions, alongside event-specific bans and violent police attacks on peaceful gatherings. The report describes hostility institutionalised under Year of the Family instructions to public institutions, hate speech from senior officials, censored broadcasts and cancelled artistic events as national practice. It contains no Afyonkarahisar-specific finding and describes the country-wide framework that governs the province.

25984515B39003465173278.name: Ağrı
25984515B39003465173278.summary:
Ağrı stands under the national legal framework of Türkiye; the source inventory records no province-specific statute, ordinance, enforcement pattern or incident series applying to the province. What a trans visitor encounters in Ağrı is Turkish national law and national police practice as described in the parent record.

Human Rights Watch reported on 29 October 2025 that a leaked draft of Türkiye's omnibus 11th Judicial Package would open the way to criminal charges against LGBT people, described there as one of the most alarming rollbacks of rights in decades. Conduct deemed 'contrary to biological sex and general morality', including its so-called 'promotion', would carry up to three years in prison, and participation in same-sex engagement or marriage ceremonies up to four years; same-sex marriage is not legal in Türkiye, so such ceremonies are by definition symbolic. The package would also restrict gender-affirming care: raising the surgery age from 18 to 25, making permanent infertility mandatory, exposing medical professionals to fines or up to seven years' imprisonment, and imprisoning transgender patients for up to three years for care outside the new limits, which would push treatment into underground settings. The package contains no Ağrı-specific provision, and whether it has since been enacted is unresolved in the sources.

Kaos GL's report on 2025, 'A Major Siege against LGBTI+ People in 2025: Hostility Turned into State Policy', documents six right-to-life violations, three recorded as hate-motivated killings, with trans people the most affected. These counts are drawn from media and civil-society reports because the state keeps no official hate-crime statistics. The report also records 89 torture or ill-treatment violations, up from 51 the previous year, mostly linked to peaceful assembly, alongside 336 assembly violations and 313 liberty violations — a roughly 2.5-fold rise in liberty violations, consisting mostly of detentions — together with event-specific bans and violent police attacks on peaceful gatherings. Hostility is presented as institutionalised under 'Year of the Family' instructions to public institutions, with hate speech from senior officials, censored broadcasts and cancelled artistic events. The report describes national practice rather than provincial choice, and no Ağrı-specific finding appears in it.

sources.title: LGBTQ rights in Turkey - Wikipedia
sources.summary: Wikipedia records the national framework that a visitor to Düzce stands under: consensual same-sex activity has been decriminalised since the 1858 Ottoman penal code, and transgender people have been able to change their legal gender since 1988, while Turkish marriage law gives same-sex relationships no legal recognition and offers no civil unions, domestic partnerships or joint adoption; no comprehensive law bans discrimination on sexual orientation or gender identity, and LGBTQ people are barred from open military service. In early 2026 Turkish media reported that the government was considering legislation criminalising public advocacy of 'behaviour contrary to biological sex', and that provision was not included in that year's judicial reform package. Pride events and LGBTQ gatherings were repeatedly disallowed in 2024 and 2025, with police detaining participants, per Amnesty International.

sources.title: LGBTQ rights in Turkey - Wikipedia
sources.summary: Turkey's national legal framework applies in Edirne. Same-sex activity has been legal since the 1858 Ottoman penal code, and trans people have been able to change legal gender since 1988. Same-sex marriage, civil unions and domestic partnerships remain unavailable, no comprehensive anti-discrimination law exists, and LGBTQ people are barred from open military service. In early 2026 Turkish media reported that the government was considering legislation criminalising public advocacy of 'behaviour contrary to biological sex', and the provision was not included in that year's judicial reform package. In May 2025 Erdoğan declared a 'Decade of Family and Population' for 2026-2035 at the International Family Forum with explicit anti-LGBTI rhetoric. Pride events were disallowed in 2024 and 2025, with police detaining participants. The European Commission's Türkiye Report 2025 concludes that the country's laws and their implementation do not properly protect LGBTQ people.

sources.summary: Human Rights Watch (29 Oct 2025) reported that the leaked omnibus '11th Judicial Package' would amend penal-code article 225 so that acts 'contrary to biological sex and general morality' carry up to 3 years and same-sex engagement or marriage ceremonies up to 4 years; amend civil-code article 40 ('Changing Sex') to raise the gender-affirming care minimum age from 18 to 25 with mandatory infertility and government-approved hospital evaluation; and imprison care providers up to 7 years and trans patients up to 3 years. The package is national legislation.

sources.title: LGBT rights in Turkey - Wikipedia
sources.summary: Manisa falls under Turkey's national rules. Homosexuality has not been a criminal offence since the Ottoman penal code of 1858, and transgender people have been able to change their legal gender since 1988, but no comprehensive law prohibits discrimination on the basis of sexual orientation or gender identity. Same-sex marriage and civil unions are not recognised. Marriage eligibility turns on the gender recorded in the civil registry, so a trans person who has legally changed the registered gender may marry a partner of the opposite registered gender. Openly LGBTQ people are barred from the military. Since 2015 authorities have banned pride events in most years, using tear gas, water cannon and mass detentions against those who defied the bans; in ILGA-Europe's 2026 Rainbow ranking Turkey placed 47th of 49. A February 2026 press report described legislation considering criminalising public advocacy of 'behaviour contrary to biological sex' with one to three years in prison, which was not included in the 2026 omnibus, the 12th judicial package. In September 2026 coordinated raids under the 'My Family is Safe' crackdown involved 162 suspects, 9 associations and 13 businesses.

sources.title: Türkiye - Amnesty International country report (Report 2025/26)
sources.summary: Amnesty International's Türkiye country report (Report 2025/26): in June 2025 authorities issued blanket bans against the Istanbul LGBTI and trans pride marches, police subjected peaceful protesters to unlawful use of force, over 90 people were arbitrarily detained, three activists were remanded in prison on 29 June and released on 8 August pending trial, and prosecutions of 92 people for participating in pride marches continued at year's end. In June 2025 the health ministry's medicines agency banned prescription and supply of hormones for gender-affirming procedures for people under 21, despite existing law permitting access from 18. In December 2025 an İzmir court ordered the dissolution of the Young LGBTI+ Association for sharing 'obscene' images incompatible with 'society's moral values'. Three draft law packages targeting LGBTI people were made public during 2025 - criminalising expression of LGBTI identities and consensual same-sex relations and making legal gender recognition nearly impossible - but were ultimately not submitted to parliament.

Amnesty also records that three draft law packages targeting LGBTI people were made public during 2025 - an unprecedented assault that would criminalize expression of LGBTI identities and consensual same-sex relations and make legal gender recognition nearly impossible - but they were ultimately not submitted to parliament.

sources.title: LGBT rights in Turkey - Wikipedia
sources.summary: Wikipedia's national 'LGBT rights in Turkey' page is the framework every Turkish province, Sivas included, stands under: homosexuality has not been a criminal offence since the Ottoman penal code of 1858, and transgender people have been able to change their legal gender since 1988 (with sex reassignment surgery, medical examination and court permission), but there is no comprehensive law prohibiting discrimination on the basis of sexual orientation or gender identity. Openly LGBTQ people are barred from serving in the Turkish military: a health regulation defines homosexuality as a 'psychosexual illness', conscripts who declare it must provide photographic proof, and the resulting 'unfit report' can leak and fuel later discrimination in public life. Same-sex marriage, civil unions and domestic partnerships are not recognised, and when the 12th judicial reform package passed in 2026 the anti-LGBTQ provisions were removed from the bill, leaving only symbolic same-sex weddings possible. Since 2015 authorities have banned Pride events in Istanbul and other cities in most years, with police using tear gas, water cannons and mass detentions against participants who defied the bans. The page also records early-2026 press reports that the government considered legislation criminalising public advocacy of 'behaviour contrary to biological sex', and that Turkey placed 47th of 49 countries in ILGA-Europe's 2026 Rainbow Europe ranking.

19177384B49506124846693.summary:
Ciudad Autónoma de Buenos Aires stands under Argentina's national framework for legal gender recognition, health care and hate-crime law. The sources identify two region-anchored findings for the city and no city-specific statute or enforcement statistic.

Trans activists based in Buenos Aires told the Washington Blade, in reporting published on 10 April 2025, that police violence against trans and travesti sex workers has become more common since the current national government took office. The same account records harassment and hate speech rising nationally.

DNU 61/2025, one of two emergency decrees published in February 2025, re-regulates the housing of transgender people deprived of liberty and invites the provinces and the City of Buenos Aires to adhere. The decree bars people who have legally changed gender from being housed in women's prisons when they are detained for sexual offences or violence against women. Whether the City of Buenos Aires has adhered is not stated in the sources.

sources.summary: The national administration eliminated the Women, Gender and Diversity Ministry, closed the National Institute Against Discrimination, Xenophobia and Racism (INADI), dismissed trans people hired under the Trans Labor Quota Law, which reserved at least 1% of public-sector jobs, and has moved to restrict the 12-year-old Gender Identity Law. Buenos Aires-based activists told the Washington Blade on April 10, 2025 that police violence against trans and travesti sex workers has become more common since the current government took office, with harassment and hate speech rising nationally.

Argentina recorded at least 227 hate crimes based on sexual orientation or gender identity in 2025, up 62% year-on-year, a ten-year record of one crime every 38 hours. According to Agencia Presentes data published on 19 March 2026, 32% of the crimes occurred in police stations and penal facilities, security-force violence multiplied from 17 cases (2024) to 64 (2025), and trans women and travestis concentrated 62.5% of victims (142 cases). Most perpetrators were security personnel and unknown assailants.

Via emergency decrees published in February 2025, DNU 62/2025 modified Article 11 of the Gender Identity Law (Law 26743) to prohibit gender-affirming interventions for persons under 18, and DNU 61/2025 re-regulates the housing of transgender people deprived of liberty, inviting the provinces and the City of Buenos Aires to adhere. The latter decree prohibits those who legally changed gender from being housed in women's prisons if detained for sexual offences or violence against women. FALGBT and legal experts call the decrees illegal and unconstitutional and are seeking judicial intervention.

14911670B90188072957077.name: Santa Catarina
14911670B90188072957077.summary:
Santa Catarina stands under Brazil's national framework. State-level protections specific to this jurisdiction have narrowed: State Law No. 12,534 of 4 April 2003, which barred discrimination on grounds of gender identity and sexual orientation, was repealed on 8 October 2015 by Complementary Law No. 656, and Complementary Law No. 527 of 28 December 2010, which also covered gender identity and sexual orientation, lost two of its operative provisions when the Supreme Federal Court declared Articles 2 VI and VII unconstitutional in ADI 5307 on 29 October 2018. The state constitution's anti-discrimination clause, in force since 2002, lists sexual orientation but does not address discrimination against transgender people.

What remains of Complementary Law No. 527 is the jurisdiction's principal conduct rule for visitors. It penalises private legal entities and, where applicable, state public servants that promote, permit or tolerate discriminatory acts based on gender or sexual orientation. The acts it defines include violent, coercive, intimidating or vexatious conduct; barring entry to or stay in places of free public access; service differentiated in ways the law does not require; refusing, preferring against or surcharging hotel, motel and pension lodging and the rental, purchase, acquisition or lease of movable and immovable property; and prohibiting expressions of affection that are permitted to others. Penalties are R$2,500, rising to R$5,000 on repeat, with 30-day suspension of an annual licence or revocation of monthly, daily or seasonal licences and a 30-day bar on renewal; complaints go to the State Secretariat of Public Security and Defence of the Citizen, fines are directed to the State Civil Police Improvement Fund, and state servants face suspension of up to 30 days.

Marriage formalities are processed locally without a sex restriction. On 29 April 2013 the Corregedoria-Geral da Justiça of Santa Catarina authorised notarial and civil-registry offices to process marriage habilitations regardless of the sex of the spouses and without observance of any gender limitation, extending Article 629 of the CGJ Code of Norms beyond the stable unions recognised since 2011; couples where both partners reside in the state could then formalise civil marriage at registry level. In Florianópolis, Judge M. C. F. Ribeiro da Silva of the 1st Civil Court blocked immigration authorities from deporting an Italian citizen who had lived more than ten years in a stable relationship with a Brazilian partner.

Documents recording a non-binary gender have been issued in Santa Catarina since 2020 through the courts and notarial offices, though no state law provides for them. In 2021 Idris Kawabe became the first person in the state to change documents judicially to reflect a neutral gender. A judicial action remains necessary in the absence of a state recognition law, and legal sex is still recorded on birth certificates.

Access to sex-segregated facilities is contested in the state. Governor Jorginho Mello signed State Law No. 19,686/2026 on 21 January 2026, requiring all public and private educational institutions from preschool through higher and vocational education to maintain strictly separate male and female restrooms and changing rooms. From 18 June 2026 the Federal University of Santa Catarina installed signage indicating that restrooms may be used in accordance with gender identity, in direct tension with the state requirement.

The leading public-accommodation case began in a Florianópolis shopping mall in 2014, when a trans woman was stopped by mall security from using the women's restroom. A lower court awarded 15,000 reais in compensation for pain and suffering under the Consumer Defence Code, the Court of Justice of Santa Catarina overturned the award, and on 6 June 2024 the Supreme Federal Court voted 8-3 to dismiss her appeal on the procedural ground that the original claim pleaded only consumer-law damages rather than constitutional provisions. The court withdrew the general repercussion it had recognised, so no binding constitutional ruling on trans restroom access was issued. In August 2025 an extraordinary appeal was taken to the Inter-American Court of Human Rights against both courts.

Florianópolis is among Brazil's broadly welcoming major cities, with active LGBTQ+ communities, pride events and legal infrastructure accustomed to processing marriages, adoptions and name or gender-marker changes. Smaller cities and rural areas of Santa Catarina may present more social friction, although the legal rights are the same.

sources.summary: Santa Catarina's constitution contains an anti-discrimination clause dating to 2002 that lists sexual orientation among non-discrimination grounds, yet as of 2019 it does not address discrimination against transgender people. Since 2020 people in Santa Catarina have obtained documents recording non-binary gender through the courts or notarial offices, although no specific law prescribes this. In Florianópolis, judge M. C. F. Ribeiro da Silva of the 1st Civil Court blocked immigration authorities from deporting an Italian citizen who had lived over ten years in a stable relationship with a lesbian Brazilian. Nationally, same-sex marriage has been legal since 2013 under CNJ Resolution 175/2013, and a 2019 Supreme Federal Tribunal ruling made discrimination on grounds of sexual orientation or gender identity a crime equivalent to racism under Law 7.716/1989.

Constitutional guarantees and federal criminal provisions adopted after the 2019 Supreme Federal Tribunal ruling prohibit discrimination and hate crimes based on sexual orientation and gender identity. A deeply conservative Congress has nonetheless generated a surge of anti-LGBTIQ proposals, including efforts to repeal the marriage equality recognised by the Supreme Court in 2013. These guarantees apply nationwide and cover visitors in Santa Catarina. In September 2025 the government reinstated the National LGBTI+ Health Technical Committee, a participatory mechanism dissolved in 2019, for shaping and monitoring inclusive public-health policy. The Superior Court of Justice ruled that nonbinary people may amend their civil registry to reflect their gender identity.

A legal guide updated 5 April 2026 names Florianópolis among Brazil's broadly welcoming major cities, with active LGBTQ+ communities, pride events and legal infrastructure accustomed to processing same-sex marriages, adoptions and name or gender-marker changes. Smaller cities and rural areas may present more social friction, though legal rights are identical nationwide. Foreign same-sex spouses and partners are treated identically for visa and residence categories, including the spousal residence permit, and foreign same-sex marriages are recognised for immigration purposes. Joint and second-parent adoption are confirmed by STF RE 846.102 (2015). Gender-marker changes proceed without surgery. ADO 26 (2019) criminalises homophobia and transphobia as equivalent to racism under Lei 7.716/1989.

sources.title: LGBTQ rights in Santa Catarina (Wikipedia)
sources.summary: State Law No. 12,534 enacted 4 April 2003 prohibited discrimination based on gender identity until repealed 8 October 2015 by Complementary Law No. 656, while Complementary Law No. 527 signed 28 December 2010 also prohibited discrimination based on gender identity until partially overturned 11 October 2018 after a 2015 Supreme Federal Court challenge on labor-law grounds, followed by a 2019 Supreme Federal Court decision banning discrimination based on gender identity. On 1 March 2018 the Supreme Federal Court ruled a transgender person has the right to change official name and sex by self-declaration of psychosocial identity without surgery or professional evaluation, and in 2021 Idris Kawabe became the first person in Santa Catarina to judicially change documents to reflect a neutral gender, though judicial actions are still required without a state law recognizing it and legal sex is still required in birth certificates. In December 2023 the Constitution and Justice Committee of the Legislative Assembly approved a bill prohibiting transgender women from participating in women's sports, still under review as of 18 August 2026, and a 2026 count recorded 271 unconstitutional laws processed since 2015 against women's or LGBTQ rights with about 70% involving the trans and travesti community and 41% ruled unconstitutional by the Supreme Federal Court. The Army provides that any person in the draft cohort expressing a gender identity other than male who holds a final, unappealable court ruling or civil registry amendment is treated as non-binary in the same manner as intersex individuals and considered exempt from mandatory military service for not meeting Federal Constitution, Military Service Law, implementing regulations and 2024 General Conscription Plan requirements. On 21 January 2026 Governor Jorginho Mello signed State Law No. 19,686/2026 requiring all public and private educational institutions from preschool through higher and vocational education to maintain strictly separate male and female restrooms and changing rooms, while the Federal University of Santa Catarina installed signs from 18 June 2026 indicating restrooms may be used in accordance with gender identity. In a 2014 Florianopolis shopping-mall case where a trans woman was denied access to the women's restroom, a lower court ordered 15,000 reais compensation for pain and suffering, the Court of Justice of Santa Catarina overturned it, and on 6 June 2024 the Supreme Federal Court voted 8-3 to reject her 2015 appeal as not involving a constitutional issue, followed in August 2025 by an extraordinary appeal to the Inter-American Court of Human Rights against both courts. Gender-neutral language was banned in state schools by decree of Governor Carlos Moises on 15 June 2021 until overturned 6 May 2025 by the Supreme Federal Court and banned in Joinville public office by law of 20 December 2021 until struck down 3 August 2022 by the Court of Justice, while on 1 April 2026 a law allowed parents to prohibit children from participating in classes on LGBTQ topics, and in 2024 three murders of trans people were recorded in the state. Same-sex sexual activity has been legal in Brazil since 1830, same-sex unions were recognized as family units with same rights and responsibilities as heterosexual couples by the Supreme Federal Court in May 2011, and same-sex marriage was authorized statewide by General Inspectorate of Justice resolution on 29 April 2013. 82249235B24619009834807.summary:
British Columbia stands under the Canadian national framework, and the province itself has no hostile legislation: no provincial statute restricts trans people's access to restrooms or other sex-segregated facilities, to gender-affirming care, or to gender-related name use in schools. The provincial layer adds no risk of its own for a trans visitor.

Human rights protection here is statutory and provincial as well as constitutional. British Columbia's human rights legislation lists gender identity and gender expression as prohibited grounds across employment, housing, and public and private accommodations, and a complaint against a private business proceeds under that statute rather than through a court. A visitor therefore has a provincial complaint route that does not depend on a court case.

Vital statistics, including birth certificates, are a provincial responsibility, and legal gender change is available in British Columbia under provincial rules. Anyone dealing with a document issued by this province does so through the provincial vital statistics authority rather than a national agency.

Sexual orientation has been covered federally since 1996, and the Criminal Code's hate-propaganda and anti-discrimination provisions protect gender identity and gender expression. A 2021 Criminal Code amendment, in force since 2022, made Canada the first country in North America to statutorily ban conversion therapy nationwide for both minors and adults. British Columbia has no hostile provincial legislation, and the national baseline score of 0.86 rests on Charter equality protection, nationwide conversion-therapy criminalisation, and legal gender change in every province including BC.

sources.title: LGBTQ rights in British Columbia (Wikipedia)
sources.summary: Federal, provincial and territorial law prohibits discrimination on the basis of gender identity or expression in employment, housing and public and private accommodations, and as of 2017 all provinces, territories and the federal government explicitly list gender identity as a prohibited ground in their human rights acts. The Supreme Court has interpreted the concepts of sex and physical disability in Charter section 15 to include transsexuality, with section 15 applying to all laws and government institutions including law enforcement authorities, while complaints against private businesses proceed under the applicable federal or provincial human rights statute. Transgender people are able to change their legal gender in all provinces and territories under varying rules, with vital statistics including identity documents such as birth certificates falling under provincial jurisdiction. In 2023 Saskatchewan passed The Education (Parents' Bill of Rights) Amendment Act, 2023 invoking the notwithstanding clause to require schools to obtain parental consent for students under 16 who request use of their gender-related preferred name or gender identity, prompting calls for repeal and legal action. In 2024 Alberta passed the Health Statutes Amendment Act, 2024, Education Amendment Act, 2024 and Fairness and Safety in Sport Act, which faced legal challenges blocked when the government passed Bill 9: Protecting Alberta's Children Statutes Amendment Act, 2025 using the notwithstanding clause. In December 2020 the Canadian Association of Chiefs of Police apologized for harm to Two-Spirit, Lesbian, Gay, Bisexual, Trans, Transgender and Queer communities, stated police must stand together against transphobia, and created an Equity, Diversity and Inclusion Committee to identify, mitigate and eliminate implicit bias and systemic barriers. Same-sex sexual activity in private between consenting adults was decriminalized on June 27, 1969 when the Criminal Law Amendment Act, 1968-69 received royal assent, and the anal-intercourse provision in section 159 of the Criminal Code was repealed on June 21, 2019 by Bill C-75, setting the age of consent at 16 for all sexual activities, 18 where there is a relationship of trust, authority or dependency, with close-in-age exceptions for ages 12 through 15. In Egan v Canada in 1995 the Supreme Court held sexual orientation is constitutionally protected under Charter section 15 as an analogous ground, and in Vriend v Alberta in 1998 it held failure to include sexual orientation in human rights law violated section 15, with all provinces, territories and the federal government explicitly prohibiting sexual orientation discrimination as of 2017. Charter equality protections apply to all laws and government institutions including law enforcement but not directly against the private sector, are subject to reasonable limits under section 1 under the Oakes Test and to section 33's notwithstanding clause, which has never been used by the federal Parliament. Canada legalized same-sex marriage nationwide on July 20, 2005 through the federal Civil Marriage Act, becoming the fourth country in the world and first in the Americas to do so, after court rulings between 2002 and 2005 struck down the opposite-sex common-law definition. Same-sex adoption is legal in all provinces and territories, beginning with British Columbia in 1996 and ending with Nunavut in 2011, and British Columbia, Ontario and Saskatchewan grant parental status to three or more intentional parents. In 2022 Canada became the third country in the world and first in North America to statutorily ban conversion therapy nationwide for minors and adults, making it a crime under the Criminal Code to subject anyone to it as defined by statute. On June 21, 2018 royal assent was granted to the Expungement of Historically Unjust Convictions Act allowing RCMP, federal departments, and notified provincial, municipal police and courts to destroy or remove judicial records for pre-1969 homosexual acts and section 159 convictions for living and deceased persons, distinct from a pardon or record suspension. Canada was ranked first in Asher & Lyric's LGBTQ+ Danger Index in 2023 indicating least dangerous, first in the Gay Travel Index in 2024, and ninth in the Equaldex Equality Index in 2024. The 2020 Pew Research showed 85% of Canada's general population, including 92% among Canadians aged 18 to 29, favoured social acceptance of homosexuality, up from 80% in 2013. June 2013 polls showed a vast majority blessed same-sex marriage available throughout Canada since 2005, with 70% agreeing same-sex couples should have the same rights to adopt as heterosexual couples and 76% agreeing they are just as likely to successfully raise children. A 2020 poll commissioned by the Privy Council Office found 91.8% of those surveyed said they would be "comfortable" if a next-door neighbour was gay, lesbian or bisexual. The same poll documented transgender-specific tolerance, finding that "87.6% said they would be 'comfortable' if a neighbour was a transgender person."

Región de Valparaíso stands under the national framework of Chile: the legal regime, document rules, entry provisions and protection machinery are those set out in the national record. What is specific to the region is the distribution of recorded anti-LGBTI discrimination cases and a municipal diversity-office structure.

13589884B3780741375954.name: Antioquia
13589884B3780741375954.summary:
Antioquia stands under Colombia's national framework: the national rules on identity documents, recognition of marriages performed abroad, access to public and commercial premises, and the treatment of detainees apply in the department as elsewhere in the country, and the inventory identifies no Antioquia-specific statute, departmental decree or court ruling of its own.

The region-specific record is a killing in Bello, in the metropolitan corridor around Medellín. On 5 April 2025 a video circulated showing Sara Millerey González Borja, a 32-year-old trans woman, beaten and thrown into a waterway in daylight while onlookers filmed; her legs, arms and hands were fractured, she could not swim, and she died of cardiac arrest the following afternoon.

She was the third LGBTQ person killed in Bello during 2025, the two earlier victims being gay men. A clinic reportedly declined to treat her as an emergency, on the stated ground that she had not been shot. Bello city hall drew criticism for referring to her by her pre-transition name. President Gustavo Petro ordered an urgent investigation, and protests followed in several cities.

sources.summary: El País English (14 April 2025), reporting from Bello, Antioquia: 32-year-old trans woman Sara Millerey González Borja was beaten and thrown into a waterway in broad daylight while onlookers filmed; the video went viral on 5 April, President Gustavo Petro ordered an investigation and protests were held in several cities. She was the third LGBTQ person killed in Bello in 2025 (the first two victims were gay men); a clinic reportedly did not treat her as an emergency 'because she didn't get shot', and she died of cardiac arrest the following afternoon. The article records 13 trans people killed in Colombia in the first quarter of 2025 alone and notes city hall was criticised for using her pre-transition name.

The Guardian (30 July 2024), reporting from Caquetá: 41 transgender women were killed in Colombia in 2023 and eight more between February and April 2024, national figures that also cover Antioquia. Armed groups in Caquetá, where ex-rebel structures persist despite the 2016 peace agreement, distributed flyers on streets and WhatsApp announcing a 'social cleansing' plan naming 'faggots, lesbians and men and women who destroy homes' as legitimate military targets, and trans women there fled after death threats. No Antioquia-specific source covers these national 2023-24 kill tallies or the southern-department flyers.

13589884B40908771570386.name: Bogota Capital District
13589884B40908771570386.summary:
Bogotá Capital District stands under Colombia's national framework, which carries the legal gender recognition regime, the identity-document markers, entry and partner-recognition rules, and the national record of lethal violence against trans people. The available sources record no district-level statute, ordinance or enforcement practice that departs from that national layer.

Prejudice and discrimination against LGBTI people remain present in a considerable part of the population. For a visibly gender-nonconforming visitor in central Bogotá, that is the social baseline the sources describe, and it sits alongside the capital's visible LGBTI presence.

Claudia López Hernández became the first openly gay person to serve as mayor of Bogotá. Pride parades in the city rank among Colombia's large LGBTI events, and a Washington Post report describes thriving gay neighbourhoods in the capital.

25490228B43154843394848.name: Comunidad de Madrid
25490228B43154843394848.summary:
Madrid stands under Spain's national framework for legal gender recognition, with the Comunidad de Madrid's own statute as a layer beneath it. Madrid is one of Europe's principal LGBT urban centres, and the region was among the first in Spain to pass a gender-identity law, adopting its statute in 2016 alongside the Islas Baleares and the Región de Murcia and after Extremadura in 2015. That regional statute was later amended by Ley 17/2023. Regional law must comply with Spain's Ley 4/2023, which sets the statutory floor that a trans visitor's recognition and protection claims in the region rest on.

What the region has withdrawn since then matters to anyone relying on local antidiscrimination machinery. After the 2023 regional election, the new government of the Comunidad de Madrid repealed the region's non-discrimination law, repealed the regional ban on conversion therapy as it applies to trans people, removed the penalties that attached to conversion therapy, and repealed several trans legal recognitions. These measures act on the region's own guarantees and leave the national framework in place.

The safety picture the region's own sources report does not follow from the legal position. Homophobic and transphobic discrimination and violence are described as significant problems in Madrid, and trans people and migrants are reported to face additional barriers within the city's LGBT population.

The community is concentrated and long established. The Chueca district is the centre of the city's LGBT life, and MADO, held annually in late June or early July, is among the largest Pride events in the world and draws millions of attendees. COGAM, founded in 1986, is the city's most influential LGBT organisation; the city government maintains an Oficina de Atención a la Diversidad Sexual y de Género; and Arcopoli works against discrimination and violence.

sources.summary: Official text (BOE) of Ley 4/2023 (28 February 2023), "for the real and effective equality of trans people and the guarantee of the rights of LGTBI people": establishes self-ID legal gender recognition (16+, no diagnosis), broad anti-discrimination guarantees, employment and health measures, and an LGTBI equality strategy. National framework that Madrid's 2023 amendments sit beside.

Human Rights Watch (Feb 2023): "Victory in Fight for Gender Recognition in Spain" - hails Spain's self-ID gender-recognition law as a hard-won victory after years of activism. National framework context.

Spanish criminal-law firm analysis (June 2026): disentangles three statutes - what Law 4/2023 does and does not do; the discrimination aggravating factor of Article 22.4 of the Penal Code (gender identity/expression motives); and the hate offences of Article 510 CP extended to trans/LGBTI people. National framework context.

The safety finding it reports is that homophobic and transphobic discrimination and violence remain significant problems in Madrid, and that marginalised LGBT groups such as migrants and trans people face additional barriers.

19338628B36302232233914.name: Hauts-de-France
19338628B36302232233914.summary:
Hauts-de-France legislates nothing of its own on detention, identity documents or anti-discrimination. The region stands under the national framework of France: custodial placement, gender markers and discrimination protections are set nationally. No regional statute, regional court ruling or regional administrative instruction on transgender detainees or visitors appears in the sources.

The single documented case in the region is Paola, a trans woman whose identity documents record her as male, transferred in 2014 to the correctional facility at Lille and held in a men's establishment. Detainees there shouted "We don't want any women here!"; a fellow inmate tried to attack her with a knife; she spent two days in solitary confinement. The account was published in a BuzzFeed News investigation of 12 January 2018.

sources.summary: BuzzFeed investigation posted 12 January 2018: under Article D248 of the criminal-procedure code men and women must be held in separate establishments, but placement follows the legal gender on identity documents, so trans women still recorded as male are held in all-male facilities - the group that, per controller-general Adeline Hazan, 'suffers the most' in prison. Region-relevant case: Paola, transferred in 2014 to Lille's northern correctional facility, was met by detainees shouting 'We don't want any women here!', a fellow inmate tried to attack her with a knife and she spent two days in solitary confinement; Kara B. was held under conditions described as worrying after her 2016 Paris protest trial; the Ministry of Justice counted 13 transgender detainees across eight facilities as of 1 November 2016.

National detention-oversight opinion of 25 May 2021 (covering every place of deprivation of liberty; prepared from referrals received since 2010 concerning transgender detainees): assignment to establishments or wards (male or female) is based exclusively on civil status, so the vast majority of transgender people are held in institutions or wards that do not correspond to their gender identity, and search procedures for persons whose civil-status sex does not match their identity add constraints such as isolation. It recommends guaranteeing every transgender detainee the possibility of choosing the sex of searching officers and of their ward, bars identity-based isolation, requires continuity of medical and hormone care with free choice of doctor, urges research funding, and faults the administration for not translating the 2016 justice-modernisation law (n° 2016-1547 of 18 November 2016) into prison rules.

19338628B57683459369229.name: Occitanie
19338628B57683459369229.summary:
Occitanie stands under the national legal framework of France. The region-specific record in the sources is the opinion issued on 25 May 2021 by the CGLPL, the national inspectorate of places of deprivation of liberty, whose visits covered two facilities in Toulouse: Toulouse-Seysses prison and the Toulouse central police station.

The opinion concerns eight transgender women held in those Toulouse facilities. It documents isolation imposed on detainees because of their trans status, and staff who had received no training on trans issues. It further finds that the depathologisation law of 18 November 2016 (n° 2016-1547) was never written into prison rules or into healthcare guidance, so the statutory change of status had no operational effect on how trans detainees were held or treated.

The inspectorate's recommendations bearing on the region call for financed research, policies against discrimination, and suitable procedures for searching and for assigning detainees whose civil-status sex does not match the identity they present. For a trans visitor, the operative exposure in Occitanie is custody: police custody at a central station and detention at a prison are the settings where the documented failures occur, and the placement and search practices described apply regardless of how a person presents in ordinary daily life.

A trans woman from Argentina whose passport lists her as female spent three days in a men's facility in Lille amid inmate threats, including an attempt to attack her with a knife; another detainee was held after a 2016 Paris protest trial. As of 1 November 2016 there were 13 transgender detainees in France, and damages obtained for one detainee's detention conditions were a symbolic 2,000 euros. No Occitanie-specific event appears in the article. The national custody framework applies unchanged in every department, including this one.

65028918B14696209246677.name: Jakarta Special Capital Region
65028918B14696209246677.summary:
Jakarta stands under Indonesia's national framework, which the national record carries; what is specific to the Special Capital Region is a police practice of raiding private LGBT gatherings under pornography and morality provisions rather than under any Jakarta statute naming LGBT people.

The raid series runs back a decade. In May 2017 police arrested 141 people at what was described as a gay sex party in Jakarta. On 21 May 2017 officers detained 144 people at the Atlantis Gym sauna, ten of whom were charged. In October 2017 police arrested 51 people at a sauna in Central Jakarta, of whom six were charged. All of these cases were pursued under the pornography law.

The pattern continued in 2025. On 1 February 2025 police detained 56 people at a hotel in South Jakarta, described in reporting as a gay party. On 24 May 2025 nine people were detained after a raid on a different hotel in South Jakarta. Offences of this kind can carry up to 15 years' imprisonment.

City government, not only the police, has acted against transgender residents. In March 2018 the Jakarta Social Agency declared transgender waria 'socially dysfunctional' and held trans women in city-run rehabilitation centres unless they signed statements promising not to repeat their offence.

For a trans visitor the operative exposure in Jakarta is attendance at a private gathering: a hotel party, a sauna, a rented venue. The charges that follow are laid under broad pornography and morality provisions with long sentences available, and the sources record no Jakarta statute creating offences specific to LGBT people.

sources.summary: An October 2025 presidential decree named 'the promotion of LGBTQ+ culture' a non-military national security threat alongside terrorism, radicalism and drug addiction. Journalists report a constant chilling effect, with editors killing LGBTQ+ stories fearing state reprisal or religious backlash. Civil-society and independent media space has contracted since 2024-25, documented amid student-led anti-government protests.

More recently it records 56 people detained at a hotel in South Jakarta on 1 February 2025, nine detained at another South Jakarta hotel on 24 May 2025, and 75 arrested at a private villa near the capital on 22 June 2025 — offences there can carry up to 15 years' imprisonment. In March 2018 the Jakarta Social Agency declared transgender waria 'socially dysfunctional' and detained trans women in city-run 'rehabilitation' centres unless they signed statements promising not to repeat their 'offence'. Transgender people may change legal gender only after surgery and a judge's approval, and there is no general anti-discrimination law, so police action in Jakarta operates on pornography and morality provisions rather than any LGBT-specific statute.

sources.title: Indonesia: Police must release 75 people arrested in discriminatory raid on "gay party" - Amnesty International
sources.summary: Amnesty International's 24 June 2025 press release responds to the arrest of 75 people in a raid on a 'gay party' at a privately rented villa in Bogor, near Jakarta, and situates it inside the capital's raid series: 56 people were detained for participating in 'a gay party' at a hotel in South Jakarta on 1 February 2025, and nine were detained following a raid on a different hotel in South Jakarta on 24 May 2025. Amnesty International Indonesia's deputy director called the villa raid 'a blatant violation of human rights and privacy' that 'exemplifies the hostile environment for LGBTI people in Indonesia', and demanded the release of those arrested. The release notes that police made the arrests without naming detainees or conducting judicial proceedings, and that those detained risk up to 15 years' imprisonment under Indonesia's broadly worded Pornography Law.

68945753B55100681051852.name: Seoul
68945753B55100681051852.summary:
Seoul stands under the national framework of South Korea. National rules on criminal law, identity documents, military service and legal gender recognition are carried by the country record; what follows is specific to Seoul.

On 2 July 2024 the Seoul Central District Court, with presiding judge Chung In-jae, dismissed the government's appeal in a damages action brought by a transgender plaintiff identified as A, and the judgment became final when neither side appealed further. The court awarded 300,000 won (about $240) of the 3 million won claimed. It held that a police officer's advice to an LGBT person in the middle of legal transition to avoid public restrooms for a period infringed personal rights, and that the right to use restrooms comfortably is a fundamental and universal human right.

The ruling addresses police conduct rather than venue policy. It establishes that advice of this kind from an officer is unlawful in Seoul. It does not by itself require any particular venue, school or business to admit a trans person to a given restroom.

The decision became final on 2 July 2024 after neither party appealed. The court held that a police officer's advice to an LGBT person mid-legal-transition to avoid public restrooms for a while infringed personal rights, stating that the right to comfortably use restrooms is a fundamental and universal human right. A 2021 NHRCK survey of 591 trans respondents found that 41% used another-gender restrooms out of fear of mistreatment, 39% avoided food and drink, and 36% forwent restroom use altogether. A 2021 Pohang branch of the Daegu District Court ruling awarded 7 million won in damages against an academy that barred a trans student's restroom use.

National judicial-framework item (Yonhap, 8 May 2024): the regional court in the central county of Yeongdong approved male-to-female gender-marker change for five transgender people without sex reassignment surgery, holding that it is against the law to determine gender change based on surgery and that every human being has the right to live according to their gender identity. The national court guidelines that previously required surgery have been downgraded to reference-only status, though some courts still apply them. The court sits outside Seoul, and the ruling bears on this jurisdiction as evidence of the national judicial trend cited for it.

31927357B30293642818187.name: Quintana Roo
31927357B30293642818187.summary:
Quintana Roo stands under the national framework of Mexico. The state's own law governs legal gender recognition, marriage, adoption, hate-crime liability and the prohibition of conversion practices.

Quintana Roo enacted legal gender recognition in 2020.

On 15 December 2023 the state congress banned conversion practices, following Morelos. The reform prohibits and sanctions efforts to correct sexual orientation and gender identity, commonly called conversion therapies, with penalties of two to six years in prison and fines of 1,000 to 2,000 times the daily UMA value. It applies across the state, including the tourist corridors of Cancún and the Riviera Maya.

The state penal code treats crimes motivated by sexual orientation or gender as hate crimes, and the state ratified the 2011 federal constitutional ban on sexual-orientation discrimination.

Marriage in Quintana Roo has been open to couples without regard to gender since 2012. Two marriages were performed in Kantunilkín in November 2011, annulled by the governor in April 2012, and reinstated on 3 May 2012 after the state conceded that its Civil Code sets no gender requirement. That silence in the Civil Code is the operative basis on which a trans visitor's marriage would be recognised in the state.

The state congress legalised adoption by same-sex couples in August 2022.

15666254B89722251658211.name: Selangor
15666254B89722251658211.summary:
Selangor stands under Malaysia's national framework: the federal Penal Code, the national rules governing identity documents and the other provisions set out in Malaysia's record apply to visitors here as elsewhere in the country. What follows is specific to Selangor, where two layers of local enforcement operate. The Syariah Criminal Offences Enactment 1995 binds Muslims, and the state's Islamic religious department polices appearance and public conduct.

In February 2021 the Federal Court struck down provisions of the Selangor Syariah Criminal Offences Enactment 1995 for exceeding the state's legislative power. The decision turned on which legislature may create such an offence, not on the substance of the cross-dressing prohibition, and it decriminalised nothing under the federal Penal Code.

Documented enforcement in the state has attached to appearance rather than conduct. In 2021 a transgender businesswoman and cosmetics entrepreneur, Nur Sajat, failed to appear in a Selangor Sharia court to answer charges of insulting Islam brought over her attire. The state's religious department issued a warrant for her arrest and announced that 122 religious-affairs officers had been mobilised to find her, and it sought her extradition from Thailand. 15666254B42356713390762.name: Johor
15666254B42356713390762.summary:
Johor is one of Malaysia's thirteen states and stands under the national framework. The federal Penal Code applies in full within its borders, and Johor's own Sharia enactment applies to Muslim residents and visitors; the substance of both is set out in the national assessment.

In November 2023 the Johor state government announced plans to establish conversion-therapy centres to "rehabilitate" LGBT people. The announcement is a formal statement of policy by the state administration rather than a criminal provision, and it indicates official hostility toward gender-nonconforming and LGBT people in Johor, for residents and visitors alike.

For a trans visitor the announcement matters as a signal of the state government's posture rather than as a rule that singles out travellers. No Johor-specific protection, countervailing policy or official statement of tolerance appears in the sources, so the practical exposure a visitor faces in Johor is set by the national enforcement pattern.

27671186B76269877687363.name: Abuja Federal Capital Territory
27671186B76269877687363.summary:
Abuja Federal Capital Territory has no territorial variation from Nigeria's national framework: the Same-Sex Marriage (Prohibition) Act 2014 and the criminal provisions it reinforces apply in the capital as they do elsewhere in the country, and the national assessment carries that layer in full.

The territory's documented trans-specific killing is that of a 33-year-old transgender woman and TikTok creator known as Abuja Area Mama. BBC News reported on 9 August 2024 that her beaten and bruised body was found along the Katampe-Mabushi expressway in the Banex/Wuse II area of Abuja on Thursday 8 August 2024, hours after she posted a final video; she had previously expressed fear for her life.

The official response misgendered the victim. A police statement described her as "a man fully dressed in female clothing with no means of identification". The Abuja police chief, Benneth Igweh, ordered a "thorough and discreet" investigation.

No charge followed. The Dial reported in February 2025, six months after the killing, that no suspects had been charged despite the public commitment to investigate. A petition carrying nearly 6,000 signatures demanded that the murder be pursued as a hate crime.

For a trans visitor or resident in the capital, the case sets the expected official posture: a trans woman killed on a city highway, recorded in police language by her clothing rather than her identity, with no prosecution recorded months later.

1875124B65618634887963.name: Lima
1875124B65618634887963.summary:
Lima department and the metropolitan area stand under the national framework of Peru, and the national assessment carried by the parent record applies here. No separate departmental or municipal regime modifying that framework was identified in the sources.

Lima's Jorge Chávez international airport had installed signage reading "for all persons with female identity" and "male identity". The national norm approved by Congress on 2 April 2025 bars such "ambiguous" signage as well as trans people's use of facilities matching their gender identity, so the airport's inclusive signs fall directly within the national prohibition.

On 12 February 2023 Rubí Torres Silvano, a 31-year-old transgender sex worker, was abducted from jirón Chancay in central Lima by the "Los Gallegos" extortion gang and killed with roughly 30 gunshots. The killing is recorded by the TLGBI Rights Observatory.

sources.summary: National-framework source (binds Lima as national policy): Infobae (20 Feb 2025) reports the Congress Women and Family Commission unanimously approved the Muñante initiative barring trans people from public bathrooms of the sex not matching their biological sex at birth, stating the text also bars “ambiguous” bathroom signage of the kind the international airport Jorge Chávez had placed (“for all persons with female identity” / “male identity”) and that the norm still required plenary backing. LGBTIQ activist Gianna Camacho is quoted calling the measure discriminatory and describing how enforcement would reduce to security staff demanding ID (DNI) based on their own judgment of whether a woman entering is trans.

1875124B43998217738279.name: Municipalidad Metropolitana de Lima
1875124B43998217738279.summary:
Lima stands under Peru's national framework: Congress and national agencies set the rules on gender identity, access to public facilities, identity documents and hate-crime protection, and no municipal ordinance of the city's own on these matters appears in the reporting reviewed. What is specific to the capital is where those national rules land, at the airport that serves it, in its public buildings and commercial venues, and in the violence documented in its central streets.

The bathroom bill approved unanimously by the Congressional Women and Family Commission on 20 February 2025 obliges the removal of "ambiguous" signage, and the text names the signage installed at Jorge Chávez International Airport, which reads "for all persons with female identity" and "male identity". The airport serving Lima is the first site where that removal obligation would apply, and the signs in question are the ones that currently direct arriving trans passengers to a facility.

Gianna Camacho, a trans human-rights defender, warns that enforcement will take the form of identity-document checks by security staff deciding who may enter a bathroom, a practice she describes as discriminatory and grounded in prejudice. In the capital that discretion would sit with staff at municipal buildings, transport terminals and private venues rather than with any single agency.

Violence in the capital is documented in the same reporting. On 12 February 2023 the gang known as Los Gallegos kidnapped Rubí Torres Silvano, a 31-year-old trans sex worker, from jirón Chancay in the central city and killed her with roughly 30 gunshots. The Observatory report on hate crimes cites the case as an example of the pattern in Lima.

25984515B47806653651907.name: Ankara
25984515B47806653651907.summary:
Ankara stands under Turkey's national framework: the sources record no Ankara-level law or municipal measure, and the city's distinct exposure is institutional, since the presidency, the Ministry of Family and the drafting machinery for national legislation sit there. The penal-code package reported by Human Rights Watch on 29 October 2025 is drafted, and would be enforced, through institutions operating in Ankara.

The leaked draft, known as the 11th Judicial Package, would amend the penal code to criminalise conduct treated as contrary to biological sex and general morality, punishable by up to three years in prison, and to punish participation in same-sex engagement or marriage ceremonies with up to four years. It would raise the minimum age for gender-affirming care, surgery included, from 18 to 25, attach mandatory permanent infertility and repeated evaluations at government-approved hospitals, expose health professionals performing such interventions to fines and up to seven years in prison and trans people receiving care the authorities deem illegal to up to three years, and allow courts to order pretrial detention. Fifteen LGBT groups and the Turkish Medical Association opposed the draft, which had not been enacted as of the reporting date.

Kaos GL's 2025 annual report concludes that hostility toward LGBTI+ people became explicit state policy, centred on the presidency and implemented through the Ministry of Family, both of them Ankara institutions. It records censored broadcasts, artistic events cancelled or banned, and an LGBTI+ association closed for the first time in years, with criminal cases opened against 11 of its members.

The same report counts six violations of the right to life over the year, three of them recorded as hate-motivated, with trans people the most affected group, alongside a rise in torture and ill-treatment violations to 89 from 51 the previous year. Turkey compiles no official hate-crime statistics, so these figures rest on the organisation's own monitoring; with no general homicide or violence denominator in the sources, the six deaths cannot be expressed as a rate or compared with the risk borne by the general population.
