25984515B12971548112787.name: Eskişehir
25984515B12971548112787.summary:
Eskişehir stands under Turkey's national framework; no Eskişehir-specific statute, municipal ordinance or local protection body appears in the source inventory, so the national assessment governs here. The region-specific record concerns public assembly.

In June 2021 police blocked Eskişehir's first Pride parade. Officers reached the area hours before the scheduled meeting time and carried out identity checks. Organisers were not permitted to hold a press meeting or conduct the parade, and police detained 20 people on the grounds of violating the ban on the march.

The ban is the clearest local signal that even in a university city, local authorities have suppressed the local Pride event. For a trans visitor, the documented exposure in Eskişehir is assembly and identity checks at LGBT-related gatherings rather than any city-level criminal provision.

sources.title: LGBT rights in Turkey - Wikipedia
sources.summary: Wikipedia's country page on LGBT rights in Turkey is the framework under which Eskişehir stands, and it names the province directly: in June 2021 police blocked the first Eskişehir pride parade, showing that even in this university city local authorities have suppressed the local Pride event. On the national frame, homosexuality has not been a criminal offence since the Ottoman penal code of 1858 and transgender people have been able to change their legal gender since 1988 (with surgery, medical examination and court permission), but there is no comprehensive anti-discrimination law and same-sex marriage, civil unions and domestic partnerships are not recognised. Since 2015 authorities have banned Pride events in most years, and participants have faced police attacks; in ILGA-Europe's 2026 Rainbow Europe ranking Turkey placed 47th of 49 countries. In early 2026 Turkish media reported the government was considering legislation criminalising public advocacy of 'behaviour contrary to biological sex', a provision that was ultimately not included in that year's judicial reform package. It also records that Kadir Has University surveys saw public support for equal rights for LGBTQ people rise from 33% in 2016 to 45% in 2020.

25984515B18786507826220.name: İstanbul
25984515B18786507826220.summary:
İstanbul stands under the national framework in force across Turkey; country-level law, detention conditions and healthcare are covered in the national assessment. What is specific to the city is the assembly ban and the policing of trans women on its streets.

The Governorship of İstanbul has denied permission for and locally banned Pride parades since 2015 on security and public-order grounds, with the 2016 to 2018 bans stated explicitly; one source dates the ban to 2014. Water cannon were used against marchers on 29 June 2015. The 2014 march drew more than 100,000 participants, the largest LGBT event recorded in Turkey.

Suppression escalated after the ban. In 2021 police blockaded the route and used tear gas, arresting 25 people. On 26 June 2022 riot police dispersed the march at Taksim Square, blockaded streets in the adjacent Cihangir neighbourhood, shut down public transport to the square and detained 373 people, among them the photojournalist Bülent Kılıç; those held were released after a night in custody. The district governor's offices of Kadıköy and Beyoğlu had banned all Pride Week events for seven days. Arrests continued at 113 in 2023 and 11 in 2024, three of them minors, after organisers moved Pride out of Taksim Square into other public spaces and issued false meeting calls to evade police.

Policing extends to trans women going about ordinary business. On 31 July 2025 İstanbul police stopped around 20 trans women in Beyoğlu for identity checks, recorded their names and filmed them; the report describes the operation as profiling.

Its monitoring counts six violations of the right to life, three recorded as hate-motivated, with trans people most affected; torture and ill-treatment violations nearly doubled to 89 from 51; one LGBTI+ association closed with criminal cases opened against 11 members; and the state keeps no official hate-crime statistics.
The underlying news report covers the 31 July 2025 roundup of around 20 trans women in İstanbul's Beyoğlu district for ID checks, with names recorded and videos taken — "this is profiling".

66186276B86072070009793.name: Puerto Rico
66186276B86072070009793.summary:
Puerto Rico is a United States territory and stands under the United States federal framework for entry, documents, federally funded care and federal custody; the findings below are the territory's own law, its own enforcement and its own institutions.

Ley Núm. 63 de 2025, the Law for the Protection of the Health and Wellbeing of Minors, was enacted in July 2025. It bars gender-affirming care for anyone under 21, withdraws public funding for that care, and penalises violations with a fixed 15-year prison term, a $50,000 fine per violation for legal persons, and permanent loss of medical licences for professionals. Article 4, the operative prohibition, is directed at medical institutions and health professionals: none may perform surgical interventions or medication treatments that alter sex biology under the pretext of gender transition or as part of gender-dysphoria treatment.

Article 3 defines the banned chemical and surgical practice more broadly than the operative clause. It expressly names the use of puberty blockers and sex hormones, including androgen blockers, oestrogen, progesterone or testosterone, when used to treat gender dysphoria, and it sets the protected class at anyone under 21. Article 6 penalises any person who violates the law's provisions.

The gap between a definition framed around patient use and an operative clause that restricts only providers leaves an unresolved question. Under ordinary criminal-law principles a successful prosecution of a visiting under-21 trans person for using their own lawfully prescribed hormones, or of a parent accompanying them, would almost certainly fail, and no test case had resolved the question at the time of writing. For an under-21 trans traveller the practical reading is that carrying and using prescribed hormone treatment on the island sits inside the law's literal definition of a banned practice, and that enforcement risk is harassment-shaped rather than conviction-shaped: questioning, detention or investigation by hostile officials, with the answer arriving only after the fact. The law's protected class is anyone under 21 and does not on its face reach patients 21 or older.

The law was pushed through non-public hearings and is written with deliberate vagueness, so doctors and affirming parents who facilitate hormone treatment or top surgery risk prosecution, a reach that extends to the accompanying parents of a travelling trans teenager. It mandates campaigns by the Education and Health departments on the risks of trans-affirming care. Health Secretary Víctor Ramos Parés proposed amendments that would have allowed puberty blockers and the continuation of existing hormone treatment; the text as enacted stands as the most restrictive care law in any United States jurisdiction according to the report documenting it. The Puerto Rico LGBTQ+ Federation announced plans to challenge the ban in court.

The ACLU of Puerto Rico urged Governor Jenniffer González Colón to veto Senate Bill 350, which it said criminalizes doctors and parents and creates two distinct categories of children divided by whether identity aligns with sex assigned at birth. Policy Counsel Lolimar Escudero Rodríguez stated that the bill allows parents to authorise treatment where a child's identity aligns with the sex assigned at birth and prohibits them the same right where it does not. Executive Director Annette Martínez Orabona said the measure discriminates against transgender people and denies the existence of trans children and youth. The bill was authored by Senate President Thomas Rivera Schatz and Senator Joanne Rodríguez Veve, passed both chambers in April, was returned for amendments suggested by Health Secretary Ramos Parés that the ACLU warned did not remedy the rights violations, and was re-approved and returned to the Governor on 28 June. Opposition was registered by the Puerto Rico College of Physicians and Surgeons, the Puerto Rico Psychology Association, the College of Social Work Professionals, the Puerto Rican Association of Professional Counseling, the Puerto Rico Bar Association and the LGBTQ+ Federation of Puerto Rico.

Puerto Rico amended its hate crime statutes in 2002 to include sexual orientation and gender identity as protected characteristics. The first hate crime charges in the territory's history were brought in 2020, after Sean Díaz de León and Juan Pagán Bonilla were charged in the murder of two transgender women on 22 April 2020; Bonilla confessed to the killings. In January 2021 Governor Pedro Pierluisi declared a state of emergency over ongoing murders, assaults and rape of transgender individuals on the island.

Anti-discrimination coverage is partial. The 2013 law that passed, Senate Bill 238, signed 29 May 2013, was amended in the House to apply only to employment discrimination, so public facilities, housing, transit and business transactions are not covered. An earlier bill, House Bill 1725, passed the House 43-6 in November 2009 with wider coverage, but the Senate held no hearings and took no action after Senate President Thomas Rivera Schatz said it would not be approved.

Marriage recognition for same-sex couples was won through federal court rather than local statute. The challenge was filed in March 2014 in the Ada Conde Vidal case, with intervention from Lambda Legal and Puerto Rico Para Todas, and in June 2014 four couples joined as plaintiffs, among them a former National Guard member and two couples already married in Canada in 2007 and in New York in 2012.

Consensual private sexual activity between adults is not criminalised. The Puerto Rico Supreme Court upheld the territory's sodomy ban in 2002; after the United States Supreme Court's 2003 ruling invalidated state and territorial sodomy statutes covering consensual private acts, Puerto Rico amended its Penal Code in 2004 to remove private, non-commercial sexual activity between consenting adults from the statute.

sources.title: Ley Núm. 63 de 2025 (LexJuris de Puerto Rico) — primary legal text
sources.summary: Ley Núm. 63 de 2025, 'Ley para la protección de la salud y el bienestar de los menores de edad en Puerto Rico' (primary legal text, LexJuris). Article 4 — the operative prohibition — is directed at medical institutions and health professionals: none may perform surgical interventions or medication treatments altering the sex biology of a minor 'bajo el pretexto de una transición de género o como parte de un tratamiento de disforia de género'. The Article 3 definition of banned 'chemical and surgical mutilation' is drafted broader than the prohibition: it expressly includes 'el uso de bloqueadores de pubertad y hormonas sexuales (incluyendo bloqueadores androgénicos, estrógenos, progesterona o testosterona) utilizados con el propósito de tratar la disforia de género' — the USE itself of puberty blockers and sex hormones for gender-dysphoria treatment — and defines 'niño o menor de edad' as any person under 21. Article 6 then penalises 'toda persona que viole las disposiciones de esta Ley' with a fixed 15-year term, plus permanent licence loss for professionals and a $50,000 per-violation fine for juridical persons. Legal analysis of this drafting notes a structural tension: the definition speaks of patient 'use' while the operative clause restricts only providers, and the penalty catch-all says 'any person'. Under standard criminal doctrines (definitions create no offence by themselves; a protected class cannot be prosecuted as the perpetrator of its own victimisation; the principle of legality bars analogy; and travel with lawfully prescribed personal medication), a successful prosecution of a visiting under-21 trans person for using their own prescribed hormones — or of their parents for enabling it — would almost certainly fail, and the statute is a textbook void-for-vagueness candidate. But the textual ambiguity is precisely what legal advocates flag as its chilling effect: it leaves interpretive room for hostile officials to question, detain or investigate trans youth and their families on the ground, with the answer coming only after the fact. For a travelling under-21 trans person the practical reading is: carrying and using prescribed HRT in Puerto Rico sits inside the law's literal definition of banned practice, enforcement risk is harassment-shaped rather than conviction-shaped, and no test case had resolved the question at the time of writing. The ACLU of Puerto Rico had urged a veto before signature, stating the bill 'criminalizes doctors and parents' and creates 'two distinct categories of children' divided by sex-assigned-at-birth identity, and the island's College of Physicians and Surgeons, Psychology Association, College of Social Work Professionals, Bar Association and LGBTQ+ Federation all registered opposition.

Washington Blade (26 Apr 2019): Gov. Rossello announced SB1253 ('clarify religious freedom principles') and SB1254 (conversion-therapy ban with pastoral exemption); LGBT council president Johanne Velez Garcia and allies said the pair would open discrimination doors, criticizing the religious-freedom carve-out as license to refuse service on orientation/gender-identity grounds.

Washington Blade (25 Jun 2014): four same-sex couples joined the federal marriage lawsuit in PR (filed March; Ada Conde Vidal case), with Lambda Legal and PR Para Todas intervening - one couple married in Canada 2007, another in New York 2012; former National Guard member among plaintiffs. Road to marriage equality in PR ran through federal court.

Washington Blade (18 Mar 2019): the pro-statehood NPP caucus in the PR House blocked a floor vote on SB1000, which would have banned conversion therapy for minors; Sen. Zoe Laboy (co-sponsor) dissented publicly. Conversion-therapy ban died in the House despite Senate passage and governor support.

Washington Blade (13 Jun 2019): Gov. Rossello asked lawmakers to withdraw SB1253/SB1254 amid sustained opposition; his April announcement had included a pastoral-capacity exemption for clergy in the conversion-therapy ban. Record of LGBT advocates defeating the religious-freedom bill pairing.

Erin in the Morning (2025): PR enacted a trans youth care ban pushed through non-public hearings; law is deliberately vague so doctors and affirming parents facilitating HRT or top surgery risk prosecution; mandates Education/Health department campaigns on 'risks' of trans-affirming care; Health Secretary Ramos Otero proposed amendments allowing puberty blockers and continuation of existing HRT, but the enacted text is the most extreme care restriction in US jurisdictions per the report. For a trans visitor the ban closes off all gender-affirming care on the island for anyone under 21, and the deliberately vague facilitation language reaches the accompanying parents of a travelling trans teenager.

sources.title: Executive Order 14168 ("Defending Women from Gender Ideology Extremism and Restoring Biological Truth to the Federal Government") - Wikipedia
sources.summary: Executive Order 14168 (signed 20 January 2025) directs US federal agencies, including the Bureau of Prisons, to recognize only two sexes, and federal practice has followed by placing transgender inmates in facilities congruent with their sex assigned at birth rather than their asserted gender identity. The ACLU said it had received reports that transgender women were being transferred to men's prisons, told they would be, or moved to solitary confinement, and the Bureau of Prisons stopped reporting the number of transgender people it holds. Advocates say the order violates the Prison Rape Elimination Act's requirement that trans inmates' housing be decided on an individual safety assessment. Federal custody rules apply in Puerto Rico as a US territory. No separate Puerto Rico Department of Corrections trans-inmate housing policy, special unit, or ruling was located.

sources.title: Wikipedia country coverage
sources.summary: Puerto Rico's sodomy ban was upheld by the Puerto Rico Supreme Court in 2002, but after the U.S. Supreme Court's Lawrence v. Texas ruling in 2003 struck down all state and territorial sodomy statutes for consensual private acts, Puerto Rico amended its Penal Code in 2004 to remove private, non-commercial sexual activity between consenting adults from the statute. In July 2025 Puerto Rico banned gender-affirming care for anyone under 21, barred public funding for it, and threatened doctors who violate the ban with up to 15 years in prison, a $50,000 fine, and permanent loss of their licenses; the Puerto Rico LGBTQ+ Federation announced plans to challenge the ban in court. An anti-discrimination bill (House Bill 1725) passed the House 43-6 in November 2009 and would have barred discrimination on the basis of sexual orientation in employment, public transportation and public facilities, business transactions and housing, but the Senate held no hearings and took no action after Senate President Thomas Rivera Schatz said it would not be approved. The 2013 law that did pass (Senate Bill 238, signed 29 May 2013) was amended in the House to apply only to employment discrimination, so public facilities remain uncovered. A 2017 religious freedom bill that would have let public businesses legally discriminate against LGBTQ people was vetoed by Governor Ricardo Rosselló in February 2018, and a similar 2019 bill was withdrawn by Rosselló on 13 June 2019 after House approval amid protests. Puerto Rico amended its hate crime statutes in 2002 to include sexual orientation and gender identity as protected characteristics, and the territory is also covered by the U.S. federal Matthew Shepard and James Byrd, Jr. Hate Crimes Prevention Act. 2020 was the first year anyone in Puerto Rico was charged with a hate crime: Sean Díaz de León and Juan Pagán Bonilla were charged after Bonilla confessed that he and Díaz de León murdered two transgender women on 22 April 2020. In January 2021 Governor Pedro Pierluisi declared a state of emergency over ongoing murders, assaults and rape of transgender individuals on the island. In 2013 the legislature passed House Bill 488 (signed 29 May 2013) extending domestic violence protections to all households regardless of sexual orientation and gender identity.

sources.title: ACLU of Puerto Rico Urges Governor to Veto Senate Bill 350 (ACLU-PR press release)
sources.summary: The ACLU of Puerto Rico called on Governor Jenniffer González Colón to veto Senate Bill 350, 'which criminalizes doctors and parents and aims to prohibit gender-affirming medical treatments for individuals under the age of 21'. Policy Counsel Lolimar Escudero Rodríguez stated the bill 'creates two distinct categories of children: one that allows parents to access and authorize treatments if the child's identity aligns with the sex assigned at birth, and another that prohibits parents the same right if their child's identity is different'. The release records that the bill was authored by Senate President Thomas Rivera Schatz and Senator Joanne Rodríguez Veve, passed both chambers in April, was returned for amendments suggested by Health Secretary Víctor Ramos Parés that the ACLU warned 'do not remedy the violation of fundamental constitutional, civil, and human rights', and was re-approved and returned to the Governor on 28 June. It states the bill's 'text is clearly and exclusively aimed at minors whose identity does not correspond to the sex assigned to them at birth' and that it disregards the specialist consultation process that precedes parents authorising puberty blockers or hormonal treatments, 'and instead, criminalizes them'. Executive Director Annette Martínez Orabona: the measure 'directly discriminates against transgender people and denies the existence of trans children and youth, whose very lives may be at risk'. The release lists local opposition from the Puerto Rico College of Physicians and Surgeons, the Puerto Rico Psychology Association, the College of Social Work Professionals, the Puerto Rican Association of Professional Counseling, the Puerto Rico Bar Association and the LGBTQ+ Federation of Puerto Rico.

sources.title: Senate Bill 350 — ACLU of Puerto Rico legislation page
sources.summary: The ACLU of Puerto Rico opposed Senate Bill 350 'because of its direct impact on access to gender-affirming care for trans people, particularly trans youth and trans children, as well as on the rights of families and minors. The measure bans gender-affirming medical treatments for people under 21 years of age.'

sources.title: Puerto Rico bans hormone therapy and gender surgery for transgender youth (AP News)
sources.summary: AP reported that Puerto Rico's governor signed a bill prohibiting hormone therapy or gender-affirming surgeries for transgender youth, a move that 'has drawn sharp criticism from activists in the largely conservative U.S. territory'. The law applies to those younger than 21 and calls for 15 years in prison for violators, a $50,000 penalty, and revocation of the licences and permits of medical staff.

sources.title: Human rights in Puerto Rico — Amnesty International report
sources.summary: Amnesty International's Puerto Rico reporting records that 'In July, the government signed Law 63-2025, prohibiting gender-affirming health care for people under the age of 21.'

sources.title: LGBTQ+ advocacy group criticizes Puerto Rico law criminalizing gender-affirming care (JURIST)
sources.summary: JURIST reported that Puerto Rico's LGBTQ+ Federation denounced the Law for the Protection of the Health and Wellbeing of Minors in Puerto Rico, which 'prohibits the use of puberty blockers, hormone treatment, and gender-affirming surgeries for anybody under the age of 21' and 'imposes a sentence of up to 15 years and a $50,000 fine on offenders'.

In March 2019 the pro-statehood New Progressive Party caucus in the Puerto Rico House blocked a floor vote on Senate Bill 1000, which would have banned conversion therapy for minors, despite Senate passage and governor support; Senator Zoe Laboy, a co-sponsor, dissented publicly. The state/province is a dependent state/province and stands under the national framework of the parent nation for entry, documents, nationally funded care and national custody; the findings below are the state/province's own law, its own enforcement and its own institutions.

A 2025 law was enacted in July 2025. It bars gender-affirming care for anyone under 21, withdraws public funding for that care, and penalises violations with a fixed 15-year prison term, a $50,000 fine per violation for legal persons, and permanent loss of medical licences for professionals. The operative prohibition is directed at medical institutions and health professionals: none may perform surgical interventions or medication treatments that alter sex biology under the pretext of gender transition or as part of gender-dysphoria treatment.

A civil-liberties organisation in the state/province urged the governor to veto the bill, which it said criminalizes doctors and parents and creates two distinct categories of children divided by whether identity aligns with sex assigned at birth. Its policy counsel stated that the bill allows parents to authorise treatment where a child's identity aligns with the sex assigned at birth and prohibits them the same right where it does not. Its executive director said the measure discriminates against transgender people and denies the existence of trans children and youth. The bill was authored by the senate president and a senator, passed both chambers in April, was returned for amendments suggested by the health secretary that the organisation warned did not remedy the rights violations, and was re-approved and returned to the governor on 28 June. Opposition was registered by the state/province's college of physicians and surgeons, its psychology association, its college of social work professionals, its association of professional counselling, its bar association and an LGBTQ+ federation.

The state/province amended its hate crime statutes in 2002 to include sexual orientation and gender identity as protected characteristics. The first hate crime charges in its history were brought in 2020, after two men were charged in the murder of two transgender women on 22 April 2020; one of them confessed to the killings. In January 2021 the governor declared a public emergency over ongoing murders, assaults and rape of transgender individuals in the state/province.

The 2013 law that passed, signed 29 May 2013, was amended to apply only to employment discrimination, so public facilities, housing, transit and business transactions are not covered. An earlier bill passed the legislature's lower chamber 43-6 in November 2009 with wider coverage, but the upper chamber held no hearings and took no action after the senate president said it would not be approved.

The challenge was filed in March 2014, with intervention from legal advocacy organisations, and in June 2014 four couples joined as plaintiffs, among them a former national guard member and two couples already married in a neighbouring jurisdiction in 2007 and in another jurisdiction in 2012.

Consensual private sexual activity between adults is not criminalised. The state/province's highest court upheld the sodomy ban in 2002; after the parent nation's highest court ruled in 2003 against state/province sodomy statutes covering consensual private acts, the state/province amended its penal code in 2004 to remove private, non-commercial sexual activity between consenting adults from the statute.

SYN-ASM.name: American Samoa
SYN-ASM.summary:
American Samoa's criminal law does not punish consensual sodomy. The 1979 revision of the criminal law, which took effect in 1980, retained prohibition only for public acts, prostitution, conduct involving minors and persons unable to consent. The first sodomy statute, enacted in 1963, criminalised male homosexual and heterosexual conduct and did not address lesbian sex. The age of consent is 16, regardless of gender or sexual orientation.

Same-sex marriage is not licensed in American Samoa. In July 2015 Attorney General Talauega Eleasalo Ale was reviewing whether the United States Supreme Court's marriage-equality ruling applied to the territory, and the Governor stated at the time that it did not, citing the territory's preamble, its constitution, Christian values and its unorganised and unincorporated political status. No same-sex couple had filed an application for a marriage licence then, and none has applied to date.

A 2026 law review article by two attorneys practising in American Samoa concludes that the 2015 ruling does apply despite those official statements, and that the territory would have to issue a marriage certificate to any same-sex couple that applied. The article sets out the litigation route: the High Court of American Samoa first, with the Territorial Registrar as defendant, then the United States Department of the Interior. Reporting from the territory in July 2024 described the local ban as still treated as operative on the island and its durability under the Fourteenth Amendment as an open question, with a survey by a constitutional and comparative law professor testing the issue.

Birth certificates in American Samoa are altered only to correct information that was erroneous at the time of recordation or to reflect a name change due to adoption, under a High Court ruling that the Office of Vital Statistics applies to applications from transgender individuals. The office changes the name on a birth certificate when presented with a name change order, and may change the gender marker with medical documentation of the sex change.

Protection machinery has been used locally. In September 2023 the United States Justice Department secured a settlement with the American Samoa Government resolving an employment-discrimination case involving harassment of a transgender employee, following a June 2023 federal civil action that cited a hostile work environment in a transgender woman's lawsuit against the territorial government over her gender identity. In February 2023 a 51-year-old man was charged with sexual abuse of a 16-year-old transgender teen.

American Samoan society is highly religious, and conservative attitudes on gender and sexuality tend to dominate. Reserved public behaviour is expected of people of all orientations, and open displays of affection between couples, same-sex or opposite-sex, may offend. Against that, fa'afafine, boys raised as girls to take an important domestic role in Samoan communal life, are described in the sources as a recognised and integral part of traditional Samoan culture, and the territory is described as tolerant and accepting of transgender people and identities.

sources.summary: The UH Manoa libraries research guide on Pacific gender identities, last updated 2026-07-23, states that the Society of Fa'afafine in American Samoa (SOFIAS) was formed in 2010 by merging the American Samoa Island Queens Association and the American 7s Association, explicitly re-anchored to cultural pride: 'we are fa'afafine Samoa'. It defines fa'afafine as born male but embodying both male and female traits, 'a recognized and integral part of traditional Samoan culture', and frames colonial suppression followed by contemporary reclaiming of Pacific gender identities.

Out Traveler 'Ask the Expert' column (Ed Salvato, 2009-07-01) answering a honeymoon question about American Samoa: the two Samoan nations share the fa'amatai chiefly system; ASM's ~57,000 residents across seven islands/atolls; 'Samoan culture tends toward traditionalism, and reserved behavior by people of all orientations is expected', yet 'unlike the homophobia rampant in Fiji, homosexuality is a widely accepted part of Samoan culture', with Western gay men reportedly courted by fa'afafine transgender locals and by officially straight men; local artist Dan Taulapapa McMullin calls the Samoan islands 'the homeland of fa'afafine culture'; ASM hotels skew business-travel (Tradewinds, Pago Pago).

The Independent (2015-07-10): American Samoa was then the only US territory unsure whether the 2015 federal marriage ruling applied — its AG said applicability was 'still being reviewed... I don't know' while Puerto Rico, USVI, Guam and CNMI moved to apply it; no licence applications had been made.

sources.title: American Samoa Senate rejects bill outlawing same sex marriages (RNZ Pacific)
sources.summary: American Samoa's Fono Senate voted down a bill that would have outlawed same-sex marriage in March 2003, after the House judiciary committee recommended the bill be killed. The bill was introduced by Representative Sua Carl Schuster, who wanted to preempt the kind of marriage lawsuits then unfolding in US states. At the committee hearing, fa'afafine resident Tifanny Poutasi testified that Samoan fa'afafine 'don't believe in marriages with other men', describing them as men expressing femininity through dress and speech who do not seek same-sex marriage, citing Christian upbringing. The territory therefore deliberately declined a formal marriage ban before Obergefell, and the hearing records contemporaneous local fa'afafine views on the question.

sources.title: American Samoa judge objects to same sex marriage (RNZ Pacific)
sources.summary: In January 2016 the American Samoa Senate unanimously confirmed former territory Attorney General Fiti Alexander Sunia as District Court judge, filling the seat left by Judge John Ward II's retirement. At his confirmation hearing Senator Tauolo Manaia Fruean, a retired associate judge of the High Court of American Samoa, asked whether Sunia had read Obergefell; Sunia replied he had not read the US Supreme Court decision and that the district court 'doesn't deal with this ruling', and said he would not perform weddings for same-sex couples unless local laws are changed. The exchange shows that eighteen months after Obergefell the territory's judiciary was operating on the premise that the ruling did not automatically apply.

sources.title: The Ambiguity that Isn't: Why Same-Sex Marriage Is Legal in American Samoa (Harootunian & Lawrence, American University JGSPL vol 33 iss 2 (2026) pp 163-207)
sources.summary: 2026 law review article by two attorneys practicing in American Samoa (American Samoa Legal Aid, with Freedom From Religion Foundation) concluding that Obergefell DOES apply in the territory despite local officials' statements, and that American Samoa would have to issue a marriage certificate to any same-sex couple that applied. It records that to date no same-sex couple has applied for a marriage license in the territory, and lays out the litigation roadmap: the High Court of American Samoa first (defendant the Territorial Registrar), then the US Department of the Interior. The article is the most recent dated authority on whether the 2015 ruling is operative in American Samoa, and it separates the law as written from the practical reality.

sources.title: Survey conducted on-island focuses on local same sex marriage ban (Samoa News, Asi Andrew Fa'asau, Pago Pago)
sources.summary: Samoa News reported in July 2024 an on-island survey by Dr Daniel Hall, a constitutional and comparative law professor at Miami University, testing whether American Samoa's same-sex marriage ban would survive a challenge under the 14th Amendment. The survey also probes cultural dimensions bearing on the question (collectivistic vs individualistic orientation; linear vs polychronic time). As of mid-2024, nine years after Obergefell and more than a year after the Respect for Marriage Act obliged recognition of outside marriages (Dec 13 2022), the local ban is treated on-island as operative and its constitutional durability as an open question.

USA TODAY (7 Mar 2025): Trump executive order requires all US identity documents to reflect sex assigned at birth; ACLU sued the State Department for seven plaintiffs; trans/nonbinary travelers report passports confiscated or blocked, leaving some stranded abroad.

Lambda Legal's FAQ sets out passport and identity-document rules for TGNCNBI people under the current federal policy change: which documents to consider, how name and gender changes interact with federal records, and the current status of document updates.

HRC (updated 2025): since Jan 2025 executive order, new/renewed US passports show sex assigned at birth regardless of gender identity or name change; the 'X' marker (available since 2022) eliminated; policy challenged in federal courts -- current passport posture for trans US travelers.

Condé Nast Traveler (Feb 2025) reports that the State Department stopped processing X-marker passports and markers not matching sex assigned at birth; existing X-marker passports remain valid until expiration; new applications are processed only as M or F per supporting documents.

sources.title: LGBTQ rights in American Samoa (Wikipedia)
sources.summary: The High Court of American Samoa has held that birth certificates should only be altered to correct information that was erroneous at the time of recordation or to reflect a name change due to adoption. The Office of Vital Statistics has interpreted this ruling to cover applications from transgender individuals. The Office will change the name on a birth certificate when presented with a name change order. The Office may change the gender marker on a birth certificate with medical documentation of the sex change. The first criminal law against sodomy was enacted in 1963 and made male homosexual and heterosexual sodomy illegal, but did not address lesbian sex. In 1979 the Fono revised criminal law so that consensual sodomy was no longer illegal unless it involved public acts, prostitution, minors or people unable to give consent due to mental illness, with the law taking effect in 1980. The age of consent is set at 16 years, regardless of gender and/or sexual orientation. The American Samoa Code does not specify the sex of the parties to a marriage but refers to the age of "the male" and "the female" and prescribes a form in which parties identify as "son" and as "daughter," and a 2003 bill to ban same-sex marriage was voted against by the House Judiciary Committee and then the full Senate. Same-sex marriages are currently not licensed in American Samoa, with the Attorney General in July 2015 reviewing applicability of Obergefell v. Hodges and the Governor stating the ruling does not apply due to preamble, constitution, Christian values and unorganized and unincorporated political status. Under the Respect for Marriage Act passed by the 117th United States Congress and signed by President Joe Biden in 2022, all territories including American Samoa are required to recognize, though not perform, same-sex marriages performed legally in another jurisdiction, with equal treatment for same-sex and opposite-sex couples. The article states American Samoa remains the only part of the United States along with select Native American tribal jurisdictions to enforce a ban on same-sex couples marrying, while same-sex couples married legally in other jurisdictions are recognized and must be treated equally under US federal law since 13 December 2022. The article states "American Samoa, like the neighboring country of Samoa, tends to be tolerant and accepting of transgender people and identities." It notes a long-standing tradition of raising some boys as girls to play an important domestic role in Samoan communal life, with such individuals known as the fa'afafine. It states nevertheless American Samoan society is highly religious and conservative attitudes regarding gender and sexuality tend to dominate. It states open displays of affection between couples, same-sex or opposite-sex, may offend. The main LGBTQ organization is the Society of Fa'afafine in American Samoa (S.O.F.I.A.S.) which annually organizes events and festivals and campaigns for the betterment of the fa'afafine community. The first Pride festival was held in August 2016 in Utulei with pageant, song, dance and poetry choral competitions, beauty pageants among the fa'afafine community are quite popular, and families generally turn up en masse to support candidates.

sources.title: 2003 Same-Sex Marriage Ban Bill by Rep. Sua Carl Schuster
sources.summary: On 20 March 2003 the American Samoa Senate rejected Representative Sua Carl Schuster's bill to outlaw same-sex marriage after the House judiciary committee recommended it be killed, with fa'afine witness Tiffany Poutasi testifying that fa'afine are men who express femininity through dress and speech and oppose marriage with other men as against Christian upbringing.

sources.title: Attorney General Talauega Eleasalo Ale - July 2015 Review Statement
sources.summary: As of July 10, 2015, American Samoa had not authorized same-sex marriage and no same-sex marriage license applications had been filed while Attorney General Talauega Eleasalo Ale reviewed the U.S. Supreme Court marriage-equality ruling for applicability to the territory, which maintained a tradition of embracing faafafine — males raised as females taking on feminine traits — alongside dominant conservative Christian churches.

SYN-GUM.name: Guam
SYN-GUM.summary:
Guam's own law governs legal gender recognition, and it requires surgery. To amend a birth certificate, a transgender person must give the Office of Vital Statistics a sworn statement from a physician confirming sex reassignment surgery, after which the office amends the certificate. The Motor Vehicle Division Supervisor issues an amended driver's licence on receipt of a sworn physician statement that the applicant's sex has been surgically changed.

A 2018 attempt to remove the surgery requirement failed. Senator Fernando Esteves introduced a bill in May 2018 to permit legal gender change on judicial permission with a letter confirming gender identity supported by documentation from a certified psychologist, social worker, therapist or other licensed professional, with no surgery required. The Legislature postponed a vote on 13 December 2018 pending medical and law enforcement process issues, and the bill failed on 17 December 2018 by a 6 to 7 vote. Surgery remains the condition for both documents.

Marriage recognition for a trans visitor in what would be locally classed as a same-sex relationship rests on the 2015 ruling. Chief judge Frances M Tydingco-Gatewood struck down Guam's prohibition on same-sex marriage in June 2015 after an April 2015 lawsuit by Loretta Pangelinan and Kathleen Aguero, who had been denied a marriage licence. The ruling took effect at 8am on Tuesday 9 June 2015, making Guam the first United States territory to recognise same-sex marriage.

Private consensual adult non-commercial sexual conduct has been lawful since the 1978 reform of the Criminal Code; the penal code in force before that, ordained in 1933, had criminalised sodomy, fellatio and cunnilingus with between one and ten years' imprisonment.

Guam hosts a large permanent United States military presence, so federal policy on transgender service members bears directly on personnel stationed on the island.

SYN-VIR.name: United States Virgin Islands
SYN-VIR.summary:
The U.S. Virgin Islands is a United States territory; entry, travel documents and airport screening follow United States federal rules. What is specific to the territory is its own anti-discrimination and family law.

The territory's human-rights statute prohibits discrimination on grounds that include sexual orientation and gender identity. That statute is the operative protection a trans visitor can invoke while in the territory.

In March 2017 the territory's Attorney General issued an official interpretation holding that the anti-discrimination law applies to transgender students, extending the protection explicitly into the education setting.

Marriage is settled in the territory. In 2015 the Superior Court of the U.S. Virgin Islands struck down the refusal of marriage licences to same-sex couples as unconstitutional, and later federal recognition settled the question nationwide. A married trans visitor can rely on their marriage in the territory, including where the couple would previously have been refused a licence as a same-sex couple.

The historic sodomy statute, applicable to the territory since 1957, has been replaced and is no longer in force.

SYN-MNP.name: Northern Mariana Islands
SYN-MNP.summary:
The Northern Mariana Islands is a US commonwealth. Travel documents, immigration and airport screening are governed by United States national rules rather than by commonwealth law, and the national layer of this assessment sits with the United States record.

Consensual same-sex conduct is not criminalised. Marriage between same-sex couples has been recognised in the commonwealth since 2015, and the first such marriage on Saipan was officiated on 27 July 2015. A trans visitor in what would be locally classed as a same-sex relationship can expect that relationship to be recognised. Adoption has been available to same-sex couples since 2015.

Legal gender change is permitted in the Northern Mariana Islands provided the applicant has undergone the specified medical process, so identity documents can be brought into line with presentation, subject to that medical requirement.

Commonwealth law provides for enhanced sentencing in hate-motivated crimes. Public Law 22-32, signed in January 2023, amends the Commonwealth Code with criteria covering offences motivated by sexual orientation and gender identity. This is the principal commonwealth-level protection with direct bearing on gender-identity-motivated violence.

There is no comprehensive commonwealth nondiscrimination statute covering gender identity. Commonwealth-level protections extend to government employees only, and recourse beyond federal complaint channels is limited.

As of 27 September 2026 the Movement Advancement Project scored the territory's sexual orientation policy at 3.5 of 22 and its gender identity policy at minus 2 of 25, an overall rating of 1.5 of 47, classified as Low with a negative gender-identity score.

A public law signed in January 2023 amends the state/province's legal code with criteria covering offences motivated by sexual orientation and gender identity. This is the principal local protection with direct bearing on gender-identity-motivated violence.

There is no comprehensive local nondiscrimination statute covering gender identity. Local protections extend to government employees only, and recourse beyond national complaint channels is limited.

As of 27 September 2026 an advocacy organisation's equality index scored the state/province's sexual orientation policy at 3.5 of 22 and its gender identity policy at minus 2 of 25, an overall rating of 1.5 of 47, classified as Low with a negative gender-identity score.
SYN-MNP.blindTangential: The state/province's first Gay Pride event was held at a nightclub, with about 60 people attending. The organiser described it as a success. Attendance of that size at the first such event points to a small organised community.
SYN-MNP.blindLocalsOnly:
Local discrimination protections extend to government employees only; residents outside government employment have no local statutory coverage and depend on national complaint channels.

Adoption has been available to same-sex couples since 2015.
SYN-MNP.blindOutOfScope:
The specific medical process required for legal gender change is not detailed in the sources reviewed, so which procedures satisfy the requirement is unresolved.

No record of how often the enhanced-sentencing provision in the public law signed in January 2023 has been applied, or of any prosecution brought under it, appears in the sources reviewed.

The advocacy index figures are a measure of policy coverage rather than a legal measure or an enforcement record, and the date of the state/province's first Gay Pride event is not established in the sources reviewed.
